en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Apadāna in the Khuddakanikāya.
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition:
Having bowed my head to the Supreme One, the Buddha, who has no equal;
Having crossed the ocean of what is to be known, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra,
he likewise [proclaims] the Dhamma— the supreme peace, profound, difficult to see, subtle,
the maker of existence and non-existence, pure, and honored by the Fully Awakened One.
In the same way, one should pay homage especially to that faultless Saṅgha, the unattached and supreme Saṅgha,
the most excellent among those worthy of offerings, whose faculties are stilled and who are free from taints.
By the act of prostrating to them, one gains a distinguished merit.
Especially out of reverence for the Three Jewels, and with particular devotion,
I [request] those who are steadfastly wise, learned in the scriptures, and discerning— that is, the elders—
to specifically compose a commentary on the *Apadāna*.
Having been entreated again and again with great reverence by those of illustrious fame,
I shall therefore illuminate, within the three Piṭakas, this Apadāna in its entirety—
along with its introduction— as a lamp for the method of exposition.
Just as there is a beautiful commentary on the meaning according to the method of the Pāḷi itself, one should first state:
"By whom was this supreme Dhamma spoken, where, when, and for what purpose was it spoken?
Having stated this, one should then explain the procedure.
For the sake of skill in the *Nidānas*, and for easy comprehension and retention,
I shall therefore explain each respective method, distinguished by its preceding and succeeding parts,
first in the Sinhalese language and according to the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
That which has been established does not accomplish what the virtuous desire.
Therefore, relying upon that [tradition], yet avoiding the method of the ancient commentaries (porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā) which contains contradictory meanings, I shall elucidate the specific meaning.
"We shall provide the excellent special commentary, which is a commentary on the meaning. Regarding the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*):
"By whom, where, and when was this supreme Dhamma spoken? and "We shall provide a commentary on the meaning."

Furthermore, because this commentary on the meaning of the *Apadāna* has been formally acknowledged, we shall explain it by first demonstrating these three types of origins—the distant origin (*dūrenidāna*), the not-distant origin (*avidūrenidāna*), and the proximate origin (*santikenidāna*).

For those who hear it being thus explained, it becomes well-understood because they comprehend it starting from its ultimate source; therefore, we shall indeed explain it by first showing those origins.
In this regard, first of all, the delimitation of those introductory causes (*nidāna*) should be understood.

From the time the Great Being made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until he passed away from that existence as Vessantara and was reborn in the Tusita heaven—the course of narrative occurring during that interval is called the "distant introduction" (*dūrenidāna*).
However, from the time he passed away from the Tusita realm until the attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [the narrative is called the proximate introduction].

A discourse that proceeds in such a manner is called a "remote nidāna. A "proximate nidāna," however, is obtained at the very place where [the Buddha] was dwelling in various locations among those [places].
1. Discourse on the Remote Nidāna.
In this regard, this is what is called the "distant cause": It is said that four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons ago, there was a city named Amaravatī.
There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both sides from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, and irreproachable.
He was unassailable by talk of his birth; he was handsome, beautiful to behold, inspiring, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Without engaging in any other work, he mastered the craft of the brahmins. While he was still in his youth, his parents passed away.
Then the treasurer, the minister, brought forth the register of wealth, which was filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth.
Opening the chest, he said, "This much, young man, belongs to your mother; this much belongs to your father;
this much belongs to your grandfathers and great-grandfathers," and having thus explained the wealth back through seven generations of his family, he said, "Take possession of this.
The wise Sumedha thought: "Having gathered this wealth, my father, grandfather, and the rest have gone to the other world."
“Those who went did not go even after taking a single kārṣāpaṇa; however, it is fitting for me to take [some] and provide the means for their journey.
Having reported this to the king, he had a drum beaten throughout the city, gave alms to the great multitude, and went forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller.
To clarify this matter, the story of Sumedha should be told here.
Although this account appears continuously in the *Buddhavaṃsa*, it is not very clear because it is presented in verse form;
therefore, we shall explain it by interspersing it with prose passages that illuminate the connections between the verses.
The Story of Sumedha.

At the conclusion of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand eons, there was a city named Amaravatī, also called Amara, which was never devoid of ten kinds of sounds. Referring to this, it is said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
“During four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand eons, There was a city named Amara, beautiful and delightful.”
“Not devoid of ten sounds, provided with food and drink. Therein, “not devoid of ten sounds” means:

the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of small drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of conchs, the sound of cymbals, and the sound of clapping hands; [and the call] “Eat!”
"Drink! Eat!"—with these ten sounds it was never devoid.
And taking only a portion of those sounds:
"The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, and the drums, conchs, and chariots..."
"Eat and drink indeed, O you who are resounded with food and drink!"—
having spoken this verse in the *Buddhavamsa*,
[he added]: "The city, endowed with every excellence, has arrived at the completion of all its tasks."
Endowed with the seven treasures, crowded with various people,
prosperous like a city of the gods, it was the dwelling place of those who perform meritorious deeds.
In the city of Amarāvatī, there was a brahmin named Sumedha.
“Accumulating many millions, possessing abundant wealth and grain;
a reciter who mastered the mantras, one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas;
and who had attained perfection in the science of marks, in history, and in his own doctrine”—so it was said.
Then one day, while seated cross-legged in solitude on the excellent upper terrace of the palace, the wise Sumedha reflected thus:
“O wise one, the taking of rebirth-linking in a new existence is suffering;
likewise is the breaking up of the body in each place where one is born. And I am subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to sickness.”
"I am subject to death; therefore, it is fitting for me, being such as I am, to seek the birthless, ageless, diseaseless, deathless, sorrowless, blissful, cool, great Nibbāna, the Deathless.
One must certainly escape from existence by means of a single path leading to Nibbāna. Thus it was said:
“Sitting down in seclusion, I then reflected thus:
‘Rebirth is indeed suffering, as is the dissolution of the body.
Subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to illness, I was then [aware of this].’”
“I shall seek the deathless, the immortal, the secure, the state of extinction.
“What if I were now to cast aside this putrid body, filled with various kinds of filth,
and go forth, indifferent and free from desire?”
“There must exist that path; it cannot be that it does not exist for me.
I shall seek that path for the sake of liberation from existence.
After that, he further reflected thus: “Just as in the world there is indeed what is called happiness, which is the opposite of suffering...”
Since this exists, there must also exist its opposite, namely non-becoming (*vibhava*).
And just as when there is heat, there is also its pacification, which is cold, so too there must be *nibbāna* through the pacification of the fire of passion and the other defilements.
Just as there is a wholesome and blameless state that serves as the opposite of evil and base states...
“It is indeed so; even when there is evil birth, since it casts aside all forms of birth, there must necessarily exist that which is designated as ‘non-birth,’ namely Nibbāna.
Therefore it was said:
“Just as when suffering exists, That which is called happiness also exists;”
While existence thus persists, non-existence must be sought.
Just as when heat exists, its opposite, coolness, is found;
so too, while the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna must be sought.
“Just as when evil exists, the good also exists;
even so, while birth exists, the unborn should be sought.
He thought further: “Just as a man submerged in a heap of excrement might see from afar a pond covered with five-colored lotuses...”
Upon seeing a great lake, it is appropriate to search for that lake, thinking, "By which path should one go there?
That one does not search for it is not the fault of the lake; it is the fault of the person alone.

Likewise, while the great lake of the deathless Nibbāna—which washes away the stains of the defilements—is present, that one does not search for it is not the fault of the great lake of the deathless Nibbāna.

It is the fault of the person, indeed, the fault of the person. And just as when a man is surrounded by thieves, if he does not flee even though a path for escape exists, it is not the fault of the path, but the fault of the man;
even so, for a person seized and surrounded by defilements, the failure to seek out the auspicious path leading to Nibbāna—even though that path exists—is the fault of the person.
It is not the fault of the path, but the fault of the person. Just as when a man afflicted by disease does not seek out a physician who exists and has the means to treat him,
and thus fails to have his illness cured— it is not the fault of the physician,

but the fault of the man— so too, it is the fault of one who, though afflicted by the disease of the defilements, does not seek out a teacher who exists and is skilled in the path that leads to the pacification of those defilements.
"It is his own fault, not the fault of the teacher who destroys the defilements. Thus it was said:
"Just as a man who has fallen into excrement, upon seeing a pond filled [with water], does not seek out that pond—it is not the fault of the pond."
“Thus, while washing away the stains of defilement, even though the lake of the Deathless exists, one does not seek that lake; there is no fault in the lake of the Deathless.
Just as one besieged by enemies, when a path for escape exists...”
That man does not flee; it is no fault of the straight path.
"Thus, though obstructed by defilements while the auspicious path exists, he does not seek that way; it is no fault of the auspicious straight path."
“Just as a man who is diseased, though a physician is present,
does not have that disease treated— no fault lies with the physician.
So too, one who is afflicted and oppressed by the diseases of the defilements...”
“He does not seek out that teacher; there is no fault in such a guide.

He thought further: “Just as a man who is fond of adornment might cast off a corpse hanging from his neck and go on happily, even so shall I cast off this putrid body and, without looking back, proceed to the city of Nibbāna.”

One must enter. Just as men and women, having voided excrement or urine upon a dung-heap, do not depart taking it up in their laps or wrapping it in their garments, but rather, loathing it, cast it away without regard and go on;
even so, I too, casting aside this putrid body without regard, shall enter the city of the Deathless Nibbāna.

It is appropriate. Just as sailors abandon a dilapidated ship without looking back and go their way, so too shall I, abandoning this body which is oozing from nine openings, enter the city of Nibbāna without looking back.
And just as a man, while traveling on a path with thieves after taking various jewels for himself...
“Out of fear of losing his jewels, he abandons that [treasure] and takes to a safe path; in the same way, this body made of flesh is like a thief who plunders one's jewels.
If I were to develop craving for this, the jewel of the noble path and the wholesome Dhamma would be lost to me.
Therefore, it is right for me to abandon this body, which is like a thief, and enter the great city of the Deathless Nibbāna. Thus it was said:
“Just as a man, loathing a corpse tied around his neck,
might set it free and go away happy, independent, and self-possessed; even so,
[one should abandon] this putrid body, a heap of various corpses.”
Having discarded it, I would go away, indifferent and without desire:
"Just as men and women, having discarded excrement in a place for refuse,
go away indifferent and without desire."
“In this very way, having cast off this body filled with various kinds of filth,
I shall depart, just as one leaves a hut after having voided excrement.
Just as an old, leaking boat that is taking on water,”
“Carpenters abandon their tools and go away, indifferent and no longer needing them.
In the same way, I shall abandon this body— with its nine openings and constant discharge—
and depart, just as owners leave a worn-out boat.”
“Just as a man traveling with thieves, taking his goods along,
sees the danger of having his goods stolen and goes on after casting them away;
even so is this body, like a great thief.”
"Having abandoned this, I shall go, out of fear of the destruction of my welfare.
Thus the wise Sumedha, having reflected on this matter connected with renunciation through various kinds of similes,
distributed his immeasurable mass of wealth within his own residence to the poor, the destitute, and others, in the manner described above.
Having given a great gift and having abandoned both sensual objects and the defilements of sensual desire, he departed from the City of the Immortals (Amaranagara).
All alone, he established a hermitage in the Himālaya mountains near a peak named Dhammika;

there, having constructed a leaf-hut and a walking-path, he dwelt in a state free from the five faults of the hindrances, as described by the method beginning with the words, "When the mind is thus concentrated."

Endowed with eight qualities of cause, he entered the ascetic life (*isipabbajjā*) in that hermitage, having discarded his garment which possessed nine defects in order to acquire the power known as direct knowledge (*abhiññā*),
and having donned the bark-fiber robe (*vākacīra*) which possessed twelve qualities.
Having thus gone forth, he abandoned that leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*) which was beset by eight defects, [and took up] that which possessed ten qualities.

Having approached the foot of a tree and abandoned all varieties of grain, he lived on naturally fallen fruit and, exerting himself through sitting, standing, and walking, within seven days he became an attainer of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Thus he reached the power of direct knowledge as he had desired. Therefore it was said:
“Having thus reflected, I gave away wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions to those who had protectors and those who were protectorless, and then I went to the Himavat mountains.
Not far from the Himavat is a mountain named Dhammika.”
“My hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully laid out.
There I established a walking path, free from five defects and endowed with eight qualities;
I brought forth the power of direct knowledge.”
“There I discarded my cloth garment, which had come to possess nine faults;
I put on a bark robe, which possessed twelve virtues.
I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight faults.”
I approached the foot of the tree, which was endowed with ten qualities.
"The grain that had been sown and planted, I abandoned entirely;
I took instead the fruit that grows spontaneously, which is possessed of manifold virtues."
“Therein I exerted effort, sitting, standing, and walking;
within seven days, I attained the power of direct knowledge.
Regarding this, by means of the passage beginning, “My hermitage is well-prepared, my leaf-hut is well-constructed,” the wise Sumedha—
The hermitage, leaf-huts, and walkways are described as if they had been constructed with his own hands. This is the meaning here:
when Sakka saw that the Great Being had entered deep into the Himalayas and was about to enter Dhammika Mountain today, he addressed the divine son Vissakamma:
"Dear one, this wise Sumedha has gone forth with the thought, 'I shall go into homelessness'; [prepare] a dwelling place for him."
“Build it,” he said. Having accepted his words, he built a delightful hermitage, a well-guarded leaf-hut, and a charming walkway.
But the Blessed One, referring to that hermitage site produced by the power of his own merit, said: “Sāriputta, on that mountain Dhammika—”
“My hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully built;
there I constructed a walking-path, free from the five defects,” he said.
In this context, “well-constructed by me” means it was properly made by me. “My leaf-hut is beautifully built” means that even the hut with its roof of leaves was well-constructed by me.

"Free from the five faults": these five are called the faults of a walking path (*caṅkama*): unevenness and hardness, having trees inside, being overgrown with thickets, being too narrow, and being too wide.
For when one walks on a walking path where the ground is uneven and hard, the feet ache, blisters arise, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) fails.
However, when the ground is soft and even, one attains a comfortable dwelling and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) succeeds.

Therefore, it should be understood that having a hard and uneven surface is one defect. If there is a tree at the end, in the middle, or at the side of the walking path, the forehead or head of one who is walking may strike it through negligence;
thus, having trees within the path is the second defect. [If the area] is covered by a thicket of grass, creepers, and so forth...
While walking back and forth on a walking path at the time of darkness, one might step on or kill living beings such as snakes, or be bitten by them and thus encounter suffering;

this concealment by thickets is the third fault. Furthermore, when walking on a walking path that is too narrow—measuring only one *ratana* or half a *ratana* in width—one may stumble at the edge, resulting in broken nails and fingers.
Being too narrow is the fourth fault. When walking on a walkway that is too wide, the mind wanders and one does not attain one-pointedness;

thus, being too wide is the fifth fault. As for the walkway itself, it should be one and a half *ratanas* in width, one *ratana* on each side, sixty cubits in length, with a smooth surface and evenly scattered sand.
It was appropriate for Cetiya Mountain, just like the walking path of the Great Elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the Island;
it was exactly like that. Therefore he said: “There I had a walking path constructed, free from the five faults.

“Endowed with eight qualities” means endowed with the eight kinds of happiness of a recluse (*samaṇa*). These eight so-called happinesses of a recluse are: the absence of property, grain, and possessions;...
The state of seeking almsfood that is blameless; the state of consuming almsfood with a sense of relief;
the absence of the defilement of oppressing the country when dealing with royal families who seize wealth, essence, or head-money by taxing the realm;
the state of having no desire or lust for requisites; the state of being fearless regarding robbery and plunder; and the state of not associating with kings, royal ministers, or high officials.
"Unobstructed state in the four directions. This is what is meant:
"Just as it was possible for one dwelling in that hermitage to experience these eight kinds of happiness, so he constructed that hermitage endowed with these eight qualities.

"He brought forth the power of direct knowledge" means that while later dwelling in that hermitage, having performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, he [attained] the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

For the sake of producing the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), I began insight meditation (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence and suffering, and brought forth the power of insight that had reached full strength.

The meaning is: "Just as I was able to bring forth that power while dwelling there, so did he construct that hermitage, making it suitable for the power of insight intended for direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*)."
"He abandoned his garment there, having fallen into the ninefold fault"—this is the sequential account here.

It is said that at that time, having established a delightful hermitage adorned with walkways and caves, covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees, possessing pools of sweet water, free from terrifying wild beasts and birds, and suitable for seclusion;
and having placed support-boards at both ends of the decorated walkway—
Having prepared a level slab of earth, the color of green mung beans, for his sitting place in the middle of the walkway, he arranged within the leaf-hut the requisites of an ascetic—
such as a circle of matted hair, bark garments, a triple staff, and a water-pot— and in the pavilion, water-jars, conch shells, and bowls;
and in the fire-hall, charcoal, embers, wood, and so forth— in this way, whatever was conducive to the benefit of those who have gone forth.
Having fashioned all that, he inscribed these words upon the wall of the leaf-hut: "Whoever desires to go forth into homelessness, let them take these requisites and go forth.

Then, when the divine son Vissakamma had departed for the world of the gods, the wise Sumedha, following the course of a mountain cave at the foot of the Himalayas, was looking for a comfortable place suitable for his dwelling when he saw a spot by the bend of a river.
Having seen the delightful hermitage, fashioned by the work of Vissakamma and granted by Sakka, he went to the end of the walking path;
not seeing any footprints, he thought, "Surely the renunciants, having sought alms in the village ahead and being weary from their journey, must have entered the leaf-hut and are now sitting there.
After waiting a short while, he thought, "They are taking far too long; I shall find out."
Having opened the door of the leaf-hut and entered within, I looked here and there;
reading the letters inscribed upon the great wall, [I thought], "These are my lawful requisites; taking these, I shall go forth," and I cast off the pair of garments I was wearing.
Therefore he said: "There I cast off the garment. Thus, Sāriputta, I entered.
In that leaf-hut, he discarded his garment (*sāṭaka*).
"Having encountered nine faults" means that while discarding the garment, he did so having seen nine defects;
this explains that for those who have gone forth into the ascetic life, nine defects regarding the garment present themselves. One defect is its high value, and because it is dependent on others...
The state of arising is one; the state of being quickly defiled through use is another—for what is defiled must be washed and dyed;
the state of wearing out through use is another—for what is worn out must be patched or provided with new leather strips;
the state of being difficult to obtain again through renewed seeking is one; and the unsuitability for the ascetic life of renunciation is another.
It has the single quality of being common to enemies; for it must be guarded in such a way that enemies do not seize it.
It has the single quality of being an object of adornment for one who uses it; and it has the single quality of being a burden upon the shoulders for one who carries it about.
"I wore a garment of bark," Sāriputta, saying this, I discarded my lower robe because I saw these nine defects in it, and [donned] a garment of bark.
"I wore" means that I took up a bark garment (*vākacīra*) made by weaving together strips of *muñja* grass after pulling them out one by one, for the purpose of wearing as a lower and upper robe.
"Possessing twelve virtues" means endowed with twelve benefits. For there are twelve benefits in a bark garment:
first, it is inexpensive, beautiful, and allowable; furthermore, it can be made with one's own hands.
This is the second; it becomes gradually soiled by use, yet there is no trouble even when it is being washed—this is the third;
even when worn out by use, there is no need for it to be sewn—this is the fourth; it can be easily made again by one seeking materials—this is the fifth;
it is suitable for the ascetic life of renunciation—this is the sixth; it is useless to enemies—this is the seventh.
The eighth is the absence of ornamentation while wearing it; the ninth is its lightness when worn;
the tenth is having few desires regarding the requisite of robes; the eleventh is being righteous and blameless in speech;
and the twelfth is being without regard even if the bark-fiber robe is lost.
"He abandoned the leaf-hut filled with eight defects"—how did he abandon it?
It is said that, while taking off his pair of fine garments, he took a red bark-cloth (*vākacīra*) hanging on the robe-stand that resembled a wreath of *anoja* flowers;
having put it on as an undergarment, he further donned over it another gold-colored bark-cloth that resembled a carpet of *punnāga* flowers.
Placing the deer-skin with its hooves over one shoulder, having bound his circle of matted hair, and having inserted a metal pin into his top-knot to keep it steady,
he hung a coral-colored water-pot from a carrying-net resembling a lattice of pearls; then, taking a tripod stand curved at three points,
he placed the water-pot on one end of the stand and the hook, axe, staff, and other implements on the other.

Having hung [his belongings] and placed his carrying-pole (khārikāja) upon his shoulder, he took a walking-stick (kattaradaṇḍa) in his right hand, emerged from the leaf-hut, and while pacing back and forth on the great walkway (mahācaṅkama) sixty cubits long, he looked at his own appearance and thought:
“My heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment; my renunciation truly shines, like that of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others.”
"This going-forth is praised and extolled by all wise men; the fetters of household life have been abandoned by me;
I have gone forth into renunciation; I have attained the supreme going-forth; I shall practice the duty of a recluse;
I shall obtain the bliss of the path and its fruit"—thus inspired with zeal, he set down his pack-burden and stood upon the stone slab the color of green gram in the middle of the walking-path.

Sitting like a golden statue, he passed the day; then, at evening time, having entered the leaf-hut and lain down on a wooden mat beside a bed of *bidala* leaves, he allowed his body to take up its natural temperature.
Waking at the powerful dawn, he reflected upon his own arrival: "Having seen the danger in the household life, [I left] my immeasurable wealth..."
Having abandoned infinite dangers, I entered the forest and went forth as one seeking renunciation.
From this moment on, it is not fitting to engage in heedless conduct; for the flies of wrong thoughts devour one who wanders about having abandoned seclusion.
Now it is fitting for me to cultivate seclusion, for I have viewed the household life as an impediment.
“I have departed from home, yet here is this delightful leaf-hut;

the ground is smoothed and colored like a ripe *veluva* fruit, the white walls are silver-colored, the thatched roof is the color of a pigeon’s foot, and the bed of split bamboo has the appearance of variegated rugs;
it is a dwelling place comfortable for living. Indeed, no greater perfection of a house than this appears to me.”
Searching for the faults in the leaf-hut, he saw eight faults.
For there are eight disadvantages in the use of a leaf-hut: first, the disadvantage of having to seek out materials and labor after collecting the building supplies with great effort;
and second, the necessity of repeatedly replacing the grass, leaves, and clay whenever they fall away.
The state of being bound to wakefulness is the second; the fact that a lodging is obtained for one who is senior is the third;
the lack of one-pointedness of mind when being awakened at an improper time is the fourth; the state of making the body delicate through protection from cold, heat, and so forth is the fifth;
and the state of concealing blame—the possibility of committing some evil once one has entered a house—is the sixth.
The sixth [danger] is the state of making it one's own possession by thinking, "It is mine.

The seventh is the fact that the existence of a house is like living with a companion. The eighth is the state of being shared with many, due to its being common to lice, bedbugs, crickets, owls, and so forth.
Having seen these eight dangers, the Great Being abandoned the leaf-hut. Therefore he said: "Crowded with eight faults..."

"Abandoning the leaf-hut," he says, "I have approached the foot of a tree, endowed with ten qualities. Having rejected the covered dwelling, he states that he has approached the foot of a tree possessed of ten qualities.
These ten qualities are as follows: (1) the quality of requiring little exertion; (2) the quality of being merely a place for approaching... [and so on].
"Because it does not exist there. (1) Non-maintenance is the second [reason]; for even if it is not properly swept, whether it has been swept or not, it remains comfortable for use.
(2) The state of not being made to perform duties is the third. (3) It does not conceal censure;
for one who commits evil therein feels shame, thus the state of not concealing censure is the fourth. (4) Like living in the open air, it does not stiffen the body.
The fifth is the state of the body being unpropped up; the sixth is the absence of making [the dwelling] one's own;

the seventh is the rejection of the household as a home-base. The eighth is the absence of the impulse to take [the dwelling] out with one, like a house shared by many, thinking, "I will look after it, come out!
The ninth is the state of delight while dwelling [there], because the lodging at the foot of a tree is easily available wherever one goes.
"Having seen these ten qualities—the tenth being the state of non-attachment—I have approached the foot of a tree," he said.
For, having observed these many reasons, the Great Being entered the village for alms on the following day.
Then, in the village he reached, the people gave him alms with great enthusiasm. He [performed] his meal-duty...
Having finished his work, he returned to the hermitage, sat down, and reflected: "I did not go forth [into homelessness] thinking, 'I shall obtain food.
This so-called 'palatable food' increases pride, intoxication, and the intoxication of manhood; and there is no end to the suffering rooted in food.
What if I were to abandon food that produces grain through sowing and planting, and subsist instead on wild fruits as they ripen?"

"May it come to pass. From that time forth, practicing and striving in that manner, within seven days he brought forth the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Therefore it is said:
"The grain that was sown and planted, I abandoned without remainder;”
I took ripe fruit endowed with manifold virtues.
There, sitting, standing, and walking, I applied myself to supreme effort;
within seven days, I attained the power of direct knowledge.
Dīpaṅkara Buddha:
Having thus attained the power of direct knowledge, while the ascetic Sumedha was passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, the Teacher named Dīpaṅkara appeared in the world.
At the moments of his conception, birth, enlightenment, and turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the entire ten-thousandfold world system—
The earth trembled, quaked, and shook violently; it let out a great roar, and thirty-two omens appeared.
Yet, as the ascetic Sumedha was passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, he neither heard that sound nor saw those signs.
Therefore it is said:
“When I had thus attained accomplishment and become a master in the Teaching,
the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World,
appeared. He appeared, was born, and awakened to the teaching of the Dhamma.”
“I did not perceive the four signs, being absorbed in the delight of jhāna.

At that time, the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand whose taints were exhausted, while wandering on a gradual tour, reached the city named Ramma and resided in the Sudassana Great Monastery. The inhabitants of the city of Ramma...
Having heard that "the Lord of Ascetics, Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma,
while wandering on his journey in due course, has arrived at our city of Ramma and is residing in the Sudassana Great Monastery," they had clarified butter,
fresh butter, and other medicinal requisites, as well as robes and coverings, prepared; and with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands—
Inclined toward, leaning toward, and tending toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and honored him with perfumes,
garlands, and other offerings. Sitting to one side, they listened to the teaching of the Dhamma,
invited him for the following day’s meal, and rising from their seats, they departed.
On the following day, having prepared a great almsgiving and adorned the city, they decorated the path by which the One of Ten Powers would arrive;
they filled the places where the ground was broken with water with earth, leveling the surface of the earth,
and scattered sand the color of silver plates, strewn parched grain and flowers, and raised banners and streamers of various colors.
They were setting up rows of plantain trees and full water-jars.
At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, having risen into the air from his own hermitage and traveling through the sky above those people, saw them joyful and delighted;
wondering, "What could be the reason for this? he descended from the sky, stood to one side, and questioned the people.
“Ho there! For whom are you decorating this uneven path here? To this it was said:
“In a border region, having invited the Tathāgata, they clear the road for his arrival with joyful minds.”
“At that time, having departed from Sakassama,
I was then traveling through the sky, shaking my bark garments.
Seeing the people filled with wisdom, joyful, delighted, and exultant— ”
Having descended from the sky, he immediately questioned the people:
"Why is the great multitude so joyful, delighted, glad, and filled with rapture?
Whose path is being cleared—the straight way, the path of travel?"

The people said, "Venerable Sumedha, you do not know that Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, having attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, is traveling on tour and has arrived at our city, staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery.
We have invited that Blessed One; this is the path by which the Blessed Buddha is coming."
“Let us adorn it. Then the ascetic Sumedha thought: “In this world, even the mere sound of the word ‘Buddha’ is rare to hear, let alone the appearance of a Buddha;
it is fitting that I too, along with these people, should adorn the path for the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
He said to those people: “Sirs, if you are adorning this path for the Buddha, [then let me do so as well].”
“Give me also one place; I too shall adorn the path along with you.

They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and knowing that the ascetic Sumedha possessed supernormal powers, they observed a spot where the ground had been broken by water and gave it to him, saying, “You adorn this place.
Taking up rapture directed toward the Buddha as his object, Sumedha reflected:
—"I am capable of adorning this place with my supernormal power (iddhi), but being thus adorned will not satisfy me;
today it is fitting for me to perform manual labor (kāyaveyyāvacca). Having brought earth, he scattered it over that spot.
Even before he had finished that spot, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, [approached] the six of great majesty who possessed the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā).
Surrounded by four hundred thousand *khīṇāsavas*, while the deities honored him with celestial perfumes, garlands, and the like,
as divine musical instruments resounded and celestial choruses proceeded, and while the humans honored him with human perfumes, garlands, and musical instruments,
he displayed the peerless grace of a Buddha upon the ground of *manosilā*, like a lion stretching its limbs.
He set out upon that road, which was like that very one, adorned and prepared. The ascetic Sumedha opened his eyes and beheld the One of Ten Powers approaching along the decorated path—
adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, graced by the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide halo,
and like streaks of various kinds of lightning in a sapphire-colored sky.
Beholding his own person, which had attained the pinnacle of physical beauty and was emitting dense, six-colored rays of a Buddha like interlacing garlands and paired strands, he thought:
"Today it is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for the One of Ten Powers;
let not the Blessed One tread upon the mud, but as if treading upon a bridge of jeweled slabs, let him cross together with [the others]."
“Let him go treading upon my back, followed by four hundred thousand arahants whose taints are exhausted;

that shall be for my benefit and happiness for a long time. Having said this, he loosened his hair, spread out his deerskin, his matted locks, and his garment of bark-fiber upon the dark-colored mud, and lay down on the surface of the mud like a bridge made of jeweled slabs. Thus it was said:
“When I asked them, they replied: ‘The Buddha, the unsurpassed in the world, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, has appeared;
his path is being cleared, the straight way for traveling.’”
“Having heard the Buddha’s own words, joy arose at that very moment;
uttering ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I experienced great gladness.
Standing there, with a heart full of rapture and agitation, I reflected.”
‘I shall plant seeds here; let not the opportune moment pass me by.
“If you would clear the way for the Buddha, grant me a single space;
I too shall clear the straight path, the way for traveling.”
“They gave me space then, so that I might clear the path;
thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I then cleared the way.
While my space was not yet finished, Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage,”
With four hundred thousand [monks], who were such-like ones possessing the six direct knowledges,
whose taints were destroyed and who were stainless, the Victor set out upon the straight path.
"Welcoming processions were underway, and many drums resounded."
The humans and gods were filled with joy and broke into shouts of "Well done!
"The gods see humans, and humans also see the gods;
both of them follow the Tathāgata with palms joined in reverence."
“Devas with celestial instruments, and humans with human ones—
both of them, playing together, follow after the Tathāgata.
Celestial Mandārava flowers, lotuses, and Pārichattaka trees;”
The gods, having ascended into the sky, sprinkle divine sandalwood powder and pure, excellent fragrance in every direction. The gods, having ascended into the sky,
sprinkle divine sandalwood powder and pure, excellent fragrance in every direction.
“Men on the surface of the earth are casting campaka, salala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga,
and ketaka flowers in every direction. There,
having loosened my hair, I [cast away] my bark garment and my skin.”
Having spread myself out upon the mud, I lay down face downwards:
"May the Buddha, together with his disciples, tread over me and pass on;
let them not tread upon the mud—this will be for my welfare."
Then, while still lying on the surface of the *kalala*, he opened his eyes again and, beholding the splendor of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Possessor of the Ten Powers, thought thus:
"If I so desired, I could burn away all defilements and enter the city of Ramma as the youngest member of the Saṅgha;
yet, by burning away my defilements in the guise of a stranger, I shall attain Nibbāna."

“There is nothing further to be done; what if I were now, like the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, board the ship of the Dhamma, ferry the great multitude across the ocean of saṃsāra, and only afterwards pass into parinibbāna? This would be fitting for me.
Then, having brought together the eight qualities and making the resolution for Buddhahood, he lay down. Thus it was said:
“As I lay upon the earth, such was the thought in my mind:
‘If I so desired, I could today burn away my defilements.
What need have I for this disguise of anonymity, now that I have realized the Dhamma here?’”
“Having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its devas.
“What is the use of my crossing alone, as a man who perceives his own strength?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.”
“By this service rendered to the Supreme Person,
having attained omniscience, may I deliver the vast multitude of beings.
Having cut the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence...”
“Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world together with its devas.
For one who aspires to Buddhahood, it is said:
“Human birth, perfection of gender, the cause, and seeing the Teacher;”
“Going forth, perfection of qualities, authority, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
For it is only while remaining in a human existence that the aspiration of one who aspires to Buddhahood succeeds, not for a nāga.
The aspiration of a nāga, or a supaṇṇa, or a deity, or even of Sakka, does not succeed. Even in the human state, the aspiration succeeds only for one established in the male gender;
it does not succeed for a woman, or for those who are paṇḍakas, napuṃsakas, or ubhatobyañjanakas.
Even for a man, within that particular existence, [the aspiration succeeds] only for one who is endowed with the causes for attaining arahantship.
An aspiration succeeds for one who possesses the causes, but not for another. Even for one who possesses the causes, the aspiration succeeds only when making it in the presence of a living Buddha;
it does not succeed for one making it near a shrine or at the foot of the Bodhi tree after the Buddha has attained final Nibbāna.
Even for one making an aspiration in the presence of Buddhas, it succeeds only if they are established in the outward signs of the going-forth (pabbajjā).
It does not succeed for one remaining in the garb of a householder.
Even for one who has gone forth, it succeeds only for one who has attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, and not for one devoid of these perfections of virtue.

Furthermore, even for one endowed with virtue, it succeeds through this specific service only for one who has sacrificed his own life for the Buddhas and is thus perfected in service, and not for another.

Even for one who possesses the necessary qualifications, success belongs only to him who has great zeal, effort, exertion, and search for the sake of those qualities that constitute a Buddha, and not to another. Herein, this is an illustration of the greatness of zeal:
suppose, for instance, there were a person who thought thus: "I shall drain out the entire interior of the world-system, which has become a single mass of water..."
He who is capable of crossing over and reaching the further shore by the strength of his own arms attains Buddhahood.

Or again, he who is capable of reaching the further shore by walking on foot after clearing away and trampling the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) as if it were covered with a thicket of bamboo attains Buddhahood.
Or again, he who [is capable of reaching the further shore] of the entire interior of the world-system...

One who is capable of reaching the far shore by trampling with his feet across a path that is densely packed with spears, having struck them down so they stand shoulder-to-shoulder, attains Buddhahood.

Or again, one who is capable of reaching the far shore by treading with his feet across the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa filled with glowing embers, attains Buddhahood. Whoever [is capable] of even one among these...

He does not consider his task difficult; rather, he is endowed with great desire, energy, effort, and inquiry, thinking, "Having crossed over this, or having gone through it, I shall reach the further shore.
It is for such a person that this aspiration succeeds, and not for another. Therefore, the ascetic Sumedha, having combined these eight qualities, [set forth].
Having made the resolution for the state of Buddhahood, he lay down.
Then the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara arrived and, standing at the head of the ascetic Sumedha as if opening a jeweled lion-window,
opened his eyes endowed with the five-colored clarity and gazed upon the ascetic Sumedha lying on the surface of the mud.
Seeing him, [he thought], "This ascetic has made a resolve for Buddhahood; will his aspiration succeed, or will it not?

Sending forth the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), he investigated and, knowing—"After four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons have passed from now, this one named Gotama will become a Buddha"—he remained standing right where he was.
In the midst of the assembly, he declared: "Do you see this ascetic of fierce penance lying on a bed of mud?
"Yes, Venerable Sir," they replied. "This one has made the aspiration for Buddhahood and lies here;
his wish shall be fulfilled. For at the conclusion of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons from now, he will be Gotama..."
He will become a Buddha named [Name]. In that lifetime, his residence will be the city named Kapilavatthu;
his mother will be Queen Māyā, his father King Suddhodana, his chief disciple the Elder Upatissa, his second disciple Kolita, his attendant Ānanda, and his chief female disciple Khemā.
The Elder, the second female disciple, will be the Elder named Uppalavaṇṇā.

This one, whose wisdom is mature, having made the Great Renunciation and exerted himself in the Great Struggle, will receive milk-rice at the foot of the Nigrodha tree, consume it on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, ascend the Seat of Enlightenment, and attain full awakening at the foot of the Assattha tree. Therefore it was said:
“Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
standing at my head, spoke these words:
‘Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair ascetic who practices fierce austerities;’”
"In an immeasurable aeon from now, a Buddha will appear in the world.
Having gone forth from the delightful city called Kapila, the Tathāgata,
after exerting himself in striving and performing difficult austerities..."
“Sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata,
having partaken of the milk-rice there, will proceed to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror will eat the milk-rice.”
“By the excellent path he has prepared, he will go to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having circumambulated the unsurpassed seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to the right,
the one of great renown will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.”
“His mother who gave him birth shall be named Māyā;
his father shall be named Suddhodana, and he himself shall be Gotama.
‘Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated.’”
Kolita and Upatissa shall be the foremost disciples;
one named Ānanda shall be the attendant who serves that Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples.
“Taintless, free from passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated,
the enlightenment of that Blessed One is called ‘Assattha.
Having heard this, the ascetic Sumedha, thinking, “Indeed, my aspiration will be fulfilled,” was filled with joy.

It happened thus. Having heard the words of the Dasabala Dīpaṅkara, the great multitude was thrilled and delighted, thinking, "The ascetic Sumedha is indeed the seed of a Buddha, the sprout of a Buddha. And this thought occurred to them:
"Just as people crossing a river, being unable to cross at a straight ford, cross at a lower ford, even so we too [regard] the Dasabala Dīpaṅkara..."

They made this aspiration: "If we do not obtain the fruits of the Path within this Dispensation, may we be capable of realizing the fruits of the Path in your presence when you become a Buddha in the future.
The Daśabala Dīpaṅkara, having praised the Bodhisatta, worshipped him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him, and departed. They too—
The four hundred thousand noble disciples whose taints were exhausted, having honored the Bodhisatta with perfumes and garlands and having circumambulated him, departed.
The gods and humans likewise, having honored and paid homage to him, departed.
When they had all gone, the Bodhisatta rose from his bed and, thinking, "I shall search for the perfections," stood upon the heap of flowers.
Having folded his legs crosswise, he sat down. When the Bodhisatta was thus seated, the deities throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world system raised a cry of "Sādhu!
and said: "Noble Sumedha ascetic, today all those very same portents that appear when ancient Bodhisattas sit cross-legged, thinking, 'I shall investigate the perfections,' are manifest."
“Since these [signs] have become manifest, you will undoubtedly become a Buddha. We know this:
‘He in whom these signs appear is, without exception, a Buddha. Therefore, exerting your own energy, apply yourself with firm vigor.
Thus they praised the Bodhisatta with various kinds of eulogies. Hence it is said:
“Having heard these words of the Peerless Great Sage,
humans and gods were filled with joy, thinking, ‘This one, it seems,
is the seed of the Buddhas. Shouts of exultation arose, and they clapped their hands and laughed.”
With palms joined in reverence, the ten thousand worlds together with their devas pay homage,
saying: "If we fail to fulfill the teaching of this Lord of the World,
then in a future time, may we be present before him."
"Just as people crossing a river, having missed a ford and fallen back,
take hold at a lower ford and cross over the great river—
so too, if we all were to release this Conqueror, [we would reach the goal]."
“In a future time, we shall stand face to face with him.
Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
having proclaimed my deed, raised his right foot.
“Those sons of the Conqueror who were there all circumambulated me;
men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.
When the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, had passed beyond my sight,”
With a heart joyful and elated, I then rose from my seat.
"Happy through happiness, delighted by gladness,
and suffused with rapture, I then sat cross-legged."
“Sitting cross-legged, I then thought thus:
‘I have attained mastery in jhāna and reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
In the ten-thousandfold world system, there is no sage equal to me.’”
"Unrivaled among those with psychic powers, I attained such bliss as this:
'While I sat cross-legged, the inhabitants of the ten thousandfold world-system raised a great cry:
"Surely you will become a Buddha!"'"
“Those signs which appeared in the past when the Bodhisattvas sat upon their excellent thrones—
those very same signs appear today.
The cold has vanished, and the heat is stilled.”
“Those [signs] appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.
The ten-thousandfold world system has become silent and free from clamor;
those [signs] appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.”
“Great winds do not blow, and the rivers do not flow;
those signs are visible today, so surely you will become a Buddha.
All flowers, whether born on land or born in water, are blooming at this very moment.”
"Today all of them have blossomed; surely you will become a Buddha.
Whether they be creepers or trees, as long as they bear fruit, today all of them have borne fruit; surely you will become a Buddha."
“As long as the jewels dwelling in the sky and those on the earth shone, so too do these three jewels shine today; surely you will become a Buddha.
As long as human and divine musical instruments resounded...”
“Those very same stars are shining brightly; surely you will become a Buddha.
Variegated flowers rain down from the sky even now;
they rain down today as well—surely you will become a Buddha.”
“The great ocean rolls back, the ten-thousandfold world system quakes, and the three realms resound; surely you will become a Buddha.
Even in the ten-thousandfold world system of hells, the fires are extinguished at that very moment.”
“Today the fires have been extinguished; surely you will become a Buddha.
The sun has become stainless, and all the stars are visible;
they too are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.”
“At that time, water burst forth from the earth in the form of a whirlpool;
even now it bursts forth from the earth—surely you will become a Buddha.
The hosts of stars and constellations shine in the circle of the sky.”
"Visākhā is joined with the moon; surely you will become a Buddha.
Those who dwell in holes and those who dwell in caves are emerging from their own abodes;
today they have abandoned those abodes; surely you will become a Buddha."
“Discontent does not arise for beings; they remain content for the time being.
Since all these are content today, you will certainly become a Buddha.
Illnesses are pacified therein, and hunger is destroyed.”
"These [signs] appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.
At that time, lust becomes thin, hatred and delusion perish;
all these have vanished today—surely you will become a Buddha."
“Then there was no fear, yet today it is seen;
by this sign we know for certain that you will become a Buddha.
Dust does not rise upward, yet today it is seen.”
"By this sign we know: you will certainly become a Buddha.
An unpleasant odor departs, and a divine fragrance wafts forth;
that fragrance blows today—certainly you will become a Buddha."
“All the gods appear, with the exception of those who are formless;
all of them appear today. Surely you will become a Buddha.
As far as there are realms called hells, they all appear at this time.”
"Today all these are visible; surely you will become a Buddha.
Walls, doors, and rocks do not act as obstructions then;
having become like space, today they are so; surely you will become a Buddha."
“Death and rebirth do not exist at that moment;
these signs are appearing before you—you will certainly become a Buddha.
Exert firm energy; do not turn back, but press forward!”
“May we too know this: you will certainly become a Buddha.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and of the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, the Bodhisatta became even more resolute and thought:
“The Buddhas are indeed those whose words are never in vain; there is no such thing as the Buddhas [failing].”
The alteration of the discourse: For just as the falling of a clod thrown into the air is certain, as death is certain for one who is born,
as the rising of the sun is certain at the end of the night, as the roaring of a lion’s roar is certain for a lion that has emerged from its lair,
and as the laying down of the burden is certain and inevitable for a woman heavy with child— even so, the word of the Buddhas is indeed certain.
“It shall not be in vain; indeed, I shall surely become a Buddha. Therefore it was said:
“Having heard the word of the Buddha, throughout the ten thousandfold world-system, I was thrilled, overjoyed, and delighted, and then I thought thus:”
“The Buddhas speak without duplicity; the Conquerors’ words are never in vain.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas: ‘I shall certainly become a Buddha.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky will certainly fall to the ground,”
In the same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is eternally true;
there is nothing false in the Buddhas, and it is certain that I shall become a Buddha.
Just as death is the eternal certainty for all beings, so too is my future Buddhahood certain.
In the same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Just as the rising of the sun is certain when the night has ended,
even so the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
“Just as the roar of a lion who has emerged from his lair is certain,
so too the word of the Supreme Buddhas is certain and eternal.
Just as the laying down of the burden by those pregnant with a fetus is certain...”
"Likewise, the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Having thus reached the conclusion, "I shall certainly become a Buddha," he began to investigate the qualities that constitute a Buddha, thinking:
"Where indeed are these qualities that make one a Buddha? Are they above, or below, or in the cardinal and intermediate directions? He proceeded in this gradual manner.
Investigating the entire realm of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), he saw that the first perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) had been practiced and cultivated by the ancient Bodhisattvas;
seeing this, he exhorted himself thus: "O wise Sumedha, from this moment forth you must fulfill the first perfection of giving.
For just as an overturned water-jar pours out its water completely until nothing remains, and does not draw it back in again,"

"In this very way, without looking back at wealth, fame, wife and children, or even my own limbs and members, I shall give everything desired by those who come as supplicants, leaving nothing remaining;
thus, sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, I shall become a Buddha.
Having thus made firm his resolve, he established the first Perfection of Giving (*dānapāramitā*). Therefore it was said:
“Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha—
upward, downward, and in the ten directions, as far as the realm of phenomena extends.
While searching, I then beheld first of all the perfection of giving.”
"This is the great path practiced by the great seers of old.
First, having firmly undertaken this,
go forth in the perfection of giving, if you desire to attain enlightenment."
“Just as a jar that is completely full, when turned upside down,
vomits out its water entirely without retaining anything within it;
even so, upon seeing supplicants— whether low, high, or middling— ”
“You give gifts without remainder, like a jar turned upside down.
Then, thinking to himself, “The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone,” he investigated further.
Seeing the second perfection, that of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*), he thought: “O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also practice the perfection of virtue.”

“You shall fulfill it. For just as the animal called the yak, disregarding its own life, protects only its tail, so too, from this moment on, by disregarding even your life and protecting only your virtue, you will become a Buddha.
Thus he made a firm resolve, strengthening the second perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). Therefore it is said:
“It will not be only these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While seeking, I then beheld the second perfection: that of virtue.”
"Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
'First, you must firmly undertake this second [perfection];
go forth to the perfection of virtue if you desire to attain enlightenment.'"
“Just as a yak, when her tail becomes entangled in anything,
meets her death there rather than wrenching her tail free;
even so, fulfill the precepts throughout the four stages.”
“Always guard your virtue, as the yak guards its tail.
Then, reflecting further—thinking, “The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot consist of these alone”—and perceiving the third perfection, renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*), he thought:
“O wise Sumedha, from this time forth, you must also fulfill the perfection of renunciation.”

You should fulfill it. For just as a man who has lived for a long time in a prison does not develop affection for it, but rather feels only weariness and desires to leave, even so you too, regarding all states of existence as similar to a prison, should become weary of all existences and, desiring liberation, turn toward renunciation. Thus spoke the Buddha.
“You shall become [a Buddha]! Thus, for the third time, he made firm his resolve and established himself in the perfection of renunciation. Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall search for others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.”
“Then, searching, I saw the third perfection of renunciation,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore, you too,
having firmly undertaken this third [perfection],’”
Go to the perfection of renunciation if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a man who has lived long in a prison, suffering in misery,
does not conceive passion for it but seeks only liberation.
“In the same way, you should see all states of existence as if they were a house of misery;
turn toward renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence.
Then, reflecting further, he thought: “It cannot be that there are only these many qualities that make one a Buddha.”
Having seen the fourth perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of wisdom as well.
Without excluding anyone among the low, the middling, or the superior, you should approach all wise men and ask them questions.
For just as an alms-collecting monk, without excluding any families—whether low or otherwise—proceeds in regular order..."
“Wandering for alms, one quickly obtains what is necessary for sustenance; likewise, you too, by approaching all the wise and asking questions, will become a Buddha.
Thus, having made firm his resolve, he established the fourth Perfection of Wisdom (paññāpāramī). Therefore it is said:
“These are not merely so many qualities of a Buddha that are yet to come;”
“I shall search for other qualities as well, those states that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the fourth perfection of wisdom,
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this fourth [perfection],
proceed to the perfection of wisdom if you wish to attain awakening.
Just as a monk, while begging for alms, [considers] the low, the high, and the middling...”
“By avoiding families [in this way], one thus obtains the means for subsistence.
Likewise, at all times, by questioning wise people,
you will reach the perfection of wisdom and attain supreme enlightenment.”

Then, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to just these," as he investigated further, he saw the fifth perfection, the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*), and this thought occurred to him: "O wise Sumedha, from now on you must fulfill the perfection of energy as well;
for just as Sīha, the king of beasts, possesses firm energy in all postures, so too must you."

"Being one of firm energy and unshrinking energy throughout all states of existence and in all postures, you will become a Buddha"—thus he made firm his resolve and established himself in the fifth perfection of energy. Therefore it is said:
"These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely so many;"
“I shall seek out other qualities as well that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the fifth perfection, energy,
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this fifth [perfection],
go forth to the perfection of energy, if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as the lion, king of beasts, whether sitting, standing, or walking,”
“He possesses unshaken vigor, his mind always uplifted.
In that same way, you too must exert firm vigor toward all states of existence;
having reached the perfection of vigor, you will attain full enlightenment.”

Then, thinking to himself, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," as he investigated further, he beheld the sixth perfection, patience (*khantipāramī*), and this thought occurred to him:
"O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you must fulfill the perfection of patience as well;
whether treated with honor or with contempt, you must remain patient. For just as upon the earth, even when pure things..."
“Even when they cast impurities upon it, the earth does not feel affection or resentment toward them; it simply endures, bears, and remains patient.
In the very same way, you too, remaining patient both in honor and in dishonor, shall become a Buddha.
Having thus made firm his resolve, he established the sixth perfection of patience (khantipāramī). Therefore it is said:
“It will not be merely these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the sixth perfection: patience.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
‘First of all, you must undertake this sixth [precept] firmly;
with a mind free from doubt therein, you shall attain full enlightenment.’”
“Just as that which is called the earth, whether pure or impure,
endures all that is cast upon it and does not harbor resentment toward you;
even so, may you too be patient with honor and dishonor from everyone.”
“Having reached the perfection of patience, you shall attain supreme enlightenment.

Then, thinking to himself, “There must be more qualities that bring about Buddhahood than just these,” as he investigated further, he beheld the seventh perfection, Truth (sacca-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him:
“O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also [practice] the perfection of truth.”
You should fulfill [this duty]; even if a thunderbolt were falling upon your head, do not utter a deliberate lie for the sake of wealth or other interests under the influence of desire and so forth.

For just as the medicinal star named Osadhī does not abandon its own path of movement in any season and does not travel by another path, but travels only by its own path, even so you too must not abandon the truth.
“Even while not speaking, you will become a Buddha”—thus he made firm his resolve, establishing the seventh perfection of truth (saccapāramī).
Therefore it is said:
“These alone shall not be all the qualities of a Buddha;”
“I shall seek out other qualities as well, those dharmas that ripen enlightenment.
While seeking, I then beheld the seventh perfection of truth,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, taking up this seventh [precept], hold it firmly and practice it;
there, with speech free from duplicity, you shall reach full enlightenment.
Just as the plant called Osadhi is the standard of measure for all things, including the world of gods...”
“In the dry season or during the rains, it does not deviate from its path.
In the same way, you too must not deviate from the path of truths;
having reached the perfection of truth, you shall attain full enlightenment.”

Then, thinking to himself, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," as he investigated further, he beheld the eighth foundation, the Perfection of Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "O Wise Sumedha, from this time forth you must fulfill the perfection of resolution;
whatever you resolve upon, you must remain unshakable in that resolution. For just as a mountain..."

"Just as a mountain peak, though struck by winds from all directions, does not tremble or shake but remains exactly where it stands, even so you too, remaining unshakable in your own resolve, shall become a Buddha.
Having thus made firm the eighth perfection of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), he made this resolve. Therefore it is said:
“Not only these alone shall be the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the eighth perfection: the perfection of determination.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old—
this eighth [precept], you should first undertake firmly.
Remaining unshakable therein, you will attain full enlightenment.”
“Just as a rocky mountain, immovable and well-established,
does not tremble before fierce winds but remains in its own place;
even so, you too should always remain immovable in your resolve.”
“Having reached the perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānapāramitā*), you will attain full enlightenment.

Then, thinking to himself, “There must be more qualities that constitute the factors for becoming a Buddha,” as he investigated further, he saw the ninth, the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettāpāramitā*), and this thought occurred to him:
“O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also fulfill the perfection of loving-kindness.”
“You shall fulfill it; you shall be single-minded toward both the beneficial and the harmful.

For just as water, indeed, pervades both wicked people and virtuous people alike, making its coolness uniform, even so, you too, being single-minded toward all beings with a heart of loving-kindness, will become a Buddha.
Thus, having made firm the ninth perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī), he said:
He made this resolution. Therefore it was said:
“These alone shall not be the Buddha-qualities;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen enlightenment.”
“Then, while searching, I beheld the ninth perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
‘Therefore, you too, having firmly undertaken this ninth perfection, practice it.’”
Be peerless in loving-kindness, if you desire to attain enlightenment.
Just as water, toward both good and evil people alike,
spreads its coolness equally and washes away dust and impurity.
“In the same way, you too should cultivate equanimity toward both the beneficial and the harmful through loving-kindness;
having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain full enlightenment.
Then, reflecting further, he thought: “It cannot be that the qualities which produce a Buddha consist of these alone.”
Having seen the tenth perfection, equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*), he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of equanimity as well;

whether in pleasure or in pain, you should remain perfectly neutral. For just as the earth remains neutral when both pure and impure things are thrown upon it, even so you too should remain neutral amidst pleasure and pain."
“Truly, you will become a Buddha!”—thus he made firm his resolve, establishing the tenth perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*). Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek out others as well, those qualities which bring enlightenment to fruition.”
“Then, while searching, I beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity (upekkhāpāramī),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore, you too,
having firmly undertaken this tenth perfection, [should practice it].’”
Becoming firm like a scale, you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as the earth, when impurity or purity is placed upon it,
regards both equally, free from anger and attachment.
“In the same way, you too should always remain as a balance between pleasure and pain;
having reached the perfection of equanimity, you will attain full enlightenment.
Then he thought: “In this world, there are qualities that bring about Buddhahood, which ripen for enlightenment and must be fulfilled by Bodhisattvas.”
“There are only these ten perfections; there are no others besides them. These ten perfections exist neither above in the sky, nor below in the earth, nor in the eastern or other directions;
they are established only within my own heart. Having thus seen that they were established in his heart, he resolved upon them all with firm determination.
Reflecting again and again, he reflects in forward and reverse order; taking up the end, he brings it to the beginning;
taking up the beginning, he brings it to the end; taking up the middle, he brings both ends together and concludes;
taking up both ends, he brings them to the middle and concludes. The relinquishing of external possessions is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*).
The renunciation of limbs is called the *upapāramī* of giving, and the renunciation of life is called the *paramatthapāramī* of giving;
thus, the ten *pāramīs*, the ten *upapāramīs*, and the ten *paramatthapāramīs* constitute the thirty *pāramīs*.
These are like Mount Meru when it is turned about like an oil-press, and they are like the great ocean of the world-system when it is churned.

He reflected. As he was thus reflecting upon the ten perfections, this great earth—two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness—trembled, quaked, and shook with a mighty roar, like a bundle of reeds trampled by an elephant, and like a sugarcane press being crushed, by the power of his Dhamma.
It was like a potter’s wheel or an oil-press wheel.
And I wandered about as if [in a dream]. Therefore it was said:
“There are only so many things in the world That ripen the factors of enlightenment;
Beyond these there is nothing else— Stand firm therein with steadfastness.”
“As he comprehends these phenomena, which possess the characteristic of their own essential nature,
the earth of the ten thousandfold world-system trembles through the power of the Dhamma.
The earth shakes and roars like a sugarcane press being crushed.”
“As the wheel spins upon its pivot, so does the earth tremble.
As the great earth shook, the inhabitants of the city of Ramma were unable to stand their ground;
like great sāl trees struck by the winds at the end of an eon, they fell down in a swoon. Clay pots and other vessels, being overturned, collided with one another.
As they struck one another, they were reduced to powder and fragments. The great multitude, terrified and trembling, approached the Teacher and said:
"What indeed is this, Blessed One? Is this a possession by a nāga, or is it a possession by some spirit, yakṣa, or deity?
For we do not know this; moreover, this entire great multitude is afflicted—what indeed has come upon this world?"
"Will this result in evil, or will it be auspicious? Tell us the reason for this," he said.
Then the Teacher, having heard their conversation, said: "Do not fear, do not worry; you have no cause for fear on this account.
He whom I prophesied today as 'the wise Sumedha shall become a Buddha named Gotama in the future'—"

"He now contemplates the ten perfections (pāramīs). As he contemplates and churns them, by the spiritual power (dhammateja) of that contemplation, the entire ten-thousandfold world system (dasasahassī lokadhātu) trembles and resounds all at once," he said. Therefore it is said:
"As far as the assembly was present at the Buddha’s meal-offering..."
Trembling there, she lay unconscious upon the ground:
“Thousands of jars and many hundreds of pots were crushed and mangled there,
clashing against one another.”
“Agitated, thirsty for news, afraid, bewildered and with trembling minds, the great multitude gathered together and approached Dīpaṅkara.
‘What will happen to the world? Will it be good or evil?’”
“The whole world is distressed; dispel that, O Visionary One!
Then Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, reassured them:
“Be confident, do not fear this trembling of the earth.”
“Today I have declared: ‘A Buddha shall arise in the world.
He now comprehends the Dhamma, that which was practiced by the Conquerors of old.
As he comprehends the Dhamma in its entirety, reaching the stage of a Buddha without exception—”
"Therefore this earth, together with its ten thousand worlds and its gods, has trembled.
Having heard the words of the Tathāgata, the great multitude was joyful and delighted;

taking flowers, perfumes, and ointments, they departed from the city of Ramma, approached the Bodhisatta, honored him with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, and paid him homage by circumambulating him.

Having done so, he entered the city of Ramma itself. The Bodhisatta, too, having contemplated the ten perfections (pāramīs) and having made his effort firm, rose from the seat where he sat with resolute determination. Thus it is said:
“Having heard the word of the Buddha, my mind was instantly extinguished;”
All of them, having approached me, again paid homage.
Having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm,
I then rose from my seat after paying reverence to Dīpaṅkara.
Then, as the Bodhisatta was rising from his seat, the devas of the entire ten-thousandfold world-system gathered together;
having honored him with celestial garlands and perfumes and having paid homage, they said:
"Noble Sumedha ascetic, today at the feet of the Great Being Dīpaṅkara you have made a great aspiration; may it be fulfilled for you without obstacle, and let there be no fear for you."
Or let there be no trembling; let not even the slightest ailment arise in your body.
Having quickly fulfilled the perfections, may you realize supreme perfect enlightenment.
Just as trees that bear flowers and fruits blossom and bear fruit in their proper season, so too may you, without overstepping that time, swiftly attain the highest enlightenment.
They recited these verses of praise and auspiciousness, beginning with "Touch [the earth]," and so forth.
Having thus offered their praise, they each returned to their own celestial abodes. The Bodhisatta too, being extolled by the deities, thought:
"Having fulfilled the ten perfections, at the conclusion of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons, I shall become a Buddha."
Making his effort firm and resolute, he rose up into the sky and went straight to the Himālaya mountains. Thus it is said:
“Celestial and human flowers—both gods and humans alike— Showered him with blossoms as he rose from his seat.”
“Both gods and humans alike proclaim your well-being:
‘May you obtain that great wish which you have desired, just as you have wished for it.
May all misfortunes be averted; may sorrow and disease perish.”
“May no obstacles arise for you; quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Just as when the proper season has arrived, flowering trees put forth their blossoms, even so, O Great Hero, may you blossom with the wisdom of a Buddha.”
