“Just as all those who were perfectly awakened fulfilled the ten perfections,
so too may you, O Great Hero, fulfill the ten perfections.
Just as all those who were perfectly awakened awakened at the seat of enlightenment...”
In the same way, O Great Hero, awaken to the enlightenment of a Conqueror.
Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
even so, O Great Hero, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
“Just as the moon on the full-moon night shines forth utterly pure,
so too do you, O one of fulfilled mind, shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
Just as the sun, released from Rāhu, outshines all with its heat;”
In that same way, having liberated the worlds, you shine with glory.
Just as whatever rivers flow toward the great ocean,
so may the worlds, together with their devas, flow toward you.
“Praised and extolled by them, having undertaken ten qualities and fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.
The Story of Sumedha is finished.
The inhabitants of Ramma City, too, having entered the city, gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher, having taught the Dhamma to them and established the great multitude in the refuges and other precepts, departed from Ramma City.
Thereafter, remaining for the remainder of his lifespan and performing all the duties of a Buddha, he proceeded in due order.

He attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue. Whatever needs to be said regarding this should be expanded in full according to the method already stated in the *Buddhavaṃsa*. For it is said there:
"Then, having fed the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha..."
They went for refuge to that Teacher, Dīpaṅkara.
The Tathāgata established some in the going for refuge,
others in the five precepts, and still others in the tenfold morality.
“To some he gives the state of recluseship, the four supreme fruits;
to some he gives the peerless states, the analytical knowledges.
To some the Bull among Men gives the eight excellent attainments.”
He bestowed upon someone the three true knowledges and the six direct knowledges.
By that means, the Great Sage exhorted the body of people;
by that means, the teaching of the Lord of the World became widespread.
“Mahāhanū, Sīha-kkhandha, and Dīpaṅkara by name—
these deliver many people and liberate them from miserable rebirths.
Having seen those who are capable of being awakened, even at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas,”
Approaching in an instant, the Great Sage awakened him:
"At the first realization, the Buddha awakened one hundred koṭis;
at the second realization, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis."
“And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the abode of the gods,
there was a third realization for ninety thousand koṭis.
There were three assemblies under the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.”
The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand times ten million [beings].
Again, when the Victor had retired into solitude at Nāradakūṭa, a hundred times ten million [beings],
whose taints were exhausted and who were free from stain, gathered together.
“At the time when the Great Hero, the Great Sage,
was offering alms to ninety thousand koṭis on the Sudassana mountain of stone,
I at that time was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities.”
Wandering through the sky, he had reached the further shore of the five higher knowledges.
There was the realization of the Dhamma for ten or twenty thousand beings;
as for the realizations of single individuals and pairs, they were beyond counting.
“Extensive, widely known, prosperous, and flourishing was it then;
the teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was well-purified.
Four hundred thousand [monks], possessing the six direct knowledges and great psychic power,”
They always attend upon Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.
"Whosoever at that time abandon their human existence,
being trainees who have not yet attained the goal of mind, they become objects of reproach."
“The well-flowered Pāvacana, by the Arahants who are such-like,
By those with taints destroyed and stainless, shines forth forever.
There was a city named Rammavatī, and a kshatriya named Sudeva;”
The mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sumedhā.
He lived in the household for ten thousand years;
there were three supreme palaces: those of the swans, the cranes, and the peacocks.
“Three hundred thousand women, beautifully adorned, were there;
that woman named Padumā was his offspring, with shoulders like a bull’s.
Having seen four omens, he went forth on an elephant vehicle.”
For ten full months the Victor exerted himself in striving.
Having practiced the course of striving, the Sage awakened his mind.
Being entreated by Brahmā, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara attained enlightenment.
“The Great Hero set the wheel in motion at the Nandārāma in Sirīghara;
seated at the foot of the Sirīsa tree, he crushed the heretics.
Sumaṅgala and Tissa were his two chief disciples.”
Sāgata was the name of the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.
Sunandā and Nandā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī.
“Tapussa and Bhallika were the foremost attendants;
Sirima and Koṇā were the supporters of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, was eighty cubits in height.”
He shines like a lamp-tree, like a flowering king of sāl trees.
His radiance spreads for twelve leagues in every direction;
the lifespan of that Great Seer is one hundred thousand years.
Remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
Having kindled the True Dhamma and brought the great multitude across, he—
like a mass of fire that has burned out— has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
“That psychic power and that glory, and those wheel-treasures under his feet—all that has vanished. Are not all conditioned things empty?
“The Victor Dīpaṅkara, the Teacher, attained Nibbāna at the Nanda Monastery.”
"Therein his Jina-stūpa is thirty-six yojanas in height.
After the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, having passed one incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya), there appeared a Buddha named Koṇḍañña.
The Teacher appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand koṭis;

in the second, one thousand koṭis; and in the third, ninety koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, numbering one hundred thousand koṭis. The Teacher—
Having prophesied that the Bodhisatta would become a Buddha, he taught the Dhamma.

Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he handed over his kingdom and went forth. Having mastered the Three Piṭakas and attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from his jhāna. [This was] under the time of Koṇḍañña Buddha.
His city was named Rammavatī; his father was the kṣatriya Sunanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā.
His two chief disciples were Bhadda and Subhadda; his attendant was named Anuruddha; his two chief female disciples were Tissā and Upatissā.
His Bodhi tree was the Sālakalyāṇī tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and the lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“After Dīpaṅkara, there was a leader named Koṇḍañña,
of infinite splendor, immeasurable fame,
unfathomable, and invincible. After his time, having passed one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), four Buddhas appeared in a single aeon.
—Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita. At the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Maṅgala, there were one hundred and ten koṭis of bhikkhus;
at the second, one hundred and ten koṭis; and at the third, ninety koṭis.
It is said that his half-brother, Prince Ānanda by name, was present in that assembly numbering ninety koṭis.
He went into the presence of the Teacher for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. The Teacher delivered a gradual discourse to him.
Together with his retinue, he attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

The Teacher, surveying the past conduct of those sons of noble family, saw the necessary condition (upanissaya) for their possessing bowls and robes made of supernormal power (iddhimaya); he then extended his right hand.
"Come, monks," he said. At that very moment, they all became endowed with proper deportment, like elders of sixty years, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*).
Having paid homage to the Teacher, they surrounded him. This was his third assembly of disciples.
However, whereas the bodily radiance of other Buddhas extended only eighty cubits all around, [his was not so].
It was thus for him. Furthermore, the radiance from the body of that Blessed One remained at all times pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
Trees, the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth—even down to cooking pots and the like—became as if covered with plates of gold.
His lifespan, moreover, was ninety thousand years. During this entire time, the moon, the sun, and the other [heavenly bodies]...
They were unable to shine by their own radiance, and the distinction between night and day was no longer discernible.

During the day, beings moved about constantly illuminated only by the light of the Buddha, as if by the light of the sun. It was only by means of flowers that bloomed at night and birds and other creatures that cried out at dawn that people could perceive the distinction between night and day.
But is it that other Buddhas do not possess this power? It is not so;

for they too, if they so desired, could pervade a ten-thousandfold world-system or even more with their radiance. However, due to a previous aspiration made by the Blessed One Maṅgala, his bodily radiance was always like that of the other Buddhas—a fathom-wide aura—yet it pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system.

Having pervaded [the world], he stood there. It is said that while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisatta, having assumed an existence similar to that of Vessantara, he dwelt with his children and wife on a mountain resembling Mount Vaṅka.

Then, a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, having heard of the Great Being’s inclination toward generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and asked the Great Being for his two children. The Great Being—
Saying, “I give them, brahmin, my two little sons,” he, overjoyed and exultant, gave both children while making the great earth tremble down to its watery boundaries.

The yakkha stood leaning against a railing at the edge of the walkway and, even as the Great Being was looking on, devoured the two children like a bundle of young grass stalks. As the Great Man gazed at the yakkha, [his mouth...]
Even upon seeing his mouth disgorging a stream of blood like a mass of fire as soon as it was opened, not even a hair’s breadth of dejection arose within him.
As he thought, "Truly, my gift has been well-bestowed," a great joy and gladness welled up in his body.
He [thought], "By the result of this gift of mine, in the future, in this very same manner..."

He made this aspiration: "May rays of light issue forth from my body. Based on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays of light issued from his body and pervaded such an extent of space. Furthermore, there is another account of his past conduct:
it is said that in the time of his existence as a Bodhisatta, having seen the stupa of a certain Buddha...
Thinking, “It is right for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha,” he wrapped his entire body according to the method of wrapping a torch-handle,
filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces]— which was the size of a jewel-encrusted crown—
with ghee, lit a thousand wicks therein, took it upon his head, set his whole body ablaze, and [approached] the Cetiya.

He spent the entire night performing circumambulations. Even though he exerted himself in this way until the rising of the dawn, not even a single pore of his body grew warm; it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus bud.
For this Dhamma indeed protects him who protects himself. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.

This is the benefit when Dhamma is well-practiced: the one who lives by Dhamma does not go to a state of woe.”—By the outflow of this very deed, the radiance from the Blessed One’s body remained pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Suruci, approached [the Buddha] with the thought, "I shall invite the Teacher.
Having heard a sweet discourse on the Dhamma, he said, "Venerable Sir, please accept alms from me tomorrow.
[The Buddha asked], "Brahmin, how many monks do you require? He replied, "But how large is your retinue of monks, Venerable Sir?"
At that time, it was the very first assembly of the Teacher; therefore, he said, "one hundred thousand koṭis.
[The brahmin said,] "Venerable Sir, please accept alms from me together with all of them. The Teacher consented.
Having invited [the Sangha] for the following day, the brahmin went home and thought: "I am able to provide such a number of monks with rice gruel, food, robes, and so forth, but—"
"But how will there be a place for sitting?
This thought of his produced a sense of heat in the stone throne of the divine king Paṇḍukambala, which stood eighty-four thousand yojanas away.
Sakka, wondering, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from this position? [looked] with his divine eye.
Looking about, he saw the Great Man and thought, “The brahmin named Suruci has invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and is contemplating a place for them to sit;
it is fitting that I too go there and take a portion of merit.
Having assumed the form of a carpenter, with axe and adze in hand, he appeared before the Great Man. “There is...”
“Is there perhaps some work to be done for hire by anyone? he asked. When the Great Man saw him, he said, “What work will you do?
“There is no craft unknown to me; whether it be a house or a pavilion, whatever anyone has built, I know how to construct it.
“In that case, I have work for you. “What is it, noble sir? “Tomorrow, for my sake, [prepare for] one hundred thousand million bhikkhus...”
“You have been invited. You shall build a pavilion for them to sit in. “I would indeed build it, if you could provide me with wages,” he said.
“I can, my son,” they replied. “Very well, I will do it,” he said, and having gone there, he looked out at a certain spot.
A stretch of land twelve or thirteen yojanas in extent became as level as a *kasiṇa* disk. He—
Thinking, "Let a pavilion made of the seven precious gems arise in this place," he looked out.
At that very moment, the earth split open and the pavilion arose. On its pillars made of gold were capitals made of silver;
on those made of silver were capitals made of gold; on the pillars made of jewels were capitals made of coral; and on those made of coral were capitals made of jewels.
Upon pillars made of the seven precious gems, there were water-pots made of the seven precious gems.
Then he looked, thinking, "Let a network of small bells hang within the pavilion. At the very moment of his looking, the network hung down.
When stirred by a gentle breeze, it emitted a sweet sound like that of fivefold musical instruments; it was as if the time for celestial music had arrived.
As he thought, "Let garlands and wreaths of perfumes hang down here and there," garlands and wreaths hung down.

He thought, "Let seats and footstools for the bhikkhus numbering one hundred thousand times ten million emerge by breaking through the earth," and at that very moment they emerged. He thought, "Let a water-jar appear in each corner."
He thought, and water-jars appeared.
Having constructed this much, he went into the presence of the brahmin and said, "Come, sir;
look at your pavilion and give me my wages. The Great Being went and looked at the pavilion. And even as he was looking, his entire body—
It became continuously suffused with five-colored radiance. Then, looking at the pavilion, it occurred to him:

"This pavilion was not made by a human being; rather, having come upon my own intention and my own virtue, this pavilion has surely been caused to be made by Sakka, the king of the gods, because his own celestial abode will become hot."
"It will be so. Then he thought, "It is not fitting for me to give alms in such a pavilion for only a single day;
I shall give them for seven days. For even that much of an external gift is unable to bring satisfaction to the Bodhisattas;
rather, it is by cutting off his own head while it is adorned, gouging out his eyes while they are anointed, and [offering] the flesh of his heart...
When something is given after having been rubbed off [from one's own body], there arises what is called "joy based on the generosity of the Bodhisattvas.
For even in our own case, when the Bodhisattva, in the *Sivirāja Jātaka*, gave away five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas daily,
distributing gifts at the four gates and in the center of the city, that gift was unable to produce such joy of generosity.
But when Sakka, the king of the gods, came in the guise of a brahmin and begged for his eyes, even as he was plucking them out and giving them away, joy arose within him;
not even a hair’s breadth of change occurred in his mind. Thus, there is no satiety for Bodhisattas in the act of giving gifts.
Therefore, that Great Being also thought: "For seven days, by me [were given] those numbering one hundred thousand times ten million..."
Thinking, "It is fitting to give alms to the bhikkhus," he had them seated in that pavilion and for seven days gave what is called *gavapāna*.
*Gavapāna* is a dish prepared by filling large jars with milk, placing them on hearths, and when the milk has been thickened by boiling,
adding a small amount of rice and cooking it until it is seasoned with honey, sugar, and powdered ghee.
It is said. However, even the humans were unable to serve [the food]. The devas also served by taking turns.
Even an area measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas was not sufficient for the monks to occupy;
yet those monks sat down through their own supernatural power. On the final day, however, after having all the monks wash their bowls—
Having filled [the robes] with ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses for the purpose of medicine, he gave them together with his three robes;
the robe-cloths received by the most junior monk of the Saṅgha were worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
As the Teacher was giving the blessing of thanksgiving, he thought: "This man has given such a great gift; who indeed will he become?"

While reflecting, he saw that "in the future, at the end of two incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kalpas, there will be a Buddha named Gotama," and addressing the Great Man, he prophesied: "After such a length of time has passed, you will become a Buddha named Gotama.
Having heard this prophecy, the Great Man thought: "It seems that I..."
Thinking, "I shall become a Buddha; what use have I for the life of a householder? I will go forth," he abandoned such prosperity as if it were a globule of spittle.

Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he mastered the word of the Buddha, attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Maṅgala was the Buddha;
the city of the Blessed One Maṅgala was named Uttara; his father was a kṣatriya named Uttara;
his mother was Queen Uttarā; Sudeva and Dhammasena were his two chief disciples; and Pālita was his attendant.
Sīvalī and Asokā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
After he had remained for ninety thousand years and attained Parinibbāna, ten thousand world-systems simultaneously became plunged into darkness.
In all those world-systems, there arose a great wailing and lamentation among human beings.
“After Koṇḍañña, the Leader named Maṅgala,
having destroyed the darkness in the world, upheld the Dhamma-faring.
Thus [spoke] the Buddha Sumana.

Thus, after that Blessed One had entered final nibbāna, having cast darkness over the ten-thousandfold world system, at a later time a Teacher named Sumana appeared in the world. He too had three assemblies of disciples:

in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus; in the second, on the Golden Mountain, ninety thousand times ten million; and in the third, eighty thousand times ten million.
At that time, there was a dragon king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty.
Hearing that "a Buddha has appeared," he departed from his dragon abode surrounded by his retinue of kinsmen.

He caused divine musical instruments to be played as an offering for the Blessed One, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand times ten million monks; he distributed a great almsgiving and presented pairs of fine cloths to each individual.
Having given [these gifts], he established himself in the refuges. The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Mekhalā; his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was Queen Sirimā.
Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta were his two chief disciples; Udena was his attendant, and Soṇā and Upasoṇā were his chief female disciples.
He had two chief female disciples, his Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree, his body was ninety cubits in height,
and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After Maṅgala, the Leader named Sumana appeared.
"Unequaled in all things, the supreme among all beings.
Subsequently to that Buddha Revata, a teacher named Revata arose. He, too, had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly...
There was no counting [of them]; in the second assembly there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus, and likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Atideva, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and established himself in the refuges.
Placing his joined palms to his head and hearing praise for that Teacher’s abandonment of the defilements, he made an offering with his upper robe.
He also prophesied of him, "He will become a Buddha. Now, the city of that Blessed One was named Sudhaññavatī;

his father was a kṣatriya named Vipula, his mother was named Vipulā, his two chief disciples were Varuṇa and Brahmadeva, his attendant was named Sambhava, his two chief female disciples were Bhaddā and Subhaddā, and his Bodhi tree was a Nāga-tree.
Bodhi, his body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
"After Sumanas, there was a leader named Revata;
peerless, incomparable, matchless, supreme, and a Conqueror."
Regarding the Buddha Sobhita:
In his later period, a teacher named Sobhita arose. He also had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta...

Having become a brahmin named Ajita and having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he established himself in the refuges and gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He, too, prophesied of him: "He will become a Buddha.
Furthermore, that Blessed One’s city was named Sudhamma; his father was King Sudhamma, and his mother was also Sudhammā.
The queen was named Nāma; the two chief disciples were Asama and Sunetta; the attendant was named Anoma;
the two chief female disciples were Nakulā and Sujātā; the Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
“After Revata, there was a leader named Sobhita;
he was concentrated, peaceful in mind, unequaled, and without rival.
Thus spoke the Buddha Anomadassī.
After a further incalculable aeon had passed, three Buddhas appeared in a single aeon:
Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. The Blessed One Anomadassī had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first there were eight hundred thousand bhikkhus, in the second seven hundred thousand, and in the third six hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was alone...
He was a general of the *yakkhas*, possessed of great psychic power and majesty, the sovereign of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *yakkhas*.
Hearing that "a Buddha has arisen," he came and gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha. As for Anomadassī...
The Blessed One’s city was named Candavatī; his father was King Yasava; his mother was Queen Yasodharā;
his two chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma; his attendant was Varuṇa; his two chief female disciples were Sundarī and Sumanā;
his Bodhi tree was the Ajjuṇa tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height; and the lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“After Sobhita, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds,
was Anomadassī of immeasurable fame, radiant and invincible.
Thus [was] the Buddha Paduma.
In a later period, a teacher named Paduma arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.

In the first assembly, there were one hundred and ten million bhikkhus; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third, two hundred thousand bhikkhus dwelling in a great forest thicket in a wilderness devoid of villages.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, [saw] the Teacher...
Seeing him who had entered the attainment of cessation, he paid homage with a clear mind, circumambulated him, and filled with joy and gladness, let out a lion’s roar three times.

Without abandoning the joy directed toward the Buddha for seven days, and departing from his feeding ground solely through that joy and happiness, he remained attending upon the Blessed One, having even renounced his own life. The Teacher—
After seven days had passed, having emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), Siha looked toward the monks and thought, "Having inspired confidence in the Saṅgha of monks, he will pay homage to the Saṅgha.
He then thought, "Let the Saṅgha of monks come! The monks arrived at that very moment.
Siha also inspired confidence in the Saṅgha of monks. The Teacher, observing his mind, [knew]: "In the future, he will become a Buddha..."
...he prophesied, "It will be so. For the Blessed One Paduma, however, there was a city named Campaka;
his father was King Asama; his mother was Queen Asamā; his two chief disciples were Sāla and Upasāla; his attendant was Varuṇa;
his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā; his Bodhi tree was named Soṇarukkha; and it was eighty-five cubits in height.
His body was [of such splendor], and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After Anomadassi, there appeared another Perfectly Enlightened One,
the supreme among bipeds, named Paduma by name— unequaled and without a peer.
Nārada Buddha:
In the period following him, a teacher named Nārada arose. He also had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there were one hundred billion bhikkhus; in the second, ninety billion; and in the third, eighty billion.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic and attained mastery over the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and performed worship with red sandalwood.
The Teacher also prophesied of him, "In the future, he will become a Buddha. Of that Blessed One...
There was a city named Dhaññavatī; his father was a kṣatriya named Sudeva; his mother was Queen Anomā;
his two chief disciples were Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta; his attendant was named Vāseṭṭha; his two chief female disciples were Uttarā and Phaggunī;
his Bodhi tree was named Mahāsoṇarukkha; and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height. Ninety...
“The lifespan was a thousand years.
Following Paduma, there appeared a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the supreme among bipeds,
named Nārada by name, peerless and without equal.”
As for the Buddha Padumuttara:

after the time of the Buddha Nārada, in a period one hundred thousand aeons ago, there arose in a single aeon a Buddha named Padumuttara alone. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly—
There were one hundred thousand times ten million monks; on the second Vebhāra mountain, ninety thousand times ten million; and on the third, eighty thousand times ten million.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a great royal chaplain named Jaṭila, gave a gift of robes to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha."
He explained it thus. However, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no so-called "heretics" (titthiyā).
All gods and humans went for refuge to the Buddha alone. His city was named Haṃsavatī;
his father was the kṣatriya Ānanda; his mother was Queen Sujātā; Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples; and his attendant was named Sumana.
Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was a *sāla* tree; his body was fifty-eight cubits in height;
the radiance of his body extended twelve *yojanas* all around; and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After Nārada, there appeared a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the supreme among bipeds:
“The Victor named Padumuttara was unshakeable, like the ocean.
After thirty thousand aeons had passed following that Buddha, there appeared two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta.
In two eons, two Buddhas were born. Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, at the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred billion who had destroyed the taints; in the second, ninety billion; and in the third, eighty billion.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Uttara, gave away eighty billion pieces of wealth that he had previously set aside and stored away.
Having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, having heard the Dhamma, and having established himself in the refuges, he went forth and was ordained.
He too prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha.
For the Blessed One Sumedha, there was a city named Sudassana; his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was Queen Sudattā.
Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were the two chief disciples; his attendant was named Sāgara; Rāmā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree was the Mahānīpa tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height; and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After Padumuttara, there was a leader named Sumedha.
“The Sage, difficult to approach, of fierce radiance, supreme over the entire world.
After him, in a later period, there arose a Teacher named Sujāta. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly...
There were six million monks at the first assembly, five million at the second, and four million at the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch, heard that "a Buddha has arisen";

he approached him, listened to the Dhamma, and having offered the sovereignty of the four great continents together with the seven treasures to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, [he remained] in the presence of the Teacher.

He went forth into homelessness. All the inhabitants of the kingdom, having taken up the office of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), constantly offered great alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha.
The city of that Blessed One was named Sumaṅgala; his father was King Uggata, and [his mother] was Pabhāvatī.
His mother was named Mātā; Sudassana and Sudeva were his two chief disciples; Nārada was his attendant;
Nāgā and Nāgasamālā were his two chief female disciples; and his Bodhi tree was the Great Veḷu tree.

It is said that this tree, with its small hollows and thick trunk, shone like a bundle of peacock feathers due to its great branches extending upward. The body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits in height.
The lifespan was ninety thousand years.
"In that very same Maṇḍa-kappa, there was a Leader named Sujāta;
he had the jaw of a lion and the shoulders of a bull, immeasurable and unapproachable."
The Buddha Piyadassī:
After him, one hundred and eighteen aeons ago, in a single aeon, three Buddhas were born—Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī.
The Blessed One Piyadassī also had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly there were one hundred and ten million bhikkhus; in the second, ninety million; and in the third, eighty million.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Kassapa who had mastered the three Vedas, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Having constructed a monastery for the Sangha by relinquishing wealth worth one hundred and ten million, he established himself in the refuges and the precepts.
Then the Teacher prophesied of him: "After the passing of eighteen hundred kalpas, he will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Anoma; his father was King Sudinna, and his mother was named Candā.
Pālita and Sabbadassī were his two chief disciples; his attendant was named Sobhita; and Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were his two chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree was the Kakudha tree; his body was eighty cubits in height; and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
"After Sujāta, the Self-Existent One, the Leader of the World, the Unassailable One, the Peerless, Piyadassī of great renown [appeared]."
As for the Buddha Atthadassī:
in the period following him, the Blessed One named Atthadassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first, there were eight million nine hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eight million eight hundred thousand; and likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a powerful ascetic named Susīma, brought a parasol of Mandārava flowers from the world of the devas and honored the Teacher;
he, in turn, prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was called Sobhana; his father was King Sāgara, and his mother was Sudassanā.
The two chief disciples were Santo and Upasanto; his attendant was named Abhaya; the two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā;
his Bodhi tree was the Campaka tree; his body was eighty cubits in height;
the radiance of his body remained pervading a full league on all sides at all times; and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, Atthadassī, the bull among men,
having destroyed the great darkness, attained supreme enlightenment.
Thus [spoke] the Buddha Dhammadassī.
In a later period, a Teacher named Dhammadassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus, in the second ninety koṭis, and in the third eighty koṭis.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, king of the gods, performed worship with divine scented flowers and divine musical instruments; he too [honored him].
The Teacher prophesied, "In the future he will become a Buddha. That Blessed One had a city named Saraṇa;
his father was King Saraṇa, and his mother was Queen Sunandā. His two chief disciples were Paduma and Phussadeva; his attendant was named Sunetta;
his two chief female disciples were Khemā and Sabbanāmā; and his Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree.
Bodhi is also called Bimbijāla; his body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
"In that very aeon of adornment (maṇḍakappa), the greatly renowned Dhammadassī, having dispelled that darkness, shone forth among the world of devas."
Siddhattha Buddha:
In a period subsequent to that, ninety-four aeons ago, in a single aeon, there arose a single Sammasambuddha named Siddhattha.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred koṭis.
There were ninety million monks in the first assembly, ninety million in the second, and eighty million in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, possessing great majesty and endowed with the power of supernormal knowledge, became an ascetic named Maṅgala;
he brought a large rose-apple fruit and presented it to the Tathāgata. After the Teacher had consumed that fruit, he declared: "In the ninety-fourth aeon hence, you will become a Buddha."
He gave this explanation. That Blessed One’s city was named Vebhāra; his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Queen Suphassā.
Sambala and Sumitta were his two chief disciples, Revata was his attendant, and Sīvalā and Surāmā were his two chief female disciples.
His Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra tree, and his body was sixty cubits in height.
“The lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World,
arose like the sun that has emerged, having destroyed all darkness.”
Tissa Buddha:
In the period following him, at the end of ninety-two aeons from now, two Buddhas—Tissa and Phussa—were born in a single aeon.
The Blessed One Tissa had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were [ninety million] bhikkhus...
In the first [assembly] there were one billion; in the second, nine hundred million; and in the third, eight hundred million.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been born as a kṣatriya named Sujāta who was of great wealth and great fame, went forth into the ascetic life of an *ṛṣi*.

Having attained great supernormal power (*mahiddhika*), he heard that "a Buddha has appeared," and taking celestial mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka flowers, he [stood] in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
He honored the Tathāgata as he was walking along, creating a canopy of flowers in the sky. The Teacher also prophesied of him:
"In the ninety-second aeon from now, he will become a Buddha. That Blessed One had a city named Khema;
his father was the kṣatriya Janasandha, his mother was Queen Padumā, and his two chief disciples were Brahmadeva and Udaya. Sumana...
His attendant was Nāma, his two chief female disciples were Phussā and Sudattā, his Bodhi tree was the Asana tree, his body was sixty cubits in height,
and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Following Siddhattha,
there appeared the Unequaled One, the Peerless One;
“Of infinite splendor and immeasurable fame, Tissa was the leader of the world.
After him, in a later period, a teacher named Phussa arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly—
There were six million monks at the first assembly, five million at the second, and thirty-two million at the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a kshatriya named Vijitāvin, renounced his great sovereignty and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.

Having mastered the Three Piṭakas, he delivered discourses on the Dhamma to the great multitude and fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). The Teacher also declared of him: "He shall become a Buddha..."
"will come to be," he prophesied. That Blessed One’s city was named Kāsi;
his father was King Jayasena; his mother was named Sirimā; his two chief disciples were Surakkhita and Dhammasena; his attendant was named Sabhiya;
his two chief female disciples were Cālā and Upacālā; his Bodhi tree was the Āmalaka tree; and his body was fifty-eight cubits in height.
"There was [a Buddha]; the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
In that very same aeon of decline (maṇḍakappa), there was an unsurpassed Teacher;
incomparable, peerless, Phussa, the leader of the world."
Vipassī Buddha:
In the ninety-first aeon prior to this, there arose a Blessed One named Vipassī. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there were six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, one million; and in the third—

There were eighty thousand [years]. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, gave a great golden throne inlaid with the seven precious gems to the Blessed One. He too prophesied of him:
"In the ninety-first aeon from now, he will become a Buddha. The city of that Blessed One was named Bandhumatī; his father was Bandhumā.
His father was named King Nāma; his mother was named Bandhumatī. Khaṇḍa and Tissa were his two chief disciples. His attendant was named Asoka.
Candā and Candamittā were his two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree.
His body was eighty cubits in height, and the radiance of his body remained pervading seven yojanas at all times. His lifespan was eighty thousand years.
"And after Phussa, the Sambuddha, the supreme among bipeds,
named Vipassī, arose in the world as one possessed of vision.
Thus [spoke] the Buddha Sikhi.
In a later period, thirty-one aeons ago from now, there were two Buddhas named Sikhi and Vessabhu.
The Blessed One Sikhi also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly there were one hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eighty thousand;
and in the third, seventy thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama.

Having offered a great almsgiving including robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and having given the elephant-treasure adorned with the seven jewels, he made it the size of an elephant and gave it as an allowable object (kappiyabhaṇḍa). The Teacher also prophesied of him:
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, he will become a Buddha. The name of that Blessed One was Aruṇavatī.
The city was named Aruṇa; his father was the kṣatriya Aruṇa, and his mother was named Pabhāvatī.
Abhibhū and Sambhava were his two chief disciples, and Khemaṅkara was his attendant. Sakhilā and Padumā were his two chief female disciples.
His Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka tree, and his body was seventy cubits in height. The radiance of his body extended for three yojanas.
Having pervaded [the world], he stood there; his lifespan was seventy thousand years.
"After Vipassi, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, there was a Victor named Sikhī, peerless and without equal."
The Buddha Vessabhū:
In the period following him, a teacher named Vessabhū appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly there were eighty thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seventy; and in the third, sixty. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sudassana.
Having become King Nāma, he gave a great alms-offering including robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having gone forth in his presence, he became perfected in conduct and virtue, and was filled with great reverence and joy toward the Jewel of the Buddha.
The Blessed One also prophesied of him: "In the thirty-first aeon from now, he will become a Buddha. Regarding that Blessed One:
There was a city named Anoma; his father was King Suppatīta, and his mother was named Yasavatī.
His two chief disciples were Soṇa and Uttara; his attendant was named Upasanta; his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā.
His Bodhi tree was a Sāla tree; his body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, peerless and without rival,
there arose in the world a Conqueror known by the name Vessabhū.
Thus [spoke] the Buddha Kakusandha.
In the subsequent period of this eon, four Buddhas appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One.
The Blessed One Kakusandha had only one assembly of disciples, consisting of forty thousand bhikkhus.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Khema, and [he attended] the assembly headed by the Buddha.

Having given a great alms-offering of robes for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, as well as medicinal requisites such as eye-salve, and having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he went forth. The Teacher also prophesied of him, "He will become a Buddha.
Now, the Blessed One Kakusandha had a city named Khema; his father was a brahmin named Aggidatta, and [his mother] was named Visākhā.
The mother was Brāhmaṇī; Vidhura and Sañjīva were the two chief disciples; the attendant was named Buddhija;
Sāmā and Campā were the two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree was the Mahāsirīsa tree; his body was forty cubits in height;
and his lifespan was forty thousand years.
"After Vessabhu, there was another Sambuddha, the supreme among bipeds,
named Kakusandha by name— immeasurable and difficult to approach.
Then there was the Buddha Koṇāgamana.
In a later period, a Teacher named Koṇāgamana arose. He too had only one assembly of disciples, consisting of thirty thousand bhikkhus.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a king named Pabbata, went into the presence of the Teacher surrounded by his retinue of ministers;
having heard the preaching of the Dhamma, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.

Having performed a great almsgiving and given away fine woolen cloths, Chinese silk, Koseyya cloth, kambala wool, dukūla linen, and a golden plate, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "He will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Sobhavatī; his father was a brahmin named Yaññadatta, and his mother was named Uttarā.
The mother was Brāhmaṇī; the two chief disciples were Bhiyyasa and Uttara; the attendant was named Sotthija;
the two chief female disciples were Samuddā and Uttarā; the Bodhi tree was the Udumbara; his body was thirty cubits in height;
and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.
“After Kakusandha, there was a Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds,
the Conqueror named Koṇāgamana, the eldest in the world, the bull among men.
Then came the Buddha Kassapa.
At a later time, a Teacher named Kassapa arose. He too had but one assembly of disciples, consisting of twenty thousand bhikkhus.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Jotipāla, was a master of the three Vedas, renowned both on earth and in the sky, and a friend of the potter Ghaṭīkāra.
He went together with him to the Teacher, and having heard a discourse on the Dhamma, he went forth.
Being diligent, he mastered the Three Piṭakas and adorned the Buddha’s dispensation through his perfection in the proper and secondary duties.
The Teacher also prophesied of him, "He will become a Buddha. The birthplace of that Blessed One was the city named Bārāṇasī; [his father] was Brahmadatta.
His father was a brahmin named Nāma, his mother was a brahmin woman named Dhanavatī; Tissa and Bhāradvāja were his two chief disciples;
Sabbamitta was his attendant; Anulā and Uruvelā were his two chief female disciples;
the Nigrodha tree was his Bodhi tree; his body was twenty cubits in height; and his lifespan was twenty thousand years.
"After Koṇāgamana, there arose another Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, named Kassapa by clan, a King of Dhamma, a maker of light.
Furthermore, in the eon in which the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara appeared, there were three other Buddhas as well. Of them—
There is no formal prophecy (byākaraṇa) concerning the Bodhisatta; therefore, they are not shown here.
However, in the Commentary, in order to show all the Buddhas starting from Taṇhaṅkara, this was said:
“Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara;”
The Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, the supreme among bipeds;
Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, the sage Sobhita;
Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.
“Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassi of great renown;
Atthadassi and Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World.
Tissa and Phussa, the Sambuddhas; Vipassi, Sikhin, and Vessabhu.”
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa the Leader—
these were the Perfectly Awakened Ones, free from passion and concentrated.
Like the rising of the sun, they dispelled the great darkness.
“Having blazed like masses of fire, they have gone out together with their disciples.
Thus spoke Gotama the Buddha.
In this regard, our Bodhisatta performed services in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas, beginning with Dīpaṅkara.
Having acted thus, he has come [to this point] after four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand kappas.
However, from the time of the Blessed One Kassapa until this present Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), there has been no other Buddha.
Thus, having received the prophecy (*byākaraṇa*) in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhisatta—
“Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.”
Having combined these eight qualities and having made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he exerted himself with the thought:
"Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that produce a Buddha. While searching, he saw the first Perfection of Giving;
thus, he beheld the qualities that produce Buddhahood, beginning with the Perfection of Giving. Even while fulfilling them, he proceeded until he reached the state of existence as Vessantara.
And as he was coming, there were those benefits described for Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution:
"Thus, men endowed with all factors are certain of enlightenment,
even after wandering through a long course of time, for hundreds of millions of eons."
“They are not reborn in Avīci, nor likewise in the Lokantarika hells;
they are free from parching thirst and hunger, and do not become Kālakañjaka spirits.
Nor are they reborn as small creatures in states of woe.”
Being born among human beings, they are not born blind from birth.
They have no deficiency of hearing, nor are they mute;
they do not become female, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
“Those men destined for enlightenment do not belong to the mundane world;
they are freed from the immediate transgressions and have a pure range of conduct in every respect.
Seeing the efficacy of kamma, they do not pursue wrong views.”
Even while dwelling in the heavens, they do not take rebirth among the non-percipient beings.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, no cause for such rebirth exists;
these true persons are inclined toward renunciation and are detached from existence after existence.
“They practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.

Having attained these very benefits, he has come here. And while fulfilling the perfections, during his time as the brahmin Akitti, his time as the brahmin Saṅkha, his time as King Dhanañjaya, his time as King Mahāsudassana, his time as Mahāgovinda, his time as King Nimi, and his time as Prince Canda—
There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of giving during the time of the merchant Visayha, the time of King Sivi, and the time of King Vessantara.
However, in the *Sasapaṇḍita-jātaka*, it is stated with absolute certainty:
"Seeing him come for alms, I renounced my own self."
“There is none equal to me in giving; this is my perfection of giving.
Thus, for one who practices self-sacrifice in this way, the perfection of giving becomes what is called a perfection in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-pāramī*).
Likewise, during his time as the Naga king Sīlavant, as the Naga king Campeyya, as the Naga king Bhūridatta, as the Naga king Chaddanta, and as Prince Jayaddisa.
Regarding the period of the Alīnasattu Kumāra, there is no limit to the number of existences fulfilled through the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*).
Indeed, in the *Saṅkhapāla Jātaka*, it is stated that he was entirely devoted to it:
"Even while being pierced with stakes and beaten with spears..."
“I am not angry with the son of the Bhojas;
this is my perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). Thus, for one who practices self-sacrifice, the perfection of virtue becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).
Likewise, during his time as Prince Somanassa, as Prince Hatthipāla, and as the wise Ayoghara, he renounced great sovereignty through the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī).
There is no limit to the number of times his personal existence was fulfilled. However, regarding this [perfection] exclusively, it is said in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka:
"I cast away great sovereignty come into my hands like a lump of spittle;
for one who renounces, there is no clinging—this is my perfection of renunciation."
Thus, for one who renounces sovereignty out of detachment and goes forth, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*) becomes what is called the "ultimate perfection.
Likewise, during the times of the wise Vidhura, the wise Mahāgovinda, the wise Kuddāla, the wise Araka, the wanderer Bodhi, and the wise Mahosadha—
those who fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*) throughout their various existences— [the same applies].
There is no measure to it. However, in the Sattubhasta Jātaka during the time of the wise Senaka, he said:
“Discerning with wisdom, O Brahmin, I liberated the brahmin from suffering;
there is none equal to me in wisdom—this is my perfection of wisdom.”
For one who showed a snake that had been placed inside a bag, the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramitā) became known as the supreme perfection (paramattha-pāramī).

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which the perfections of energy (vīriya-pāramitā) and the others were fulfilled. However, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka, it is stated categorically:
"Those who do not see the further shore were all destroyed in the midst of the waters."
“There is no alteration in my mind; this is my perfection of energy.
Thus, for one crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy becomes what is called the perfection in the ultimate sense. In the *Khantivādijātaka*:
“Even as they were striking me with a sharp axe as if I were insentient...”
“I am not angry with the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.
Thus, for one who endures great suffering as if it were insentient, the perfection of patience becomes what is called the perfection in the ultimate sense. In the *Mahāsutasoma Jātaka*:
“Protecting the word of truth, even at the cost of my own life...”
“I released one hundred kṣatriyas;

this is my perfection of truth.”—Thus, for one who sacrificed his life to protect the truth, the perfection of truth became known as the ultimate perfection (*paramatthapāramī*). In the *Mūgapakkha Jātaka*:
“My mother and father are not to be given away, nor is great glory to be given away.”
“Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, I resolved upon the vow.
Thus, for one who resolves upon a vow even at the cost of giving up life, the perfection of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā*) becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*).
In the *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka*: “No one terrifies me, nor do I fear anyone.”

“Supported by the power of loving-kindness, I then delight in the forest.”—Thus, even disregarding his own life, as he practiced loving-kindness, the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramitā) became for him a perfection in the ultimate sense. In the *Lomahaṃsa-jātaka*:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground, using a human skeleton as my pillow.”
"Having come to the village circle, they display their forms in no small measure.

Thus, even when village children cause pleasure and pain by spitting on him and so forth, or by offering garlands, perfumes, and the like, for one who does not transcend equanimity, the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramitā) becomes a perfection in the ultimate sense (paramattha-pāramī). This is the summary here.
But this matter in detail should be taken from the *Cariyāpiṭaka*. Having thus fulfilled the perfections while established in the Vessantara existence, he declared:
“This earth is insentient; it does not perceive pleasure or pain.
Yet even it shook seven times by the power of my giving.”
Having thus performed great meritorious deeds, such as causing the great earth to tremble, he passed away at the end of his lifespan and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Thus, from the time he first stood at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until his rebirth in the city of Tusita—
this entire extent should be understood as the "Remote Past" (dūrenidāna).
The Story of the Remote Past is finished.
2. The Story of the Not-Remote Past:
While the Bodhisatta was still dwelling in the Tusita heaven, the so-called "Buddha-proclamation" arose. For in this world, there are three [such proclamations].
Great tumults arise: the tumult of an aeon (*kappa-kolāhala*), the tumult of a Buddha (*buddha-kolāhala*), and the tumult of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-kolāhala*).

In that regard, when it is said, "After the passing of one hundred thousand years, the emergence of an aeon will occur," the gods of the sense-sphere realm known as Lokabyūhas—having loosened their turbans, with disheveled hair, weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, and dressed in crimson garments—become exceedingly [distressed].
Assuming hideous disguises and wandering along the public highways, they proclaim: "Sirs, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the end of the aeon will come;

this world will be destroyed. Even the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be consumed and destroyed, until the destruction of the world reaches as far as the Brahma-world."
“There will be, friends, cultivate loving-kindness; cultivate compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, friends;
attend upon your mother; attend upon your father; be respectful toward the elders of the family. This is called the "clamor of the aeon.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Fully Enlightened One (Sabbuññubuddha) will arise in the world—thus [proclaimed] by the world-protecting deities.
“Friends, after a thousand years from now, a Sammasambuddha will appear in the world,” they proclaim as they wander about.

This is called the “Buddha-announcement. Likewise, deities proclaim, “Friends, after a hundred years from now, a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti-rāja) will appear in the world,” as they wander about.
They wander about. This is what is called the "clamor of the wheel-turning monarch. These three clamors are great.
Upon hearing the sound of the clamor of a Buddha among them, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world-system assemble together;
knowing that "such-and-such a being will become a Buddha," they approach him and make their request. While making their request—

And when the preliminary signs had appeared, they made their entreaty. At that time, all of them gathered together in a single world-system along with the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmā;
then, having gone into the presence of the Bodhisatta in the Tusita heaven, they said:
"O Noble One, while you were fulfilling the ten perfections, it was not for the sake of the attainment of Sakka, nor the attainment of Māra, Brahmā, or a Wheel-turning Monarch."
"Filled by those who made aspirations, and filled by those who aspired for omniscience for the sake of delivering the world—now is the time for you, dear sir, to become a Buddha;
this is the moment, dear sir, to become a Buddha. Thus they entreated him.
Then the Great Being, without yet giving his promise to the deities, [considered] the factors of time, continent, country, family, parentage, and the limit of lifespan.
He performed what is called the five great observations (*pañcamahāvilokana*). Therein, he first observed the time, thinking: "Is it the right time, or is it not the right time?
In this regard, a period when the lifespan has increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not the right time.
Why? Because at such a time, birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings; and the teaching of the Dhamma by Buddhas is characterized by the three marks (*tilakkhaṇa*).
There is no such thing [as a suitable time for the Dispensation]. When they speak of "impermanence, suffering, and non-self," people think, "What is this they are talking about?
and thus consider it neither worth hearing nor worth believing. Consequently, there is no realization; and when that is absent, the Teaching fails to lead to liberation.
Therefore, that is not the right time. Even a period when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is not called the right time. Why?

For at that time, beings have defilements that are rampant; and advice given to those with rampant defilements does not remain in its proper place, but quickly vanishes like a line drawn with a stick upon water. Therefore, that too is an improper time.
From a hundred thousand years downwards, and from a hundred years upwards, is the period of life-span called "the proper time. And at that time, it is the period of a hundred-year lifespan.
Then the Great Being perceived that the time for his birth had come.

Looking toward the continents, he surveyed the four continents along with their surrounding islands and saw: "Buddhas are not born on three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa. Then he considered:
"Jambudīpa is vast, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region, indeed, are Buddhas born?"
Looking for a place where beings are being reborn, he saw the Middle Country. As for what is called the Middle Country:
to the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsālā, and beyond that are the bordering districts;
on this side of that is the middle. To the southeast is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts.
To the east, the bordering districts are from the middle [of the country]. To the south, there is a market town named Setakaṇṇika;
the bordering districts are beyond that, and the central districts are within. To the west, there is a brahmin village named Thūṇa;
the bordering districts are beyond that, and the central districts are within. To the north, there is a mountain named Usīraddhaja; the bordering districts are beyond that...
"Janapadas, from the edge to the middle"—this is the region described thus in the Vinaya.
It is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.
In this region, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Wheel-turning Monarchs, and other beings of great influence [arise].
“Kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, and great landowners arise [there]. And here is the city named Kapilavatthu;
it is my conclusion that I must be reborn there.
Then, surveying the family, he reflected: “Buddhas are not born into the merchant class or the *śūdra* class. They are born into a family esteemed by the world...”
Furthermore, [beings] are reborn in only two types of families: either in a khattiya family or in a brahmin family. Now, the khattiya family is honored by the world; therefore, I shall be born there.
King Suddhodana shall be my father. Thus he surveyed the family. Then, looking for a mother, [he considered]:
“The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful, addicted to liquor, or a gambler; for a hundred thousand aeons...”
"But one who has fulfilled the perfections is possessed of the five precepts unbroken from birth onwards.
This queen named Mahāmāyā is such a person; she shall be my mother. How long, however, will her lifespan be?
He saw that it would be seven days more than ten months.

Having thus performed these five great observations, and having given his promise while gathering the devas by saying, "The time for my Buddhahood has come, sirs," he dismissed those devas with the words,
"Go, you," and surrounded by the Tusita devas, entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita heaven. For indeed, the Nandana Grove exists in all the celestial worlds.

There, deities wander about reminding him of the sphere of wholesome kamma performed in the past, saying, "Pass away from here and go to a happy destination; pass away from here and go to a happy destination.
Surrounded by these deities who were thus reminding him of his wholesome deeds, he wandered there and, upon passing away, took rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

To clarify this, here is the sequential account: At that time, it is said, the festival of the Āsāḷhi constellation had been proclaimed in the city of Kapilavatthu, and the great multitude was enjoying the festivities.

Queen Mahāmāyā, too, from the seventh day prior to the full moon, abstained from intoxicating drinks and enjoyed the festival celebrations, adorned with garlands, perfumes, and finery. On the seventh [day]...
Rising early one morning, having bathed with scented water, having bestowed four hundred thousand pieces of gold and given a great almsgiving,
adorned with all her ornaments, having eaten excellent food, and having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha,
she entered the decorated bedchamber; lying down on her royal couch and falling asleep, she saw this dream:
It is said that the four Great Kings, lifting her up along with her bed, brought her to the Himālaya mountains;
having placed her beneath a great sāla tree sixty *yojanas* in height on a surface of mind-made stone (*manosilā*) seventy *yojanas* wide, they stood to one side.
Then their queens came, led the queen to Lake Anotatta, and bathed her in order to remove the impurities of human birth.
Having had her dressed in celestial garments, anointed with perfumes, and adorned with celestial flowers, they then led her to a silver mountain not far from there.
Inside it was a golden palace; having prepared a celestial couch there with its head toward the east, they laid her down upon it.
Then the Bodhisatta, having become a magnificent white elephant, [stood] on a golden mountain not far from that place.
There he wandered about, then descended from there and ascended the Silver Mountain;
coming from the northern direction, he took a white lotus with his trunk, which was the color of a silver garland, let out a trumpeting cry, entered the golden celestial mansion,
circumambulated his mother’s bed three times from left to right, and appeared as if entering her womb by splitting open her right side.
"Thus it was. In this way, he took conception under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha.
On the following day, having awakened, the queen reported that dream to the king.

The king summoned about sixty-four eminent brahmins and, upon a ground smeared with cow dung and green grass and adorned with auspicious ceremonies such as parched grain, [offered them] most costly...
Having prepared seats, he filled golden and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar for the brahmins seated there;
having covered them with golden and silver lids, he gave them to them.
Furthermore, he satisfied them with other gifts such as new garments and tawny cows. Then, when they had been satisfied with all their desires—
Having had the brahmins interpret his dream, he asked, "What will happen? The brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King.
A fetus has been conceived in the womb of your queen; moreover, it is a male fetus, not a female one. You will have a son.
If he lives the life of a householder, he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin). If..."
“Having gone forth from the home life, he will renounce the world; he will become a Buddha in the world, one who has removed the veil.
At the very moment the Bodhisatta took rebirth in his mother’s womb, the entire ten-thousandfold world system shook, trembled, and quaked all at once. Thirty-two omens appeared:
An immeasurable radiance pervaded ten thousand world-systems. As if desiring to behold his splendor, the blind regained their sight,
the deaf heard sounds, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight-limbed, the lame regained the ability to walk on their feet,
and all beings who were in bondage— such as those bound in fetters— were released from their shackles and other constraints.
The winds ceased, the fires in all the hells were extinguished, hunger and thirst were stilled in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya),
fear vanished among the animals, the disease of all beings was pacified, all beings became speakers of kind words,
horses neighed with sweet voices, elephants trumpeted, and all musical instruments emitted their respective sounds even without being struck.
The ornaments on the hands and other limbs of human beings resounded; all directions became serene;
a soft, cool breeze blew, bringing happiness to living beings; unseasonable clouds rained; water welled up and overflowed from the earth;
birds abandoned their flight through the sky; rivers stood still without flowing; and the great ocean...
The water became sweet; its entire surface was covered with five-colored lotuses; all flowers, both land-born and water-born, blossomed;
on the trunks of the trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses bloomed;
and on the creepers, creeper-lotuses bloomed; even splitting through solid rock surfaces, they appeared as layers upon layers of hundred-petaled flowers.
Stalked lotuses emerged; hanging lotuses appeared suspended in the sky; showers of flowers rained down on every side.

Celestial musical instruments resounded in the air, and the entire ten-thousandfold world system was like a mass of loose garlands rolled up, or like a cluster of garlands pressed together and bound, appearing as a throne of garlands fully adorned and prepared.
And it was as if adorned with a single garland, fanned by waving yak-tail whisks, perfumed with flowers, incense, and scents,
and had reached the pinnacle of supreme beauty. Thus, from the very moment the Bodhisatta took conception,
four sons of gods with swords in hand stood guard to ward off any misfortune for both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother.
They took her. No lustful thought arose in the mind of the Bodhisatta’s mother toward men;
she attained the pinnacle of gain and the height of fame, being happy and with a body free from fatigue.
And she saw the Bodhisatta within her womb like a yellow thread wound around a clear gem. For a womb inhabited by a Bodhisatta is indeed like the interior of a shrine.
It is not possible for another being to dwell in or utilize it;
therefore, seven days after the Bodhisatta was born, the Bodhisatta’s mother passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Furthermore, unlike other women who give birth while standing, sitting, or lying down—even before or after the ten months—so it was not with the Bodhisatta’s mother. She...
However, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months, she gives birth while still standing. This is the natural law regarding the mother of a Bodhisatta.
Queen Mahāmāyā also, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months like oil in a vessel, and being full-term, desired to go to her father’s home;
she informed King Suddhodana: "I wish, O Lord, to go to my family's home."
"to go to the city of Devadaha. The King, having consented by saying "Very well," had the road made level from Kapilavatthu as far as the city of Devadaha;

having had it adorned with decorations such as plantain trees, full water-pots, banners, and flags, he had the Queen seated in a golden palanquin, had it carried by a thousand ministers, and sent her forth with a great retinue.
Between the two cities, however, there was a grove of auspicious sal trees called Lumbinīvana, inhabited by the residents of both cities.
At that time, from its roots up to its topmost branches, the entire grove was in full bloom;
and from within the branches and the flowers, swarms of bees of five colors and various flocks of birds [emerged].
They wandered about warbling with sweet voices. The entire Lumbinī grove became like a forest of *cittalatā* creepers, resembling a well-prepared drinking circle for a king of great majesty.
Upon seeing it, a desire arose in the Queen to sport in the *sāla* grove.
The ministers took the Queen and entered the *sāla* grove. She approached the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree and [grasped] a *sāla* branch.
Desiring to grasp it, the *sāla* branch bent down like the well-polished tip of a bamboo cane and approached the vicinity of the Queen’s hand.
She extended her hand and seized the branch. At that very moment, the winds born of the Queen’s karma stirred;
then, having had a curtain drawn around her, the great multitude withdrew while she remained standing, holding the *sāla* branch.
And thus was her delivery from the womb. At that very moment, four Great Brahmas with purified minds arrived, carrying a golden net.
Having received the Bodhisatta in that golden net and standing before his mother, they said:
"Be joyful, O Queen! A son of great power has been born to you."
However, unlike other beings who emerge from the mother’s womb smeared with loathsome impurities,
the Bodhisatta does not do so. Rather, like a preacher descending from a Dhamma-seat or a man descending from a ladder,
he emerges with his two hands and two feet outstretched, as if already standing, without being defiled by anything born of the mother’s womb.
Untainted by impurity, pure and stainless, he emerged from his mother’s womb shining like a precious gem placed within a cloth of Kāsī silk.
Even so, for the sake of honoring both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother,
two streams of water issued forth from the sky and provided warmth to the bodies of both the Bodhisatta and his mother.
Then, having been received by the Brahmās standing with golden nets, the Four Great Kings took it from their hands upon a deerskin rug that was considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch;
from their hands, men took it upon a cushion of fine linen (*dukūla*);
and when it was released from the hands of the men, it settled upon the earth and [proceeded] toward the eastern direction.
He looked out, and thousands of world-systems became a single open space. There, gods and humans, worshipping with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said:
"Great Being, there is no one else here equal to you; how could there be anyone superior?
Having thus surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—he, by himself...

Seeing no one equal to him, he took seven steps with the stride of a lion, thinking, "This is the northern direction," while being followed by Mahābrahmā holding a white parasol, Suyāma holding a yak-tail fan, and other deities carrying the remaining royal insignia in their hands.
Then, standing at the seventh step, he uttered this bold proclamation: "I am the foremost in the world," and so forth.
He let out a lion’s roar.

For indeed, in three of his existences—the existence as Mahosadha, the existence as Vessantara, and this present existence—the Bodhisatta uttered speech immediately upon emerging from his mother’s womb.
It is said that in the existence as Mahosadha, while he was still in his mother’s womb...
As he was departing, Sakka, the king of the gods, came and placed a piece of choice sandalwood in his hand and departed.
He left having taken it in his fist. Then his mother asked him, "Dear, what have you brought back?
"Medicine, Mother," he replied. Because he had come having taken medicine, they gave him the name "Osadhadāraka" (The Medicine Boy).
Having taken that medicine, they placed it in a jar; for those who came one after another—the blind, the deaf, and others—it became the very remedy for the subsiding of all diseases.
Then, because of the words that arose, "This medicine is great! This medicine is great!", his name became "Mahosadha.
However, when he was emerging from his mother’s womb during his existence as Vessantara—
Stretching out his right hand, he went forth saying, "Mother, is there anything in the house that I might give as an offering?

Then his mother, saying to her son, "My dear, you were born into a wealthy family," placed her own palm against her son's hand and set down a purse containing a thousand coins. But in this present existence, he uttered this lion’s roar:
"Nadi"—thus, in three successive existences, the Bodhisatta uttered these words as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb.
And just as at the moment of conception, so too at the moment of birth did the thirty-two omens appear.
At the very same time that our Bodhisatta was born in the Lumbinī grove, Queen Rāhulamātā...
The Elder Ānanda, the minister Channa, the minister Kāḷudāyī, the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka, the Great Bodhi Tree, and four treasure-pots were born.

Among them, one treasure-pot was a quarter-league (gāvuta) in size, one was half a league (yojana) in size, one was three-quarters of a league in size, and one was a full league in size. In depth, they reached as far as the very limits of the earth.
These seven are called the co-natives (*sahajāta*).
The inhabitants of both cities took the Bodhisatta and went to the city of Kapilavatthu itself. On that very day, [the proclamation was made]:
"In the city of Kapilavatthu, a son has been born to the Great King Suddhodana; this prince, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree..."
Thinking, “He will become a Buddha,” the hosts of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, joyful and delighted, sported, tossing their garments and performing other such acts.
At that time, a forest-dwelling ascetic named Kāla-devala, a follower of King Suddhodana who had attained the eight meditative attainments,
having finished his meal, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his midday rest and stayed there for his day’s abiding.
Sitting there, he saw those deities playing in such a manner and asked, "For what reason do you play with such joyful hearts?
Tell me the cause of this. The deities replied, "Venerable sir, a son has been born to the great king Suddhodana;
having sat at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and become a Buddha, he will set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. Of him—"
“We are joyful for this reason: ‘We shall see the infinite grace of a Buddha and hear the Dhamma.
Having heard their words, the ascetic quickly descended from the world of the gods, entered the royal palace, and sitting on the prepared seat, said:
“It is said, Great King, that a son has been born to you; I shall see him. The king [brought forth] his son, adorned and arrayed...
Having had the prince brought, they carried him forward to make him pay homage to the ascetic. The Bodhisatta’s feet turned around and rested upon the ascetic’s matted locks.
Indeed, for that particular existence, there was no one else worthy of being saluted by the Bodhisatta.
For if those who were unaware had placed the Bodhisatta’s head at the feet of the ascetic, [the ascetic] would have split into seven pieces.
His head would have burst asunder. The ascetic, thinking, "It is not right for me to destroy myself," rose from his seat and extended his joined palms in reverence toward the Bodhisatta.
Seeing that marvel, the king paid homage to his own son.
The ascetic recollected eighty eons—forty eons in the past and forty eons in the future. Regarding the Bodhisatta...
Having seen the perfection of his marks, he reflected, "Will he become a Buddha, or will he not?
As he investigated and examined this, he knew with certainty, "He will surely become a Buddha," and smiled, thinking, "This is a marvelous man.
Then, as he further investigated, "Shall I have the opportunity to see this marvelous man when he has become a Buddha, or shall I not? he pondered.
