Seeing that "I shall not obtain [the opportunity]; having died in the interval, I will be reborn in the formless realm (arūpabhava), which cannot be reached even by a hundred or a thousand Buddhas coming to awaken one," she wept, thinking:
"I shall not be able to see such a marvelous person when he has become a Buddha; alas, a great loss will be mine!"
When people saw him, they asked, "Our noble sir has just now laughed and then wept and stood up;
what, venerable sir, will some obstacle befall our noble son? "There is no obstacle for him;
he will undoubtedly become a Buddha. "Then why, venerable sir, did you weep?"
“I shall not have the opportunity to see such a person when he has become a Buddha;
thinking, ‘Alas, my grief will be great,’ I weep while mourning for myself,” he said. Then, reflecting, “Will anyone among my kinsmen have the opportunity to see one who has become a Buddha?
he saw his own nephew, the boy Nālaka. He [sent him] to his sister...
Having gone home, [she asked], "Where is your son Nālaka? "He is in the house, noble lady," he replied. "Call him here," she said;
and having had him summoned, when the youth had come into her presence, she said to him: "Dear child, a son has been born into the family of the Great King Suddhodana;
he is a sprout of a Buddha. After thirty-five years have passed, he will become a Buddha. You must go to see him."
“You shall obtain it; go forth this very day! The boy, born into a family possessing seven hundred and eighty million in wealth, thought, “My maternal uncle will not lead me into what is harmful.

Thinking thus, he immediately had saffron robes and an earthen bowl brought from the market, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron garments, and [approached] him who is the supreme person in the world.
“My renunciation was for his sake,” he said, and extending his joined palms toward the Bodhisatta, he paid homage by prostrating himself on his five limbs.
He then placed the bowl in its bag, slung it over his shoulder, entered the Himālaya mountains, and practiced the duty of a recluse.
Later, having approached the Tathāgata who had attained supreme perfect enlightenment, he requested the discourse on the Nālaka practice.
Furthermore, having entered the Himālayas and attained *arahantship*, he practiced the austere path (*ukkaṭṭha-paṭipadā*);
after maintaining his life for seven months, while standing beside a golden mountain, he passed away into the *nibbāna*-element without remainder (*anupādisesa*).
On the fifth day, the Bodhisatta also had his head washed and [the king] went to the royal palace, thinking, "We shall perform the naming ceremony."
Having anointed [the child] with four kinds of perfumes, having scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth, and having prepared unbroken milk-rice,
they invited one hundred and eight brahmins who had mastered the three Vedas, seated them in the royal palace, fed them a fine meal,
and after performing great honors, they had the marks examined, wondering, "What indeed will happen? Among them—
“Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, and Mantī, Yañña, Subhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta—these were the eight brahmins at that time who, possessing the six factors, interpreted the signs.
These eight brahmins were the ones who examined the marks. On the day of the conception, there was also a dream...
He was indeed examined by these very men. Among them, seven persons raised two fingers and declared of him:
"One endowed with these marks, if he dwells in the household life, will become a universal monarch (cakravartin);
if he goes forth into homelessness, he will become a Buddha. They described all the glorious majesty of a universal monarch.
Among them, the youngest, a young brahmin named Koṇḍañña by clan, observed the Bodhisatta’s perfection of the excellent marks and gave a categorical prediction, raising a single finger:
"There is no reason for him to remain in the midst of a household; he will certainly become a Buddha with the canopy of his hair uncovered.
For this one had already performed his meritorious service.

The being destined for his final existence, having surpassed the other seven persons through his wisdom, saw only one thing—the absolute state of Buddhahood—belonging to this Bodhisatta who was endowed with these marks;
therefore, raising a single finger, he made this declaration.
And when they were choosing a name for him, because he would bring about the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world, they gave him the name "Siddhattha."
Then those brahmins, having gone to their respective homes, addressed their sons: "Dear ones, we are old;
whether or not we shall believe that the son of the Great King Suddhodana has attained omniscience, once that prince has attained omniscience, you should go forth into his teaching. Those seven...
When the people had remained for the duration of their lifespan and departed according to their karma, the young man Koṇḍañña alone remained free from illness.
As the Great Being grew up, he made the Great Renunciation, went forth, and in due course arrived at Uruvelā.
He thought: "Truly delightful is this spot of earth; it is indeed fit for a clansman seeking to strive."
Having resolved, "I shall go forth," and having gone there to dwell, they heard that "the Great Man has gone forth.
Then, approaching the sons of those brahmins, he said to them: "It is said that Prince Siddhattha has gone forth;
he will undoubtedly become a Buddha. If your fathers were healthy, they would have departed this very day."
"Let us go forth. If you also desire it, come; we shall follow that Great Man into the homeless life.
They were not all able to become of one mind; among them, three persons did not go forth.
With the brahmin Koṇḍañña as their leader, the other four went forth. Those five persons became known as the Pañcavaggiya Theras.
Then King Suddhodana asked, "What did my son see that he will go forth? [The reply was: "The four portents.
"Which ones, and which ones? "An old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a renunciant.
The king said, "From now on, do not allow such people to approach my son; for me—"
"Because my son has become a Buddha, he has no further karmic duty;

I wish to see my son exercising the sovereignty and lordship of a wheel-turning monarch over the four great continents and the two thousand surrounding islands, traveling through the sky surrounded by a retinue thirty-six *yojanas* in circumference. Having spoken thus, to these...
To prevent the four kinds of omens from coming within the prince’s range of vision, he established a guard at intervals of one *gāvuta* in each of the four directions.
On that day, among the eighty thousand kinsmen assembled at the auspicious site, each one adopted a son, saying: "Whether this child becomes a Buddha or a king..."
“We shall give him this one son alone. Even if he becomes a Buddha, he will wander surrounded by a host of kshatriya ascetics;
even if he becomes a king, he will wander preceded and surrounded by kshatriya princes.
The King also appointed for the Bodhisatta nurses endowed with the most excellent beauty and free from all defects.
The Bodhisatta grew up with a great retinue and with great splendor and majesty.
Then one day, there was a festival for the King known as the "Blessing of the Sowing. On that day, they decorated the entire city like a city of the gods;
all the slaves, laborers, and others were dressed in new garments and adorned with perfumes, garlands, and other ornaments.
They assemble at the royal palace and harness a thousand ploughs for the King’s work;
on that day, however, seven hundred and ninety-nine ploughs, together with their oxen, reins, and traces, are adorned with silver.
But the King’s own guiding plough is adorned with red gold. Even the horns, reins, and goads of the oxen [are likewise adorned].
They were indeed adorned with gold. As the king was departing with a great retinue, he went along taking his son with him.
At the site of the work, there was a single *jambu* tree with thick foliage and abundant shade.
Having prepared a bed for the prince beneath it, having had a canopy inlaid with golden stars fastened above, and having had it enclosed by a screen of cloth, [he stayed there].
Having established guards and adorned himself with all his ornaments, the king, surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the place where the plowing was to be done.
There, the king took up a golden plow; the ministers took seventy-nine silver plows less one;
and the farmers took the remaining plows. Having taken them, they plowed here and there. But the king [plowed] from this side to the other.
He goes, or he comes from the further shore to this side.

At that place there was great prosperity. The nurses sitting around the Bodhisatta, thinking, "Let us see the king’s prosperity," stepped out from behind the curtain. The Bodhisatta, looking here and there, [saw] no one...
Seeing this, he rose up with speed, sat cross-legged, and by attending to the breath (*ānāpāna*), he attained the first *jhāna*.
The nurses, wandering among the food and snacks, were delayed for a short while.
While the shadows of the other trees had passed away, the shadow of that *jambu* tree remained fixed in a complete circle. The nurses [thought], "The noble son is alone."
Hurrying, they raised the curtain and, entering within, saw the Bodhisatta seated cross-legged on his bed and that miracle;
having gone [to the king], they reported to the king: "Your Majesty, the prince is seated thus;
while the shadows of other trees have passed away, the shadow of the rose-apple tree remains perfectly circular. The king came with great speed.
Having witnessed the miracle, the king said, "This, dear son, is your second salutation," and he bowed to his son.
Then, in due course, the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen years. The king had three palaces built for the Bodhisatta, suitable for the three seasons:
one nine stories high, one seven stories high, and one five stories high.

He also provided forty thousand dancing girls as attendants. Like a god surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs (accharā), the Bodhisatta dwelt in three palaces according to the seasons, enjoying great prosperity while attended by adorned dancing girls and entertained by instrumental music performed without men present.
His queen, however, was the mother of Rāhula, who served as his chief consort (aggamahesī).
While he was thus enjoying such great prosperity, one day this discussion arose within the circle of his kinsmen:
"Siddhattha wanders about merely intent on play; he does not learn any craft. When a battle is presented, what will he do?
The King, having summoned the Bodhisatta, said: "Dear son, your kinsmen say that Siddhattha..."
“They say you wander about addicted to games without having trained in a craft; what do you think of this, enemy, when the time has come?
“Your Majesty, there is no need for me to train in a craft. Have the drum beaten in the city to announce my demonstration of skill:
‘On the seventh day from now, I shall show my craft to my kinsmen. The king did so. The Bodhisatta—

Having assembled archers skilled in hitting targets by sound and by sight, he displayed before the great multitude his twelvefold craft, which was not shared by other archers, for the sake of his kinsmen. This should be understood according to the method set forth in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka.
At that time, the assembly of his kinsmen became free from doubt.
Then one day, desiring to go to the pleasure grove, the Bodhisatta addressed his charioteer, saying, "Yoke the chariot.

He replied, "Very well," and having adorned a magnificent, supreme chariot with every ornament, he harnessed four auspicious Sindhava horses, the color of lotus petals, and announced its readiness to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta—
Having mounted a chariot resembling a celestial palace, he set out toward the pleasure grove.
The deities, thinking, "The time for Prince Siddhattha’s full awakening is near;

we shall show him the preliminary sign," manifested a young god as an old man—decayed, with broken teeth, grey hair, crooked and hunched in body, holding a staff and trembling—and presented him to his view.

Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him. Then the Bodhisatta, following the method described in the Mahāpadāna Sutta, asked the charioteer, "Good man, who is this person? His hair is not like that of others.
Having heard his reply, he was moved with deep emotion, exclaiming, "Alas, fie upon birth! For where there is birth, aging is bound to appear for one who has been born."
Then, turning back from there, he ascended the palace itself. The king asked, "For what reason has my son returned so quickly?
"Because he saw an old man, Your Majesty," [the messenger replied]. "They said that upon seeing an old man he would go forth into homelessness;
why do you destroy me? Quickly prepare the entertainments for my son; while experiencing prosperity, he will not go forth."
"He will not pay heed," he said, and having increased his guard, he stationed protectors at every half-yojana in all directions.
On another day, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park in the same manner, he saw a sick man created by a deity;
having questioned him in the same way as before, his heart was filled with agitation, and he turned back and ascended to the palace. The king also—
Having asked [the question] and made arrangements in the manner described below, he increased the security further by stationing guards in an area extending three *gāvutas* all around.
On another day, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park in the same way, he saw a person created by a deity who had passed away;
having asked [the question] in the previous manner, his heart was moved with agitation, and he turned back once more.

He ascended the palace. The king, having inquired and made arrangements in the same manner as described below, further increased the guard and stationed them for protection over an area measuring one *yojana* on all sides.
Then, on another day, while going to the pleasure garden, he saw a renunciant created by a deity, well-clad and properly robed, and asked, "Who is this, good sir?"

He questioned the charioteer. Although the charioteer did not know of the appearance of a Buddha, nor of the going-forth (pabbajjā) or the qualities of one who has gone forth, by the power of a deity he said, "This one, O Lord, is called a 'one who has gone forth,'" and he praised the virtues of the going-forth.
The Bodhisatta, having conceived a desire for the going-forth, went to the pleasure grove on that day. [Thus say] the Dīgha-bhāṇakas.
They say: "Having seen all four omens on that very same day, he departed.
Having sported there for a portion of the day and bathed in the Maṅgala lotus pond, when the sun had set, he sat down upon the auspicious stone slab, desiring to have himself adorned;
then his attendants brought garments of various colors and of various kinds.
Taking various kinds of ornaments, garlands, perfumes, and ointments, they stood surrounding him on all sides.
At that moment, Sakka’s seat became hot. Reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from this position?
he perceived the Bodhisatta’s desire to adorn him and addressed Vissakamma: "Friend Vissakamma,..."
“Prince Siddhattha will depart on the Great Renunciation this very day at the hour of midnight;
this is his final adornment. Go to the pleasure garden and adorn the Great Being with celestial ornaments.
Having assented with “Very well,” he approached the Bodhisatta at that very moment through the power of the gods and [adorned him].
Acting like a barber, he wrapped the Bodhisatta’s head with celestial cloth. By the mere touch of his hand, the Bodhisatta recognized him, thinking, "This one is a human;
this is a son of the gods. As soon as the head was wrapped, a thousand folds of cloth rose up from the head in the form of a crest-jewel (*moḷi*) made of precious gems.
As he wrapped it again, another thousand folds appeared; thus, for every ten times he wrapped it, a thousand folds emerged.
Ten thousand lengths of cloth were raised up. One should not wonder, "The head is small and the cloths are many;
how did they rise up? For among them, the largest was the size of an *āmalaka* flower, while the remaining ones were the size of *kadamba* flowers.
The Bodhisatta’s head became like a *kuyyaka* flower, covered with filaments.
Then, while all the musicians displayed their respective skills,
while the brahmins uttered words such as "Victory and joy!", and while Sumanangalika and others honored him with various kinds of auspicious words and songs of praise,
he mounted that excellent chariot adorned with every ornament. At that moment, Rāhula’s mother—
Having heard that she had given birth to a son, King Suddhodana sent a message saying, "Announce my joy to my son.
When the Bodhisatta heard this, he said, "Rāhu is born; a bond is born. The king asked, "What did my son say?
and upon hearing those words, he declared, "From now on, let my grandson’s name be Rāhula Kumāra."
The Bodhisatta, too, having mounted his excellent chariot, entered the city with exceedingly great glory, exceeding delight, and magnificent splendor.

At that time, a noble maiden named Kisāgotamī, who was on the upper terrace of the palace, beheld the beauty of the Bodhisatta’s form as he was circumambulating the city; filled with joy and gladness, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Truly extinguished is that mother; truly extinguished is that father;
truly extinguished is that woman who has such a husband as this.
When the Bodhisatta heard this, he thought: “This person says thus: ‘For a mother who beholds such a physical form as this...’”
“The heart is extinguished; the father’s heart is extinguished; the mother’s heart is extinguished.
“In what being extinguished, indeed, is it said that the heart is extinguished? Then, with a mind dispassionate toward the defilements, this occurred to him:
“When the fire of lust is extinguished, it is said to be extinguished; when the fire of hatred is extinguished, it is said to be extinguished.”
“When the fire of delusion is extinguished, it is called ‘extinguished’ (nibbūta); when all the fevers of the defilements, such as conceit and views, are extinguished, it is called ‘extinguished.
“This man proclaims what I have long heard. For I wander about seeking Nibbāna;
it is fitting that this very day I should abandon the household life, go forth, and seek Nibbāna.”
Thinking, "Let this be the teacher's fee for her," he removed from his own neck and sent to Kisāgotamī a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces.
She was filled with joy, thinking, "Prince Siddhattha, having set his heart on me, has sent me this gift."
The Bodhisatta, too, having ascended his own palace with great splendor and majesty, lay down upon his royal couch. At that very moment, female dancers— adorned with every ornament,
highly trained in dance, song, and the like, and possessing a beauty equal to that of celestial maidens— surrounded him,
holding various musical instruments and providing him with delight through dance, song, and instrumental music.
They performed [the dances]. Because his mind was detached from the defilements, the Bodhisatta took no pleasure in the dancing and other performances, and he fell asleep for a moment.
Those women thought, "He for whose sake we perform these dances and other arts has fallen asleep; why should we trouble ourselves now?
Thus, they cast aside the musical instruments they had taken up and lay down, as did the lamps filled with fragrant oil.
They were meditating. The Bodhisatta, having awakened and sitting cross-legged on the back of his bed,
saw those women sleeping with their musical instruments strewn about— some with saliva trickling from their mouths and limbs drenched in sweat,
some gnashing their teeth, some snoring, some muttering incoherently, and some with their mouths wide open.
Some were stripped of their clothes, their private parts exposed in a state of loathsome nakedness.
Seeing this transformation in them, his mind became even more intensely detached from sensual pleasures.

To him, that great terrace—though once adorned and prepared like the palace of Sakka—appeared like a raw charnel ground filled with various kinds of filth; the three realms of existence appeared like a house on fire.
They cried out, “Alas, we are afflicted! Alas, we are beset! and uttered this exclamation;
his mind was exceedingly inclined toward the life of renunciation.
Thinking, “It is fitting for me to go forth on the Great Renunciation this very day,” he rose from his bed and went near the door.
Having gone there, he asked, "Who is here? Channa, who was lying with his head on the threshold, replied, "I am Channa, noble son.
[The Prince] said, "Today I wish to go forth in the Great Renunciation; prepare a horse for me.
He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and taking the horse-accoutrements, he went to the stable while fragrant oil lamps were burning.

Seeing the horse-king Kaṇḍaka standing on a delightful stretch of ground beneath a canopy of *sumana* flowers, [the Bodhisatta] thought, "Today it is fitting that I should saddle this very one," and he saddled Kaṇḍaka. Even as he was being saddled, Kaṇḍaka perceived:
"This saddling is exceedingly tight; it is not like the saddling used on other days when going for pleasure excursions to the parks and such."
"It cannot be; my noble son will today desire to go forth on the Great Renunciation.
Then, with a joyful heart, he let out a great laugh. That sound would have spread throughout the entire city, but the deities suppressed it and did not allow anyone to hear it.

The Bodhisatta, having sent Channa away and thinking, "I shall first see my son," rose from his sitting-couch and went to the dwelling place of Rāhula’s mother; he opened the door of the inner chamber.
At that moment, a lamp fed with scented oil was burning within the room, and Rāhula’s mother had [filled] a vessel to the brim with jasmine, mallika, and other flowers.
While his son was sleeping on a bed strewn with flowers, the Bodhisatta placed his hand upon the child’s head and fell asleep.
Standing there with his foot upon the threshold, he looked down and thought: “If I remove the queen’s hand and take my son, the queen will wake up;
thus there will be an obstacle to my departure. Only after becoming a Buddha shall I come back and take my son.”

"I shall go forth," he thought, and descended from the palace roof. As for what is stated in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*—"At that time, Prince Rāhula was seven days old"—this is not found in the other commentaries;
therefore, this [latter version] alone should be accepted.
Thus, having descended from the palace roof and approached his horse, the Bodhisatta spoke as follows: "Dear Kaṇḍaka, you..."
"Today, for one night, save me; relying upon you, once I have become a Buddha, I shall save the world together with its devas.
Then, having leaped up, he mounted the back of Kaṇḍaka. From the neck upward, Kaṇḍaka was eighteen cubits in length;
he was endowed with a corresponding height, possessed of strength and speed, and was entirely white like a polished conch shell.
Thus, had he laughed or made even the sound of a footfall, his voice would have pervaded the entire city;

therefore, by her own supernatural power, the deity suppressed the sound of his laughter so that no one could hear it, and at every step of his walking, she presented the palms of her hands beneath him.
The Bodhisatta was seated upon the middle of the horse’s back.
Having had the horse’s tail covered, he reached the vicinity of the great gate at the hour of midnight. At that time,

however, the king, thinking, "In this way my son will not be able to leave the city by opening the city gates at any time whatsoever," ordered that each of the two door-panels be opened by a thousand men.

The Bodhisatta, however, endowed with strength and power, possessed the strength of ten thousand million elephants by the count of elephants, and the strength of ten thousand million men by the count of men. He thought:
"If the gate is not opened, today, while seated on Kaṇḍaka’s back, I shall take hold of his tail, and with Channa standing [there],"
“Together with Kaṇḍaka, by pressing against him with my thighs, I shall leap over and cross the wall which is eighteen cubits high.

Channa also thought: “If the gate is not opened, I will place my master, the noble son, upon my shoulder, and taking Kaṇḍaka between my knees, encircling him with my right hand, I shall carry him across.”
“I shall leap over the wall and pass beyond. Kaṇḍaka also thought:

“If the gate is not opened, I shall take my master, while he remains seated exactly as he is on my back, along with Channa who stands holding the tail, lift him up together with me, leap over the wall, and pass beyond. If the gate were not opened, it would have been exactly as they had intended.
One of those three men would prepare [the way]. However, the deity dwelling at the gate opened the gate.
At that very moment, Māra the Evil One, thinking, "I shall turn the Bodhisatta back," arrived and stood in the air, saying:
"My dear sir, do not go out! On the seventh day from now, the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) will appear to you, [ruling] over the two thousand minor islands surrounding [Jambudīpa]."
“You shall rule over the four great continents; turn back, dear sir. “Who are you? “I am Vasavatti.
“Māra, I know of the appearance of my Wheel-Treasure; I have no need for kingship. Having made the ten-thousandfold world-system resound, I shall become a Buddha,” he said.
Then Māra thought, “From this moment on, whether it be a thought of sensual desire or a thought of ill will...”
“Or, at the time of reflection, I shall know whether there is a thought of sensual desire or a thought of ill will. Thus, seeking an opportunity, he followed after him like a shadow.

The Bodhisatta, however, having cast aside the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands as if it were a globule of spittle, without regard for it, departed from the city with great honor.
Having departed on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, while the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā was prevailing—

Furthermore, he became desirous of looking back at the city. And as soon as this thought arose in his mind—the great earth, as if saying, "Great Being, you have not yet performed the act of looking back," split and turned like a potter's wheel.
The Bodhisatta stood facing the city, looked back at it, and [gazed] upon it.
Having pointed out to him on the ground the site of the Kaṇḍakanivattana Cetiya,
he turned Kaṇḍaka toward the path that was to be traveled and set forth with great honor and sublime majesty and splendor. At that time, it is said,
deities held sixty thousand torches before him, sixty behind him, sixty on his right side, and sixty on his left side.
"Sixty. Another deity held immeasurable torches at the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*).
Other deities, as well as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others, proceeded while making offerings with divine perfumes, garlands, powders, and incense;
they were adorned with *pāricchattaka* flowers and *mandārava* flowers, like torrents of rain falling from thick clouds.
The sky became continuous [with sound], and divine songs resounded;
eight musical instruments on all sides, and sixty—that is, six million eight hundred thousand musical instruments—were played.
Their sound rolled like the thundering of clouds within the belly of the ocean, and like the roar of the sea within the belly of Mount Yugandhara.
Proceeding with this glorious splendor, the Bodhisatta reached the bank of the Anomā River, a distance of thirty *yojanas*, having traversed three kingdoms in a single night.
But was it that the horse was unable to go further than that? No, it was not;
for he was like one who crushes the circumference of the rim of a wheel standing upon its hub, as he traversed the entire extent of a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Having gone out early in the morning, he was able to return and eat the meal he had prepared for himself.
However, on that occasion, his body was covered as far as the thighs by perfumes, garlands, and other offerings cast down from the sky by devas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others;
thus, as he dragged it along and cut through the mass of those garlands and flowers, there was great delay. Therefore, [he could only go] about thirty yojanas.
He arrived. Then the Bodhisatta, standing on the riverbank, asked Channa, "What is the name of this river?

"It is named Anomā, O Lord," he replied. "Our renunciation, too, shall be 'Anomā' (Incomparable)," he said, and giving the horse a signal by nudging him with his heel, the horse leaped over and stood on the opposite bank of the river, which was eight usabhas in width.
The Bodhisatta, having dismounted from the back of the horse and stood upon the sandy shore that resembled a silver plate, addressed Channa:
“Friend Channa, take my ornaments and Kaṇḍaka and go; I shall go forth.
“I too will go forth, O Lord,” [Channa replied]. The Bodhisatta said, “It is not possible for you to go forth; you must go.”
Having refused him three times and caused both the ornaments and Kaṇḍaka to be hidden away, he thought:
"These hairs of mine are not suitable for a recluse; there is no one else fit to cut the Bodhisatta’s hair.
Then, thinking, "I shall cut them myself with a sword," he took a blade in his right hand and [held the head] with his left hand.
Taking the topknot together with the fillet, he cut it off. The hair, being only two finger-breadths long, curled to the right and clung to the head.
That remained their length for as long as they lived, and the beard was proportionate to it; thus, there was no further need for the task of shaving the hair and beard.
The Bodhisatta, taking the topknot together with the fillet, [said]: "If I..."
"If I am to become a perfectly enlightened Buddha, let it stay in the sky; if not, let it fall to the ground," he said, and threw it into the atmosphere.
That crest-jewel rose up to a height of one *yojana* and remained suspended in the sky.
Sakka, the king of the gods, beheld it with his divine eye, caught it with a golden net one *yojana* in size, and established it in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the Cūḷāmaṇi Shrine.
“Having cut off his crest-lock, which was perfumed with excellent scents, the Bull of the Sakyans cast it into the air.
Vāsava, the thousand-eyed one, received it upon his head with his most precious jeweled casket.
Then the Bodhisatta thought: “These Kāsī garments are not suitable for a recluse. Thereupon, he—
In the time of Buddha Kassapa, Ghaṭīkāra Mahābrahmā, who had been his old friend for an entire interval between Buddhas, thought:
"Today my friend has gone forth on the Great Renunciation; I shall go to him, taking with me the requisites of a recluse."
“Three robes and a bowl, an axe, a needle, and a belt;
together with a water-strainer—these eight are for a bhikkhu devoted to yoga.
Having brought these eight requisites, he gave them [to the Bodhisatta]. The Bodhisatta, having donned the Arahat’s banner and the supreme garb of one who has gone forth...
Having taken him, he said, "Channa, speak of my parents' health in my name," and dismissed him.
Channa paid homage to the Bodhisatta, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
But Kaṇḍaka, while listening to the words of the Bodhisatta as he was deliberating with Channa, thought, "I shall never see my master again."
Having reflected thus and leaving the range of his vision, he was unable to endure his grief;
with a broken heart, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a son of the gods named Kaṇḍaka.
Channa initially experienced only one sorrow, but being oppressed by a second sorrow due to Kaṇḍaka’s death, he entered the city weeping and lamenting.
Having gone forth, the Bodhisatta spent seven days in that very place in the mango grove named Anupiya, enjoying the bliss of renunciation.
Then, traveling on foot for a distance of thirty yojanas in a single day, he entered Rājagaha.
Having entered, he wandered for alms from house to house in regular succession. The entire city was [moved] by the mere sight of the Bodhisatta’s form.
When Dhanapālaka entered, it became as turbulent as Rājagaha when the asura lord enters the city of the gods.
The king’s men went and reported, "Sire, a being such as this is wandering for alms in the city;
we do not know whether he is a god, a human, a nāga, a supaṇṇa, or someone named so-and-so. The king was on the terrace of his palace.
Standing there and seeing the Great Man, his heart filled with wonder and amazement, he commanded his men: "Go, my men, and investigate!
If he is a non-human spirit, he will depart from the city and vanish;
if he is a deity, he will travel through the air; if he is a naga, he will sink into the earth and depart."
“If he becomes a human, he will consume whatever alms-food he receives.
Then the Great Man, having gathered the mixed food and knowing, “This is sufficient for my sustenance,” departed from the city by the very gate through which he had entered;
sitting down with his face toward the east in the shade of Mount Paṇḍava, he sat to partake of the food.
He began. Then his bowels turned back and reached the state of coming out through his mouth.
Thereupon, because he had never before even seen such food with his own eyes, he was distressed by that repulsive meal;
yet, even so, he exhorted himself in this way: "Siddhattha, you were born into a family where food and drink are easily obtained."
"Even after being reborn in a place where one eats three-year-old fragrant śāli rice with various exquisite flavors, upon seeing a single paṃsukūlika, he thought:
'When indeed shall I too become like this, wandering for alms and eating? Will that time ever come for me?
Having departed while thinking thus, why now do you act in this manner?"—having thus exhorted himself, [he spoke].
He consumed his food without any agitation.
When the king’s men saw what had occurred, they went and reported it to the king.
Upon hearing the messengers’ words, the king departed from the city in haste and approached the Bodhisatta; even at the mere sight of his deportment, he was filled with faith toward the Bodhisatta.

He relinquished all his sovereignty. The Bodhisatta said, “Great King, I have no need for either sensual pleasures of the objects (*vatthukāma*) or sensual pleasures of the defilements (*kilesakāma*);

I have gone forth aspiring for supreme perfect enlightenment. Although the king entreated him in many ways, he could not gain his consent and said, “Surely you will become a Buddha; but when you have become a Buddha...”
She took a vow, saying, "You must first come to my victory. This is the summary here;

however, the detailed account should be understood by consulting the *Pabbajjā-sutta* together with its commentary, beginning with the verse: "I shall proclaim the going-forth, how the One with Vision went forth."
The Bodhisatta, having given his word to the king, traveled by stages on his journey until he approached Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta;
after having attained their meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and realizing, "This is not the path to enlightenment," he did not find satisfaction even in the cultivation of those attainments.
Then, for the purpose of demonstrating his own strength and vigor to the world including its devas, [he proceeded further].
Desiring to undertake the Great Struggle, he went to Uruvelā; thinking, "How delightful indeed is this spot of earth," he took up residence right there and undertook the Great Struggle.

Meanwhile, those five companions of the group, headed by Koṇḍañña, while wandering for alms among the villages, market towns, and royal capitals, arrived there at the place where the Bodhisatta was. Then, [they witnessed] his six-year Great Struggle.

As he was walking about, those who were his close attendants remained near him, performing their duties such as sweeping the courtyard, thinking, "Now he will become a Buddha; now he will become a Buddha.

The Bodhisatta, however, thinking, "I shall perform the practice of asceticism to its ultimate limit," passed the time even on a single sesame seed or grain of rice, and eventually practiced the total cessation of all food.
He did so. Even the deities, contributing nutritive essence through his pores, infused it into him.
Then, due to that lack of food and his extreme emaciation, his body, though once golden-hued, became dark-colored, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man became obscured.
At times, he would even practice the meditation on breathlessness (ānāpānaka-jhāna).
Overwhelmed by great pain and losing consciousness, he fell at the edge of his walking path.
Then some deities said, "The ascetic Gotama has passed away," while others said, "This is merely the dwelling-place of an Arahant.
Among them, those who had the perception that he was dead went and informed King Suddhodana: "Your son..."
“He has passed away. “Has my son passed away after becoming a Buddha, or without having become one? “He was unable to become a Buddha;
he fell down right on the ground of his striving and passed away. Having heard this, the king rejected it, saying: “I do not believe it;
for my son, there is no such thing as passing away without attaining enlightenment. But why did the king not [believe it]?
“Does he have faith? [The King replied: “Because I witnessed the miracles at the foot of the rose-apple tree on the day when the ascetic Kāladevala was sent to pay his respects.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisatta regained consciousness and arose, those deities went and announced, “Your son is well, O Great King.
The King said, “I already knew that my son would not die. Regarding the Great Being—
For six years, while he was performing austerities, it was as if a knot were being tied in the air.
He realized, "This practice of austerities is not the path to enlightenment," and so he began to take substantial food, wandering for alms in villages and market towns to sustain himself.
Then his thirty-two marks of a Great Man became manifest once again.
His body also became golden-hued. The group-of-five monks thought: "Even though he practiced austerities for six years, he was unable to penetrate omniscience.
Now, wandering for alms among villages and market towns and consuming substantial food, what will he be able to achieve?
He has become luxurious and has abandoned his striving; he is like one who wishes to bathe his head [after having previously endured hardship]."
"Discerning any distinction from him is like examining a drop of dew; what use have we for him?
Thus, abandoning the Great Man and taking their respective bowls and robes, they traveled the eighteen-yojana road and entered Isipatana.
Now at that time, Sujātā had been born in the house of Senāni the householder in the village of Senānigama in Uruvelā.
When the maiden Nāma reached marriageable age, she made a vow at a banyan tree:
"If, after going to a family of equal birth, I obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall perform an annual offering to you by giving away one hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Her vow was fulfilled. She [then performed] the Great Being’s practice of austerities...
When the sixth year was completed, wishing to perform the *balikamma* offering on the full moon day of the month of Visākha,
she first had a thousand cows graze in the *laṭṭhi-madhuka* grove; she had their milk given to five hundred cows,
and their milk to two hundred and fifty, continuing in this manner until the milk of sixteen cows was yielded by eight cows.
While they were drinking, she—desiring the thickness, sweetness, and nutritive essence of the milk—performed what is known as the "milk-turning" ritual.

On the full moon day of the month of Visākha, thinking, "I shall perform the offering ceremony early in the morning," she rose at the first flush of dawn during the night and had those eight cows milked.
However, the calves did not come to the udders of the cows.
But at the foot of the tree, as soon as the nine vessels were brought forward, streams of milk flowed forth by their own natural law.
Seeing this marvel, Sujātā took the milk with her own hands, placed it in the nine vessels,
and began to cook it over a fire lit by her own hand.
As that milk-rice was cooking, large bubbles arose and moved about turning to the right.
Not even a single drop splashed out, and not even a trace of smoke rose from the hearth.
At that moment, the four World-Protectors arrived and took charge of guarding the hearth, while Mahābrahmā held a parasol over it.

Sakka, gathering firebrands, kindled the fire. By means of their own divine power, the deities collected the nourishment suitable for gods and humans throughout the four great continents and the two thousand surrounding islands—just as one might collect honey by squeezing a honeycomb bound upon a stick—and cast it into that fire.
For at other times, the deities [place] morsels...
They added nutritive essence to the morsels; however, on the day he attained full enlightenment and on the day of his final nibbāna, they placed it directly into the cooking pot itself.
On that very same day, Sujātā, having witnessed many wonders manifest there, addressed her slave girl named Puṇṇā:
"Mother Puṇṇā, today our deity is exceedingly well-pleased with me..."
“Indeed, in all this time such a marvel as this has never been seen before; go quickly and attend to the place of the deity.
Having accepted her words with the reply, “Very well, noble lady,” she went in great haste to the foot of the tree.
As for the Bodhisatta, having seen five great dreams during that portion of the night, he reflected: “Without a doubt...”
"Today I shall become a Buddha. Having thus made his resolve, at the end of that night, having attended to his physical needs, he waited for the time of the alms-round.
Coming there early in the morning, he sat down at the foot of that tree, illuminating the entire area around the tree's base with his own radiance.
Then Puṇṇā arrived and saw the Bodhisatta at the foot of the tree.
Seeing him seated, gazing toward the eastern world-system, and seeing that the entire tree had become golden-colored by the radiance streaming from his body, she thought:
"Today our deity must have descended from the tree and is sitting here, I believe, to receive the offering with his own hands.
Overcome with excitement, she came in haste and reported this matter to Sujātā.
Having heard her words, Sujātā became joyful in heart and said, "From this day forward,
you shall stand in the place of my eldest daughter," and she gave her all the ornaments suitable for a daughter.
Since it was necessary to obtain a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] on the day he would attain Buddhahood, she [prepared] the milk-rice in a golden bowl.
Having formed the thought, "I shall put [the rice] inside," she had a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces brought out.
Desiring to pour the milk-rice into it, she looked toward the cooking vessel.
All the milk-rice swirled out like water from a lotus leaf and settled into the bowl; it filled exactly one bowl. She [then] took that bowl with another bowl...
Having closed it and wrapped it in white cloth, she herself adorned her body with all her ornaments, placed that bowl upon her head, and went to the foot of the Nigrodha tree with great majesty.
Upon seeing the Bodhisatta, she was filled with intense joy; perceiving him as a "tree deity," she bowed lower and lower from the very spot where she had seen him.
Having gone there, he lowered the bowl from his head, opened it, and taking scented water with fragrant flowers in a golden pitcher, he approached the Bodhisatta and stood before him.
The clay bowl given by the Great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra had remained with the Bodhisatta for all that time, but at that moment it vanished from sight; the Bodhisatta, not seeing the bowl—
Stretching out his right hand, he received the water. Sujātā placed the milk-rice together with the bowl into the Great Being’s hand;
the Great Being looked at Sujātā. Perceiving his gesture, she said, “Noble sir, this has been surrendered by me to you;
take it and do with it as you please,” and having paid homage, she added, “Just as my heart’s desire has been fulfilled...”
"May it likewise come to pass for you," he said, and having renounced even the golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces like a withered leaf, he departed without looking back.
The Bodhisatta, too, rising from his seat, circumambulated the tree and, taking the bowl, went to the Nerañjarā River.
Having gone to the bank, on the day of the full awakening of many hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattvas,
there is a bathing place called Supaṭṭhita where they descended; having placed his alms-bowl on its shore and descended into the Supaṭṭhita ford to bathe,
he put on the lower robe of an Arahant, which had been the dwelling-place of many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and sat down facing the east.
Having made forty-nine lumps, each the size of a single standing palm fruit, he consumed that entire milk-rice mixed with honey and water.
This was his sole sustenance for the forty-nine days while he remained at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) during the seven weeks after becoming a Buddha.
During this period, there was no other food; he did not bathe, nor wash his face, nor perform any bodily grooming.
He spent his time in the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Having eaten that milk-rice, he took the golden bowl and said, "If I am to become a Buddha today, let this bowl go against the current;
if not, let it go with the current," and he cast it into the river's flow. Cutting through the current, it went to the middle of the river.
Like a horse endowed with speed that has traveled eighty cubits upstream by way of its middle course, he submerged in a whirlpool and went to the abode of the Naga King Kāḷa.
There, making a "kili-kilī" sound as he struck the alms-bowls used by the three Buddhas, he stood at the very bottom of them all. Kāḷa—
Upon hearing that sound, the Nāga King said, "Yesterday one Buddha was born, and today another has been born," and he rose up,
uttering praises in many hundreds of verses. Indeed, his ascent today was equal to his ascent yesterday,
filling the sky over an area of one yojana and three gavutas across the great earth.

The Bodhisatta, having spent the day’s rest on the riverbank in a grove of blossoming *sāla* trees, set out toward the Bodhi tree at the time of evening, when the flowers were beginning to detach from their stalks.
Striding like a lion along a path eight *usabha* in width, adorned by the deities, he proceeded.
The *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *supaṇṇas*, and others honored him with divine perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
They set celestial music and other sounds in motion; the ten-thousandfold world system became one with fragrance, one with garlands, and one with cries of "Well done!
At that time, a grass-cutter named Sotthiya, coming along the opposite path carrying grass, recognized the demeanor of the Great Being and offered eight handfuls of grass.
The Bodhisatta took the grass, ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and sat down.

He stood facing north in the southern direction. At that moment, the southern world-system seemed to sink down as if reaching the Avīci hell below, while the northern world-system seemed to rise up as if reaching the peak of existence above.
The Bodhisatta thought, "I suspect this is not the place where I shall attain supreme enlightenment," and [he turned] clockwise.
While doing so, it went toward the western quarter and stood facing the east;
then, the western world-sphere sank down as if reaching the Avīci hell below, while the eastern world-sphere rose up as if reaching the peak of existence above.
It is said that at every place where it stood, its rim was marked by the track of its circumference.
The great earth became uneven, like a large chariot wheel resting upon its hub.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I suspect this place also will not be the site for attaining full enlightenment," circumambulated it and went toward the northern quarter, where he stood facing south.
Thereupon, the northern world-system sank down, reaching as far as the Avīci hell below.
It was as if it had surpassed the southern world-system and reached the very peak of existence above.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I suspect this place too will not be the site for attaining full enlightenment," circumambulated it and went toward the eastern quarter, standing there facing the west.
For the eastern quarter is the place where all Buddhas sit cross-legged.

It was not shaken nor did it tremble. The Bodhisatta, knowing that "this is the unshakeable place never abandoned by all Buddhas, the place where the cage of the defilements is shattered," took those grasses by their tips and shook them;
instantly, they became a seat fourteen cubits long in the form of a cross-legged posture. Those grasses likewise assumed such a shape.
There was no painter or book-illustrator so skilled that he would have been capable of painting [the likeness].
The Bodhisatta, placing the trunk of the Bodhi tree behind him and facing eastward, with a firm mind, resolved:
"Let skin, sinew, and bone remain; let only my flesh and blood waste away; I will not relax this effort until I have attained what is unattained."
"Let the flesh and blood in my body dry up entirely;

yet I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment. Having thus folded his legs into the invincible *pallaṅka*—which would not have yielded even under the simultaneous strike of a hundred thunderbolts—he sat down.
At that moment, Māra the Evil One thought: "Prince Siddhattha wishes to escape from my power; now I must no longer let him go."
Thinking, "I shall go to overcome him," he went into the presence of Māra’s army, reported this matter, and having caused the so-called "Proclamation of Māra" to be proclaimed,
he set out taking Māra’s army with him. That army of Māra was twelve yojanas in front of Māra, twelve yojanas to his right and left,
and stood extending as far as the edge of the world-system behind him.
It was nine yojanas in height, and when it trumpeted, the sound of its roar could be heard from as far as a thousand yojanas, like the sound of an earthquake.

Then Māra the Devaputta, having mounted his elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, manifested a thousand arms and seized various weapons. As for the rest of Māra’s retinue...
There were no two people who were alike, nor did they take up identical weapons.
Appearing in various colors and with various facial expressions, they approached, overwhelming the Bodhisatta while taking up diverse weapons.
However, the devas of ten thousand world-systems stood praising the Mahāsatta, and Sakka, the king of the gods, [did likewise].
He stood blowing his conch shell, the Vijayuttara. It is said that this conch was one hundred and twenty cubits long;
once it had caught the wind and was blown, it would continue to sound for four months before becoming silent.
The Great Black Naga King stood there, praising [the Buddha] with more than a hundred verses, while Mahābrahmā held a white parasol over him.
He stood there. But when the hosts of Māra approached the seat of enlightenment, not even one among them was able to remain;

they fled from their very positions face-to-face. Even the Nāga king named Kāḷa submerged into the earth and went to his own Nāga abode, Mañjerika, five hundred yojanas away, where he lay down covering his face with both hands. Sakka, the king of the gods, [took] the conch Vijayuttara...
Placing it on his back, he stood upon the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*); Mahābrahmā, taking hold of the white parasol by its tip, departed for the Brahma-world itself.
Not even a single deity was able to remain there. The Great Man, however, sat all alone.
Māra also said to his own retinue: "Sirs, there is no other man equal to Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana."
“There is no way out; we will not be able to give battle face-to-face, so we shall do so from the rear.
The Great Being, too, looked toward the three sides and saw that they were empty because all the deities had fled.
Then, seeing Māra’s army overwhelming him from the northern side, he thought: “This entire host is directed against me alone.”
He makes a great effort, thinking: "In this place I have no mother, father, brother, or any other relative;
rather, these ten perfections alone are like a family long nurtured by me.
Therefore, making the perfections my army and striking with the very essence of the perfections, I shall destroy this host."
"It is fitting," he said, and sat down while reflecting upon the ten perfections (*pāramī*).
Then Māra, the son of the gods, thinking, "I shall blow Siddhattha away with the wind alone," unleashed a whirlwind.
At that very moment, winds of various kinds—eastern and the rest—arose, measuring half a league, one league, two leagues, and three leagues in extent.

Though they were capable of splitting mountain peaks, uprooting forests, thickets, and trees, and reducing villages and towns on all sides to dust and ashes, their power was neutralized by the majesty of the Great Being’s merit;
upon reaching the Bodhisatta, they were unable to move even the hem of his robe. Then—“With water we shall [wash] him...”
Thinking, "I shall kill him by overwhelming him," he raised a great rain. By its power, clouds consisting of layers of hundreds and thousands of layers arose one above the other and rained down.
Due to the force of the torrential downpour, the earth became perforated here and there.
Yet, although the great cloud approached from above the forest trees and such, it was unable to moisten even as much as a drop of dew upon the Great Being’s robe.
He was unable [to harm him]. Thereupon, he raised a rain of stones.
Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the air and, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, were transformed into divine garlands and bouquets.
Then, he raised a rain of weapons: single-edged swords, double-edged swords, spears, javelins, and so forth, all smoking...
Blazing, they came through the air and, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, became divine flowers.
Then he raised a rain of embers; embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers came through the air and, having become divine flowers, scattered at the feet of the Bodhisatta.
Then he raised a rain of hot ashes; extremely hot, fire-colored ashes came through the air and—
It fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta as sandalwood powder. Then it raised a shower of sand;
the exceedingly fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the air and fell at the feet of the Great Being as celestial flowers.
Then it raised a shower of mud; that mud, smoking and blazing—
Having come through the air, it fell at the Bodhisatta’s feet as divine ointment.

Then, thinking, "By frightening him with this, I will cause Siddhattha to flee," he conjured up darkness. That darkness, possessing the four characteristics, became a great gloom like pitch-black night;
but upon reaching the Bodhisatta, it vanished like darkness struck down by the radiance of the sun.

Thus, when Māra was unable to frighten the Bodhisatta away by means of these nine showers—of wind, rain, stones, clubs, glowing embers, hot sand, mud, darkness, and thunder—he commanded his own host, saying, "Hey! What are you waiting for?
Seize this Prince Siddhattha, kill him, drive him away! and he himself mounted the elephant Girimekhala.
Seated upon his shoulders and taking up his discus weapon, Māra approached the Bodhisatta and said, "Siddhattha, rise from this couch! This does not belong to you; it belongs to me.

Having heard his words, the Great Being replied, "Māra, neither have you fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs), nor the secondary perfections (upapāramīs), nor the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs)."

"Nor were the five great renunciations performed by you; nor was the conduct for the welfare of relatives fulfilled, nor the conduct for the welfare of the world, nor the conduct for the welfare of Buddhahood.
All those were fulfilled by me alone. Therefore, this couch does not belong to you; it belongs to me alone.
Enraged and unable to endure the force of his anger, Māra discharged the discus-weapon at the Great Being. It struck him—his ten...
As he was reflecting upon the perfections (*pāramitā*), that wheel-weapon with a razor-sharp edge—
which on other occasions, when released by an angry man, would pass through solid stone pillars as if they were bamboo reeds— stood above him transformed into a canopy of garlands.
Now, while it stood there as a floral canopy, the rest of Māra’s assembly thought, "Now Siddhattha..."
“Having risen from his cross-legged seat, he will flee! they hurled down massive mountain peaks;
yet, as the Great Being brought to mind the ten perfections (*pāramī*), those peaks turned into bouquets of flowers and fell upon the ground.
Devas standing at the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) stretched out their necks, raised their heads, and cried: “Alas, he is lost! Alas, he is ruined!”
"O, what indeed will he do with this physical form of Prince Siddhattha, which has reached the pinnacle of beauty?"—thus they gazed upon him.
Then the Bodhisatta said, "The seat upon which Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections sit when the day of their awakening arrives, now falls to me," and addressed Mara standing there:
"Mara, who is the witness to the fact that you have given gifts?"
Māra thought, “These people alone are my witnesses,” and extended his hand toward the host of Māra’s forces.
At that moment, the sound arising from Māra’s assembly crying out, “I am a witness! I am a witness! was like the roar of the earth-shaking earthquake.
Then Māra said to the Great Being: “Siddhattha, who is your witness to the fact that you have given alms?”
The Great Being said: "As for your gift, there are sentient beings who can bear witness to its having been given;
however, in this present state of mine, there is no sentient being whatsoever who can act as a witness.

Let alone my gifts given in all other successive existences—even regarding the giving of the great gift of the seven hundred in my Vessantara existence, though it was insentient [matter], it was indeed given."
“This solid great earth is my witness,” he said, and extending his right hand from within his robe-chamber,

he stretched it out toward the great earth, saying, “In my existence as Vessantara, were you or were you not a witness to the giving of my great gift of seven hundred? The great earth replied, “I was your witness at that time.”
It roared as if trampling the host of Māra with ten, a hundred, a thousand, and a hundred thousand roars. Then,
while the Great Being was reflecting upon the Vessantara gift, thinking, "Siddhattha, you have given a great gift,
a supreme gift," the elephant Girimekhala, measuring one hundred and fifty yojanas, knelt upon the earth with his knees.
Māra’s retinue fled in every direction and intermediate quarter; there was not even two who went by the same path.
Casting off their head-ornaments and their lower garments, they fled in all directions, right before his very eyes.
Then, seeing Māra’s army fleeing, the hosts of devas exclaimed, "Victory has been won by Māra; defeat has come to Prince Siddhattha!"
“Let us perform a victory-offering! Thus the deities proclaimed to the deities, the nāgas to the nāgas, the supaṇṇas to the supaṇṇas, and the brahmas to the brahmas.
With perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, they approached the Great Man at the seat of enlightenment.
Now, when they had thus departed—
“Victory indeed belongs to the glorious Buddha, and defeat to Māra the Evil One!
Thus did the hosts of gods, filled with joy, proclaim the victory of the Great Seer at the seat of enlightenment.
“Victory indeed belongs to the glorious Buddha, and defeat to Māra the Evil One!”
Delighted, the hosts of nāgas then proclaimed victory for the Great Sage at the seat of enlightenment:
“This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha and the defeat of Māra, the Evil One.
Delighted, the throngs of supaṇṇas also proclaimed victory for the Great Sage at the seat of enlightenment.
“Victory indeed belongs to the Glorious Buddha, and defeat to Māra the Evil One!
Thus did the hosts of Brahmās, filled with joy, proclaim the victory to the Great Seer at the seat of enlightenment.
The remaining deities in the ten thousand world-systems, honoring him with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, [offered] various kinds [of worship].
And they stood praising him with hymns. While the sun was still shining, the Great Being,
having shattered the host of Māra and being honored as if by coral petals falling from the Bodhi tree onto his robe,
recollecting his past lives during the first watch, purifying the divine eye during the middle watch, and [contemplating] dependent origination during the last watch—

He applied his knowledge. Then, as he was comprehending the twelvefold formula of dependent origination in its forward and reverse order according to the cycle of existence and its cessation, the ten-thousandfold world-system, bounded by the waters, shook twelve times.
Having caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to resound, at the time of sunrise, the Great Being attained omniscience.
As he penetrated [this realization], the entire ten-thousandfold world system became adorned and prepared.
The banners and flags raised at the eastern rim of the world-system struck against the western rim of the world-system;
likewise, the banners and flags raised at the western rim of the world-system struck against the eastern rim of the world-system; and at the southern rim of the world-system...
The banners and flags raised on the northern rim of the world-sphere struck the eastern rim of the world-sphere;
the banners and flags raised on the eastern rim of the world-sphere struck the southern rim of the world-sphere;
the banners and flags raised upon the surface of the earth stood reaching as far as the Brahma-world; and the banners and flags fastened in the Brahma-world...

They were established upon the surface of the earth; in the ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), flowering trees burst into bloom, and fruit-bearing trees became laden with heavy clusters of fruit.
Lotus flowers blossomed from the trunks, lotus flowers from the branches, lotus flowers from the creepers, and hanging lotus flowers appeared in the sky, even from solid stone surfaces.
Having split open, they rose up as *daṇḍaka-paduma* lotuses with a hundred petals each, one upon another.
The ten-thousandfold world system became strewn with flowers like a loose cluster of garlands or like a well-spread carpet of blossoms.

Even within the intervals between the world-systems, the eight thousand *yojanas* of the Lokantarika hells—which had never before been illuminated even by the radiance of seven suns—[were filled with light].
At that time, all things became one in radiance. The great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, became sweet water;
rivers ceased to flow. Those blind from birth saw forms; those deaf from birth heard sounds;
those who were cripples from birth walked on their own feet; and fetters and bonds were severed and fell away.

Thus, being honored with immeasurable splendor and majesty, and when manifold kinds of wonderful phenomena had appeared, the Great Being, having realized omniscience, uttered this inspired utterance never abandoned by all Buddhas:
“Through many births in saṃsāra I have wandered without finding rest,
seeking the builder of the house, for birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the state of disintegration; it has attained the destruction of craving.”

Thus, from the Tusita heaven up until this attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this extent of the narrative should be understood as the "Not-Remote Origin" (avidūrenidāna).
The Discourse on the Not-Remote Origin is concluded.
3. The Discourse on the Near Origin (santikenidāna).

"Regarding the introduction (*nidāna*), however, it is said: 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery,' and likewise, 'He was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall'—it is found thus in each respective location.
Although this has been stated, nevertheless, even that [introduction] should be recited from the very beginning as follows:
It should be understood as follows: after uttering this inspired utterance (*udāna*), it occurred to the Blessed One as he sat upon the victory throne (*jayapallaṅka*):
"For four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons, I have run about for the sake of this throne;
for so long a time, for the sake of this very throne, I have given away my head, adorned with ornaments, by cutting it from my neck."

“His well-anointed eyes and even the flesh of his heart were torn out and given away; sons like Prince Jālī, daughters like Princess Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Queen Maddī were surrendered by him for the sake of others’ service. This is my couch, the couch of victory, the firm couch;
while seated here, my resolves have been fulfilled, and I shall not rise from this until they are so.”
Entering into many hundreds of thousands of millions of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he sat right there for seven days.
It was with reference to this that it was said: “Then the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then, some deities thought: “Surely there is still some duty to be performed by Siddhattha; for he remains in the cross-legged posture...”
The thought arose: "He does not abandon the *ālaya*. Knowing the deities' reflection, the Teacher rose into the air to still their thoughts and displayed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
For he had previously displayed the miracle at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*), the miracle at the assembly of kinsmen, and the miracle at the assembly of Pāṭikaputta.
Everything was just like the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree.
Thus, having stilled the thoughts of the deities by means of this miracle, the Teacher rose from his cross-legged seat, stood slightly to the north-eastern side of the seat, and said:
"On this very seat, indeed, omniscience was realized by me. Then he [performed] the four...

Gazing with unblinking eyes at the seat where he had attained power through the fulfillment of perfections over incalculable hundreds of thousands of eons, as well as at the Bodhi tree, he spent seven days;
that place became known as the Animisa Cetiya. Then the Teacher established a walking path between the seat and the spot where he stood.
He spent seven days walking back and forth upon a jeweled walkway extending from east to west;
that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya.
On the fourth week, however, deities constructed a jeweled hall to the north-west of the Bodhi tree.
There, the Blessed One sat cross-legged and spent seven days discerning the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and specifically the *Anantanaya-Samantapaṭṭhāna* within it.
However, the masters of the Abhidhamma say: "The so-called 'Jewel House' (*Ratanaghara*) is not a house made of the seven precious gems;
rather, the place where the seven treatises were contemplated is called the 'Jewel House. For...
In this regard, both these explanations are applicable; therefore, both should indeed be accepted.
From that point on, that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya.
Thus, having spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, on the fifth week the Teacher approached the Ajapāla Nigrodha from the foot of the Bodhi tree.
There too, he sat down, investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.
At that time, Māra the Evil One, thinking, "Though I have followed him for so long, seeking an opening, I have seen no lapse in him;
now he has escaped from my power," became despondent and sat down by the great road.
Reflecting upon the sixteen causes, he drew sixteen lines upon the ground: "I did not fulfill the perfection of giving as this man did;
therefore, I was not born equal to him"—thus he drew one line. Likewise: "I did not fulfill the perfection of virtue...
[and so on] ...the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience... [he drew another line for each].
“I did not fulfill the perfection of truth, the perfection of resolve, the perfection of loving-kindness, and the perfection of equanimity;
therefore, I was not born equal to him. Thus he drew out the tenth letter. Likewise:
“I did not fulfill the ten perfections that serve as the necessary support for the penetration of the unique knowledge of the degrees of others’ faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*), as he did.”
"Therefore, I was not born equal to him," he said, drawing forth the eleventh letter. Likewise:

"Like him, I did not fulfill the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) which serve as the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the penetration of the uncommon knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*), ... [and so on] ... the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya-ñāṇa*), the unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*); therefore, I..."
“None such as he has ever been born,” he drew the sixteenth line. Thus Māra, having drawn sixteen lines upon the great highway for these reasons, sat down.
And at that time, the three daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā—thought, “Our father is not to be seen.”
“Where indeed is he now? As they looked about, they saw him sitting there, overcome with dejection, scratching the ground.
Going to their father’s presence, they asked, “Father, why are you so distressed and dejected?
He replied, “Daughters, this Great Ascetic has escaped my power; for all this time I have been watching to find an opening against him.”
“I was unable; therefore, I am suffering and dejected.
“If that is so, do not worry,” they said, “we shall bring him under our own control and take him away. “It is impossible, mothers;
this man cannot be brought under anyone’s control, for he is established in unshakable faith. “Dear son, we are women; right now, with the snares of passion—”
“Having bound him, we shall bring him; you need not worry,” they said, and having approached the Blessed One, they said, “O ascetic, let us serve at your feet.
The Blessed One paid no heed to their words, nor did he open his eyes to look at them;
experiencing only the bliss of seclusion in the unsurpassed liberation through the destruction of the substrata of existence, he sat there.
Again, the daughters of Māra thought, "The inclinations of men are indeed diverse:
some have affection for girls, some for those in the first stage of life, some for those in the middle stage of life, and some for those in the final stage of life.
What if we were to entice him with various forms and capture him? Thus, each one assumed the appearance of a young girl and so forth.

Each having manifested her own individual form, they became young maidens, those who had not yet borne children, those who had borne once, those who had borne twice, middle-aged women, and elderly women;
having approached the Blessed One six times, they said, "O ascetic, let us serve your feet.
Yet the Blessed One paid no heed to them, as he was liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata of existence (*upadhi*). Some...
Other teachers say: "When the Blessed One saw that they had approached in the form of great female elephants, he resolved:
'Let these have broken teeth and grey hair. That should not be accepted; for the Blessed One did not make such a resolution.
Rather, the Blessed One said: "Go away! Having seen what do you strive thus? Such a thing as this [is not for those] who are not free from lust and so forth."
"It is fitting to place [the Tathāgata] at the forefront. For the Tathāgata, lust has been abandoned, hatred has been abandoned, and delusion has been abandoned.
Referring to his own abandonment of the defilements, he said:
"He whose victory is never lost, whose victory no one in the world can undo—"
“By what track can you lead that Buddha of infinite range, who is trackless?
For him, the ensnaring and clinging craving that leads one anywhere no longer exists—
by what track can you lead that Buddha of infinite range, who is trackless?”

While reciting these two verses from the *Buddhavaṅga* of the *Dhammapada*, he taught the Dhamma. Upon hearing them, they said, "It seems our father spoke the truth: 'The Arhat, the Sugata, is in the world; he cannot be led astray by passion,'" and so forth, and they returned to their father's presence.
The Blessed One, having spent seven days right there, then went to the foot of the Mucalinda tree.
There, when a seven-day storm arose, for the sake of warding off the cold and other discomforts, the Naga king named Mucalinda [shielded him] with his coils seven times.

Having spent seven days in the Perfumed Chamber—which was surrounded for his own comfort—experiencing the bliss of liberation as if dwelling there, he approached the Rājāyatana tree; and there too, experiencing the very same bliss of liberation, he spent another seven days.
At this point, the seven weeks were completed. During this interval, he did not even wash his face.
There was no tending of the body, nor was there any need for food; he passed the time solely through the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of the fruit [of Arahantship].
Then, on the forty-ninth day, at the end of those seven weeks, as he sat there, the thought arose in him, "I shall wash my face.
Sakka, the lord of the devas, brought and gave him *agada* (medicine) and *harītaka* (myrobalan), and the Teacher—
He consumed it, and because of that, his body became covered in excrement.

Then Sakka himself provided him with a *nāgalatā* tooth-stick and water for rinsing his mouth. The Teacher chewed that tooth-stick, rinsed his mouth with the water from Lake Anotatta, and sat down right there at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.
At that time, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling from the country of Ukkala to the Middle Country with five hundred carts,
were stopped by a deity who had previously been their own kinswoman and blood relative;
encouraged by her to provide food for the Teacher, they took some parched grain and honey-cakes and said, "May he accept from us..."
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this food out of compassion,” they said, and having offered it to the Teacher, they stood by.
On that very day of receiving the milk-rice, because his bowl had vanished, the Blessed One thought, “Tathāgatas do not receive food in their hands; in what, then, shall I receive it?
Then, knowing his mind, four [deities] from the four directions...
The Great Kings offered bowls made of sapphire, but the Blessed One declined them. Again, they offered four bowls made of emerald-colored stone.
To preserve the faith of all four Great Kings, the Blessed One accepted all four bowls, stacked them one upon another, and resolved: "Let there be one. Thus, all four became a single bowl at the rim.
Becoming visible lines, they attained unity with a medium-sized measure.
The Blessed One, having accepted food in that excellent stone bowl and having partaken of it, gave a blessing of thanksgiving.
Those two brothers, the merchants, went for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma and became lay followers by the formula of the two refuges. Then, [the Blessed One said] to them: "One..."
Saying, “No, venerable sir, please give us a portion to be venerated,” they touched their own heads with their right hands and gave him the hair-relics.
They placed those relics inside a golden casket in their own city and established a shrine over them.
The Perfectly Enlightened One, having emerged from that state, went once more to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree and sat down at its foot.

Then, as soon as he was seated there, while reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, the habitual tendency common to all Buddhas arose in him—the inclination not to teach others, thinking: "This Dhamma has been attained by me with great difficulty."
The thought arose [in the Blessed One]. Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, "Alas, the world is perishing!
Alas, the world is being destroyed!", took with him the Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Nimmānarati, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmās from ten thousand world-systems and approached the Teacher.
He requested the teaching of the Dhamma in this manner, beginning with the words: "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma."
The Teacher, having given him his consent and reflecting, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
formed the thought, "Āḷāra is wise; he will quickly understand this Dhamma.
Looking further, however, he perceived that Āḷāra had died seven days prior and directed his attention to Uddaka. He likewise perceived that Uddaka had died the previous evening.
Knowing, "The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me," he directed his attention toward them and, reflecting, "Where are they dwelling now?
he perceived that they were at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī.
Having stayed for a few days wandering for alms in the vicinity of the Seat of Enlightenment, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha—
"Having gone to Bārāṇasī, I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
Thus, on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, rising at dawn during the early morning hours, he took his bowl and robe and set out upon the eighteen-yojana journey.
On the way, he encountered an Ājīvika named Upaka; having declared to him his state as a Buddha, on that very day—
In the evening, he arrived at Isipatana.
When the group of five monks saw the Tathāgata approaching from afar, they said, "Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama, who has turned back to a life of abundance in requisites;
he is coming with a full body, his faculties refreshed, and possessing a golden complexion. [We should not pay him homage, etc.]”
“We will not do so; however, as he is born of a great family, he deserves the offering of a seat. Therefore, we shall prepare a mere seat for him.

Thus they made an agreement. Then the Blessed One, having reflected with his knowledge—which is capable of knowing the mental conduct of the world including its devas—“What indeed are these people thinking? he understood their thoughts. Then, among all those gods and humans...
Having condensed his loving-kindness—which was capable of pervading in an unspecified manner—he pervaded them with loving-kindness in a specified manner.
Touched by the Blessed One’s loving-kindness, they were unable to maintain their agreement when the Tathāgata approached;
they went out to meet him and performed all the customary duties, such as prostrating and so forth. [They recognized] his state as a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
Since they did not know him, they addressed him merely by name and with the term "friend" (āyuṣmān).
