Then the Blessed One, making known his own state as a Buddha by saying, "Bhikkhus, do not address the Tathāgata by name or with the term 'friend.
Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One," sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.
Seated while the constellation Uttarāsāḷha was in conjunction, surrounded by eighteen koṭis of Brahmas,

he addressed the five bhikkhus of the group and taught the unsurpassed Discourse on the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, which has three turnings and twelve aspects and manifests six types of knowledge.
Among them, the Elder Koṇḍañña, directing his knowledge according to the course of the teaching, [attained it] at the conclusion of the sutta— by means of the eighteen...
Together with ten million Brahmās, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
The Teacher, having entered the rains retreat right there, sat in the monastery itself on the following day while instructing the Elder Vappa; the other four [disciples] went out for alms.
The Elder Vappa attained the fruit of stream-entry that very morning. By this same method, on the next day, [he instructed] the Elder Bhaddiya.
On the following day he established Mahānāma Thera in the fruit of stream-entry; on the next day, Assaji Thera.
Having thus established all five elders in the fruit of stream-entry, on the fifth day of the fortnight, he assembled all five elders and taught them the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all five elders were established in Arahatship. Then the Teacher [considered] the spiritual predisposition (*upanissaya*) of the young man Yasa.
Seeing him depart from his home in the middle of the night out of world-weariness, she called out to him, "Come, Yasa!
On that very same night, she established him in the fruit of stream-entry, and on the following day, she established him in Arahatship;
furthermore, she ordained his fifty-four companions through the "Come, monk" formula and led them to Arahatship.

Thus, when sixty-one arhats had been born in the world, the Teacher, having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, sent sixty bhikkhus in various directions with the words, "Go forth on tour, bhikkhus," while he himself went toward Uruvelā.
On the way, in a cottonwood forest grove, he disciplined thirty young men of the Bhaddavaggiya group.
Among them, the last to attain realization became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the foremost became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

He became [the Buddha]. Having ordained all of them by the mere utterance of "Come, monk," he sent them out in various directions. Then, going to Uruvelā, he displayed one thousand four hundred miracles.
Having converted the three brothers, the Jaṭilas, along with their thousand followers led by Uruvelakassapa, he ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula.
Seating them at Gayāsīsa, he established them in Arahatship through the teaching of the "Discourse on the Burning" (Ādittapariyāya). By that...
Surrounded by a thousand arahants, [the Buddha] went to the Laṭṭhivana grove on the outskirts of the city of Rājagaha, thinking,

"I shall release King Bimbisāra from his promise. When the king heard from the park-keeper that "the Teacher has arrived," he approached the Teacher accompanied by twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders, beneath a golden canopy with a variegated wheel-patterned floor.
As they were emitting a radiance like that of a mass of light, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and sat down to one side together with the assembly.
Then, this thought occurred to those brahmins and householders: "What now is the reason that the Great Ascetic [is acting thus] toward Uruvelakassapa?"

“Is it you who are living the holy life, or is it Uruvela Kassapa who lives the holy life under the Great Ascetic? The Blessed One, knowing the thoughts in their minds with his own mind, addressed Uruvela Kassapa in verse:
“What did you see, O dweller of Uruvela, that you, called ‘the emaciated one,’ abandoned the sacrificial fire?”
“I ask you this matter, Kassapa: how has your fire-sacrifice been abandoned?
The Elder, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, replied:
“Sacrifices proclaim forms, sounds, tastes, and women who are desired.”
"Having known this impurity in acquisitions (*upadhi*), therefore he did not delight in sacrifice or offering.

Having spoken this verse, for the purpose of declaring his status as a disciple, he placed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple," and then [clapped] once, twice, and thrice.
Having ascended into the air seven times to the height of seventy palm trees and then descended, he paid homage to the Tathāgata and sat down to one side.
Seeing that miracle, the great multitude exclaimed, "Oh, how majestic are the Buddhas!
For even Uruvelakassapa—who was considered an 'Arahat' by those with such deeply rooted views—has broken through the net of his own dogmatic beliefs."
He spoke only of the Teacher’s virtues, saying, "The Tathāgata has tamed him. The Blessed One said, "It is not only now that I tame Uruvelakassapa;
in the past, too, he was tamed by me. Having spoken thus, on this occasion of the arising of the matter, he related the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka and proclaimed the Four Truths.
Together with eleven hundred thousand followers, the king attained the fruit of stream-entry.
He established himself [in the refuges] and declared his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by the tens of thousands.

While still seated in the presence of the Teacher, the king proclaimed the five assurances, went for refuge, and having invited [the Buddha] for the following day, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One, and departed.
On the following day, all the inhabitants of Rājagaha—both those who had seen the Blessed One the previous day and those who had not—[assembled].
Eighteen koṭis of people, desiring to see the Tathāgata, departed from Rājagaha early in the morning for the Laṭṭhivana Grove.
The road, though three gavutas long, was insufficient; the entire Laṭṭhivana Grove became packed without any space between them.
Although the great multitude beheld the Blessed One’s physical form, which had attained the pinnacle of beauty, they were unable to reach satiety.

This is called the "Ground of Praise" (*vaṇṇabhūmi*). For in such places, all the splendor of the Blessed One’s form-body (*rūpakāya*), distinguished by the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), should be described.

Thus, when the great multitude, beholding the body of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*) which had attained the pinnacle of physical beauty, crowded the pleasure grove and the path of travel without interval, there was not even space for a single monk to exit.
It did not happen. It is said that on that day the Blessed One’s meal might have been interrupted; therefore, thinking, "Let it not be so," Sakka manifested a sign of heat upon his own seat.

Sakka, reflecting and understanding the reason for this, assumed the form of a young brahmin and stood before the One of Ten Powers, uttering praises connected with the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Having descended by means of his divine power and made way for himself,
the Blessed One— tamed together with those tamed, formerly matted-hair ascetics, and liberated together with those liberated—
entered Rājagaha, he who has the color of refined gold.
“Freed by those who are freed...
[as before] ...Crossed over by those who have crossed over...
[as before] ...Peaceful with those who are peaceful... Thus the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.
“Ten-dwelling, ten-powered, knower of the ten dharmas, endowed with the ten [virtues];
surrounded by a retinue of a thousand, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.
Speaking these verses in praise of the Teacher, he walked ahead. At that time, the great multitude [beheld] the young man’s beauty and splendor...

Seeing him, he thought, "How exceedingly handsome this young man is! Indeed, I have never seen anyone like him before," and he asked, "Where has this young man come from, or whose is he? Hearing this, the young man said:
"The wise one who is self-controlled in every way, pure, and peerless..."
“The Arahant, the Sugata, is in the world; I am his attendant,” he said, reciting this verse.
Having followed the path prepared by Sakka, the Teacher entered Rājagaha surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus.
After the king had given a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he said: “Venerable sir, without the Three Jewels...”
"I shall not be able to stay [there]; I will come to the presence of the Blessed One at any time, whether it be the right time or not.
Furthermore, the Laṭṭhivana grove is very far away, but this Veḷuvana grove of ours is neither too far nor too near; it is a lodging fit for a Buddha, with easy access for coming and going.
May the Blessed One, O Venerable Sir, accept this from me," he said, pouring water from a golden pitcher.
Taking water scented with flowers and fragrances that was the color of a jewel, he poured it into the hand of the One Possessing Ten Powers while dedicating the Veḷuvana monastery.
At the very moment that the monastery was accepted, the great earth shook, as if to signify: "The roots of the Buddha’s dispensation have taken hold.
Indeed, apart from Veḷuvana, there was no other place on the surface of Jambudīpa that had caused the great earth to tremble.
There was no other dwelling place that had been taken up by shaking the earth even in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, except for the Mahāvihāra.
Having accepted the Veḷuvana monastery and offered words of thanksgiving to the king,
the Teacher rose from his seat and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to Veḷuvana.
At that time, two wanderers named Sāriputta and Moggallāna were living near Rājagaha, seeking the Deathless.
Among them, Sāriputta, seeing the Elder Assaji entering for alms, approached him with a devout heart;
having paid his respects and heard the verse beginning with "Those phenomena that arise from a cause," he attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having established himself, he recited that same verse to his companion Moggallāna as well. He too was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Both of them, having looked toward Sañjaya, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One together with their own retinues.
Among them, Moggallāna attained arahantship in seven days, and Sāriputta in half a month. Both of them...
The Teacher established them in the position of chief disciples. On the very day that the Elder Sāriputta attained Arahatship, he convened a great assembly.
While the Tathāgata was dwelling in that same Veḷuvana Monastery, King Suddhodana heard:
"My son, it is said, having practiced austerities for six years and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, has now set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma."
Having heard that [the Buddha] was dwelling at Veḷuvana in dependence on Rājagaha, he addressed a certain minister:
"Come, my good man; go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and, speaking in my name, say: 'Your father, the Great King Suddhodana, desires to see you.
Then, taking my son, return. He replied, "So be it, Your Majesty," and accepted the king's command.
Having accepted [the message] with his head, surrounded by a thousand men,
he quickly traveled the sixty-yojana road and entered the monastery at the time of the Teacher’s preaching of the Dhamma while the Dasabala was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking,
"Let the message sent by the king wait for now," he stood at the edge of the assembly and, having heard the Teacher’s preaching of the Dhamma, remained exactly where he was.
Having attained arahantship together with a thousand men, he requested the going forth. The Blessed One extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became as if sixty-year-old elders, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power.
For from the moment one attains arahantship, those known as Noble Ones (ariya) remain ever equanimous.

He did not deliver the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers. The king, thinking, "He neither goes nor does his message reach me," sent another minister with the same instruction, saying, "Come, my man, you go.
He too went and, having attained Arahatship together with his retinue in the same manner as before, remained silent. Again the king said, "Come..."
“Go, sir! Go, sir! In this very manner, he dispatched seven other ministers as well.
All nine ministers, each accompanied by a retinue of nine thousand men, completed their respective duties and remained right there in silence.
Since the king could not find anyone even to bring back a mere message or report it to him, he thought: “Even so many people [have failed me] regarding me...”
"Because they lacked affection, they did not accept even my teaching; who indeed will carry out my instruction?
Looking over the entire royal force, he saw Kāḷudāyin. It is said that he was the king’s chief minister, a confidant who accomplished all his purposes, and an exceedingly trusted counselor;
he had been born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, was his playmate from childhood, and a close friend.
Then the king addressed him: "Dear Kāḷudāyi, desiring to see my son, I dispatched nine thousand men and nine ministers;
yet not even one among them has returned to report so much as a message.
Indeed, the threat to my life is difficult to foresee, and I wish to see my son while I still live. Will you be able to do so?"
“Show me my son. “I shall be able to do so, Your Majesty, if I am permitted to go forth,” he replied.
“Dear son, whether you have gone forth or not, show me my son. Saying, “Very well, Your Majesty,” he took the king’s message and went to Rājagaha;
standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s time for preaching the Dhamma, he listened to the Dhamma.
Having heard this, he and his retinue attained arahantship, went forth by means of the "Come, monk" formula, and lived there.
After the Teacher had become a Buddha, having spent his first rains retreat at Isipatana, and having completed the rains and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he went to Uruvelā.
While staying there for three months, he converted the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics; then, surrounded by a thousand monks, on the full moon day of the month of Phussa—
Having gone to Rājagaha, he dwelt there for two months. At that point, five months had elapsed since his departure from Bārāṇasī, and the entire winter season had passed.
Seven or eight days had already gone by since the day the Elder Kāḷudāyī arrived.
On the full moon day of the month of Phagguṇa, the Elder reflected: "The winter has now passed; the spring season has arrived."
"Men have harvested the crops and cleared the roads at every turn;
the earth is covered with green grass, the forest groves are in full bloom, and the paths are fit for travel. It is time for the One of Ten Powers to perform an act of kinship.
Then, having approached the Blessed One—
“Now the trees, O Blessed One, are like glowing coals, having shed their foliage and bearing fruit;
they shine forth as if possessed of flames. This is the season, Great Hero, when the juices abound...
[etc. ...It is neither too cold nor too hot, nor is there excessive famine or drought.”
“The ground is green with young grass; this is the time, Great Sage!
Thus, with about sixty verses, he praised the journey to the Teacher’s native city.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Udāyi, why are you praising the journey with such a sweet voice? [Udāyi replied: “It is for you, Bhante...”
“Your father, the great king Suddhodana, desires to see you; show hospitality to your kinsmen.
“Very well, Udāyin, I shall show hospitality to my kinsmen. Announce this to the community of monks, so that they may fulfill the duties of those traveling.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the Elder announced it to them.

The Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted—ten thousand from among the noble sons dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha, and ten thousand from among those dwelling in Kapilavatthu—departed from Rājagaha and traveled a league day after day.
From Rājagaha, it was sixty leagues to Kapilavatthu; he reached it in two months.

"I shall reach him," he thought, and set out on his journey with unhurried pace. The Elder, thinking, "I will inform the king that the Blessed One has departed," rose into the air and appeared within the king's palace. Upon seeing the Elder, the king was filled with joy;
he had him seated upon a magnificent couch, filled the bowl with various choice delicacies from his own prepared meal, and presented it to him.
The Elder rose and made as if to depart. “Sit down and eat, dear one,” [the king said].
“I shall eat after going into the presence of the Teacher, Great King. “But where is the Teacher, dear one?
“He has set out on a journey, Great King, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, for the purpose of seeing you. With a joyful heart, the king said: “You...”
“Having consumed this, until my son reaches this city, provide him with almsfood from right here,” he said.

The Elder consented. After the king had served the Elder, he rubbed the bowl with fragrant powder, filled it with the finest food, and placing it in the Elder’s hand, said, “Give this to the Tathāgata.”
While everyone was looking on, the Elder threw his alms-bowl into the air;
he himself ascended into the sky, brought back the alms-food, and placed it in the Teacher’s hand. The Teacher consumed it.
By this very means, the Elder brought alms-food day after day. The Teacher, meanwhile, consumed the alms-food of the king himself along the way.
At the conclusion of his meal, the Elder also, day after day, spoke of the Buddha’s qualities—saying, "Today the Blessed One came this far;
today he came that far"—and thus caused the entire royal household to conceive faith in the Teacher even without having seen him.
For this very reason, the Blessed One declared of him: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus, this is the foremost..."
He placed Kāḷudāyī at the foremost position among those who inspire confidence in families.
When the Sākiyas arrived, thinking, "We shall see our most excellent kinsman," they gathered together;
while searching for a place for the Blessed One to stay, they observed that the Nigrodha Sāka’s park was delightful.
There, having performed all the rites of reception, they went out to meet him with perfumes and flowers in their hands;
first they sent forth the youngest city boys and girls adorned with every ornament,
then the princes and princesses, and immediately after them, [the King himself] while personally worshipping with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Taking the Blessed One with them, they went to the Nigrodha Monastery.

There, the Blessed One sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed. The Sakyans, being of a proud nature and stiff with pride, thought, "Prince Siddhattha is younger than we;
he is our junior, our nephew, our son, and our grandson," and so they [seated him] according to their seniority.
The princes said, “You pay homage; we shall sit behind you.
When they had sat down thus without paying homage, the Blessed One, observing their disposition, thought, “My kinsmen do not pay homage to me;
well now, I shall have them pay homage. He then entered the fourth jhāna, the basis for direct knowledge, and emerging from that, he—
Rising up into the sky, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, he performed a miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree similar to the Twin Miracle at the root of the Yaṃaka tree.

Having seen that marvel, the king said: "Venerable sir, even when I saw on the day of your birth that the soles of your feet had been turned upward and placed upon the head of the brahmin Kāla-deva for the purpose of paying him homage..."

"I paid homage at your feet; this was my first homage. And on the auspicious day of the Vappa festival, when you were reclining upon the couch of glory in the shade of the rose-apple tree, even after seeing that the shadow of the rose-apple tree did not shift, I paid homage at your feet; this was my second homage.
But now, having seen this unprecedented miracle, I [pay homage] at your feet."

“I pay homage; this is my third salutation. When the king had paid homage, not a single member of the Śākya clan was able to remain standing without bowing to the Blessed One; they all paid homage indeed.
Thus, having caused his kinsmen to pay homage, the Blessed One descended from the sky and sat upon the prepared seat. While the Blessed One was seated,
The gathering of kinsmen reached its conclusion; they all sat down with one-pointed minds.
Then a great cloud rained down a shower of lotus-like droplets. The copper-colored water flowed away below with a roar;

it drenched only those who wished to be drenched, while not even a single drop fell upon the bodies of those who did not wish to be drenched. Seeing this, they were all filled with a sense of wonder and amazement.
They broke out into the exclamation, “Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how marvelous! The Teacher thought, “It is not only now that a rain of lotuses falls upon my gathering of kinsmen;
it fell in the past as well. With this as the occasion for instruction, he related the Vessantara Jātaka.
Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, they all rose, paid homage, and departed. Not even a single king or royal minister remained.
Or, having said, "Come and take alms from us," he had not departed.
On the following day, the Teacher entered Kapilavatthu for alms, surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus.
No one went out to invite him, nor did anyone take his bowl. Standing right at the city gate, the Blessed One directed his attention inward.
“How indeed did the previous Buddhas wander for alms in their native towns?
Did they go to the houses of wealthy people out of order, or did they practice systematic wandering (sapadānacārika)? Then, seeing that not even a single Buddha had gone out of order, [he thought]:
“Now I too must uphold this very tradition of theirs, and in the future my disciples...”
"Training after me alone, they will fulfill the conduct of one who lives on alms.
Having said this, he went for alms in regular succession, starting from the house at the end of the street. "The noble Prince Siddhattha is indeed going for alms," people exclaimed;
and in palaces of two or three stories high, the great multitude opened their window-lattices and busied themselves with looking on.

The Queen, Rāhulamātā, thought: "It is said that my noble son, having wandered through this very city with great royal splendor in golden palanquins and the like, now has his hair and beard shaved off, wears saffron robes, and wanders for alms with a bowl in hand;
does he indeed shine? Opening the lion-window, she looked out and [beheld] the Blessed One, resplendent with various colors...
Having seen him shining with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha— illuminating the city streets with the radiance of his body, surrounded by the halo of his fathom-wide aura,
resplendent with the light of the eighty minor marks, and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—
he beheld him from the crown of his head down to the soles of his feet.
“With glossy, dark-blue, soft, and curly hair; with a forehead like the stainless surface of the sun; with a well-proportioned, high, and soft-featured nose;
a lion among men, radiant with a web of rays”—having thus praised him with these ten verses on the Lion Among Men, [he said]: “Your son is wandering for alms.”

He informed the king. With a heart deeply moved, the king, pulling at his upper garment with his hand, hurriedly went out, proceeded with speed, and standing before the Blessed One, said: "Venerable sir, why do you put us to shame?
For what purpose do you wander for alms? Do you think, 'It will not be possible to obtain food for so many bhikkhus'?"
“Did you form such a perception? “This is our family custom, Great King. “But, venerable sir, our lineage is the Kṣatriya lineage of Mahāsammata;
and herein, not even a single Kṣatriya is known as a mendicant wanderer.
“Great King, this so-called ‘Kṣatriya lineage’ is your lineage. But ours is: ‘Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña... [and so forth].”
"This is the lineage of Buddhas known as Kassapa.
Standing right there in the middle of the street, he said:
"Arise and do not be negligent; practice the Dhamma of good conduct."
“The practitioner of Dhamma dwells in happiness, both in this world and in the next.
Having spoken this verse, at its conclusion the king was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
“One should practice the Dhamma well-conducted; one should not practice what is ill-conducted.”

Having heard this verse: “The one who lives by the Dhamma dwells in happiness, both in this world and in the next,” he was established in the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmiphala*). Having heard the *Mahādhammapāla Jātaka*, he was established in the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
At the time of his death, while lying upon a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol, he attained *arahantship*.
Due to his dwelling in the forest, the king had no need for the practice of strenuous exertion.

Having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he took the Blessed One’s bowl and, having escorted the Blessed One together with his retinue up to the great palace, served him with excellent hard and soft foods.
At the conclusion of the meal, the entire harem came forward.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she set aside Rāhula’s mother.
Although her attendants told her, "Go, pay homage to the noble son," she replied, "If I possess any virtue, the noble son will come to me of his own accord;
I shall pay him homage only when he has arrived," and so she did not go.
The Blessed One had the king take his bowl and, together with his two chief disciples, went to the princess’s bedchamber.
Saying, "The princess may pay homage as she wishes; she is not to be told anything," he sat down on the prepared seat.
She came forward in haste, grasped his ankles, and resting her head upon the backs of his feet, [she paid homage] according to her desire.
She paid homage. The King spoke of the princess’s perfection of qualities, such as her affection and great respect for the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, when my daughter heard that you were wearing saffron robes, from then on she began to wear saffron robes herself.
When she heard of your practice of eating only one meal a day, she too began to eat only one meal a day. When she heard of your [abandonment of] large beds...”
“Having heard that her state had been abandoned, she lay down right there on the couch with its cloth coverlet.
Knowing that you had ceased using garlands, perfumes, and such, she herself became one who abstained from garlands and perfumes.

Even when her own kinsmen sent word saying, ‘We shall look after her,’ she did not look upon even a single relative. Thus endowed with virtues is my daughter, Bhante. “It is no wonder,” [the Buddha replied].
"Great King, this princess, now being protected by you, would protect herself once her wisdom has matured;
yet previously, while wandering at the foot of the mountain unprotected, she protected herself even though her wisdom was not yet mature.
Having said this, he related the Canda-Kinnarī Jātaka and, rising from his seat, departed.
On the following day, while the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s entry into his consecration hall and his marriage were taking place, [the Elder] went to his house.
Desiring to have the prince take up the alms-bowl and go forth into homelessness, he offered words of blessing, rose from his seat, and departed.
Seeing the prince leaving, Janapadakalyāṇī said, “Noble son, please return quickly.”
Having spoken thus, he craned his neck and looked back. Unable to bring himself to say to the Blessed One, "Take the bowl," he went back to the monastery itself.
Even though he was unwilling, the Blessed One ordained him. Thus, having gone to Kapilavatthu, the Blessed One ordained Nanda on the third day.
On the seventh day, Rāhula’s mother also had the prince adorned and sent him into the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
“Look, dear son, at this ascetic of golden complexion and the appearance of a Brahmā, surrounded by twenty thousand ascetics;
this is your father. Great treasures belonged to him, yet since the time of his departure, we have seen none of them.”
“Go and ask for your inheritance, saying: ‘Father, I am the prince; having received the consecration, I shall become a wheel-turning monarch.
I have need of wealth; give me wealth. For a son is the master of what belongs to his father.
And the prince, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One and received his father’s affection, with a joyful heart said, “May you have a pleasant shadow, O ascetic.”
He stood there speaking much more that was appropriate to himself. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and delivered a blessing, he rose from his seat and departed.
The prince followed after the Blessed One, saying, "Give me my inheritance, ascetic! Give me my inheritance, ascetic!
But the Blessed One did not make the prince turn back, nor did his retinue [persuade him].
He was unable to turn back the one who was going along with him. Thus, he went to the monastery together with the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One thought: "The wealth from his father’s estate that he desires is part of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and fraught with suffering;
well then, let me give him the sevenfold noble wealth (*ariyadhana*) obtained by me at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which is the supramundane inheritance."
“I shall make him my master,” he said, and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: “In that case, Sāriputta, let Rāhula go forth.
The Elder caused him to go forth. But when the prince had gone forth, an exceeding sorrow arose in the king;
unable to endure it, he approached the Blessed One and said: “It would be well, venerable sir, if the masters...”
He requested this boon: "May you not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father. The Blessed One granted him the boon;
then, on another day, having finished his meal at the royal residence, the King sat to one side and said:
"Venerable Sir, during the time when you were practicing austerities, a certain deity approached me and said, 'Your son has died.'"
When it was said, "Not believing her words, he rejected them, saying, 'My son does not die without having attained full enlightenment,'" [the Buddha remarked],
"Now what will you believe, you who previously did not believe even when your bones were shown to you and told,
'Your son is dead'? It was on this occasion that the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka was related.
He preached. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Thus, having established his father in the three fruits, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), returned once more to Rājagaha and dwelt in the Sītavana grove.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika [was traveling] with five hundred carts...
Taking his merchandise, he went to Rājagaha and approached the house of his own dear friend, the merchant.
There, having heard that the Buddha, the Blessed One, had appeared, he went to the Teacher at the break of dawn when the gate was opened through the power of the deities.
Having heard the Dhamma and established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), on the second day [he invited] the community headed by the Buddha...

Having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha and obtained the Teacher’s permission to return to Sāvatthī, he gave one hundred thousand pieces of money at every forty-five-yojana interval along the way, having monasteries built at each yojana.
Having purchased the Jeta Grove for eighteen crores of gold by covering it with ten million pieces of gold, he commenced the construction work. In the middle...
He had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) built for the One Possessing the Ten Powers; surrounding that, he provided separate dwellings for eighty great elders in a single settlement,
consisting of individual huts, double huts, circular haṃsavaṭṭaka-style buildings, long halls, short halls, pavilions, and so forth,
along with other lodgings such as lotus ponds, walking paths, night-quarters, and day-quarters— making a delightful place through a gift of eighteen koṭis.
Having caused a delightful monastery to be built on a piece of land, he dispatched a messenger for the sake of the arrival of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
Having heard his words, the Teacher departed from Rājagaha accompanied by a great community of monks and, traveling by stages, reached the city of Sāvatthī.
The Great Merchant, having prepared the festival for the monastery, [sent] his son on the day the Tathāgata was to enter Jetavana.
Having adorned him with every kind of ornament, he sent him forth together with five hundred princes who were likewise dressed and adorned.
Accompanied by his retinue, he took five hundred banners radiant with five-colored cloths and stood before the One of Ten Powers;
behind them followed the two daughters of the treasurer, Mahāsubhaddā and Cūḷasubhaddā, with five hundred...
Taking full water-jars, they went out together with hundreds of young girls;
behind them, the merchant’s wife, adorned with all her ornaments, went out taking full bowls together with five hundred women;
and behind them all, the great merchant, dressed in new garments, [went out] with five hundred others likewise dressed in new garments.
Together with hundreds of wealthy merchants, he approached the Blessed One. Placing this assembly of lay disciples before him and surrounded by the great community of monks,

the Blessed One entered the Jetavana Monastery with the infinite grace of a Buddha and immeasurable splendor of a Buddha, making the forest groves appear as if they were being sprinkled with streams of molten gold by the radiance of his own body.
Then Anāthapiṇḍika asked him, "Venerable sir, how should I proceed regarding this monastery?
"In that case, householder, establish this monastery for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from the four quarters, both those who have come and those yet to come.
"Very well, venerable sir," the great merchant replied, and taking a golden water-pitcher, he poured water into the hand of the One of Ten Powers.
“I give this Jetavana monastery to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters, present and future, headed by the Buddha,” he said, and thus gave it.
Having accepted the monastery, the Teacher delivered a blessing of thanks:
“It wards off cold and heat, and likewise wild beasts;”
“From snakes and mosquitoes, from the cold and also from rains;
then the fierce wind and heat that have arisen are warded off—
for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the purpose of meditating and attaining insight.”
“The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as the foremost by the Buddha.
Therefore, a wise person, seeing his own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those learned in the Dhamma to dwell therein.”
To those who have become upright, one should give food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings,
with a mind full of serene confidence. They, in turn,
teach him the Dhamma that brings about the destruction of all suffering.
“Having understood that Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints”—thus he spoke of the benefits of the monastery.
From the second day onward, Anāthapiṇḍika began the festival for the monastery.
Visākhā’s festival for her monastery was completed in four months, but Anāthapiṇḍika’s festival for his monastery took nine [months].
He completed it within months. Even during the festival of the monastery, eighteen *koṭis* were offered as gifts.
Thus, he bestowed wealth amounting to fifty-four *koṭis* upon that single monastery alone.
Furthermore, in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, a merchant named Punabbasumitta [constructed] a floor inlaid with golden bricks.
Having purchased it, he built a monastic complex (saṅghārāma) measuring one *yojana* on that very spot.

During the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, however, a merchant named Sirivaḍḍha purchased it by covering the ground with a layer of gold ingots and built a monastic complex measuring three *gāvutas* on that very same spot.
During the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, a merchant named Sotthiya [purchased it] by covering the ground with a layer of golden elephant tracks...
Having purchased it, he built a monastic complex (saṅghārāma) measuring half a yojana on that very spot.
During the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha, a merchant named Accuta purchased it with a layer of golden bricks and built a monastic complex measuring one gāvuta on that very same spot.
During the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, a merchant named Ugga [purchased it] with a layer of golden tortoises...
Having purchased it, he built a monastic park (saṅghārāma) of the measure of half a gāvuta on that very spot.

During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, a merchant named Sumaṅgala purchased it by covering it with a layer of gold bars and built a monastic park of the measure of sixteen karīsas on that very spot.
However, during the time of our Blessed One, a merchant named Anāthapiṇḍika [purchased it] by covering it with ten million coins (kahāpaṇa).
Having purchased it, he had a monastery built on that very spot measuring eight *karīsa* in extent.
Indeed, this place is one that has never been abandoned by any of the Buddhas.

Thus, from the attainment of omniscience at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*Mahābodhimaṇḍa*) until the couch of the Great Parinibbāna—whatever places the Blessed One inhabited during that time—this should be understood as the "proximate nidāna."
The introductory narrative of the presence is finished.
The Introductory Narrative is finished.
The *Therāpadāna*.
1. The Chapter on the Buddhas (Buddhavagga):
Explanation of the Internal Introduction "Now, with pure minds, listen to the exploits of the Buddhas."
“Having fulfilled the thirty perfections, the Dharma-kings are beyond counting.

Here, *atha* is a particle (*nipāta*) used in the sense of indicating a change of subject (*adhikārantara*). Among the two types of particles—those connected with case endings and those not so connected—it is a particle connected with a case ending. Alternatively:
“In the sense of a heading (*adhikāra*), a blessing (*maṅgala*), a completed state (*nipphanna*), a meaning, and a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*);”
The word *atha* occurs when there is immediate succession.
For it is said:
“It expresses purpose (*adhikicca*), determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and special meaning (*adhiattha*);”

Because it is stated: “The office is established by way of being the most excellent and the eldest,” the words are joined with the term *atha* in the sense of office (*adhikāra*) with respect to the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) of the Buddhas, by virtue of their excellence and seniority.
And because of the nature of the threefold Bodhisattvas’ worship and auspiciousness, [it is said] “worship (*pūjā*)...”
Because of the statement, “Of those worthy of worship, this is the supreme blessing,” they are phrases joined with the word *atha* in the sense of being auspicious (*maṅgala*).

Because the perfected function of the Blessed Ones, such as the Buddhas, is accomplished through the path of arahantship, they are phrases joined with the word *atha* in the sense of being accomplished (*nipphanna*).
[Furthermore,] because of the wholesome states of the Buddhas and others, such as the path of arahantship, as well as other wholesome states...
The words are connected with the term *atha* in the sense of exclusion (*avadhāraṇa*), in the sense of warding off (*nivāraṇa*), and in the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*).
The words are connected with the term *atha* in the sense of immediate succession (*anantara*), because it was compiled immediately after the compilation of the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
The words are connected with the term *atha* in the sense of departure (*apagama*), meaning "starting from this *Khuddakapāṭha*."
Regarding the term "Buddha": here, he is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the world; he is a Buddha by virtue of omniscience;
he is a Buddha by virtue of all-seeing vision; he is a Buddha by virtue of not being led by others; he is a Buddha by virtue of his flowing wisdom; he is a Buddha as one whose taints are exhausted;
he is a Buddha as one free from defilements; he is a Buddha as one who has gone forth; and he is a Buddha in the sense of being without a second.

He is a Buddha because he has abandoned craving; he is a Buddha because he has gone along the path traveled by the One (the *ekāyana-magga*); he is a Buddha because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*);

he is a Buddha because his non-enlightenment has been destroyed and he has attained true wisdom (*buddhi*). Wisdom (*buddhi*), the enlightened one (*buddha*), and enlightenment (*bodhi*)—these are not different in meaning.
Just as a cloth is called a "blue cloth" or a "red cloth" due to its association with colors such as blue and so forth, [so too is he called a Buddha].
Thus, he is called a Buddha because of his possession of the qualities of a Buddha. Alternatively, "Bodhi" refers to the knowledge within the four paths;
because one has exhausted the entire host of enemies that are the one thousand five hundred defilements by means of that knowledge and thereby attained Nibbāna, that knowledge is called "Bodhi.
The person who possesses that [knowledge] through its association is a Buddha. By means of that very same knowledge, even a Paccekabuddha [is so called] regarding all defilements...
Having exhausted [the defilements], one attains Nibbāna. But as for the Buddhas, because they have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*) over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons,

and because they have attained the knowledge of enlightenment (*bodhiñāṇa*), and because they have acquired the unique knowledges— the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*), the knowledge of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇa*), the knowledge of the twin miracle (*yamakapāṭihīrañāṇa*), the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),
the unobstructed knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (*āsayānusaya*), and so forth— they [are able to do so] even with a single teaching of the Dhamma.

Because it causes the nectar of the Dhamma to be drunk by incalculable multitudes of beings and leads them to Nibbāna, and because that very knowledge exists in a superior degree only in the Buddhas, it is the "Apadāna of the Fully Enlightened Ones" (Sambuddhāpadāna), meaning the cause or ground for their status as Buddhas. That [apadāna] is twofold, according to the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome.
However, Paccekabuddhas are not capable of acting in such a way; even when they provide support to those who give requisites such as food—
“May what you desire and have prayed for be fulfilled very quickly;
may your heart’s intentions be realized just like the moon on the fifteenth day.
May what you desire and have prayed for be fulfilled very quickly.”
“May their mental aspirations be fulfilled, like a radiant wish-fulfilling gem.
Teaching the Dhamma with these two verses alone, they are unable to awaken even an incalculable multitude of beings;
therefore, because they are not like a *sabbaññubuddha* (an omniscient Buddha) but are enlightened individually and separately, they are called *paccekabuddhas*.
The account of their deeds is the *apadāna*, the *apadāna* of the Paccekabuddhas.
They are called "Theras" because they have long endured. Alternatively, they are Theras because they are endowed with qualities such as firmness of virtue, conduct, and gentleness.
Or else, they are Theras because they are endowed with the qualities of firm, excellent virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Or again—
The Elders (theras) are so called because they have attained the supreme peace of Nibbāna, which is refined and reckoned as most stable; the *apadānas* of the Elders are the *Therāpadānas*.
Likewise, the Elder-nuns (therīs) are so called because they are endowed with such qualities; the *apadānas* of the Elder-nuns are the *Therīpadānas*.
Among these, there are exactly five *apadānas* and exactly five Suttantas concerning the Buddha. Thus the ancients said:
“Five Apadānas and five Suttas for whom [they were told];
this is the ‘Buddha-Apadāna,’ first in the forward order.
Regarding the Paccekabuddha-Apadāna as well, there are likewise five Apadānas and five Suttantas. Thus said the ancients:
“Five apadānas and five suttas for whom [they were told];
this is the ‘Apadāna of the Paccekabuddhas,’ the second [section] in forward order.
In the *Therāpadāna*, there are five hundred and ten apadānas, and fifty-one chapters by division. Thus said the ancients:
“Five hundred and ten verses, divided into fifty-one chapters;
this is the *Therāpadāna*, the third [section] in forward order.
In the *Therīapadāna*, there are forty apadānas, arranged into four chapters. Thus say the ancients:
“Forty apadānas, and those belonging to the four groups;
this is the *therī-apadāna*, the fourth in the direct order. Regarding the word *apadāna*:
here the term *apadāna* is seen in the senses of cause, taking away, departure, sequence, accusation, and so forth.
For this term is seen in the sense of "cause" in such passages as “the *apadāna* of the khattiyas, the *apadāna* of the brāhmaṇas,” meaning the cause of the khattiyas, the cause of the brāhmaṇas.

It is seen in the sense of "grasping" in such passages as “the *apadāna* of the upāsakas,” meaning a firm grasping. [It is also seen] in such passages as “the *apadāna* of the vāṇijas, the *apadāna* of the suddas.”
In the sense of departing, it is seen as "departing from here and there," meaning their departure from those places.

In such passages as "The alms-collecting bhikkhu wanders for alms by means of the systematic round" (*sapadānacāra*), it is seen in the sense of sequence; the meaning is that he wanders house by house in regular order.
In such passages as "He reviles them, saying, 'These recluses have departed [from virtue], these brahmins have departed,'" it is seen in the sense of abuse; he reviles.
The meaning is "he reviles. However, here it is used in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*). Therefore, the "exploits of the Buddhas" (*buddhāpadāni*) means the exploits belonging to the Buddhas;

the meaning is "the causes for becoming a Buddha. It should be understood that the cause for the many Buddhas, who are like the sands of the Ganges, is the perfection of the thirty pāramīs, beginning with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Now, the connection is: "Listen, you of pure mind, to the appropriate exploits concerning [the topics of] the subject matter (*adhikāra*) and so forth."

In this context, "those with pure minds" refers to the five hundred *khīṇāsavas* (those whose taints are destroyed) who, having eliminated one thousand five hundred defilements by means of the knowledge of the path to *arahantship*, abide with pure minds, purified hearts, and cleansed inner beings;
they are seated here in this Dhamma assembly. The meaning is: "Listen with attentive ears and apply your minds."
In this context, however, instead of saying "the Apadānas," even though the *Apadānas* of Paccekabuddhas, Theras, and Therīs exist, the expression "then the Buddhapadānas" is used;
this is like using the term "Root Yamaka" because of its preeminence and its position as the beginning,

even though the *Khandha*, *Yamaka*, *Āyatana*, *Dhātu*, *Sacca*, *Saṅkhāra*, and *Anusaya Yamakas* also exist— just as among the thirteen *Saṅghādisesas*, the two *Aniyatas*, and the thirty *Nissaggiyas*.

Even though [other sections] exist, it should be understood that here too it is stated by way of prominence and by way of beginning, just as the expression "Pārājika-khaṇḍa" is used despite the existence of other sections.
This is according to the method of grammar (nirutta), which states:
"In the case of what ought to be called 'Sammāsambuddhāpadānāni' (Deeds of the Perfectly Enlightened One), there is the addition of a vowel... [and so on]... the fivefold grammar."

Alternatively, by applying the rule "there is elision, addition, modification, and substitution of opposites" (*tesu vuddhilopāgamavikāraviparītādesā*), having effected the elision of the indeclinable particle *sammā*—which expresses the sense of the third case—and the prefix *sa-*—which expresses the sense of the word *sayaṃ*—one takes only the word *buddha*, which ends in the suffix *-kit*.

For the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition, it is stated as "the exploits of the Buddha" (*buddhāpadānāni*). Therefore, the meaning is "the exploits of the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddhāpadānāni*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Internal Introduction to the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, entitled *Visuddhajanavilāsinī*. 1.
Commentary on the *Buddha-apadāna* (The Deeds of the Buddha).
Now, immediately after the internal introduction (*abbhantaranidāna*), wishing to explain the commentary on the *Apadāna*,
[the author says]: “The *Apadāna* in sequential order,
with its teaching of diverse methods, which the great seers recited within the *Khuddakanikāya*— ”
"Now the turn has arrived for its commentary on the meaning.
In this regard, since it is said that "the entire word of the Buddha has the single flavor of liberation," the Apadāna is included within the category of that single flavor;
furthermore, within the twofold classification into Dhamma and Vinaya, it is included in the Dhamma; and among the word of the Buddhas of the first, middle, and final periods—
It is included within the Word of the Buddha; among the three baskets of the Vinaya, Abhidhamma, and Sutta Piṭakas, it is included in the Sutta Piṭaka;
among the five Nikāyas—the Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara, and Khuddaka—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya;
specifically, it consists of the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, and Abbhutadhamma.
Regarding the term *vedalla*: among the nine branches of the teaching (*sāsanaṅga*), it is included within the category of verses (*gāthā*).
As it is said: “I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus;
these are the eighty-four thousand teachings that have come forth.”
Thus, among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma that have been mentioned, [this Apadāna] is included within a certain number of those aggregates.
Now, in order to show that Apadāna, he said: "The Kings of Dhamma, who have fulfilled the thirty perfections, are beyond counting.

In this context, the ten perfections alone—by way of their being inferior, middling, and superior—are comprised of the ten perfections, the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*).

By means of these, he is endowed with the thirty perfections (*pāramī*). Fully developed, filled, possessed of, equipped with, attained to, and associated with these—thus he is "one perfected in the thirty perfections" (*tiṃsapāramisampunnā*).

Through the four sublime abidings (*brahmavihāra*) known as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, or through the dwelling in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he has, by way of a single state of mind, [extended this] toward the entire mass of beings dwelling in the three worlds.

And because they delight in and cause others to adhere to the body, they are called *rājāno* (kings); those who are kings by way of the Dhamma are *dhammarājā* (Dhamma-kings), and such are the Buddhas.

Ten hundred is a thousand; ten thousand is a hundred thousand; ten hundred thousand is a million (*koṭi*); ten million is ten million (*pakoṭi*); ten times ten million is a hundred million (*koṭippakoṭi*);
then *nahuta*, *ninnahuta*, *akkhobhiṇi*, *bindu*, *abbuda*, *nirabbuda*, *ahahaṃ*, *ababaṃ*, *aṭaṭaṃ*, *sogandhikaṃ*.

By way of the Uppala, Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and Paduma [Buddhas], and by way of the Kathā, Mahākathā, and Asaṅkhyeyya [Buddhas], the Dhamma-kings—incalculable, beyond reckoning, and devoid of conceptual constructs—have passed away, departed, ceased, and gone to their final end; this is the intended meaning.
6. Among those past Buddhas, one has performed service, and having himself been a Bodhisatta, he became a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*).
When the Elder Ānanda asked about the equipment [for enlightenment], the Blessed One said, "The supreme enlightenment of the Buddhas," and so forth.
The intention is: "O Ānanda, listen to my *apadāna* (account of past deeds).

Ānanda, in former times, while fulfilling the equipment for enlightenment, I was a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) who [provided] the supreme enlightenment of the Buddhas—the most excellent ones who have penetrated the Four Noble Truths.
The connection is: "I pay homage with my head to the knowledge of the four truths and the path, or to the knowledge of omniscience.

Having paid homage and worshipped with both hands joined with the ten fingers before the Buddha—the Leader of the World, the Eldest of the World, who is accompanied by the Saṅgha, that is, the community of disciples—I bow down with my head;
the meaning is: "Having performed a reverential salutation with devotion, I offer praise."
"Throughout the Buddha-fields" means throughout the ten thousand world-systems that constitute the Buddha-fields.

Therein, those things situated in space or in the sky, and those situated on the earth or on the ground—namely, the seven jewels beginning with beryl—which are incalculable and beyond reckoning, as many as there may be:
all of these one should gather together with the mind, having firmly resolved upon them with the heart.
The meaning is "I shall bring"; the meaning is "I shall make a heap around my palace.
8. In that context, "on the silver floor" means that on that palace of many stories, a floor made of silver—that is, made of white metal—was fashioned.
I [shall build] a palace made of jewels, constructed with the seven kinds of gems, consisting of many hundreds of stories.
The meaning is: they are building one that is lofty, risen up, ascended into the sky, and shining in the atmosphere.
9. Describing that very palace, he says "with variegated pillars" and so forth. It is raised up with many variegated pillars of various colors such as *masāragalla* (lapis lazuli) and others;
it is well-made, excellently constructed, endowed with auspicious marks, and well-proportioned in terms of height and circumference.
It was magnificent because it was constructed with many hundreds of millions of toraṇa-gates. Furthermore, how was it distinguished?

It was a palace adorned and beautified by golden *saṅghāṭa*-roofs—meaning it was equipped with gold-made *tulā-saṅghāṭa* rings—and by banners and parasols raised up therein. This is the connection [of the words].
10. Furthermore, describing the splendor of the palace itself, he said, "The first floor was of beryl," and so forth.

The meaning is that the first floor of that palace, which had many hundreds of stories, was beautiful, desirable, lovely, pleasing, cloud-like, resembling a mass of clouds, stainless, pure, made of beryl gems, blue in color, and covered—endowed—with excellent water-born lotuses and lilies.
The meaning is that it shines like the highest golden ground, like a land of gold. 11.
Of that very palace, some floors were made of coral, consisting of coral parts and having the color of coral;
some floors were red, having a crimson hue; and some floors were beautiful and charming, emitting rays of light with the luster of the color of *indagopaka* insects.
The meaning is that a certain floor illuminates the ten directions. 12.

In that very palace, the *niyyūha* (turrets) and the *niggata-pamukha-sālā* (projecting front halls) were well-proportioned—meaning they were perfectly divided and arranged into distinct sections—and there were lion-window lattices and lion-doors. "Four railings" refers to four circular railings.
And from the lattice-windows hang delightful, heart-entrancing fragrant garlands and perfumed wreaths; this is the meaning. 13.
In that very palace there were gabled chambers adorned with the seven jewels, beautified by the seven precious substances.
Of what nature were they? Blue, blue-colored; yellow, yellow-colored, golden-colored; red, red-colored, crimson-colored; and white.
White in color, bright white in color, pure black, unmixed with any other black color;
"furnished with excellent gabled chambers" means that the palace was endowed and possessed of excellent gabled chambers and excellent pinnacle-gabled chambers.
In that very palace, lotuses made of precious gems, facing upwards and in full bloom, shone brilliantly; [there were] lions, tigers, and so forth...
The meaning is that this palace was beautified by herds of wild beasts and by flocks of birds such as swans, cranes, and peacocks.

Being exceedingly high and having risen up into the sky, it was strewn with constellations and stars, and adorned with the moon and sun—that is, with the forms of the moon and the sun. This is the meaning.
15. Thus, the palace of the wheel-turning monarch was covered with nets of gold and nets of silver;
"endowed with golden bells" means it was provided and possessed with networks of golden bells. "Delightful" means they were pleasing to the mind.
"Golden garlands" means rows of golden flowers that "hummed"—that is, made sounds—by the force of the wind, by the impact of the wind.
16. Mañjeṭṭhaka means crimson-colored; lohitaka means red-colored; pītaka means yellow-colored; haripiñjara means the color of Jambūnada gold;
and pañjaravaṇṇa refers to a banner of various dyes and many colors, a banner dyed with blended hues, raised—that is, hoisted—upon that palace.
[The term] "Dhajamālinī" is used by way of a grammatical shift in gender.
It is said: "That palace was adorned with a garland of banners"—this is the meaning.
(17) Describing the coverings and other features of that palace, he says, "There was nothing there that was not abundant," and so forth.
In this context, "nothing" means that there was no part of that palace which was not present in abundance; it was variegated with many diverse coverings of various colors and patterns.
There were many hundreds, indeed many hundreds in number, of couches, seats, and other types of bedding that were resplendent;

what were they like? They were made of crystal—composed of crystal gems—or made of silver, constructed from silver; some were made of gems, constructed from blue sapphires; some were made of rubies, constructed from red-colored gems;
some were made of emeralds, constructed from dark-colored gems; and they were spread with fine Kāsika cloth, that is, with soft and delicate fabrics.
Woven from Kāsī cloth. 18. *Pāvūrā* means coverlets. Of what kind?
Woolen blankets (*kambala*) made from woolen threads; *dukūla* cloths made from *dukūla* fibers; Chinese silks (*cīna*) made from Chinese fabrics;
Pattuṇṇa cloths made from fabrics produced in the Pattuṇṇa region; *paṇḍu*, meaning yellowish-white in color; and variegated rugs (*vicittattharaṇa*).
The meaning is: "I shall mentally design every bed, variegated with many coverlets and rugs.
19. Describing that very palace, he said, "In those very floors," and so forth.
Therein, "adorned with jeweled peaks" means it was beautified and decorated with peaks made of jewels and jeweled capitals (*kaṇṇikā*). "Lamps of radiant gems" (*maṇiverocanā ukkā*)...
“Made with *verocana* gems and red gems” refers to torches and staff-lamps.
“Holding them well aloft” means that many hundreds of people, holding [the lamps] high in the air, stand there firmly; the sense is that they remain well-established.
(20) Again, describing that very palace, he said, “The pillar-standards shine,” and so forth. Therein, “pillar-standards” (*esikāthambhā*)...
The pillars set up for the sake of beauty at the city gates are beautiful and desirable;

the arches (*toraṇa*) made of gold are golden, and those made of *jambūnada* are of *jambūnada* gold; the arches made of heartwood are of the heartwood of the *khadira* tree and of silver, and they shine.
The meaning is that the stakes and the arches beautify that palace.

21. In that palace, the various well-proportioned joints, adorned with panels and bolts, and the decorated enclosures of those joints, "shone"—this is the meaning. "On both sides" means on both flanks of that palace;
"full jars," joined with many lotuses and many water-lilies, were full and beautified that palace—this is the meaning.

22–23. Having thus described the splendor of the palace, he spoke the words beginning with “And to all the Buddhas of the past,” etc., in order to manifest both the jewel-adorned palace and the honor and respect [shown to them].
Therein, “of the past” (*atīte*) means those who have passed away, departed, occurred, or existed in former times;

“all the World-Leaders, the Buddhas, together with their Saṅghas” means accompanied by the assembly of disciples (*sāvakasamūha*), all the Buddhas who are leaders of the world, in their essential nature (*sabhāva*), their natural color (*pakativaṇṇa*), and their physical form (*rūpa*).
Having fashioned the Buddha together with his disciples, complete in form, he entered the palace through whichever gate it was to be entered;

then all the Buddhas, together with their disciples, sat upon seats made entirely of gold—meaning they were composed of pure, solid gold—and became noble assemblies, groups of noble ones. This is the meaning.
24–25. At this present time, those Buddhas who exist and are found— supreme, being without superior— as well as the many hundreds of Paccekabuddhas,
who are self-become (*sayambhū*), having become so by themselves without reliance on another teacher,
unconquered, undefeated by the Māras consisting of the aggregates, the defilements, formations, death, and the son of a god— they will satisfy those who have attained victory.
The meaning is as follows: "In the past and in the present, all Buddhas have ascended (*samāruhuṃ*), that is, they have well (*su*) ascended, my palace (*pāsādaṃ*) called Bhavana. 26.

Those which are divine (*dibbā*), meaning existing in the heavens (*divi bhavā*), born in the world of the gods (*devaloke*); and those many wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) that exist; and those...

The connection is as follows: "Having gathered all the cloth from the humans born among men and from the many *kappa*-trees that exist, and having well-prepared it, I shall have three robes made and clothe those *paccekabuddhas* with the triple robe (*ticīvara*). 27.
Having thus clothed them with the triple robe and caused them to wear it, when those *paccekabuddhas* were seated, [the offering] was complete.
Sweet solid food such as cakes and the like was to be eaten; sweet soft food and nourishment were to be consumed; sweet drinks and syrups were to be sipped;
and excellent, sweet eightfold beverages and meals were to be enjoyed—all of which I gave, having filled beautiful, fine bowls made of jewels and stone to their full capacity.
The meaning is "they caused them to be received. 28.
All those noble circles, all those noble assemblies, having become possessed of the divine eye, were polished—meaning they were smooth because they were free from defilements;
they were sleek and radiant, endowed with robes, being equipped with the three robes (ticīvara).
The meaning is: they were satisfied, provided for, and fulfilled by me with sweet syllables, with oil, with honey and molasses, and with the finest rice-porridge and the most excellent food.
Having been thus satisfied, those noble circles [entered] the jewel-chamber, a chamber fashioned from the seven jewels.
Having entered the dwelling, reclining in one cave after another like maned lions,
they prepared the lion’s posture upon a costly and most noble couch— just as the lion, king of beasts,
lies on his right side with one foot placed over the other, his right hand used as a pillow for his head, and his left hand extended straight out.
Having placed his tail between his thighs, he lay motionless; the meaning is that they made their bed in this manner. 30.

Having thus made the lion’s posture (sīhaseyyā), being fully aware and endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sampajañña), they rose up well—that is, having risen properly—and on the bed they folded their legs crosswise (pallaṅka); the meaning is that they assumed the bound-thigh posture (ūrubaddhāsana).
31. "The range of all Buddhas" means the range, which has become the object (ārammaṇa), of all Buddhas of the past and the future.
"Devoted to the delight of meditation" means they were thoroughly absorbed in and possessed of the delight of meditation;
"teaching other teachings" means that among those paccekabuddhas, some teach certain other doctrines,
while others sport and take pleasure in the play of the first and subsequent jhānas through supernormal powers (iddhi).
32. Some others have attained mastery over the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*);
they have reached, gone to, and acquired mastery through the five forms of mastery—namely, adverting, entering, emerging, resolving, and reviewing—regarding the five direct knowledges;
they apply themselves to and enter them. Some others [perform] thousands of transformations.
The meaning is that they perform various transformations of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*), such as becoming many after being one, or becoming one after being many. 33.

"Buddhas [asking] Buddhas": when *paccekabuddhas* have thus assembled, the Buddhas ask those *paccekabuddhas* questions that fall within the range of their omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) and serve as its object;
this is the meaning. Those Buddhas, because of the profundity of the meaning...
They penetrate with wisdom that which is profound, subtle, and delicate—the state and the cause—awakening to it specifically and without remainder.
At that time, even the disciples assembled in my palace ask questions of the Buddhas, and the Buddhas ask questions of their disciples;
those Buddhas and disciples, having asked each other questions, [answer] one another.
They explain and answer. 35.
Showing them all together once more, he said, "The Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas," and so forth. Therein, "Buddhas" refers to the Sammasambuddhas;
"Paccekabuddhas," as well as disciples (*sāvaka*), pupils (*sissa*), attendants (*paricāraka*), and those who rely on others (*nissitaka*)—all these [are included].
The meaning is: "Delighting in their respective pleasures, they dwell in seclusion, finding joy in my palace.

(36) Having thus demonstrated the excellence of the conduct of the Paccekabuddhas in that Vejayanta Palace, the Cakkavatti King Tilokavijaya now, displaying his own majesty, spoke the words beginning with, "Let the jeweled parasols stand."
In that regard, the meaning is as follows: let the parasols made of the seven precious gems, with their golden handles and fringes, hang suspended by nets of gold;
let all the parasols, encircled and surrounded by nets of pearls, be held over my head.
As soon as he thought this, the parasols appeared.
37. May canopies adorned with golden stars, shining with golden stars, come into being;

may they be produced. "Variegated" means of many colors; "stretched with garlands" means covered with flowers. The meaning is: may all these various canopies be held above the place where the seat is located at the top.

38–40. The connection is as follows: the lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*) is "stretched over" (*vitata*) and "strewn with" (*parikiṇṇa*) garlands of flowers (*mālyadāma*), that is, garlands of many fragrant blossoms;

it is "resplendent with" (*sobhita*) garlands of perfumes (*gandhadāma*), such as sandalwood, saffron, tagara, and other fragrant substances. It is strewn with garlands of cloth (*dussadāma*), namely, priceless cloth-garlands made of fine cotton, silk, and so forth;

the lotus pond is adorned and decorated with garlands of the seven precious gems (*sattaratana*). It is "covered with flowers" (*pupphābhikiṇṇa*), meaning it is strewn with fragrant blossoms such as the *campaka*, *saḷala*, and *sogandhika*.
It was strewn [with flowers], very variegated, and beautiful. Furthermore, what was the pond like?

It was adorned and perfumed with fragrant scents. It was decorated all around with "five-finger" marks of perfume—adorned with five fingers' worth of applied scents—and it was covered with golden canopies, that is, covered with golden awnings and golden roofs, [belonging to] the palace.
The lotus ponds in the four directions, well-spread and carpeted with red and blue lotuses, are like golden forms, possessing a golden hue;
let them shine, covered with the pollen of the lotuses and strewn with the dust of the *paduma* flowers—this is the meaning. 41.
Let all the trees surrounding my Vejayanta Palace, such as the *campaka* and other species, come into full bloom.
Flower-trees: having themselves released their blossoms, let them fall and go to sprinkle my dwelling;
the meaning is that once strewn, they shall form a canopy above the palace.
42. Therein, upon that Vejayanta Palace of mine, let peacocks dance; "divine swans" means celestial swans.
Let the *pakūjara* birds make their sound; let the *karavīka* birds, sweet-voiced, sing their songs;
and let other peerless flocks of winged creatures (*dijasaṅghā*) all around the palace utter sweet cries—this is the meaning. 43.
Let all the drums, such as the *ātatā* and *vitata*, all around the palace, be struck and beaten; let them all...
"Let the lutes with their many strings resound, let them produce sound; let all kinds of musical ensembles proceed, circulate, and sing all around the palace"—this is the meaning.
(44–5) "As far as," that is, in whatever extent of space within the Buddha-field—namely, the ten-thousandfold world-system and beyond those world-systems—[let them do so].
Let there stand golden couches and gold-laden couches, endowed with radiance, possessed of splendor, unbroken, vast, made of jewels on all sides, and inlaid with the seven precious gems;
let lamp-trees bearing lamps and oil-trees blaze all around the palace, and let them burn with lamps, ten thousand upon ten thousand.
The meaning is: "May the ten thousand lineages shine forth, becoming like a single lamp, a single light.
(46) Let courtesans skilled in dance and song, dancing women, and *lāsikā* who produce sound with their mouths, dance all around the palace;
let throngs of *accharā*—multitudes of divine nymphs—dance; and let circles of many colors, of various hues, [shine forth].
"Let them dance all around the palace; let them be visible, let them be manifest"—this is the meaning.

47. At that time, having become a universal monarch named Tilokavijaya, [I saw] throughout the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*)—on the tops of trees along the roads, on the peaks of mountains, at the summits of the Himalayas, the world-system mountains, and so forth, and upon the crest of Mount Sineru—in all such places.
"Variegated" means manifoldly variegated; "five-colored" means consisting of the five colors, such as blue, yellow, and so forth; the meaning is: "I shall raise every banner. 48.
Let humans from the world of men, and nāgas from the nāga-world, and gandhabbas and gods from the world of the gods—all approach, let them come;
those humans and others, paying homage, performing salutation to me with palms joined (katahatthapuṭā).
The meaning is: "They shall surround my Vejayanta Palace.

(49) Thus, having praised the majesty of both the palace and himself, that Cakkavatti King, the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, now spoke the words beginning with "Whatever wholesome deed" in order to encourage others toward the fruit of the merit he had attained for himself.
Whatever action consisting of wholesome karma that ought to be performed, all of that has been well done by me through my body,
speech, or mind— via these three doors; the meaning is that it was properly executed and made worthy of arising in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
50. Again, while exhorting [others], he said, “Those beings who possess perception,” and so forth. Therein, the meaning is:
“Whatever beings there are—whether humans, gods, or Brahmās—who possess perception (saññino), that is, who are endowed with perception;

and whatever beings there are who are non-percipient (asaññino), that is, devoid of perception—all those beings, may they partake of the fruit of the merit performed by me; may they become possessed of merit.”
51. Furthermore, while exhorting [others], the Bodhisatta spoke the verse beginning with "Yesaṃ kataṃ. The meaning is:
by whomsoever—whether they be humans, nāgas, gandhabbas, or devas—my performed merit is well-known and understood, to them I give the fruit of that merit;
and as for those humans and others who do not know that the state of having been given exists within the merit performed by me, the devas go and announce it to them.

52. "Whatever beings in the entire world live dependent upon food, may all those beings obtain every kind of pleasing food through my mind, through my intention; they shall obtain it by the power of my merit—this is the meaning. 53.

"With a clear mind and a heart of faith, I brought forth confidence in that gift which was given by me. And all the Fully Enlightened Ones, the Pacceka Buddhas, and the disciples of the Conquerors were honored by me while I was a Wheel-turning Monarch."

54. By virtue of that pleasant karma performed with faith, through wholesome deeds, and by means of the aspirations and mental resolves formed in my heart, I abandoned and cast off this human body—the physical frame of a mortal—and went to the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world;
the meaning is that I was reborn there as if waking from sleep.

55. Then, after the universal monarch Tilokavijaya had passed away, from that point onward I knew two existences—two births—namely, existence as a deity in the state of being a god, and existence as a human in the state of being a man.

Beyond those two births, I know no other destiny, nor do I see any other rebirth; this is the fruit of aspiration, the meaning being "the fruit of the aspiration one has made," known through the mind and consciousness.
56. "May I be superior to the gods": if born among the gods, may I be superior to the gods in lifespan, beauty, strength, and splendor;
that is, may I be the eldest and most excellent among them. If born among humans, may I become a lord of men, a ruler and master over human beings;
likewise, having become a king, may I possess beauty through the perfection of form and the characteristics of physical proportions such as height and girth.
And being endowed with and perfected in it, in every birth that arises, he is peerless through his wisdom—the wisdom that knows the ultimate truth—and is without equal;
the meaning is that there is no one like me.
57. By the fruit of merit from the accumulation of merit performed by me, in every birth that arises, [he experiences] what is excellent, sublime, and sweet.

Various kinds of food in manifold ways, and no small amount of many jewels for beings, as well as various garments of diverse types such as cotton and silk, quickly and swiftly approach and come into my presence from the sky, the atmosphere. 58–66.
Whatever [thing] on the earth, on mountains, in the sky, in water, or in the forest—wherever it may be—whatever [it may be].
When I stretch out my hand and place it down, from here and there divine foods and divine nourishments come toward me, approach me;
the meaning is that they manifest. Likewise, in due order: all jewels; all fragrances such as sandalwood and so forth;
all vehicles and conveyances; all garlands and flowers such as the *campaka*, *nāga*, and *punnāga*.
All ornaments and decorations; all celestial maidens; all honey and sugar;
and all cakes and other foods to be chewed—these come and approach me.
(67–68) "For the attainment of the supreme enlightenment" means for the purpose of reaching the attainment of the knowledge of the supreme Fourfold Path. By me, that which...

The supreme gift was performed and fulfilled; by that supreme gift, making the entire mountain known as Sela resound with a single cry, thundering with a thick voice and a broad resonance, and causing the world with its devas—the entire realm of humans and gods—to laugh and attain joy, the meaning is:
"I am the Buddha, whose veil has been removed throughout the three worlds."
69. "The ten directions in the world": in the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-loka*), the directions consist of ten kinds or ten divisions.
The meaning is that for one who traverses those divisions, moving and proceeding, there is no end.

During the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*), in whichever direction or region I have gone, there are Buddha-fields and Buddha-spheres (*buddha-visaya*) that are incalculable and beyond reckoning.

70. "The radiance was manifested": at that time, during the era of the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), my radiance—the light of the wheel-treasure, the jewel-treasure, and so forth—was manifested, made visible, as pairs and couples of beams, emitting rays and acting as vehicles for those rays;
within this interval, throughout the ten thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa), there was a web of rays, a mass of rays, a vast and abundant light.
The meaning is: "May it be so.

(71) "In this much of the world-system" means: "May all people in the ten-thousandfold world-system see me, may they behold me. "May all the gods, as far as the abode of Brahmā, as far as the Brahma-world, follow after me and be favorable to me.
(72) "With a distinguished, sweet sound" means with a wide-spread, melodious voice; "beating the drum of the Deathless" means [beating] the drum of the *amata*.
I struck the divine drum; meanwhile, within this ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*), may all people hear and attend to the sweet voice and sound of my mind.

73. While raining down the cloud of Dhamma—the thunderous roar consisting of the teaching of the Dhamma—there falls a rain of profound, sweet, and subtle meanings that transcend conventional designations and reach the ultimate truth.

While it rains and continues to rain, by the power of the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), may all the monks, nuns, and others become free from taints (anāsava) and devoid of defilements (nikkilesa).

Regarding the phrase "those beings who are last": among these four groups of beings gathered here, the intention is that those beings who are "last"—meaning inferior in terms of their qualities—may all become stream-enterers (sotāpanna).
74. At that time, during the era of King Tilokavijaya Cakkavatti, having given what was to be given and what was appropriate to give, having performed acts of generosity,
