and having fulfilled morality— the perfection of morality— without remainder or exception, and having reached the pinnacle of the perfection of renunciation,
may I attain supreme enlightenment, the knowledge of the four paths.
75. Having questioned those who are wise, possessed of wisdom, and intelligent—asking, "Venerable sir, what should be done? What should not be done? What is wholesome? What is unwholesome?

By doing what does one become a partaker of both heaven and liberation?"—in this way, the meaning is that he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*). "Having exerted supreme energy" means having exerted the highest, most excellent energy while standing, sitting, and so forth.

"Having exerted uninterrupted energy, having fulfilled the perfection of energy"— this is the meaning. "Having reached the pinnacle of the perfection of patience through enduring the contempt shown by all hostile people,
and having fulfilled the perfection of patience, may I attain, may I become, supreme enlightenment, the state of a Supreme Buddha."

76. "Having made a firm resolve" means: having established the perfection of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) with unshakable steadfastness, thinking, "Even if my body and life were to perish, I shall not desist from meritorious deeds";
and having fulfilled the pinnacle of the perfection of truth (sacca-pāramitā), thinking, "Even if my head were being cut off, I shall not speak a falsehood";
and [reciting] "May all beings be happy and free from enmity," etc.
The meaning is that he reached the pinnacle of the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramitā*) and attained supreme enlightenment.

77. Whether in the gain or loss of the grounds for being called "living" or "non-living," and likewise in bodily and mental pleasure or pain, as well as in honor and contempt performed by respectful people—he was equal in all respects, possessing an even mind.
The meaning is: having fulfilled the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*), may he attain supreme enlightenment.
78. Having seen and known laziness—the state of being indolent—as a danger, by way of its being a danger, [thinking] "it is one that shares in the suffering of the states of misery" (*apāya-dukkha*);
and having seen and known non-laziness—the state of being non-indolent, a conduct free from dejection—as a security, by way of its being a security, [thinking] "it leads to Nibbāna."
Be energetic; be so. This is the instruction of the Buddhas, this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

79. Having seen dispute as fear—having seen and known that dispute and quarrel lead to the states of deprivation—and having seen non-dispute, the refraining from dispute, as the attainment of Nibbāna, and having seen it as security, [be] united with one-pointed minds.

The meaning is: "May you be friendly, smooth, and radiant with a love that has reached its peak. This discourse is a consultation, an utterance, an instruction of the Buddhas, and the giving of advice. 80.
He dwells regarding negligence—living with the absence of mindfulness while standing, sitting, and so forth—as a danger: "In whatever place I am born..."
Having seen and known that [the eightfold path] leads to being afflicted, ugly, lacking food and drink, and so forth, as well as rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and so on;
and having seen and directly known it as "the attainment of Nibbāna," growing from a state of security—[one cultivates] the eightfold path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, [right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].
"Cultivate, increase, and attend to the eight-factored path to perfect enlightenment—right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration;
this is the discourse, the proclamation, the utterance, the instruction of the Buddhas, the teaching of the Buddhas"—this is the meaning. 81.
"Many Buddhas have gathered" means that many Pacceka-Buddhas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, have gathered and assembled as a multitude.
In every way and in all their various forms, hundreds of thousands of Arahants whose taints are exhausted have gathered together in a great multitude.
Therefore, while they are worshipping the Buddhas and the Arahants who are worthy of worship, you too should pay homage by prostrating with all your limbs and parts,
and you should worship them.
82. Thus, by this manner spoken by me, the "Buddhas" and "Buddha-qualities" are the four foundations of mindfulness...

[and so on] ...the eightfold path, the five aggregates, and such phenomena as the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), which are inconceivable (*acintiya*), meaning impossible to conceive;
or else, they are the intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) of the Buddhas, which are inconceivable and impossible to conceive.

The ripening for faithful gods and humans—which is beyond the sphere of thought and transcends the conceivable—consists of the attainment of excellence among gods and humans and the attainment of Nibbāna; it is impossible to conceive and it transcends all calculation.
Thus, to this extent, just as one traveling on a journey, when asked, "Show us the way," might say, "Having released the left..."
When it was said, "Take the southern road," they completed whatever duties were to be performed in the villages, market towns, and royal capitals along that path, and having been released again,
they likewise completed the duties to be performed in the villages, market towns, and so forth even when traveling by another, northern road; in the same way,

having completed the Buddha’s legacy (Buddhāpadāna) by way of the legacy of the wholesome, this interrogation is undertaken to expand upon that very same subject by way of the legacy of the unwholesome:
“The false accusation that was difficult to endure, and another false accusation;
the false accusation involving the shooting of a stone, and the pain from the splinter.
Nāḷāgiri, the cutting of the seven [limbs], the suffering of the head, and the eating of barley.”
“Backache and indigestion—these are the causes of unwholesomeness.
Regarding the first question: “Difficult to do” refers to the practice of austerities for six years.

In the past, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a young brahmin student named Jotipāla; by virtue of his birth into the brahmin caste, he [entered] the Dispensation...

Lacking faith in that Blessed One, due to the ripening of his past action involving a rag, he heard the name “Blessed Kassapa” and said, “Where is the enlightenment of this shaven-headed ascetic? Enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain.

Because of the ripening of that action, after experiencing the suffering of hell and other realms for many hundreds of births, immediately following that very Blessed One, by means of that same prediction he had received—
Having exhausted the cycle of births through karma, at the conclusion of that process he attained the state of Vessantara; passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
By the entreaty of the deities, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Sakyan clan.

Due to the full ripening of his knowledge, he renounced the sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa, cut off his mass of hair together with its topknot using a well-sharpened sword on the banks of the Anomā River, and [was received] by the Brahmā who had arrived.
During the period of the world’s formation in the age of supernormal power (*iddhimaya-kappa*), having been born within the calyx of a lotus and received the eight requisites,
he went forth into homelessness; yet, because his vision of the knowledge of enlightenment was as yet unripened and he did not know the path and the non-path toward Buddhahood,
for six years in the district of Uruvelā he lived by means of a single meal, a single morsel, a single person [as alms-giver], a single road, and eating at a single sitting.

With his body reduced to mere skin, sinews, and bones, resembling a fleshless and bloodless corpse, he performed austerities and great exertions involving difficult practices according to the method described in the *Padhāna-sutta*.

Thinking that these difficult practices were not the path to full enlightenment (*sambodhi*), he partook of refined food in villages, market towns, and royal capitals; thus, with his faculties refreshed and his thirty-two marks of a Great Man fully perfected, he [proceeded].
"In due course, having approached the seat of enlightenment and conquered the five Māras, he became a Buddha.
“Then I, Jotipāla, spoke to the Sugata Kassapa:
‘Whence indeed can there be enlightenment for one shaven-headed? Enlightenment is exceedingly difficult to attain.’”
“By the ripening of that karma, I practiced many hardships for six years at Uruvelā; from that, I attained enlightenment.
It was not by this path that I attained supreme enlightenment.”
“I shall seek the path by a wrong way, but I am obstructed by my past karma.
With merit and evil exhausted, free from all burning fevers,
without sorrow, without despair, and without taints, I shall attain Nibbāna.”
In the second question: *abbhakkhānaṃ* means an accusation, a false attribution, or an insult.
It is said that in the past, when the Bodhisatta was born into a clan of *suddas*, he lived as an obscure and unknown rogue named Munāḷi.
At that time, a Paccekabuddha named Surabhi, possessed of great psychic power and majesty, arrived at his dwelling on some business. Upon seeing him, he...
“He falsely accused [the Buddha], saying, ‘This ascetic is immoral and of evil character,’ and so forth. Due to that outflow of unwholesome karma,
after experiencing suffering for many thousands of years in the hells and other realms, in this final existence,
when the heretics first became prominent during the Blessed One’s residence in the Tusita heaven, they deceived all the people with the sixty-two views.”
Having thus illuminated [the world], they wander about. Then, having passed away from the Tusita heaven and been reborn in the Sakyan royal family, he gradually became a Buddha.
At that time, like glow-worms at the rising of the sun, the heretics—having lost their gains and honor—wandered about harboring resentment toward the Blessed One.
On that occasion, the merchant of Rājagaha was playing by casting a net in the Ganges.
Seeing the red sandalwood bowl, [the king thought], "There is much sandalwood in my house;
having had this bowl mounted on a frame and having had it inscribed with letters by carpenters, I shall have it suspended from a succession of bamboo poles and beat the drum, proclaiming:
'I shall provide food for whoever comes and takes this bowl by means of psychic power. Thus he caused the drum to be beaten.
Then the sectarians, thinking, “We are lost! We are truly lost! said to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta in his own assembly:
“I shall go near the bamboo grove and perform a feat of leaping into the air;
you must seize me by the shoulders and stop me, saying, ‘Do not perform miracles on account of a mere wooden bowl! They went there and did exactly as he had instructed.
At that time, Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja and Moggallāna, standing on the summit of the Sela mountain three gavutas away, were putting on their robes to receive alms-food when they heard that clamor.
Among them, Moggallāna said to Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, "Go through the air and fetch that bowl.
He replied, "Venerable sir, you yourself have been declared by the Blessed One as the foremost of those possessing psychic power..."
“Place it in the foremost position; you alone shall take it,” he said.

Nevertheless, being commanded by him, “You alone must take it as I have ordered,” he pressed the three-league rocky mountain upon which he stood against the sole of his foot and covered the entire city of Rājagaha like the lid of a cooking pot.
At that time, the city-dwellers [beheld it] like a red thread wound around the Phalika rock.
Seeing the Elder, they cried out, "Venerable Bhāradvāja, protect us! Terrified, they placed their heads upon the pestles.
Then the Elder, releasing that mountain from its standing place and traveling by means of psychic power, seized the bowl;
at that moment, the city-dwellers raised a great clamor.
The Blessed One, sitting in the Veḷuvana Monastery, heard that sound and asked Ānanda, "What is this sound?
He replied, "Venerable Sir, because Bhāradvāja has accepted the bowl, the city-dwellers, being well-pleased, have raised a shout of acclamation.
Then, for the sake of future liberation from the reproach of others, the Blessed One had that bowl brought, had it broken, and [used] the ointment powder...
Having prepared them, he had them given to the bhikkhus; and having had them given, he laid down a training rule: "Bhikkhus, no transformation by psychic power (iddhi-vikubbanā) should be performed.
Whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Thereupon, the sectarians said:
"It seems that the ascetic Gotama has laid down a training rule for his disciples; even for the sake of their lives, they..."
“They will not surpass him; we shall perform a miracle of psychic power! Thus they gathered in heaps here and there and raised a great clamor.
Then King Bimbisāra, having heard this, went into the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sitting to one side, said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the sectarians are shouting, ‘We shall perform a miracle of psychic power!’”
“I too shall do it, Great King. “But surely, Bhante, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One for his disciples?

“Great King, I will ask you this very thing: when you were establishing punishments for those eating mangoes and other fruits in your own park, did you not establish them by taking all [the cases] together? “Bhante, there is no punishment for me. “In that case,”...
“Great King, no training rule has been laid down by me. “Venerable sir, where will the miracle take place?
“Near Sāvatthī, at the foot of a *kaṇḍama* tree, Great King. “Excellent, venerable sir;
we shall see it. Then the sectarians heard, “It is said that the miracle will take place at the foot of a *kaṇḍama* tree.”
Upon hearing this, they had the mango trees cut down in the vicinity of the city. The citizens erected tiered platforms and watchtowers in the great courtyard;
inhabitants from all over Jambudīpa gathered like a single mass and stood filling twelve yojanas toward the eastern direction alone.
They likewise assembled in corresponding formations in the other directions as well.
When the time had arrived, on the full moon day of Āsāḷhi, the Blessed One completed his morning duties and went to that place, where he sat down.

At that moment, a park keeper named Kaṇḍa saw a perfectly ripe mango fruit inside a cluster of ants and thought, "If I were to give this to the King, I would receive a reward such as a kahāpaṇa coin; but if it is offered to the Blessed One—"
"However, there will be prosperity in both this world and the next. Having said this, he offered it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One accepted it and instructed the Elder Ānanda: "Grind this fruit and give me a drink. The Elder did so.
After the Blessed One had drunk the mango juice, he gave the stone to the park-keeper, saying, "Plant this. He then cleared away some sand.
The Elder Ānanda planted it and poured water from his water-pot over it.
At that moment, a mango sprout emerged and, even as the great multitude looked on, it appeared laden with branches, twigs, flowers, fruits, and shoots.
Even though all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa ate the fallen mango fruits, they were unable to exhaust them.

Then the Blessed One, from the eastern world-system as far as the western world-system, having established a jeweled walkway upon the summit of Mount Mahāmeru in this world-system, caused many assemblies to roar the lion’s roar;

and having performed a great miracle of psychic power in the manner described in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, he crushed the heretics and brought them to utter confusion. At the conclusion of the miracles—
In accordance with the practice of previous Buddhas, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and, having spent the rains retreat there, taught the Abhidhamma continuously for three months.
Having enabled numerous deities, headed by his mother, to attain the path of stream-entry, and having completed the rains retreat, he performed the descent from the heavens.
Surrounded by a multitude of gods and brahmās, he descended at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa.
He performed a favor for the world. At that time, the Blessed One’s gain and honor were like five great Ganges rivers overflowing across Jambudīpa.
Then the heretics, deprived of gain and honor, sat down miserable and dejected with their shoulders slumped and heads cast down.
Seeing them sitting thus, a female lay devotee named Ciñcā Māṇavikā, who was exceedingly beautiful, approached them.
“Venerable sir, why are you sitting here so distressed and dejected? he asked. “But sister, why are you so unconcerned?
“Why, venerable sir? “Sister, from the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been deprived of gains and honor;
the city-dwellers no longer hold us in any regard. “What can I do about this? “By you, sister, [the ascetic]...”
"It is fitting to incite dispraise toward Gotama. She replied, "It is no burden for me," and showing her enthusiasm for the task, she went to the Jeta Grove Monastery at an improper time.

Staying in the lodgings of the sectarians, she rose early in the morning, took perfumes and other offerings from the city-dwellers, and set out from the Jeta Grove as if she were going to pay homage to the Blessed One.
When asked, "Where did you sleep? she replied, "What business is it of yours where I slept? and departed.
As time passed, when questioned again, she said, "I have just emerged from the same fragrant chamber where the ascetic Gotama slept.
The foolish worldlings believed her, but the wise—those who had attained the fruit of stream-entry and beyond—did not believe her. One day...

Having tied a wooden ring around her belly and draped a red cloth over it, she went before the Blessed One, who was seated for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to an assembly including the king, and spoke thus: "O ascetic, you preach the Dhamma;
yet, because of you, you do not allow me—who am pregnant with a child—garlic, black pepper, and other such things? [The Blessed One replied: "It is so."
"Sister, both you and I understand this. She replied, "In the same way, at the time of sexual intercourse, only two people know it, and no others.
At that moment, Sakka’s stone throne of yellow silk (paṇḍukambala-silāsana) showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on this—
Having understood the cause, he commanded two sons of the gods: "One of you, assuming the form of a mouse, must sever the binding cord of that wooden wheel;
the other, raising up a whirlwind, must blow the cloak she wears upward.
They went and did exactly so. As the wooden wheel fell, it broke the instep of her foot. [In the Hall of Truth...]
All the commoners who had assembled there cried out, "Hey, you wicked thief! How could you make such a false accusation against the Lord of the Three Worlds?
Rising up, they each struck him with a handful of earth and cast him out from the assembly hall;
as soon as he passed beyond sight, the earth opened up. At that moment, flames rose from the Avīci hell, and by means of a family heirloom red woolen cloth, [he was drawn out].
Having slandered him, he cast him into Avīci; the gain and honor of the Blessed One became even greater. Therefore it was said:
“Nanda was a disciple of the Buddha Sabbābhibhū;
having falsely accused him, I wandered for a long time in hell.”
“For ten thousand years I wandered long in hell;
having attained human form, I received much false accusation.
By the remainder of that karma, Ciñcā Māṇavikā [accused] me.”
“He slandered with what was untrue, in the presence of the multitude.
Regarding the third question: *abbhakkhānaṃ* means speaking falsely (*abhi-akkhānaṃ*), that is, reviling.

It is said that in the past, when the Bodhisatta had been reborn in an obscure birth as a rogue named Munāḷi, through the power of association with wicked people, he [reviled] the Paccekabuddha named Surabhi.
“He is an immoral monk of evil character,” he reviled him. Because of that unwholesome verbal action, he was boiled in hell for many thousands of years;

yet, in this final existence, through the power of having perfected the ten perfections, he was born as a Buddha and attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of glory. Again, the heretics became emboldened and asked: “How indeed...?”
“We shall bring infamy upon the ascetic Gotama,” they said, and sat down miserable and dejected.
Then a female wanderer named Sundarī approached them, paid homage, and stood there; seeing them silent and saying nothing, she asked, “What is my fault?
They replied, “While we were being harassed by the ascetic Gotama, you remained unconcerned.”
“You will dwell [there]; this is your fault. “What shall I do there?
“Will you be able to produce dispraise of the ascetic Gotama? “I will be able, noble ladies,” he said.
From then on, according to the method described, whenever anyone was seen, he would say, “They have come out after sleeping in the same fragrant chamber as the ascetic Gotama.”
Having said this, he reviled and abused him. Even the members of other sects reviled and abused him, saying, "Behold, sirs, the deed of the ascetic Gotama! For this has been said:
"In former births, I was a rogue named Munāḷi."
I falsely accused the fragrant Paccekabuddha, who was without fault.
Because of the ripening of that karma, I wandered for a long time in hell;
for many thousands of years, I experienced painful sensations.
“By the remainder of that karma, in this final existence, I received false accusations on account of Sundarī. Regarding the fourth question:
*abbhakkhānaṃ* means a specific kind of accusation, namely, reviling and abusing. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta...
Born into a brahmin family, highly learned, and honored and revered by many, he went forth into the ascetic life.

Dwelling in the Himalayas, subsisting on forest roots and fruits, he lived there teaching many young men the mantras. A certain ascetic who had attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments came into his presence.
Upon seeing him, the other became consumed with envy and, though the seer was innocent, accused him of being a seeker of sensual pleasures.
Thinking, "This ascetic is a deceiver," he slandered him; and he said to his own disciples, "This ascetic is such a person of improper conduct.
They too reviled and abused him in that very same way.

Due to the ripening of that unwholesome kamma, after experiencing suffering in hell for a thousand years, having become a Buddha in this final existence, he attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of glory.
She became as manifest as the full moon in the sky. Just so, the heretics, dissatisfied even with that previous slander, again had Sundarī slandered;
they summoned drunkards, gave them a bribe, and commanded them, "Kill Sundarī and cover her body with flower refuse near the gate of Jetavana. They did exactly as instructed.
Then the heretics, saying, "We do not see Sundarī," informed the king. The king said, "Search for her.
They took her from the place where she had been cast down, placed her upon a litter, and showed her to the king, saying, "Behold, sirs, the deed of the disciples of the ascetic Gotama!
And they spread disrepute throughout the entire city regarding the Blessed One and the community of monks.
They wandered about making this proclamation. They placed Sundarī upon a wooden platform in the raw charnel ground. The king issued an order: “Search for the murderers of Sundarī!
At that time, some rascals, having drunk liquor, fell into a quarrel, crying out, “You killed Sundarī!
You killed her! The king’s men seized those rascals and presented them to the king. The king asked, “Tell me, what did you do with Sundarī?”
“Has she been killed? “Yes, Your Majesty. “By whom was she ordered? “By the heretics, Your Majesty.
The king had the heretics brought before him and bound them, saying, “Go, men! Proclaim: ‘We ourselves have had Sundarī put to death for the sake of slandering the Buddha;
the Blessed One and his disciples are innocent. They did exactly as they were told. All the inhabitants of the city—
They became free from doubt. The king, having had the heretics and the rogues executed, caused them to be discarded.
Thereupon, the gain and honor for the Blessed One increased even more than before. Therefore it was said:
“I was a learned brahmin, honored and revered.”
In the Great Forest, I was teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins.
There, the formidable seer Āgata, possessed of the five super-knowledges and great psychic power, arrived.
Seeing him come, though he was innocent, I slandered him.
Then I said to my students, “This seer is a seeker of sensual pleasures”;
and even as I spoke, the young men gave their approval.
Thereupon all the young men followed that mendicant from family to family.
They said to the great multitude, "This seer was a consumer of sensual pleasures.
By the ripening of that karma, all these five hundred bhikkhus have received false accusations on account of Sundarika."
Regarding the fifth question: "A stone-thrower" means he threw a stone with a struck mind. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta and his younger brother were both sons of the same father.
After their father passed away, they became hostile toward one another, quarreling over the slaves.
By virtue of his own strength, the Bodhisatta overwhelmed his younger brother.

He hurled a stone at him. Due to the ripening of that karma, after experiencing suffering for many thousands of years in the hells and other realms, he was born as a Buddha in this final existence. Devadatta was the maternal uncle of Prince Rāhula;
formerly, during the time when they were merchants of Sīrī, he was a trader together with the Bodhisatta. They [went] to a certain port town...
Having reached [the house], they both entered, saying, "You take one row; I too shall take one row.
Of those two, in the row entered by Devadatta, there were only two people: the wife of an aged merchant and her granddaughter.
A large golden bowl of theirs, covered in grime, had been placed inside another vessel. Not recognizing it for a golden bowl, she said, "This..."

“Take the bowl and give me the jewelry,” he said. He took it, drew a line with a needle, and realizing it was a golden bowl, thought, “I will take it after giving him a small amount,” and then departed.
Then, seeing the Bodhisatta approaching the door, he said, “Niece, noble lady, give me my tortoise-shell jewelry.”
She had him summoned, seated him, and gave him the bowl, saying, "Take this and give it to my granddaughter to wear as an ornament.
The Bodhisatta, taking it and realizing it was a golden bowl, understood that he had been deceived;
he then gave her the eight kahāpaṇas he had kept in his own bag, along with the remaining goods, and [received] the bracelet.
Having had the jewelry fastened upon the hand of the young girl, he departed. When that merchant returned and asked about her, they replied, "Father, you did not take her;
my son gave this and that to him, and having taken her, he went away.
Upon hearing this, as if his heart were torn asunder, he ran after him. The Bodhisatta, having boarded a ship, set sail.
Saying, "Stay! Do not flee! Do not flee! he made this aspiration: "May I be able to destroy him in every birth where he is reborn.
By virtue of that aspiration, after harassing one another through many hundreds of thousands of births, in this present existence—

Having been born into the Sakyan clan and having gradually attained omniscience under the Blessed One, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, he went into the presence of the Blessed One together with Anuruddha and others.
Having gone forth and become an attainer of the jhānas, he became well-known and requested a boon from the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, let the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus undertake the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), such as the practice of living on almsfood."
“Let the entire community of bhikkhus be my burden,” he said. The Blessed One did not grant permission.

Having conceived enmity and fallen away from meditative absorption, Devadatta, desiring to kill the Blessed One, one day stood atop Mount Vebhāra and hurled a mountain peak down upon the Blessed One as he was standing at its base.
Through the Blessed One’s supernatural power, another mountain peak [arose] to meet that falling one.
He accepted it. By the friction of those [stones], a splinter arose and came to strike the top of the Blessed One’s foot. Therefore it was said:
“In the past, for the sake of wealth, I killed my half-brother;
I cast him into a mountain ravine and crushed him with a stone.”
“By the ripening of that karma, Devadatta hurled a stone;
It crushed my toe with a pebble from the rock.
In the sixth question—*sakalikā-vedho* means being struck by a splinter. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta...
Born into a noble family, while playing in the main street during his childhood, he saw a Paccekabuddha walking for alms along the road.
Thinking, "Where is this shaven-headed ascetic going? he took a piece of stone and threw it at the back of the man's foot.
The skin on the back of the foot was cut and blood flowed out. Because of that evil deed, for many thousands of years...

Having experienced great suffering in hell, even after becoming a Buddha, he suffered the shedding of blood due to the impact of stones and potsherds on the soles of his feet, as a result of the remnants of his past karma.
Therefore it was said:
“Formerly, when I was a young boy playing on the high road...”
“Having seen a Paccekabuddha, I threw a piece of wood onto the path.
By the ripening of that kamma, in this my final existence,
Devadatta incited assassins against me for the purpose of killing.”
In the seventh question: Nāḷāgirī was the elephant Dhanapālaka, who had been sent for the purpose of killing [the Buddha].
It is said that in the past, when the Bodhisatta had been reborn as an elephant-keeper, he was wandering about mounted on an elephant.

Seeing a Paccekabuddha on the great highway, he spoke with a provoked mind and became filled with resentment, saying, "Where is this shaven-headed man coming from? and he attacked him with the elephant. By that kamma...
Having experienced suffering in the states of misery for many thousands of years, he was born as a Buddha in his final existence.
Devadatta, having made King Ajātasattu his ally, persuaded him, saying, "Great King, kill your father and become king;
I shall kill the Buddha and become the Buddha. One day, with the king’s permission, [he went] to the elephant stable...
Having gone there, he commanded the elephant keepers: "Tomorrow, after you have given sixteen jars of liquor to Nāḷāgiri, send him forth at the time when the Blessed One goes for alms.
A great clamor arose throughout the entire city;
thinking, "We shall witness the battle between the Elephant-Nāga and the Buddha-Nāga," people erected tiered platforms along both sides of the royal highway even before dawn.
They gathered together. The Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs, entered Rājagaha for alms surrounded by the community of monks.
At that moment, they released Nāḷāgiri according to the previously described procedure. He came along, obstructing the streets, crossroads, and other thoroughfares.
At that time, a certain woman carrying a child was walking from street to street; the elephant [caught sight of] that woman.
Having seen him, he pursued him. The Blessed One said, "Nāḷāgiri, you were not sent here to kill me; come toward me.

Hearing those words, he ran toward the Blessed One. The Blessed One directed his loving-kindness (*mettā*), which is capable of pervading infinite beings throughout immeasurable world-systems, toward Nāḷāgiri alone.
Touched by the Blessed One’s loving-kindness, he became free from fear.
Having made the offering, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One placed his hand upon the man’s head.

At that moment, the gods, Brahmās, and others, their hearts filled with wonder and amazement, honored him with flower pollen and other offerings. Throughout the entire city, there were heaps of wealth reaching as high as the knees.
The king [declared]: "Let the wealth at the western gate belong to the city-dwellers; let the wealth at the eastern gate..."
“Let them be in the royal treasury,” he caused the drum to be beaten. All did accordingly. At that time, Nāḷāgiri was named Dhanapāla.
The Blessed One went to the Veḷuvana monastery.
Thus it is said: “In the past, I was an elephant trainer; [I served] the supreme Paccekabuddha.”
As he was wandering for alms, I assailed him with an elephant.
By the ripening of that karma, the elephant Nāḷāgiri, being frantic,
came upon me in the excellent city of Giribbaja in a most terrible manner.
Regarding the eighth question: "Cutting with a blade" (*satthacchedo*) means splitting a tumor with a blade, or cutting with an axe or a knife.
It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was a king in a border region. Due to association with wicked people and because he resided in a border region, he became a rogue and a violent man.
One day, wandering through the city on foot with a sword in hand, he [attacked] innocent people...
He went along splitting the ground with a sword. Due to the ripening of that evil deed,

after being boiled in hell for many thousands of years and experiencing suffering among animals and other realms, by the remainder of that karma, even though he had become a Buddha in his final existence,
he developed a boil on account of the blow from the stone splinter thrown by Devadatta in the manner described above.
With a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), Jīvaka lanced that abscess. For Devadatta, who possessed a mind of enmity, the act of shedding blood was an immediate retribution (*ānantarika*);
for Jīvaka, who possessed a mind of loving-kindness, the lancing of the abscess was purely meritorious. Therefore it is said:
“I was once a king, walking on foot, and I struck a man with a spear;”
"By the ripening of that karma, I suffered intensely in hell.
By the remainder of that same karma, my entire skin on the feet has now been peeled away; for indeed, karma does not perish."
Regarding the ninth question: "Headache" means a disorder of the head, a pain in the head.
It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the village of Kevaṭṭa as a fisherman.
One day, having gone with other fishermen to a place for killing fish, he saw them killing the fish and felt joy there; his attendant likewise felt joy in the same way.

They committed that unwholesome deed. Having experienced suffering in the four states of misery (*apāya*) because of that unwholesome karma, he was reborn in his final existence within the Sakya royal family along with those men.
Even though he eventually attained Buddhahood, he himself experienced a headache.
And as for those Sakyans, according to the method described in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, they [were slain] in the battle at Viḍaḍūbha.
All have met with destruction. Therefore it was said:
“In the village of the fishermen, I was once a fisherman’s son;
seeing the fish being killed, I felt a surge of joy.”
“By the ripening of that kamma, there was pain in my head;
and all the Sakyans were slain when Viṭaṭūbha slaughtered them.
In the tenth question—“eating barley”: this refers to eating barley grains in Verañjā. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta...

Having been reborn in a certain family, by virtue of his birth and his state as a blind fool, he saw the disciples of the Blessed One Phussa eating sweet food and drink, such as rice-meat (*sālibhojana*), and reviled them, saying: "O shaven-headed ascetics!
Eat barley; do not eat rice-meat! Due to the ripening of that unwholesome karma, for many thousands of years...

Having experienced suffering in the four states of misery, and having attained Buddhahood in this final existence, he moved through villages, market towns, and royal capitals to provide for the world.
On one occasion, he arrived at the foot of a *pucimanda* tree, rich with branches and foliage, near the brahmin village of Verañjā.
The brahmin of Verañjā approached the Blessed One and, by way of many discourses, [addressed him].
Failing to defeat the Blessed One, he became a stream-enterer and announced, "Venerable Sir, it is fitting that I enter the rains retreat right here.

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Then, from the following day onward, Māra the Evil One began to instigate the inhabitants of the entire brahmin village of Verañjā against him. As the Blessed One entered for alms—
Due to Māra’s interference, not even a single person gave so much as a spoonful of alms-food.
The Blessed One returned with his bowl empty, surrounded by the community of monks.
When he arrived there, the horse-dealers who had been staying right there offered a gift on that very day; from then on, they invited the Blessed One along with his retinue of five hundred monks.
Having divided five hundred loads of barley from the food supply and having had it threshed, they placed it into the bowls of the monks.
The deities of the entire thousandfold world-system added divine essence to it, just as they did on the day Sujātā cooked the milk-rice.
The Blessed One partook of it; in this manner, he consumed barley for three months. At the end of those three months, Māra’s obstruction ceased.
On the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Brahmin of Verañjā, having remembered [his transgression], was overcome with great spiritual urgency.
He gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and after bowing down, he asked for forgiveness. Thus it is said:
"In the dispensation of Phussa, I reviled the disciples..."
"Eat and consume barley, but do not eat it with longing.
By the ripening of that karma, I ate barley for three months;
invited by a brahmin, I then dwelt in Verañjā.
In the eleventh question: "Back pain" refers to an ailment of the back. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a householders’ family;
he was endowed with great strength but possessed short limbs.
At that time, there was a wrestler who, while wrestling matches were being held in all the villages, market towns, and royal capitals throughout Jambudīpa, had defeated men and achieved victory.
Kama reached the city where the Bodhisatta resided, and having struck down the people there as well, he began to depart.
Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, "He is leaving after achieving victory in my own dwelling place," approached the city moat, slapped his arms, and said, "Come back!
Come and fight with me before you go! Kama laughed and said, "I am a great man..."
"I threw him down; this short-limbed dwarf is not even a match for one of my hands! Having said this, he slapped his arms and came forward roaring.

Both of them grasped each other's hands; the Bodhisatta lifted him up, whirled him around in the air, and as he brought him crashing to the ground, he broke his backbone and cast him down. All the inhabitants of the city raised a great shout.
Having performed the act, they honored the Bodhisatta by clapping their hands and offering garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
The Bodhisatta laid the wrestler flat on his back, straightened his spine, and sent him away, saying, "Go; from now on, do not act in such a manner.
Due to the ripening of that karma, he experienced suffering in the head, body, and other parts of his frame in every successive birth.
Even though he had become a Buddha in this final existence, he experienced suffering such as backache.
Therefore, whenever back pain arose, he would say to Sāriputta and Moggallāna, "From now on, you two teach the Dhamma," and he himself would spread out the Sugata’s robe and lie down;
for even a Buddha is not released from what is called the "remnant of karma. Thus it has been said:
“When the wrestling match was underway, I struck down the son of a wrestler;
by the ripening of that kamma, there was pain in my back. Regarding the twelfth question:
*atisāra* means a purgative for dysentery. It is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of householders.
Having been reborn, he made his living through the practice of medicine. While treating a merchant’s son who was afflicted by disease, he prepared medicine and cured him;
however, due to negligence regarding the gift to be given, he administered another drug and performed emetics and purgatives.
The merchant gave him much wealth. By the ripening of that kamma, in each successive birth...

He was afflicted by the ailment of bloody dysentery. Even in this final existence, at the moment of his Parinibbāna, as soon as he had eaten the *sūkaramaddava* cooked by Cunda the smith together with food into which the deities of the entire Cakkavāḷa had infused divine seeds, there occurred a purging of bloody dysentery. [It was as if] for hundreds of thousands of millions of elephants...
His strength went to destruction. As the Blessed One was traveling toward Kusinārā for his final passing away on the full moon day of Visākha, he sat down at many places;
becoming thirsty, he drank water, and with great suffering he reached Kusinārā and attained parinibbāna at the time of dawn.
Such is the nature of the net of karma; it does not abandon even the Lord of the three worlds. Therefore it is said:
“I was once a physician and purged the son of a merchant;
by the ripening of that kamma, I have this dysentery.
Thus the Victor explained before the assembly of monks.
"Having attained the power of all direct knowledges, at the great lake Anotatta.
Thus, by way of setting forth the table of contents for the questions thus promised, the "Account of the Unwholesome" (Akusalāpadāna) is said to be completed.
"Itthaṃ sudanti": *itthaṃ* means "in this manner," according to the method stated below; *sudanti* is a particle used for the purpose of completing the meter.
The Blessed One has arrived— the one endowed with good fortune, the Great Being who has fulfilled the perfections— [according to the definition]: "He is the Blessed One because he possesses fortune,
because he has broken [defilements], because he is joined with [virtues],
because he has analyzed excellences, because he has enjoyed [the Dharma], because he has cast out [defilements], and because he has gone beyond all states of existence."
Endowed with such qualities as these, the Blessed One— the God of Gods, the Sakka beyond Sakka, the Brahma beyond Brahma, the Buddha beyond Buddha— that Greatly Compassionate One,
reflecting upon His own conduct as a Buddha and the causes for His Buddhahood, made them manifest and spoke, preached,
and recited this Dharma discourse and sutta known as the *Buddhāpadāniya*, which elucidates the causes for Buddhahood.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Buddha-apadāna* within the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Visuddhajanavilāsinī*. 2.
Commentary on the *Paccekabuddha-apadāna*.

Immediately following that, while reciting the *Apadāna*, when asked, "Friend Ānanda, where was the *Paccekabuddhāpadāna* laid down by the Blessed One?", he replied, "Now, listen to the *Paccekabuddhāpadāna*. The meaning of their *Apadānas* has already been stated above.
(83) Explaining the phrase "Listen! by way of its origin and production, he spoke the passage beginning with, "The Tathāgata dwelling in Jetavana... and so forth.
Therein, in the monastery known by the name of Prince Jeta, he dwells—whether abiding in the four postures or in the divine, brahma, and noble dwellings.

He is called the Tathāgata because, just as the previous Buddhas such as Vipassī and others arrived after fulfilling the thirty perfections, so too has our Blessed One arrived. [The phrase] "dwelling in the Jeta Grove" refers to that Tathāgata.
The connection [is as follows]: "Vedehamuni" means that she was born in the kingdom of Videha, thus she is Vedehī; the son of Vedehī is Vedehiputta. "Mona" is said to be knowledge (*ñāṇa*);
one who has gone to or proceeded by means of that is a "muni. He is both the son of Vedehī and a muni, thus he is called "Vedehiputtamuni.

In what should have been stated as such, by the method of etymology (*nirutti*) beginning with "the addition of a vowel" (*vaṇṇāgamo*), there is the substitution of *a* for the letter *i*, and the elision of the word "putta."

Having done so, it was said, “The sage of Videha. The Venerable Ānanda, who had been placed in this foremost position by the Blessed One—“Bhikkhus, among my disciples, monks who are mindful, resolute, possessed of understanding, learned, and attendants, this is the foremost, namely Ānanda”—bowed his limbs, bent his body, and with palms joined, asked:
“Venerable sir, what are those called Paccekabuddhas like?”
The connection is with the phrase "they exist," which was asked. By what causes and by what reasons do those Paccekabuddhas come into being, that is, arise?
The word "Vīra" is an address to the Blessed One. 84–85.
Following that, in order to show the manner in which [the question] was answered, he said: "Then the Supreme All-Knowing Great Sage... and so forth.

He is called "Omniscient" (*sabbaññū*) because he knows everything—divided into the past and so forth—as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand. He is the "Supreme Omniscient One" (*sabbaññuvara*) because he is both omniscient and the most excellent (*vara*).

He is a "Great Sage" (*mahesi*) because he seeks (*esati*) and searches for the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*), and the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha*). [He addresses him] with the auspicious name "Ānanda" in a sweet voice...
The connection is: "At that time, when asked, he spoke by way of his voice.

O Ānanda, those Paccekabuddhas who, having performed service under former Buddhas—those past Buddhas of the previous ages—and having accumulated a store of merit, did not obtain liberation within the teachings of the Jinas and did not reach Nibbāna—all those wise Paccekabuddhas, in this world, by way of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), [regard] one person...
The meaning is that they became Paccekabuddhas by making an effort. "With very sharp wisdom" means with exceedingly keen wisdom.
"Even without Buddhas" means even when deprived of the exhortations and instructions of the Buddhas.
Even by means of a limited or insignificant object, they attain—that is, they penetrate—the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, an enlightenment that follows immediately after that of a Sammasambuddha.
86. In the entire world, throughout the whole triple world, there is no one equal to me—setting me aside, that is, excluding me—not even among the Paccekabuddhas.
I shall speak, I shall explain to you well and thoroughly this praise, this quality of those Great Sages, the Paccekabuddhas; this is the meaning.
87. Having become teacherless, you yourselves— among the Buddhas who have realized [the truth] by themselves and among the great seers (isī)—
like a small honey-bee amidst a cluster of honey, desiring and longing for Nibbāna as the excellent, sweet words, the utterances of inspired speech,
the unsurpassed medicine and remedy free from superior [to it], all of you with well-clarified minds.
"With well-pleased minds, listen and attend"—this is the meaning.
88–89. "Of the Paccekabuddhas who have assembled" means of those Paccekabuddhas who have arisen and gathered together in a group.
[They are] Ariṭṭha, Upariṭṭha, Tagarasikhī, Yasassī, Sudassana, Piyadassī, Gandhāra, Piṇḍola, and Upāsabha.
Nitha, Tatha, Sutavā, Bhāvitatta, Sumbha, Subha, Methula as the eighth,
Sumedha, Anīgha, Sudātha, Hiṅgu, Hiṅga, Dvejālina, Aṭṭhaka, Kosala, Subāhu, Upanemisa, Nemisa, Santacitta, Sacca, Tatha, Viraja,
Paṇḍita, Kāla, Upakāla, Vijita, Jita, Aṅga, Paṅga, and Guttijita.
Passī, Jahī, Upadhi, Dukkhmūla, Aparājita, Sarabhaṅga, Lomahaṃsa, Uccaṅgamāya,
Asita, Anāsava, Manomaya, Mānacchida, Bandhumā, Tadādhimutta,
Vimala, Ketumā, Kotumbaraṅga, Mātaṅga, Ariya, Accuta, Accutagāmi, Byāmaka, Sumaṅgala, Dibbila, and so forth— of these one hundred Paccekabuddhas.
Those apadānas which are individual explanations handed down in succession; the danger [of attachment] and the ground for dispassion (*virāga*);
the reason for not clinging; and how, and by what cause, they attained enlightenment and realized the knowledge of the four paths. "In grounds of passion" (*sarāgavatthusu*) means:

in those grounds where one should thoroughly cling—namely, in the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*)—one perceives them as dispassionate (*virāgasaññī*).
Possessing perceptions of dispassion toward the world that is full of passion, in a world whose nature is clinging,
they have minds detached from it and intentions free from clinging. Having abandoned *papañca*— for passion is *papañca*, hatred is *papañca*,
and all defilements are *papañca*— having abandoned the defilements designated as *papañca*, and having conquered the "throbbings," that is, the sixty-two types of speculative views, even so...
For that reason, they thus attained enlightenment; the meaning is that they realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment) through direct experience.

90–91. "Having laid aside the rod toward all beings": having laid aside—meaning set aside—threatening, striking, killing, and binding, and not harming, not injuring even a single being among all those sentient creatures.

Not causing suffering with a mind of loving-kindness, thinking, "May all beings be happy," he is one who possesses loving-kindness, whose nature is to feel compassion for their welfare through a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
Alternatively, "having laid aside the rod toward all beings":
the word "all" (*sabbesu*) is an expression that encompasses everything in every way, entirely, without remainder, and exhaustively. "Toward beings" (*bhūtesu*)...

"Beings" (*bhūta*) refers to both the mobile (*tasa*) and the stationary (*thāvara*). Those whose craving (*taṇhā*) has not been abandoned, and those whose fears and terrors have not been abandoned, are the mobile.

For what reason are they called "mobile"? They tremble (*tasanti*), they are terrified, they are distressed, they fear, and they fall into a state of panic; for that reason they are called "mobile. Those whose craving has been abandoned, and those...
Fear and terror have been abandoned; they are steadfast. For what reason are they called steadfast?
Because they do not tremble, do not fear, do not become terrified, do not shrink back, do not feel dread, and do not fall into panic—therefore they are called steadfast.
There are three rods: the rod of body, the rod of speech, and the rod of mind. The threefold misconduct of body is the rod of body.
The fourfold misconduct of speech is the verbal rod; the threefold misconduct of mind is the mental rod.

Having laid down, having set aside, having lowered, having fully lowered, having deposited, and having stilled this threefold rod toward all beings and all creatures—meaning not taking it up for the purpose of harming—all beings, [this is expressed as] "having laid down the rod toward all beings."
"Without harming even one among them" means: not harming even a single being with the hand, or a clod of earth, or a staff, or a sword, or a sling, or a rope;
and not harming all beings with the hand, or a clod of earth, or a staff, or a sword, or a sling, or a rope—without harming even one among them.
For them: "One should not desire a son, much less a companion"—this is the negation. "Son" refers to four kinds of sons:
the son born of one's own body (*atrāja*), the son born of the field (*khettaja*), the son given in adoption (*dinnaka*), and the pupil-son (*antevāsika*).
"Companion" is said of one with whom coming is easy, going is easy, standing is easy, sitting is easy, conversing is easy, and chatting is easy.
It is comfortable to converse [alone]. One should not desire a son;
how much less a companion? Thus, one should not desire, approve of, long for, yearn for, or crave even a son;
how much less should one desire, approve of, long for, yearn for, or crave a friend, a relative, an associate, or a companion? Thus, "one should not desire a son."
"Whence [comes] a companion? One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn"—thus the Paccekasambuddha is "one" in the sense of being designated as having gone forth;

he is "one" in the sense of being without a second; he is "one" in the sense of the abandoning of craving; he is "one" as one who is entirely free from lust; he is "one" as one who is entirely free from hatred;
he is "one" as one who is entirely free from delusion; he is "one" as one who is entirely without defilement; he is "one" as one who has gone the single path; he is "one" as one who is unsurpassed...
"He has awakened to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha" refers to being alone. How is that Paccekabuddha "alone" by way of the going-forth?

For that Paccekabuddha, having severed all the impediments of household life, having severed the impediment of wife and children, the impediment of relatives, and the impediment of friends and companions...
Having severed the impediment of hoarding, having shaved off his hair and beard, having donned saffron-colored robes,
and having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, he attained the state of possessing nothing; thus, as a Paccekabuddha,
he was "one" by virtue of what is termed renunciation, for he wandered, dwelt, moved, conducted himself, protected, maintained, and sustained himself all alone.
In what sense is that paccekasambuddha “one” in the sense of being without a second?

Having thus gone forth, he resorts to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats—places that are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, suitable for private seclusion, and fit for solitary living.
He stands alone, walks alone, sits alone, and lies down alone.
One enters a village for alms alone; one returns alone; one sits in seclusion alone; one walks in meditation alone;
and he lives, dwells, conducts himself, carries on, protects, maintains, and sustains himself alone—thus he is "one" in the sense of being without a second.
How is that paccekabuddha "one" in the sense of the abandoning of craving? He is alone, without a second, diligent, and ardent.
Dwelling with resolute self-exertion and striving at the Great Exertion, he shattered Māra, the dark one, the kinsman of negligence, together with his host.
He abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and utterly eliminated the spreading and clinging net of craving.
“A person with craving as his companion wanders for a long time through the cycle of existence.”
“From this state to another state, one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having understood this danger— that craving is the origin of suffering—
a bhikkhu should wander mindfully, free from craving and without grasping.”
Thus, that Paccekasambuddha is "one" in the sense of having abandoned craving.
How is that Paccekasambuddha "one" as being entirely free from lust? He is one because lust has been abandoned;
he is one because hatred has been abandoned, thus he is entirely free from hatred; he is one because delusion has been abandoned, thus he is entirely free from delusion.
He is "one" because he is entirely free from defilement due to the abandoning of the defilements; likewise, that Paccekasambuddha is "one" because he is entirely free from lust.
How is that Paccekasambuddha "one" because he has gone by the path traveled by only one?
The "path traveled by only one" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.
“The one who sees the destruction of birth knows this single way, the path that leads to welfare and compassion.
By means of this path, those of old have crossed over, and those yet to come will cross, as do those crossing now, the flood.”—
Thus, he is "one" because he has gone upon the path of the single way (*ekāyanamagga*).
How is that Paccekasambuddha "one"? He is one because he has awakened alone to the unsurpassed, individual enlightenment (*paccekasambodhi*).

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is said to be the knowledge (*ñāṇa*) in the four paths; it is wisdom (*paññā*), the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), the power of wisdom (*paññābala*), and the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*).

Investigation is insight; it is right view. That paccekasambuddha, by means of that knowledge of paccekabodhi, awakened to the fact that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," he awakened to the fact that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering," and he awakened to the fact that "all phenomena are non-self.

He awakened to the fact that "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," he awakened to the fact that "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises," and with consciousness as condition...
He awakened to: "name-and-form"; he awakened to: "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases"; he awakened to: "with the six sense bases as condition, contact";
he awakened to: "with contact as condition, feeling"; he awakened to: "with feeling as condition, craving";
he awakened to: "with craving as condition, clinging"; he awakened to: "with clinging as condition, existence"; he awakened to: "with existence as condition, birth."
He awakened to: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be. He awakened to: “With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease”; he awakened to:

“With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases”… [and so on] …he awakened to: “With the cessation of existence, birth ceases”; he awakened to: “With the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases.
He awakened to: “This is suffering”; he awakened to: “This is the origin of suffering”; he awakened to: “This is the cessation of suffering.”
He awakened to: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He awakened to: "These are the taints," and he awakened to:
"This is the origin of the taints" … [and so on] … he awakened to: "This is the way. He awakened to: "These phenomena are to be directly known," he awakened to:
"These phenomena are to be abandoned," and he awakened to: "These phenomena are to be realized. These phenomena...
He awakened to the thought, "They are to be developed. He awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact;
he awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging;
and he awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the four great elements.
He awakened; he awakened to the fact that "whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.

Alternatively, whatever is to be awakened to, to be fully awakened to, to be thoroughly awakened to, to be completely awakened to, to be attained, to be touched, and to be realized—all that he awakened to, fully awakened to, by means of that knowledge of the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.
"He awakened, fully understood, attained, touched, and realized"—thus that Paccekasambuddha alone has perfectly awakened to the unsurpassed Paccekabodhi; he is "one.
He practices the eight modes of conduct: the conduct of postures, the conduct of sense bases, the conduct of mindfulness, and the conduct of concentration.
The conduct of knowledge, the conduct of the path, the conduct of attainment, and the conduct for the welfare of the world. Conduct in the postures refers to the four postures;
conduct in the sense bases refers to the six internal and external sense bases; conduct in mindfulness refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
conduct in concentration refers to the four jhānas; conduct in knowledge refers to the four noble truths; and conduct in the path refers to the four...
"Conduct pertaining to the noble paths" refers to the four fruits of asceticism;
"conduct for the benefit of the world" refers to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, partially to the Paccekabuddhas, and partially to the disciples.
There is also "conduct regarding the modes of deportment" for those endowed with aspiration, and "conduct regarding the sense bases" for those who guard the doors of the faculties.
The practice of mindfulness for those dwelling in heedfulness; the practice of concentration for those devoted to higher consciousness;
the practice of knowledge for those endowed with wisdom; the practice of the path for those who have entered correctly; the practice of attainment for those who have realized the fruits;
the practice for the welfare of the world for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and [the practice] in part for the Paccekabuddhas.
These eight modes of conduct are partial to the disciples.
There are another eight modes of conduct: one who is resolving conducts with faith; one who exerts conducts with energy;
one who establishes conducts with mindfulness; one who brings about non-distraction conducts with concentration; one who understands conducts with wisdom.
One who acts while cognizing acts by way of the conduct of consciousness (*viññāṇacariyā*). For one practicing in this way, wholesome states become a basis;
thus, one acts by way of the conduct of the sense bases (*āyatanacariyā*). One who practices in this way attains distinction; thus, one acts by way of the conduct of distinction (*visesacariyā*).

These are the eight conducts. There are another eight conducts: the conduct of seeing (*dassanacariyā*) through right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), and the conduct of directing toward (*abhiniropanacariyā*) through right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).
The practice of non-possessiveness is for right speech; the practice of undertaking is for right action;
the practice of purification is for right livelihood; the practice of exertion is for right effort; the practice of establishment is for right mindfulness;
and the practice of non-distraction is for right concentration. These are the eight practices.
"Like the rhinoceros's horn": just as the horn of a rhinoceros is indeed single and without a second, even so that Paccekasambuddha is like that, similar to that, of that same nature.

Just as what is excessively salty is called "salty-like," what is excessively bitter is called "bitter-like," what is excessively sweet is called "sweet-like," and what is excessively hot is called...
"A fire-like age" is said of an era of extreme cold; "an ocean-like age" is said of a great mass of water;
and a disciple who has attained the power of great direct knowledge is called "teacher-like.

In the same way, that Paccekabuddha is like the horn of a rhinoceros—resembling a rhinoceros horn, like a rhinoceros horn, and its counterpart—solitary and peerless, with bonds released, he moves, dwells, and conducts himself rightly in the world.
He exists, protects, maintains, and sustains—thus one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. Therefore the Paccekabuddhas have said:
“Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, not harming even one among them;
one should desire no son, much less a companion—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
“For one born of association, affections arise; from these affections, this suffering comes into being.
Seeing the danger born of affection, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Out of compassion for friends and companions, one whose mind is bound to them ruins his own welfare.”
Seeing this danger in social attachment, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Just as a wide-spreading bamboo is entangled by its own growth, so too is attachment to children and wives;
like a new shoot on that bamboo, one who remains unattached should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Just as a deer in the forest, unbound, goes wherever it pleases for its range,
so should a wise man, seeing his own freedom, wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
There is conversation in the midst of companions, whether in staying, standing, going, or wandering.”
Beholding the uninhabited forest as a desirable state, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Amidst companions there is play and delight, and toward children there is great affection;
loathing the separation from those who are dear, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Being impartial toward all four quarters and free from aversion, content with whatever comes his way,
undaunted by hardships and patient, let him wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Some who have gone forth are difficult to restrain, as are some householders living at home.”
Free from anxiety regarding the children of others, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the insignia of a householder, like a *koviḷāra* tree with its leaves stripped away,
the hero, having severed the bonds of household life, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“If one should find a prudent companion to walk with— one who is steadfast, lives rightly, and is wise— then,
having overcome all dangers, one may wander with him, joyful and mindful.
“But if one does not find a prudent companion to walk with— one who is steadfast, lives rightly, and is wise— ”
Having abandoned his conquered kingdom like a king, one should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest.
"Truly, we praise the attainment of good companions; companions who are equal and excellent are those with whom one should associate.
Failing to find such, one who eats blameless food should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."
“Having seen two golden armlets, radiant and well-finished by a smith’s son,
clashing against each other upon my arm, let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
May I have no conversation or even angry outbursts with a second person.”
Foreseeing this danger in the future, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and enchanting; they agitate the mind in their diverse forms.
Having seen the peril in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Calamity, tumor, and affliction, disease, arrow, and fear—this is what they are.
Seeing this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind and sun, gadflies and serpents;”
Having overcome all these things, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like an elephant, having avoided the herds, with its trunk grown long, magnificent and lotus-adorned,
dwelling in the forest as it pleases, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience occasional liberation;
having heeded the words of the Kinsman of the Sun, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having transcended the thorns of views, having attained the path and secured the state of certainty.”
I have attained knowledge and am no longer led by others; let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirsting desire, free from hypocrisy, with the dross of passion and delusion burnt away, and having become one who has no expectations for the whole world—let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“One should avoid an evil companion, one who sees no harm and is intent on what is wrong;
one should not associate with one who is addicted to and negligent in sensual pleasures. One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One should cultivate a friend who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, noble, and eloquent.”
Having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Without adorning oneself with play, delight, or sensual pleasure in the world, and without looking back at them;
abstaining from the grounds for vanity and speaking the truth, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

“Having abandoned son and wife, father and mother, wealth and grain, and kinsmen—having renounced sensual pleasures as they arise—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. This is a bond;
here there is but little happiness; there is little gratification, but suffering indeed is more abundant here.”
Knowing that this is a fetter, the wise man should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having torn asunder the fetters, like a water-dweller breaking through a net in the water,
like a fire that does not turn back once it has burnt its fuel, he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
With downcast eyes and not fidgeting with his feet, guarding his sense-faculties and protecting his mind,
untainted and unburning, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the insignia of a householder, like a *pārichatta* tree with its leaves completely fallen away.
Having gone forth clad in saffron robes, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Free from greed for flavors, not lustful, not supporting others, and wandering from house to house in regular succession;
with a mind unattached to family after family, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Having abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind, having dispelled all secondary defilements,
being independent and cutting off the fault of attachment— one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having turned one’s back on both pleasure and pain, and even before that, on joy and grief...”
Having attained equanimity and purified tranquility, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Arousing energy for the attainment of the supreme goal, with a mind undaunted and conduct untiring,
firm in exertion and endowed with fortitude and strength, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Never abandoning the jhānas of seclusion, always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma regarding all phenomena,
contemplating the peril in states of existence— one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Aspiring for the destruction of craving, heedful, not dull-witted or deaf-mute, learned and mindful— ”
One who has mastered the Dhamma, who is resolute and exerts himself, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Like a lion undaunted by sounds, like the wind unentangled in a net,
like a lotus unsullied by water— one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
“Just as a lion, powerful with its fangs, moves having overcome [all] by force, so should the king of deer move having overcome [all].
One should frequent remote lodgings; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Practicing loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, liberation, and sympathetic joy at the proper times;”
Unopposed by the entire world, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and having torn asunder the fetters,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, remaining undaunted at the end of life.
“They resort to and serve [others] for a purpose; friends without a motive are rare these days.
People are impure in their wisdom regarding their own welfare; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Therein, “toward all beings” refers to the *Khaggavisāṇa-paccekabuddhāpadāna-sutta*. What is its origin? It is the origin of all suttas.
There are four ways of origin: from one’s own inclination, from another’s inclination, from the occasion of a specific event, and from the prompting of a question.
In this regard, the origin of the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta* is generally from the prompting of a question;

specifically, however, some verses therein were spoken by various Paccekabuddhas when questioned, while others were spoken without being asked, in accordance with the method of the path they had personally realized.
Since it is indeed an *udāna* (inspired utterance) that is being uttered, therefore, in some cases the origin is occasioned by a question, while in others it arises from one's own inclination.
Therein, this origin which is occasioned by a question without distinction should be understood as follows from the very beginning:
"At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then, when the Venerable Ānanda had gone into seclusion..."

While in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind: "The aspiration and the formal resolution of the Buddhas are seen, as well as those of their disciples; however, they are not seen in the case of the Paccekabuddhas.
What if I were to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this? Emerging from seclusion, he approached the Blessed One and, in due order, [inquired].
He asked about this matter. Then the Blessed One spoke to him the Pubbayogāvacara Sutta:
“Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one who practices the preliminary yoga:
either he attains final knowledge right here and now, or if he does not attain final knowledge right here and now, then he attains final knowledge at the time of death.”
"Then, as a son of the gods, he propitiates another [Buddha]. Then, in the presence of Buddhas, he becomes one who attains the higher knowledges quickly.
Then, in his final time, he becomes a Paccekasambuddha.
Having said this, he spoke again:

“Ānanda, those called Paccekabuddhas are endowed with the initial resolve (abhinīhāra) and have practiced the preliminary exercises (pubbayoga); therefore, the aspiration and the resolve of all Buddhas and disciples of the Buddhas are to be desired.
He asked: “Venerable sir, for how long does the aspiration of the Buddhas last?
“Ānanda, at the minimum limit, it lasts for four incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand kappas; at the middle limit, it lasts for eight incalculable eons.”
One hundred thousand kappas, and at the upper limit, sixteen asaṅkhyeyyas and one hundred thousand kappas.
These divisions should be understood according to those who are preeminent in wisdom, preeminent in faith, and preeminent in energy.
For those preeminent in wisdom, their faith is dull and their wisdom is sharp; for those preeminent in faith, their wisdom is middling and their faith is sharp.
For those in whom energy (*vīriya*) predominates, faith (*saddhā*) and wisdom (*paññā*) are dull, while their energy is sharp.

However, even if one were to give gifts day after day equal to the Vessantara gift for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and a hundred thousand aeons (*kappa*), and were to accumulate the corresponding perfections of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, it is impossible that such a person would become a Buddha in the interim. Why is this?
Knowledge does not conceive, it does not reach growth, and it does not come to maturity.

Just as a crop that is to be produced after three, four, or five months would, if one were to tend to it a hundred or a thousand times every day and water it with water, yet [fail] in the interim... [by a fortnight...]
Or that it will be produced within a month—such a thing is impossible. Why?
Because the grain does not take root, does not reach fullness, and does not go to maturity.
Even so, without having reached four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, it is impossible for one to become a Buddha in the interim. Therefore, it is exactly as previously stated.
The time must be spent in fulfilling the perfections for the sake of maturing one’s knowledge.
Furthermore, for one who aspires to Buddhahood even during such a period, eight accomplishments must be sought when making the formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
For it is said: “Human birth, the perfection of gender, the cause, and seeing the Teacher;”
“Going forth, the perfection of qualities, the requisite, and zeal—through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
“Resolution” (*abhinīhāra*) is a designation for the original aspiration (*mūlapaṇidhāna*). In this context, “human state” (*manussatta*) means birth as a human being. Apart from...
For indeed, even for one established in the state of a deva or any remaining states of existence other than the human birth, a resolution does not succeed.
However, one established in those states who aspires to Buddhahood must perform meritorious deeds such as giving and so forth, and aspire specifically for human status;
having established oneself there, the resolution should be made. For it is in this way that it succeeds. "Perfection of gender" means the male state.
For even those standing within the human race—women, eunuchs, and hermaphrodites—do not succeed in their aspiration.
However, one standing there who aspires to Buddhahood should perform meritorious deeds such as giving and so forth, and aspire specifically for the male state;
remaining in that state, one should make the aspiration. For it is in this way that it succeeds. "The cause" refers to the cause of Arahantship.

The perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya-sampatti*). For one who, striving in that particular existence, is capable of reaching *arahantship*, their aspiration succeeds, but not that of another, such as the case of the wise Sumedha.
He, indeed, having gone forth at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, was capable of reaching *arahantship* in that very existence. "Beholding the Teacher" means...
It is the direct vision of the Buddhas. For it succeeds only in this way and not otherwise, as was the case with the wise Sumedha.
He, indeed, having seen Dīpaṅkara face to face, made his aspiration. "Going forth" means the state of homelessness;

and that may take place either within the Dispensation or within the orders of ascetics and wanderers who maintain the doctrine of karma and the efficacy of action, as was the case with the wise Sumedha.

For indeed, having become an ascetic named Sumedha, he made a vow (*paṇidhi*). "Perfection of qualities" (*guṇasampatti*) means the attainment of qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
For even one who has gone forth, success is achieved only by one endowed with such qualities and not by another, just as in the case of the wise Sumedha.

He, having become possessed of the five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhiññā*) and the master of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), made his vow. "Service" (*adhikāra*) means the act of superior service.

The meaning is "renunciation. For one who has made the renunciation of life and so forth, the aspiration succeeds only for that person and not for another, as was the case with the wise Sumedha. Indeed, he said:
"Let the Buddha step over me and proceed together with his disciples;..."
"Do not step upon this mud; it will be for my benefit.
Thus, having made the sacrifice of himself, he made his aspiration. *Chandatā* means the desire to act.
