That aspiration succeeds for one in whom that desire is powerful. And if someone were to say: "Who, for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons..."
"Having been cooked in hell, he desires Buddhahood. Upon hearing this, it should be understood that for one who dares to say "I," [the aspiration] is powerful.
Likewise, if someone were to say: "Who desires Buddhahood after treading upon an entire world-system filled with glowing embers?
Who, treading upon an entire world-system strewn with spears and spikes..."
“Who desires Buddhahood after having crossed over the entire Cakkavāḷa filled to the brim with water?
Who desires Buddhahood after having crushed and passed through the entire Cakkavāḷa covered without interval by thickets of bamboo?
Upon hearing this, it should be understood that the power of whoever is able to say, “I [can do it],” is great.
And endowed with such a desire for action, the wise Sumedha made this aspiration.
Thus, having successfully accomplished his resolve, the Bodhisatta does not encounter these eighteen impossible conditions.
For from that time forth, he was never born blind, nor born deaf, nor insane, nor mute, nor a cripple.
He is not born among the barbarians; he is not reborn from the womb of a slave-girl;
he is not one whose wrong view is fixed; his gender does not change; he does not commit the five deeds of immediate retribution;
he is not a leper; he is not one who has turned back from the animal realm; he is not in his final existence as a human being who is inferior to a handstander (a dwarf).
It arises among the hungry ghosts (petas) who are emaciated by hunger and thirst, but it does not arise among the Kālakañjika Asuras, nor in the Avīci Hell, nor in the Lokantariya hells.

Furthermore, among the sense-sphere beings (kāmāvacara), it does not become Māra; among the fine-material-sphere beings (rūpāvacara), it does not arise in the non-percipient realm (asaññībhava), nor in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa);
it does not arise in the immaterial realms (arūpabhava), and it does not migrate to another world-system (cakkavāḷa).
And he is endowed with these four stages of Buddhahood: zeal, ingenuity, steadfastness, and conduct for the welfare of others.
Regarding these: "Zeal is said to be energy; ingenuity is called wisdom;
steadfastness is resolve; and conduct for the welfare of others is the cultivation of loving-kindness."

These should be understood. Furthermore, these six inclinations—which are the inclination toward renunciation, the inclination toward seclusion, the inclination toward non-greed, the inclination toward non-hatred, the inclination toward non-delusion, and the inclination toward escape—lead to the maturation of enlightenment.
Because they possess these, Bodhisattvas who are inclined toward renunciation perceive the defects in sensual pleasures, and those who are inclined toward seclusion...
And it is said that Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in socializing, have a disposition toward non-attachment; Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in greed, have a disposition toward non-greed;
Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in hatred, have a disposition toward non-hatred; Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in delusion, have a disposition toward non-delusion;
and Bodhisattvas, having a disposition toward renunciation, see the fault in all states of existence.
And he is endowed with those [qualities].
But for how long must the aspiration of Paccekabuddhas last? For Paccekabuddhas, it lasts for two *asaṅkhyeyya* kalpas and one hundred thousand *kappas*;
it is not possible for it to be less than that. The reason for this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
Furthermore, for one who aspires to the state of a Paccekabuddha, five perfections must be fulfilled when making the formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
For them: "Human birth, perfection of gender, Vision free from the taints (*āsava*),..."
“Qualification and zeal—these are the causes for the resolution.
Herein, “seeing those free from taints” means the seeing of anyone among the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Buddha. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Now, one might ask: “How much is required for the aspiration of disciples? For the two chief disciples, it is one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
For one hundred thousand eons, and for eighty thousand eons for the great disciples;
likewise for the Buddha’s mother, father, attendant, and son—it is not possible to do so in less than that time, and the reason for this is as already stated.
Furthermore, for all of these individuals, the resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is endowed with two factors: both the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*) and the zeal (*chanda*).

Thus, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) over the aforementioned period of time through this aspiration and this resolve, the Buddhas who arise in the world do so either in a khattiya clan or a brahmin clan;
the Paccekabuddhas arise in one of the khattiya, brahmin, or householder clans;
whereas the Chief Disciples (aggasāvakas), like the Buddhas, arise only in khattiya or brahmin clans.
All Buddhas do not appear during a contracting aeon (*saṃvaṭṭamāna-kappa*); they appear during an expanding aeon (*vivaṭṭamāna-kappa*). The same is true for Paccekabuddhas.
However, they do not appear at the time when Buddhas appear. Buddhas awaken by themselves and awaken others;
Paccekabuddhas awaken by themselves alone and do not awaken others. [They experience] only the flavor of the Dhamma (*attharasa*).
They penetrate [the truth], yet they do not experience the flavor of the Dhamma. For they are unable to teach the supramundane Dhamma by applying it to conventional designations;
their realization of the Dhamma is like a dream seen by a mute person, or like the taste of seasoned broth experienced in a city by a forest-dweller.
They attain every variety of psychic power, meditative attainment, and analytical knowledge.
Due to their distinguished qualities, they stand below the Buddhas and above the disciples; they do not ordain others and then merely instruct them in the training of outward conduct.
Instead, they perform the Uposatha by means of this brief recitation: "The extraction of the arrow of the mind must be performed;
one must not fall into complacency," or simply by saying, "Today is Uposatha. And while performing the Uposatha, they were at Gandhamādana, at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree.

“Having assembled in the Jewel Chamber, they perform [the rites]. Thus, having explained to the Venerable Ānanda the aspirations and the formal resolves (*abhinīhāra*) of the Paccekabuddhas in all their aspects, the Blessed One now spoke of those various Paccekabuddhas who had arisen through such aspirations and such resolves: “Having laid down [all enmity] toward all beings...”
By way of the method beginning with "The staff," he spoke this Khaggavisāṇasutta. This, then, is the origin of the Khaggavisāṇasutta as determined by the question in general.
Now, it must be told in detail. In that regard, first, the origin of this very verse should be understood as follows: this—
It is said that the Paccekabuddha, while entering the stage of a Paccekabodhisatta, fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons;
then, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a forest-dweller and practiced the ascetic life, fulfilling the duty of going forth and returning.
It is said that had he not fulfilled this duty, he would not have attained Paccekabodhi.
There is no such thing. But what is this so-called "practice of going and returning"?
It is "taking and bringing back. We shall explain how that comes about.
Here, one certain bhikkhu takes but does not bring back; another brings back but does not take; another neither...
One takes [the bowl] but does not bring it back; another both takes it and brings it back.

In this regard, a certain bhikkhu, having risen early, performed the duties at the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard, poured water at the Bodhi-tree, filled the water-jar, and placed it in the water-hall;
he then performed the duties toward his teacher and his preceptor, as well as the eighty-two duties prescribed in the Khandhaka.
And having undertaken the fourteen great precepts (*mahāvatta*), he conducts himself accordingly.
Having attended to his bodily needs and entered his lodging, he passes the time in a secluded seat until it is time for the alms-round.

Knowing the time has come, he puts on his lower robe, fastens his waistband, arranges his upper robe, places his outer cloak over his shoulder, hangs his bowl from his neck, and [takes up] his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Mindfully proceeding to the courtyard of the shrine, he pays homage to the shrine and the Bodhi tree.
Having put on his robe near the village and taken his bowl, he enters the village for alms.

Having thus entered, the fortunate monk, who is a recipient of gains and is honored and respected by the lay devotees, returns either to the family that supports him or to the refectory, where he is met by the lay devotees.
Being asked various questions, he abandons that attention by answering those questions and by diverting his discourse with Dharma teachings, and thus departs.
Even when he has returned to the monastery, being questioned by the monks, he speaks, recites the Dharma, and engages in various activities.
This continues after the meal, during the first watch of the night, and during the middle watch.

Having thus engaged in such idle chatter with the bhikkhus, being overcome by physical indisposition, he sleeps even during the last watch of the night and does not attend to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
This is called "carrying away but not bringing back.
However, one who is frequently afflicted by illness finds that food eaten at the time of dawn does not digest properly; how much more so if he has risen [from sleep] earlier?
Being unable to perform the duties as prescribed or to attend to the meditation subject,
he instead enters the village at the very early hour, taking his bowl and robes, longing only for rice gruel, solid food, medicine, or a meal.
Having obtained there rice gruel, solid food, medicine, or a meal, he fills his bowl...

Having brought [the almsfood] out and finished his meal, he sits on the prepared seat, attends to his meditation subject, and—whether or not he has attained distinction—returns to the monastery and dwells with that very same mental attention. This is called "he brings back but does not take.
For such bhikkhus, having drunk the rice-gruel and increased their insight (vipassanā) in the Buddha’s teaching...
Those who have attained Arahatship exceed the path of calculation;
even in the island of Sīhaḷa alone, in this or that village, there was no sitting hall where monks, having sat down and drunk rice-gruel, did not attain Arahatship.
But he who dwells in negligence, having cast aside his burden and broken all the observances, has a mind bound by the five kinds of mental obstructions and fetters.

While dwelling thus, not devoted to attention to the meditation subject, he enters a village for alms and, distracted by extensive talk with householders, goes out empty-handed. This is called "neither carrying it away nor bringing it back.
But he who, having risen early, fulfills all the duties in the aforementioned manner until the time for the alms-round—
Having sat down cross-legged, he brings the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to mind. The meditation subject is twofold:

that which is universal (*sabbatthaka*) and that which is to be carried (*pārihāriya*). Among these, the universal consists of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*).
For it is because these must be practiced and desired everywhere that they are called "universal. As for loving-kindness:
It is desirable in all places, such as dwellings and so forth. For a bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness toward his dwellings becomes dear and pleasing to his fellow celibates;
through that, he dwells in comfort, free from conflict. Toward deities, one who dwells in loving-kindness dwells happily, protected and guarded by those deities.
Toward kings, royal ministers, and others, one who dwells in loving-kindness dwells happily, being cherished by them.
One who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārī*) is honored and respected by people everywhere—in villages, market towns, and so forth—and dwells happily during alms-rounds and other activities.
By the cultivation of the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*), one abandons attachment to life and dwells heedfully (*appamatta*).
Furthermore, that which is always to be carried about, taken up according to one’s temperament, is found among the ten foulness subjects (*asubha*), the kasiṇas, and the recollections (*anussati*).

Alternatively, it is the definition of the four elements itself; because it must be maintained, guarded, and developed, it is called "that which is to be maintained" (*pārihāriya*), and that very thing is also known as the "root meditation subject" (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*).
For sons of good family who desire the welfare [of others] and have gone forth in the Dispensation, even ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred living together in one place—
Having made a formal agreement, they dwell thus: "Friends, you have not gone forth out of debt, nor out of fear, nor because you were driven by a livelihood;
rather, you have gone forth here desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, whatever defilements arise while walking, subdue them right there while walking;
whatever defilements arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, subdue them right there while lying down."

Having thus made this agreement, when they go on their almsround, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, or one gāvuta; with that as a signpost, they go along while attending to the meditation subject.
If defilement arises in anyone while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stops, and then [his companion] from behind—
Even one who is coming along stands still. Thinking, "This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you;
this is not suitable for you," he reproaches himself, develops insight, and right there enters the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).
If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then even one who is coming behind him sits down. This same method applies to the plane of the Noble Ones.
Even if he is unable to fall asleep, he goes along suppressing that defilement and attending only to the meditation subject;
he does not lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject.
If he should so lift it, he turns back and stands right where he was before, just like the Elder Mahā Phussadeva, who dwelt at the Ālindaka.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived in this manner, fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning.

People along the road—whether plowing, sowing, threshing, or performing other labors—saw the Elder walking in such a way and thought, "This Elder goes back again and again; is he perhaps lost, or has he seen something?"

"You have forgotten! they exclaimed. But he, disregarding them, performed the duties of a recluse with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and within twenty years he attained *arahantship*.
On the very day he attained *arahantship*, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there having lit a lamp with her fingers, as did the Four Great Kings and Sakka.
Sakka, lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahampati came to attend upon him.
Seeing that radiance, the forest-dwelling Mahātissa Thera asked him on the following day: "Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night;
what was it? The elder, wishing to avoid the matter, replied: "Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or the light of a gem."

He spoke these words and others such as these. Being pressed with the command, "You must conceal [this]," he admitted, saying "Yes," and then confessed it—just like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavalli bower.

It is said that while fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning, he thought, "First, I shall honor the Blessed One’s Great Striving (Mahāpadhāna)," and for seven years he engaged only in standing and walking meditation.
He made a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāsi*), and after fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning for sixteen years, he attained *arahatta*.

Thus, lifting his foot with a mind devoted to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and turning back from where he had lifted it with a detached mind, he went near the village and stood in a suspicious place, wondering, "Is that a cow, or is it a renunciant? and [took up] his outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
Having put on his robes and taken his bowl, he reaches the village gate, takes water from a streamlet, and rinses his mouth before entering the village.
He does this thinking, "May there be no distraction from my meditation subject even by the mere words 'Long life to you! when people approach to give alms or pay homage.
However, if someone says to him, "Venerable sir, today..."
When people ask, "Is it the seventh day or the eighth? he swallows water and indicates the answer.

If there are no such questioners, at the time of departure he spits out [the water] at the village gate and then goes forth, just like the fifty monks who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery on the island of Sri Lanka. It is said that on the Uposatha day of their entry into the rains retreat...
They made a formal agreement: "Until we have attained arahantship, we shall not speak to one another.

When entering a village for alms, they would rinse their mouths with water at the village gate before entering; when asked about the day's food, if they had been questioned, they would swallow the water and report back;
if not questioned, they would spit it out at the village gate and return to the monastery. There, people [pointed out] the place where they spat.
Having seen them, they recognized: "Today one has come; today two. And they thought: "Why is it that these do not converse with us, or perhaps even with each other?
If they do not converse with each other either, they must certainly have fallen into a dispute;
come now, let us reconcile them with one another. They all went to the monastery.
There, when fifty bhikkhus had entered upon the rains retreat, two bhikkhus did not see each other in a single place.
Then, a man with good eyesight among them said: "Sirs, such is not the dwelling place of those who cause quarrels;
the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard have been well-swept, the brooms have been neatly set aside, and [the water] has been well-placed."

Thinking, "This is water for drinking and water for washing," they turned back from there. Those monks, having spent the rains retreat right there and having increased their insight (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship* and performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) of purity during the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*).
Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavalli bower, the monks who entered the rains retreat at the Kalambatittha monastery [attained the same].
And as if lifting his foot with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he goes near the village;
having rinsed his mouth with water and observed the streets, he enters that path where there are no drunkards, gamblers, or other quarrelsome people, nor fierce elephants, horses, and the like.
And while wandering there for alms, he does not move with hurried haste or speed.

He goes along; there is no such thing as a "speedy alms-collecting ascetic practice" (*javanapiṇḍapātika-dhutanga*), but rather he proceeds remaining motionless like a water-filled cart that has reached uneven ground.

Having entered from house to house, observing whether a person wishes to give or not, and taking alms at the appropriate time for each, he sits down in a suitable place and [engages in] his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
While attending to this, having established the perception of repulsiveness in food, he reflects upon it by way of the similes of axle-oil,
wound-ointment, and the flesh of one’s own son, and partakes of the eightfold food neither for sport nor for intoxication...
[as before] ...and having finished eating, performed his water-rites, and dispelled the fatigue from the meal for a short while, just as he did before the meal, so too...
After the meal, during the first watch and the last watch of the night, he attends to his meditation subject.
This is called "carrying it out and bringing it back. Thus, this process of carrying out and bringing back is called the "practice of going and returning.
If, while fulfilling this, one is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), one attains *arahantship* in the very first stage of life. If not...
If he does not attain it in the first stage of life, then he attains it in the middle stage of life. If he does not attain it in the middle stage of life, then he attains it at the time of death.
If he does not attain it at the time of death, then he attains it having become a son of the gods.
If he does not attain it having become a son of the gods, then he attains final Nibbāna having become a paccekabuddha. If he does not become a paccekabuddha...

Having offered [the oblation], he attains final nibbāna; or else, in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of quick higher knowledge, just like the elder Bāhiya, or one of great wisdom, just like the elder Sāriputta.
Now, this Paccekabodhisatta, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, became a forest-dweller.
Having fulfilled this practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, she passed away and was reborn in the world of the sense-sphere devas.
Falling from there, she took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Skilled women can discern the position of the embryo on that very day; she was one of them, and therefore she too—
She informed the king of that conception. It is a natural law that when a meritorious being is conceived in the womb, the woman receives special care regarding her pregnancy.
Therefore, the king granted her such care.
From then on, she was permitted to consume nothing that was too hot, nor too cold, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too pungent.
It is not too bitter. For when it is swallowed by the mother while she is too hot, it is as if the embryo were living in a cauldron of molten iron;

when she is too cold, it is as if living in the intermediate space between worlds (*lokantarika*); and when she eats what is excessively sour, salty, pungent, or bitter, the limbs of the child experience intense pain, as if they had been cut with a knife and sprinkled with the sour liquids and so forth. Also from excessive walking, standing, sitting, or lying down...
They do not prevent her [from moving], thinking, "May there be no suffering from the movement of that which is within the womb.
Because the ground is covered with soft rugs, she is permitted to perform walking-meditations and other activities in moderation;
she is permitted to consume food and drink that is delicious, suitable, and endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and so forth. Having taken care of her, they cause her to walk, sit, and stand up.

While she was being cared for in this manner, at the time when her pregnancy had matured, she entered the birth chamber and gave birth at dawn to a son who resembled a lump of red arsenic smeared with clarified butter, endowed with the marks of merit and grain.
Then, on the fifth day, they presented him, adorned and prepared, to the king; the king, being delighted, had him attended by sixty-six nurses. He...
Increasing in all perfections, he attained maturity before long. When he reached the age of sixteen, the king consecrated him in the kingship and provided him with various theatrical performances.
Having been consecrated, the prince ruled the kingdom under the name Brahmadatta over twenty thousand cities throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Indeed, formerly in Jambudīpa...
There were originally eighty-four hundred thousand cities; as they declined, there were sixty thousand; declining further from that, there were forty thousand;
but at the time of their total decline, there were twenty thousand. And this Brahmadatta arose during the period of total decline;
therefore, he possessed twenty thousand cities, twenty thousand palaces, and twenty thousand elephants.
Twenty thousand horses, twenty thousand chariots, twenty thousand foot soldiers, twenty thousand women—
both those of the harem and female dancers— and twenty thousand ministers.
While exercising great sovereignty, he performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
And he brought them forth. Since one who has been anointed king must necessarily sit in the court of justice, he therefore partook of his morning meal early one day and sat in the place of judgment.
There they made a great clamor and a loud noise; thinking, "This sound is an obstacle to meditative attainment," he ascended to the palace roof and [entered] meditative attainment.
While sitting with the thought, "I shall attain [concentration]," he was unable to attain it; his meditative absorption (samāpatti) was lost due to the distraction of kingship.
Then he reflected: "Which is better, kingship or the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma)?

Thereupon, knowing that "the pleasure of kingship is limited and fraught with many dangers, whereas the pleasure of the duty of a recluse is vast, possesses many benefits, and is practiced by the supreme persons," he [chose] another...
He commanded his minister, "Rule this kingdom with righteousness and justice;
do not act unrighteously," and having handed over everything to him, he ascended the palace and spent his time in the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
No one was permitted to approach him, except for those who brought water for rinsing the mouth, tooth-sticks, or food.
When half a month had passed, the chief queen asked, "The king is not seen anywhere—at the pleasure gardens, the review of the army, or at the theatrical performances;
where has he gone? They reported the matter to her. She sent a message to the minister:
"Since the kingdom is concealed, I too am concealed; let him come and enjoy union with me."
Thus, covering both his ears, he refused, saying, "This is not to be heard.
She sent him again two or three times, and when he would not consent, she threatened him, saying, "If you do not do it, I shall remove you from this place; I shall even take your life.
Terrified, he thought, "Women are indeed firm in their resolve; perhaps she will even do such a thing as this. One day, in private...
Having gone there, he enjoyed amorous dalliance with her upon a luxurious couch. She was virtuous and possessed a pleasant touch;
he, being infatuated by his passion for that touch, went there frequently, feeling increasingly bold.
Gradually, he began to enter as if he were the master of her own house, free from all hesitation.
Then the king’s attendants reported that matter to the king. The king did not believe it. They reported it a second and a third time;
then the king, having seen it himself while he was hiding, summoned all his ministers and informed them.
They said, "This man is a criminal against the king; he deserves the severing of his hands, he deserves the severing of his feet," and so on, up to being impaled upon a stake.
Then they pointed out all the various punishments. The king said, "If I were to have him executed, imprisoned, or flogged, cruelty would arise within me;
if I were to deprive him of life, it would be the taking of life; if I were to seize his wealth, it would be theft.
Enough with such things being done! Expel this man from my kingdom. The ministers then banished him from the realm.
They did so. Taking his own wealth and essence, as well as his wife and children, he went to another kingdom.
There, having heard of him, the king asked, "Why have you come? He replied, "Your Majesty, I wish to serve you. The king accepted him.
After a few days had passed and he had gained the king's confidence, the minister said this to the king: "Great King, [there is] no fly..."
“I see honey, but there is no one to eat it. The king did not hear him, thinking, “What is he saying, wishing to mock me?
Finding an opportunity, the man praised it even more highly and spoke again.
The king asked, “What is this? “The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, Your Majesty. The king said, “Do you wish to take me away and kill me? He replied, “No.”
“Your Majesty, speak thus: ‘If you do not believe me, send men. He sent men.
They went there, dug through the city gate, and rose up in the king’s bedchamber.
When the king saw them, he asked, “Why have you come? “We are thieves, Great King. The king [took] their wealth...
Having caused them to give it, he exhorted them, saying, "Do not act thus again," and then dismissed them. They returned and reported this to the king.
After testing him in that same manner two or three more times, [the king] concluded, "This is a virtuous king.
He then arrayed his fourfold army, approached a certain city on the border, and sent a message to the minister there: "Give me either the city or battle."
Thus he had King Brahmadatta informed of the matter: “Sire, please command him:
‘Shall I fight, or shall I give you the city? The king sent word back: “There is no need to fight;
having given me the city, come here. He did accordingly. The opposing king, having seized that city, likewise dispatched a messenger to the remaining cities.
The border ministers reported this to Brahmadatta exactly as it was; having been told by him, "You must not fight, you should come here," they returned to Bārāṇasī.
Then the ministers said to Brahmadatta, "Great King, let us fight with him. The king [replied], "There would be the taking of life for me..."
"it will happen," he said, and stopped them. The ministers said, "Great King, we shall capture him alive and bring him right here.
Having persuaded the king with various means, they began to go, saying, "Come, Great King! The king said, "If you do not commit the act of killing, wounding, or plundering, I shall go.
The ministers replied, "No, Your Majesty; we shall not do it. We shall frighten him and cause him to flee."
Having arrayed the fourfold army and placed lamps inside jars, they marched forth at night.
On that day, the opposing king captured a city near Bārāṇasī; now, thinking "What shall I do?", he removed his armor at night and fell asleep with his troops in a state of negligence.
Then the ministers took King Brahmadatta and [delivered him] to the opposing king.
Having gone to the royal camp, they had all the lamps brought out from the jars and, having made it a single blaze of light, raised a shout of triumph.
Seeing the great army, the minister of the opposing king became terrified; he approached his own king and cried out with a loud voice, "Arise!
Eat honey free from flies! A second and likewise a third minister did the same. Then the opposing king—
Waking up at that sound, he fell into fear and terror. Hundreds of shouts arose.
Thinking, "Having believed the words of another, I have fallen into the hands of my enemies," he lamented various things throughout the entire night.
On the second day, thinking, "The king is righteous; he would not cause harm, so I will go and ask for his forgiveness," he approached the king.
Having approached and knelt on his knees, he said, "Forgive me, Great King, for my offense.
The king, having exhorted him, said, "Arise; I forgive you. As soon as the king had spoken thus, he attained supreme relief.
He obtained a kingdom in a district right near the realm of the King of Bārāṇasī. They became friends with one another.
Then, seeing both armies standing together in harmony, Brahmadatta thought:
"By the mere protection of my own mind alone, not even a single drop of blood, sufficient for a tiny fly to drink, has been shed among this great multitude of people; oh, how wonderful!
Oh, how excellent! May all beings be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction. Thus he entered the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā).
Having generated that [insight], taking it as a foundation, he comprehended conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, and attained self-enlightenment.
While he was seated upon the back of an elephant, made happy by the bliss of the path and its fruition, his ministers prostrated themselves before him and said:
"It is time for the departure, O Great King; honor should be paid to the victorious army."
“Food and provisions must be given to the defeated army. He replied, “I am not a king, my man;
I am called a Paccekabuddha. “What does Your Majesty say? Such as these do not become Paccekabuddhas. “My man, what kind of people are Paccekabuddhas?
“Paccekabuddhas, sire, have hair and beard two finger-breadths long and possess eight requisites. He [pointed] with his right hand...
As soon as he touched his head, the marks of a householder disappeared and the appearance of a renunciant manifested.
With hair and beard two finger-breadths long and provided with the eight requisites, he appeared like an elder of a hundred years.
Having attained the fourth jhāna, he rose up from the elephant’s shoulder into the air and sat upon a lotus flower. The ministers, having paid homage, asked: “What—”
“Venerable sir, what is your meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and how did you attain it? they asked.

Since his meditation subject was the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā), and he had attained it after having practiced insight (vipassanā) upon that, he spoke this very verse—both as a verse of exultation (udāna) and as a verse of explanation—to show that matter: “Having laid aside the rod toward all beings...”
In this context, "in all" means without exception. "Beings" means sentient beings. This is the summary here;
however, we shall explain the detailed exposition in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta. "Having laid aside" means having set down. "The rod" refers to the rod of body, speech, and mind;
it is a designation for bodily misconduct and so forth. For bodily misconduct is called a "rod" because it punishes (daṇḍayati) and afflicts.
It means that one brings about ruin and calamity. This applies likewise to verbal misconduct and mental misconduct.
Alternatively, "the rod" refers specifically to the weapon; thus it is also said, "having laid aside that [rod]. "They do not harm" means being without malice.

"Even any one [of them]" means even any single one whatsoever. "Of those" means of all those living beings. "One should not desire a son" refers to one born of the womb (*atrāja*) or one born of the field (*khetta-ja*).
Among these four types of sons—the given son and the pupil—one would not desire any of them as a son;
how much less so a "companion," for how could one possibly desire that?

"Alone" means alone by way of the going-forth (pabbajjā), alone in the sense of being without a second, alone in the sense of the abandoning of craving, and alone because he has utterly departed from the defilements.

"He is alone" means he has awakened to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha alone. For even while moving in the midst of a thousand ascetics, he is "alone" because the fetters of a householder have been severed;
thus he is alone by way of his renunciation. He stands alone, walks alone, sits alone, lies down alone, and conducts himself alone; thus he is alone in the sense of being without a second.
“With craving as his companion, a person wanders through the long course of saṃsāra;
from this state of existence to another state of existence, he does not transcend the cycle of rebirth.
Having understood this danger—that craving is the origin of suffering—”
“Free from craving, without grasping, let the mindful bhikkhu wander.”—Thus, in the sense of the abandoning of craving, he is one.
All his defilements are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future;
thus, in the sense of being entirely free from defilements, he is one. Having become teacherless, he is self-become (*sayambhū*).
"Having himself awakened to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha"—thus he is "one" because he alone has awakened to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.

He "conducts himself" by means of these eight modes of conduct (*cariyā*). That is to say: for those endowed with aspiration, there is the conduct of posture (*iriyāpathacariyā*) regarding the four postures;
for those who guard the doors of the sense faculties, there is the conduct of the sense bases (*āyatanacariyā*) regarding the six internal sense bases.
The practice of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness for those dwelling in heedfulness;
the practice of concentration in the four jhānas for those devoted to higher consciousness; the practice of knowledge in the four noble truths for those endowed with wisdom;
the practice of the path in the four noble truths for those who have entered correctly; and the practice of attainment in the four fruits of recluseship for those who have reached the fruit.
The world-benefiting conduct of the three Buddhas extends to all beings; therein, it is partial in the case of the paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha.
As it is said: "Conduct (cariyā) refers to the eight types of conduct, beginning with the conduct of the postures," and so on in detail.

The meaning is that one should be endowed with those modes of conduct. Alternatively, it refers to those who, while resolving, proceed by means of faith, and while exerting, proceed by means of energy.
He practices; attending with mindfulness he practices; undistracted by concentration he practices;
understanding with wisdom he practices; cognizing with consciousness he practices. One who practices thus, wholesome states increase—thus he practices the practice of the bases (*āyatanacariyā*).
One who practices thus attains distinction—thus he practices the practice of distinction (*visesacariyā*). Such is another [set].
The eight modes of conduct have been taught; the meaning is that he should be endowed with those as well. Regarding the phrase "like the rhinoceros horn" (*khaggavisāṇakappo*):
here, "rhinoceros horn" refers to the horn of the *khagga* deer. We shall explain the meaning of the word *kappa* in detail in the commentary on the *Maṅgala Sutta*;
however, in this context, it is used in the sense found in the passage: "Alas, sir, they were indeed conversing with a disciple who is like the Teacher."
In such cases as these, the counterpart image (*paṭibhāga*) is to be understood. "Like the horn of a rhinoceros" means it is similar to a rhinoceros horn.
This, first, is the explanation of the meaning according to the words.

However, from the perspective of the underlying intention and the connection of the discourse, it should be understood as follows: this aforementioned kind of rod, when being applied toward living beings...
He is one who has laid aside the rod; by not directing it toward them, by promoting the welfare of others through loving-kindness which is its opposite,
and by laying aside the rod toward all beings, and because he has laid aside the rod, he does not harm beings with a rod,
a sword, a hand, or a clod, unlike those beings who, having not laid aside the rod, do harm to living creatures.

The intended meaning is this: by resorting to one or another of those subjects of meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*), having practiced insight (*vipassanā*) into whatever has come under feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness therein—and following that, into other formations as well—one attains this *paccekabodhi*.
This, at least, is the underlying intention.
This is the connection: When this had been said, those ministers asked, "Now, venerable sir, where are you going?
Then, having reflected and known—"Where did the paccekabuddhas dwell in the past?"—he replied, "On Mount Gandhamādana.
They spoke again, "Venerable sir, do you now abandon us? You do not wish [to stay]? Then the paccekasambuddha—
He said: “One should not desire a son,” and so forth. The intended meaning therein is this:
“I do not now desire even any kind of son, whether born of my own womb or otherwise; how much less a companion such as you?
Therefore, even among you, whoever wishes to go with me or to become like me, let him wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. Or alternatively, by them [it was said]: “Us...”
When he said, "Venerable sir, abandon it now; do not desire it," that Paccekabuddha replied, "One should not desire a son, much less a companion.

Having spoken thus, and seeing the virtue of the solitary life according to his own purpose, he was gladdened and filled with joy and happiness, and uttered this inspired utterance: "One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. Having said this, he—
While the great multitude was still looking on, he sprang up into the air and went to Gandhamādana.
Gandhamādana is located beyond seven mountains in the Himavat—namely, Cūḷakāḷapabbata, Mahākāḷapabbata, Nāgapaliveṭhana, Candagabbha, Sūriyagabbha, Suvaṇṇapassa, and the Himavanta mountain. There...
There is a mountain cave named Nandamūlaka, a dwelling place for paccekabuddhas, and three grottoes:
the Golden Grotto, the Jewel Grotto, and the Silver Grotto. At the entrance of the Jewel Grotto stands a tree named Mañjūsaka, one yojana in height and one yojana in width.
It causes all flowers, whether in water or on land, to bloom.
Especially on the day of the arrival of a Paccekabuddha. Above that is a pavilion made of all kinds of jewels.
There, the sweeping wind discards the refuse; the leveling wind makes the sand made of all kinds of jewels even;
the sprinkling wind brings water from Lake Anotatta and sprinkles it; and the fragrance-making wind [brings] from the Himālaya all the fragrant trees.
The wind called *āneti* brings the fragrance; the wind called *ocinaka* gathers the flowers and causes them to fall; the wind called *santharaka* spreads them everywhere.
Furthermore, the seats there are always well-prepared, upon which all the Paccekabuddhas assemble and sit on the day of a Paccekabuddha’s appearance and on Uposatha days.
This is the natural order there. This is the Paccekabuddha.
Having gone there, he sits on the prepared seat. Then, if other paccekabuddhas are present at that time, they too assemble at that very moment and sit on the prepared seats.
Having sat down, they enter some meditative attainment (samāpatti) and emerge from it.
Then, the senior elder of the Saṅgha [addresses] the newly arrived paccekabuddha for the purpose of giving thanks for the meal to all of them.
"How was it attained?"—thus he asks regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). At that time, he recites that very same verse which is his own utterance of realization (*udāna*).
Again, the Blessed One, being questioned by the Venerable Ānanda, recites that same verse. Ānanda [recited it] at the Great Recital (*saṅgīti*);
thus, each single verse was spoken at the place where the Pratyekabuddha attained full awakening, namely, in the Mañjūsaka grove.
At the time when Ānanda asked the question, it was spoken four times as part of the *saṅgīti* (council).
The commentary on the first verse is finished. 92.
As for the verse beginning with "Of one born of association" (*saṃsaggajātassa*), what is its origin? This [being] was also a *paccekabodhisatta* under the Blessed One Kassapa.

Practicing the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years in the Dispensation according to the previous method, he performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, attained the first jhāna, and having defined name-and-form, practiced the comprehension of characteristics;
yet, without attaining the Noble Path, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. Passing away from there, he [was conceived] by the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.

Having been born from the womb and growing according to the previous manner, from the time he first discerned the distinction that "this is a woman" and "this is a man," he no longer delights in the hands of women;
he does not even consent to being anointed, bathed, or adorned. Men alone nourish him. At the time of suckling, the nurses put on bodices...
They fed him milk by means of men. Having smelled the scent of women or heard their voices, he would weep;
even when he had reached the age of discretion, he did not wish to see women. Therefore, they knew him as Anitthigandha (Scentless to Women).
When he was sixteen years old, the king, thinking, "I shall establish a family lineage," [sent for him] from various clans.
Having brought suitable maidens, he commanded a certain minister, "Entertain the prince.
Desiring to entertain him by means of a stratagem, the minister had a curtain enclosure constructed not far from him and employed dancers there.
Hearing the sound of singing and instrumental music, the prince asked, "Whose sound is this? The minister replied, "That, Your Majesty, belongs to the dancing girls."
"Sire, such theatrical performances belong to those possessed of merit. Delight yourself, O King; you are one of great merit," he said.
The prince had the minister beaten with a staff and had him driven out. He reported this to the king.
The king went together with the prince’s mother, asked the prince for forgiveness, and commanded the minister once more. Being thus excessively pressured by them, the prince...
Having given them the finest gold, he commanded the goldsmiths, "Fashion a beautiful female form.
They fashioned a female form adorned with every ornament, resembling one created by Vissakamma, and presented it to him.
Upon seeing it, the prince nodded his head in wonder and sent word to his parents: "If I may obtain such a woman as this, I shall take her."
The parents thought, “Our son is of great merit; surely some maiden who has performed meritorious deeds must have appeared in the world together with him.
Placing that golden image upon a chariot, they gave it to the ministers, saying, “Go, search for such a maiden as this.
Taking it with them, they traveled through each of the sixteen great provinces.
Having gone to the village, wherever they saw a crowd of people— at water crossings and other such places— they would place a golden image as if it were a deity,
perform worship with various flowers, garments, and ornaments, and having hung up a canopy,
they would stand to one side, thinking, "If anyone has previously seen such a thing, how will he produce it?"
By this means, having wandered through all the other provinces except for the Madda kingdom, they disregarded it as a "small district" and, not going there first, turned back.
Then it occurred to them: "Let us go to the Madda kingdom first; let it not be that we enter Bārāṇasī [only after it has been taken]."
“The king sent [messengers] again,” they said, and they went to the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda.
In the city of Sāgala there was a king named Maddava. His daughter was sixteen years of age and was beautiful.
Her handmaidens used to go to the bathing place for the sake of bathing water. There, having seen that golden image set up by the ministers from afar, they said, “Us—”
"She sent her for water, but the princess came herself," they said. Approaching them, they replied, "This is not our mistress;
our mistress is more beautiful than she. When the ministers heard this, they went to the king and requested the girl in a fitting manner.
He gave her to them. They sent word to the King of Bārāṇasī: "We have obtained her..."
“Your Majesty, shall the princess come herself, or shall we bring her?
He replied, “If I go, there will be oppression of the countryside; you yourselves must bring her,” and he sent her.
The ministers, taking the girl, departed from the city and dispatched her to the prince, saying: “We have found one who resembles a golden image...”
“...the maiden. As soon as the prince heard this, he was overcome by passion and fell away from the first jhāna.
He sent word through a succession of messengers: “Bring her quickly! Bring her quickly! They reached Bārāṇasī after traveling at a single night’s pace everywhere along the way;
standing outside the city, they sent word to the king: “Should we enter this very day, or not? The king said, “From a family of the highest status...”
“The girl has been brought; having performed the auspicious rites, we shall lead her in with great honor. For now, take her to the park,” he said. They did so.
That maiden, who was exceedingly delicate, was afflicted by the jolting of the carriage and, due to the exhaustion of the journey, developed a wind-disease (vātaroga).
Becoming like a withered garland, she passed away during the night. The ministers thought, “We have failed in our honors.”
They lamented. Both the king and the citizens lamented, crying out, "The lineage is ruined! The entire city was filled with a great clamor.
As soon as the prince heard this, a profound sorrow arose within him.
Thereupon, the prince began to dig up the very root of that grief. He thought to himself: "This thing called sorrow..."

"It occurs for one who is not yet born, and it also occurs for one who is already born. Therefore, dependent on birth, there is sorrow. But dependent on what does birth occur? Dependent on existence (bhava), birth occurs.

Thus, through the power of prior cultivation, as he applied his mind methodically and saw dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and further contemplated the formative forces (saṅkhāra) in their forward sequence while sitting right there, he attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.

He realized the Truth. Seeing him sitting there, his faculties calmed and his mind at peace, happy with the bliss of the Path and its Fruit, the ministers prostrated themselves and said, "Do not grieve, O King!
Jambudīpa is vast; we shall bring you another maiden more beautiful than her. He replied, "I do not grieve; I am a Paccekabuddha, free from sorrow. Hereafter—
Everything is exactly as stated in the preceding verses, with the exception of the commentary on the verses.

The commentary on the verses, however, should be understood as follows: *saṃsaggajātassa* means "of one who has come into association. In this context, association (*saṃsagga*) is fivefold, consisting of:
seeing, hearing, physical contact, conversation, and sharing enjoyments. Among these, passion that arises through the process of the visual consciousness upon seeing one another—

This is what is called "contact through sight. In this regard, a daughter of a householder in the village of Kāḷadīghavāpī on the island of Sri Lanka, having seen a young *dīghabhāṇaka* bhikkhu residing at the Kalyāṇavihāra while he was wandering for alms, became infatuated with him. Not being able to obtain him by any means, she died.
Upon seeing a fragment of her undergarment, [the bhikkhu thought]: "I did not obtain cohabitation with one who wore such clothing."
His heart failed and he passed away; that very youth serves as the illustration.

Furthermore, hearing of the excellence of form and so forth being described by others, or hearing the sounds of one’s own laughter, speech, or singing, and thereby experiencing lust through the cognitive process of ear-consciousness, is called "contact through hearing.
In this regard, there is the example of the smith’s daughter living in a mountain village and her five companions...
Having gone together with her to the Padumassara lake, bathed, and offered a garland, Tissadāhara—the dweller of the Pañcaggaḷa cave—heard the sound of her singing loudly;
while traveling through the air, he fell away from his excellence due to sensual lust and met with ruin.
This is the illustrative example.
Sexual contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) is defined as lust arising from the mutual touching of limbs.
In this regard, the young monk who preached the Dhamma and the king’s daughter serve as the illustration. It is said that at the Mahāvihāra, a young monk was preaching the Dhamma.
A great crowd of people had gathered there, and the king also went along with his chief queen and the king’s daughter. Then, the king’s daughter—
Strong lust arose in him because of that form and sound, even though he was young.
Seeing this, the king observed the situation and had them enclosed by a curtain. They touched one another and embraced.
When the curtain was removed again and they looked on, they saw that both had already passed away.
Furthermore, lust arising from the act of conversing and chatting with one another is called "contact through conversation.
Lust arising when a bhikkhu engages in the use of requisites together with bhikkhunīs is called "contact through shared enjoyment.

In both of these cases, the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī who have fallen into a *pārājika* offense serve as the illustration. [This was spoken] during the festival of the Great Monastery named Maricavaṭṭi.
It is said that King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, having prepared a great almsgiving, was serving both Saṅghas.
There, when hot rice-gruel had been served, a young novice nun gave a set of ivory rings to a young novice monk who was without support and engaged in conversation with him.
Both of them, having received full ordination and reached sixty years of age—
Having reached the opposite shore, they regained their former recognition through conversation with one another;
immediately, affection arose, and having transgressed the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), they became those who have committed a defeat (*pārājika*).
Thus, in these five kinds of association, for one who has become associated by any such association, affection arises, and depending on that prior passion, powerful lust (*balavarāga*) emerges.

From that, this suffering arising from affection (*sneha*) comes into being; following after that very affection, this suffering—consisting of various kinds such as sorrow and lamentation pertaining both to the present life and the future—comes into being, originates, and arises.
Others say: "The release and attachment of the mind toward an object is *saṃsagga*. From that comes affection, and from that comes this suffering of affection.
Having spoken this half-verse concerning the analysis of the self in this way, that Paccekabuddha said:
"This very root of suffering which follows upon affection— the suffering consisting of grief and the like that arises from it— I have attained Paccekabodhi by digging up that very root of suffering."
When this was said, those ministers asked: "Venerable sir, what should we do now? Then he said:

"Whether it be you or anyone else who desires to be freed from this suffering, everyone should perceive the danger born of affection and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. And here, as for that which was said: "This suffering arises from affection..."
It should be understood that this was said with reference to that very same point;

or else, having connected it thus: "Through association as previously described, affection arises for one who has associated, and from affection follows this suffering"—thus, seeing the danger born of affection as it truly is, I have attained [this state].
The fourth line should be understood as having been spoken by way of affection according to the method already explained.
All that follows thereafter is exactly like what was stated in the preceding verse.
The commentary on the verses concerning association is finished.

93. What is the origin of the *Suhajja*? This Paccekabuddha, having arisen in the same manner as described in the preceding verse, was ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī. Having attained the first jhāna, he reflected, "Which is better:
the practice of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) or kingship? After testing this, he handed over the kingdom to his ministers and practiced the dharma of a recluse.
Although the ministers were told, "Act according to the Dhamma and with justice," they accepted bribes and acted unjustly.
Having accepted bribes, while defeating the owners [in court], they once defeated a certain royal favorite.
That man entered together with the king's cooks and reported everything. On the following day, the king went to the seat of justice himself.
Then the great multitude, crying out, "Sire, the ministers are making those who are not masters into masters!", raised a loud clamor and made it like a great battle.
Then the King, rising from the seat of justice and ascending to his palace, sat down to enter a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Distraught by that noise, he was unable to attain it. He thought, "Of what use is this kingship to me? The duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*)..."

"Excellent! Having abandoned the pleasures of kingship, he again attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and by practicing insight (*vipassanā*) in the manner previously described, he realized the enlightenment of a *paccekabuddha*.
When asked about his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he recited this verse.

In it, they are "friends" (*mittā*) by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*); they are "dear friends" (*suhajjā*) because of their well-disposed hearts. Some say they are simply "friends" due to the desire for their absolute welfare.
There are those who are not good friends. Some are indeed good friends by producing mental happiness through coming and going, standing, sitting, and conversing, but they are not [true] friends.
Some are both good friends and friends by virtue of both [those qualities]. These are of two kinds: householders and those who have gone forth.
Among them, householders are of three types: the benefactor, the one who shares in pleasure and pain, and the compassionate one.
The homeless ones, in particular, are those who explain the goal; they are endowed with four factors. As it is said:
"Householder’s son, a helpful friend who wishes one well is to be known by four grounds: he protects one when one is negligent;
he protects one’s property when one is negligent; he is a refuge when one is afraid; and he assists one in matters that arise and must be done."
“He bestows double that enjoyment.
Likewise:
“Householder’s son, a friend who is easy to please should be known by four grounds as one who shares in both pleasure and pain: his secret...”
“He discloses [his secrets], he guards his secrets, he does not abandon him in times of misfortune, and even his own life is surrendered for his sake.
Likewise:

“Householder’s son, a compassionate friend who is easy to please is to be recognized by four grounds: he does not rejoice in one’s misfortune, he rejoices in one’s prosperity, he restrains one when one speaks ill [of others], and he commends one when one speaks well.”
Likewise:

“Householder’s son, a friend who speaks for one’s benefit and is well-disposed should be known by four grounds: he restrains one from evil, establishes one in what is wholesome, makes one hear what has not been heard, and points out the path to heaven.

Here, those intended are householders; however, in terms of meaning, all [types of friends] are applicable. “Feeling compassion for those friends and well-wishers” means feeling sympathy for them, desiring to bestow happiness upon them and wishing to remove their suffering.
"He ruins his welfare" (*hāpeti atthaṃ*): welfare is threefold, according to the mundane, the supramundane, and the ultimate sense;

likewise, it is also threefold according to one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both. He ruins or destroys it in two ways: by the loss of what has been gained and by the non-arising of what has not yet been gained.
"With mind bound" (*paṭibaddhacitto*) means: "Without this person I cannot live; he is my resort, he is my final refuge"—thus placing oneself in a low position.
Even when placing [beings] in a high position, one is bound by attachment. Thinking, "These cannot live without me;
I am their refuge, I am their ultimate resort," even when placing oneself in a high position, one is bound by attachment.
But here, it is this kind of bound attachment that is intended. "This fear" means this fear of losing one's purpose, [the fear] of oneself...

This is said with reference to the loss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-hāni*). "Familiarity" (*santhava*) is threefold, by way of familiarity through craving (*taṇhā*), familiarity through views (*diṭṭhi*), and familiarity through friendship (*mitta*).
Among these, even the hundred-and-eightfold craving is familiarity through craving; even the sixty-two-fold views are familiarity through views;
and the compassionate concern for friends due to a bound mind is familiarity through friendship. Of these, it is the latter that is intended here. For by that...
He has fallen away from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Therefore he said: "Perceiving this danger in intimacy, I have attained [this state]. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses concerning friends and kinsmen is finished.

94. Regarding the verse beginning "The bamboo is broad-based": what is its origin? It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were three *paccekabodhisattvas*.
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of coming and going for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the gods.
Passing away from there, the eldest was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī, while the other two were reborn in the families of frontier kings.
Both of them, having mastered a meditation subject and renounced their kingdoms to go forth, eventually became Paccekabuddhas.
While dwelling in the Nandamūlaka cave, one day, having emerged from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), they reflected, "What deed did we perform to attain this supramundane bliss?
As they examined this, they saw their respective past conduct during the time of the Buddha Kassapa.
Then, reflecting on where the third was, they saw him ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī.
Having seen him and recollected his virtues, they thought: "He is naturally endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires;
he is our very instructor, one who corrects us, is patient with our words, and censures evil. Come now, let us show him an object and inform him.
Seeking an opportunity, they saw him one day going to the park adorned with all his ornaments, and arriving through the air, they said:
They stood at the gate of the park at the base of a bamboo thicket. The great multitude, insatiable in their desire to see the king, gazed up at him.
Then the king, looking about to see if there was anyone who did not exert themselves to behold him, beheld the Paccekabuddhas.
At the very moment of seeing them, affection arose within him for them. Descending from the back of his elephant, with a tranquil...
Having approached with due decorum, he asked, "Venerable sirs, what is your name? They replied, "Great King, we are named 'The Unattached' (Asajjamānā).
"Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of 'the unattached'? "It means 'not clinging,' Great King.
Then, pointing to a clump of bamboo, they said: "Great King, just as this clump of bamboo is entirely..."
Just as a man with a sword in hand, unable to pull out a bamboo thicket that stands interwoven by its roots,
trunks, branches, and sub-branches even after cutting it at the base, so too are you entangled both within and without by this tangle,
clinging to it and attached to it. Or rather, it is like this bamboo stalk standing in the middle, because its branches have not yet grown.
"Just as it stands unattached to anything, yet can be pulled out by cutting it at the tip or the root, even so we go in all directions without being stuck anywhere.
Having said this, they immediately entered the fourth jhāna and, while the king was still watching, they departed through the air for the Nandamūlaka Crag. Then the king thought: "When..."
"Could I too, perhaps, become one who is thus unattached? While standing right there, practicing insight (vipassanā), he realized Pratyekabuddhahood.
When asked about his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the same manner as before, he spoke this verse.
In that context, *vaṃsa* means bamboo; *visāla* means broad. The letter *va* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇattha*), or it is the word *eva*.

Here, the letter *e* has been elided by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*). It is connected with the following word; we shall join it later. "As" (*yathā*) means in the counterpart-image (*paṭibhāga*).
"Entangled" (*visatta*) means stuck, matted, and woven together. "In children and wives" (*puttesu dāresu ca*) means among sons, daughters, and spouses.
"That longing" (*yā apekkhā*) means that craving (*taṇhā*) or that affection (*sineha*). "Like a bamboo shoot, not clinging" (*vaṃsakaḷīrova asajjamāno*) means like a bamboo sprout, not adhering.

What is meant? Just as a bamboo is "clinging" (visatta) because it is wide-spreading and attached, so too the concern for children and wives is likewise clinging, because it stands fastened to those objects.
Thus, "I am one who has concern through that concern, clinging like a wide-spreading bamboo"—having thus seen the danger in concern, [he abandons] that concern.

Cutting through with the knowledge of the path, like this bamboo shoot, he did not cling—whether to forms and so forth, or to gains and so forth, or to sensual existence and so forth, or to views and so forth—by way of craving, conceit, or false view, and thus he attained private enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*). The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the verse of the bamboo shoot is finished.

95. As for the origin of the verse beginning "The deer in the forest": It is said that a certain monk, a practitioner of yoga under the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa, passed away and was reborn in Bārāṇasī into a family of a wealthy merchant, one of great riches and vast possessions. He was handsome;
however, having become an adulterer, he died and was reborn in hell. After being cooked there, by what remained after he had been roasted...
She took rebirth as a female in the womb of the merchant’s wife.

Since the bodies of beings who have come from hell are warm, the merchant’s wife—with her burning belly—carried that fetus with great difficulty and hardship, and in due time she gave birth to a girl.
From the very day of her birth, [the child] [brought distress] to her parents, her other relatives, and her attendants.
She was unloved by her parents. When she reached marriageable age and was given to a family, there too she remained unloved, disliked, and unpleasant to her husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law.
Then, when a festival had been proclaimed, the merchant’s son, unwilling to amuse himself with her, brought a courtesan and sported with her.
Hearing of this from the female slaves, she approached the merchant’s son and [accused him] in various ways.

Having conciliated him, she said: "Noble son, as for women, even if one were the youngest of ten kings or the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), she must still perform service for her husband.
When the husband does not speak to her, she experiences suffering as if she were being impaled on a stake. If I am worthy of favor and should be favored, [then do so]; if not—"
“[The goods] must be sold. I shall go to my own family’s home. The merchant’s son said, “Very well, lady; do not grieve. Be ready for recreation;

we shall celebrate the festival. At that mere conversation, the merchant’s daughter became filled with enthusiasm and prepared a great quantity of hard and soft food, thinking, “Tomorrow we shall celebrate the festival. The merchant’s son—
On the second day, without having informed her, he went to the place of recreation. She sat watching the road, thinking, "He will send word now; he will send word now.
Seeing that it was past noon, she dispatched men. They returned and reported, "The merchant’s son has gone.
Taking all that had been prepared, she mounted a carriage and set out for the park.
Then, on the seventh day, the Paccekabuddha emerged from cessation (*nirodha*) in the Nandamūlaka Cave;
having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* and washed his face in Lake Anotatta, he reflected, "Where shall I go for alms today?
Seeing that merchant’s daughter, he thought, "If I cause her to manifest an act of faith, that karma will be exhausted."
Knowing that he would go there, he stood upon a sixty-yojana stretch of the Manosilā plateau near the mountain slope;

taking his bowl and robe, he attained the jhāna that serves as the basis for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and traveling through the air, he descended on the opposite side and proceeded toward Bārāṇasī.
Upon seeing him, the slave girls informed the merchant’s daughter. She descended from her carriage and paid him due respect.

Having paid homage, she filled the bowl with various kinds of hard and soft foods, covered it with a lotus flower, placed another lotus flower beneath it, and holding the cluster of flowers in her hand, she placed the bowl into the hands of the Paccekabuddha.
Having paid homage, with the cluster of flowers still in her hand, she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, just as..."
“May this flower ensure that wherever I am reborn, there I shall be dear and pleasing to the great multitude.
Having thus made his aspiration, he made it a second time: “Venerable sir, the dwelling in a womb is suffering;
may my rebirth-linking occur right here upon this lotus flower, without entering a womb. And a third time he made his aspiration: “Venerable sir, womenfolk are loathsome...”
“Even the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch falls under the power of another. Therefore, may I not enter into the female state, but become a man.
For a fourth time he made this aspiration: “Venerable sir, having transcended this suffering of saṃsāra, may I attain the Deathless which you have reached at the end.
Having thus made these four aspirations and worshipped that cluster of lotus flowers, he departed.
Having prostrated with the fivefold salutation, he made this fifth aspiration: "May my fragrance and my complexion be exactly like those of a flower.
Then the Paccekabuddha, taking both the bowl and the bouquet of flowers, stood in the air and said:
"May what you desire and pray for be fulfilled quickly;
may all your intentions be accomplished, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Having offered this blessing of thanksgiving with this verse to the merchant’s daughter, [he thought], "Let the merchant’s daughter see me as I go."
Having made a resolution, he went through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave. As the merchant’s daughter watched him, great joy arose within her.
The unwholesome karma she had committed in a previous existence was exhausted due to the lack of opportunity for its fruition;

she became pure, like a copper vessel washed with sour tamarind juice. At that very moment, everyone in both her husband’s family and her own kin was delighted. They spoke affectionate words, asking, "What shall we do?"
He also sent various gifts. The husband likewise sent men, saying, "Bring the merchant’s daughter here quickly;

I came to the park having forgotten her. From that time forth, he cherished her, holding her dear like sandalwood paste smeared upon his chest, like a pearl necklace worn around his neck, or like a garland of flowers.
There she enjoyed, for as long as her life lasted, the happiness associated with sovereignty and wealth.
Having experienced [the results of his merit] and passed away, he was reborn in the world of the gods as a male being within a lotus flower.
That son of the gods, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, remained within the interior of that very lotus flower.
They called him "The Great Lotus Son of the Gods" (Mahāpaduma-devaputta). Thus, by the power of that supernormal success (iddhi), he moved both forward and backward.
He transmigrates only within the six celestial worlds.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī had twenty thousand women, yet not even one among them conceived a son.
The ministers petitioned the king: "Your Majesty, a son who will sustain the royal lineage must be desired; [for] among one's own kin..."
“Even one who is not born of noble lineage can become a sustainer of the family line.
Then the king said, “Except for the chief queen, let all the other women perform the Dhamma-dance for seven days,” and he allowed them to go out as they pleased; yet even so, he did not obtain a son.
Again the ministers said, “Great King, the chief queen is indeed pre-eminent among all women in merit and wisdom.”
“O foremost one, perhaps the King might obtain a son from the womb of the chief queen. The king reported this matter to the chief queen.
She said, “Great King, only a woman who is virtuous and truthful may obtain a son; how can there be a son for one devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing?
Having ascended the palace, she undertook the five precepts and reflected upon them again and again. Being virtuous—
As the princess was reflecting upon the five precepts, the very moment a thought of longing for a son arose, Sakka’s throne trembled.
Then Sakka, perceiving this matter through his own reflection, thought: “I shall grant a noble son to the virtuous princess.
Coming through the air and standing before the queen, he asked, “What do you choose, O Queen? “A son, Great King,” she replied. “I give it to you.”
"O Queen, do not worry about your son," he said, and having departed for the world of the gods, he reflected:
"Is there anyone here whose lifespan has been exhausted? Perceiving that this Mahāpaduma intended to go to the higher celestial realms, he went to his palace and entreated him:
"Dear Mahāpaduma, go to the human world. He replied: "Do not say so, Great King."
“Speak! The world of humans is loathsome. “Father, you have been reborn here after performing merit in the human world;
remaining right there, you must fulfill the perfections (pāramitās). Go, father! “Great King, dwelling in the womb is suffering;
I am unable to dwell there. “Father, for you there is no dwelling in a womb, for such was the deed you performed.”
"Go, dear one, so that you shall be reborn right within the heart of a lotus," he was told again and again;
thus, having passed away from the world of the devas, he was reborn within the heart of a lotus in a stone-slab pond in the royal park of the King of Bārāṇasī.
And on that night, at the time of dawn, the chief queen, surrounded by twenty thousand women, saw him in a dream as she was entering the park.
Having gone there, she felt as though she had obtained a son within the heart of a lotus in the stone-slab pond.
When the night had turned to dawn, she went there while observing her moral precepts and saw a single lotus flower; it was neither on the bank nor in deep water.
At the very moment of seeing it, maternal affection for a son arose within her. She herself then—
Having descended, she took hold of that flower; as soon as the flower was grasped, its petals unfolded.
There she saw a boy like a golden image, and upon seeing him, she cried out, "I have found a son! The great multitude raised thousands of shouts of approval.
She sent word to the king, who, having heard it, asked, "Where was he found? and upon hearing the place where he had been found, [acted accordingly].
“The grove, the lotus pond, and the lotus belong to us alone; therefore, because he was born in our field, this son shall be named Khettaja (Field-born),” she said.
Having thus spoken, she brought him into the city and had twenty thousand women perform the duties of nurses for him.
Whichever woman, having ascertained the prince’s preference, fed him with whatever kind of food he desired, received a thousand [pieces of gold].
He received them. All of Benares was stirred up, and every person sent a thousand gifts for the prince.
As the prince passed from one place to another, being told, "Eat this, eat that," he became weary of food and grew despondent;
going to the city gate, he played with a ball of lac.
At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha was dwelling at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī.

Having risen early and performed all his duties—such as the observance of the rules for the lodging, the bodily preparations, and mental reflection—he emerged from seclusion and, reflecting on where he should seek alms today, saw the boy’s prosperity and thought: "This [boy] in the past..."
Inquiring, "What deed did he do? and reflecting, [the deity thought]: "Having given alms-food to one such as me, he made four aspirations;
three of them have been fulfilled, but one still remains unfulfilled. By a skillful means, I shall show him the object of that aspiration.
With this in mind, he approached the prince while on his alms-round. Upon seeing him, the prince said: "Ascetic, do not come here! For these..."
“‘Eat this! Consume this! they would say. Having said this, he turned back from there at that very word and went to his own lodging.
The prince said to his attendants: “This ascetic turned back as soon as I spoke;
is he perhaps angry with me? They replied to him: “Those who have gone forth are not given over to anger; rather, by the mere sight of another’s serene mind...”
Even when it was said, “They subsist on whatever is given,” he thought, “Such a wicked ascetic! I shall ask for his forgiveness.
Having informed his parents, he mounted an elephant and went to Isipatana with great royal splendor.
Seeing a herd of deer, he asked, “What are these? “These, sir, are called deer. “Of these—‘this’...”
"Are there any who, having said, 'Eat this, consume this, taste this,' look after them? "There are none, sir;
they dwell wherever grass and water are easily obtained.
The prince thought, "Just as these people dwell wherever they wish, even without being guarded, when indeed shall I too—"
He took as his object of meditation: "May he dwell thus. The Paccekabuddha, knowing of his arrival, swept the dwelling place, the path, and the walking-pavilion, making them smooth;

after walking up and down there once or twice or three times to show the impression of his footsteps, he swept and smoothed the area for his midday rest and the leaf-hut, [leaving] the impression of his footsteps upon entering.
Having shown [the way] and without indicating where he had set foot upon his departure, he went elsewhere.
The prince went there, swept that spot, and seeing it made smooth, he said, "I suppose that Paccekabuddha was staying here," after hearing what the attendants had said.
"That ascetic must have been troubled even at dawn; now, with elephants, horses, and so forth, his own..."
"Seeing that he has stepped upon my space, he will surely sleep even more poorly; you yourselves stay right here!
Having said this, he dismounted from the elephant's back and entered the lodging alone. Seeing the footprints left in a place well-swept according to the rules of conduct, he thought:
"This ascetic, while walking here, did not think of trade or other such business; certainly, he is intent only on his own welfare."
"I think he reflected thus," it is said. With a mind full of serene confidence, he ascended the walking path; having cast aside worldly thoughts, he went and sat upon a stone slab.
