Becoming one-pointed in mind, he entered the leaf-hut and, practicing insight (vipassanā), attained the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi.
Then, being questioned about his meditation subject by the chaplain in the same manner as before, while seated in the sky, he uttered this verse.
In this context, "deer" refers to two kinds of deer: the eni-deer and the pasada-deer; moreover, it is a designation for all four-footed forest animals.
However, they say that here the pasada-deer is intended. "In the forest" means the remainder of the land excluding the village and its precincts;
but here, a pleasure garden is intended, therefore it is said, "in the pleasure garden."
It is so. "As" means in the counterpart image (*paṭibhāga*). "Unbound" means unbound by ropes, fetters, and the like;

by this, he illustrates his unrestrained conduct. "He goes wherever he wishes for the sake of his range" means that in whichever direction he wishes to go, in that very direction he goes for the sake of his range. And this was said by the Blessed One:
“Just as, monks, a forest deer wandering in the forest glade goes with confidence, stands with confidence, sits with confidence, and lies down with confidence. Why is that?
Because he has not come within the range of the hunter. Even so, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above]... remains.”
“He enters and dwells in the first jhāna. This, monks, is called a monk who has made an end of Māra, rendered him trackless;
having struck down the eye of Māra, he has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One,” thus it is said in detail.
“At ease” means living according to one’s own will or being independent of others; this is what is meant: just as a deer in the forest...
"Unfettered, he goes wherever he wishes for his range of activity; likewise, when shall I too go thus, having severed the bond of craving?
Thus does a wise and learned man wander alone, looking toward freedom.
The commentary on the "Deer in the Forest" verses is finished.
96. Regarding the phrase "there is an invitation": what is its origin? It is said that during a great assembly of the King of Bārāṇasī, ministers approached him.
Among them, one minister requested to go aside, saying, "Your Majesty, there is something to be heard. He rose from his seat and departed.
Again, another requested [to speak] while the King was seated in the great assembly; another while he was seated on the neck of an elephant; and another while he was on the back of a horse.
One begged him while he was seated; another, while he was seated in a golden chariot; and another, while he was traveling to the park seated in a palanquin.
The king dismounted from there and departed. Another begged him while he was going on a tour of the countryside;
having heard his words as well, he dismounted from the back of the elephant and went aside. Thus, having become disillusioned by them, he went forth.
The ministers grew in power. One among them went and said to the king, "Great King, grant me such-and-such a district. The king replied, "That is being enjoyed by so-and-so.
Disregarding the king's words, he thought, "I shall go, take that district, and enjoy it," and having gone there, he started a quarrel.
Again, both of them came into the presence of the king and reported their mutual faults.

The king, seeing that it was impossible to satisfy them and perceiving the danger in greed, attained *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) through insight (*vipassanā*). In the manner previously described, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Its meaning is as follows: while standing in the midst of his companions, during his stay known as the daytime rest, and during the great audience known as...
In staying [at home], in the journey known as going to the pleasure grove, and in the wandering known as traveling through the countryside,
there is addressing [others] in various ways such as, “Listen to this for me,” or “Give this to me. Therefore, having become disillusioned with that,
although there is this state which is frequented by noble persons, possesses manifold benefits, and is exclusively blissful, yet because of those overcome by greed—

"Renunciation is not coveted by any base men; seeing it as a privilege for a person capable of attaining it—since it is uncraved by others and cannot be brought under their control—I applied myself to insight and gradually attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
The rest is exactly as previously stated."
The commentary on the Āmantā verses is finished. 97.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Delighting in play" (Khiḍḍāratī): It is said that in Benares there was a king named Ekaputtaka-Brahmadatta.
He had an only son who was dear to him, pleasing, and as dear to him as his own life; the king would take his son with him in all his postures.
It was customary for him to go to the pleasure garden one day, having left the boy behind. On that very day, the prince died of a sudden illness.
Fearing that "the king’s heart might burst from affection for his son," the ministers did not inform him but cremated him instead.
Intoxicated by liquor in the garden, the king did not even remember his son; likewise on the second day as well.
At the time of bathing and eating, he sat down after having finished his meal; remembering [his son], he said, "Bring my son.
They reported the matter to him according to the proper protocol. Then, overcome by grief while sitting there, he applied his mind wisely (*yoniso manasākāsi*) thus:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. In this way, step by step...
By contemplating dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and reverse order, he realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The remainder is exactly as stated in the commentary on the *Saṃsagga-gāthā*, with the exception of the explanation of the meaning of the verses.
As for that explanation of the meaning: *khiḍḍā* means play. It is twofold: bodily and verbal. Therein—
"Bodily" means such things as playing with elephants, horses, chariots, bows, and javelins, and so forth.

"Vocal" means such things as singing, reciting verses (*siloka*), and the sounds of mouth-drums (*mukhabherī*) and hanging drums (*ālambara-bherī*), and so forth. "Delight" refers to the delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
"Vast" means extending throughout the entire physical existence, reaching even to the marrow of the bones. The rest is self-evident.
The connection (*anusandhi*) here should also be understood according to the method stated in the verse on association (*saṃsaggagāthā*), as well as everything following that.
The commentary on the verse on play and delight (*Khiḍḍāratigāthāvaṇṇanā*) is finished. 98.
As for the origin of the term *cātuddisa*: formerly, it is said, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were five Pacceka-Bodhisattvas.
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, the eldest of them became the King of Bārāṇasī, while the others became ordinary kings.
All four of them, having mastered a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and renounced their kingdoms to go forth, eventually became Paccekabuddhas at the Nandamūlaka cave.

One day, having emerged from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), Vasantā—reflecting upon and understanding her own past karma and her companion according to the method described in the *Vaṃsakaḷīra-gāthā*—sought an opportunity to present a means for the King of Bārāṇasī to perceive the object of his fear.
That king was terrified three times during the night; frightened, he let out a cry on the great terrace.
He ran off. Although the chaplain rose early and asked after his comfortable sleep, he replied, "Teacher, where is there comfort for me?
and related the whole situation. The chaplain thought, "This disease cannot be cured by any medicinal treatment such as emetics or purgatives; however, a means of food has occurred to me."
“Great King, this is a foretoken of obstacles such as the loss of your kingdom or even your life,” he said, greatly terrifying the king.

Then, in order to pacify that [evil omen], he urged him to perform a sacrifice, saying, “Having given such and such numbers of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, as well as gold and silver as the sacrificial fee, you must offer the sacrifice. Thus he incited him to the performance of the sacrifice.
Then the Paccekabuddhas, seeing thousands of living beings gathered for the sake of a sacrifice, thought:
"When this deed is done, he will become difficult to enlighten; come now, let us go beforehand and observe him.
Arriving by the method described in the *Vaṃsakaḷīra* verses, they went in a procession through the royal courtyard while wandering for alms. The king was at the lion-window.
Standing there, he looked out over the royal courtyard and saw them; at the very sight of them, affection arose within him.
Then, having summoned them and had them sit on seats prepared on the roof-terrace, he respectfully fed them.
When they had finished their meal, he asked, "Who are you? "We are called the Cātuddisas, Great King. "Venerable sirs, regarding this term 'Cātuddisa'..."
“What is the purpose? “Great King, we have no fear or mental terror from any quarter whatsoever in the four directions. “Venerable sir, for what reason does that fear not exist for you?

“Great King, we cultivate loving-kindness (*mettā*), we cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*), we cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and we cultivate equanimity (*upekkhā*). Because of that, that fear does not exist for us.”
Having said, "There is no [fear]," they rose from their seats and went to their own dwelling places.

Then the king thought: "These recluses say that through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the like there is no fear, yet these brahmins praise the slaughter of many thousands of living beings; whose word, then, is the truth? Thereupon, this occurred to him:
—“The recluses wash the unclean with the clean, but the brahmins wash the unclean with the unclean.
Indeed, it is not possible to wash the unclean with the unclean; the word of those who have gone forth alone is true.
Having thus developed the four divine abidings, beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*), according to the method starting with “May all beings be happy,” he [radiated] welfare.
With his mind, he commanded his ministers: “Release all living beings; let them drink cool water, eat green grass, and let a cool breeze blow upon them. They did so.
Then the king, thinking, “By the word of my virtuous friends, I am liberated from evil karma,” sat right there and attained insight (*vipassanā*).

He realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. When his ministers said at mealtime, "Eat, Great King, it is time," he replied, "I am not a king," and having spoken everything according to the previous method, he uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna) as a declaration:
"Therein, 'one who dwells in the four quarters' means one who dwells at ease in the four directions, as described in such passages as, 'having pervaded one direction, he dwells [therein]'..."
He is "four-quarded" (*cātuddiso*) because he has pervaded the four directions with the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) according to the method.
He is "non-reactive" (*appaṭigho*) because he does not resist any beings or conditioned phenomena in those four directions out of fear.
He is "contented" (*santussamāno*) by way of the twelve kinds of contentment. "With this or that" (*itarītarena*) refers to requisites that are high or low.

Regarding the phrase "enduring dangers without fear": here, they are called *parissaya* because they afflict (*parissayanti*) body and mind, or because they cause their excellence to decline (*parihāpenti*), or because they lie in wait (*sayanti*) depending upon them.

This is a designation for external physical and mental calamities such as lions and tigers, and internal ones such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). One endures those dangers through patience (*adhivāsanakhanti*).
He is "enduring" (*sahitā*) because he endures through such qualities as energy (*vīriya*). He is "unfrightened" (*achambhī*) due to the absence of fear that causes rigidity.
What is meant? Just like those four ascetics, being content with various requisites, he stands here in this state of practice upon contentment;
and by means of the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] in the four directions, he is "four-directional" (*cātuddiso*).

Because there is an absence of fear regarding the resistance found among the seven formations, he is non-resistant (*appaṭigho*). Because he endures the aforementioned kinds of perils due to his state of being "belonging to the four quarters" (*cātuddisattā*), and because he is non-resistant, he is undaunted (*achambhī*).
Having thus seen the virtue of such practice, and having practiced with wise attention (*yoniso*), I have attained Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Alternatively, like those ascetics, being content with whatever is available...
"Having understood that one is 'four-faced' in the manner already described, and aspiring to such a state of being four-faced, I have attained it by practicing with wise attention (*yoniso*).

Therefore, another who aspires to such a station should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, fearless because of his endurance of dangers and his lack of resentment toward them due to his four-faced nature. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Cātuddisagāthā* is finished. 99.
What is the origin of the verse beginning with "Dussaṅgahā"? It is said that the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī passed away.
Then, after the days of mourning had elapsed, one day the ministers [said]: "For kings, in various matters of business, the chief queen is certainly..."
“[She] should be desired; it would be well, O Lord, if you would bring another queen as well,” they requested.
The king said, “In that case, my men, find out. While they were searching, they learned that in a neighboring kingdom a king had died and his queen was ruling the realm;
she was pregnant, and the ministers, knowing she was a suitable match for the king, made their request to her. She replied, “As for being pregnant, people...”
"It is unpleasant. It would be well if you would wait until I have given birth; if not, seek another," she said.
They reported this matter to the king as well. The king said, "Let her be pregnant; bring her here. They brought her.
The king, having consecrated her, gave her all the wealth of the chief queen and various kinds of provisions for her attendants.
He favored him with gifts. In due time, she gave birth to a son. The king, like his own son, dwelt with him, holding him on his lap and against his breast in all postures.
At that time, the queen’s attendants thought: “The king favors him excessively and places great trust in the prince;
come, let us cause a rift between them.”
Then they said to the prince, "My dear son, you are the son of our king, not the son of this king.
Do not place your trust in him. Then, although the king called out, "Come, my son," and tried to pull him toward him by the hand, the prince did not draw near to the king as he had done before.
The king, wondering "What is the reason? and investigating, learned of that occurrence.
Thinking, "Even though they have been gathered by me, they still behave in a repulsive manner," he became disillusioned, renounced his kingdom, and went forth.

When it was heard that "the king has gone forth," many among his ministers and attendants also went forth. Although the king had gone forth along with his retinue, people continued to bring him excellent requisites;
the king, however, caused those excellent requisites to be distributed according to seniority. In that regard:
Those who receive what is beautiful are satisfied, while the others grumble, saying, "We sweep the cells and perform all the duties, yet we receive coarse food and worn-out robes.
Knowing this as well—thinking, "Even when things are given according to seniority, these people grumble;
alas, how difficult this assembly is to manage"—he took his bowl and robe and went alone.
Having entered the forest and begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
When questioned about the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) by those who came there, he spoke this verse. Its meaning is indeed clear; however, the construction [of the commentary] is as follows:
"Some, even though they have gone forth, are difficult to restrain, being overcome by non-contentment; and likewise, such are some householders."
"Living at home"—it was while loathing this state of being difficult to maintain that I undertook insight meditation and attained [the goal].
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the "Dussaṅgaha" verse is finished.
100. As for "having removed": what is the origin [of this]? It is said that in Benares, a king named Cātumāsika-Brahmadatta went to his pleasure garden during the first month of summer.

There, seeing a *koviḷāra* tree covered with dense, dark green foliage on a delightful spot of ground, he said, "Prepare my couch at the foot of the *koviḷāra* tree," and after sporting in the garden, at the time of evening...
There he made his bed. Again, in the middle month of summer, he went to the park;
at that time the *koviḷāra* tree was in full bloom, and he acted exactly as before. Once more, in the last month of summer, he went there;
at that time the *koviḷāra* tree had its leaves fallen off and was like a withered tree, yet even then the king, not seeing the tree, remained right there due to his previous familiarity with it.
He gave orders for a bed to be prepared there. Although the ministers were aware of it, they prepared the bed there at the king’s command.

Having sported in the park, as he was making his bed there in the evening, he saw that tree and thought: "Ah! Previously this tree had leaves that were lush and beautiful to behold, like if made of jewels;
then, from among its branches which were the color of jewels, [there appeared] things resembling coral sprouts placed there."

“With its flowers, it was once beautiful to behold; its lower ground was strewn with sand like a net of pearls and covered with blossoms fallen from its branches, appearing as if spread with red woolen cloth. But today it stands like a withered tree, reduced to mere branches.
Alas! The *kovidāra* tree has been ravaged by old age. Having thought this, [he saw] even that which is not yet subject to grasping...
“By that very old age one is struck; how much more so, then, by what is clung-to (upādiṇṇa)!”—thus he acquired the perception of impermanence.
Following that very line of thought, while practicing insight into all conditioned phenomena as suffering and non-self, he made this aspiration:
“O, may I too become like the koviḷāra tree with its fallen leaves, having removed the marks of a householder. While thus aspiring, he gradually [passed away] upon that couch on his right side.
While lying on his side, he practiced insight (vipassanā) and realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
Then, at the time of departure, when his ministers said, "It is time to go, Your Majesty," he spoke these verses in the same manner as before, saying, "I am not a king," and so forth.

In that context, *oropayitvā* means having removed. *Gihibyañjanāni* refers to the marks of a householder: hair and beard, fine garments, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, ointments, sons, wives, female slaves, male servants, and so on.
These indicate the state of a householder; therefore, they are called "the marks of a householder. "With his bowl shattered" means his bowl has fallen [from its purpose].
"Having cut" means having cut with the knowledge of the Path (*magga-ñāṇa*). "A hero" means one endowed with the vigor of the Path (*maggavīriya*).
"The bonds of a householder" refers to the bonds of sensual desire (*kāmabandhana*); for sensual desires are indeed the bonds of householders. This, then, is the meaning of the words.
The intended meaning here is this: "O, may I too, having laid aside the marks of a householder, become one whose bowl is [properly] held, like the *koviḷāra* tree.
Thinking thus, he applied himself to insight (*vipassanā*) and attained [the goal]. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the *Koviḷāra* verse is finished.
The First Chapter is concluded. 101–2.

As for the origin of the phrase "If one should obtain": it is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, two individuals destined for solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhisattas) went forth into homelessness.
Having fulfilled the practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the gods. From there...
Of those two, the elder was the son of the King of Bārāṇasī, and the younger was the son of the royal chaplain.
Having conceived on the same day and emerged from their mothers' wombs on the same day, they became companions who played together in the dust.
The chaplain’s son was wise; he said to the prince, "Friend, you..."
"After your father passes away, you shall obtain the kingdom; I shall take the position of chaplain.

Since it is possible to govern a kingdom only when one is well-trained, come, let us learn a craft. Then, having both accumulated the merit of sacrifices, they wandered for alms through villages, market towns, and other settlements, until they reached a village in a frontier province.
At the time of their alms-round, five paccekabuddhas [arrived] at that village.
They entered. There, when the people saw the Paccekabuddhas, they were filled with enthusiasm;
they prepared seats, offered them excellent hard and soft food, and paid them honor. Then it occurred to them:
"There are none among us who are of equal high birth; yet these people, if they so desire, give alms to us."
"If they do not give [it] when we ask, yet they perform such honors for these renunciants, then surely these people know some craft; well then, let us learn that craft from them.
When those people had departed, they found an opportunity and said, "Venerable sirs, please teach us whatever craft you know."
They requested [ordination]. The Paccekabuddhas said, "It is not possible to train without having gone forth. They requested going-forth and were ordained.

Then the Paccekabuddhas, having explained the rules of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) to them in the manner beginning with, "In this way you must dress; in this way you must clothe yourselves," said: "The perfection of this craft consists in delighting in solitude; therefore..."
"One should sit alone, one should walk alone, one should stand alone, and one should lie down alone.
Thus they gave each of them a separate leaf-hut; then, having entered their respective leaf-huts, they sat down.
From the moment the chaplain’s son sat down, he attained concentration of mind and acquired meditative absorption (jhāna). The prince, however, [attained it] in a mere moment.
Becoming weary, he came into his presence. Seeing him, the other asked, "What is it, friend?
He replied, "I am weary. "In that case, sit here," he said.
After sitting there for a moment, he asked, "Friend, is delight in solitude the accomplishment of this craft? The chaplain's son replied, "It is so, friend; therefore, you yourself—"
“Go back to your own place; I shall master the perfection of this craft,” he said.
He went, but after only a moment, becoming weary once more, he returned three times in the same manner as before.
Then the chaplain’s son dismissed him in that very way, and when he had gone, he thought: “This man has his own work to do...”
“He neglects me and comes here constantly. So he left his leaf-hut and entered the forest.

The other remained sitting in his own leaf-hut; after a short while, becoming weary once more, he went to him and, though searching here and there, did not see him. He thought: “He who, when he was a householder, used to take gifts...”
"Even though he came, he did not obtain the sight of me; now that I have arrived, he has departed, unwilling even to grant me a look.
Alas, you wretched mind! Are you not ashamed that you have brought me here four times? Now I shall no longer act under your control;
on the contrary, I shall bring you entirely under my own control. Having thus spoken, he entered his own dwelling and applied himself to insight (vipassanā).
Having undertaken the practice for private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) and realized it, he went through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave.
The other one also entered the forest, undertook insight meditation (vipassanā), realized private enlightenment, and went to that very same place.
Both of them sat down on a slab of ruby (manosilā) and each individually recited these verses of inspired utterance (udānagāthā).
In this context, "nipaka" means one who is naturally prudent, wise, and skilled in the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and so forth.
"Sādhuvihārin" means endowed with either the attainment of absorption (appanā) or access concentration (upacāra). "Dhīra" means possessed of fortitude.

Here, the perfection of fortitude was already mentioned by way of being "nipaka"; however, the meaning here is specifically "one who is endowed with fortitude. Fortitude (dhiti) is defined as unwavering perseverance.
“‘Willingly, skin and sinews’—this is a designation for one whose energy proceeds in such a manner.
Furthermore, he is wise (dhīra) because he has condemned evil. ‘Just as a king, abandoning a conquered kingdom’:

just as a natural-born king, realizing that a conquered kingdom brings no benefit, abandons his sovereignty and wanders alone, so too should one abandon companions who are fools and wander alone. Or else, [it means] just like a king.”
"Kingdom": this also means that he wandered alone, just as King Sutasoma did when he abandoned his conquered kingdom and wandered alone, and just as King Mahājanaka did;
the rest can be understood according to what has already been said, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
The commentary on the verse concerning companions is finished.

103. Regarding this verse beginning with “Truly, praise...,” the origin of this story is exactly like the origin of the *Cātuddisa* verse, up until the point where the Pratyekabuddhas sat upon seats prepared on the surface of the sky. However, this is the distinction:
that king was terrified three times during the night, whereas this one was not; nor was a sacrifice presented to him.
Thus, having had the Paccekabuddhas seated on the seats prepared upon the surface of the sky, he asked, "Who are you?
"Great King, we are known as the 'Blameless-Eaters' (Anavajjabhojino)," they replied. "Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of this term 'Blameless-Eaters'?
"Great King, whether we receive something beautiful or unattractive, we eat it without any change of expression. Having heard that, the king—

It occurred to him: "What if I were now to examine these men to see whether they are such as I have described or not? On that day, he served them with broken rice and sour gruel as their second course.
The Paccekabuddhas ate it without any change of expression, as if it were the Deathless (amata).
The king thought, "Because they have given their word, they remain without any change of expression for one day; tomorrow I shall find out," and so he invited them for the following day.
On the second day as well, he did exactly the same. They too ate in that very same manner.

Then the king, thinking, "I shall test them by giving them something exquisite," invited them once more. For two days, having rendered great honor, he served them with choice and most varied kinds of solid and soft food.
They likewise ate without any change of expression, and [pronounced] a blessing for the king.
Having spoken thus, they departed. Not long after they had gone, the king thought, "These men eat blameless food; oh, that I too might become one who eats blameless food!
Having abandoned his great kingdom and undertaken the life of a wanderer, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā).
Having become a Paccekabuddha, he sat at the foot of a Mañjūsaka tree, clarifying his own meditative object in the midst of the other Paccekabuddhas, and uttered this:
He spoke this verse. Its meaning in terms of the words is quite plain.

However, regarding the phrase "perfection of companions," it should be understood that "companions" refers specifically to those endowed with the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to the state of one beyond training (asekha); this alone constitutes the "perfection of companions. This is the application [of the commentary] here: we certainly praise this aforementioned perfection of companions.
It is said that one should praise [them] with absolute certainty. How so? Because they are the best companions to be associated with.

Why? For one who associates with those superior in their own virtue and other qualities, qualities such as virtue that have not yet arisen do arise, and those already arisen reach growth, increase, and fullness. For one who associates with equals, there is mutual sharing regarding remorse.
And by means of diversion, those [pleasures] once obtained do not decline. However, failing to find such excellent and equal companions,
a clansman who desires his own welfare should abandon wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like, and subsisting on food acquired through righteous and equitable means—
neither giving rise to aversion nor attachment toward it— he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, living a life free from blame.
"I too, practicing in this way, have attained this success.
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of praise for the duration [of life]. 104.
As for the verse beginning "Having seen gold": what is its origin? It is said that a certain king in Bārāṇasī, during the summer season, while lying down for his midday rest...
He approached, and in his presence a courtesan named Vaṇṇadāsī was grinding *gosīta* sandalwood. On one of her arms was a single golden bracelet, and on the other arm were two.
These [two] brushed against each other, while the other [single one] did not brush against them.
Seeing this, the king thought, "In this very way, there is friction in living in a group, but no friction in living alone," and reflecting thus again and again—
He looked at a female slave. At that time, the queen, adorned with all her ornaments, was standing there fanning him.
Thinking, "The king seems to be infatuated with this low-caste slave," she raised the slave up and began to grind the rice herself.
Then, as many golden bracelets on both her arms struck against one another, they made a great noise.
They gave birth. The king, becoming even more deeply disenchanted, while still lying on his right side, applied insight and realized Pratyekabuddhahood.
As he lay there, blissful with that unsurpassed happiness, Queen Candanahatthā approached him and said, “I shall anoint you, Great King.
He replied, “Go away; do not anoint me. She asked, “Why?”
"Are you the Great King? He replied, "I am not the king. Having heard this exchange between them, the ministers approached;
when he was addressed by them with the title "Great King," he said, "Truly, I am not the king. The rest is exactly as stated in the first verse.
This, then, is the commentary on that verse: therein, *disvā* means having looked upon. *Suvaṇṇassa* means of gold. *Valayāni* means bracelets.
This is a remainder of the text; for this meaning has its word-meaning still remaining. "Radiant" (*pabhassarāni*) means having the nature of shining;
it is said that they are "possessing luster. The rest has its word-meaning already explained. This, however, is the construction:
having seen the golden bracelets on his arm, and having reflected thus—"When living in a group there is clashing, but when living alone there is no clashing"—he [applied] insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having begun [the practice], I have attained it. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Suvaṇṇavalaya-gāthā* is finished.
105. Regarding "Thus by the second": what is its origin? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, while still young, desired to go forth into homelessness.
The king commanded his ministers, “Take the queen and administer the kingdom; I shall go forth into homelessness.
The ministers persuaded him, saying, “Great King, we are unable to protect a kingdom without a ruler; neighboring kings will come and plunder it.
Wait until at least one son has been born. With a gentle heart, the king consented.
Then the queen conceived. The king commanded them again: "The queen is pregnant;
once a son is born, consecrate him in the kingdom and you govern the realm; I shall go forth into the religious life.
The ministers said, "This is difficult to know, Great King—whether the queen will give birth to a son or a daughter. Wait, therefore, until the time of delivery."
Again they exhorted the king. Then she gave birth to a son. At that time too, the king commanded his ministers in the same manner.
The ministers again exhorted the king with many reasons, saying, "Wait, Great King, until he is capable.
Thereafter, when the prince had become capable, [the king] summoned the ministers and said, "He is now capable..."

"Having consecrated him in the kingdom, proceed [to the forest]," he said; and without giving the ministers an opportunity to speak, having had all his requisites such as saffron robes and other items brought from the marketplace, he went forth right there in the inner palace. Having departed like Mahājanaka, he went away.
All his attendants followed after the king, lamenting in various ways, until he reached the boundary of his own kingdom.
Having gone there, he drew a line with a wooden staff and said, "This line must not be crossed.
The great multitude, making the line their head, lay prostrate on the ground lamenting, "Now, dear child, you have the King's command; what will you do?
Thus they made the prince cross the line. The prince ran toward them, crying out, "Father! Father!"
He reached the king. Upon seeing the prince, the king thought, "I have governed the kingdom while looking after such a great multitude of people;
why then should I not be able to look after a single child? Taking the prince with him, he entered the forest.
There, seeing a leaf-hut where former paccekabuddhas had dwelt, he made his home together with his son.
Then the prince, being unaccustomed to sleeping on excellent beds and such, would weep while lying on a spread of grass or a bed of ropes.
When touched by cold winds and the like, he would cry out, "It is cold, father! It is hot, father! Mosquitoes are biting me, father!
I am hungry, father! I am thirsty, father! The king spent the night merely trying to console him.
During the day as well, he would go for alms and offer him food;

the prince, though it was a mixed meal consisting mostly of *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, *mugga*, and other such grains, ate it despite its lack of flavor due to the force of his hunger, and after a few days, he withered like a lotus placed in the heat.
The King, however, ate without any change of expression through the power of reflection. Then, seeking to persuade the prince, [the King said]:
He said, "Father, excellent food is available in the city; let us go there. The prince replied, "Yes, father.

Then, placing him in front, they returned by the very same path they had come. The prince’s mother, the queen, thinking, "The king will not now stay long in the forest with the prince; he will return in just a few days," [prepared] for the king a walking-stick...
Having had a fence constructed right where he had written, he took up residence there.
The king, standing not far from that fence, sent him forth, saying, "My dear son, your mother is sitting here;
go to her. He stood watching until the prince reached that place, thinking, "May no one harm him. The prince then ran toward his mother.
The guards, seeing the prince approaching, informed the queen. The queen, surrounded by twenty thousand female dancers, went out to meet him and received him.
She then inquired about the king’s well-being. Upon hearing that he was coming from behind, she dispatched men.
At that very moment, the king also returned to his own quarters. When the people did not see the king, they...
They turned back. Then the queen, having become despondent, took her son and went to the city, where she had him consecrated in the kingdom.
The king, while sitting in his own dwelling place, attained insight and reached the state of a Paccekabuddha;
then, at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree in the midst of the Paccekabuddhas, he uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*). As for its meaning, it is quite plain.

This, however, is the intended meaning here: "When I was living together with this one prince who informed me of the cold, heat, and so forth, my verbal expression toward him—whether it was an outburst of anger born of affection—arose because of that intimacy.
If I do not renounce him now, then in the future it will be exactly as it is now; likewise, [it will be] with the second."

"His speech was abusive and provocative. Seeing that "both of these are obstacles to the attainment of distinction," and perceiving this danger in the future, I abandoned them, practiced with wise attention (*yoniso*), and attained Pratyekabuddhahood.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses concerning fear of the future is finished. 106.
"For desires are variegated"—how did this come about? It is said that in Benares, the son of a merchant obtained the position of a merchant while still young.
He had three palaces suited to the three seasons. With all his prosperity, he was like a young god.
He attended upon them as if they were his own parents. Then, while still young, he asked his parents for permission, saying, "I shall go forth into homelessness. They tried to dissuade him.
He persisted in the same way. Again, his parents sought to dissuade him in various ways, saying, "My dear son, you are delicate;
the life of renunciation is difficult, like walking upon the edge of a razor's blade."
Thus he remained bound to that very thought. They thought: “If he goes forth, we shall suffer grief;
if we try to stop him, he will suffer grief. Nevertheless, let it be our grief rather than his.
With this, they gave him permission. Then, disregarding all his weeping attendants, he went to Isipatana and [approached] the Paccekabuddhas.
He went forth into the presence [of the Buddha]. He did not obtain a magnificent dwelling; instead, he slept on a wooden plank spread upon a couch.
Having been accustomed to excellent beds, he suffered greatly throughout the entire night.
At dawn, having performed his bodily grooming, he took up his bowl and robes and entered for alms together with the Paccekabuddhas. There, the elders [received] the seat of honor...
They received only the first portion of alms, while the novices received whatever coarse seats and food remained. He became exceedingly distressed even by that coarse food.
Within just a few days, having become emaciated and disfigured, he grew disillusioned because his practice of the ascetic life had not yet reached maturity.
Then, having sent a messenger to his parents, he left the order. After only a few more days, he regained his strength.
Again he desired to go forth; having gone forth for a second time, he went forth again and then left the order once more.

But on the third occasion, having gone forth and practiced correctly, he attained insight, realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and after uttering this verse of exultation, he further recited this very verse of prophecy in the midst of the Pratyekabuddhas.

In this context, "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) are twofold: sensual pleasure as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure as defilements (*kilesakāma*). Here, sensual pleasure as objects refers to phenomena that serve as objects of perception, such as agreeable forms and so forth;
sensual pleasure as defilements refers to every variety of lust (*rāga*). However, it is sensual pleasure as objects that is intended here.

They are "variegated" (*citrā*) by way of their many forms, such as visible forms and so forth. They are "sweet" (*madhurā*) by way of worldly gratification. They are "delightful to the mind" (*manoramā*) because they gladden the minds of foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*). "By means of various forms" (*virūparūpena*)...

"By various forms" means by many kinds of intrinsic natures; for they are variegated by way of visible form and so forth, and even within visible form and the rest, they possess diverse forms such as blue and so on.
Thus, by displaying gratification in this or that manifold and varied way, they churn the mind and do not allow it to delight in the going-forth. The rest here is self-evident.
The conclusion should also be understood by joining two or three phrases according to the same method stated in the preceding verses.
The commentary on the verses concerning sensual pleasures is finished.
107. As for the verse beginning "Ītī ca" (And calamities): what is its origin? It is said that in Benares a boil arose upon the king; his intense pains increased.
The physicians said, "Without surgical treatment, there will be no relief. The king granted them immunity from punishment and had the surgical procedure performed.
Having cut him open and extracted the pus and blood, they reported their success and bound the wound with a cloth.
They also properly instructed him regarding a diet of coarse meat. Due to this coarse food, the king’s body became emaciated.
A boil appeared on him and it began to fester. Thinking he was feeling well, he ate rich, succulent food;
consequently, his strength returned and he indulged in sensual pleasures once again. His boil then returned to its former state.
In this manner, after having the surgical treatment performed three times and being shunned by the physicians, he became disillusioned, renounced his great kingdom, and went forth into homelessness.
Having entered the forest and begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he realized the enlightenment of a *paccekabuddha* within seven years.
After speaking this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*), he went to the Nandamūlaka Cave.
In that context, "calamity" (*īti*) means that which comes; it is a designation for those adventitious, unwholesome causes of misfortune. Therefore...
These strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are also a plague (*īti*) in the sense that they bring about manifold calamities and in the sense that they are a gathering place for misfortunes.

A boil (*gaṇḍa*) also exudes impurity; it becomes swollen, ripened, and burst open. Therefore, these [sensual pleasures] are a boil because they exude the impurity of the defilements (*kilesa*), and because through their arising, aging, and dissolution, they possess the state of being swollen, ripened, and burst open. That which afflicts is an affliction (*upaddava*).
The meaning is that it "overcomes" and "envelops" by producing harm; this is a designation for the tumor of lust (*rāgagaṇḍa*) and so forth.

Therefore, even the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are a calamity (*upaddava*), because they bring about the non-attainment of the goal of Nibbāna and because they are surrounded by all manner of misfortunes and karmic actions.
Furthermore, because these [defilements] produce a state of illness consisting of the defilements, they cause greed toward health, which is to say, virtue (*sīla*).
Or, by arising, they plunder one's natural health; therefore, in the sense of plundering health, it is a "disease" (*roga*).
In the sense of having entered inside, in the sense of piercing within, and in the sense of being difficult to extract, it is a "dart" (*salla*).
Because it brings about fear pertaining to both the present life and future lives, it is "fear" (*bhaya*). "It is mine" is *metaṃ*. The rest here is self-evident.
The conclusion should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Ītigāthā* is finished. 108.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Cold...": it is said that in Benares there was once a king named Sītālukabrahmadatta.
Having thus gone forth, he lived in a grass hut in the forest. And in that place, because it was an open space, it was cold when it was cold and scorching when it was hot.

In the village where he went for alms, he did not receive enough food, drinking water was scarce, and he was troubled by wind, heat, gadflies, and reptiles. It occurred to him: "Only half a yojana from here..."
“This region is excellent; there are none of these dangers there at all. Suppose I were to go there;
while dwelling in comfort, it would be possible for me to attain happiness. Then it occurred to him again: “Those who have gone forth are not greedy for requisites;
they bring such a mind under their own control, and do not let themselves be controlled by the mind.”
“They are engaged in worldly affairs; I will not go there. Having reflected thus, he did not go. In this manner, having reflected on his arising thoughts up to three times, he turned back.
Then, dwelling right there for seven years and practicing correctly, he realized pratyekabodhi (solitary enlightenment).
Having uttered this verse of exultation, he went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.
In this context, "cold" (*sīta*) is twofold: that caused by an internal disturbance of the elements and that caused by an external disturbance of the elements;
the same applies to "heat" (*uṇha*). "Gnats" (*ḍaṃsa*) are brown flies. "Crawling things" (*sarīsapa*) are any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling.
The rest is self-evident. The conclusion should also be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Sītālukā Gāthā is finished. 109.

What is the origin of the story of Nāga? It is said that in Benares, a certain king, having ruled the kingdom for twenty years, passed away and was reborn in hell, where he suffered for exactly twenty years. Thereafter, he was reborn in the Himalayan region in the womb of an elephant.
He became a magnificent leader of the herd, a great elephant with fully developed trunks and a body as beautiful as a lotus.

The female elephants ate the broken-off branches from his drooping limbs like elephant-grass, and they smeared him with mud in the fords; everything was just as it had been for the Nāga of Pālileyyaka.
Having become disillusioned with the herd, he departed. Then the herd followed after him by his footprints, and so—
They followed him even as he fled for a third time. Then he thought: "Now my nephew is ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī;
what if I were to go to the park belonging to my previous birth? There he will protect me.
Then, while the herd was fast asleep during the night, he left one group after another and entered that very park. Seeing him, the park-keeper—
He informed the king. The king, thinking, "I shall capture the elephant," surrounded it with his army.
The elephant proceeded directly toward the king. The king, thinking, "It is coming toward me," stood there having fixed an arrow to his bow.
Then the elephant, thinking, "He might even pierce me," spoke in a human voice: "Brahmadatta, do not pierce me; I am your grandfather."
The king asked him everything, "What are you saying? The elephant also related the entire account of his existence in the kingdom, in hell, and in the womb of an elephant.
The king said, "It is well; do not fear, and do not frighten anyone," and he provided for the elephant's maintenance, appointed guards, and established elephant-keepers for him.
Then one day, the king, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, thought: "Having ruled for twenty years, this man was boiled in hell;
with what remained of that karmic residue, he was reborn in the animal realm. Even there, unable to endure the crowding and friction of living in a herd, he has come here.
Alas, living in a crowd is suffering; indeed, solitude alone is happiness. Having reflected thus, he—
Having begun insight meditation right there, he realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
While he was thus made happy by supramundane bliss, his ministers approached him, prostrated themselves, and said, "It is time for the vehicle, Great King.
Then, saying, "I am not a king," he spoke this verse in the same manner as before. As for its meaning, it is quite evident.
This, however, is the intended application here— and that indeed by way of logical reasoning, not by way of mere hearsay.
Just as this elephant is called a "nāga" because he has been tamed (*danta*) by means of the virtues dear to the Noble Ones and thus does not reach the state of the untamed,
or because of the greatness of his body, so too, when will I also— by being tamed through the virtues dear to the Noble Ones and by not reaching the state of the untamed— [be called a nāga]?
I might be called a "Nāga" because of my non-returning to this state of existence and because of the greatness of my body of qualities.
And just as he, having avoided herds, dwells as he pleases in the forest alone in the bliss of solitary wandering like the horn of a rhinoceros—
when indeed shall I too, having avoided the crowd, dwell thus in the bliss of solitary abiding?
Dwelling in the forest as he pleases, in whatever way brings him happiness, let him dwell in the forest for as long as he desires;
"let him wander alone like the rhinoceros horn" means that he should wander alone.
And just as this [elephant] has grown a trunk due to the great size and firmness of its body, when indeed shall I too become thus?
May I become one who has produced a great mass of virtue through the greatness of the aggregate of the virtues of the Asekhas.

And just as he is called "Padumī" (Lotus-like) because his limbs resemble a lotus or because he was born into the family of the lotuses, when indeed shall I too likewise become "Padumī" because my straightness resembles a lotus or because I am born into the noble-born lotus of the Ariyans? And just as he is sublime in terms of strength, power, and so forth...
"When shall I too become so eminent through such things as perfectly pure bodily conduct, or through virtue, concentration, and penetrative wisdom?
Thinking thus, he applied himself to insight and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The commentary on the Nāga verses is finished.
110. As for the *Aṭṭhānata* Sutta, what is its origin? It is said that the young son of the King of Bārāṇasī, while still a child, desired to go forth and asked his parents for permission.
His parents tried to dissuade him, but even though he was being restrained, he persisted, saying, "I shall go forth.
Then, after they had told him everything as previously related in the case of the merchant’s son, they finally gave their consent. "And having gone forth, [he stayed] right there in the park..."
They made him promise, "You must dwell [in seclusion]," and he did accordingly. His mother, accompanied by twenty thousand dancing women, would go to the park early in the morning;

after having her son drink rice-gruel and eating snacks and other foods with him, she would converse with him until midday and then enter the city. His father also would come at midday, feed him, and—
Having himself eaten and conversed with him throughout the day, he would station attendants at evening time and enter the city.
In this way, he lived day and night without being separated from him.
Now, at that time, a Paccekabuddha named Ādiccabandhu was dwelling in the Nandamūlaka cave.
Thus reflecting, he saw: "This prince was able to go forth, yet he is unable to cut off his matted locks.
He then reflected further: "Will he become disillusioned through his own natural disposition, or not?

Then, knowing that if he were to become disillusioned through his natural disposition, it would take too long, [the deity] thought, "I shall provide him with an object of focus," and proceeded in the same manner as before.
Having come from the surface of Mount Manosilā, he stood in the park. When the king’s retinue saw him, they announced, “A Paccekabuddha has arrived, Your Majesty!
The king, his heart filled with joy, thinking, “Now my son shall dwell here without longing, in the company of a Paccekabuddha,” attended upon the Paccekabuddha with great respect.
Having requested him to reside right there, he provided everything, including leaf-huts, pavilions, and walking-paths for meditation.
Having had it built, he made him dwell there. While living there, on one occasion, having found an opportunity, he asked the prince:

"Who are you? "I am a renunciant," he replied. "Those who have gone forth are not like this," [the prince said]. Then, when [the prince] asked, "Venerable sir, what are they like? What is it that is unsuitable for me?
[the other replied], "You do not perceive what is unsuitable for yourself."
"Is it not the case that your mother, accompanied by twenty thousand women, comes in the morning and keeps the park unoccupied;
and your father, with a great army, keeps watch in the evening and throughout the entire night?
Those who have gone forth are certainly not like you; rather, they are exactly like this," he said while remaining right there through his supernormal power (iddhi).

He showed him a certain monastery in the Himalayas. There, seeing the Paccekabuddhas standing by a support-board, walking to and fro, and performing tasks such as dyeing and sewing, he asked: "Did you not come here before?
And was the going-forth (pabbajjā) permitted by you? "Yes, the going-forth was permitted; from the time we went forth..."
"From the time they become ascetics, they are permitted to seek their own deliverance and to go to whatever place they desire or long for;
this much alone is sufficient," he said. Then, standing in the air, he spoke this half-stanza: "It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience that temporary liberation.
Having spoken thus, while still visible, he traveled through the air to the Nandamūlaka Crag.
He departed. When the Paccekabuddha had thus gone, he entered his own leaf-hut and lay down.
The guard, thinking, "The prince is asleep; where will he go now? fell into a careless sleep.
Knowing that he was negligent, he took his bowl and robe and entered the forest. Standing there, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.

Having realized it, he attained the state of a Paccekabuddha. And there, when asked by the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha), "How was this attained?", he spoke the half-stanza that had been uttered, completing it.
Its meaning is as follows: *aṭṭhānaṃ taṃ* means "that is not a basis"; it is said to be "not a cause. [Note: *anunāsikalopo* refers to the elision of the nasal vowel.]
It is used in such contexts as “the seeing of the Noble Truths. *Saṅgaṇikārattassa* means one who delights in company.
*Yaṃ* is a word denoting a reason, as in “that for which one feels shame regarding what should be shunned. *Phusaye* means he would attain.
*Sāmayikaṃ vimuttiṃ* refers to mundane meditative attainment (*lokīya-samāpatti*), for that [attainment] is [lost] by its adversaries at the very moment it has been entered.
Because it is a liberation [attained] at a specific time, it is called "temporary liberation" (*sāmayikā vimutti*). Regarding that temporary liberation: it is impossible;
no such cause exists for one who delights in social company by which means they might touch that liberation.
Having reflected upon these words of the Paccekabuddha Ādiccabandhu, one who abandons delight in social company and practices with proper wisdom thinks: "I have attained it."
He said: "The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Aṭṭhānagāthā* is finished.
The second chapter is finished.
111. As for the "forks of views," what is their origin? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, having gone into seclusion, reflected:
"Just as there exist things like heat which counteract cold and so forth, does there likewise exist a 'turning away' (nibbāna) that counteracts the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), or not?
He asked his ministers: "Do you know the turning away? They replied: "We know it, Great King. The king—
“What is that? they asked. Then, by way of the formula beginning with “The world is finite,” they spoke of eternalism and annihilationism.

The king thought, “These do not know; all these are proponents of false views. Seeing for himself their contradiction and irrationality, he reflected, “There exists the turning away from the cycle of existence (vivaṭṭa) which strikes down the cycle (vaṭṭa); that must be sought. Having thus abandoned his kingdom and gone forth into homelessness, he—

While practicing insight, he realized Paccekabodhi (the enlightenment of a Private Buddha). And amidst the company of the Paccekabuddhas, he uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*) as well as a verse of proclamation.

Its meaning is as follows: "The snares of views" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views. For these are "snares of views" in the sense that they are snares (*visūka*) because they are pierced by the right view of the Path, because they are struck down, and because they are contrary to it;
thus they are snares of views, or the views themselves are the snares.
"Transcending the diversities of views": having surpassed them by means of the path of vision (*dassanamagga*). "Attained to certainty" (*niyāma*):

having reached the state of necessity due to being subject to non-falling away and being destined for enlightenment; or, it refers to the first path known as the "certainty of rightness" (*sammattaniyāma*).
By this much, both the accomplishment of the function of the first path and its acquisition have been described. Now, [the phrase] "having acquired the path" (*paṭiladdhamagga*)...
By this, he shows the attainment of the remaining paths. "I am one whose knowledge has arisen" means that I am one who has attained the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment).
By this, he shows the fruit. "Not to be led by others" means that he cannot be led by others [to realize] "this is the truth.

By this, he shows self-become-ness (*sayambhutā*); or rather, because there is an absence of being led by others once the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* has been reached, it is self-determined. [This is through] serenity and insight.

Or, one who has transcended the thorns of views, who has entered the certainty of rightness (*niyāma*) by means of the first path, who has attained the remaining paths, whose knowledge has arisen through the knowledge of fruition—since all this has been realized by himself, he is "not to be led by others.
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the verse concerning the thorns of views is finished.

112. As for the origin of the term *nillolupa* (free from greed): it is said that the king of Bārāṇasī’s cook, having cooked an intermediate meal, presented it to him—food that was pleasing to behold and sweet in taste—thinking, "Perhaps the king might grant me some wealth.
By its very fragrance, it aroused the king's desire to eat; it caused saliva to arise in his mouth. However, as soon as the first morsel was placed in his mouth...
Seventeen thousand people were as if touched by the nectar of immortality. The cook thought, "Now he will give me [a reward], now he will give me [a reward].

The king also thought, "This cook is worthy of honor," yet, fearing that if he tasted the flavor and honored him, an evil reputation would spread—namely, "This king is greedy and fond of flavors"—he said nothing at all.
In this manner, until the conclusion of the meal, the cook thought, "He will give me now; he will give me now.
The king, out of fear of disrepute, said nothing at all. Then the cook thought, "I suppose this king has no faculty of gustatory consciousness.
On the second day, he served him food that was tasteless. While eating, the king remarked, "Alas, the cook is truly worthy of punishment today!"
Although he knew, he reflected as before and said nothing out of fear of ill repute.
Then the cook thought, "The king knows neither what is good nor what is bad," and taking all the proceeds himself, he cooked something and gave it to the king.
The king exclaimed, "Alas, what greed! Here I am, enjoying twenty thousand cities..."
"Through greed for this, I do not even receive a mere morsel of food. Having become disillusioned and renounced his kingdom, he went forth into homelessness;
while practicing insight (vipassanā), he realized pratyekabodhi. He spoke this verse in the same manner as before.
In that context, *nillolupa* means one who is free from greed (*alolupa*). For whoever is overcome by craving for flavors (*rasataṇhā*) is repeatedly and excessively plundered (*luppati*).
He is "greedy" (*lolupa*) because he is seized; therefore, rejecting that, he says "free from greed" (*nillolupa*).

Regarding "free from guile" (*nikkuha*): although one who lacks the three bases of guile is called "free from guile," the intended meaning here is that he is "free from guile" because he does not fall into astonishment over pleasant food and the like.

"Free from thirst" (*nippipāso*): here, "thirst" (*pipāsā*) is the desire to drink; by the absence of that, he is "free from thirst," meaning he is devoid of the longing to eat due to greed for delicious flavors.
"Free from hypocrisy" (*nimmakkho*): here, "hypocrisy" (*makkho*) is characterized by the destruction of another's virtues; by the absence of that, he is "free from hypocrisy.

He says this with reference to the absence of hypocrisy regarding the cook’s virtues during his own time as a householder. "With delusion whose dregs have been blown away" (*niddhantakasāvamoho*): here... [text continues]

The three beginning with lust—namely, lust, hatred, and delusion—and the three beginning with bodily misconduct—namely, bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct—these six states should be understood as "bitter" (kasāva) in the sense that, according to their occurrence, they cause one to abandon one's own nature and take on another nature by way of being unpleasing, by way of causing the assumption of a different state, and by way of being dregs. As it is said: "In this context, what are the three bitter things?

The bitterness of lust, the bitterness of hatred, and the bitterness of delusion. These are the three bitter things. In this context, what are the other three bitter things? The bitterness of body, the bitterness of speech, and the bitterness of mind."

Among those, having set aside delusion (*moha*), because the five stains (*kasāva*) and the delusion that is their root have been blown away, he is one who has "blown away the stain of delusion" (*niddhantakasāvamoha*).
Alternatively, because the three stains of body, speech, and mind, as well as delusion, have been blown away, he is one who has "blown away the stain of delusion.
Among the others, through non-greediness and so forth, the stain of lust (*rāga-kasāva*) [is removed], and through freedom from flattery, the stain of hatred (*dosa-kasāva*) [is removed].
The state of being "shaken off" (niddhanta) is indeed established. "Free from longing" (nirāsaya) means devoid of craving.

"Having existed in the whole world" (sabbaloke bhavitvā) means having become free from the craving for existence and non-existence in the entire world—whether in the three realms of existence or in the twelve sense-bases; this is the meaning.

The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. Alternatively, after speaking of the three feet, [the phrase] "one should wander alone" (eko care) means that one would be able to wander alone.
In this case, the connection should be made in this way.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "Nillolupa" is finished. 113.
As for the origin of the verse "Pāpaṃ sahāyaṃ": it is said that in Benares, a certain king, by means of his great royal power...
While performing a circumambulation of the city, he saw people carrying out old grain and other goods from the storehouses to the outside, and he asked his ministers, "What is this, sirs?
The ministers replied, "Great King, new grain and other crops will soon be produced;
these people are discarding the old grain and other goods to make room for them."
The king said, "Tell me, is the service of the women’s quarters, the army, and so forth, being performed in full? "Yes, Great King, it is complete.
"In that case, my good man, have an alms-hall built; I shall give gifts. Let these grains not go to waste without benefit.
Then a certain minister holding wrong views said to him, "Great King, there is no..."

Starting from the words "It has been given," and continuing until he said, "Fools and the wise alike, having run their course and wandered through saṃsāra, will make an end of suffering," [the Elder] stopped him.
When the king saw the storehouse being plundered for a second and even a third time, he gave the same command.
For a third time, the Elder stopped him by saying, "Great King, this so-called 'giving' is merely a matter of what has been assigned as a gift," and so forth.
Thus, thinking, "Alas! I cannot even give away what belongs to me; what use have I for these evil companions?", he became disillusioned.

Abandoning his kingdom, he went forth into homelessness and, practicing insight (vipassanā), realized pratyekabodhi. And while censuring that evil companion, he uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna).
This is the summary of its meaning: A clansman who desires his own welfare should avoid that evil companion who, because he is possessed of ten bases of evil views, is "evil";

who sees harm even for others, thus being a "seer of harm"; and who is settled in what is uneven, such as bodily misconduct and so forth—that evil companion, a seer of harm, settled in the uneven. He himself should not...
"One should not associate" means one should not associate with such a person by one's own will. However, if it is under the power of another, what can be done?
"Addicted" (pasuta) means entangled; the meaning is that they are stuck here and there due to their views.

"Negligent" (pamatta) means one whose mind is cast away toward the strands of sensual pleasure, or one who is devoid of the cultivation of wholesome states. One should not associate with such a companion.
"I do not associate with them, nor do I wait upon them; rather, I shall wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The commentary on the verses concerning evil companions is finished. 114.

As for the origin of the verse beginning "The learned one": it is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were eight individuals destined for solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhisatta).

Having gone forth and fulfilled the duties of one who has returned from his travels, he was reborn in the world of the devas; all such details are exactly as described in the verse concerning the "one who eats blameless food.
However, this is the distinction: after the Paccekabuddha had been seated, the king asked, "Who are you?
They replied, "Great King, we are known as the 'Highly Learned' (Bahussuta). The king said, "I am Sutasoma by name, the son of Brahmadatta."
“I do not reach satiety with what I have heard; come now, I shall listen to their diverse and methodical teaching of the Dhamma.

Thus, being delighted, he offered water for the guest-offering, served the meal, and at the conclusion of his meal duties, sat down beside the senior monk of the Saṅgha and said, “Venerable sir, please give a discourse on the Dhamma. He replied, “May you be happy, Great King; the destruction of lust—”
Having said, "May there be [the destruction of hatred]," he rose. The king thought, "This one is not very learned; the second one will be learned.
Tomorrow I shall hear his diverse teaching of the Dhamma," and he invited him for the following day. In this manner, he invited them all until their turn had come.
They all [said], "May there be the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of rebirth, and the destruction of existence."

“May there be the destruction of the cycle of existence, the destruction of the substrata, the destruction of craving! Having thus distinguished each phrase individually and spoken the remainder exactly as in the first instance, they rose from their seats.
Then the king thought, “These say, ‘We are learned,’ yet they have no varied discourse; what is it that they have said?
He began to examine the meaning of their words. Then, while examining the phrase, “May there be the destruction of passion,” he—
Knowing that "when lust is exhausted, hatred and delusion, as well as various other defilements, are also exhausted," he was satisfied, thinking:

"These recluses are truly learned in the non-figurative sense (nippariyāya). For just as when a man points to the great earth or the sky with his finger, it is not merely the finger-tip that is pointed out; rather—"
"The entire earth and space itself are thus indicated. In this way, by indicating each single meaning through these [words], immeasurable meanings are indicated.

Then, aspiring for such a state of great learning as he thought, "When indeed shall I too become so very learned?", he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight (vipassanā), attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
Having realized this, he spoke this verse of inspired utterance (*udāna*).

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: “One of great learning” (*bahussuta*) is twofold—there is the one of great learning in the scriptures (*pariyatti-bahussuta*), who has mastered the three Piṭakas in their entirety according to the letter and the meaning;

and there is the one of great learning through penetration (*paṭivedha-bahussuta*), who has realized the knowledge of the path and fruit along with the superknowledges (*abhiññā*). One whose tradition has been handed down...
One who upholds the Dhamma is a "Dhammadhara. One who is endowed with sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind is "sublime" (ulāra).
One who possesses ready wit is "eloquent" (paṭibhānavā), being one whose wit is appropriate, one whose wit is liberated, and one whose wit is both appropriate and liberated.

Alternatively, one who possesses ready wit should be understood as being of three kinds according to study, inquiry, and realization. For he in whom the study [of the scriptures] flashes forth is one whose wit regarding study is ready.

One for whom an inquiry regarding the meaning, the knowledge, the characteristics, and the possible and impossible occurs as a ready response is one possessed of inspired ingenuity in inquiry (*paripucchā-paṭibhānavā*).
One for whom the Path and so forth have been penetrated is one possessed of inspired ingenuity through realization (*adhigama-paṭibhānavā*).
One should associate with such a person of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, a sublime friend endowed with inspired ingenuity. From him...

By the power of that [knowledge], having understood the manifold kinds of welfare—distinguished as one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, or distinguished as pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—he has dispelled doubt and removed uncertainty regarding those points that give rise to doubt, such as "Did I exist in the past? and so forth; thus he has performed all his duties.
"One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
The commentary on the *Bahussuta-gāthā* is finished. 115.
As for the origin of the verse "Delight in play": it is said that in Benares there was a king named Vibhūsaka-Brahmadatta.
In the morning, having eaten either gruel or a meal, and having had himself adorned with various kinds of ornaments, he would look at his entire body in a large mirror;
whatever he did not like, he would remove and have himself adorned with something else.
While he was doing this one day, the time for his midday meal arrived. He remained with his adornment still unfinished.
Having wrapped his head with a silk cloth and eaten, he went to sleep during the day.

When he rose again and did exactly the same, the sun had already set. This happened on the second day as well, and on the third day too. As he was thus addicted to adorning himself, a back ailment arose.
He thought to himself: "Alas! Even though I am adorning myself with all my might, in this..."
"Being dissatisfied with my barber and ornaments, I gave rise to greed; and indeed, this greed is a state that leads to rebirth in the woeful states.
Come now, let me subdue this greed. Having thus abandoned his kingdom and gone forth, he attained insight and realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and uttered this verse of exultation:
In this context, "play" (*khiḍḍā*) and "pleasure" (*rati*) have already been explained previously. "Sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukha*) refers to the pleasure derived from sense objects (*vatthukāma*).
For even sense objects are called "pleasure" by virtue of being the domain and so forth of pleasure. As it has been said: "There is form that is pleasant, associated with pleasure.
Thus, having neither adorned nor deemed sufficient this world-sphere with such play, pleasure, and sensual pleasure, [they departed].
Not grasping at this as being "pleasing" or "essential. "Disregarding" means having a disposition that does not look back toward that ornament—being without longing, without craving.
"Abstaining from the basis of adornment, speaking truthfully": herein, adornment is twofold—adornment for householders and adornment for those who have gone forth.
[The latter includes] adornment such as garments, head-wraps, garlands, perfumes, and so forth.
The adornment of a householder is called *agārikavibhūsā*. The adornment of bowls, ornaments, and so forth is the adornment of one who is not a householder (*anagārikavibhūsā*).

Adornment itself is the basis for adornment; therefore, he is "abstinent from the three bases of adornment. He is a "speaker of truth" (*saccavādī*) because his speech is not false; thus the meaning should be understood.
The commentary on the verse concerning the bases of adornment is finished.
116. What is the origin of the verses beginning with "Son and wife"? It is said that in Benares, a king’s son was consecrated to the throne while still a child.
Like the Paccekabuddha mentioned in the first verse, he experienced the glory of sovereignty and one day reflected:
"While I rule the kingdom, I cause much suffering; what is the use of this for the sake of a single meal?"

"By means of this evil, alas, I shall produce happiness! Having thus abandoned his kingdom and gone forth, he realized *paccekabodhi* through insight and uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*).
In that context, "wealths" (*dhanāni*) refers to gems such as pearls, jewels, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold. "Grains" (*dhaññāni*)...
The seven types of grain—rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, fine rice, and kudrūsa grass—as well as the remaining other foods;
"relatives" refers to the fourfold relatives by way of kinship, family, clan, friendship, and craft;
"according to their respective spheres" means they remain established within their own particular domains. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Puttadāragāthā* is finished. 117.
What is the origin of the verse beginning with "This is a bond"? It is said that in Benares there was a king named Pādalola-Brahmadatta.
Having eaten rice gruel or a meal early in the morning, he would watch three kinds of theatrical performances in three palaces.
There were three kinds of dancers: those who had come from former kings, those who had come from the immediately preceding king, and those who appeared in his own time.
One day, early in the morning, he went to the palace of the young dancers.

Those dancing women, thinking, "We shall delight the king," performed dance, song, and instrumental music that was exceedingly enchanting, like the celestial nymphs (*accharā*) of Sakka, the lord of the devas. The king—
Thinking, "It is not surprising that young women [act thus]," he became dissatisfied and went to the Middle Hall of the Dancing Girls;
those dancing girls did exactly the same there. Being dissatisfied even there, he went to the Hall of the Old Dancing Girls;
they too did exactly the same. Because of their state of old age, after two or three royal turns had passed, the king—

Having seen a dance resembling a play with bones and having heard a song that was not sweet, he wandered again to the palace of the young actresses and again to the palace of the middle-aged actresses; yet, finding no satisfaction anywhere, he thought:
"These female dancers desire to delight me, just as the apsarases delight Sakka, the lord of the gods, by dancing, singing, and playing music with all their might."
They applied themselves [to their duties]. But I, being dissatisfied with anything, increased my greed. Now, this greed is indeed a state that leads to rebirth in the woeful states;

come now, let me subdue this greed. Having thus renounced his kingdom and gone forth into homelessness, he practiced insight (vipassanā), realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and uttered this verse of exultation (udāna).
The meaning of this is as follows: "This is a fetter" (saṅgo) points to one's own enjoyment.
For living beings become stuck there, like an elephant sunk in mud; thus it is a "fetter. "Therein, happiness is meager" (parittaṃ ettha sokhyaṃ):

here, during the time of enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, it is called "happiness" only in a contemptuous sense, because it must be produced through perverted perception or because it is included within the phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
"Trifling" means it is brief, like the fleeting pleasure of watching a dance illuminated by the light of a flash of lightning; this is what is meant by "temporary.
Regarding the statement, "The gratification here is slight, while suffering is greater," this refers to that which was said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification in sensual pleasures."
Thus, when it is said here, "And what, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures?
Here, monks, a clansman earns his livelihood by some craft, whether by calculation or by accounting," and so forth, compared to that [suffering], this [suffering] is but a mere drop of water;
rather, suffering is much more abundant in the four [realms].
In the oceans, it is like water. Therefore it is said: "The gratification is slight, but here suffering is much more. This is a hook;
having shown the gratification, it is like a fishhook by way of its power to drag [one in], namely, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇā*).
Knowing this thus, a wise and intelligent person, having understood this, should abandon all this and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The commentary on the Saṅgāmagāthā is finished. 118.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Having torn apart": it is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a king named Anivattabrahmadatta.
