Once he had entered into battle, he would not turn back until he had either won the victory or completed another task he had undertaken.
Therefore, they perceived him in this way. One day he went to the pleasure grove. At that time, a forest fire broke out.
That fire, burning both dry and green grasses and other vegetation, proceeded without turning back.
Seeing it, the king gave rise to a corresponding mental image: "Just as this forest fire is, so too is the elevenfold [aging]."
"The fire, burning all beings, goes on without turning back, producing great suffering.
When, alas, shall I too—like this fire—burn away the defilements with the fire of the knowledge of the Noble Path and go on without turning back for the sake of putting an end to this suffering?
Then, after going a short distance, he saw fishermen catching fish in the river.
A certain large fish, having entered among their nets, broke through the net and escaped. They cried out, "The fish has broken the net and gone!
When the king heard those words, he conceived a corresponding aspiration:
"When indeed shall I too, by means of the knowledge of the Noble Path, break through the net of craving and views and go forth unattached? He [renounced] his kingdom...
Having abandoned [the world] and gone forth, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha, and uttered this verse of exultation (udāna).
Regarding its second line: *jāla* refers to a net made of thread. *Ambu* means water;
one who moves therein is an *ambucārī*, which is a designation for a fish. A fish that moves in the water is a *salilambucārī*. In that river-water, there was a net...
"Having broken through, it goes where water cannot move"—this is what is meant. Regarding the third line, "burnt" (*daḍḍha*) refers to a place that has been burnt.

Just as fire does not return to a place it has burnt and does not come back to it again, so too, the fire of the knowledge of the Path, having burnt the place of the sense-qualities (*kāmaguṇa*), does not return there and does not come back to it again—this is what is meant. The rest is according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Sandāla-gāthā is finished.

119. Regarding "With downcast eyes": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was a king named Cakkhulola-Brahmadatta, who, like Pādalola-Brahmadatta, was devoted to watching theatrical performances. However, this is the distinction: he was dissatisfied.
He goes here and there. Having seen various performances and rejoiced exceedingly in them, he wanders about increasing his craving by alternating between different spectacles.
It is said that upon seeing a certain householder’s wife who had come for the sake of a performance, lust arose within him.
Thereafter, having fallen into a state of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he thought again: "Alas! If I continue to increase this craving..."
"I shall become one who fills the states of misery; come now, I will restrain him.

Having thus gone forth and attained *paccekabodhi* through insight (*vipassanā*), he censured his own former practice and uttered this inspired verse (*udānagāthā*) illustrating its opposite qualities:
"Therein, 'with downcast eyes' means with eyes cast downward; having placed seven neck-vertebrae in succession..."
This is said for the purpose of showing what is to be avoided and what is to be adopted: namely, looking only as far as the distance of a yoke.
It does not mean, however, that one should strike the heart-bone with the jaw-bone; for such downward-looking would not be befitting a recluse.
Nor should one be "fidgety with the feet," meaning one who scratches their feet out of a desire to enter the midst of a group—such as a second person following one, or a third following two.
Being as if he were not [present], he abstained from long journeys and from journeys involving no return.

"Guarded in his faculties" means that since the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) has been mentioned separately here among the six faculties, he is one whose remaining faculties are protected. "One who has guarded the mind-stream":
*mānasānaṃ* is simply *mānasaṃ*; he is "one who has guarded the mind-stream" (*rakkhitamānasāno*) because he has guarded that mind. Thus, he is not plundered by the defilements (*kilesa*).
Thus, it is said that "the mind is guarded. "Untainted" (anavassuta) means being free from the influx of defilements (kilesa-anvassava) toward various objects by means of this practice.
"Not burning" (apariḍayhamāna) means not being consumed by the fires of the defilements.
Or, externally untainted and internally not burning. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Okkhittacakkhu* verses is concluded.
120. Regarding the phrase "having caused [the food] to be brought out": what is its origin?

It is said that in Benares there was another king named Cātumāsika-Brahmadatta, who used to go for a pleasure excursion to the park every four months. One day, during the middle month of the summer...
As he was entering the park, he saw at the park gate a *pāricchattaka* and *koviḷāra* tree with branches and twigs covered in leaves and adorned with flowers;

taking a single flower, he entered the park. Then, thinking, "The king has taken the finest flower," another minister standing on the back of an elephant took only a single flower. By this same means, the entire army [did the same].
They took them; those who could not satisfy themselves with the flowers even took the leaves. That tree became nothing more than a trunk, stripped of both leaves and flowers.
As the king was departing from the park in the evening, he saw it and thought, "What has been done to this tree?
At the time of my arrival, it was adorned with coral-like flowers amidst its jewel-colored branches; now it has become bare of leaves and flowers."
While reflecting thus, he saw nearby a tree that was not yet in flower but was covered with foliage. Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him:
"This tree, because it was laden with flowers, became an object of desire for many people; consequently, in a mere moment, it met its destruction.
But this other tree, because it was not desirable, remains just as it was. This kingdom, too, is like the flowering tree."
"Like a tree in full bloom, it is alluring; but the state of a bhikkhu, however, is like a tree without flowers and is not alluring.
Therefore, as long as even this [kingdom] is not plundered like this tree, you should go forth, clothed in the saffron robe, just as another [tree] is covered with leaves like the Pāricchattaka.
Having abandoned his kingdom and gone forth, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā).
Having realized private enlightenment (paccekabodhi), he uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udānagāthā).

Regarding the line "having gone forth clad in saffron robes" (kāsāyavattho abhinikkhamitvā), its meaning should be understood as: "having departed from home and being clothed in saffron robes. The remainder can be understood according to the method already explained; therefore, it has not been elaborated upon.
The commentary on the Pāricchattaka verses is concluded.
The Third Chapter is finished. 121.
Regarding "In flavors": what is the origin [of this]? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī was sporting with his ministers' sons on a stone slab by a lotus pond in a park.
His cook, having taken the essence of all kinds of meat, prepared an exceedingly well-prepared [dish].
Having cooked an "intermediate meal" that was like the nectar of immortality, he offered it to him.
Having become greedy for it, he did not give anything to anyone but ate it all by himself. While playing in the water, he emerged very late and ate with great haste.
He did not remember anyone with whom he used to eat in the past. Then, having later given rise to reflection—
“Alas! A wicked deed has been done by me, in that, overcome by craving for flavors, I forgot all people and ate all alone.
Come now, I shall subdue this craving for flavors. Having thus renounced his kingdom and gone forth, he realized pratyekabodhi through insight;
then, censuring his former conduct and illuminating the qualities that are its opposite, he uttered this inspired verse (udāna-gāthā).
In this context, "in flavors" (*rasesu*) refers to various kinds of things to be tasted, such as sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, astringent, and alkaline.
"They do not show greed" (*gedham akaruṃ*) means they do not become greedy; that is to say, they do not give rise to craving.

"Not fickle" (*alolo*) means not agitated by specific flavors, thinking, "I shall taste this," or "I shall taste that. "Not supporting others" (*anaññaposī*) means being devoid of those who must be supported, such as fellow residents (*saddhivihārika*).

It means being content with merely maintaining the body. Or alternatively, instead of being as one was previously—a consumer of others' food who, in the pleasure gardens, had the habit of greedily grasping at flavors—one has abandoned that craving by which, being fickle, one grasps at flavors;
thus, by not producing another future personal existence rooted in craving, one is said to be "not a consumer of others."
[The word] *hoti* [is used]. Alternatively, in the sense of being that which destroys one’s welfare (*atthabhañjanaka*), the defilements (*kilesā*) are called "other" (*aññe*);

by not nourishing them, he is "one who does not nourish others" (*anaññaposī*)—this is the meaning here. "One who goes from house to house" (*sapadānacārī*) means one who does not skip over houses, one who goes in regular succession;
the meaning is: entering for alms continuously, without omitting either a wealthy family or a poor family. "With a mind unattached to this family or that family" (*kule kule appaṭibaddhacitto*).
With a mind that does not cling due to the defilements to any place whatsoever, such as among the kṣatriya clans and so forth—this is the meaning of being "ever-new like the moon.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verse regarding craving for flavors is finished.
122. Regarding the origin of the verse beginning with "Having abandoned the five hindrances": It is said that in Benares there was a certain king who had attained the first *jhāna*.

For the sake of protecting his meditative absorption, he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *paccekabodhi* (private enlightenment).
Demonstrating the perfection of his own practice, he uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*).
In this context, "five hindrances" refers to the five *nīvaraṇas* themselves, which are explained in their essential meaning in the *Uragasutta*.
Because they shroud the mind just as clouds and other phenomena shroud the moon and sun, they are called "hindrances of the mind.

The meaning is that one has abandoned or relinquished them, either by way of access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*). Regarding "defilements" (*upakkilesa*), they approach the mind...
"Vibādhente" means they are obstructing unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*), or else covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth as described in the *Vatthūpama-sutta* and other texts.
"Byapanujja" means having dispelled them, that is, having abandoned them by way of insight (*vipassanā*). "Sabbā" means without exception.

Thus, one who is perfected in serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) is "independent" because the basis for views has been abandoned by the first path; having severed the three realms (*tedhātuka*) by the remaining paths—
"Sticky fault" (*sineha-dosa*) means craving as a flood (*taṇhā-rāga*). For it is "sticky" itself that is called the "sticky fault" because it is the opposite of virtue (*guṇa*).
The rest is exactly according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the verses on the hindrances (*āvaraṇa-gāthā-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
123. Regarding the phrase "having turned one's back": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was a certain king who had attained the fourth *jhāna*.
For the sake of guarding that *jhāna*, he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and by practicing insight (*vipassanā*), realized *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment).
While illustrating the perfection of his own practice, he uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*).

In this context, "having turned one's back" means having placed behind oneself; the meaning is having discarded or abandoned. "Pleasure and pain" refers to bodily agreeable and disagreeable sensations.
"Joy and grief" refers to mental agreeable and disagreeable sensations. "Equanimity" refers to the equanimity of the fourth jhāna.
"Tranquility" refers specifically to the concentration of the fourth jhāna. "Purified" [means] by way of the five hindrances, initial application, sustained application, rapture, and pleasure.
It is "exceedingly pure" because it is liberated from the nine opposing states; the meaning is that it is free from adventitious defilements like refined gold.

This, however, is the construction [of the verse]: "having turned one's back on pleasure and pain beforehand"—the intention being that "pain" refers specifically to the vicinity of the first jhāna, and "pleasure" refers specifically to the vicinity of the third jhāna. Then, the word *ca* (and) mentioned at the beginning [is to be applied] later...
The governing phrase is: "Having turned one's back on both joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*), even before [the fourth jhāna].

By this, it is indicated that joy belongs to the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the fourth jhāna, while grief belongs specifically to the preliminary stage of the second jhāna. For these are, in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*), the points at which these are abandoned;
but in a literal sense (*nippariyāyato*), the first jhāna is the abandonment of pain (*dukkha*), and [the second jhāna] is the abandonment of grief.
The second jhāna is the place for the abandoning of pain, the third jhāna for pleasure, and the fourth jhāna for mental joy.

As it is said: "Entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder," and so forth—all of which is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Just as...
"Having previously turned one's back on" means that having turned one's back on pain, mental grief, and pleasure in the three [preceding] jhānas beginning with the first,

and likewise here in this fourth jhāna having turned one's back on mental joy (*somanassa*), one "should wander alone" with the equanimity obtained by this practice, which is purified through serenity (*samatha*).
The rest is exactly as described in the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Vipiṭṭhigāthā* is concluded.
124. As for the origin of the verse beginning "One who has aroused energy":

It is said that there was a certain frontier king who, though small in his kingdom and possessing an army of only a thousand warriors, was great in wisdom. One day he thought, "Although I am small in my kingdom..."
"But it is possible for one possessed of wisdom to seize the whole of Jambudīpa," he thought; and having reflected thus, he dispatched a messenger to the neighboring king, saying:
"Within seven days, either grant me your kingdom or give me battle. Thereupon, he summoned his own ministers and said:
"Without even consulting you, I have committed this rash act; such a message has been sent to that king."
"What should be done? they asked. He said, "It is possible, Great King, to turn that messenger back.
"It is not possible; he must have already gone. "If that is so, we have been ruined by you.
It would be better to die at the hands of another sword; come now, let us kill one another, or kill ourselves, or hang ourselves."
"Let us eat poison! Thus, each one among them extolled death alone. Then the king said, "What use have I for these?
My good man, do I not have warriors? Thereupon, a thousand warriors stood up, crying out, "I am a warrior, Great King! I am a warrior, Great King!"
The king, thinking, "I shall investigate these matters," had a large funeral pyre prepared and said:
"My men, I have committed this act of rashness, for which my ministers reproach me; therefore, I shall enter the pyre.
Who will enter with me? Who has surrendered their life for mine? When he had spoken thus, five hundred warriors stood up.
“We shall enter, Great King,” they said. Then the king said to the other five hundred: “Now what will you do, dear ones? They replied:
“This, Great King, is not a manly deed; this is the behavior of women.
Nevertheless, a messenger was sent by the Great King to the rival king; we shall fight with that king and die.”
Then the king, thinking, "You have surrendered my life," arrayed his fourfold army and,
surrounded by those thousand warriors, went and sat down at the border of the kingdom.
That opposing king, having heard of this news, thought, "Ah, that petty king is not even a match for my slave!"
Having corrupted his entire army, he set out to do battle.
When the minor king saw that expedition approaching, he said to his army: "Sirs, you are not numerous;
all of you, joining together and taking up swords and shields, go quickly and directly right before this king. They did exactly so. Then his army—
Having split him in two, he gave him over as a hostage. They seized that king alive and handed him over to their own king, who was coming with the intent, "I shall kill him.
The rival king begged for his life. The king granted him safety, made him take an oath, and brought him under his own control;
then, together with him, he marched against another king and [defeated] him.
Standing at the frontier of his kingdom, he sent word: "Either give me the kingdom or give me battle.
He replied, "I cannot endure even a single battle," and thus surrendered the kingdom. By this means, he captured all the kings, and finally seized even the King of Bārāṇasī.
Surrounded by one hundred and one kings, as he ruled over the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa, he thought: "Formerly I was insignificant..."
“I was [once] so, but now, through the perfection of my own knowledge, I have become a king, the lord of the entire circle of Jambudīpa.
Yet that knowledge of mine is associated with worldly effort; it leads neither to disenchantment nor to dispassion.
What if I were to seek the supramundane Dhamma by means of this very knowledge? Then, [he relinquished] the kingship of Bārāṇasī.
Having given away his wife and children, and having established them in his own country alone, he renounced everything, went forth into homelessness, and began the practice of insight (*vipassanā*).
Having realized *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment), he uttered this verse of exultation (*udānagāthā*) while illustrating his own perfection of energy (*vīriya*).
In that context, "one who has initiated energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*) means one whose energy has been set in motion; by this, he demonstrates his own great vigor.

"Paramattha" (the ultimate goal) is said to be Nibbāna; "paramatthappatti" (the attainment of the ultimate goal) is the reaching of that Nibbāna; [the phrase] "tassā paramatthappattiyā" refers to that attainment of the ultimate goal.
By this, he shows the fruit to be attained through the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*).

By the term "alīnacitto" (one with an undaunted mind), he shows the non-languor of the mind and mental factors that support energy. By the term "akusītavutti" (one of untiring conduct), he shows [the non-languor] of the body in standing, walking, and so forth...

This shows non-despondency. By the term "firm exertion" (*daḷhanikkamo*), he shows the energy of striving that occurs in such passages as, "Willingly, let skin and sinews [waste away]," which one who strives in the gradual training and so forth is said to "realize the ultimate truth with the body.
Alternatively, by this he shows the energy associated with the Path (*magga-sampayutta-vīriya*); that too is firm.

Because he has reached the full perfection of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and because he has entirely emerged from all opposing factors (*paṭipakkha*), the person who possesses these qualities is called "firmly emergent" (*daḷhanikkama*).
"Endowed with fortitude and strength" means endowed at the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*) with both bodily fortitude and the power of knowledge;
or alternatively, endowed with a strength that has become firm—that is, endowed with the firm power of knowledge.
This has been said. By this, while demonstrating the association of that energy with the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa), he establishes its status as the primary exertion.
Alternatively, all three feet may be construed according to the categories of initial, intermediate, and intense energy. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "Ardent Energy" is concluded.
125. As for “seclusion” (*paṭisallāna*): what is its origin? Its origin is the same as that of the introductory verse;
there is no difference whatsoever. However, regarding the commentary on its meaning:

“seclusion” (*paṭisallāna*) means withdrawing from those various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and settling down (*sallāna*), which is to say, dwelling apart, being alone, and physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). “Meditative absorption” (*jhāna*) is so called because it burns away (*jhāpana*) opposing factors.
And mental seclusion is spoken of by way of contemplation upon the characteristics of the object.

In that context, the eight attainments are called "jhāna" because they burn away (jhāpana) opposing factors such as the hindrances and because they contemplate (upanijjhāna) objects such as the kasiṇas.

Insight, the path, and the fruit are called "jhānas" because they burn away opposing factors such as the seven perceptions and because they contemplate the characteristics [of phenomena]. However, here only contemplation of the object is intended.

Thus, not neglecting, not abandoning, and not relinquishing both this seclusion and meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "In regard to phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means in regard to the phenomena such as the five aggregates that have come under the scope of insight (*vipassanā*).
"Constantly" (*niccaṃ*) means continuously, uninterruptedly, and without interval.

"Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārī*) means practicing the Dhamma of insight that follows by way of being directed toward those very phenomena. Alternatively, "in regard to phenomena" means...
Here, "states" (*dhammā*) refers to the nine supramundane states; "conformity to those states" (*anudhamma*) means a state that accords with them, which is a designation for insight (*vipassanā*).

In this context, although one should say "constantly practicing in conformity with the states" (*dhammānaṃ niccaṃ anudhammacārī*), it may have been stated as "in the states" (*dhammesu*) for the sake of metrical convenience through a change in grammatical case.
"Having comprehended the danger in states of existence" (*ādīnavaṃ sammasitā bhavesu*)—by means of that practice in conformity with the Dhamma...

Perceiving the defects such as impermanence in the three realms of existence through insight (vipassanā), one may be said to have attained the path known as insight that has reached the pinnacle of physical and mental seclusion;
thus, the construction of the verse "One should wander alone" should be understood.
The commentary on the verses on seclusion (paṭisallāna) is finished.
126. What is the origin of "the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaya*)? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī was circumambulating the city with great royal splendor.
Beings, their hearts captivated by the beauty of his person, even those walking in front turned back to gaze at him;
likewise those walking behind and those walking on both sides did the same. This was simply his natural [beauty].
For the world is never satiated with the sight of a Buddha, nor with the sight of the full moon or the king of the ocean.
Now, a certain householder’s wife, having gone to the upper terrace of her palace, stood there looking out through an open lattice window.
When the king saw her, his heart became bound to her, and he commanded his minister: "Go, find out whether this woman has a husband or not."
Having understood this, he reported, "O King, they have their husbands. Then the king reflected:
"These twenty thousand dancing women delight me alone, just like celestial nymphs; yet now, not being satisfied even with them, I have conceived a craving for another's wife.
Once arisen, that craving drags one only toward the states of misery. Having thus seen the danger in craving, [he renounced it].

Thinking, “Come now, I shall restrain him,” he abandoned his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and through insight realized pratyekabodhi (enlightenment of a solitary buddha), whereupon he uttered this verse of inspired utterance (*udānagāthā*).
Therein, “the destruction of craving” (*taṇhakkhaya*) refers to *nibbāna*, or the non-occurrence of craving once its dangers have been thus seen. “Heedful” (*appamatta*)—
One who acts with constancy, one who acts with diligence. "Not lisping" means not having a lolling mouth; or alternatively, "not lisping and not deaf," which is to say, he is wise and competent.
"Possessed of learning" (sutavā) means one who possesses the hearing that brings about welfare and happiness; it is to say, he is endowed with the scriptures (āgama).
"Mindful" means one who recollects what was done long ago and so forth. "One who has scrutinized the Dhamma" means through the investigation of the Dhamma.

One who has fully understood the Dhamma. "Fixed" means having attained the state of certainty through the Noble Path. "Exerting" means endowed with the energy of the right efforts. This reading should be construed in reverse order.
Thus, one who possesses those qualities such as diligence and so forth is "exerting" by means of the exertion that brings about certainty;
because of that exertion, one is "fixed" due to the certainty attained; and from that, through the attainment of Arahatship...
"One who has fully understood the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammo*). For an Arahant is called "one who has fully understood the Dhamma" because there is nothing further to be understood. As it is said:
"Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and those many trainees here. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verse on the destruction of craving is finished.
127. What is the origin of the lion simile? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī had a pleasure grove situated at a distance.
Rising early in the morning, as he was going to the grove, he alighted from his carriage on the way and approached a body of water, thinking, "I shall wash my face.
In that place, a lioness had given birth to a lion cub and had gone out for prey. Seeing it, the king’s man thought, "This is a lion cub."
“Sire,” he announced. The king, thinking, “It is said that Sīha fears no one,” had drums and other instruments beaten to test him.
Although the lion cub heard that sound, he lay down exactly as before. Then they had them beaten a second and even a third time.
On the third occasion, he raised his head, looked at the entire assembly, and lay down just as before. Then the king [thought], “As long as...”
Saying, "Let us go while our mother has not yet returned," he went along and thought:
"Even a lion cub born only this very day does not tremble or fear; when indeed shall I too, having cast off the terror of craving and wrong views, neither tremble nor fear?
Taking that as his mental object, he continued on his way until the fishermen again caught fish.
Having tied it to the branches, he saw that when the net was cast out, the wind passed through it without any obstruction; seeing this, he took it as a sign:
"When indeed shall I too, having torn asunder the net of craving, views, and delusion, go forth without such attachment?
Then, having gone to the park, he sat on the bank of a stone-slab lotus pond, where the lotuses, struck by the wind, bent down.
Having touched the water, when the wind had subsided, he saw that they remained in their original places, unsullied by the water;

he took that as his sign: "When indeed shall I too, though born in the world, remain unsullied by the world, just as these things, though born in the water, remain unsullied by the water? Again and again he thought: "Just as a lion..."

Having reflected, "Just as the wind [passes through] lotuses, so too should one who is not yet fully enlightened become unattached and unsullied," he renounced his kingdom, went forth, and while practicing insight (vipassanā), realized Pratyekabuddhahood and uttered this verse of exultation (udāna).
In that context, regarding "the lion," there are four kinds of lions: the grass-lion, the pale-yellow lion, the black lion, and the maned lion (*kesara-sīha*). Of these, the maned lion...
It is declared to be the foremost; that is what is intended here. Wind is of many kinds, such as the eastern wind and so forth. The lotus is of various kinds, such as the red, white, and others.

Among those, any kind of wind or any kind of lotus will do. In this context, since what is called "terror" arises from self-attachment (*attasineha*), and self-attachment is indeed the smear of craving (*taṇhālepa*), and that [craving] is associated either with views (*diṭṭhi*) or dissociated from views—
Or it arises through greed, and that too is simply craving (*taṇhā*). However, in the case of a virtuous person, it arises through delusion (*moha*) when they lack investigation and so forth;
and delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*). In this regard, craving is abandoned by serenity (*samatha*), and ignorance by insight (*vipassanā*).
Therefore, having abandoned attachment to self through serenity, like a lion, being unperturbed by sounds such as impermanence and suffering, [one proceeds] through insight.
Having abandoned delusion, like the wind [passing] through a net, he is unattached to the aggregates, bases, and so forth;

having abandoned greed and the views associated with greed by means of serenity (samatha) alone, he is unsullied by greed for the enjoyments of all states of existence, just as a lotus is unsullied by water.

And here, since two factors have been established—namely, that virtue is the proximate cause of serenity, serenity is the proximate cause of concentration (samādhi), and concentration is the proximate cause of insight (vipassanā)—[the path is perfected].

The three aggregates are indeed established. In this regard, by means of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), he is a hero. Like a lion, he does not tremble at sounds that are grounds for resentment, nor does he feel anger.

By means of the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*), having penetrated the true nature of things, he is not caught, like the wind in a net, amidst the various phenomena such as the trunk and so forth.

By means of the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), being free from passion, he is not defiled by passion, like a lotus by water. Thus, through serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*)—

Furthermore, he should be understood as being non-existent, unattached, and untainted by virtue of the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and by way of the abandoning of craving, ignorance, and the three unwholesome roots as they occur. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses beginning with "The Lion" is finished.

128. What is the origin of the verse beginning "Just as a lion"? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, in order to pacify a rebellion on the frontier, set aside the regular road from village to village and traveled with a great army by taking a direct forest path.
At that time, a certain lion was lying down at the foot of a mountain, basking in the heat of the rising sun.

Seeing him, the king’s men reported it to the king. Thinking, "It is said that the lion does not tremble," the king had the sounds of kettledrums, small drums, and other instruments made to be played;
yet the lion lay down exactly as he was. He had them play a second time, and the lion lay down exactly as he was.
He had them play a third time; then, thinking, "I have a rival," the lion planted all four feet firmly upon the ground.
He let out a lion’s roar. Hearing it, the elephant-riders and others dismounted from their elephants and entered the thickets of grass;
the herds of elephants and horses fled in every direction. The king’s elephant also seized the king and fled, crushing him against the dense forest thickets.
Unable to sustain himself, the king hung from a tree branch, fell to the ground, and proceeded along a narrow footpath.
As he was going, he arrived at the dwelling place of the Paccekabuddhas.
There he asked the Paccekabuddhas: "Venerable sirs, did you hear any sound? "Yes, Great King. "Whose sound was it, venerable sirs?
"First that of drums, conchs, and so forth; afterwards, that of a lion. "Were you not afraid, venerable sirs? "We were not afraid, Great King."
“I am afraid of any sound whatsoever. “But is it possible, Bhante, for me also to do the same?
“It is possible, Great King, if you will go forth. “I shall go forth, Bhante.

Then, having ordained him, they instructed him in the training of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) in the manner previously described. He too, practicing insight (*vipassanā*) in the manner previously described, attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
Having realized this, he spoke this inspired verse (*udāna-gāthā*).

In this context, a *sīha* is so called because of its endurance (*sahanā*), its slaying (*hananā*), and its swift speed (*sīghajavatā*). Here, it is specifically intended as the maned lion (*kesara-sīha*).

One who possesses fangs and strength is "fang-strong" (*dāṭhabalī*). Both terms—“having overcome” (*pasayha*) and “having surpassed” (*abhibhuyya*)—should be construed with the word “moving” (*cārī*).
"One who moves by force" (*pasayhacārī*) and "one who moves having overcome" (*abhibhuyyacārī*). Therein, he is "one who moves by force" because he moves by means of suppressing [others];

he is "one who moves having overcome" because he moves by means of overcoming, intimidating, and bringing [them] under his control. This one moves by force through bodily power and moves having overcome through his fiery energy (*tejas*).
In that regard, if someone were to ask, "By what does he move by force and having overcome? then—
"Migānaṃ" (of deer) is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative; it should be understood as "roaming having subdued and overcome the deer.
"Pantāni" means remote. "Senāsanāni" means dwelling places. Since the remainder can be understood according to the method already stated, it has not been explained in detail.
The commentary on the Dāṭhabhāgīya verses is finished.

129. What is the origin of the verses beginning with "Loving-kindness and equanimity"? It is said that there was once a certain king who had attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna) such as loving-kindness.

Thinking, "Sovereignty is an obstacle to the bliss of jhāna," he renounced his kingdom for the sake of protecting his meditation, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight (vipassanā), realized Pratyekabuddhahood and uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna).
In this context, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the desire to bring about welfare and happiness for all beings by way of the formula: "May all beings be happy.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the desire to remove harm and suffering by way of the formula: "O, may they be freed from this suffering!
Appreciative joy (*muditā*) is the desire for the non-separation of beings from welfare and happiness by way of the formula: "How the noble beings rejoice! How well and truly they rejoice!"
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is the state of looking on with equanimity toward pleasure and pain, [thinking], "They will be known by their own karma.
However, for the sake of the ease of versification, loving-kindness (*mettā*) was mentioned first and equanimity last, and sympathetic joy was mentioned afterwards.

As for "liberations" (*vimutti*): all four of these are liberations because they are liberated from their respective opposing states (*paccanīkadhamma*). Therefore it was said: "Loving-kindness, equanimity..."
“Cultivating compassion and liberation, and joy at the proper time.
In this context, “cultivating” means developing [compassion] by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas, and developing equanimity by way of the fourth jhāna.

“At the proper time” means that after cultivating loving-kindness, one emerges from that and cultivates compassion; after emerging from that, one cultivates joy; and after emerging from that, one [cultivates the others].
Or, having emerged from a jhāna devoid of rapture, one who cultivates equanimity is said to be "cultivating at the proper time," or [one who cultivates] at a time when it is convenient to cultivate.
"Not being obstructed by the whole world" means not being obstructed by the entire world of sentient beings in the ten directions;
for because of the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], sentient beings become non-repulsive, and one is no longer in opposition toward them.
Aversion is stilled. Therefore it is said: "Unopposed by the entire world. This is the summary here;

the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* (The Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī) within the discussion on loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables]. The remainder is exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the verses concerning the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) is concluded.
130. As for the origin of the passage beginning "lust and hatred": it is said that near Rājagaha there lived a Paccekabuddha named Mātaṅga, the very last of all the Paccekabuddhas.
Then, when our Bodhisatta had appeared in the world, the deities who were coming to pay homage to the Bodhisatta saw him and exclaimed, "Friends, friends! A Buddha has arisen in the world!"
They said this. Upon emerging from cessation and hearing that, he foresaw his own death.
He went through the air to the mountain in the Himalayas called Mahāpapāta, the place where Paccekabuddhas attain final Nibbāna.
There, having cast the skeletal remains of a Paccekabuddha who had previously attained final Nibbāna into the precipice, he sat down on a stone surface and uttered this verse of exultation:
Therein, lust, hatred, and delusion have already been explained in the *Uragasutta*. "Fetters" refers to the ten fetters, and these are to be torn asunder by the respective paths.
"Fearless at the dissolution of life": the dissolution of life is said to be the breaking up of the death-consciousness.
And at that dissolution of life, because attachment to life has been abandoned, one is fearless. Up to this point...
Having shown his own *nibbāna*-element with residue remaining (*sopādisesa*), at the conclusion of the verses he attained final *nibbāna* in the *nibbāna*-element without residue (*anupādisesa*).
The commentary on the "Verses on the Exhaustion of Life" is finished. 131.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "They resort": it is said that in Benares there was a certain king who, in the manner described in the opening verse, [acted].
He ruled over a prosperous kingdom. A severe illness arose in him, and painful sensations set in.
Twenty thousand women surrounded him, massaging his hands and feet and performing other services.
The ministers thought, "This king will not live; come, let us seek our own refuge," and [they went] to a certain king.
Having gone into his presence, they requested attendance. They continued to attend upon him there, yet they received nothing at all.
When the king recovered from his illness, he asked, "Where are so-and-so and so-and-so?
Upon hearing that report, he merely shook his head and remained silent. Those ministers, hearing that "the king has recovered," went there...
Finding nothing at all and oppressed by extreme destitution, they returned once more, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side.
When the king asked them, "Where have you been, dear ones?
they replied, "Your Majesty, seeing that you were weak, we went to such-and-such a district out of fear for our livelihood. The king shook his head and reflected:

—"What if I were to display that very same illness? Would they do this again, or not? Thinking thus, as if he had been afflicted by disease before, he displayed intense pain and made his bed of illness. The women surrounded him and did everything exactly as they had done previously.
Those ministers likewise departed once more, taking even more people with them.
In this way, the king repeated everything as before up to three times, and they likewise departed.
Then, seeing them return for a fourth time, the king thought: "Alas! These men have performed a difficult task, in that they have departed without concern, leaving me while I am ill.
Becoming disillusioned, he abandoned his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and through insight, realized the state of a Pacceka-Buddha.
He spoke this verse of inspired utterance (*udāna*).

In that context, "they resort to" (*bhajanti*) means they attend upon him by clinging to his person. "They serve" (*sevanti*) means they attend to him with such acts as joining their palms in salutation and by being ready to carry out whatever is commanded.
"Those whose purpose is the cause" (*kāraṇatthā*) refers to those for whom the purpose consists of resorting and serving; there is no other [purpose] than these two.
There is a reason; their very purpose is the reason. What is meant is that they serve for the sake of some purpose.
"Friends without cause are hard to find today" means they are without cause [only] by way of seeking personal gain, thinking, "I shall receive something from this person. As it is said:
"A friend who is helpful, a friend who shares in both happiness and suffering..."
“And the friend who explains the Dhamma, the friend who is compassionate.
Friends endowed with such noble friendship as this are rare to find today.
“Attattha-paññā” means their wisdom is established within themselves; the sense is that they look only to themselves, not to others. It is also [spelled] “attattha-paññā.”
The reading [is such that] its meaning is that one looks only to one's own welfare, not to the welfare of others.
"Wisdom regarding what is seen" (*diṭṭhatthapaññā*)—this too, it is said, is an ancient reading; its meaning is that their wisdom concerns only the welfare presently seen, not the future.
It is stated that one looks only to the welfare pertaining to this present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), not to the welfare pertaining to the life hereafter. "Impure" (*asuci*)...
They were possessed of impure, ignoble deeds of body, speech, and mind.

Regarding the term *khaggavisāṇakappa*: just as one cutting trees and the like with a sword (*khaggena*), or reducing mountains and the like to powder and dust with one's own horn (*sakasiṅgena*), so he wanders;
thus he is a "rhinoceros-horn" (*khaggavisāṇa*). An order (*āṇā*) that is like poison (*visa*) is a "poisonous horn" (*visāṇā*). Like a sword (*khagga*), it is therefore a "sword" (*khagga*).
The horn of a rhinoceros belongs to that deer which is the "rhinoceros-deer"; the mode of life of that rhinoceros-horn is the "rhinoceros-horn mode.
The meaning is: like the rhinoceros-horn, a paccekabuddha should wander, dwell, conduct himself, live, and subsist alone, without a second, and without a companion.
132. *Visuddhasīlā* means especially pure in virtue; their virtue is purified by the fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhi*).

*Suvisuddhapaññā* means well-purified wisdom; because they are free from lust and other defilements, their wisdom consists of the path, the fruits, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and so forth.
*Samāhitā* means well-composed; their minds are firmly established and placed in proximity [to concentration]. *Jāgariyānuyuttā*: vigilance is *jāgaro*; [those devoted to it are *jāgariyānuyuttā*].
The meaning is "the overcoming of sleep. The state of being awake is *jāgariya*; those devoted to wakefulness are *jāgariyānuyutta*.
"Vipassakas" means those whose nature it is to see specifically that "it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"; the meaning is that they dwell having established insight (*vipassanā*).
"One who sees the distinction of phenomena" refers to the ten wholesome phenomena, the phenomenon of the Four Noble Truths, and the nine supramundane phenomena.

Or, they are those whose nature it is to see with distinction. "Included in the path-factors and enlightenment-factors" means the noble states that are associated with and have entered into the path-factors such as right view and so forth, and the enlightenment-factors such as the mindfulness enlightenment-factor and so forth.
"One should discern" means one should know with distinction; the meaning is "one who knows. 133. "Emptiness, the wishless, and the signless":
by way of the contemplation of non-self, there is the emptiness liberation; and by way of the contemplation of suffering...

The liberation of the wishless (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) by way of the contemplation of the impermanent (*aniccānupassanā*), and the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*). "Having cultivated" means having increased [them].
Those wise people who have completed the necessary preparations within the teaching of the Victor do not enter—that is, do not reach—the state of a disciple (*sāvakatta*);
those wise ones who have completed the preparations become self-become (*sayambhū*), that is, they become Pacceka-jinas or Pacceka-buddhas on their own.

134. Of what nature are they? They are possessed of great qualities (*mahantadhamma*), having fulfilled the great equipment (*pūritamahāsambhāra*), possessing a body of manifold teachings (*bahudhammakāya*), and having a physical form consisting of the essential nature of numerous phenomena (*anekadhammasabhāvasarīra*).

Furthermore, of what nature are they? They have the mind as their lord (*cittissara*), follow the course of the mind (*cittagatika*), and are endowed with meditative absorption (*jhānasampanna*)—this is the meaning.

Having crossed the flood of all suffering (*sabbadukkhoghatinna*), they have crossed and transcended the entire flood of saṃsāra; with uplifted minds, they possess hearts of joy because they are free from defilements such as anger and pride.

"Santamanā" means peaceful-minded. "Paramatthadassī" means those whose nature it is to see the ultimate reality (paramattha)—the supreme goal—by way of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the thirty-two aspects, the truths, dependent origination, and so forth.
"Sīhopamā" means like a lion, in the sense of being unshakable and fearless; the meaning is that they resemble a lion.
"Khaggavisāṇakappā" means like the horn of a rhinoceros; the meaning is that they are like the horn of a rhinoceros-like deer due to their absence of attachment to social groups.
135. *Santindriyā* means those whose faculties (*indriya*) have a peaceful nature because the eye-faculty and the others do not function toward their respective objects.

*Santamanā* means those with peaceful minds; the meaning is that their mental intentions (*cittasaṅkappa*) have a peaceful nature due to the absence of defilements (*nikilesabhāva*). *Samādhī* means those with well-concentrated, one-pointed minds.
*Paccantasattesu paṭipaccārā* means those who act with compassion, pity, and so forth toward beings in the border regions.

"Those whose virtue consists in following [the path]. "Lamps shining there and here"—the meaning is that they are like lamps or torches, shining both in the world beyond and in this world by means of bringing benefit to the entire world.
"The Paccekabuddhas always seek welfare"—the meaning is that these Paccekabuddhas are at all times engaged in the welfare of the entire world.
136. "O lords of people who have abandoned all hindrances": those Paccekabuddhas are the lords (*inda*) of people;

they are "those who have abandoned all hindrances" because of having abandoned all five hindrances, such as the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). "Possessing the luster of solid gold":

the meaning is that their radiance is like the splendor of red gold or Jambūnada gold. "Undoubtedly worthy of the world's offerings": they are exclusively worthy of the world’s excellent gifts (*sudakkhiṇeyya*).
"They are worthy to receive the supreme gift" means they are fit for it; because they are free from defilements (*nikkilesattā*), they are worthy of receiving beautiful offerings.

"These Buddhas, who have attained individual knowledge, are constantly satisfied" means these Buddhas—who have attained individual enlightenment—are always, at all times, satisfied, contented, and fulfilled;
even though they have gone without food for seven days, they remain fulfilled by way of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
137. Paccekabuddhas are those who are distinct from a Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), being other and unique Buddhas not shared with others. Alternatively, as the etymologists say:
“Prefixes, particles, and suffixes—these three have various and single meanings respectively.
Thus [the term *pacceka* is explained].
Because of the statement regarding the prefix, the term *pati* functions as a primary prefix (*eka-upasagga*).
Being pre-eminent and acting as a master (*sāmī*), it signifies that by accepting even a small amount of food from many donors, one attains heaven and liberation.
For instance, after accepting a portion of rice from Annabhāra, [the Buddha] ate it while he was still looking on, caused the deities to give their applause, and on that very day—
By leading that poor man to the position of a wealthy merchant and causing him to produce wealth amounting to ten million;

and by receiving the alms-food given by the Bodhisatta after he had stepped upon the pericarp of a lotus flower that had arisen over a pit of acacia charcoal conjured up by Māra in the *Khadirangāra Jātaka*, and by inspiring joy through his departure into the sky even as the man looked on.
By means of pleasing Queen Padumavatī— the mother of the sons of King Mahājanaka— and by accepting her gift after arriving through the air from Mount Gandhamādana,
he caused joy to arise in both the Bodhisatta Mahājanaka and his queen;
likewise, when a drought had arisen throughout the whole of Jambudīpa during a time when no Buddha had appeared, he [relieved] the drought-fear of the merchant of Bārāṇasī.
Having depended [on these], they exhausted the sixty thousand koṭis of storehouses that were being guarded;
having exhausted the grain buried in the earth and the grain filled in thousands of jars;
and having exhausted the grain ground with water and smeared upon all the walls of the palace, there remained then only a single measure of rice, thinking, "Having eaten this, we shall die today."
As he lay there having formed this thought, a certain Paccekabuddha came from Gandhamādana and stood at the door of his house.
Upon seeing him, the merchant felt such serene confidence that, even while giving up his life, he poured [his wealth] into the Paccekabuddha’s bowl.
The Paccekabuddha went to his dwelling place, and by means of his own supernatural power, while the merchant was still looking on, [he arrived] with five hundred Paccekabuddhas.
They ate together. At that time, they covered the cooking pot of boiled rice and set it aside.
When the hunger of the merchant arose as he fell asleep, he woke up and said to his wife, "Look at the rice;
see if there is even a little bit left. She, being well-trained, did not say, "Has it all been given away? but [looked] into the pot.
She opened the lid. At that very moment, the cooking pot became filled with fragrant rice resembling clusters of jasmine flowers.
She and the merchant were satisfied; they, along with all the inhabitants of the house and all the inhabitants of the city, ate.
Each time a portion was taken with the ladle, the spot from which it was taken was filled again. [This occurred] in all sixty thousand koṭis of storehouses.
They filled [the vessels] with fragrant *sāli* rice. All the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, having taken seeds of grain from the merchant’s house alone, became happy.

Because he is the master who has fallen [into the world] for the purpose of leading many classes of beings across [to safety], protecting them, and establishing them in heaven and liberation, he is called a *paccekabuddha*.
"The well-spoken words of the *paccekabuddhas*" refers to those spoken by the *paccekabuddhas*.

"Words well-spoken and uttered by way of exhortation and instruction. "They roam through the world together with its devas" means they move about and circulate throughout the world of beings, including the realm of the devas.
"The fools who, having heard it, do not act accordingly" refers to those foolish people who, having heard such well-spoken words of the Paccekabuddhas, do not act upon them or take them to heart.
Those fools wander and proceed—meaning they run—again and again through the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, that is, through the sufferings of rebirth.
138. "The well-spoken words of the *paccekabuddhas*" means words spoken very well for the sake of liberation from the four states of misery (*apāya*).
Of what nature are they? They are like sweet honey that is oozing and flowing; such are their sweet words.

The meaning is as follows: even those wise people who are engaged in practice, acting in accordance with what has been taught regarding those practices, become doers of the word upon hearing such sweet speech;
those wise people become "seers of truth," meaning they perceive the Four Truths, and they become "possessed of wisdom," meaning they are endowed with discernment. This is the meaning.
139. "Spoken by the Paccekabuddhas and the Jinas": they are called *jina* (conquerors) because they conquer (*jinanti*) or have conquered (*jiniṃsu*) the defilements.
By those *jinas*, the Paccekabuddhas, [this] was spoken, uttered, and declared. These discourses (*kathā*) are sublime, rich in essence, manifest, existent, and active.
Those discourses were [spoken] by the Lion of the Sakyans—the Lion of the royal lineage of the Sakyans, Gotama, the Tathāgata—who, having gone forth, became a Buddha.
The connection is as follows: they were "proclaimed" (pakāsitā), meaning made manifest and taught, by the Supreme among Men, the Best of men.

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the purpose of knowing the Dhamma. The meaning is: for the purpose of causing one to know specifically the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma).
140. "Out of compassion for the world, these [teachings] are theirs": out of compassion for the world, that is, based on compassion for the world, these [teachings] are theirs.
These words are verses (*gāthāyo*). "The transformations of those *paccekabuddhas*" means they were spoken with particular skillful transformation.

"For the purpose of increasing agitation, non-attachment, and intelligence" means for the sake of increasing agitation in the wise, for the sake of increasing non-attachment, for the sake of increasing unity, and for the sake of increasing intelligence—that is, for the sake of increasing wisdom—by the self-become lion who has no teacher.

Having sacrificed, these words were proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Lion, the Fearless One, Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One—this being born, having arisen, and having fully penetrated [them].
The meaning is that these verses were proclaimed, revealed, and made plain.
The word *iti* is a particle used in the sense of completion.
Thus ends the commentary on the Apadānas of the Paccekabuddhas in the *Visuddhajanavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Apadānas. 3-1.
Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sāriputta.
Immediately following that, in order to explain the verses comprising the *Therāpadāna*, he said: "Now, listen to the *Therāpadāna*.
The meaning of the words *atha* and *apadāna* has already been stated above. However, this word *thera* (elder) is used in many senses, such as duration of time, designation, name, and seniority.
For instance, in passages such as "the elder’s *vassika* flowers have withered and become like powder," it refers to time.
*Therovassikāni* means "having rained for a long time"; that is the meaning. In such passages as "The Elder is indeed great," the meaning is "one whose character is firm" (*thira-sīlo*).
In such passages as "This venerable one is an elder, he is advanced in years," the meaning is "a mere designation," referring simply to worldly convention.
In such passages as "Cunda the Elder, Phussa the Elder," the meaning is "one by whom this name was given. "And this Elder..."
In such phrases as "the prince among my sons," the meaning is "the eldest. However, here it is used in the sense of both "time" and "firmness.
Therefore, one who has stood for a long time is called a *thera* (elder); or, one who is endowed with qualities such as exceedingly firm virtue, conduct, and gentleness is called a *thera*.
One who is a *thera* and another who is a *thera* are [collectively] *therā*; the *apadāna*, which is the cause or account, of those *theras* is the *Therāpadāna*.

The connection is: "Listen to that *Therāpadāna*. Regarding the passage beginning "Not far from the Himavat mountain is a mountain named Lambaka," etc., this is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta;
the account of that Venerable One and of the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna should be understood as follows:
It is said that in the past, more than a hundred thousand aeons ago—at the end of one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*)—the Venerable Sāriputta...
Having been reborn in a great brahmin family, he was known by the name Sarada Māṇava.
Mahāmoggallāna, having been reborn in a great householder family, was known by the name Sirivaḍḍhana the householder. Both of them were companions who played together in the dust.
Among them, after his father passed away, Sarada Māṇava took charge of the wealth belonging to the family; one day—
Going into solitude, he thought: “Death is certain for these beings;
therefore, having gone forth into the religious life, I must seek the path to liberation. He approached his friend and said, “Friend, I wish to go forth.
Will you be able to go forth as well? When the other replied, “I will not be able,” he said, “Very well, I alone shall do so.”
Thinking, “I shall go forth,” he had his treasuries opened and gave a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, and others;
then, going to the foot of a mountain, he went forth as an ascetic. After he had gone forth, seventy-four thousand sons of brahmins followed him and went forth as well.
He attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
Having manifested them, he also explained the preliminary practice of the kasiṇas to those jaṭilas. They all likewise developed the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
At that time, the Sammasambuddha named Anomadassī had arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma.
Having delivered beings from the great flood of saṃsāra, and desiring on one day to show favor to the ascetic Sarada and his disciples, he took his bowl and robe and traveled through the air alone.

Thinking, "Let him know my state as a Buddha," he descended from the sky right before the ascetic's eyes while he was watching, and stood firm upon the earth. The ascetic Sarada [beheld] the Teacher...

Having examined the marks of a Great Man on his body and reached the conclusion, "This one is indeed an omniscient Buddha," the ascetic Sarada went out to meet him, prepared a seat, and offered it to him. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The ascetic Sarada sat down to one side in the presence of the Teacher.
At that time, his seventy-four thousand disciples, the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila), arrived bringing various kinds of most excellent and nutritious fruits.

Upon seeing the Teacher, they were filled with faith; observing the manner in which both their teacher and the Teacher were seated, they said, "Teacher, previously we thought, 'There is no one greater than you.'"
"We think, however, that this man is greater than you," they said. "What are you saying, dear ones?
Do you wish to make Mount Sineru, sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas high, equal in height to a mustard seed?
Do not attempt to weigh me against an omniscient Buddha! Then those ascetics, having heard the words of their teacher, [fell silent].
“O how great is this Supreme Person! Saying this, they all prostrated at his feet and paid homage to the Teacher.
Then the teacher said to them: “Dear ones, we have no gift suitable for the Teacher;
yet the Teacher has come here at the time for wandering for alms. Come now, let us give a gift according to our means. By you—”
"Bring whatever choice fruits have been brought," he said; having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them in the Tathāgata’s bowl.
As soon as the Teacher had accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence.
The ascetic himself filtered the water and gave it [to him]. Then, the meal was finished.
When he had finished and the Teacher was seated, he summoned all his resident disciples and sat down conversing with the Teacher on a friendly and memorable discourse.
The Teacher thought, "Let the two Chief Disciples come together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
At that very moment, the two Chief Disciples, surrounded by a retinue of a hundred thousand who were free from the taints (khīṇāsavā), arrived, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his pupils: "Sirs, an offering of flower-seats must be made for the Teacher and the community of monks;

therefore, bring flowers. They immediately brought back, by means of their psychic power, flowers endowed with exquisite color and fragrance, and prepared a flower-seat one league in extent for the Buddha, as well as for the two chief disciples.

They assigned a distance of thirty *gāvutas* for the Buddha, a variety of distances such as half a *yojana* for the other monks, and a space the size of a bull (*usabha*) for the youngest member of the Saṅgha.

When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Sarada extended his joined palms before the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable Sir, please ascend this flower-seat out of favor toward me. The Blessed One sat down upon the flower-seat.
While the Teacher was seated, the two chief disciples and the rest of the bhikkhus sat down each upon their own respective seats.
The Teacher, thinking, "May this be of great fruit for them," entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Knowing that the Teacher had attained cessation, the two chief disciples and the rest of the bhikkhus also entered the attainment of cessation. The ascetic [remained] continuously for seven days.
He stood holding a flower parasol over the Teacher. The others, having consumed forest roots and fruits, stood with palms joined in reverence for the remainder of the time.
At the end of seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and addressed the chief disciple, the Elder Nisabha:
“Offer words of thanksgiving for the flowers and seats of these ascetics. The Elder, regarding the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple—

Having stood there, he offered an expression of appreciation for their flower-seats. At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher addressed Anoma Thera, the second chief disciple, saying, "You too, preach the Dhamma to them.
He, having reflected upon the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, preached the Dhamma to them.
Yet, through the preaching of both, there was no realization of the Dhamma. Then—
The Teacher, standing upon the ground of the Buddha’s domain, began his discourse on the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, with the exception of the ascetic Sarada, all the remaining seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship.

The Teacher extended his hand to them, saying, "Come, monks. Instantly, they vanished from their appearance as ascetics and appeared wearing the eight requisites of a monk, looking like elders of sixty years' standing.

But the ascetic Sarada, thinking at the time of the teaching, "Oh, may I too become a disciple of a future Buddha just like this Elder Nisabha," was distracted by that arisen reflection and was unable to penetrate the paths and fruits.
Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, he made such an aspiration. The Teacher [prophesied] that there would be no obstacle...

Seeing that his aspiration was being fulfilled, [the Buddha] prophesied: "After one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons have passed from now, you will become the foremost disciple named Sāriputta of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama.
Having delivered this prophecy and spoken a discourse on the Dhamma, he leapt into the air, surrounded by the community of monks. Sarada the ascetic also [regarded] his friend...

Having gone into the presence of Sirivaḍḍha, he said, "Friend, at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassi, I have made a resolution for the position of chief disciple of the future Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Gotama;
you too should resolve upon the position of his second disciple. Having heard this instruction, Sirivaḍḍha, at the door of his own residence—
Having had a level area measuring eight *karīsa* prepared, having scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth element,
having had a pavilion constructed with a canopy of blue lotuses, having arranged a seat for the Buddha and seats for the monks,
and having prepared a great show of honor and hospitality, he invited the Teacher together with the ascetic Sarada to offer a great almsgiving for seven days.
Having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and clothed them in costly garments, he made a formal aspiration for the state of being a second disciple.
The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him a prediction in the manner previously described;
then, after expressing his appreciation for the meal, he departed. Sirivaḍḍha, with a heart overflowing with joy, performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived.
In the second cycle of thoughts, he was reborn in the world of the sense-sphere devas. The ascetic Sarada, having cultivated the four divine abidings (brahmavihāras), was reborn in the Brahma-world.
From that point on, no further account of their deeds is told for either of them. But as for our Blessed One—
Even before his birth, the ascetic Sarada took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī in the village of Upatissa, not far from Rājagaha.
On that very same day, his companion also took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman Moggalī in the village of Kolita, not far from Rājagaha.
Therefore, he was called Moggallāna after the brahmin woman Moggalī.
"Putto" means Moggallāna. Or, he is called Moggallāna because he was born into the Moggallī clan.
Alternatively, while she was still a maiden, her parents gave her the name "Muggalī," based on their saying, "Do not be arrogant (mā uggali, mā uggalī).
He is Moggallāna because he is the son of that Muggalī. Or else, it refers to the obtaining or taking up of the paths, beginning with the path of stream-entry.
"Moggallāna is one who is capable and able to penetrate [the truth]. It is said that those two families were close allies for seven successive generations.
On one and the same day, they provided the care for the pregnancies of both women.
When the ten months had passed and the children were born, they appointed sixty-six nurses for each of them. On the day of their naming ceremony, the brahmin woman Rūpasārī...
Because he was the son of the eldest family in Upatissa Village, they gave him the name Upatissa;
because the other was the son of the eldest family in Kolita Village, they gave him the name Kolita.
Both of them, growing up with a great retinue, reached the further shore of all arts and sciences as they attained maturity.
Then one day, while they were watching a mountain-top festival in Rājagaha and seeing the great multitude gathered together, their knowledge reached maturity;
emerging through wise reflection, they attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: "All these people too shall enter the jaws of death within a mere hundred years.
Having thus gained this realization, they thought: "The Dhamma of liberation must be sought by us; and while seeking it, [we must find] one..."
Having made the firm resolve, “It is right for us to receive the going-forth,” they went forth in the presence of the wanderer Sañcaya together with five hundred young brahmins.
From the time they had gone forth, Sañcaya attained the highest gain and the highest fame.
Within just a few days, they mastered the entire system of Sañcaya; yet, finding no essence therein, they [discarded it].
Then, having become disillusioned, they went here and there to ask questions of those ascetics and brahmins esteemed as wise;
when questioned by them, those teachers could not provide satisfactory answers, but instead merely had their own questions answered by those very seekers.
Thus, while searching for liberation, they made an agreement: "Whichever among us first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other."
And at that time, when our Teacher— having attained full enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma—
had gradually tamed the thousand matted-hair ascetics headed by Uruvela Kassapa and was dwelling in Rājagaha,
one day the wanderer Upatissa, while going to the wanderers’ park, [beheld] the Venerable Elder Assaji in Rājagaha.
Seeing him wandering for alms, [the man] thought, "I have never before seen a renunciant so perfected in his deportment;
there must surely be a state of peace here. With faith having arisen, he followed closely behind the Venerable One, watching him in expectation of asking a question.
The Elder, having received the alms-food, went to a suitable place to eat it.
The wanderer prepared his own wanderer’s seat and gave it to him. At the conclusion of the meal, he gave him water from his own water-pot.
Having thus performed the duties toward his teacher, and having exchanged greetings with the Elder who had finished his meal, he asked: "Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you find pleasing?"
The Elder pointed to the Perfectly Enlightened One.

When he was asked again by him, "But what does the Venerable One’s Teacher teach?", the Elder—thinking, "I shall demonstrate the profundity of this dispensation"—declared his own status as a novice and, speaking the Dhamma of the dispensation in brief, recited the verse beginning, "Those phenomena that arise from a cause. The wanderer [understood] only the first two lines.
Having heard [the first verse], he was established in the fruit of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-phala*), which is endowed with a thousandfold reasoning.

The other two lines were completed at the time of his becoming a stream-enterer. However, at the conclusion of the verses, having become a stream-enterer, and observing that no further distinctions arose, he reflected, "There must be a reason for this," and said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, do not increase the teaching of the Dhamma further."
“This much is enough; where does our teacher dwell? “In Veḷuvana. “Venerable sir, you go on ahead;
I will release my companion from his promise, take him with me, and return,” he said.
Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, circumambulated the elder, and dismissed him, he went to the wanderers’ park.
When the wanderer Koliya saw him approaching from afar, he thought, "His complexion is not like it was on other days;
surely he has attained the Deathless through his journey. Anticipating his extraordinary achievement, he asked about his attainment of the Deathless.
The other replied to him, "Friend, the Deathless has been attained," and recited that very verse. At the conclusion of the verse—
Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, Kolita asked, "Where is our Teacher? "In the Veḷuvana," he replied.
"Then come, friend; let us go to see the Teacher. Upatissa was always a worshipper of his teacher;
therefore, having proclaimed the virtues of Sañcaya, he desired to lead him as well into the presence of the Teacher. He was driven by a longing for gain.
Not wishing to be a resident pupil, he refused, saying, "I cannot become a water-carrier by acting as a ladle.
Unable to persuade him through various means, they went to Veḷuvana together with two hundred and fifty resident pupils who were following their own instructions.
Seeing them approaching from afar, the Teacher said, "This..."

Having said, "I shall have a pair of disciples, a supreme and auspicious pair," he taught the Dhamma according to the conduct of their assembly, established them in Arahatship, and granted them the higher ordination by the "Come, monk" formula.
Just as it was for them, so too for the Chief Disciples, magical bowls and robes appeared of their own accord. [The task of the three higher paths...]
But he did not reach the end. Why? Because of the greatness of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (pāramīñāṇa).

Among them, on the seventh day after his going forth, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was practicing the duties of a recluse at the village of Kallavāla in the kingdom of Magadha, he fell into sloth and torpor; being stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled that sloth and torpor.
While listening to the meditation subject on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna), he attained the three higher paths and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s supreme knowledge (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa).
After half a month had passed since his going forth, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling with the Teacher at Rājagaha in the Sūkarakhatā Cave;
there, in the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta, [he spoke] to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha.

While the teaching was being delivered, he sent forth his knowledge according to the discourse and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*), like one eating a meal served by another.
Thus, the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge was attained by the two chief disciples in the very presence of the Teacher.

Thus, having attained the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple, the Venerable Sāriputta, reflecting on what deed had brought about this success, understood it and, moved by joy and gladness, uttered this inspired utterance beginning with, "Not far from the Himalayas... Therefore it was said:
"Not far from the Himalayas, a mountain named Lambaka;..."
“My hermitage is well-prepared, my leaf-hut is well-constructed.
In this context, “of the Himavat” means: that which has snow (*hima*) is the Himavat;
[the phrase] refers to the vicinity, not far from that Himavat, namely the forests connected to the Himalayas. “The mountain named Lambaka” refers to a mountain of loose soil bearing that name.
"Assamaṃ sukato mayhaṃ": on that Lambaka mountain, my *assama*—a forest dwelling built for my sake—is "assama" because it is level (*sama*) on all sides.
Or alternatively, it is called *assama* because there is no fatigue (*parissama*) for those who have entered it.
Such a forest dwelling has been well-constructed; it is beautiful by way of night-quarters, day-quarters, huts, pavilions, and so forth.
“Katā” means made. “Paṇṇasālā” means a leaf-hut covered with leaves such as those of the *usīra* and *pabbaja* plants; the meaning is a dwelling hut made of leaves.
“A river with shallow banks, with beautiful landing-stairs, delightful, strewn with very pure sand, not far from my hermitage.”
In this context, "with shallow banks" means a river that is not deep. "With beautiful landing places" means having lovely fords.
"Delightful, charming, and pleasing" [is the description]. "Strewn with very pure sand" means covered with sand resembling very white pearls;
the meaning is that it has become dense [with sand]. Such a small river (*kunnadī*) was near my hermitage, in close proximity to my dwelling.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, "in the hermitage" (*assame*) should be understood as the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.
"A stream flows there, free from gravel and precipices, sweet and without foul odor, beautifying my hermitage."
In this context, "without pebbles" (*asakkharā*) means free from pebbles, because it is described as "strewn with sand.

"Without cliffs" (*apabbhārā*) means devoid of precipices; the meaning is that its banks are not deep. "Sweet and odorless" (*sādu appaṭigandhikā*) means having water of pleasant taste and free from foul odors.
The meaning is that a small river (*nadikā*), a minor stream, flows and courses along, beautifying my hermitage.
“Here there are *kumbhīla* fish, *makara* fish, *susumāra* crocodiles, and tortoises;
a river flows there, beautifying my hermitage.
Therein, the *kumbhīla* fish, *makara* fish, *susumāra* crocodiles, fierce fish, and tortoise fish are present here.
The connection is: "They were playing in this river. The connection is: "Adorning my hermitage, the *nadikā*—a small river—flows and runs. [As it is said:
"The *pāṭhīna*, *pāvusa*, *balaja*, *muñja*, and *rohitā* fish..."
“Leaping up and falling down, they beautify my hermitage.
The pāṭhīna fish, the pāvusa fish, the balaja fish, the muñja fish, the rohita fish, and the vaggaḷa fish—
all these species of fish leap here and there, moving along with the river, [beautifying] my [hermitage].
The meaning is: "beautifying the hermitage grounds.
[As it is said: "On both banks of the river, trees in flower and bearing fruit hang down on both sides, beautifying my hermitage."
In that context, "on both banks" means that trees with perpetual flowers and perpetual fruit, hanging down from both sides and leaning downward toward both banks of that river,
beautified my hermitage. "Mangoes, sal trees, tilakas, pāṭalis, and sinduvārakas—
blooming in my hermitage, they waft a divine fragrance."
In this context, "mangoes" refers to the *madhupiṇḍika* mango trees, *sāla* trees, *tilaka* trees, *pāṭali* trees, and *sinduvāra* trees;
these trees are in full bloom at all times. The meaning is that they waft forth divine fragrances from my hermitage, blowing scents in every direction.
“Campaka, saḷala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka trees—
having blossomed in my hermitage, they emit divine fragrances. In that place,
the campaka trees and saḷala trees have flowers resembling golden rings, as do the nīpa trees.

The *nāgaka* trees, the *punnāga* trees, and the fragrant *ketaka* trees—all these divine trees have blossomed and flowered in my hermitage, wafting forth their sweet fragrance; that is to say, they are exhaling a most excellent scent.
And the *asoka* trees—both the *adhimutta-asoka* and the *bhaginī-mālā-asoka*—have also blossomed.
“The *aṅkola* and *bimbijāla* trees have blossomed in my hermitage.
