The connection is as follows: there, the *adhimuttaka* trees have blossomed, the *asoka* trees have blossomed, the *bhaginīmālā* trees have blossomed, the *aṅkola* trees have blossomed, and the *bimbijāla* trees have blossomed; these trees, having flowered, beautify my hermitage.
“Ketaka trees and kandalī plants, godhuka trees and tiṇasūlika shrubs, wafting a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.
Therein, *ketakā* refers to groves of fragrant ketaka trees; *kandalī* refers to kandalī trees; *godhuka* refers to godhuka trees; and *tiṇasūlika* refers to tiṇasūlika shrubs.
And all these species of trees, wafting divine fragrance, beautify my entire hermitage— this is the meaning.
"The *kaṇikāra* and *kaṇṇika*, the *asana* and many *ajjuna* trees,
wafting divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage."
The connection is as follows: "These trees, such as the *kaṇikāra* and others, beautifying my entire hermitage, waft forth a divine fragrance.
[And: "The *punnāga*, the mountain *punnāga*, and the *koviḷāra* trees, all in full bloom, wafting a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage."
The meaning is: "Punnāga trees and others, wafting divine fragrances, beautify my hermitage.
"Uddālaka, kuṭaja, kadamba, and many bakula trees, wafting divine fragrances, beautify my hermitage."
The connection is as follows: trees such as the *uddālaka* and others, emitting divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.
“The *āḷaka*, *isimugga*, *kadali*, and *mātuluṅgi* trees, nurtured by fragrant water, bear their fruits.”

In this context, the meaning is that these trees, such as the *āḷaka* and others, having been nourished with fragrant scented water from sandalwood and other sources, bear golden fruits and thus beautify my hermitage.
"Other lotuses bloom, others are born as *kesari*;
some lotuses are in bud, while others have already blossomed in the pond at that time."
In that regard, "others bloom as lotuses": not far from my hermitage, in a pond, some lotuses are blooming;
some *kesari* lotuses are being born and produced; and some lotuses are "in full flower," meaning their petals and filaments have fallen away.
"The lotuses conceive a womb; the *muḷāli* plants run forth."
“Then the ponds shine, strewn with *siṅghāṭika* flowers.
Regarding that: “The lotuses conceive buds”—at that time, during my period of dwelling there as an ascetic, some lotuses within the pond took up their buds and blossoms.
The *muḷāliya* roots—the roots of the lotuses—stretched out from within the mud.
The meaning is that they go along like elephant tusks. The meaning is that the crossroads, strewn with fallen flowers and having become dense thickets, are beautifying [the place].
“Then, in that pond, the *nayitā*, the mango-scented, the *uttalī*, and the *bandhujīvaka*—all in full bloom—emit a divine fragrance.”
Then, at the time of my dwelling, near the pond, there were the Nayita grove, the Ambagandha grove, the grove called Uttalī,
and the Bandhujīvaka groves; all these groves were in full bloom, bearing flowers, wafting sweet fragrances,
and beautifying the pond— this is the meaning.
“Pāṭhīna, pāvusa, balaja, muñja, rohita, saṅgula,
and maggura fish dwell then in the pond. The connection is that at that time,
during my period of residence, the Pāṭhīna and other fish dwelt in the pond without fear.
“Crocodiles and water-monsters, water-owls and *rakkhasas*, *oguhās* and pythons dwell then in that pond. The connection is as follows:
at the time of my dwelling, these crocodiles and other fish lived fearlessly and without distress in the pond near my hermitage.
“Doves, sun-swan birds, ruddy geese, river-dwellers, cuckoos, parrots,
and mynahs all depend upon that lake.
Therein, near my hermitage, depending on that lake, there were birds such as doves, sun-swan birds, and river-dwellers.
The connection is that the cakravāka birds, cuckoos, parrots, and mynahs live depending upon that lake. “The kukutthakas,
the kuḷīrakas, and the pokkharasātakas in the forest;”

“Kukutthakas and kuḷīrakas, as well as dindibhas, suvapotas, and pokkharasātakas—these birds all dwell near my hermitage. In this context, “kukutthakas” refers to birds of that name; “kuḷīrakas” refers to birds of that name;
and “dindibhas,” “suvapotas,” and “pokkharasātakas” are also birds—all these birds [reside] near my hermitage.
The connection is: "They live depending on the lake.
"Swans, cranes, and peacocks, cuckoos and *tambacūḷaka* birds, *pammaka* birds and *jīvaṃjīva* birds—all depend upon that lake for their livelihood."
All these birds, such as the swans and others, live depending upon that lake; the meaning is that they maintain their livelihood there.
"The kosikas and poṭṭhasīsas, many kuraras and senakas, and the mahākāla birds—all depend for their livelihood upon that lake."
Therein, the *kosika* birds, the *poṭṭhasīsa* birds, the *kurara* birds, the *senaka* birds, the *mahākāla* birds,
and many other birds on dry land lived and made their living by that lake, in the vicinity of that lake— this is the meaning.
"The *pasada* deer, the boars, the *camara* antelopes, and many *gaṇḍaka* antelopes..."
“Ruddy geese and white pigeons depend upon that lake.
Here, the meaning is that these animals, such as the deer and so forth, dwell near that lake—in the accusative case used in the sense of the locative—sustaining their lives there.
“Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, and jackals...”
“Elephants of three-fold breed depend upon that lake.
The connection is that these four-footed animals, such as lions and the rest, live near the lake free from affliction.
“Kinnaras and monkeys, as well as forest-dwellers;”
“Slaves and hunters alike subsist upon that lake.
Here, the meaning is that these beings, such as the *kinnaras* and others of such names, dwell in the vicinity of that lake.
“*Tinduka* fruits, *piyāla* nuts, *madhūka* flowers, and *sumārikā* berries;”
“Surely these trees bear fruits, not far from my hermitage.

Herein, the connection is as follows: these trees, such as the *tinduka* and others, surely bear sweet fruits at the three seasons reckoned as winter, summer, and the rainy season, in a place not far from my hermitage.
“The *kosamba*, *saḷala*, and *nimba* trees are endowed with sweet fruit;”
“They surely bear fruit not far from my hermitage.

In this context, the meaning is that these trees, such as the *kosaṃba* and others—possessing heartwood, sweet fruit, and excellent fruit—are well-joined, thoroughly joined, and fully endowed, shining constantly near my hermitage while bearing fruit.
“The *harītakī*, the *āmalaka*, the mango, the *jambu*, and the *vibhītaka*;”
“Kolā, bhallātakā, and billā—these trees bear fruit.
The connection is that those *harītakī* and other trees, grown near my hermitage, constantly bear fruit.
“And *āluva*, *kaḷamba*, and *biḷālītakkaḷa*;”
“Jīvakas and even Sutas, many are they in my hermitage.
The connection is that these *ālu* and other roots and fruits, small yet sweet in taste, exist in great abundance near my hermitage.
“Not far from the hermitage, there are well-constructed ponds;”
“With clear water, cool water, beautiful landing-stairs, and enchanting. Not far from that hermitage,
near the hermitage itself, it was well-constructed— meaning it was fashioned so as to be perfectly suitable for ascending and descending—
with clear water (acchodaka) meaning limpid water, cool water (sītajala) meaning cold water, and beautiful landing-stairs (supatittha) meaning lovely bathing-places.
The ponds were delightful and joy-inducing; this is the meaning of "they were.
"Covered with lotuses and water-lilies, joined with white lotuses, and strewn with mandārava flowers, they waft a divine fragrance."

There, the ponds were covered with lotuses and water-lilies, filled and endowed with white lilies, and possessed of mandārava flowers; they were so densely covered that they became impenetrable, and divine fragrances wafted forth, blowing from all sides—this is the meaning.
“Thus, in that forest endowed with every excellence, in full bloom and laden with fruit, in that well-made and delightful hermitage, I dwelt at that time.”

In that context, "thus endowed with all its parts" means: at that time, when I had become an ascetic, I dwelt in a well-constructed and delightful hermitage in the forest—a forest that was complete and perfect with various components such as streams and the like, and which had become a dense thicket with flowering and fruiting trees.
Having thus far shown the excellence of the hermitage, he now shows the excellence of his own qualities, such as virtue (sīla), etc.: [the following passage].
“He is virtuous, perfected in his vows, a meditator always delighting in meditation,
and has attained the power of the five super-knowledges— the ascetic named Suruci,” he said. In this context,
“virtuous” means one who is complete in the five kinds of virtue, which are similar to the fourfold purification of virtue associated with meditative absorption.
The meaning: "Endowed with vows" means endowed by the undertaking of a vow, thinking, "From this day forward, I shall not indulge in household life or the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"A meditator" means one who meditates and whose nature is to meditate by means of characteristic-contemplation (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and object-contemplation (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).

"Delighting in meditation" means delighting in, attached to, and always fully absorbed in these meditations. "Attained to the power of the five supernormal knowledges" refers to those known as the various psychic powers (*iddhividha*), the divine ear (*dibbasota*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavijānana*), the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*), and the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"Endowed with the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the specific wisdoms, and possessed of the powers"—this is the meaning of "perfected.
The connection is: "I dwell having become an ascetic named Suruci by name.
Having thus shown his own perfection of qualities, he now shows the perfection of his assembly:
“Twenty-four thousand disciples attended upon me;
all these brahmins were of noble birth and possessed of fame,” he said at the beginning.

Therein, the connection is as follows: “All these twenty-four thousand brahmins, my disciples—being of noble birth (*jātimanto*), endowed with lineage, and possessed of fame (*yasassino*) through their retinue—attended upon me.”
“In the science of marks (*lakkhaṇa*), in history (*itihāsa*), together with the glossaries (*nighaṇḍu*) and ritual manuals (*keṭubha*);
in grammar (*padaka*) and etymology (*veyyākaraṇa*), they have reached perfection in their own Dhamma.
Therein, “in the science of marks” means in the treatise on marks. Regarding all worldly men and women: “By these marks... [they discern].
One knows the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) thus: "When endowed with these, beings are suffering; when endowed with these, they are happy.

The treatise that elucidates this is the *Lakkhaṇa*; [the phrase] "in that *Lakkhaṇa*" refers to that work. Regarding *itihāsa*: it refers to the treatises that illustrate statements such as "Thus it was, thus it was" (*itiha āsa itiha āsā*).
The connection is: "They have reached the perfection (*pārami*), the culmination, in both the *Lakkhaṇa* and the *itihāsa*. [This applies to] trees, mountains, and so forth.
A text that elucidates names is called a *nighaṇḍu*. A *keṭubha* is a treatise that assists poets in the various forms of ritual action (*kriyā*) and prosody (*kappa*).
That which exists together with the *nighaṇḍu* is "with the *nighaṇḍu*" (*sanighaṇḍu*); that which exists together with the *keṭubha* is "with the *keṭubha*" (*sakeṭubha*). The connection is:
"having reached perfection in those three Vedas, together with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*. As for the term *padaka*:
They were experts in words consisting of nouns, compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), verbs, and formations such as *kita* and *ka*.

They were experts in the grammars, namely the grammatical systems of Canda, Pāṇini, Kalāpa, and others. "Reached perfection in their own Dhamma" means they had reached, attained, the perfection—the ultimate limit—in their own Dhamma, that is, the Dhamma of the Brahmins, the three Vedas.
"They were skilled in portents, omens, and bodily marks..."
“My well-trained disciples are experts in the earth, the ground, and the sky.

In this context, they are skilled and proficient regarding portents such as the falling of meteors and earthquakes, as well as in signs of beauty and signs of ugliness, and in the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, and the characteristics of a Great Man (mahāpurisa).
“In the earth, on the ground, throughout the entire world, and in the sky—that is, in the atmosphere”—thus, they are experts in all these areas.
"My disciples are well-trained:
'These ones are few in desires, prudent, moderate in food, and free from greed;
content with gain and loss alike, they always attend upon me.'"
In this context, "of few wishes" means those who subsist with even a little. "Clever" means endowed with wisdom characterized by skillfulness (*nepakkasaṅkhātāya paññāya*).
"Eating little" means having one meal a day, that is, eating only once. "Not greedy" means those in whom greedy craving does not arise.
"Contented with gain and loss"—these disciples of mine always and at all times surround me, being joyful whether there is gain or loss.
The meaning is "they attend upon me.
"The wise ones, meditators who delight in jhāna, with peaceful minds and concentrated,
aspiring for nothingness, always surround me."

In this context, "meditators" (*jhāyī*) refers to those endowed with the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and the contemplation of objects (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), or those whose nature is to meditate.
"Delighting in meditation" (*jhānarata*) means they are fond of and attached to those meditations. "Wise" (*dhīra*) means perfected in steadfastness (*dhiti*).

"Tranquil-minded" (*santacitta*) means those whose minds are calmed. "Concentrated" (*samāhita*) means those whose minds are one-pointed. "Nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*) refers to a state free from impediments. "Aspiring" (*patthayanta*) means desiring it.
The connection is: "My disciples, being thus, always surround me.
"Having attained perfection in the higher knowledges, delighting in their ancestral domain, those wise ones who move through the air always surround me."
In this context, "having attained perfection in the higher knowledges" means having reached the limit or completion in the five higher knowledges;
the sense is that they have fulfilled them. "Delighting in their paternal domain" means delighting in food obtained through intimation authorized by the Buddhas.
"Wandering through the air" means coming and going by way of the air, that is, the sky. "The steadfast" means those who have become firm.
The meaning is that they are by nature undaunted even in the face of dangers such as lions and tigers. The meaning is that my ascetics, being such as these, always surround me.
"Restrained in the six doors, unshakable, with their faculties guarded..."
"And those wise ones are unassociated; my disciples are difficult to overcome.
In this context, "restrained" means they are closed, shut, and concealed regarding the six doors of the eye and so forth with respect to the six objects such as visible forms;
the meaning is that their doors are guarded and protected. "Unshaken" means free from craving; "with guarded faculties" means their faculties, such as the eye and so forth, have been protected.
"Not associating with relatives" means not being mixed with householders. "Difficult to approach" means difficult to get near;
the meaning is that they are incapable of being approached or disturbed.
"By sitting cross-legged, by standing, and by walking..."
"My disciples, difficult to approach, spend the night [in this way].

Here, the connection is as follows: "My disciples, having abandoned lying down with their legs crossed in the *pallaṅka* posture, spend and pass the entire night specifically through sitting, standing, and walking.
"They do not become attached to what is attractive, nor do they feel aversion toward what is repulsive."
"My disciples, who are difficult to assail, are not deluded by that which leads to delusion.

Being such as this, my disciples—the ascetics—do not become attached to, nor do they give rise to attachment for, an object that is "to be delighted in," that is, an object fit for the arising of lust.
They do not become hateful toward, nor do they give rise to hatred for, an object that is "to be hated," that is, an object fit for the arising of aversion.

They do not act [with delusion]. In a situation liable to cause delusion and appropriate for being deluded, they are not deluded; they do not produce delusion. The meaning is that they become endowed with wisdom.
“Investigating psychic power, they proceed at all times;
they cause the earth to tremble, difficult to approach because of their zeal.”

The connection is as follows: those disciples of mine live constantly testing their supernormal transformations (*iddhi-vikubbana*), such as "having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one," and so forth.
The meaning is that those disciples of mine, having fashioned the earth even in the sky or in water, perform the postures of daily life.
[This is done] through agitation, through seizing upon opposing views, and through the making of quarrels.
The meaning is: "They are not to be approached.
"And while playing, those disciples of mine play the game of jhāna;
they bring back fruit from the rose-apple tree—my disciples are difficult to approach."
My disciples, while playing, play the game of the first jhāna and so forth; the meaning is that they sport and delight.

"Bringing fruits from the rose-apple tree" means that, having gone by means of psychic power to the rose-apple tree on Mount Himavanta which is one hundred yojanas high, they bring back rose-apple fruits the size of water-jars; this is the meaning.
“Some go to Goyāna, others to Pubbavideha;
others still to Uttarakuru—difficult to approach in their quest.
Among those disciples of mine, some go to the island of Goyāna (Aparagoyāna), while others [go elsewhere].
They go to the island of Pubbavideha, and some go to the island of Uttarakuru;
the connection is that they go to these places for the purpose of seeking, searching, and looking for requisites.
"They send a load ahead, and they follow behind."
“The sky was covered by twenty-four thousand [monks].
The meaning is that as my disciples were traveling through the air, they sent the basket filled with the requisites of an ascetic and the carrying-pole ahead of them;
having sent that first toward the front, they themselves followed behind it. While they were traveling in this manner...
The connection is that the sky, the expanse of the atmosphere, was covered and concealed by twenty-four thousand ascetics.
[They were as follows: “Some were fire-cookers and some were fireless;
some used their teeth as mortars, while others pounded with stones; some ate food consisting of fallen fruit.”
In that regard, some of my disciples cook fruits, roots, leaves, and so forth with fire and eat them;
some, being fire-avoiders (*anaggi*), do not cook with fire but eat them raw; some, being toothless (*dantika*), strip off the bark with their teeth and eat it;
some, using mortars (*udukhalika*), pound [the food] in mortars and eat it; and some eat what has been pounded with stones.
They eat [the fruit] after pounding it with stones. Some have "those who feed on fruits that have fallen of their own accord" as the connection [of the verse].
"Some of my disciples are those who descend into water, who are pure and steadfast at evening and dawn, and who perform ritual sprinklings with water; they are difficult to overcome."

“Some of my disciples are difficult to approach; they are very long-enduring and desire purity, bathing in water morning and evening—the meaning is that they enter the water. Some perform ablutions with water—the meaning is that they sprinkle themselves with water.
With their armpits, nails, and body hair grown long, with teeth stained by dirt and hair grey, yet perfumed by the fragrance of virtue, my disciples are difficult to approach.”

In that regard, those disciples of mine are difficult to approach; the meaning is that long nails and hair have grown and sprouted upon their flanks, both sides of the flanks, and their hands and feet.
Because they are devoid of grooming, the intention is that they are unadorned and unembellished.
"With mud-stained teeth" means that their teeth are covered in grime because they have not been whitened with brick powder, lime, stone powder, or similar substances.
The meaning is as follows: "Dust-covered" (*rajaṃsirā*) means their heads are smeared with dust because they are devoid of anointing with oil and such.

"Fragrant with the scent of virtue" (*gandhitā sīlagandhena*) means that because they are endowed with the virtue associated with the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), they have become fragrant everywhere with the worldly scent of virtue.
"My disciples are difficult to approach" (*mama sissā durāsadā*) is because they are possessed of these aforementioned qualities.
The connection is: "My disciples are impossible to approach or to disturb.
"At dawn, having assembled together, those matted-hair ascetics of fierce austerities, having proclaimed their gains and losses, then depart through the sky."

In that context, "having assembled early in the morning" (*pātova sannipatitvā*)—the suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of the locative case—the meaning is: "having gathered into a heap in my presence at the very time of the morning meal.
"Those with high asceticism" (*uggatāpanā*) means those whose heat of penance is manifest, whose heat is spread abroad; "jaṭilas" are ascetics who wear matted hair.
"Having proclaimed gain and loss" (*lābhālābhaṃ pakittetvā*) means having made small and great gains public, at that time, on that occasion.
The connection is that they travel in the sky, upon the surface of the atmosphere.
(192) Furthermore, illustrating their very qualities, he said: "Of these, as they set forth," and so on.
Therein, for these ascetics as they set forth—that is, as they go—whether in the air or on land, a great sound produced by their bark garments (*vākacīra*) arises.

The meaning is as follows: "The deities are delighted" means that as they departed after raising such a great clamor, the deities—satisfied by the sound of the antelope skins and filled with joy, exclaiming "Excellent, excellent, noble ones!"—became glad and contented; this is the connection. 193.
"In every direction": those seers, moving through the atmosphere and traveling through the sky, set out toward the southern direction and its intermediate quarters.

"They go" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Supported by their own power" means that, endowed with either the strength of their own bodies or the power of *jhāna*, wherever they wish to go, they go right there; this is the connection.
(194) Again, demonstrating the majesty of those very same beings, he said: "These are the shakers of the earth," and so forth. At that time, these [beings] were everywhere...
They move at will; they cause the earth to quake, being of a nature that makes the ground tremble; they move through the sky, traveling in the atmosphere.
Possessing lofty splendor—those of exalted and pervasive majesty—they are "difficult to overcome" (*duppasaha*), meaning they cannot be suppressed or overcome by others.
Like the ocean, they are unshakeable; like the sea, they are unshakeable and undisturbed by others.
The connection is that they are "incapable of being shaken.
(195) "Some who stand and walk" means: among those disciples of mine, some seers are endowed with the postures of standing and walking;
some seers are "sitters," endowed with the posture of sitting; and some seers subsist on food that has been brought to them or on food consisting of fallen leaves.
The connection is: "Because they are endowed with such qualities, they are difficult to assail.

(196) Praising them all, he said, "Those who dwell in loving-kindness," and so forth. In that context, they dwell having pervaded [the world] with loving-kindness—characterized by affection—in the manner of: "May immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems be happy," and so on; [they do this] toward their own person...
"They cause [this] to proceed" means: "These dwellers in loving-kindness are my disciples. All those seers were seekers of the welfare of all breathing things, seekers of the benefit of all beings.

Not exalting themselves—meaning they did not elevate themselves, being free from pride—they did not disparage any person whatsoever; the meaning is that they did not hold anyone in contempt by degrading them.

197. The connection is as follows: because they are endowed with the qualities of virtue, concentration, and meditative attainment, these disciples of mine come into my presence like lion-kings—undaunted and fearless;
like elephant-kings—possessing strength and perfected in both physical power and the power of jhāna;
and like tiger-kings—difficult to approach and impossible to provoke.
198. Then, demonstrating his own majesty by way of its manifestation, he spoke the verse beginning with "Vidyādharas... and so forth.

Therein, the *vidyādharas*—who possess the sciences (*vijjā*) such as the recitation of mantras—and the earth-dwelling deities (*bhummadevatā*) who reside in trees, mountains, and the like; the *nāgas* dwelling on the ground and on dry land;
the *gandhabbas*, *devas*, fierce *rakkhasas*, *kumbhaṇḍa* gods, and *dānava* gods—all of whom are capable of creating whatever they desire—[were present].
The connection is that the *garuḷas* subsist upon that lake; the meaning is that they dwell in that lake or in its vicinity.

(199) Furthermore, praising the virtues of those very disciples of his who were ascetics, he said: "Their matted hair fills the *khāris*, etc. All of that is of plain meaning. "*Khāribhāra*" refers to the requisites of an ascetic, such as the water-pot (*udañcana*), the water-strainer (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth.
(207) Again, manifesting his own virtues, he said: "In portents and in dreams, etc. In that context, regarding the skills of the Brahmins...
Because he had attained perfection and was skilled in the recitation of astrology, when asked about the occurrence of the rising signs of constellations for this prince—
whether they were auspicious or inauspicious— he spoke on the interpretation of the arising of signs and dreams, saying, "This dream is auspicious;
this is inauspicious," and he spoke on the characteristics of the hands and feet of all men and women.

The connection is as follows: "And having been well-trained, at that time during my period as an ascetic, I retained all the mantra-words circulating throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, including the entire section on the mantras of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
(208) He spoke the verse beginning with "Anomadassī," etc., while proclaiming his own prophecy preceded by the qualities of the Buddha. Therein—

"Not low" means "not inferior. Seeing—that is, the vision—of all sentient beings by means of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the universal eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye, is called "vision";
the Blessed One who possesses such an "inferiorless vision" is the Blessed One Anomadassī.
Because of qualities such as being fortunate, and because he is the eldest and most excellent in the world, the Blessed One is the "Eldest of the World" (Lokajeṭṭha).
*Usabha*, *nisabha*, and *āsabha* are the three [terms for] the leaders of cattle. In this context, the leader of a hundred cows is an *usabha*;
the leader of a thousand cows is a *nisabha*; the leader of a hundred thousand cows is an *āsabha*. The "bull among men" (*narāsabha*) is one who has penetrated all phenomena;
the Fully Awakened One (*sambuddha*), desiring seclusion and wishing for solitude, approached the Himavanta, the Himalayan mountain—this is the connection [of the passage].
209. "Having plunged into the Himavat" means having entered into the vicinity of the Himavat mountains; the rest is self-evident.

210–1. Like a blooming blue lotus flower (*indīvara*), like a blazing sacrificial fire (*hutāsana*)—the seat of the oblation—like a mass of flames burning and endowed with radiance, like lightning flashing in the sky, and like a king of *sāla* trees in full bloom.
The connection is that they saw the Leader of the World seated. 213.
The God of gods among gods—having seen that God of gods, for the purpose of recognizing his marks, namely the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, I pondered and investigated:
"Is he a Buddha or not? The One with Eyes [possesses] five eyes.
The connection is: "For what reason do I behold the Visionary Conqueror?
(214) On his supreme feet, on the soles of those most excellent feet, wheel-marks with a thousand spokes are seen;
having seen those marks of that Blessed One, I reached a conclusion regarding the Tathāgata, I arrived at certainty, free from doubt.
"Is" (āsinti) is the meaning. The rest is self-evident. 218. *Sayambhū*:
self-existent (*sayameva bhūtā*). *Amitodaya*: the arising and source of immeasurable (*amitānaṃ*), that is, limitless (*aparimāṇānaṃ*), qualities.
These two phrases are merely forms of address. "Thou well upliftest this world"—this world of sentient beings—from *saṃsāra*.
The meaning is: "Having pulled them out, he caused them to reach the ground of Nibbāna.
The connection is: "All those beings, having come and approached your sight, cross over—that is, transcend—the stream of doubt, the great flood of perplexity. 219.
Praising the Blessed One, the ascetic spoke the words beginning with "You are the Teacher," and so forth. In that context, "O Venerable One, Omniscient One... [the text continues].
You are the Teacher of the world including the devas; in the highest sense, you alone are the lofty banner (*ketu*).
In the sense of illuminating the entire world, you alone are the standard (*dhaja*). Because you have risen above the three worlds, you alone are the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), like a raised pillar.
For all living beings, you alone are the supreme refuge (*parāyaṇa*); you alone are the goal to be reached, the foundation, and the place of support.
Because you dispel the darkness of delusion for the world, you alone are a lamp, like an oil-lamp;
"the supreme among bipeds" (*dvipaduttama*) means you are the most excellent and best among bipeds—namely, gods, brahmas, and humans. This is the connection.
(220) Again, praising the Blessed One himself, he said, "It is possible [to know] the water in the ocean," and so forth. Therein, [the ocean is] eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep.

"Venerable sir, it might be possible to measure and weigh the water in the ocean by the *āḷhaka*, but it is not at all possible to measure or weigh your omniscient knowledge as being 'this much' in extent; this is the meaning. 221.
It might be possible, venerable sir, to place the earth upon a scale-pan and hold up the Medinī, but it is not at all possible to sustain your omniscient knowledge; such is the connection."

222. Venerable Sir, it might be possible to measure the entire expanse of space with a cord or even a finger; but the meaning is that your knowledge—the space of knowledge—cannot be measured in such a way.

223. "The water in the great ocean" means that one would have to abandon—that is, pass beyond—the entire water in the sea, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, as well as the entire earth, which is two hundred and forty-four thousand yojanas thick.

One might make it equal to the Buddha’s knowledge by taking it up, grasping it, and weighing it; one might make it equal. By way of comparison—that is, through the medium of a simile—it would not be fitting, nor could it be joined.
The meaning is that knowledge alone is superior. 224. "O Visionary One" (*cakkhumā*):
you possess eyes by means of five kinds of vision; this is an address. Of that which proceeds together with the devas...

"Of the world": the genitive case is used here in the sense of the locative. "In the world including the devas," among whomsoever so many beings have minds active—these so many sentient beings possessing minds are "caught within the net of your knowledge," meaning they have entered within the net of your knowledge;
the sense is that you see all beings with the net of your knowledge.
225. Venerable sir, O Omniscient One, Knower of all phenomena:

the connection is that by means of that knowledge associated with the four paths, through which you attained and reached the entirety of supreme enlightenment and Nibbāna, by that same knowledge you have crushed and overcome the followers of other sects and those of alien religions.
226. The Elders who compiled the Dhamma, demonstrating the manner in which they had been praised by that ascetic, said: "Having praised [him] with these verses.
In this context, "these verses" means having praised—that is, having performed the act of praise—with so many verses.

By name, he was an ascetic named Suruci; however, in the other commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), he appears as "the youth Sarada. According to the method of the commentaries, this is simply the reading [of the text].
*Pamāṇaṃ*. Alternatively, he is *suruci* because his taste (*ruci*), inclination (*ajjhāsaya*), and abiding (*ālaya*) are beautiful (*sundara*).
He is *sarado* because he remembers (*sarati*), goes toward (*gacchati*), and proceeds for the sake of taming the sense faculties (*indriyadamanāya*); thus both are names for him.

That ascetic Suruci, having spread out a deerskin (*ajinacamma*) upon the earth, sat down—meaning he sat in the *sarada* posture, avoiding the six faults of sitting such as being too close, and so forth.
227. Sitting there, the ascetic, praising the knowledge of that Blessed One, spoke the words beginning with "eighty-four thousand.
In this context, "eighty-four thousand" means eighty-four thousand; "the king of mountains, Meru, the monarch of peaks," is submerged—plunged deep and entered—into the great ocean, the sea;
and to that same extent, it rises up [above the water] by those same eighty-four thousand.
The connection is: "Now he is called 'exceedingly lofty' (ati-uggata). 228.

To that extent it was "lofty" (accuggata), and thus it is "exceedingly lofty" (ati-uggata). That great Nera, the king of mountains, so vast in length, height, and breadth—that great Nera, the sovereign of mountains—has been ground into a hundred thousand millions of atoms, reduced to a state of pulverized dust. 229.
"Venerable Sir, O Omniscient One, when your knowledge is placed against [the measure of] knowledge, it is as if a hundred or a thousand [grains] were set against a *lakkha*."
The connection is as follows: even if one were to place each drop of water from the great ocean into a hundred thousand [jars], that very powder of Mount Mahāmeru would eventually be exhausted;
yet it is impossible to measure or establish a limit for your knowledge.
230. If one were to cast a net with fine mesh and fine openings across the entire great ocean and drain the water...
One would enclose it on all sides; the meaning is that once thus enclosed, whatever living beings are born in the water, they would all come to be caught within the net. 231.
Showing the object of comparison, he said, "For just so," and so forth. Therein, just as the water-born creatures are caught within the net...
It is so, O Great Hero; exert your energy for the attainment of great enlightenment.
There are various and numerous other sectarian teachers who are false, having plunged into the thicket of views and entered the dense forest of dogmatic opinions.
They are deluded and obstructed by their own attachment—a view characterized by grasping at things as being otherwise than they truly are.

232. By means of your pure, stainless knowledge (*ñāṇa*), which sees without obstruction—that is, by virtue of seeing all phenomena free from hindrance—all these sectarians (*titthiya*) have entered within the net;
they have been brought inside the net of knowledge, or rather, they remain exactly so—this is the connection.
"Your knowledge does not let them pass" means that those sectarians do not transcend your knowledge.
233. At the conclusion of the praise thus spoken, the Blessed One said, "At that time," and so forth, in order to show the occasion for his own prophecy.

Therein, at the moment when the ascetic praised the Blessed One—that is, at the time of the completion of that praise—the Blessed One Anomadassī, who possessed great fame due to having an entourage beyond counting, [overcame] the Māras of the defilements and so forth.

He is a *Jina* (Victor) because he has conquered. The connection is as follows: having emerged from the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) into which he had been absorbed, he surveyed the entire Jambudīpa with his divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). 234–5.
Of that Blessed One, the Sage Anomadassī, who was endowed with the knowledge designated as "wisdom" (*mona*),...
The disciple named Nisabha was surrounded by one hundred thousand Tādi-s— those whose minds were tranquil, whose defilements and conceits were stilled,
who were free from taints, pure, endowed with purified bodily actions and so forth, possessed of the six supernormal powers,
and whose nature was unshakable by the eight worldly conditions due to their being imperturbable toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. Having understood and known the Buddha’s mind, [he spoke].
The connection is that they approached the Leader of the World; at that very moment, they came into his presence.
Having arrived there in that manner, standing in the sky—that is, in the atmosphere—they circumambulated the Blessed One.
With all their hands joined in reverence, they descended from the sky into the presence of the Buddha.
The connection is "they descended.
(237) Again, in order to reveal the preliminary cause for giving the prophecy, he said, "He manifested a smile," and so forth; all of that is of plain meaning.
(241) "Who with a flower... refers to the ascetic who, having inspired confidence in his mind toward me, honored me with many flowers.
"I shall praise and proclaim that ascetic;
listen to my words as I speak, bring them within the range of your hearing, and attend to them.
(250) The Blessed One spoke thus while bestowing a prophecy regarding his final birth. In this context, "final" means being at the very end.
When existence has been attained: he will go to the human state, to the human birth; the meaning is that he will arise in the human world.

He will be carried in the womb of a brahmin woman named Sārī, so called because she possesses essence (*sāra*) through her essential beauty, essential wealth, essential youth, essential lineage, essential prosperity, and essential merit.
253. He begins the exposition of the root of the prophecy: "In immeasurable eons from now.

Here, although the two chief disciples fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand eons, nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated thus by taking intermediate eons into account for the sake of the ease of metrical composition.
254. “By the name Sāriputta, he shall become the foremost disciple”—thus he gave this prediction.
Having given the prediction, the Blessed One, praising him, spoke these words beginning with, “This Bhāgīrathī.
Among these five rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarabhū, Mahī, and Aciravatī—this first great Gaṅgā named Bhāgīrathī flows from the Himālayas.
Manifested from the Himālayas, originating from Lake Anotatta,
they flow into and reach the great ocean, the vast mass of water; just as they enter and approach the great sea, the great ocean,
even so this Sāriputta is confident in his own three [Vedas], being confident in the three Vedas that prevail in his own lineage.

"Unfaltering in knowledge, expansive in knowledge. Having reached the perfection of wisdom and having attained the ultimate limit of the knowledge of his own disciples, he will satisfy, gladden, and bring contentment to all living beings—this is the meaning. 257.
"Starting from the Himalayas" means beginning with the Himalaya mountain range, up to the great ocean, the vast sea, the burden of water.

Taking the ocean as its limit, whatever sand there is within this interval—in the midst of these two, the mountains and the ocean—that is incalculable (*asaṅkhiya*), meaning it exceeds all number by way of calculation.
(258) "That too could be counted without remainder" means that even that sand could be counted completely; it would be possible, it might be so.
The connection is: "How that counting comes to be. The meaning is: "In that way, there will never be an end or limit to Sāriputta’s wisdom.
(259) Regarding the passage beginning with "In a hundred thousand...

it would come to pass": the meaning is that if knowledge were placed for even a single moment within a hundred thousand units of knowledge, the sands of the Ganges would be exhausted and reach their total depletion.

260. Just as in the Great Ocean—the four great seas with a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas—there are waves of various kinds such as a *gāvuta* in height, masses of billows that are incalculable (*asaṅkhiya*) by number, being devoid of any count;
even so, there will be no end or limit to the wisdom of Sāriputta. This is the connection [of the verse].

261. Thus, having pleased the Fully Enlightened One—the Gotama by virtue of belonging to the Gotama clan, the eldest in the Sakyan family, and the bull among Sakyans—Sāriputta, being thus possessed of wisdom, performed the pleasing of his heart through the practice of duties, conduct, virtue, and proper behavior;
and having reached the perfection and culmination of the disciple’s knowledge through wisdom, he will become the foremost disciple of that Blessed One—this is the connection.

262. Thus, having attained the position of chief disciple, he will follow the True Dhamma—the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Blessed One, the Son of the Sakyans, which functions through an unshakable nature toward both the desirable and the undesirable, and has been made manifest;
he will maintain it without letting it perish. Shedding rains—that is, pouring forth, teaching, clarifying, and expounding the rains known as the teachings of the Dhamma—[he will do so].
The meaning is that it will proceed by being analyzed and made clear. 263.

The connection is as follows: the Blessed One Gotama, the bull among the Śākyas, having directly known (*abhiññāya*)—that is, having understood all this through specific knowledge (*visesa-ñāṇa*)—will, while seated in the midst of the community of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) within the Saṅgha of monks, establish [the disciple] in the foremost place, in a high position that delights in the entire multitude of qualities such as wisdom.
264. Thus, having received his prediction, he was filled with joy; and through the power of that rapture and joy, uttering an inspired exclamation (*udāna*), he said:
"Ah, what well-performed karma I have done! and so forth. In this context, *aho* is a particle used in the sense of wonder.

Regarding the "well-performed" (*sukata*)—meaning well-done, performed with full faith—in the presence of the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Venerable Anomadassi, it refers to a portion of merit; "aho" expresses amazement.

The meaning is "of inconceivable power. Having performed meritorious deeds as service to that Blessed One, I have reached the perfection—the culmination and the highest limit—regarding the entire multitude of qualities in every respect;
that Blessed One is indeed a source of wonder—this is the connection. 265. *Aparimeyye* means in a time exceeding all calculation;
*kataṃ kusalakammaṃ* means wholesome karma performed; *me* means by me; *idha* means in this [world].
In his final existence, he manifested the fruit of that result. "Sumutto" means well-liberated; "suṭṭhu vimutto" means thoroughly liberated.
Just as the speed of an arrow shot by a skilled archer [is checked], I have, by the fruit of that merit, burnt away and caused the defilements to be burnt away—this is the meaning.
(266) Displaying his own energy, he spoke the verse beginning with "asaṅkhataṃ. Therein, "asaṅkhataṃ" means not conditioned (*na saṅkhataṃ*).
The meaning is: "It has not been made by the coming together of conditions.

Seeking and searching for that unconditioned Nibbāna—the immovable because of the absence of the turbidity of defilements, and the "footing" (pada) in the sense of being a foundation for those who have completed their provisions—one investigates and examines all the various sectarians, all the founders of sects, and all individuals who give rise to wrong views, thinking: "Is this it? Is this it? (esāhaṃ eso ahaṃ bhave).
The connection [of the verse] is: "I have wandered and transmigrated through existence, beginning with the realm of sensual desire" (kāmabhava).
267–8. To reveal his own intention, he said: "Just as a man afflicted by disease," and so forth.
Therein, "afflicted" (byādhitō) means a person (posō), a man, oppressed by illness; "just as he would seek medicine, so did I [seek] the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) and deathless (amata)."

The connection is as follows: seeking the state of Nibbāna, throughout five hundred successive births, in five hundred individual existences, I went forth into the ascetic life without interruption, without break, and without interval. 271.
"I wandered at Kutittha" means that I wandered along a lowly ford, that is, on a path for crossing over.
272. "A man seeking essence, a person searching for substance": having cut down the plantain tree (*kadali*), he would split it open—he would cut the trunk of the plantain tree and split it in two.

"He would not find essence therein" means that even after splitting it, he would not find or obtain any essence within that plantain trunk; the connection is that this man is devoid of essence, empty.

273. Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is void and empty of pith, even so the many people among the world’s sectarians who follow various views are void and empty of the unconditioned Nibbāna; this is the connection [of the verse]. *Seti* is merely a particle. 274.
In my final existence, at the conclusion of my births, I was born into a brahmin family as a "brahmin-kinsman" (*brahmabandhu*);
such is the meaning. "Having abandoned great wealth" means having cast away a vast mass of possessions like a globule of spittle.
"I went forth into the homeless life"—the meaning is that I undertook the ascetic renunciation which is devoid of such activities as agriculture and trade.
The commentary on the first section of recitation is finished.
275–7. "A reciter... [up to] ...the sage absorbed in silence": "silence" (*mona*) is said to be knowledge; he was endowed with that silence.
"Muni" means that his mind is properly placed, established, and concentrated in that silence (mone). He is called "Nāga" because he does not commit evil characterized by agitation;
this refers to the Elder Assaji. The meaning is that he shines like a great Nāga, like a lotus flower that is well-blossomed and fully opened.
278–281. “Having seen me... [etc. ...to ask about the state of the deathless” is of plain meaning.
282. “In the middle of the street”: the connection is that having approached—that is, having reached and come near—that elder who had arrived in the middle of the street, I asked.
284. “Of what sort are you, O Great Hero?”: regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma for the first time among all the disciples, both women and men, among the Arahants.

"O Great Hero who has attained Arahatship, O one of great fame due to the abundance of your attendant followers who have followed you—what is the nature of your Buddha’s *sāsana*, that is to say, the Dhamma known as the teaching of the Dhamma? This is the connection.
'O gentle-faced one, tell me, speak to me; it is well and auspicious for me,' is the meaning."
285. Then, demonstrating the manner in which he had spoken, he said to me, "When questioned by me," and so forth. Therein, "he" refers to the Elder Assaji;
"when questioned by me" means that when I asked, "What is the nature of the Teaching? he related the entire account.

The whole Teaching is profound due to the profundity of the Suttas, and it is profound due to the profundity of the teaching, the penetration of the Dhamma, and the manifestation of the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), and so on.

The connection is as follows: *nipuṇaṃ padaṃ* (the subtle state) refers to Nibbāna, which is the slayer of the arrow of craving, the destroyer, the remover of all the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and that which brings about its exhaustion; this is the *dhamma*. 286.
Showing the manner in which it was spoken by him, he said, "Those *dhammas*," and so forth. *Hetuppabhavā* means originating from a cause, from a reason.

The connection is as follows: those phenomena (dhammas) which have arisen, been born, come to be, fully produced, manifested, and fully brought forth—those phenomena which possess conditions, which have intrinsic nature (sabhāva), and which exist, are found, and are apprehended.
Of those phenomena, the Tathāgata has spoken, he has declared, their cause and reason;
and also their cessation—that is, the cessation of those causal phenomena, their nature of ceasing.

"One who speaks thus is a Great Recluse" (evaṃvādī mahāsamaṇo): because of the greatness of his retinue of qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and because he has stilled evil and destroyed evil, the Blessed One is a "Great Recluse. "One who speaks thus" means one whose nature is to speak of the pacification of causes and so forth; this is the meaning. 287.
Then, having heard the Dhamma thus spoken, [the interlocutor] spoke the verse beginning with "They shine," etc., showing the manner in which he himself had directly realized it. That is self-evident.

289. "This very Dhamma, 'if only this much'": even if there is nothing beyond this, this alone is the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) that is to be attained. Thus, the meaning is: "This very Dhamma.
You have realized and penetrated the sorrowless state, Nibbāna. Indeed, for us, this state has passed away, unseen for many millions of eons.

290. “I who was seeking the Dhamma” means: I, while seeking and searching for the Dhamma—the state of peace—wandered and roamed about at evil fords, wretched fords, and censurable fords. “That goal has been attained by me” means:
that goal which was to be sought has been reached and attained by me; now, however, for me...
The meaning is: "It is time to be non-negligent; it is time to be diligent. (291) The meaning is:

"Satisfied and filled with joy by the elder Assaji, having reached and attained the unshakable and immovable state of Nibbāna, I went to the hermitage seeking and searching for my companion, the young man Kolita.
(292) "Having seen me from afar" means: having seen me as I was approaching from a distance away from the hermitage, [he who was] well-trained...
"My companion," meaning one who is endowed with and possessed of the modes of conduct such as standing and sitting, "spoke"—that is, he said—the following words which are about to be stated. 293.
"O companion, you have a serene face and eyes; your face and eyes are serene, beautiful, and radiant."
"You are endowed [with these qualities]. A sage-like state is seen and discerned in you. Being thus, you have attained the Deathless;
you have reached *nibbāna*, which is deathless. I ask: 'Have you indeed attained, or will you attain, the deathless state of *nibbāna*?'—this is the meaning.
(294) 'You come in a form corresponding to beauty' means that you come, having assumed a form corresponding to beauty, a clear and radiant complexion."
"Like one made immovable": like an elephant made immovable by spears and other weapons, or like a well-trained tusker after three months of training, because he has cast out evil;
O Brahmin, one who is tamed and disciplined, whose training is complete, and who is stilled in the state of Nibbāna—thus he asked.
(295) Being questioned by him, the Blessed One said, "I have attained the Deathless," and so forth. The meaning of that is plain.
299. "One whose intention is unfulfilled" means one whose intention has not reached the culmination of the aspiration thus prayed for: "May I become the chief disciple of a certain future Buddha.
I wandered and roamed along a path where it was improper to go, namely, at a narrow ford (*kutittha*).
O Venerable Gotama, Foremost One in the World, having come into and attained the sight of you, my intention—that is, my aspiration—[is fulfilled].
The intention is that it is "filled" by the attainment of the path of Arahatship and "perfected" by reaching the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). 300.
"Established upon the earth": having arisen upon the earth, they bloom and open at the proper time during the winter season;
possessing divine fragrance, they are sweet-smelling and waft forth most excellently, delighting all living beings—both gods and humans.
"Just as they act while possessed of joy,
so too, O Great Hero— O you who possess great prowess, born of the Śākya clan, and surrounded by a great retinue— having established myself in your teaching,
I shall establish myself [therein] and wait for the time and opportunity to blossom, to open out through the knowledge of the path to Arahatship."
The connection is: "I seek, I search for, in that very way.

(302) "Seeking the flower of liberation" means seeking and searching for the flower known as the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship—either because it is liberated from or because it effects liberation from all defilements—and specifically that which brings release from the cycle of existence (*bhava-saṃsāra*), the wandering through existences such as the realm of sensual desire (*kāma-bhava*).
Going is the wandering in existence (*bhava-saṃsāra*); liberation from that is "liberation from the wandering in existence" (*bhava-saṃsāra-mocana*).

Regarding the phrase "by the attainment of the flower of liberation": liberation is so called because it liberates, or because by means of it those who have completed the necessary equipment are liberated; it is the supreme fruit (*agga-phala*). It is called a "flower" (*puppha*) because by means of it those to be trained (*veneyya*) blossom or expand.
Liberation itself is the flower; thus, it is the "flower of liberation. Attainment is "attaining" (*lābha*); [it refers to] the attainment of the flower of liberation.

"Gain" is the gain of the flower of liberation (*vimuttipuppha*). By means of that attainment of the gain of the flower of liberation, "I satisfy all breathing things and all beings"—the meaning is that I cause them to experience joy.

Regarding the passage beginning with "As far as the Buddha-field," O Visionary One (*cakkhumā*), you are possessed of vision by means of the five kinds of vision; to whatever extent... [the field extends].
In such places, the power and efficacy of protective charms (paritta) such as the Ratana-sutta prevail;

however, within that entire Buddha-field consisting of hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷa), with the exception of the Great Sage, the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), among all other beings, there is no one else who is equal to or like your son in wisdom—this is the connection [of the text]. The rest is self-evident.

308. "Those who have entered the path" refers to those possessing the four paths, those established in the fruit—namely the noble learners (sekha) abiding in the fruit of arhatship—and those endowed with the three lower fruits;
these eight types of noble bhikkhus, longing for and seeking the supreme goal, Nibbāna, always surround it—meaning they serve, resort to, and attend upon it at all times—possessing wisdom.

310. You shine like the moon, the king of stars, being devoted to and intent upon the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment—beginning with the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor—which consist of the four foundations of mindfulness known as the contemplation of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, and which are skillful and expert. 315.
That which bears trees, mountains, jewels, sentient beings, and so forth is the "earth" (dharaṇī). [Those things] grown, produced, and increased upon that earth are "earth-born" (dharaṇiruhā).
And "dharaṇīruhā" refers to trees. Having taken root in the earth, they grow, increase, reach maturity, and attain full development;
those trees, in due course, manifest fruit and become bearers of fruit.
317–9. Furthermore, praising the Blessed One alone, he spoke the verse beginning with “The Sindhu and the Sarassatī.
In this context, the rivers named Sindhu, Gaṅgā, Sarassatī, Nandiyagaṅgā, Candabhāgāgaṅgā, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarabhū, and Mahī are those that flow. Of these flowing [rivers]...
Just as the ocean alone receives, accepts, and holds these Ganges rivers as they flow toward it,
so too at that time all these Ganges rivers abandon and cast off their former names and designations— such as Sindhū, Vidiśā, Gaṅgā, and so forth—
and become known and manifest only as "the ocean," just as the ocean is indeed called "the ocean. In the same way...
In the same way, these four castes— known as the Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—
having gone forth in your presence, in your vicinity, wearing the received saffron robes, and attending upon you, they abandon and relinquish their former names,
such as "Khattiya" and so forth, which are conventional designations; they become "sons of the Buddha," the legitimate offspring of the Buddha.
They would become manifest according to the proper method. 320–4.
The moon, being free from the five defilements—namely, clouds, mist, dust, smoke, and Rāhu—is stainless, devoid of impurity, and immaculate;
moving through the womb of space within the element of space, it outshines all the hosts of stars.
Just as one who overcomes the world with radiance shines and glows intensely, so too are you... [as before] ...325-7.

Just as many water-born lotuses and mandārava flowers, though born in the water and grown in the water, are smeared and adhered to by the water, the mud, and the silt; even so are many beings, immeasurable in number.
Beings born and raised in the world, tormented and bound by passion and hatred, grow up in a state of distress.
Just as a white water-lily (*kumuda*) grows and is produced in the mud, so it is with the lotus (*kesarī*).
[This occurs] in the month of *Rammaka*, that is, the month of *Kattika*, because it is said, "on the full moon day of the fourth month. The "water-born" refers to lotus flowers and the like.
Many flowers bloom and blossom; they do not pass beyond that month, namely the month of Kattika—this is the connection.
"The time for their blooming is that" means that the month of Kattika is the time or season for blooming and blossoming.
Just as those flowers bloom, even so, O Son of the Sakyans, you have blossomed and are in full bloom. You have blossomed...

"Those [who have blossomed] through liberation": those disciples of yours, monks who have completed the necessary preparations, have blossomed—that is, they have fully opened—through liberation, which is the knowledge of the fruit of Arahatship.
Just as a water-born lotus does not exceed its time for flowering, so too they do not overstep, that is, they do not go beyond, your teaching, advice, and instruction; this is the meaning.
333-4. Just as the mountain Himavā—meaning the mountain range consisting of rock—is the medicine for all living beings, possessing medicinal herbs for all creatures afflicted by disease;

and just as it is the abode and dwelling place for all *nāgas*, all *asuras*, and all *devas*, even so, O Great Hero, you are the medicine for all living beings because of your liberation from old age, sickness, death, and the like.

Just as that Himālaya is the abode of the *nāgas* and others, so too you have reached and attained the perfection and culmination of the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*), the sixfold direct knowledge (*chaḷabhiññā*), and supernormal power (*iddhi*); they dwell depending upon you—this is the connection [between the verses].
Whether by way of the preceding or the following, the method of connecting the verses through the relationship of simile and subject of the simile is indeed easy to understand.

342. "Having known the underlying tendency (āsaya) and the latent disposition (anusaya)": here, *āsaya* means inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) or temperament (*cariyā*), while *anusaya* means a firmly rooted defilement (*thāmagata-kilesa*).

The meaning is: having known the underlying tendency and the latent disposition—that is, the manifestation of defilements—by way of [distinguishing] "this one is of a lustful temperament," "this one is of a hateful temperament," "this one is of a deluded temperament," and so forth;

and [having known] the strength and weakness of the faculties (*indriya*), that is, the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*), such as [knowing] "this one has sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriyo*).
"Having understood their strength and weakness thus— whether one has dull faculties or keen faculties, a good disposition or a bad disposition, is easy to instruct or difficult to instruct—
and having known who is capable and who is incapable, [thinking] 'This person is capable and able to penetrate the Dhamma taught by me;
this person is incapable,' you, O Blessed One, the Omniscient One, are like a great cloud over the four continents."
With the lion’s roar of the teaching of the Dhamma, you thunder with a fearless cry, making the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) resound with a single voice.
343–4. "As far as the limits of the world-system" means that the assembly might be seated, filling the interior of the world-system on all sides.
Seated thus, they—holding various views and diverse opinions—dispute, having fallen into doubt and contention.
To cut through their doubt and for the purpose of severing their poor understanding,

you— O Sage, skilled in similes and expert in both the simile and the thing illustrated— having known the minds and perceived the mental movements of all beings, even while speaking a single question,
dispelled with that very same discourse on the question the doubt and uncertainty of all living beings seated within the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa.
"It makes one free from doubt" is the meaning of "chindasi.
(345) Regarding the phrase "upadisasadiseheva": here, *upadisā* refers to moss, because it is seen—that is, made manifest—upon the water.
Those who are similar to *upadisā* are "upadisasadisa," namely, human beings. For just as the *upadisā* moss [makes] the water invisible...
Having done so, they stood spread out over it; likewise, the earth— the world—
would be filled with those men standing packed together like the very tips of the hairs, all of them covering the earth and standing with palms joined,
holding their hands in *añjali* at their heads, praising the Leader of the World before the Leader of the World.
They might speak of the Buddha’s virtues.
Even if all those gods and humans were to praise him for an entire eon, extolling his virtues through various colors and diverse aspects,
they still would not be able to measure or fully describe the extent of his qualities.
They would fail to reach it, they would not succeed. The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is immeasurable and his excellence of qualities is boundless.
By this, he illuminates the greatness of his virtues. 347.
By his own power, by his own strength—referring to the relationship between the lower comparison and the object compared—the Conqueror (Jina), who has conquered the defilements, is the Buddha.

The meaning is: just as I have praised and extolled him, even if all gods and humans were to praise and celebrate him for ten million eons (*kappakoṭi*) or even a hundred times ten million eons, they would speak [of his qualities] in exactly that same way.
(348) Furthermore, in order to illustrate the immeasurability of his virtues, he said: "If some god... and so forth. "He might drag away what has been filled" means...
One might draw out water from the great ocean filled with water on all sides; the meaning is that such a person would meet only with exhaustion and suffering.
"I maintain the teaching of the Victor" means that I maintain, promote, and protect the entirety of the Three Pitakas spoken by the Victor.
"General of the Dhamma" means [one who leads] by means of the Dhamma, that is, by wisdom, for the sake of the Blessed One’s fourfold assembly.
"Because he strove for the sake of the assembly, he is the Dhamma-Senāpati (General of the Dhamma).

The meaning is that, in the dispensation of the Blessed One, the Son of the Sakyans, during this present time, he protects the entire Buddha-sāsana like the eldest son of a universal monarch (cakkavatti-rāja).
352–3. Showing his own wandering through *saṃsāra*, he said, "Whatever man bears the burden," and so forth. Whoever...
Suppose a man, a human being, were to place a burden, a load upon his head, and carry it;
for all time, that man would be pained, oppressed, and overwhelmed by that burden. The burden is "borne," meaning it is carried, excessively carried.
In that same manner, I [am overwhelmed] by the three fires known as the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
The connection is as follows: "Being burned by fires, like one who has been dragged up a mountain"—meaning having been dragged up, lifted, and placed upon the head of Mount Mahāmeru;

"burdened," meaning burdened by the weight of existence (*bhava*), that is, the weight of arising in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); "oppressed," meaning I wandered and roamed through various states of existence.
354. "The burden has been laid down by me": from this time forth, from the moment of my going forth, that burden of existence has been laid down and set aside by me.
"Existence has been shattered by me": all nine types of existence have been destroyed by me.

That which was to be done, that which was to be accomplished in the teaching of the Blessed One, the Sakyan Son—namely, the work of destroying the defilements through the successive stages of the path—has been performed.
The meaning is: "Whatever exists, all that was done by me.
(355) Again, demonstrating his own distinction, he said, "As far as the Buddha-field," and so forth.

In that context, "as far as" (*yāvatā*) means within the extent of the Buddha-field, which consists of ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*); [therein] the Bull of the Sakyans, the eldest-born of the Sakyan clan...
This demonstrates that, with the exception of the Blessed One, there is no one among the remaining beings who is my equal in wisdom.
Therefore he said: "I am the foremost in wisdom; my peer is not to be found.
(356) Again, manifesting his own power, he spoke the verse beginning with "In concentration," and so forth. That is indeed easy to understand.

360. "One who quickly attains the jhānas and liberations" means one who swiftly reaches and quickly obtains the eight supramundane liberations—which are designated as "liberations" because the jhānas, beginning with the first, liberate one from the world. 362.
Thus, demonstrating his own great reverence and esteem for his fellow celibates despite his own great power, he said: "Free from arrogance and impurity," and so forth.
Therein, like a snake whose venom has been removed or a bull whose horns have been cut off,
I now approach and draw near to the assembly in the presence of the Saṅgha with heavy reverence,
earnest respect, and great esteem, having laid aside pride and arrogance and having cast away the conceit of lineage and the like.
363. Now, demonstrating the greatness of his own wisdom, he said, "If it were of such a form," and so forth.

The intention is this: "If my great wisdom, which is actually formless (*arūpinī*), were to possess form (*rūpinī*), then it would equal—that is, be the same as—the wisdom of those lords of wealth, the kings who rule over the earth. Having thus shown the magnitude of his own wisdom, [he continues].
Then, having recollected his former karma by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), he spoke the words beginning with "Anomadassī.
In that context, the meaning is: "This greatness of my wisdom is the fruit of the praise of knowledge (*ñāṇathomanā*) offered by me to the Blessed One Anomadassī.
Regarding the phrase "the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion" (*pavattitaṃ dhammacakkaṃ*): here, this word *cakkra* (wheel) is used in such expressions as "a four-wheeled carriage" (*catucakkayānaṃ*).

It occurs in the sense of a vehicle in such passages as “The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Blessed One. It occurs in the sense of teaching in such passages as “Set the wheel in motion for all living beings.
It occurs in the sense of meritorious action consisting of giving in such passages as “He sets the wheel in motion day and night.

It occurs in the sense of bodily posture in such passages as “The wheel revolves upon the head of the man overcome by desire. And it occurs in the sense of a razor-wheel in such passages as “The king...”
In such passages as "a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī) who turns by the power of the wheel," it refers to the jewel-wheel (*ratana-cakka*).

But here, in this teaching, I correctly and without error follow and turn the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*)—comprising the three baskets (*piṭaka-ttaya*)—which was set in motion and taught by the Sakyan son, the Fully Awakened One Gotama, who is "Such" (*tādi*) and endowed with the qualities of one who is "Such. I teach the teaching.

"I perform. The connection is as follows: having followed this "conformity" (*anuvattana*) taught [in the previous verse], the subsequent teaching bears fruit through the praise of the knowledge (*ñāṇathomanā*) performed for the former Buddhas.

(365) Then, showing the fruit of merit consisting of reliance upon true persons (*sappurisūpanissaya*), appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and so forth, he said: "May I never have evil desires," and so on.
In this context, a person who is "one of evil desires" (pāpiccha)—possessing base desires; a person who is "of evil conduct" (pāpacārī);

one who is "lazy" (kusīta) in performing duties and services while standing, sitting, and so forth; one who is "weak in energy" (hīnavīriya) regarding the cultivation of meditative absorption, concentration, the Path, and so on; one who is "of little learning" (appassuta) due to being devoid of the burden of study and the burden of insight;
and one who is "of bad conduct" (anācāra) due to being devoid of proper behavior toward teachers, preceptors, and others—such a person at some time...
"In some place, may there not be one who has met or come together with me"—this is the connection [of the verse]. 366.
"One of great learning" (*bahussuta*) refers to a person who is learned in two ways: by way of mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and by way of penetration (*paṭivedha*).

"Wise" (*medhāvī*) means endowed with intelligence (*medhā*), that is, wisdom (*paññā*). "Well-composed in the precepts" (*sīlesu susamāhita*) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), virtue associated with the path, the eightfold Uposatha precepts, and so forth.
"Suṭṭhu āhito ṭhapitacitto ca": one whose mind is well-placed and established. "Cetosamathānuyutto": a person devoted to the unification of the mind.
"Api muddhani tiṭṭhatu": let such a person stand even upon my head; the meaning is "let him stand even on my crown.
(367) Having stated the benefit of the fruit attained by himself, he says "taṃ vo vadāmi bhaddante" and so forth, enjoining others therein. That is indeed easy to understand.

368–9. When I first saw the Elder Assaji at the beginning, he who struck [the path] for me—because of his attainment of the path of stream-entry, he had become stainless and free from impurity through the abandoning of defilements such as the view of a self-body—that Elder Assaji was my teacher, the instructor in the training of the supramundane Dhamma.
It was by his instruction that I heard [the Dhamma].
Today I am the Dhammasenāpati. Having reached perfection in all qualities and attained the ultimate goal, I dwell free from taints and devoid of defilements.
(370) Demonstrating his reverence for his own teacher, he said, "He who was my teacher," and so forth. This refers to the Elder named Assaji.
"The Teacher’s disciple was my teacher; that elder dwells in whichever direction, in whichever quarter—that direction I place upon the crown of my head, above my very skull. This is the connection.
Then, showing the fact of having attained his own high station, he said, "My work," and so forth. [This refers to] the Blessed One Gotama.

The connection is as follows: the Bull of the Sakyas, the Banner of the Sakya clan, having remembered and known my past deeds through his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, established me in the foremost position, the position of the chief disciple. 374.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
These are the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and their classification is explained in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* itself.

Furthermore, by way of the four paths and four fruits, or by way of the form and formless meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the eight liberations (*vimokkha*)—which are qualities that liberate one from the cycle of existence—and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) beginning with the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhā*) have been realized and made manifest. Thus, "the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Regarding the Buddha:
The meaning is that the instruction—known as the teaching consisting of exhortation—has been accomplished, brought to completion by means of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship.
Regarding the phrase *itthaṃ sudaṃ*: here, *itthaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of indication, meaning "in this manner.
By this, he indicates the entire *Sāriputtāpadāna*. *Sudaṃ* is a particle used for the purpose of completing the metrical foot. *Āyasmā* is a term of great respect.
"Sāriputta" is the name given to the Elder by way of his mother's name.

"These verses" means he spoke and recited these entire verses of the *Sāriputtattherāpadāna*. The word "iti" is a particle used in the sense of completion; the meaning is that the entire *Sāriputtāpadāna* is finished.
The commentary on the *Sāriputtattheraapadāna* is complete.
3–2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Moggallāna begins with the words “The Blessed One Anomadassī...”.

This elder had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; having accumulated there, in various states of existence, the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the turning away from rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), [he was born] under Anomadassī...
The passage beginning with "At the time of the Blessed One" and so forth has already been told in the account of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.

For on the seventh day after his going forth, while the Elder was practicing the duties of a recluse near the village of Kallavāla in the kingdom of Magadha, as dullness and drowsiness were descending upon him, the Teacher said: "Moggallāna, let not your bowl be empty."
Being thus stirred by the words beginning with "Exertion," the Venerable One dispelled sloth and torpor;

while listening to the meditation subject on the elements as it was being taught by the Blessed One, he attained the three higher paths through the sequence of insight and reached the pinnacle of disciple-knowledge at the moment of the supreme fruit (arahantship).
Having thus attained the status of a second chief disciple, the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna [related] his own past karma:
Having recollected [this], and proclaiming his former conduct (*pubbacariyā*) by way of joy (*somanassa*), he spoke the words beginning with "The Blessed One Anomadassī.
In this context, he is called *Anomadassī* because his vision (*dassana*)—his seeing—is not inferior (*anomam*, i.e., not base).

For, because his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), even those who gazed upon him for an entire day, an entire month, an entire year, or even a hundred thousand years, [could never tire of it].
Because his appearance brings no satiety to gods and humans, or because he is one whose nature is to see the peerless, incomparable Nibbāna, he is named Anomadassī.

By reason of his good fortune and other such qualities, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā). He is the "Elder of the World" (Lokajeṭṭha), meaning the eldest and most preeminent among the entire world of beings.
Because he resembles a bull (āsabha), he is a bull; a bull among men is a "man-bull" (narāsabha). He is that Elder of the World, the man-bull.
The Blessed One Anomadassi was honored by the host of devas and surrounded by the assembly of devas; he dwelt in the Himalayas—this is the connection.

376. When he made his aspiration for the second time toward the state of being a second disciple, the meaning is that he was reborn as a king of nāgas named Varuṇa. Therefore it was said: "Varuṇa by name, a king of nāgas..."

"At that time, I... "Capable of assuming any form at will" (*kāmarūpī*) means one whose nature is to create whatever forms one desires. "I transformed myself" (*vikubbāmi*) means I performed various miraculous transformations.

Regarding "the great ocean-dwelling ones": among these—namely, the *mañjerika* nāgas, the earth-dwelling nāgas, the mountain-dwelling nāgas, the Ganges-flowing nāgas, and the oceanic nāgas—I was an oceanic nāga in the great ocean.
"I dwelt" means "I made my residence. 377.
"Having left the assembly, having abandoned the group" means having left behind one's own constant retinue, that host of *nāgas*, and being without them.
"Let the music be struck up" means "I had the music struck up," that is, I had it played.
"Surrounding the Fully Enlightened One" means that the celestial nymphs and Naga maidens, attending upon the Buddha Anomadassi from all sides, played divine instruments;
they sang with songs and verses, and they performed in accordance with what was appropriate—this is the meaning.
"While the musical instruments were being played" means while the fivefold human and Naga instruments were being sounded. The gods [played] the instruments...
The gods of the Four Great Kings struck divine musical instruments; "struck" means they played them.

"Having heard the sound of both" means having heard the sound of the drums from both the gods and the humans. Although the Buddha is equal to the Teacher of the Three Worlds, he "awoke"—that is to say, he knew and he heard.
