379. Having invited the Fully Awakened One together with the community of disciples—having invited the Fully Awakened One for the following day and surrounded him—I approached my own abode, the Nāga realm.
And having gone there, "having prepared a seat" means having arranged and adorned the places for standing at night and by day, the inner chambers, the pavilions, the couches, and the sitting areas.
"I announced the time" means that I, having thus performed the preliminary rites, said, "The time has come."
"Venerable sir, the meal is ready," I announced the time and made my request. 380. "Surrounded by a thousand whose taints were destroyed":
the meaning is that at that time the Blessed One, the Leader of the World, having arrived, approached my residence while illuminating all directions, accompanied by a thousand Arahants.

381. Showing the Blessed One taking his seat in the manner of eating as he entered his own residence, [the poet] spoke the verse beginning with "The Great Hero who had entered. That is indeed easy to understand.

386. "Born in the lineage of Okkāka" means that a teacher named Gotama will appear in the world of humans—one born in the royal dynasty descended from King Okkāka, or one born in a royal family renowned throughout all of Jambudīpa—by virtue of his clan (*gotra*) and through his lineage.

388. "Having later gone forth" means that this Nāga king, subsequently urged and impelled by the roots of merit and the accumulation of merit from his final existence, will go forth in the Dispensation and become the second chief disciple of the Blessed One Gotama; thus did he give this prophecy.

389. "One of aroused energy" means one who possesses energy in the postures such as standing, sitting, and so forth. "One with a resolute mind" means one whose consciousness is directed toward Nibbāna.

"One who has reached the perfection of psychic power" refers to [the powers] such as the psychic power of resolve, the psychic power of transformation, the psychic power of action-result, and so on, [regarding whom it was said]: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus possessing psychic power, namely Mahāmoggallāna."
He has reached and attained the ultimate limit (pāramiṃ). Regarding "all taints" (sabba-āsava):

because they flow (savana) and proceed from all sides (ā), these phenomena—consisting of sensual desire, existence, views, and ignorance—which have received the name "taints," he has fully understood (pariññāya), known them completely through final knowledge (aññāya), abandoned them, and is thus without taints (anāsava) and free from defilement (nikkilesa).

"He will attain extinction" (nibbāyissati) is connected to the meaning that he will attain extinction through the complete extinguishing of the defilements and the aggregates (kilesa-khandha-parinibbāna).

390. Thus the Elder, having stated how he received his prediction of enlightenment through the power of his own merit, spoke the verse beginning with "By relying on evil friends" (*pāpamittopanissāya*) while further explaining his past conduct of evil.
In this context, "by relying on evil friends" means by taking as a support evil, wicked, and base friends;
the sense is that he came into association with them.

In this regard, this is the sequential account: On one occasion, the followers of other sects gathered together and deliberated, saying, "Friends, do you know for what reason such great gain and honor have arisen for the ascetic Gotama?
"We do not know. "But you do not know? "Yes, we do—we know it was by relying on a certain monk named Moggallāna."
He had arisen [in the world]. For having gone to the celestial realm and questioned the deities about their deeds, he would return and tell people:

"By doing such-and-such, they obtain such-and-such prosperity. Having also questioned those reborn in hell about their deeds, he would return and tell people: "By doing such-and-such, they experience such-and-such suffering."
When people heard his words, they brought him great wealth and honor. Thinking, "If we can kill him, that wealth and honor will accrue to us;
there is this means," they all became of one mind and incited their own attendants, saying, "By whatever means necessary, we shall kill him.
Having obtained a thousand kahāpaṇas, they [sent them] to the assassins.
Having summoned their chief, they gave them that thousand pieces of money, saying, "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, dwells on Kāḷasilā; go there and kill him.
Accepting it for the sake of the wealth, the bandits went with the intent, "We shall kill the Elder," and surrounded his dwelling place. The Elder—
Realizing that he was surrounded by them, the Elder slipped out through a keyhole and departed. On that day, the thieves did not see the Elder;
however, on another day, they surrounded his dwelling place once more. Knowing this, the Elder broke through the circular window and leapt into the air.
In this manner, they were unable to capture the Elder during the first month, nor even during the middle month.
They were unable [to move him]. But when the last month arrived, the Elder, knowing that the force of his own past karma was drawing him back, did not depart.
As the robbers struck him, they shattered his bones until they were reduced to the size of grains of rice.
Then, perceiving him to be dead, they threw him onto the back of a bush and went away.
The Elder thought, “Having seen and paid homage to the Teacher, I shall attain final Nibbāna.
Wrapping his physical body in the shroud of jhāna, he went through the air into the presence of the Teacher. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said, “Venerable Sir, I shall attain final Nibbāna.
“Will you attain final Nibbāna, Moggallāna? “Yes, Venerable Sir. “Where will you go to attain final Nibbāna?”
“Venerable sir, to the region of Kāḷasilā. “In that case, Moggallāna, go after preaching the Dhamma to me.
For now, there is no more seeing of such a disciple as I have.
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he rose into the air and, like the Elder Sāriputta on the day of his Parinibbāna, performed various kinds of [miracles].
Having performed miracles and preached the Dhamma, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he went to the site of Kāḷasīla and attained final Nibbāna.
The report, "It is said that bandits killed the Elder," spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
King Ajātasattu dispatched secret agents for the purpose of searching for the bandits. Among those bandits, at a drinking bout, [one drank] liquor...
While they were drinking and getting intoxicated, one struck another on the back and knocked him down. The latter, threatening him, said:
"Hey, you ill-behaved man! Why did you strike me on the back and knock me down?
But what about it, you wicked thief—was not the Elder Mahāmoggallāna struck by you first? "How so? Was I the one who struck him first?"
"Do you not know? When the king had heard these men saying, "I struck him!
I struck him!", those secret agents seized all those thieves and reported it to the king. The king summoned those thieves and asked, "Was the elder killed by you?
"Yes, Your Majesty. "By whom were you incited? "By naked ascetics, Your Majesty."

The king had five hundred naked ascetics seized, and together with five hundred thieves, he had them buried up to their navels in pits in the royal courtyard, covered them with straw, and set fire to them.
Then, knowing them to be burnt to death, he had them ploughed with iron ploughs and had all of them cut into pieces. At that time, the monks were in the Dhamma hall...
How did they raise the discussion? "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna has met with a death that is unworthy of himself.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?
and they replied, "For this one, venerable sir," he said, "Monks, for Moggallāna, even this very body was unworthy of such a death."
"However, it is merely in accordance with the karma he performed in the past," he said. When asked, "But what, venerable sir, was his past karma? he related it in detail:
"In the past, monks, in Bārāṇasī, a certain son of good family was personally performing the work of pounding, cooking, and so forth for his mother and father."
He looked after it. Then his parents said, "Dear son, you are wearying yourself by doing the work alone both at home and in the forest;

we shall bring a young woman for you. Although he refused, saying, "Mother and father, as long as you live, I will serve you with my own hands," they repeatedly entreated him and brought a young woman for him.
After attending upon them for only a few days, she later refused even to see them, complaining,
"It is not possible to live in one place with your mother and father. When he would not accept her words,
she took pieces of bark-cloth and froth from rice-gruel and scattered them here and there while he was away.
When she returned and was asked, "What is this?", she replied, "This is the work of these old, blind people;
they wander about making the entire house filthy, and it is impossible to live in one place with them.
As she spoke thus again and again, even such a being who had fulfilled the perfections was separated from his parents.
Thinking, "Very well, I shall know what action must be taken against them," he fed them and said, "Mother and father, your relatives are waiting for your arrival at such-and-such a place;
let us go there. Having placed them on a carriage and set out with them, when they reached the middle of a forest, he said, "Father, take the reins; the oxen will move by the sign of the whip."
"Thieves dwell in this place; I shall dismount and go about," he said, and handing the reins to his father, he dismounted and went on.
Changing his voice, he made the sound of thieves rising up.
Hearing the noise, the parents, thinking "the thieves have risen up," said, "Dear son, the thieves have risen up! We are old; you must protect yourself!"
They said: "Even while his parents were crying out, he made the sound of a thief, beat them, killed them, threw them into the wilderness, and returned.

The Teacher, having related this past deed of his, said: "Monks, after Moggallāna had performed such karma and been boiled in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remainder of that very same karma, in as many as a hundred births..."
Having been pounded and crushed to pieces, he met his death; thus Moggallāna received a death that was exactly in accordance with his own karma.
Together with the five hundred thieves, the five hundred heretics also defiled my blameless son and received a death that was likewise appropriate.
For one who offends against those who have not offended is subject to ten consequences.
“Indeed, he meets with ruin and disaster. Having thus established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
“He who, with a staff, strikes those who are unarmed, or harms those who are innocent, will swiftly fall into one of ten states.”
“One may experience harsh feelings, the breaking apart of the body,
or even a severe affliction, or one may fall into a state of mental derangement.
Or one may encounter a calamity from a king, or a terrible false accusation.”
“Like the destruction of kinsmen, or the ruin of wealth,
so too his houses are consumed by fire;
at the breaking up of the body, that one of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.”
"Devoted to solitude" (*pavivekamanuyutto*) means being devoted to, engaged in, and properly applied to solitude in the sense of being one-pointed.
"Delighting in the cultivation of concentration" (*samādhibhāvanārato*) means being fond of and attached to the cultivation of the first jhāna and so forth. The connection is:

"Having fully understood—that is, having known and abandoned—all taints, which is to say all defilements, I dwell taintless and free from defilement. (*sabbāsave* = *sakalakilese*; *pariññāya* = *jānitvā pajahitvā*; *anāsavo* = *nikkileso viharāmi*).
394. Now, demonstrating the fruit of his former conduct by way of his own accumulation of merit, he spoke the verse beginning with “The earth, so very deep.
Herein, this is the sequential narrative: “Urged on by the Buddha” means urged and dispatched by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“While the community of monks looked on” means while the great assembly of monks was watching. [He struck] the Palace of Migāra’s Mother with his big toe...
At the Eastern Park, he caused the great palace built by the female lay devotee Visākhā—which was adorned with a thousand pillars—to tremble with his big toe.

For on one occasion, while the Blessed One was dwelling in that aforementioned palace at the Eastern Park, many junior bhikkhus were sitting on the upper floor of the palace; without even considering the Teacher, they [were engaged in idle talk].

They began to engage in frivolous talk. Hearing this, the Blessed One, wishing to stir them up and make them fit vessels for his own teaching of the Dhamma, addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera:
“Moggallāna, do you see these new bhikkhus intent on frivolous talk? Having heard this, the Thera [perceived] the Teacher’s intention.
Having understood this, he attained the fourth jhāna based on the water-kasiṇa as its object;
then, emerging from that state, he resolved: "Let there be water in the place where the palace stands.
He struck the pinnacle at the top of the palace with his big toe, and the palace tilted and stood on one side. He struck it again, and it stood on another side.
Terrified and agitated by the fear that the palace might collapse, those bhikkhus emerged from it and stood near the Blessed One.
The Teacher, observing their disposition, taught them the Dhamma.

Having heard it, some among them were established in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, some in the fruit of non-returning, and some were established in the fruit of arhatship.
This very point is to be illustrated by the *Pāsādakampana-sutta*.
Regarding the "Vejayanta Palace": that Vejayanta Palace in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is ten thousand yojanas in height and adorned with many thousands of turrets and gabled chambers.
It arose when Sakka, the lord of the gods, having conquered the asuras in the battle between the gods and asuras and standing in the middle of the city, was victorious.
The palace named "Vejayantī" was so called because it had arisen [by divine power]; referring to that, he says, "the Vejayanta Palace.

This elder also causes even that to tremble with his big toe. For on one occasion, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Eastern Park, Sakka, the king of the gods, approached him and asked about liberation through the destruction of craving. The Blessed One gave him the answer.
Having heard this, he was satisfied and gladdened; after paying homage and keeping him to his right, he departed for his own celestial realm.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought: "This Sakka approached the Blessed One and asked such a profound question concerning Nibbāna, and the Blessed One has answered that question."
"Did he go having understood, or did he go without understanding? Suppose I were to go to the world of the gods and learn that matter?
He went at once to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and asked Sakka, the lord of the devas, about that matter.
Sakka, being intoxicated by his divine prosperity, made an evasion. The Elder, for the purpose of producing a sense of spiritual urgency in him, [pointed to] the Vejayanta Palace.
He shook it with his big toe. Thus it is said:
“He who, firm in the power of his psychic potency, shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe and stirred the deities.”
This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the *Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta*. The manner of his trembling has already been described above.
The phrase, “He questioned Sakka,” refers specifically to the elder’s inquiry regarding liberation through the destruction of craving as previously stated.
Therefore it was said: “Do you know, friend, [the distinction between] the destruction of craving and liberation? To him, Sakka replied.

This was said with reference to the fact that the Elder, having been moved to spiritual urgency (*saṃviggahadayena*) when the palace shook, abandoned negligence and applied his mind thoroughly (*yoniso manasikaritvā*), thereby answering the question. For he spoke at that time precisely according to the fixed method taught by the Teacher.
Therefore it is said: "When asked the question, [he answered] as it truly is. In that context, "he questioned Sakka" refers to Sakka, the king of the gods.
The Elder Mahāmoggallāna asked whether the liberation through the destruction of craving taught by the Teacher had been correctly grasped.
For here, the present tense is used in the sense of the past. "Do you know, friend? means, "Friend, do you indeed know?
What do you know? "Liberation through the destruction of craving" means that the liberations through the destruction of craving were taught to you by the Teacher.
Likewise, he asks, "What do you know? Or else, he asks for the teaching of the *Taṇhakkhayavimutti* (Liberation through the Destruction of Craving) Sutta.

"Of the Brahmas" means of the Great Brahmas. "In the Sudhammā assembly hall" means in the Sudhammā hall. This Sudhammā hall, however, is in the Brahma-world, not in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There is no such thing as a divine realm devoid of the Sudhammā hall.
"There is none. 'Friend, do you still hold that same view which you held before? There is no ascetic or brahmin capable of reaching this Brahma-world.
Was the view you held prior to the Teacher's arrival here not abandoned even now? Do you see [him] transcending into the Brahma-world?"

"Radiant" means: do you see the space occupied by the Blessed One together with his disciples, who—surrounded by disciples such as Mahākappina and Mahākassapa—had entered the fire-element and was seated in the Brahma-world, having descended from there?
For on one occasion, the Blessed One had gathered and sat down in the Sudhamma assembly hall in the Brahma-world.

While the Brahmā was thinking, "Is there perhaps some ascetic or brahmin of such great psychic power that he would be able to come here?", Mahāmoggallāna, perceiving the Brahmā’s thought, went there and sat in the air above the Brahmā’s head.
Entering the fire-element attainment and emitting radiance, he considered the arrival of Mahāmoggallāna and the others. As soon as he had this thought—

They too went there, paid homage to the Teacher, and having understood the Teacher’s intention, entered the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), sat down in the various directions, and emitted radiance. The entire Brahma-world became one mass of light.
The Teacher, knowing the Brahma’s mind was ready, taught the Dhamma that reveals the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the teaching,
Many thousands of Brahmās were established in the fruits of the path. Addressing him with this in mind, he spoke the verse:
"Even today, friend, that view of yours remains. This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the *Baka-Brahma Sutta*. For it is said:
"On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. By him..."
Now at that time, a certain Brahmā had such an evil view arisen as this:
“There is no ascetic or brahmin who could come here. Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in that Brahmā’s mind, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm, or...
Just as one might extend an arm and then bend it back again, even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he reappeared in that Brahma-world.
Then the Blessed One sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahma, having entered the fire-element.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?”
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
the Blessed One sitting cross-legged in the upper atmosphere above that Brahmā, having attained the fire-element. Having seen him,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [he vanished from Jeta’s Grove and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma-world. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna,
having attained the fire-element, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahma, leaning toward the eastern direction and lower than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling at present?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahākassapa saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged above that Brahmā, having entered the fire-element meditation. Having seen him, just as...
Just as a strong man... [as before] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma-world.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, leaning toward the southern direction, sat cross-legged in the air above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākappina: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling now?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Mahākappina saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s palace, having attained the fire-element meditation. Having seen him, just as...
Just as a strong man... [as before] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma world.

Then the Venerable Mahākappina, leaning toward the western direction, sat cross-legged in the upper atmosphere above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element concentration, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Where is the Blessed One dwelling now?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One seated cross-legged in the upper story of that Brahmā’s palace, having attained the fire-element meditation. Having seen him, just as...
Just as a strong man... [as before] ...even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he appeared in that Brahma-world.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, relying on the northern direction, sat cross-legged in the upper air above that Brahma, having attained the fire-element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that Brahmā in verse:
“Friend, even today you still hold that same view which you held before.
Do you see [the world] transcending it, shining brightly in the Brahma-world?”
“O worthy sir, that view which I formerly held is no longer mine.
I see one who has transcended [the world] and shines radiantly in the Brahma-world;
how then could I now maintain, ‘I am eternal and permanent’?”
Then the Blessed One, having inspired that Brahmā with a sense of urgency—just as a strong man might...
[as before] ...even so, he vanished from that Brahma-world and reappeared in Jeta’s Grove. Then that Brahmā addressed a certain member of his assembly:
“Come, dear sir, go to where the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is; having approached him, [say this:]”

“Please say this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: ‘Is there, dear Moggallāna, any other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great supernormal power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha?
“So be it, dear sir,” replied that member of the Brahma assembly to that Brahmā.
Having heard this, he approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and, having approached him, said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Is there, dear Moggallāna, any other disciples of that Blessed One who possess such great psychic power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha? Then...
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that member of Brahmā’s retinue with this verse:

“Many are the Buddha’s disciples— those who possess the threefold knowledge, those who have attained supernormal powers, those skilled in discerning the minds of others, and the Arhats whose taints are destroyed.”
Then that member of Brahmā’s assembly, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s words,
approached that Brahmā and, having approached him, said this to him: “Venerable sir,
the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna speaks thus:”

“‘There are many disciples of the Buddha who possess the threefold knowledge, have attained supernormal powers, are skilled in understanding the minds of others, and are arahants whose taints are destroyed.
This is what that member of the Brahma’s retinue said. And that Brahmā, being pleased, rejoiced in the words of that member of the Brahma’s retinue.”
With reference to this, it was said: "This matter, however, should be illustrated by the *Baka-brahma Sutta*.
By the phrase "the peak of Mount Mahāmeru," you mean the entire King of Mountains, Sineru, by way of its summit.

"He reclined with liberation" means that he reclined with the support of the liberations of jhāna and the supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*); this is the intended meaning. "The forest" refers to Jambudīpa. He...
Indeed, it is called "forest" (*vana*) because of its abundance of woods. Therefore, he said, "the lord of Jambumaṇḍa. Regarding "of the Pubbavidehas":
the meaning is that both the region of Pubbavideha and the people of Pubbavideha are so called. And as for those humans who dwell on the earth:
"humans who dwell on the earth" refers to the people of Aparagoyāna and Uttarakuru. For they are called "earth-dwellers" (*bhūmisaya*) because they lack houses. These too—
The connection is: "He saw them all. This meaning, however, can be illustrated by the taming of Nanda and Upananda.

It is said that on one occasion, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept almsfood at my home tomorrow with five hundred bhikkhus," and then departed. And on that very day...
At dawn, as the Blessed One was surveying the ten-thousandfold world system, the Naga king named Nandopananda came within the range of his vision.
The Blessed One, reflecting, "This Naga king has come within the range of my vision;
what will become of him? perceived that he possessed the necessary support for taking refuge. Seeing that he was one of wrong view, [the Blessed One thought: "This one..."
"Who indeed could liberate this man of wrong view, who has no faith in the Three Jewels? While reflecting thus, he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, having attended to his bodily needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, announce to five hundred bhikkhus: 'The Tathāgata is going on a journey among the devas.'"

On that very day, they prepared the drinking hall for Nanda and Upananda. Seated upon a divine couch of jewels, with a divine white parasol being held over him, surrounded by the three kinds of dancers and the assembly of nāgas, he sat gazing at the food and drink served in divine vessels.
Then the Blessed One appeared in such a way that the nāga king saw him.
Having done so, he set out toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with five hundred bhikkhus, passing directly over the very summit of that celestial palace.
Now at that time, a wicked and erroneous view had arisen in the Nāga king Nandopananda:
"These shaven-headed ascetics are indeed passing above our abode, the realm of the Tāvatiṃsa gods."
“They enter and they exit; from now on, I will no longer allow them to pass while scattering the dust from their feet upon my head.
Having risen and gone to the foot of Sineru, he abandoned that form, encircled Sineru seven times with his coils, spread his hood over it, and [proceeded] to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Having enveloped him with his hood turned downwards, he made him disappear from sight.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One:
“Previously, Bhante, standing in this place, I saw Sineru, I saw the ridges of Sineru, I saw the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and I saw the Vejayanta palace.”

“I see it! I see the crest of the Vejayanta Palace! But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, that at present I no longer see Sineru... nor do I see the crest of the Vejayanta Palace?
“Raṭṭhapāla, this Nāga king named Nandopananda is angry with you; seven times he has [shaken] Sineru...”
“Having surrounded him with his coils and covered him above with his hood, he stands there having created darkness.

“I shall subdue him, Blessed One,” [said Ānanda]. But the Blessed One did not grant him permission. Then the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Rāhula, and so on, until all the bhikkhus rose up. The Blessed One granted them permission.
At the conclusion, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Venerable Sir, I shall tame him.
"Tame him, Moggallāna," the Blessed One permitted. The Elder, casting off his own form, manifested the great appearance of a royal nāga;
he encircled Nandopananda fourteen times with his coils and placed his own hood upon the tip of the other's hood.
Setting him aside, he pressed him down together with Mount Sineru. The Naga king emitted smoke.
The Elder also thought, "Smoke exists not only in your body; it exists in mine as well," and he too emitted smoke.
The Naga king's smoke did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder's smoke did afflict the Naga king. Thereupon the Naga king burst into flames, and the Elder also thought, "It is not only you..."
“There is fire in the body; I have it too,” he said, and he blazed up.
The majesty of the nāga king did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder’s majesty afflicted the nāga king. The nāga king, thinking, “This man is oppressing me with Mount Sineru;
he is smoking and blazing,” asked, “Sir, who are you? “I am indeed...”
“Nanda, Moggallāna. “Venerable sir, remain in your own state as a bhikkhu.
The elder abandoned that form and entered through the opening of his right ear and emerged from the opening of his left ear;
he entered through the opening of his left ear and emerged from the opening of his right ear. Likewise, [he did so] through the opening of his right nostril...
Having entered, he emerged through the left nostril; having entered through the left nostril, he emerged through the right nostril.
Then the Naga king opened his mouth, and the Elder, having entered through the mouth, walked back and forth within the belly from east to west.
The Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, pay attention; this Naga is of great psychic power. The Elder—

“Venerable sir, my four bases of psychic power have been developed, cultivated, made the vehicle, made the foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken. Let alone Nandopananda, venerable sir;
I could tame even a hundred or a thousand royal nāgas like Nandopananda,” he said, and so forth.
The Nāga king thought: “He was not seen entering; now, at the time of his departure, I shall seize him between my fangs and devour him.
Having thought this, he said: “Come out, venerable sir; do not trouble me by pacing back and forth inside my belly.
The Elder came out and stood outside. The Nāga king [thought]: “This is he!”
Seeing this, he did not release his breath; the Elder entered the fourth jhāna, and even the wind was unable to move a single pore of his skin.

It is said that while the remaining bhikkhus might have been able to perform all the miracles from the beginning, they would not have been able to enter such a state so swiftly upon reaching this point.
The Blessed One did not grant them permission to subdue the nāga king.
The nāga king thought, "I was unable to move even a single pore of this ascetic’s body with the wind from my nostrils; that ascetic possesses great psychic power.
The Elder, casting off his own form, manifested himself in the shape of a garuḍa and [sent forth] a garuḍa-wind.

As he was showing [the way], he followed the Naga king. The Naga king, having abandoned that form and manifested the appearance of a young brahmin, said, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you," and bowed at the Elder's feet.
The Elder, having tamed the Naga king and rendered him free of venom, said, "Nanda, the Teacher has arrived; come, let us go. Thus he subdued the Naga king and made him harmless.
Having taken him, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. The Naga king, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you.
The Blessed One, saying, "May you be happy, O Naga king," departed for the residence of Anathapindika, surrounded by the community of monks.
Anāthapiṇḍika said, “Venerable sir, why have you arrived so late?
“There was a battle between Moggallāna and Nandopananda. “But who won, venerable sir, and who lost? “Moggallāna won;
Nanda was defeated. Anāthapiṇḍika said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from me a stay for seven days.”

Having said, "We shall pay honor to the Elder for seven days by providing him with meals in a single succession," he performed great honors for seven days for the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Therefore it was said: "It should be illustrated by the taming of Nanda and Upananda.

For on one occasion, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Eastern Park in the palace built by the great female lay devotee Visākhā, which was adorned with a thousand chambers... [and so on] ...and he inspired the deity to a sense of urgency. Therefore it was said:
“Having reached the perfection of psychic power (iddhi), I could, with the tip of my left toe, shake even the very deep, thick, and unshakable earth. In this context,
“having reached the perfection of psychic power” means having arrived at, having attained the culmination of psychic powers such as the power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi) and others.
395. "The conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" means the conceit such as "I am one perfected in wisdom, virtue, and concentration.
"I do not see it, nor do I proclaim it" is the meaning. Explaining that very point, he said, "Conceit does not exist in me.
"Beginning with the novices" means starting from the novices, I maintain a mind of respect, a mind of reverence, and great esteem toward the entire community of monks; this is the meaning.
396. "In immeasurable eons from now"—that is, beyond the intermediate eons (*antarakappa*) and so forth since our own current eon;
the meaning is that it was at the very top of a hundred thousand eons above one incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*). "I brought forth that karma" means:
I fulfilled the perfection of merit which is the basis for the state of being an Aggasāvaka (Chief Disciple). "I have reached that stage" means: I have attained that ground. That... [text ends].
"I have reached the stage of a disciple; I am one who has attained Nibbāna, which is defined as the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). This is the meaning.
(397) The four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), beginning with the analytical knowledge of meaning; the eight liberations (*vimokkha*) beginning with the path of stream-entry;
and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), beginning with the various supernormal powers—these have been realized and directly experienced by me. Of the Buddha, the Blessed One...
The meaning is that the teaching known as exhortation and instruction has been completed by me through the accomplishment of the practice of virtue.
"In this way" means in this manner, according to the sequence stated above.
Thus, he received a prophecy twice in the presence of the single Buddha Anomadassi. How? By the method stated above, having become a treasurer, to him...
Having received a prophecy from the Blessed One, he passed away from there and was reborn in a nāga abode in the ocean.
Because of his long life, he made an offering to that same Blessed One, invited him, fed him, and performed a great act of worship.
At that time as well, the Blessed One gave a prophecy. *Sudam* is a particle used for filling out the verse. *Āyasmā* is a term of endearment.
This is a designation for profound respect. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna spoke and recited these verses of the Apadāna.
The word *iti* is a particle used in the sense of completion.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is finished.
3-3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākassapa.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa begins with the words, "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara...

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and accumulating stores of merit conducive to the attainment of liberation throughout various existences, [encountered] the Blessed One Padumuttara.
In the city of Haṃsavatī, at that time, there was a householder named Vedeha, possessing eighty crores of wealth.
Being devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha, he lived as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
On a certain Uposatha day, having eaten a fine meal early in the morning and resolved upon the Uposatha precepts, he took perfumes, flowers, and other offerings and went to the monastery.
Having honored and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side.
At that moment, the Teacher placed the third disciple, the Elder Mahānisabha, in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are exponents of the ascetic practices (dhuta), this Nisabha is the foremost. [The lay follower...]

Having heard this, he was filled with faith. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, when the great multitude had risen and departed, he paid homage to the Teacher and invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow. "The community of monks, lay follower, is large," [the Teacher replied].
"How many, Venerable Sir? "Six million eight hundred thousand monks. "Venerable Sir, even for a single novice..."
“Without leaving anything behind in the monastery, take alms from me. The Teacher consented.
Knowing the Teacher’s consent, the lay follower went home, prepared a great offering, and on the following day announced the time for the Teacher’s arrival.

The Teacher took his bowl and robe and, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the lay follower’s house and sat upon the prepared seat. At the conclusion of the water-offering of dedication, he—
Accepting the rice gruel and other offerings, he performed the distribution of the meal. A lay devotee also sat down near the Teacher.
In the meantime, while the Elder Mahā-Nisabha was wandering for alms, he entered that very street.
Seeing him, the lay devotee rose, went up to the Elder, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, give me your bowl. The Elder gave his bowl.
He gave it to him, saying, "Venerable sir, please enter right here; the Teacher is also sitting at home.
"That will not do, lay follower," [the Elder replied]. The man took the Elder's bowl, filled it with almsfood, and gave it to him.
Then, having followed the Elder and returned, he sat down in the presence of the Teacher and said: "Venerable sir, the Elder Mahā-Nisabha said, 'The Teacher is also sitting at home.'"
Even when this was said, he did not wish to enter. [The Teacher asked: "Is there perhaps someone among you who possesses qualities superior to his?
Now, Buddhas have no such thing as stinginess regarding praise; therefore the Teacher spoke thus:
"Lay follower, we sit in the house awaiting almsfood, yet that bhikkhu does not sit like this and look for almsfood. We [stay] in lodgings within the village..."
“We dwell in sheltered places, but he dwells only in the forest. We dwell under cover, but he dwells only in the open air.
Thus the Blessed One, as if filling the great ocean, recounted his virtues, saying, “Such and such are his qualities.
And the lay follower, naturally like a lamp already burning, became even more deeply inspired with faith, as if drenched with oil, and thought:

“What is the use of this other attainment for me? Suppose now that I were to make a resolution in the presence of a future Buddha, for the sake of being foremost among those who preach the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
He again invited the Teacher, and by that same method, having given a great almsgiving for seven days, on the seventh day, to the Great Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha...
Having given the three robes and prostrated at the feet of the Teacher, he spoke thus:

“Venerable Sir, whatever bodily, verbal, and mental acts of loving-kindness were established in me while I was giving alms for seven days—I do not, by means of this, aspire for any other celestial success, whether that of the Sakkas, Māras, or Brahmas; rather, this—”

"May my merit become a qualification for attaining the foremost position among those who observe the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), so that in the future I may reach the rank attained by the Elder Mahānisabha in the presence of a certain Buddha. The Teacher,
observing whether this great position sought by him would be fulfilled or not, saw that it would indeed be fulfilled.
He said: "A pleasant state has been aspired to by you. At the end of a hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise;
you shall become his third disciple, the Elder Mahākassapa.
Having heard this, the lay follower thought, "There are no two kinds of speech from Buddhas," and on the following day, he regarded it as something already attained.

He considered this a great success. Having given gifts for as long as he lived, having undertaken and guarded moral conduct, and having performed various kinds of meritorious deeds, he passed away and was reborn in the heavenly realms.
From then on, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, [he appeared] ninety-one aeons ago during the time of the Sammasambuddha Vipassi.
While [the Buddha] was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, [the Bodhisatta], having passed away from the world of the gods, was reborn into a certain family of aged brahmins.
At that time, in his seventh year, the Blessed One Vipassī was preaching the Dhamma, and there was a great clamor.
The deities throughout the entire Jambudīpa [cried out]: "The Teacher is preaching the Dhamma!"
“...will speak? they announced. The brahmin heard that message. He had only a single lower garment (*nivāsana-sāṭaka*), and likewise his wife had only one;
moreover, they shared a single upper robe (*pārupana*). Thus, throughout the entire city, he became known as the “One-Garment Brahmin.
On one occasion, when there was an assembly of brahmins for some business, that brahmin left his wife at home.
Setting that cloth aside, he would put it on himself and go;
when there was a gathering of brahmin women, he would remain at home while the brahmin woman would put that cloth on and go. On that particular day, however, he said to the brahmin woman:
"Madam, will you listen to the Dhamma by night, or by day? She replied: "Husband, I am a woman..."
“I am of a timid nature; I cannot hear at night, but I shall hear by day.
Having thus left the brahmin in her house, she put on that garment, went to the monastery with the female lay disciples, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
After hearing the Dhamma, she departed together with the female lay disciples. Then the brahmin, having left her in the house—
Having put on that cloth, he went to the monastery.
At that time, the Teacher, seated upon the Dhamma-throne adorned with jewels in the midst of the assembly,
took up his fan and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend, and as if churning Mount Sineru and stirring the ocean.
He preached the Dhamma. As the brahmin sat at the very edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, a five-colored rapture arose that filled his entire body even during the first watch of the night.

He gathered up the garment he was wearing and thought, "I shall give it to the One of Ten Powers. Then, a stinginess arose in him, displaying a thousand dangers. He [thought], "To the brahmin lady..."
"You have only this one garment; you have no other upper robe at all, and I cannot go outside without wearing one," he said, being entirely unwilling to give it up.
Then, as the first watch of the night was passing away, joy arose in him just as before.
Thinking in that same way, he remained unwilling to give it up. Then, during the middle watch...
When the first watch had passed, in the last watch as well, joy arose in him in the same way.

Then, having overcome his stinginess, he folded the cloth and placed it at the feet of the Teacher. Thereupon, folding his left hand and striking with his right hand, he cried out three times, "Victory is mine! Victory is mine!"
At that time, King Bandhumā was sitting behind the Dhamma-throne within the curtain, listening to the Dhamma.
To the king, the sound "I have conquered" was indeed unpleasant. The king commanded a man: "Go, my good man, and ask him: 'What is he saying?
When the brahmin approached and was asked by him, [he replied: "The rest [are] the elephant-vehicles and so forth."
"Having mounted [a horse] and taken up swords, shields, and other weapons, they conquer the enemy army—that is not wonderful.

But I, having conquered the mind of stinginess as if striking off the head with a mallet and driving away a rogue ox coming from behind, gave the garment I was wearing to the One of Ten Powers; that victory over my stinginess is truly wonderful," he said.
So he went and reported that news to the king. The king thought, "My good man, we do not know what is appropriate for the One of Ten Powers;
the brahmin knows. Having gained confidence in him, he sent a pair of garments. Seeing this, the brahmin reflected:
"The king did not give me anything at all while I was sitting in silence, but as soon as I spoke of the Teacher's virtues—"
Thinking, "This has arisen in dependence upon the virtues of the Teacher;
it is truly suitable for the Teacher alone," he gave that pair of cloths as well to the One of Ten Powers. The king asked, "What was done by the brahmin?
and having heard that "he too gave that pair of cloths to the Tathāgata alone," he sent two other pairs of cloths, which he [the brahmin] also gave to the Teacher.
He gave them. Again, the king, saying, "And four more," sent thirty-two pairs of garments in this manner.

Then the brahmin, thinking, "This is like taking what has been increased again and again," took two pairs of garments for himself—one for himself and one for his wife—and gave the remaining thirty pairs to the Tathāgata alone.
From that time forth, he became a trusted confidant of the Teacher.
Then one day, seeing him listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher during the cold season,
the king gave him his own red woolen cloak worth a hundred thousand pieces and said, "Henceforth, listen to the Dhamma wearing this."
Thinking, "What is the use of this woolen blanket being brought to this putrid body?
he went away after making it into a canopy over the Tathāgata’s bed within the Fragrant Chamber.
Then one day, the king went to the monastery early in the morning and sat down in the presence of the Teacher inside the Fragrant Chamber. At that moment, the six-colored rays of the Buddha—
They struck against the blanket, and the blanket shone exceedingly. Looking up, the king recognized it and said, "Venerable sir, this is our blanket; it was given by us to a single-garment brahmin.
"Great King, you honored the brahmin, and the brahmin has honored us. The king thought, "The brahmin understood what was appropriate, not we."

Having gained confidence, he took everything that was beneficial to human beings and, having arranged it all into groups of eight, gave a gift called the "All-Eight" (*sabbaṭṭhaka*) and appointed him to the position of royal chaplain.
He too, thinking, "The 'Eight-Eight' (*aṭṭhaṭṭhaka*) consists of sixty-four," provided sixty-four sets of daily meals;
and having given such gifts for as long as he lived and guarded his virtue, from there—
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in heaven.

Passing away again from there, in this present kappa, between the times of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana and the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī into a householder’s family. As he grew up and lived the life of a householder, one day—
He was wandering on foot through the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha, while making robes by a riverbank, began to fold and set them aside because the wind was not blowing.
Seeing this, he asked, "Venerable sir, why are you folding and setting them aside?
"Because the wind is not blowing," [the Paccekabuddha replied]. "Venerable sir, use this," and he offered him his upper garment (*uttarāsāṭaka*).
Having given [the gift], she made this aspiration: "In every place where I am reborn, may there be no decline for me.
While his wife was quarreling with her sister-in-law at home, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms.
Then his sister-in-law, having given alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, said, referring to his wife: "Such a one..."
“I would rather avoid a fool for a hundred leagues,” she made this aspiration. Standing on the courtyard of her house, she heard this and thought, “May he not eat the food given by this woman!
She took the bowl, threw away the rice, filled it with mud, and gave it to him.
Seeing this, the other said, “Foolish girl, you may insult me or strike me, but for one such as this, two incalculable aeons...”
"It is not fitting to discard the meal from the bowl of a Paccekabuddha who has fulfilled the perfections and instead give him mud," he said.
Then his wife’s reflection arose; she cried out, "Wait, venerable sir!
and having discarded the mud, washed the bowl, rubbed it with scented powder, and filled it with fine food and the four sweets, [she offered it].
Having placed the bowl, which was shining with ghee poured over it and possessing the color of the interior of a lotus, into the hand of the Paccekabuddha, he made this aspiration:
"Just as this alms-food has become radiant, may my body likewise become radiant.
After the Paccekabuddha had expressed his appreciation, he soared into the sky. Those two, the husband and wife, [lived] for as long as their lifespan lasted.

Having remained there, they passed away from that state and were reborn in heaven. Passing away from there once more, the lay follower was reborn during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa in a family possessing eighty million in wealth in Bārāṇasī;
the other woman was also reborn as the daughter of a merchant of similar means. When he reached maturity, they brought that very merchant’s daughter to him as a wife. Regarding her former...

By the power of that evil karma which has an undesirable result, as soon as she entered her father-in-law’s house, the entire residence became foul-smelling from the very center of the compound, like a latrine with its lid removed. The prince asked, "Whose smell is this?
and upon hearing it was the merchant's daughter, he said, "Take her away," and sent her back to her own family home.
She sent it. By that very same means, she turned back at seven locations.
At that time, the Fortunate One Kassapa, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers, attained final Nibbāna.
They began constructing a stupa for him, one yojana in height, using golden bricks worth a hundred thousand pieces each. While that stupa was being built, that merchant’s daughter thought:
—“I have turned back from seven points; what is the use of my life? she thought.
Having had her own jewelry and ornaments broken up, she had a golden reliquary made, one span long, one cubit wide, and four finger-breadths high.
Then, taking lumps of yellow orpiment and realgar, and carrying eight handfuls of blue lotus flowers, she went to the site where the stupa was to be built. And at that moment—
As she was coming along, having laid out a single row of bricks, she was short of one brick for the corner.
The merchant’s daughter said to the mason, "Place this brick here for me. "Mother, you have come at an auspicious time; you place it yourself," he replied.
She climbed up, mixed oil with a lump of yellow orpiment and red arsenic, and used that as an adhesive.
Having established a brick foundation and performed an offering above it with eight handfuls of blue lotus flowers, she paid homage and made this aspiration:
“In every place where I am reborn, may the fragrance of sandalwood issue from my body and the fragrance of the blue lotus from my mouth.
Having thus made her aspiration, she paid homage to the Cetiya, circumambulated it, and returned home.
At that very moment, mindfulness regarding the merchant’s son to whom she had first been led home arose in him.
A festival was also proclaimed throughout the city. He said to his attendants, "Where is the merchant’s daughter who was brought here?
"In her family home, sir. "Bring her back; we shall enjoy the festival," he said. They went and [brought her].
Having paid homage, she stood there. When asked by her, "What is it, dear ones, that you have come for? they explained the matter to her.
She said, "Dear ones, I have already worshipped the Cetiya with my own ornaments; I have no ornaments left. They went and informed the merchant’s son:
"Bring her here; she shall receive the jewelry. They brought her. As soon as she entered the house—

The fragrance of sandalwood and the fragrance of blue lotuses wafted throughout the entire house. The merchant’s son asked her, “My lady, previously a foul odor issued from your body, but now the fragrance of sandalwood issues from your body and the fragrance of blue lotuses from your mouth;
what is this? She related to him, from the beginning, the deed she had committed. The merchant’s son—

Having gained confidence, thinking, “The teaching of the Buddha is indeed leading to liberation,” he covered a golden cetiya extending for a league with a woolen cloak (*kambalakañcuka*) and adorned it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels. Their hanging tassels were twelve cubits long.
Having lived there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in heaven; then, passing away from there, [he was reborn] from Benares...

He was reborn in a certain minister’s family at a place only a *yojana* away. His wife, however, having passed away from the world of the gods, was reborn in the royal family as the eldest daughter of the king.
When they had reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the prince lived.
He said to his mother, "Mother, give me a garment; I shall go to enjoy the festival. She—
He brought out a cotton cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this is too coarse," he said. She brought out another and gave it to him.
He rejected that as well. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, in a house such as ours where we were born, there is no merit for us to obtain anything finer than this.
"In that case, Mother, I shall go to a place where I can obtain it," he replied.
“Son, I desire that you receive the kingdom of the city of Bārāṇasī this very day. He paid homage to his mother and said, “I am going, Mother.

“Go, dear son,” she replied. Having departed according to his meritorious destiny, he went to Bārāṇasī and lay down in the royal garden upon the auspicious stone slab, covering himself with his upper robe down to his head. And while the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away...
The seventh day arrived.
Having performed the funeral rites for the king, the ministers sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated:
"The king has only one daughter and no son; the kingdom will perish without a ruler. Who is worthy to become king? "You—"
“Go! You, go! The chaplain said, “It is not proper to look about too much;

we shall release the Phussa-chariot. Having yoked four horses the color of white water-lilies and placed the fivefold royal insignia and the white parasol upon it, they released the chariot and had musical instruments played behind it. The chariot [went out] by the eastern gate.
Having departed, he went toward the park. Some said, "He is going toward the park out of habit;
let us turn him back. The chaplain said, "Do not turn him back. The chariot went forward, circumambulated the prince, and stood ready for him to mount.
The chaplain drew back the corner of his upper garment and looked at the soles of the prince's feet.

“Let this island be; he is fit to rule over the four great continents within the two thousand minor islands,” he said, and then, saying, “Sound the musical instruments! he had them sounded three times.
Then the prince, opening his mouth and looking out, asked, “For what purpose have you come? “O Lord, for you...”
“He shall attain the kingship. “Where is your king? “He has passed away, sir. “How many days have elapsed?
“Today is the seventh day, sir. “Has he no son or daughter? “He has a daughter, sire, but no son.
“In that case, I shall exercise the kingship. They immediately had a consecration pavilion constructed and [prepared] the princess for the coronation.
Having adorned him with all manner of ornaments and brought him to the pleasure garden, they performed the prince’s consecration ceremony.
Then, when his consecration was completed, they presented him with a garment worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold. He asked, "What is this, dear ones?
"It is a lower robe, Your Majesty. "Is it not too thick, dear ones? "Among garments used by humans, there is nothing softer than this."
"O gods! [he asked]. "Does your king wear such garments as these? "Yes, O gods," they replied.
"I do not think your king is a man of merit," he said. "Bring a golden pitcher; I shall obtain the cloth.
Having had a golden pitcher brought, he stood up, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and [facing] the eastern direction...
He sprinkled [water]. Having split the solid earth, eight *kappa* trees sprang up. Again, taking water, he sprinkled it in the southern, western, and northern directions;
thus, having sprinkled in all four directions, making eight in each, thirty-two *kappa* trees sprang up.
He, having dressed in one divine cloth and wrapped himself in another, [stood there].
Having said, "Let a drum be beaten throughout King Nanda’s realm, proclaiming: 'Let no women spin thread!
he raised his royal parasol, adorned himself, mounted the back of a noble elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.
As time passed in this way, the queen, seeing the king’s prosperity, displayed an expression of compassion, saying, “Oh, what austerities!
When asked, “What is this, O Queen? she replied, “Your majesty, your prosperity is truly great;
it is the fruit of wholesome deeds performed in the past through faith in the Buddhas. Now, do not fail to perform the merit that will serve as a condition for the future.”
He said, "To whom shall we give? There are no virtuous ones. He replied, "Your Majesty, Jambudvīpa is not empty of Arahants;
Your Majesty, prepare the gift, and I shall find the Arahants. On the following day, the king had the almsgiving prepared at the eastern gate.
Early in the morning, the queen, having undertaken the observance precepts (uposathaṅga), stood on the upper terrace of the palace facing the east.
Having lain down with his head toward the north, he said, "If there are any Arahants in this direction, may they come tomorrow and accept our almsfood.
There were no Arahants in that direction; they gave that honor to the poor beggars.
On the following day, having made preparations at the southern gate, he likewise failed to find anyone worthy of offerings. On the next day as well, [he did so] at the western gate.

It was exactly the same. On the day the northern gate was prepared, as the queen was likewise inviting them, the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas living in the Himālaya—the sons of Padumavatī—namely the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, addressed his brothers:
"Sirs, King Nanda is inviting you; please accept his invitation. They accepted.
On the following day, having washed their faces at Lake Anotatta and come through the air, they descended at the northern gate.
When people saw them, they went and informed the king, saying, "Your Majesty, five hundred paccekabuddhas have arrived.
The king, together with his queen, went forth, paid homage, and escorted the paccekabuddhas up into the palace; there he gave them alms, and at the conclusion of their meal,

The king prostrated at the feet of the senior elder of the Saṅgha, and the queen prostrated at the feet of the junior member of the Saṅgha, saying, "Venerable sirs, may you not be distressed for lack of requisites, and may we not fall away from merit; please grant us your promise to reside here for as long as we live.
Having thus obtained their promise, he constructed five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walking-paths in the park.
Having prepared dwelling places in every respect, they had them inhabited there.
As time passed in this way, when the border regions revolted, the king instructed the queen, saying, "I am going to suppress the border regions;
do not neglect the Paccekabuddhas," and then he departed. Even before he had returned, the Paccekabuddhas—

The life-formations were exhausted. Having sported in the play of jhāna throughout the three watches of the night, the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, at the time of sunrise, grasped his support-board and, while still standing, attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. By this same method, all the others did likewise;
they all attained final Nibbāna. On the following day, the queen prepared the seating places for the Paccekabuddhas.
Having scattered flowers and perfumed the air with incense, she sat waiting for their arrival;
but seeing no sign of them, she sent men, saying, "Go, dear sirs, and find out what is troubling the masters.
They went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma’s leaf-hut, and not finding him there, proceeded to the walkway and [saw] the leaning board.
Seeing him standing there leaning against it, they paid homage and said, "It is time, Bhante.
Thinking, "What will the body of one who has attained final nibbāna say? He is likely sleeping," they touched the back of his feet with their hands;
perceiving that he had attained final nibbāna by the coldness and rigidity of the feet, they went to the second [monk] and, having perceived the same, again—
"Of the third": having thus learned that all had attained final nibbāna, they returned to the royal palace.
When asked, "Where are the paccekabuddhas, dear ones?", they replied, "They have attained final nibbāna, Your Majesty.
The queen, weeping and wailing, went out and, accompanied by the citizens, went to that place; she had the funeral rites performed for the paccekabuddhas.
Having had the relics collected, he enshrined them in a cetiya.
When the king returned after having pacified the border regions, he went out to meet the queen who had come to welcome him and asked:
"My lady, have you not neglected the Paccekabuddhas? Are the noble ones free from illness? "They have passed away, Your Majesty," she replied. He—
Having heard this, the king thought: “If even for such wise men as these death occurs, from what shall we escape?
Without entering the city, he went straight to the pleasure grove, summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingdom to him, and himself went forth into the homeless life of a recluse.
The queen also thought, “Now that the king has gone forth, what shall I do? and did likewise.
He went forth in the park. Having developed the two jhānas, when they passed away from there, they were reborn in the Brahma-world.
While they were dwelling right there, our Teacher appeared in the world, set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, and eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
While the Teacher was residing there, this young brahmin Pippali lived in the brahmin village of Mahātittha in the Magadha country.
He was reborn in the womb of the wife of the brahmin Kapila. This Bhaddakāpilānī was reborn in the womb of the wife of a brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom.
As they gradually grew up, when the young man Pippali reached his twentieth year and Bhaddā her sixteenth, their parents, having looked upon their son, said:
“Dear son, you have reached the age of maturity; it is fitting that you establish the family lineage,” they urged him with great persistence.
The young man said, “Do not speak such words within my hearing. I shall look after you as long as you live;
after your passing, I will go forth and enter the religious life. For several days, they...
Having passed over [the time], they spoke again. He, too, rejected it once more. From then on, his mother spoke of it incessantly.
The young man, thinking, "I shall persuade my mother," gave a thousand *nikkhas* of red gold to goldsmiths and had a female figure fashioned.
At the conclusion of the work—its washing, polishing, and so forth—he dressed her in that red garment.
Having adorned her with flowers of exquisite gold and various ornaments, she said, "Mother, if I obtain such an object as this, I shall live at home;
if not, I shall not live here. The wise Brahmin woman thought:
"My son is meritorious, one who has practiced giving and made his resolution in the past; while performing meritorious deeds, he did not do so alone. Surely—"
“By means of this, those who have performed merit will become like golden statues. Having summoned eight brahmins and satisfied them with all his possessions,
he placed a golden statue on a chariot and said, “Go, dear ones,
and wherever you see a girl of such a kind from a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, wealth, and so forth, there leave this very golden statue.”
“Make a solemn promise and give [us the money],” he urged them.
Thinking, “This is indeed our business,” they departed and said, “Where shall we find it?
There is a royal harem in the kingdom of Madda; let us go to the kingdom of Madda. Thus they went to the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. Then...
Having placed the golden image at the bathing ford, they sat down to one side.
Then Bhaddā’s nurse, after having bathed and adorned Bhaddā, went to the water-ford herself to bathe; seeing the golden image, she thought, “What untrained woman is this who has come and stood here?
and striking it on the back, she recognized it as the golden image and said, “My lady’s daughter—”
She formed the perception that it was beautiful, yet she said, "But this noble lady’s daughter is incomparable even to this [image] which has been accepted as her lower garment.
Then those brahmins asked her, "Is your own daughter indeed like this?
She replied, "My noble lady’s daughter is more beautiful than this golden image by a hundredfold, even a thousandfold; for even in the absence of a lamp, within a space of twelve cubits—"
“Seated in the womb, she dispels the darkness with the radiance of her body,” he said. “In that case, let us go to her parents.
Having placed the golden image in the chariot and followed the nursemaid, they stood at the door of the house of the Kosiya clan and announced their arrival.
The brahmin, having offered them hospitality, asked, "From where have you come?
They replied, "We have come from the house of the brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha, for this specific reason. "Very well, dear ones;
that brahmin is of the same caste, clan, and wealth as we are. We shall give him our daughter," he said, and he accepted their gifts. Then they [went] to the brahmin Kapila...
They sent a message: "We have found a girl named Bhaddā; please let us know what should be done.

Having heard that message, they informed the young man Pippali, saying, "The girl has been found. The young man Pippali thought, "I thought they would not find her, yet they send word that she has been found.
Since I have no desire for her, I shall send a letter. And so, having gone into seclusion, he wrote a letter.
She wrote: “May Bhaddā obtain a husband worthy of her own birth, clan, and wealth;

as for me, I shall go forth and take ordination, so that you do not later feel regret. Bhaddā, having heard that they intended to give her to such-and-such a man, went into seclusion and wrote a letter:
“May my noble son obtain a maiden worthy of his own birth, clan, and wealth; as for me, I shall go forth.”
"Do not have cause for regret later. The two letters met on the way. "Whose letter is this?
"It was sent by the young Brahmin Pippali to Bhaddā. "And whose is this? "It was sent by Bhaddā to the young Brahmin Pippali.
When this was said, they both read them aloud and remarked, "Behold the deeds of these children!"
Having torn up [the original letter] and discarded it in the forest, they wrote another letter of similar content and sent it back and forth. Thus,
because the letters of the prince and the princess were identical and worthy of the world's admiration,
the two of them came together even though they did not desire it.
On that very same day, the young brahmin Pippali had Bhaddā prepare a single flower garland.
Bhaddā placed it in the middle of the bed. When they had both finished their evening meal, they began to ascend the bed.
The young brahmin climbed onto the right side of the bed, while Bhaddā climbed onto the left side and said: "On whichever side the flowers wither, [that is the one who will die]."
"We shall know when a mind of lust arises in him; then this flower-garland must not be placed upon him.
However, out of fear of physical contact with one another's bodies, they spent the entire night without even descending into sleep.
By day, they did not even allow a smile. Remaining unattached to worldly pleasures as long as their parents lived, they passed their time.
Until then, they had not investigated the family estate; when those [ancestors] passed away, they began to investigate it. Great was the young man’s prosperity.
One day, after his body had been lifted up and discarded, he managed to obtain exactly twelve *nāḷis* of gold dust—measured by the Magadhan *nāḷi*—which would otherwise have had to be thrown away.
There were sixty great reservoirs equipped with water-lifting machines, a plantation twelve *yojanas* in extent, and [buildings] equal in size to Anurādhapura.
There were fourteen villages, fourteen elephant divisions, fourteen cavalry divisions, and fourteen chariot divisions.
One day, having mounted a decorated horse and surrounded by a great multitude, he went to his place of business;
standing at the edge of a field, he saw crows and other birds picking up and eating the worms, such as earthworms, that had been turned up by the ploughs from the spot where the ground had been cut.
Seeing them, he asked, "Father, what are these people eating? "Worms, my lord. "To whom does the evil committed by these belong?
"To you, my lord. He thought: "If the evil committed by these belongs to me, what will eighty-seven crores of wealth avail me?
What will twelve leagues of agricultural estates avail me? What will the machines bound together [by my labor] avail me?"
“Having given away these ponds, these fourteen villages, and all this else to Bhaddā Kāpilānī,
I shall go forth into homelessness. At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, having spread out three jars of sesame seeds at Antaravatthu and sitting surrounded by her nurses,
saw crows eating the sesame seeds and asked, “Mistresses, what are these eating?”
“‘A living being, noble lady. ‘Whose demerit is it? ‘Yours, noble lady. She thought:
‘I have received a four-cubit cloth and a measure of boiled rice;
yet, if this demerit committed by them becomes mine, I shall not be able to lift my head from the cycle of existence even for a thousand lifetimes. [What will become of] the noble son?”’”
“As soon as he has arrived, I will hand over everything to him and, having departed, go forth into the homeless life.
When the young man had come, bathed, and ascended the palace, he sat down upon a costly couch; then they brought him food fit for a wheel-turning monarch.
After both had eaten and the attendants had departed, [the young man] went into private in a secluded place.
They sat down. Then the young man said to Bhaddā: "Bhaddā, when you come to this house, how much wealth do you bring?

"Fifty-five thousand carts, noble sir. "All of that, as well as the eighty-seven crores in this house, the sixty irrigation reservoirs bound by machinery, and all such varieties of prosperity as exist—all that belongs to you alone."
“I am departing. “But where are you going, noble lady? “I shall go forth into homelessness.
“Noble lady, I too have been sitting here waiting for your arrival; I too shall go forth.
For them, the three realms of existence appeared like a hut of burning leaves. Saying, “We shall go forth,” they [bought] from the marketplace robes dyed with yellow ochre...
Having had their robes and clay alms-bowls brought, they shaved one another's hair, saying, "Our going forth is dedicated to those who are Worthy Ones (arahants) in the world.
Having thus gone forth, they placed their bowls in bags, slung them over their shoulders, and descended from the palace.
Neither in the house nor among the slaves or laborers did anyone recognize them.
Then, as they were departing from the brahmin village and traveling through the gateway of Dāsagāma, the inhabitants of Dāsagāma recognized them by their distinctive appearance.
Weeping, they fell at their feet and said, "Why do you leave us behind, noble sirs, as if we were helpless? [The Teacher replied:
"Friends, we have gone forth because we considered 'the three states of existence to be like a leaf-hut on fire. If you would each provide one person from among yourselves who is a free man..."
“Let us do it; even a hundred years would not suffice. You yourselves must wash your own heads and live as free men,” he said, and while they were still weeping, they departed.
As the Elder walked on ahead, he turned back and looked at them, thinking: “This Bhaddā Kāpilānī is worth the entire wealth of Jambudīpa.”
“A woman is following behind me. It is possible that someone might think, ‘Even these renunciants cannot remain apart; they are acting unbecomingly.
If anyone, having been defiled by such an evil thought, were to fill the states of misery, it would be right for me to go on after leaving her behind.”
Having generated that thought, he went forward and, seeing a forked path, stood at its head.
Bhaddā also arrived, paid homage, and stood there. Then he said to her:
"Bhaddā, when the great multitude sees such a woman following behind me, they will become hostile toward us, thinking, 'Even these who have gone forth are unable to exist without women.'"
“He would fill the states of misery. On this forked path, you take this one; I shall go by the other.
“Yes, noble sir, women might show us fault, saying, ‘Women are an impediment to those who have gone forth; even those who have gone forth cannot do without them.
Having thus circumambulated him three times, keeping him to his right, she prostrated herself at four places with the fivefold salutation.
Having paid homage and raised her hands in salutation, radiant with the ten fingers joined together, she said:
"The friendship formed over the course of a hundred thousand eons is broken today. You are indeed called 'the Right,' and the right path suits you;
we women, however, are of a left-handed nature, and the left path suits us. Having spoken thus, she paid homage once more and set out upon her way.
At the time when they were split asunder, this great earth trembled and roared as if saying,
"Though I am able to support the world-system, Mount Sineru, and the other mountains, I am unable to bear your virtues.
A sound like a thunderclap occurred in the sky, and the mountain of the world-system resounded.
The Fully Enlightened One, while seated in his hut at the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana, heard the sound of the earth’s trembling.
Reflecting, "Why is the earth shaking? he perceived: "The young brahmin Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī have gone forth, renouncing immeasurable prosperity for my sake;
this [trembling] occurs at the place of their separation through the power of the virtues of both."
"A great earthquake has occurred; it is fitting that I too should provide for their welfare.
Having thus emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, he took his own bowl and robes and, without informing any of the eighty great elders, traveled twenty-four kilometers (three gavutas) to meet them halfway.
Between Rājagaha and Nālandā, at the foot of the Bahuputta Nyagrodha tree, he sat down cross-legged.
He sat down. But instead of sitting like some other wearer of rag-robes, he assumed the appearance of a Buddha and sat down, emitting eighty cubits of Buddha-rays.

Thus, at that moment, Buddha-rays—equal in size to leaf-shaded canopies, cartwheels, and gabled houses—spread out and radiated here and there, like the time when a thousand moons and a thousand suns rise together.
Making it appear as if it were so, they made that forest interior one mass of light.
With the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the forest interior shone like the sky with a cluster of stars, or like water with fully blossomed lotuses and water-lilies.
The trunk of the banyan tree was naturally white, while its leaves were green and its fruits ripe.
They were red. On that day, however, the entire *nigrodha* tree was the color of gold.
When the Elder Mahākassapa saw this, he thought, "This one will be our Teacher; it is for his sake that I have gone forth.
Starting from the spot where he had seen it, he walked bowing low, prostrated at three places, and said: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher."
“I am a disciple, Bhante; the Blessed One is my Teacher, I am a disciple,” he said. Then the Blessed One said to him:
“Kassapa, if you were to perform this act of prostration upon the great earth, even she would not be able to bear it.
But this act of prostration has been performed by you who know such greatness of virtue in the Tathāgata.”
“He cannot even cause a single hair on my body to quiver. Sit down, Kassapa; I shall give you my inheritance.
Then the Blessed One conferred full ordination upon him with three exhortations.

Having done so, he departed from the foot of the Bahuputta-Nigrodha tree and set out on the road, making the Elder his attendant monk. The Teacher’s body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Mahākassapa, adorned with the seven marks of a great man, followed step by step behind the Teacher like one trailing behind a golden ship.
Having traveled a short distance along the road, the Teacher stepped off the path and made a gesture of sitting down at the foot of a certain tree.
The Elder, perceiving that the Teacher desired to sit, [offered] his own tattered rag-robe.
Having folded his outer robe (saṅghāṭi) into four layers, he spread it out.
The Teacher sat there and, stroking the robe with his hand, said, "Kassapa, this outer robe of yours, made of rags from a dust-heap, is indeed soft.
Thinking, "The Teacher has spoken of the softness of my outer robe; he wishes to wear it," he—
Knowing that this would be so, he said, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One put on his outer robe.
"What will you wear, Kassapa? "I shall wear what I receive as my undergarment, venerable sir.
"But how, Kassapa, will you be able to wear this rag-robe worn out by use? For I have [already] given this rag-robe..."
"On the day it was received, the great earth shook as far as the limits of the ocean.
