This worn robe, a possession of the Buddha, cannot be worn by one of meager virtue; it is fitting that it be worn by one who is capable, a true wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika) who is able to fulfill the practice," he said, and then exchanged robes with the Elder.
Having thus exchanged their robes, the Blessed One put on the elder’s robe, and the elder put on the Teacher’s robe.
At that moment, even this great earth, though insentient, cried out: "It was difficult to do, Bhante!
You have performed a deed never before done by a disciple: you have exchanged your own worn robe for that of your follower. I am unable to bear your virtue!"
It quaked as if declaring, "Having made the ocean its boundary. The Elder, too, without conceit, thinking, "I have obtained the robe used by the Buddhas;
what more remains for me to do now," undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaguṇa) right there in the presence of the Teacher.
For only seven days he remained an ordinary person (puthujjana). On the eighth day, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arahatship.

He attained [this state]. Then the Teacher, having praised him with such words as, "Bhikkhus, Kassapa approaches families like the moon, keeping his body withdrawn and his mind withdrawn, ever-new among families, free from arrogance," later on, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, declared:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are exponents of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas):"
"Namely, Mahākassapa," he said, and thus placed him in the foremost position among those who preach the ascetic practices (*dhuta*).
Having been thus established by the Blessed One in this preeminent rank, the Venerable Mahākassapa, having attained the status of a Great Disciple,
recalled his own past karma and, out of joy, proclaimed his *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds) under Padumuttara Buddha.
He spoke the passage beginning with "The Blessed One," and so forth. Regarding that, "of Padumuttara":

it is said that from the time of that Blessed One’s emergence from his mother’s womb, at every moment he set foot down, lotuses with a hundred thousand petals sprang up, piercing the earth as soon as each step was taken.
Therefore, that became his name. Among the entire multitude of beings, by each individual [performing] a hundred-fold merit...
The meaning is: "Because he has performed a hundredfold merit compared to that merit [of others], he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā). Regarding "the eldest of the world, the Stable One (Tādi)":
he is the "Stable One" because he has attained an unshakable state amidst the desirable and undesirable, being the foremost being in the world of sentient beings.
Regarding "when the Lord of the World had passed away": when the Blessed One, who was the refuge for the world of sentient beings, had attained final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the aggregates.

The meaning is "having gone to non-appearance. The connection is as follows: they perform worship while offering praise, that is, they pay homage by celebrating the "well-played" (sādhukīḷa) [performance] of the Blessed One, who has received the name "Teacher" from the world including the devas.
399. "The multitude of people pile up a fire" means that groups of people pile up a fire for the purpose of a funeral pyre, making a heap.
The connection is: "rejoicing and being satisfied on all sides, rejoicing and being satisfied in a manifold way, they performed worship.

Regarding the phrase "when a sense of spiritual urgency had arisen among them": when that multitude of people had attained a sense of urgency and were experiencing trepidation, joy and laughter arose in me—that is, they became manifest—such is the meaning.
"Having gathered our kinsmen and friends" means having brought together my relatives and companions and made them into a multitude.
"The Great Hero, the Blessed One, has attained final Nibbāna and gone beyond sight"—this is the connection with the words "I spoke," meaning I said this.
"Come now, let us perform an offering"—here *handā* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation; for that reason, we have all come together.
The meaning is: "I shall perform worship. *Sā* is a particle. 401.
"Having agreed to them, saying 'Excellent'": having assented to my words, saying "Excellent," "Fine," "Auspicious," those kinsmen and friends of mine accepted my speech;
the meaning is that they produced and gave rise to even greater laughter and joy for me.
402. Then, showing his own accumulation of merit, he said, "In the Buddha, the Lord of the World," and so forth.

It is connected as follows: having built and caused to be built a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) that rose a hundred cubits high and was one hundred and fifty cubits wide—an elevated, magnificent structure in the sky, well-constructed and fashioned in a beautiful form—he made and performed an accumulation of merit, a heap of merit.
403. “Having made a canopy there” means: having had a canopy made—decorated and beautified with rows of palm trees—at that place of worship for the cetiya;
and “having gladdened his own mind” means: having pleased his own heart, he worshipped the cetiya.
The connection is: “he worshipped the supreme cetiya,” meaning the most excellent cetiya in which the relics of the Buddha were enshrined.
404. To demonstrate the majesty of that cetiya, he spoke the verse beginning with "Like a mass of fire.

In this context, "like a mass of fire" means like a blazing mass of fire or a heap of flames; "that cetiya shines with the seven gems" means it blazes like a king of *sāla* trees in full bloom with blossoming flowers;
and "in the four directions" means like Indra’s staff and like a rainbow in the sky.
The connection is: "it shines and glows in all directions. 405.

Therein, "having gladdened the mind" means: having gladdened the heart and mind within that womb of the radiant relic-element, and having produced joy, and by means of that gladness of mind, having performed much merit consisting of various kinds of wholesome deeds, [one should dedicate it] "in the relic-womb..."

"Having thus recollected my meritorious deeds, thinking, 'I have performed such merits in the Teaching,' I passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven of the Thirty-three, just as one awakens from sleep;
this is the connection [of the verse] with the words 'I was born.
(406) Showing the prosperity he had obtained in the celestial world where he was reborn, he said, 'yoked with a thousand [elephants],' and so forth. Therein..."
He stood upon a divine chariot yoked with a thousand horses drawn by steeds.
My palace, a celestial mansion (vimāna), rose well up and was loftily elevated through seven stories; such was the meaning.
In that mansion, there were thousands of gabled chambers (kūṭāgāra) made entirely of gold, composed wholly of gold.
The meaning is as follows: by its own power and majesty, it illuminates, radiates, shines, and glows, making all ten directions resplendent—this is the connection [of the words]. 408.
In that celestial mansion (vimāna) manifested for me, there are also other turrets and front porches; they exist and are present. What [is there]?
"Of what are they made?"—they are made of ruby (*lohitaṅga*) and red gems. Then, the connection is that those four turrets also shine with splendor and radiance toward the four directions.

(410) "I surpass all the gods"—that is, I overcome the gods in the entire world of the devas. If one asks, "Whose fruit is this? the meaning is: "This is the fruit of the meritorious deed performed by me."
411. Then, demonstrating the excellence of his human rebirth, he said, "In sixty thousand kappas," and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:

sixty thousand kappas below this present kappa, having become a Universal Monarch (cakkavattī) named Ubbiddha—conqueror of the four quarters, possessing the four great continents, victor who has conquered all adversaries—I dwelt upon the earth and exercised sovereignty.
In that same way, he makes [the aeon] auspicious because it is adorned by five Buddhas; thus it is called the Bhaddaka aeon.

Thirty times—over thirty lifetimes—he was a sovereign lord over the four continents, preeminent, endowed with and possessed of the seven treasures such as the wheel-treasure, delighted by his own deeds, and devoted to and established in the ten royal virtues of his own duty as a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī).

The connection is: "I was a king. Demonstrating the prosperity he experienced during his time as a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), he said, "There too, my palace," and so forth. In that regard, "there" refers to that reign as a wheel-turning monarch;
"my palace" means my mansion, which rose up like a pillar of Indra, standing in the sky like a flash of lightning shining aloft, with its various divisions such as the seven stories.
The connection is that it was twenty-four *yojanas* in height and length, and twelve *yojanas* in width.
The meaning is that there was a city named Rammaṇa, so called because it was delightful by virtue of captivating the minds of all people.
This shows that it was endowed with high walls and gate-towers, twelve or thirty cubits in height and made of solid material.
"Then a half-aḍḍhaka" means a half of two hundred and fifty *yojanas*. "Twenty-five were placed" means that twenty market-stalls were placed [there], forming a continuous boundary for the street.
"Born into a brahmin family" means well-born in a brahmin lineage. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākassapa is completed. 3–4.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Anuruddha begins with the verse, “Sumedha the Blessed One said...”. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a wealthy family of householders. When he reached maturity, one day he went to a monastery and,
while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, the Teacher placed a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Seeing him making the offering, he himself also aspired to that same gift;

having performed a great almsgiving for seven days for the Blessed One and his retinue of one hundred thousand monks, on the seventh day he gave the most excellent robes to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks and made a formal resolution (paṇidhāna).
The Teacher, seeing that this would be fulfilled without obstacle, [said:]
“He will become the foremost among those possessing the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) in the future dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Gotama,” he prophesied.
Thereupon, while performing meritorious deeds there, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna,

he offered a magnificent lamp-offering at the seven-yojana golden stupa, using many bronze bowls along with lamp-trees and lamp-bowls, thinking, “May this be the necessary support for the knowledge of the divine eye.”

He performed [these deeds]. Having thus performed meritorious acts for as long as he lived, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa in a householder’s family in Bārāṇasī.

Upon reaching maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna and the golden stupa one league in height had been completed, he filled many bronze bowls with the cream of ghee and placed a single lump of sugar in the middle of each.
Setting aside one rim of the bowl against another rim, he had the stupa encircled.

Having filled the bronze bowl he himself was carrying with the finest clarified butter, and having lit a thousand lamps, he placed them upon his head and circumambulated the stupa throughout the entire night.
Thus, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived even in that existence, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and there he remained for the full span of his lifespan.
Having remained there, when he passed away, he was reborn in a family of the poor in Bārāṇasī itself, at a time when no Buddha had arisen;
his name was Annabhāra. He lived by performing work in the house of a merchant named Sumanaseṭṭhi.
One day, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha, who had emerged from the attainment of cessation and was traveling through the air from Mount Gandhamādana.
Having descended at the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī and put on his robe, he saw [the Paccekabuddha] walking for alms in the city.
With a mind full of faith, he took the bowl and placed into it the portion of food set aside for himself, intending to give it to the Paccekabuddha;
he then began to lead him away. His wife also placed her own portion of food right there into the same bowl. He, taking that [food], led him away.
He placed it in the hand of the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha took it, offered words of thanksgiving, and departed.
On that day, the deity residing in the parasol of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi uttered a great sound in praise: “Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift! It is well-established upon Upaṭṭhila!
Hearing this, the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi thought: “Thus has the deity offered her thanks.”
Thinking, "This alone is the supreme gift," he requested the merit from that act. Annabhāra then gave him the merit.
With a mind full of faith, the merchant Sumanas gave him a thousand [pieces of gold] and said, "From now on, you have no need to perform manual labor with your own hands;
build a suitable house and dwell here permanently."

Because almsfood given to a Paccekabuddha who has emerged from the attainment of cessation yields a magnificent result on that very day, the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi took it with him as he went into the presence of the king.
The king, however, looked at it with great respect. The merchant said, "Your Majesty, this is indeed worthy of being looked upon."
Having spoken thus, he described the deed committed by that man and also explained how he himself had given him the thousand pieces of money. Upon hearing this, the king was pleased with him;
having granted him the thousand pieces, he commanded him, saying, "Build a house in such-and-such a place and dwell there," and thus assigned him a site for his home.
As he had that place cleared, large jars of treasure rose up from the ground.
Having seen them, they informed the king. The king, having had all the wealth brought out and seeing it piled up, asked:
“In whose house in this city is there such an amount of wealth? “In no one’s, Your Majesty,” they replied.
“In that case, let this Annabhāra be known as the Great Wealthy Merchant (Mahādhanaseṭṭhi) of this city. On that very day, he raised the merchant’s parasol over him.
Having been a merchant, he performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and was reborn in the world of the devas.

After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a long time, at the time of our Blessed One’s appearance, he took conception in the house of the Sakyan Sukkodana in the city of Kapilavatthu.
When he was born, they gave him the name Anuruddha. He [was the son] of Mahānāma the Sakyan...
The younger brother of the Blessed One, the son of his father’s younger brother, was exceedingly delicate and possessed of great merit.
His food appeared in a golden bowl alone. Then one day, his mother thought, “My son does not even know the word ‘there is not’;
I shall make him understand it. Thinking thus, she took an empty golden bowl and covered it with another golden bowl.
Having closed it, he sent it to him; along the way, deities filled it with divine cakes.
Thus, possessing great merit, surrounded by adorned dancing girls in three palaces suited to the three seasons, he enjoyed great prosperity like a god.
At that time, for us as well, the Bodhisatta descended from the Tusita heaven and was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Suddhodana.
Having gradually reached maturity and lived for twenty-nine years in the midst of the household life,
he made the Great Renunciation and, having gradually realized omniscient knowledge at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), remained there for seven weeks.
Having spent time at Isipatana in the Deer Park and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he went to Rājagaha to bring benefit to the world and dwelt in the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, King Suddhodana said, "It is said my son has arrived in Rājagaha;
go, I say, and bring my son back," and he dispatched ten ministers with a retinue of a thousand each.
They all went forth by means of the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination.
Among them, when the Elder Udāyin requested that the Blessed One go on a tour, the Blessed One departed from Rājagaha accompanied by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed.
He traveled to the city of Kapilavatthu, displayed many miracles at the assembly of kinsmen, and delivered a Dhamma discourse distinguished by its wonders.
Having caused the great multitude to drink the drink of the Deathless, on the following day he took his bowl and robe, stood at the city gate, and reflecting,
"What indeed is the custom of all Buddhas who have come to a noble city?"— knowing that "wandering for alms from house to house in regular order is the custom"—
he wandered for alms from house to house in regular order. The king [thought], "Your son is wandering for alms."
Having heard this, he arrived in great haste; after hearing the Dhamma in the street, he entered his own residence and offered great honor and hospitality.

The Blessed One, having performed the duty of supporting his kinsmen there and having ordained Prince Rāhula, set out from the city of Kapilavatthu on a journey through the Malla country and before long reached the Anupiya Mango Grove.
At that time, King Suddhodana, having assembled the Śākya clan, said:
"If my son had lived as a householder, he would have become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven treasures and surrounded by a host of kṣatriyas;
even my grandson, Prince Rāhula, would have followed him, surrounding him along with the host of kṣatriyas. You too..."
"Understand this matter: now that my son has become a Buddha, let the kshatriyas be his retinue;
each of you give one boy from your respective families. When this was said, eighty-two thousand kshatriya youths went forth all at once.
At that time, Mahānāma Sakka was the head of a household; he [took] his own younger brother, Anuruddha Sakka...
Having approached him, he said this: "Dear Anuruddha, at present many well-known Sakyan youths are following the Blessed One who has gone forth by going forth themselves.
Yet, in our family, no one has yet gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
Therefore, either you go forth, or I shall go forth. Having heard this, Anuruddha—
Having no desire for the household life, he went forth from the home into homelessness with himself as the seventh.

The sequence of his renunciation is recorded in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka itself. Thus, after they had gone to Anupiya and gone forth, during that very same rainy season, the Elder Bhaddiya attained arahantship, and the Elder Anuruddha developed the divine eye.
Devadatta attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); the Elder Ānanda was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*);

and the Elders Bhagu and Kimila later reached arahantship. For all these elders, their former aspirations and resolutions (*pubbapatthanābhinīhāra*) will become manifest at the respective places where they were reborn. This Elder Anuruddha [is the disciple] of the General of the Dhamma...

Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher’s presence, Anuruddha went to the Pācīnavaṃsa grove in the Cetiya country and, while practicing the duties of a recluse, reflected upon the seven thoughts of a Great Man;

he grew weary at the eighth. The Teacher, knowing that "Anuruddha is wearying at the eighth thought of a Great Man," and thinking, "I shall fulfill his aspiration," went there and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.

Having sat down and fulfilled the eighth thought of a Great Man, and having expounded the practice of the Great Noble Lineage adorned by contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation, he rose into the air and returned to the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
As soon as the Tathāgata had departed, the Elder became one who possessed the threefold knowledge and was a great destroyer of the taints, thinking: "The Teacher, knowing my mind..."
Having come and fulfilled the eighth thought of a Great Man, he gave it to me, and my heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment.
Then, concerning the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dhamma and his own realization of the Dhamma, he uttered these verses of inspired utterance:
“Knowing my intention, the Teacher, supreme in the world, [fulfilled it].”
With a mind-made body, he approached by means of psychic power.
"When a thought arose in me, he taught even further than that:
the Buddha, who delights in the unproliferated, taught the unproliferated."
“Having understood his Dhamma, I dwelt delighting in the Teacher’s dispensation;
the threefold knowledge has been attained, and the Buddha’s instruction is fulfilled.

Later on, while residing at the Great Monastery in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher placed Anuruddha in the foremost position, declaring: “Among the bhikkhus possessed of the divine eye, Anuruddha is the chief.”

421. Thus, having received from the Blessed One the position of being foremost among those possessing the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), he recalled his own past karma and, out of joy, proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), beginning with the words: "Sumedha, [you said] 'I am the Blessed One'.

In that context, "beautiful" refers to the wisdom of establishing [the path], the wisdom of the paths and fruits, the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā*), and that which is comprised of the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "I saw" (addasaṃ) that Blessed One— who possesses wisdom (medhā), thus being "well-wisened" (sumedha)—
the one endowed with good fortune, the elder of the world, the most excellent, the foremost, who has first emerged from saṃsāra, the leader among men, the peerless one,
who dwells having gone before others, withdrawn, secluded, and departed from the delight of social company and crowds.

422. *Sambuddhaṃ*: because he has awakened to all phenomena by himself; "having approached" means having gone into his presence. *Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna*: having placed the ten fingers joined together upon the head;

this is the meaning. The rest is of plain meaning. 430. *Divā rattiñca passāmi*: "I see by day and by night"; the meaning is that at that time, both in the world of the devas and in the world of humans, I saw a league (yojana) all around with the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).

431. *Sahassalokaṃ ñāṇena*: "The thousandfold world-system by knowledge"; the meaning is that with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), I saw a thousand world-systems (*sahassacakkavāḷa*). [Of] the Teacher...
"In the teaching" (*sāsane*) means: now, in the teaching of the Blessed One Gotama. "This is the fruit of the gift of a lamp," that is, of the offering of a lamp;
by this fruit, he has attained, acquired, and produced the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*)—this is the meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Anuruddha is complete.
3–5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta begins with the words, “A reciter, a bearer of mantras,” and so forth.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation in various states of existence, [attained this state].

Even before the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a prominent brahmin family and gradually attained maturity. Later, when the Blessed One Padumuttara had appeared and was teaching the Dhamma to those capable of being trained,
he went to the monastery together with a great multitude of people, in the manner described above.
Sitting at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who preach the Dhamma.

Thinking, "In the future, it is fitting that I too become like this," he approached the Teacher after the assembly had risen at the conclusion of the teaching, invited Him [for a meal], and [proceeded] in the manner described below.
Having paid great honor to the Blessed One, he said this to him: "Venerable Sir, by virtue of this service, I do not aspire for any other success;

rather, just as this bhikkhu was established by you on the seventh day as the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma, may I too, in the future, in the dispensation of a certain Buddha, [be the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma]."
He made an aspiration, saying, "May I become the foremost. The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied:
"In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise;
having gone forth in his dispensation, you shall become the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma."
Thus, having performed wholesome deeds for the duration of his lifespan, when he passed away from there, he accumulated a store of merit for one hundred thousand eons.

Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn at the time of our Blessed One in a prominent brahmin family in the brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu, as the nephew of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña.
They gave him the name Puṇṇa. After the Teacher had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually came to reside near Rājagaha.

There, Puṇṇa went forth under Aññā Koṇḍañña, received full ordination, and while applying himself to diligent effort, brought all the duties of a renunciant to their ultimate fulfillment. Then, [he thought: “In the presence of the One Possessing the Ten Powers...”
Saying, “I shall go,” he came into the presence of the Teacher together with the Elder Mātula;

however, having stayed right in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu, he applied himself to practice through systematic attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and, before long, having brought his insight (*vipassanā*) to maturity, attained Arahatship.
Furthermore, five hundred sons of noble family who had gone forth under the Elder Puṇṇa were there, and the Elder [instructed] them...

He exhorted them with the ten bases of discourse. Having all been exhorted with the ten bases of discourse, they stood firm in his instruction, attained arahantship, and realizing that the purpose of their going forth had reached its culmination, they approached their preceptor and said:
"Venerable sir, we have reached the culmination of the purpose of our going forth; and as for the ten bases of discourse..."
"The time has now come for us to see the One of Ten Powers. When the Elder heard their words, he thought:
"The Teacher knows that I have attained the ten bases of discourse. When I teach the Dhamma, I do so without ever departing from those ten bases of discourse.
Furthermore, if I go, all these bhikkhus will follow me, surrounding me on all sides."
"It is not fitting for me to go with my retinue to see the One of Ten Powers; let these people go first to see the One of Ten Powers.
Then he said to them: "Friends, you go on ahead and see the One of Ten Powers;
pay homage at the feet of the Tathāgata in my name, and I too shall come by the path you have taken."

All those elder monks—residents of the kingdom that was the Blessed One’s birthplace, all of whom were destroyers of the taints and had attained the ten topics of discourse—having set aside their preceptor’s instruction and paid homage to the Elder, proceeded on tour by stages.
Having traversed a road of sixty yojanas, they arrived at the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana in Rājagaha; there, having bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
They sat down. Now it is the custom for the Blessed Buddhas to exchange greetings with visiting monks;

therefore, the Blessed One, having performed a sweet greeting with them according to the method beginning with, "Is it bearable, monks?", and having asked, "From where have you come, monks?", [spoke] again.
When they replied, "From his native land," the Blessed One asked, "Who, monks, among the bhikkhus born in that native land and living as fellow celibates there,
is so highly esteemed as one who is himself few in desires and who speaks to the bhikkhus on the theme of fewness of desires?
He then questioned the bhikkhu who had attained the ten bases of discourse, and they informed him, "Venerable sir, it is the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta."
Having heard their conversation, the Venerable Sāriputta desired to see the Elder.

Then the Teacher went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. When the Elder Puṇṇa heard that the One of Ten Powers had arrived there, he thought, "I shall see the Teacher," and having gone, he reached the Tathāgata right inside the Fragrant Chamber. The Teacher [expounded] the Dhamma to him.

He taught the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, the Elder went to the Blind Men’s Grove for seclusion and sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
The Elder Sāriputta, having heard of his arrival, followed behind him, and after observing a suitable spot, he approached the one sitting at the foot of that tree.
Having exchanged greetings with the Elder, he asked him about that sequence of purification.
As the Elder explained each point he was asked, he greatly delighted his mind with the Parable of the Chariot. They both rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken words.
Then, at a later time, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Teacher declared the Elder to be "foremost."
“Monks, among my disciples who are monks preachers of the Dhamma, this Puṇṇa stands foremost”—thus he placed him at the head of that list.
Recalling his former karma and, through a state of joy, expounding the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he spoke the words beginning with “ajjhāyako.
Therein, “ajjhāyako” means one who causes many brahmins to recite and train [in the Vedas]. “Mantadhāro” means one who upholds the mantras.
“Meaning”: it is said that one should preserve [it] by means of reciting, hearing, and giving the fourth Veda, which is reckoned as the *Veda*.

Regarding the phrase “of the three Vedas”: among the three Vedic texts known by the name “Veda”—namely those reckoned as the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*—the meaning is that he has reached the further shore, the culmination, through knowledge of these three Vedas which ought to be preserved by means of wisdom. “I am placed before... [is the remainder].
"Surrounded by my disciples" means I was encircled by those disciples who were my constant retinue.
"I approached the Supreme among Men" means I went near the Blessed One, the highest of men; this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.
(Verse 438) "Knowing the method of the Abhidhamma": at that time, during the era of that Buddha, I was one skilled in the method of the Abhidhamma.
The meaning is as follows: "Through purity in the *Kathāvatthu*": one who is skilled in the purity found in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise;
or one who is skilled in the ten topics of discussion (*kathāvatthu*), such as the discourse on fewness of wishes and contentment.
Having made known and awakened all the wise members of the Saṅgha through that purity in the *Kathāvatthu*, I dwell—free from taints and free from defilements—and I pass my time.

439. "In five hundred aeons from here"—that is, in five hundred aeons from this auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*) adorned by these five Buddhas—they were well-proclaimed and well-known as the four great Wheel-turning Monarchs (*cakkavatti-rāja*), lords and preeminent rulers over the four continents beginning with Jambudīpa, endowed with the seven treasures such as the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*). This is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Puṇṇamantāṇiputta is completed.
3–6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upāli begins with the verse "In the city of Haṃsavatī... This [Elder] also [made offerings] during the time of previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great wealth within the city of Haṃsavatī as a brahmin. One day,
while listening to a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he heard the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Seeing him being appointed, he performed a service for the Teacher and aspired to that position.
Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until this arising of a Buddha, when he was reborn in the household of a barber.
They gave him the name Upāli. When he reached maturity, [he became a servant] to the six khattiyas, beginning with Anuruddha.

Having become a dear companion, when the Tathāgata was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove, he went forth together with six khattiya princes who were departing for the homeless life, and he himself received the going-forth. The procedure for his ordination is recorded in the Pāḷi itself.
Having gone forth and been fully ordained, he received a meditation subject from the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, for me..."
“Grant permission for me to dwell in the forest,” he said. [The Teacher replied: “For a bhikkhu dwelling in the forest, only one burden will increase;
but for one dwelling in my presence, both the burden of insight (vipassanā-dhura) and the burden of study (gantha-dhura) will be fulfilled.
Having accepted the Teacher’s word, he applied himself to the practice of insight and before long attained Arahantship.
He attained it. The Teacher himself also had him master the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
Later on, he adjudicated these three cases: the Bhārukaccha case, the Ajjuka case, and the Kumārakassapa case.

The Teacher, applauding each decision, established those three adjudications as the origin of the rules (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya.

441. Thus, having attained this foremost position and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming that *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the words beginning with "In the city of Haṃsavatī.

Therein, "Haṃsavatī" refers to that city which has a wall or enclosure (*vati*, *pākāra*) surrounding it in the shape of a circle of swans (*haṃsa*). Alternatively, it is so called because of the many swans [there].
It is called Haṃsavatī because swans (*haṃsa*) dwell there, running hither and thither among ponds, lotus-pools, lakes, marshes, and so forth;
[it is the genitive] "of that Haṃsavatī. "A brahmin named Sujāta" means one who is well-born (*sujāta*);

according to the expression "uncensured and unreviled," the meaning is that he was born without being subject to reproach. "One with a hoard of eighty crores" means one possessing a heap of wealth amounting to eighty crores.
The connection is as follows: there was a well-born brahmin named Sujāta, who possessed abundant wealth and grain, indeed possessing incalculable wealth and grain.
(442) Furthermore, demonstrating his great majesty, [the author] said "ajjhāvako" and so forth. Therein, "ajjhāvako" means one who teaches others the three Vedas and so on.
"Mantadhara": "manta" refers to wisdom (*paññā*); thus, it means one who possesses the wisdom that knows the *Athabbana-veda*, grammar (*byākaraṇa*), and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: "One who has reached the further shore of the three Vedas" means one who has attained the culmination of the three Vedas known as the *Iruveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*.

"In the science of marks" (*lakkhaṇe*) means in the treatise on marks, that is, in the books explaining the marks visible on the hands, feet, and so forth of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Wheel-turning Monarchs (*cakkavattis*), women, and men. "In history" (*itihāse*) means "thus indeed it was."
*Itihāsa-āsā* refers to a text that elucidates ancient narratives (*porāṇakathā*). *Sadhamme* means in one’s own doctrine, the Brahmin doctrine;
the meaning is that he has reached the perfection, the end, the limit, or attained it.
443. *Paribbājā* refers to those disciples of the Nigaṇṭhas; the connection is that they were all of various views wandering then upon the earth, the surface of the world.
445. The meaning is that for as long as a time as it takes for a Jina not to arise, for that long there is no such term as "Buddha.
446. *Accayena ahorattan* means day and night (*ahoratta*); the meaning is "after the passing of many years. The rest is easily understood. 454.

*Mantāṇiputto* means the son of the barber’s daughter named Mantāṇī; the meaning is that he received the name Puṇṇa because of his fullness of months and fullness of days. The connection is: "He will be a disciple of that Teacher; he will become one."

455. "Thus he praised the Buddha"—this means that the Blessed One Padumuttara, in this manner and in a beautiful way, praised Sunanda, who was a giver of joy, and thus gave him a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
Making all people—the entire multitude of people—laugh heartily and feel gladness, he manifested his own power, his own strength.
The connection is with the word "doing" (*karonto*). 456.
Immediately after that, showing his own power by means of another's instruction, he spoke the passage beginning with "with palms joined" (*katañjali*).
At that time, prior to the appearance of the Buddha, all people were worshipping the ascetic Sunanda with their hands joined in reverence.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Having performed service for the Buddha"—meaning that although he was honored by all people, he did not harbor the conceit of thinking "I am honored";
rather, by performing great service to the Buddha's teaching, he purified his destiny and birth; this is the meaning. 457.
"Having heard the words of the Sage" means having heard the speech of that Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*); [this is stated] for the sake of the ease of the metrical composition.
Having shortened the vowel *ā* to *a*, it is stated as “vaca. Having heard these words of the Sage, “In a future time, a teacher named Gotama will appear in the world,” [he thought]:
“In whatever manner, by whatever means, I may see the Blessed One Gotama, in that same manner I shall perform, I will perform, the *kāra*—the additional task, the accumulation of merit.”
The connection is: "me" means "my"; "saṅkappo" means "there was an intention, a volition, and an act of attention.
458. "Having thought thus" means having thought, "I shall perform a work of merit.
"I reflected on the deed for myself" means I reflected on the deed, the task to be performed, thinking, "What kind of merit ought to be done by me?"
The meaning is: "What kind of action am I performing?"—that is, "What kind of meritorious deed (*puññakamma*) am I performing? Am I fulfilling it?
The phrase "in the unsurpassed field of merit" means in the Triple Gem (*ratnattaya*), which is devoid of anything superior and serves as the vessel for all merit.
"And this reciter of the scriptures, a monk" means this monk because he recites the texts by way of *sara-bhañña* (chanting with melody).
A monk who has received the name "Pāṭhika" because of his recitation;
among all those who are learned, readers, and reciters within the Buddha’s teaching, he was placed at the very head and established as the foremost in the Vinaya.
The meaning is: "I aspire to attain that position, which has been reached by that monk."
460. Thereafter, showing the means by which he himself performed meritorious deeds, he said: "This immeasurable wealth of mine," and so forth.

"Me" means for me; "immeasurable" (amita) means devoid of measure; "mass of wealth" (bhogarāsi); "unshakeable" (akkhobha) means incapable of being shaken; "resembling the ocean" (sāgarūpama) means like the ocean. The connection is:
"With such wealth—that is, with such riches—he caused a monastery (ārāma) to be built for the Buddha."
The remainder has its meaning already explained.

474. The connection is as follows: having sat in the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha), the Fully Enlightened One, having accepted the monastery (saṅghārāma) well-constructed and caused to be built by him, spoke—that is, uttered—this speech which illuminates the benefits of that monastery.
475. How so? "He who" refers to the ascetic who was the donor of the monastery; "well-constructed" means [constructed] with huts, caves, pavilions, palaces, watchtowers, walls, and so forth.
He gave the well-prepared monastery to the Buddha with a mind associated with joy (*somanassa-sampayutta-citta*).
"I shall praise him" means that I shall make that ascetic known, I shall make him manifest.
"Listen to my speech" means listen to the words of me as I speak, with attentive ears and undistracted minds.
The meaning is: "Keep this in mind.
(476) Showing the fruit of the pleasure grove given by him, he said: "Elephants, horses, chariots, infantry," and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand.
(477) "This is the fruit of the monastic park": the meaning is that this desirable fruit, consisting of prosperity to be experienced in the future, is the fruit, the result of giving a monastic park.
"Sixty-eight thousand" means sixty thousand and eighty thousand women who were well-adorned, meaning beautifully decorated and prepared;
"women with variegated garments and ornaments" means they were endowed with various and manifold kinds of clothes and jewelry.
"With pendants of jewels and earrings" means their ears were adorned with hanging pearl necklaces and jeweled ear-rings.
479. Describing the excellence of the physical beauty of those women, he said, "With large eyes," and so forth.
In this context, "āḷārapamhā" means those women whose eyes are large (āḷāra), like clusters of jewels; the sense is that they have eyes as round as bees.
"Hasulā" means having a nature for smiling; the sense is that they possess grace and charm. "Susaññā" means those whose bodily parts are beautiful to perceive.
"Thin-waisted" means having a small abdominal region. The rest is self-evident. 484. "An heir to his Dhamma":
an heir to the Dhamma of that Blessed One Gotama, a sharer in the portions of the Dhamma. "Legitimate son" (*oraso*):

born from the breast (*urasi jāto*). [He is one] endowed with the tenfold phonetic qualities—such as the lax and the tight—and produced in the five locations of the throat, palate, lips, and so forth.

The meaning is: "one whose son was born upon his chest" because, having heard the Dhamma taught by striking [the lute], he heard it and—having exhausted all defilements through the successive stages of the paths beginning with the path of stream-entry—stood in the state of Arahantship.

"Fashioned by the Dhamma" means that you will become manifest, fashioned by the Dhamma, by the righteous, without the use of the rod or the sword. "By name Upāli"—although his mother... [text continues]

By name he will be Mantāṇiputta; however, because he went forth together with Anuruddha and others and thus became one who is closely attached (*upālī*) to the Kṣatriyas—being joined (*yutta*) and endowed (*samaṅgībhūta*) in both body and mind—he will be a disciple of the Teacher by the name Upāli; this is the meaning. 485.
“Having reached perfection in the Vinaya” means having reached, having attained the limit and the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Regarding “in the *ṭhānāṭṭhāna*... [the text continues].
And "learned" (*kovidā*) means skilled in what is the cause and what is not the cause; "clever" (*cheko*) is the meaning.

"Bearing the Victor’s teaching" (*jināsanaṃ dhārento*) means bearing the instruction spoken by the Victor, or the Victor’s Three Baskets (*piṭakattaya*), by way of reciting, hearing, reflecting, and memorizing;

"observing" (*sallakkhento*) is the meaning. "He will dwell free from taints" (*viharissati anāsavo*) means being without defilements, with a personal existence (*attabhāva*) that does not falter in the four modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).
"Harissati pavattessatīti" means "he will carry on and cause it to proceed.
(487) "Aparimeyyupādāyā" means beginning from many hundreds of thousands [of years ago]. "Patthemi tava sāsananti" means:
"I aspire to your teaching"—that is, I desire your teaching with the thought, "May I become the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya within the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama."
The meaning is as follows: "This is my goal" means that this goal, which is reckoned as the state of being foremost, has been attained by me—this is the sense.
"The destruction of all fetters" is connected with the idea that the destruction of all fetters has been attained by me; the meaning is that Nibbāna has been realized.

488. Just as a person—a man—who is threatened by royal punishment, oppressed, or impaled upon a stake (sūlāvuta = one who is fixed or pierced on a stake), not finding—that is, not experiencing—any satisfaction or sweet pleasure on the stake, desires only liberation, so it is the connection [of the simile].
489–90. O Mahāvīra, the best of heroes among heroes, I have been struck by your rod of birth;

thus defeated and oppressed, bound by the stake of karma—being entangled and caught within the stake of wholesome and unwholesome karma—I am tormented and overcome by the sensation of thirst, distressed by the state of being afflicted with thirst, and made to suffer for the sake of *sāta*, that sweet pleasure within *saṃsāra*.
"I do not find, I do not obtain. The connection is as follows:

"I seek and search for liberation—the means of being fully released—from one who is being consumed by the three fires known as the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; or alternatively, from the three fires known as the fire of hell, the fire of the world's conflagration, and the fire of suffering.
Just as one who has gone hence and fallen under a royal punishment seeks liberation, so too have I fallen under the punishment of existence (*bhava*).
The connection is: "I seek complete liberation.
(491–2) Again, demonstrating the release from *saṃsāra* by way of a simile and its subject, he says:
"Just as by poison," and so forth. Therein, one who has been bitten all around (*āsamantato*) by a snake's venom is "poisoned" (*visāda*), meaning one who is bitten by a snake.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, one who eats—that is, swallows—poison such as *halāhala* poison is a "poison-eater" (*visāda*); this is the meaning.

A man who is a poison-eater, being afflicted by such poison, would seek and search for an antidote (*agada*), a medicine that serves as a means (*upāya*) for the alleviation and destruction of that poison. While searching for it, he [seeks] a destroyer of poison...
One might see and behold an antidote (*agada*), a medicine (*osadha*) that destroys poison.
Having drunk that medicine seen by himself, he would become happy for the sake of being released, for the sake of liberation from the poison, from the poison—such is the connection. 493.
"Just so it is said" means: just as, in whatever manner, that man [who was] bitten by a venomous snake, a poison-eater, [was freed] from the poison...
Just as one might become well after drinking a medicinal herb, in that very same way, I am thoroughly oppressed by the delusion of ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Seeking the medicine of the True Dharma" means seeking the medicinal herb known as the True Dharma (*saddhamma*). 494–5.
"Searching for the medicine of the Dharma" means searching for the medicinal herb of the Dharma for the destruction of the poison of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
"I have seen the teaching of the Sakyans" means that one has heard the teaching of Gotama, who was born of the Sakyan lineage.
"The foremost of all medicines" means that among all medicines, this medicine known as the Dhamma—the teaching of the Sakyans—is the foremost and supreme.
"The dispeller of all arrows" means the dispelling of all arrows, such as the arrow of passion and so forth.

The connection is as follows: having drunk the medicine known as the Dhamma—the medicine designated as "Dhamma" which brings about pacification—one eradicates and destroys all poison, namely the poison of the suffering of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Having eradicated that poison of suffering, one attains Nibbāna, which is ageless (*ajara*) because it is free from aging, deathless (*amara*) because it is free from dying, and cool (*sītibhāva*) because it has become cooled by being free from the fever of passion and other defilements.
"I have touched [it] and made it manifest"—this is the connection.
(496) Again, showing a simile for the darkness of the defilements (*kilesatama*), he said, "Just as one possessed by a spirit," and so forth. Therein, "just as" (*yathā*) means in whatever manner;

"possessed by a spirit" (*bhūtaṭṭhito*) means a person (*puruṣo*) who is seized and oppressed by a *bhūta* demon (*yakkha*). By the seizure of a *bhūta* (*bhūtaggāhena*), that is, by the seizure of a *yakkha*.
Afflicted and suffering, he would seek out a physician for spirits (*bhūtavejja*) for the sake of release and liberation from the spirit-possession (*yakkhaggāha*).
While seeking him, he might see a physician for spirits who is well-versed and skilled in the science of spirits (*bhūtavijjā*);
that physician for spirits would then dispel and destroy the possessing spirit (*āvesabhūta*) of that man seized by the *yakkha*, together with its very root.
The connection is: "having made it so that it will not be cultivated in the future along with its root, one should destroy and disintegrate it.
498. O Great Hero, supreme among heroes! I am oppressed by the seizing of darkness—that is, the seizing of the darkness of defilements.
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, for the sake of being released from that very darkness of defilements, [I seek] the light of knowledge, the light of wisdom.
"I seek" is the connection [of the sentence].
499. Then, immediately after that, the meaning is: they saw the Sakyan Sage, who purifies the darkness of the defilements and destroys the gloom of the defilements.
That Sakyan Sage [removed] my darkness, my gloom, the dimness of the defilements, just as a physician of the real [removes] a living being.
The connection is that he "dispelled" as if one possessed by a *yakkha*, meaning he drove it far away. 500.
Being thus liberated, I thoroughly cut—that is, I severed—the stream of *saṃsāra*, the flow of cyclic existence;
I warded off the stream of craving, the great flood of craving, leaving nothing behind and bringing it to non-arising. This is the meaning. Existence (*bhava*)...
"I have opened up everything" means that I have opened up—that is, destroyed—all the nine realms of existence, beginning with the realm of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*).
The connection is: "just as a physician for spirits (*bhūtavejja*) destroys from the root, so too have I opened them up from the root.
(501) Then, showing a simile for the search for *nibbāna*, he said "Just as," and so forth. In that context, "heavy" (*garuṃ*) means burdensome (*bhāriyaṃ*).
He swallows a *nāga*, thus he is a *garuḷa*. Or, he takes (*lāti*) or seizes (*ādadāti*) a heavy (*garuṃ*) *nāga*, thus he is a *garuḷa*, the King of the *garuḷas*.
He swoops down and descends upon a *pannaga*—a *nāga* so named because it does not go into the hands of others but remains in its own range as food for himself—in order to seize it;
[he does this] all around, extending over a hundred *yojanas* in every direction.
The connection is as follows: [he] agitates and churns the great lake, the great ocean, by means of the wind from his own wings.

502. That bird, a *supaṇṇa*—one whose nature is to travel through the air—having seized a serpent by its name, having hung it with its head downwards, and afflicting it here and there with various forms of torment, having taken hold of it firmly, goes wherever he desires.
The connection is: "Wherever one desires to go, there one sets out and goes.

(503) "Venerable Mahāvīra, just as a powerful, mighty garuḷa sets out after seizing a serpent, even so do I, seeking the unconditioned Nibbāna—which is not made by conditions—and searching for it by way of fulfilling the practice," [he said].
The connection is as follows: "I have washed away all the thousands of defilements (*kilesa*)—half of which are enumerated—and especially purified them through their total eradication.

(504) Just as a *garuḷa* dwells having seized and consumed a serpent, so too, seeing this supreme Dhamma—the highest Dhamma—I behold this state of peace, the state of *nibbāna*, which is unsurpassed (*anuttara*), meaning devoid of anything higher, by means of the paths and fruits.
The connection is: "Having taken it up, having grasped it, and having employed it, I dwell.
(505) Now, demonstrating the rarity of Nibbāna, he said: "The creeper named Āsāvatī," and so forth.
In that context, because the hope (*āsā*)—the desire—of all the gods exists in this creeper, it is called the creeper named Āsāvatī; [it grows] in the forest of the mind-creeper (*cittalatāvana*).
The meaning is that it was born and produced in a grove that had become dense with many kinds of creepers.
From that creeper, one fruit is produced after a thousand years; having elapsed a thousand years, one takes one fruit.
"That god" refers to that Āsāvatī creeper, which, after such a long time has passed since its fruit was so distant.
The gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm attend upon and honor that excellent creeper named Āsāvatī, which is found bearing fruit;
such was her status as the most supreme among creepers, dear to the gods—this is the connection [of the passage]. 507.
"Starting from a hundred thousand" means beginning from a period of one hundred thousand years. "I shall serve her, O Sage."
"Venerable sir, 'mona' is said to be wisdom; a muni is one possessed of wisdom, an omniscient one. I attend upon and serve that Blessed One.

'I pay homage morning and evening' means that I pay homage and offer salutation twice—both at the time of evening and at the time of morning—just as the gods of the Thirty-three [do] with the *āsāvatī* creeper morning and evening."
The connection is: "they attend upon. 508.

Regarding "fruitful service": because the attainment of Nibbāna occurred through the cause of seeing the Buddha, therefore the service rendered to the Buddha—the performance of duties and observances—is fruitful and not empty;
likewise, the acts of reverencing and prostrating are not in vain and are not empty. Thus...
Indeed, even though he had come from afar—from far away by way of abandoning cyclic existence—he did not fail or bypass this moment;
that is to say, he did not pass me by. (509) By means of seeing the Buddha, I have attained *nibbāna*;
[he ensured] my rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in a future state of existence.
The connection is: "While searching and examining, I do not see [it]. The connection is:

"I wander, being 'without acquisitions'—meaning devoid of and liberated from the acquisitions of the aggregates and the acquisitions of the defilements; separated from all defilements; and with a peaceful mind due to the absence of the fever of defilements."
510. Again, showing a simile for his own vision of the Buddha, he said, “Just as the lotus,” and so forth.
By the sun’s rays—that is, by contact with the sun’s rays—the lotus indeed blooms and unfolds, O Great Hero, O Supreme Hero;
likewise, by the Buddha’s rays—that is, by the radiance of the Dhamma-rays taught by the Blessed Buddha—it has bloomed. This is the meaning.
511–12. Again, demonstrating that through the sight of the Buddha there is the sight of Nibbāna, he said: "Just as the crane... and so forth. In this context:
in the womb of the crane—that is, among the species of cranes—there is never, at any time, a male to be found.
If it is asked, "Since no male exists, how does the conception of the cranes' offspring occur? [The answer is: when the clouds thunder, [they hear] the sound...
Having heard the thundering of the clouds, those female cranes always—meaning at all times—conceive a fetus;

that is to say, they carry an egg. For as long as the cloud does not thunder, for as long as the cloud does not make a sound, for that long they carry the fetus—the egg—for a very long time. When, at whatever time, the cloud rains...
When it thunders in various ways and rains, and the stream of rain pours down, at that time they are released from the burden of being held in the womb;
the meaning is that they cast out the egg. 513.
Thereafter, showing the perfection of the simile, he said: "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth. Of Padumuttara...

The connection is as follows: "At that time, by following the sound of the rain-cloud of Dhamma— meaning the thundering of the Buddha as he roared with the rain-cloud of Dhamma consisting of the teachings on conventional and ultimate truth— I grasped, indeed took up, the womb of Dhamma,
which is the womb of the accumulation of merit such as generosity and virtue, and which serves as the necessary condition for the unfolding [of enlightenment]."
514. Beginning from a hundred thousand aeons ago, I have carried and fulfilled the womb of merit—the accumulation of merit consisting of generosity, virtue, and so forth.
As long as the Dhamma-cloud of the Buddha’s teaching does not thunder—that is, as long as it is not preached by a Buddha—I am not released, nor do I release myself, from this burden;
that is, I do not become separate from the burden of the womb of saṃsāra. This is the connection [of the verse].

515. Venerable Sir, when the Sakyan Sage, born of the Sakyan lineage, roared and proclaimed the Dhamma like a rain-cloud in the delightful and charming city named Kapilavatthu—your father, the great King Suddhodana—at that time, I was liberated and released from the burden of the womb of saṃsāra; such is the connection.

516. After that, demonstrating the path and fruit attained by himself, he said, "Emptiness," and so forth. Therein, it is "emptiness" (suññatā) because of the absence of self and what belongs to self;
it is the "signless liberation" (animitta-vimokkha) because of the absence of all signs of lust, hatred, delusion, and the defilements;
and it is the "wishless liberation" (appaṇihita-vimokkha) because of the absence of craving and longing. Thus, I have attained the Noble Path.
The connection is with the word "bhāvesiṃ" (I cultivated). "And all four fruits" means that I realized all four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
"Thus I unraveled the phenomena" means that I unraveled—that is, destroyed—the tangle or thicket of all phenomena.
The commentary on the second recitation section is completed. 517.
Following that, demonstrating the specific distinction he himself had attained, he said, "Immeasurable with respect to the basis," and so forth.
In this context, "immeasurable" (*aparimeyya*) means that which is not measurable; it is that which cannot be measured or calculated by way of counting years.
The goal (*attha*). Taking that immeasurable eon as the starting point, I aspire for your teaching—your teaching—to be thus:
"In the future, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama, may I become the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
The present tense is used here in the sense of the past; the meaning is "I have aspired. "That goal of mine" means that goal, consisting of this aspiration, belongs to me.
The meaning is "attained and accomplished. The connection is: "the unsurpassed state of peace, Nibbāna, has been attained and reached.
518. Because I have attained it, I have reached perfection and reached the culmination in the Vinaya, that is, in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Just as the seer (isi) Pāṭhika was the foremost among the bearers of the Vinaya in the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
"He became well-known as a reciter" means that he was indeed so called.

"There is no one equal to me" means that there is no other person equal to me in being a bearer of the Vinaya. "I uphold the teaching" means that I maintain and fulfill the teaching, which consists of the instructions and admonitions.
519. Furthermore, demonstrating his own distinction, he said, "In the Vinaya and in the Khandhaka," and so forth.

Therein, "Vinaya" refers to the two Vibhaṅgas. "Khandhaka" refers to the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. "And in the Tikaccheda" refers to the groups of three such as the Saṅghādisesas, the Tikas, the Pācittiyas, and so on.
"And in the fifth" refers to the Parivāra. Herein, in this entire Vinaya Piṭaka, my doubt (*vimati*) and perplexity (*dveḷhaka*) [have been resolved].
"There is not" means it does not exist. "In the vowels" (*akkhare*) refers to the vowels beginning with *a*, which are included within the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"In the consonants" (*byañjane*) refers to the consonants beginning with *ka*. The connection is: "I have no uncertainty or doubt regarding these.

(520) "In the suppression and the rehabilitation" (*niggahe paṭikamme ca*) refers to the suppression of wicked monks and the granting of the *parivāsa* probation and so forth to monks who have committed offenses.

"Skilled" means one who is expert in the restoration of discipline (*paṭikamma*), in what is proper and improper (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), and in what constitutes a valid reason and what does not (*kāraṇe ca akāraṇe ca*).

"And in reinstatement" (*osāraṇe ca*) means in the reinstatement or readmission by way of the cessation of formal acts such as censure (*tajjanīyakamma*). "And in rehabilitation" (*vuṭṭhāpane ca*) refers to being skilled in rehabilitating from an offense—that is, in making one free from offense.
In all these respects, he has "reached perfection" (*pāramiṃ gato*); that is, in every respect... [the sentence continues].
"Reached the conclusion in the work on the Vinaya" means he was skillful and clever.
"In the Vinaya and in the Khandhakas" refers to the aforementioned types of Vinaya and Khandhakas;
having set down and established the words, that is, the words of the Sutta. "Having disentangled from both" means from both the Vinaya and the Khandhakas.

"Having produced [the meaning], having disentangled it, and having brought forth the method. "From the flavor" means from the function (*kicca*). "I shall resolve" means "I shall perform the resolution" (*osāraṇa*); this is the sense.
"And skilled in etymology" (*niruttiyā ca kusalo*) means expert in conventional designations such as "tree," "cloth," "pot," "garland," "picture," and so forth.

"And proficient in what is meaningful and what is meaningless" means proficient—that is, discerning—in prosperity (*vaḍḍhi*) as being meaningful and in decline (*hāni*) as being meaningless; this is the sense.
"There is nothing unknown by me" means that throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka or the Three Piṭakas, there is nothing unknown,

unperceived, or obscure to me. "I am the foremost in the Teacher’s Dispensation" means that within the Buddha’s Dispensation, I alone am the foremost, the best, and the most excellent among those who uphold the Vinaya.
523. "Today, in this very time, in the teaching and the word of the Blessed One, the Son of the Sakyans, I am one skilled in form;
in the vision of form—that is, in the discernment of the Vinaya—I dispel and eliminate all doubt and every uncertainty.
This is the connection. "I cut through all uncertainties" refers to [doubts such as]: "Did I exist in the past? and so forth.
The meaning is: "I cut off, pacify, and utterly destroy all sixteen kinds of doubt arising with respect to the three times.
(524) "Word by word and also phrase by phrase" means: the preceding word (*pada*) and the subsequent word (*anupada*), and each individual syllable (*akkhara*).
"Phrasing" (*byañjana*) refers to the tenfold manner of phrasing, such as the soft and the hard consonants, as well as the rules of phonology.

"In the introduction" (*nidāne*) means in the introductory setting, beginning with the words "At that time. "In the conclusion" (*pariyosāne*) means in the summary. "Skilled in all respects" (*sabbattha kovidō*) means one who is proficient in all six of these points. 525.
Following that, in order to manifest the qualities of the Blessed One himself, he spoke the verse beginning with "Just as a king endowed with power," and so forth. Therein:
Just as a powerful king, endowed with physical strength and the power of an army,
having subdued, completely captured, or driven away the army of another rival king, might scorch, burn, and cause suffering;
"having conquered the battle" means having won, having especially triumphed over the encounter with the enemy's army in combat.

"Having achieved victory": "Let him establish a city there"—the meaning is that in that conquered place, he should cause a city to be built, a dwelling-place adorned with palaces, watchtowers, and so forth.
"And a rampart and a moat": in that city thus established, [he should build] a rampart, a rampart made of bricks white with plaster.
The connection is with the word "kāraye" (should cause to be made). One should also cause a moat (*parikhā*) to be made—namely, a mud moat, a water moat, and a dry moat.

One should also cause a watchtower (*esikā*), a gatehouse (*dvārakoṭṭhaka*), and a large quadrangular gatehouse (*koṭṭhaka*) such as a four-storied one to be built for the sake of beautifying the city;
and various types of watchtowers (*aṭṭālaka*) of different kinds, such as those with four stories.
The connection is: "He should cause many various and manifold high watchtowers to be built, or have them built.

(527) Regarding "crossroads and squares": the connection is that he should not only build walls and such, but should also cause crossroads—where four roads meet—and squares—interior streets—to be built. "Well-apportioned marketplaces" means well-divided.
The meaning is: "He should cause a marketplace consisting of many thousands of shops to be built, divided into its various sections.
"He should cause an assembly hall (*sabhā*) to be built there" means that in that constructed city, he should have a hall for legal proceedings (*dhammādhikaraṇasālā*) built.
The connection is: "He should cause a hall of justice to be built for the purpose of deciding what is beneficial and what is harmful, as well as for determining prosperity and decline."
"528. For the purpose of crushing enemies" means for the purpose of repelling rival kings. "To know the defective and the non-defective" means to know both what is faulty and what is faultless.
"For the protection of the army" means for the sake of guarding the military force consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—that is, the entire host;
[the king] who is the lord of the city [appoints] the commander-in-chief (senāpati).
"He appoints a general, a high minister" means he establishes him in that position.
"For the protection of the king's property" means for the purpose of guarding and protecting from all sides the royal goods such as gold, silver, pearls, and gems;
[he appoints one] skilled in storing, skilled in preservation, [thinking], "Let my property not be lost."
The connection is as follows: "He appoints a clever man, a guardian of goods, who is guarding the goods, to be stationed in the treasury.
(Verse 530) "He is devoted to the king" means that the wise man is devoted to, or partial toward, the king.
"And he desires his prosperity" means that he wishes for and desires the growth and increase of that king who is thus situated.
The connection is as follows: the king grants the wise man the authority and sovereignty over legal cases so that he may act toward his friend with true friendship.
(531) *Uppātesu* means in the case of portents such as falling meteors, fires in the quarters of the sky, and so forth.

*Nimittesu* means in the case of omens such as those [signs] cut by mice, and in the treatises for knowing omens, thinking, "This omen is auspicious; this omen is inauspicious. *Lakkhaṇesu*... [the text continues].

The connection is as follows: that king appointed him to the office of *porohicca* (royal chaplain)— a wise man, skilled and expert in the manuals for discerning the marks on the hands and feet of women and men,
a reciter (*ajjhāyaka*), an expounder of grammar to many disciples, a bearer of mantras,
a keeper of the mantras known as the Three Vedas, and a scholar.

532. "Endowed with these factors": the connection is that the king who is endowed (*sampanna*)—that is, possessed of—the aforementioned factors or limbs (*aṅga*) is called, or spoken of, as a "Khattiya. "They always protect the king":
these ministers, beginning with the commander-in-chief, always—at all times—protect and guard that king. Like what? Like the *cakkavāka* bird.
The meaning is: like a cakravāka bird protecting its own kin who are afflicted and fallen into suffering.

533. "In that very way, O Great Hero"—O supreme hero—just as that king, endowed with all the constituent parts such as the army and the ministers, remained stationed having closed the city gates, even so do you, having slain the enemies and struck down the adversaries, [stand] like a kṣatriya over the world including the devas.

The connection is as follows: for the world including the devas, for the world that is currently evolving, he is called and spoken of as a "Dhamma King" (*dhammarājā*) because, having become a king through the fulfillment of the Dhamma of the ten perfections, he rules by means of the Dhamma and with justice.
534. "Having expelled the sectarians" (*titthiye nīharitvāna*): having expelled all the sectarians who were his adversaries by virtue of his status as a Dhamma King.
Having completely carried away [the enemy], having rendered him defenseless, and having even driven out Māra—the wielder of power—along with his army and his weapons;
"having dispelled that darkness" means having dispelled and shattered the darkness of delusion known as *tama*;

"the city of Dhamma" refers to that which is comprised of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), and that which is comprised of the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), the profound methods, and the *Samantapāsādikā* (the Compendium of Dhamma).
"Or he measured out and built a city" means that he established it. 535.
"Virtue is the rampart there" means that in that established City of Dhamma, the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is the rampart.

"Knowledge is your gate-tower" means that for you, it is precisely the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), the knowledge of latent tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*), the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), the knowledge of the past (*atītaṃsañāṇa*), and so forth.
"Knowledge is the gateway-tower"—this is the meaning. "Faith is your pillar, O Hero"—the meaning is:

"O Venerable One, from the time you were at the feet of Dīpaṅkara until now, for the sake of attaining omniscience, your pillar has been raised and adorned with the ornament of resolute faith (*saddhā*), characterized by unremitting exertion.
And "Restraint is your gatekeeper"—the meaning is: "Your restraint regarding the six sense-doors is your gatekeeper, providing protection, warding off, and guarding."
The meaning is "gatekeeper. 536.
"The watchtower of the foundations of mindfulness" means that for you, O Sage (muni), there is a watchtower with a flat roof consisting of the four foundations of mindfulness.
"Your wisdom is the crossroads, O Sage," venerable one; for you, O Sage, there is wisdom of many kinds, such as the three marvels (pāṭihāriya).
"Crossroads" (*caccara*) means the meeting of paths; the meaning is "city street.

"And the crossroads of the bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda-siṅghāṭa*) means that your four bases of psychic power—consisting of desire, energy, mind, and investigation—are the crossroads where the four paths meet.

"The city street well-constructed of Dhamma" (*dhamma-vīthi sumāpita*) means it is well laid out and prepared by the street consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment; the meaning is "that city of Dhamma."

537. “Suttantaṃ abhidhammañca”: here, in this City of Dhamma, for you, there is the Suttanta, the Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya—the entire, complete ninefold word of the Buddha, beginning with the Sutta and Geyya; "Dhammasabhā" means the hall of legal proceedings concerning the Dhamma.
538. “Suññataṃ animittañca”: the dwelling in emptiness obtained by way of the contemplation of non-self, and [the dwelling in the signless] by way of the contemplation of impermanence.
"And the dwelling in the signless" means the dwelling in the signless attained by way of the contemplation of suffering.

"And the wishless" means the wishless dwelling attained by way of the contemplation of suffering. "And the imperturbable" means the imperturbable dwelling—unmoving and unshaking—consisting of the four fruits of recluseship.
"And cessation" means Nibbāna, the cessation of all suffering. "This is your Dhamma-hut" refers to this entire collection of the nine supramundane states.
"Your Dhamma-hut" means your dwelling-place for the Dhamma. 539.
"Ranked foremost by wisdom" means foremost among those possessing wisdom by virtue of his wisdom.
Thus the Elder was ranked and established by the Blessed One as one skilled in ready wit and in the duties to be performed through wisdom, or in the employment of appropriate and excellent eloquence.

"By name Cheko, you are renowned as Sāriputta; O Dhammasenāpati, because you have mastered the collection of the Dhamma consisting of the Three Piṭakas, you act as the leader of the army, being preeminent therein—this is the meaning.
(540) 'O Sage, you are skilled in death and rebirth' means, venerable one, you are expert and proficient in both death and rebirth."
"Having reached the perfection of psychic power (*iddhi*)" means that he has reached—the limit, the culmination—of the various types of psychic power described as "having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one," and so forth. By name he is Kolita, the Elder Moggallāna, the family priest;
the connection is that he was your personal priest.
541. "O Bhante Muni, one who upholds the ancient lineage" means one who possesses knowledge (*ñāṇavanta*) and is a bearer of the ancient lineage, or one who knows it through tradition;
"of exalted power" (*uggatejo*) means of manifest power (*pākaṭatejo*); "difficult to approach" means difficult to assail or disturb, being unassailable—this is the meaning.

"Foremost by virtue of being a proponent of the ascetic practices" (*dhutavādiguṇenaaggo*) means he speaks and exhorts the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), such as the practice of wearing only three robes (*tecīvarikaṅga*). By virtue of being a proponent of the ascetic practices—that is, by virtue of the qualities of the ascetic practices.
The Elder Mahākassapa is the foremost and best; he is your "eye for the dice," meaning he is preeminent in the administration of legal affairs.
542. "O Sage, O Blessed One, you are one who has heard much and who upholds the Dhamma.

This means that because you have heard the many eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*), and because you have mastered them from the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, you are one who has heard much—namely, the many [teachings] numbering six hundred thousand.
Ānanda is a "bearer of the Dhamma" (dhammadhara) because he has retained the Dhamma of the scriptures as well as the ultimate Dhammas such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
He is called "Sabbapāṭhī" because he is the foremost and best among all those who recite and rehearse the texts within the Buddha’s Dispensation;
thus, the elder named Ānanda is known by the name Sabbapāṭhī. [The phrase] "Dhammārakkho tava" means...
"Of you"—that is, of you who are the guardian, protector, and keeper of the Dhamma-store consisting of the Triple Piṭaka; the meaning is "the treasurer of the Dhamma.

(543) "Having passed over all these"—the Blessed One, the Fortunate One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having passed over and set aside even these highly powerful elders such as Sāriputta and others, sent for me alone;
the meaning is that he made me his authority, he took me into account. [The] decision.
"Me pādāsi": the wise who know the Vinaya have taught and elucidated this;
"the determination of the Vinaya and the investigation of faults, the Blessed One gave (*pādāsi*) to me—that is, he gave it to me in a thorough manner—made it my very burden. This is the connection.
"Whatever question regarding the Vinaya": whatever question concerning the Vinaya any bhikkhu, a disciple of the Buddha, [poses] to me...
"He asks"; regarding that question asked therein, "I have no thought, doubt, or uncertainty.
"I shall explain that very matter"—this is the connection: "I shall speak upon that very point which was asked.
(545) "As far as the Buddha-field extends"—that is, to whatever extent within the sphere of the Buddha's authority, [one should approach] that Great Sage.
"Except for the Perfectly Enlightened One, there is no one like me, equal to me, in the Vinaya, in the Vinaya-piṭaka, or in the making of Vinaya decisions;
I alone am the foremost. From where could there be anyone superior to me?"—this is the connection. 546.
Sitting in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, Gotama, the Blessed One, thunders thus.
He utters the lion’s roar. How so? In the Vinaya—namely, in the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, the Mahāvagga, and the Cūḷavagga—and by the word "and" (ca), including the Parivāra—he roars thus:
"There is no one equal to Upāli, no one like Upāli. 547.
"As far as" (yāvatā) means as much of the Buddha’s speech as has been spoken and taught by the Buddha—the ninefold teaching of the Teacher, beginning with the Sutta and Geyya.
For one who thus sees: "All that has been proclaimed by the Teacher, that depth of the Vinaya, is contained within the Vinaya and is rooted in the Vinaya. 548.
"Recalling my own deed": Gotama, the bull among the Sakyas, the preeminent one of the Sakyan lineage, [recalled] my deed.
Having recalled my past aspiration through knowledge of the past lives and having known it directly, he went into the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and placed me in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are experts in the Vinaya, namely Upāli.
This is the connection [of the passage].
