549. “Starting from a hundred thousand [aeons]” means: beginning from a hundred thousand aeons, that goal which I sought—that which I aspired to—has been reached, attained, and acquired by me; it has reached its perfection in the Vinaya and its ultimate limit. This is the meaning. 550.
“In former times, in the past, I was a barber who brought joy to the Śākyas, the kings of the Śākya lineage, and who caused them happiness.
Having abandoned—that is, having especially relinquished and cast off—that birth, that family, and that womb—of the Great Seer (Mahesi).
The meaning is that he was born as a son of the Perfectly Enlightened One and attained the designation "Sakyaputta" (Son of the Sakyas) because he upheld the Dispensation.
551. Thereafter, showing the account of his own birth into a family of slaves, he said, "In the second aeon from this one," and so forth.
In that context, in the second aeon prior to this Bhaddakappa, there was a certain Kṣatriya king named Añjaso.

The connection is as follows: he was one of infinite splendor, of splendor exceeding all calculation, of immeasurable fame, with a retinue beyond measure, possessing great wealth, a lord of hundreds of thousands of millions of riches, a protector of the earth, a guardian of the world, and a defender. 552.
"Of that king" means: I am the son of such a monarch, a noble prince named Candana.
The connection is with the word *ahosi*. "I was" means that I was propped up, stiffened, and arrogant by the intoxication of birth, the intoxication of fame, and the intoxication of wealth.
(553) "A hundred thousand nāgas" refers to a hundred thousand elephants (*mātaṅga*), born of the lineage of Mātaṅga, with their temples split in three ways.

The connection is as follows: "Adorned with all ornaments, decorated with every kind of hand-ornament, and flowing with rut from the three places known as the eyes, ears, and temples, they constantly surrounded me at all times.
(554) "Surrounded by hosts of brindled ones" means that at that time, I was surrounded by my own army forces consisting of brindled elephants.
The connection is as follows: surrounded [by his retinue] and desiring to go to the park, wishing for [the elephant] named Sirika, he mounted that elephant and departed from the city.
(555) "Endowed with conduct" means being possessed of the fifteen factors of conduct, such as the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), and having guarded sense-faculties.
The Fully Enlightened One named Devala—a Paccekabuddha whose doors of the eye and other senses were closed, who was well-restrained, and whose body and mind were perfectly guarded—came before me;
that is to say, he arrived in my presence.
(556) Having sent for the nāga named Sirika, and having seen that Paccekabuddha who had arrived, I [sent] the nāga named Sirika.
"Having sent [the elephant] toward him, he assailed the Buddha; 'he provoked' means he incensed him.

Then, "having become enraged"—that is, because I had sent it after having pressed it excessively, that noble elephant became enraged at me and did not lift its foot; the meaning is that it remained perfectly still.
557. "Having seen the elephant with a wicked mind" means: having seen the elephant with a wicked mind—that is, with a hostile heart—I directed anger toward the Buddha and the Paccekabuddhas;
the sense is that I gave rise to hatred. "Having harassed the Sambuddha" connects as follows:
having harassed and tormented the Paccekasambuddha Devala, I went to the park.
"558. 'I find no pleasure therein' means that I find no pleasure in that biting; the meaning is that I do not obtain the sweet happiness caused by the biting.
'As if my head were aflame' means that my head, my own skull, is as if it were burning, as if it were on fire.
'I am consumed by a feverish heat' is because of the anger directed toward the Paccekabuddha."
"I am burning with the fever of remorse; my heart is hot"—this is the meaning.

559. "As far as the ocean's edge": by the power of that very evil deed, the entire great earth, reaching to the ocean and bounded by the sea, appears to me as if it were blazing and aflame—this is the meaning. "Having approached my father's presence"—thus...
When fear had arisen, I approached my father, the king; having approached him, I spoke these words—this is the meaning. 560.
"Like an enraged venomous snake" means like a venomous snake that is entirely provoked and angry; "like a mass of blazing fire";
"like a rutting elephant," meaning a supreme tusker with three-fold temporal flow, possessing tusks, who has arrived.

The connection is: "I encountered—that is, I struck—the Paccekabuddha, who is self-become and awakened by himself. (561) "The Buddha was encountered by me": that Paccekabuddha was encountered and struck by me;
he is "terrible" because he is incapable of being struck by others; he is one of "exalted asceticism," meaning his asceticism is manifest;
he is a "conqueror" (*jina*) because he has conquered the five Māras—one endowed with such qualities.
The meaning is: "I have offended a Paccekabuddha. "Before all are destroyed" means:
through our lack of respect for that Paccekabuddha, we shall all be destroyed; we shall perish in various ways, becoming like ashes—this is the meaning.
"We shall ask forgiveness of that Sage" means: of that Paccekabuddha, the Sage, before we are destroyed. As long as [we are not destroyed], so long...
"I shall ask for forgiveness"—this is the connection [of the sentence].

562. "If we do not cause him to reflect"—if we do not cause that Paccekabuddha, who is self-tamed, whose mind is subdued, composed, and one-pointed, to reflect [on his transgression], we shall ask for forgiveness.
Within seven days—from within seven days—[the end of the sentence follows].
"Within seven days from now, my entire kingdom will be scattered and destroyed.

(563) "Sumekhalo and Kosiko"—these four kings, beginning with Sumekhalo, having encountered and provoked these seers, having shown them disrespect, became ruined along with their kingdoms; that is to say, they perished together with the inhabitants of their realms and provinces.
(564) "When the seers become angry"—when, at whatever time, those who are self-restrained, restrained by bodily restraint and so forth, [become enraged].

The connection is as follows: when the *isayo*—those who practice the holy life (*brahmacārino*), those of supreme conduct, those of best conduct—become angry and experience dejection, they destroy the world together with its oceans, mountains, and devas.
(Verse 565) "Within three thousand *yojanas*" means that, having recognized the power of those *isayo*, [the king] sought to appease them for his transgression (*accaya*) and offense (*aparādha*).
The connection is: "He caused men to assemble in a region measuring three thousand *yojanas* for the purpose of instruction and for the purpose of clarification.
"I approached the Self-Become One" (*sayambhuṃ upasaṅkamim*) means I went near the Self-Become One, the Paccekabuddha; this is the meaning. 566.
"All in wet garments" (*allavatthā*): all the people gathered together with me were in wet garments, meaning their upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*) were soaked with water.

With their veins showing and their hair disheveled, with palms joined and hands placed upon their heads, they fell down and lay prostrate at the feet of the Buddha, the Paccekabuddha, and spoke these words: “Forgive us, O Great Hero,” and so forth;
the meaning is that they uttered and spoke such words.
567. O Great Hero, supreme among heroes, O Blessed One, Paccekabuddha: please forgive the offense committed by me through ignorance toward you;
dispel it, do not take it to heart—this is the meaning. The people, the multitude of people, specifically entreat that Blessed One:
"Dispel our fever—the fever of mental suffering caused by hatred and delusion."
"Make it thin; do not destroy our kingdom, do not cause the destruction of those dwelling in all the provinces and districts of the entire realm"—this is the meaning.

568. "All, including gods and humans": all humans together with the gods, along with the *dānavas* such as Pahārāda and others, and together with the *rakkhasas*, [may they] always, at all times, [strike] my head, my crown, with an iron-made club, a great mallet.
They would break it; they would shatter it.
569. Thereafter, demonstrating the Buddhas’ state of forgiveness and their absence of anger, he said: "Fire does not remain in water," and so forth.
In this regard, just as fire does not remain—that is, does not find a footing—in water, and just as a seed [does not grow] on a rock, on a mountain made of stone—

It does not grow; just as a worm or insect cannot remain in a medicinal herb, so too anger, mental agitation, and dejection do not arise or occur in Buddhas who have penetrated the truth or in Paccekabuddhas—this is the meaning.
(570) Furthermore, demonstrating the majesty of the Buddhas, he says "And just as the earth," and so forth. Therein, "and just as... [is explained as follows].
The earth is the ground, immovable and unshakable; likewise, the Buddha is immovable—this is the meaning.
Just as the ocean, the great sea, is immeasurable, impossible to measure or to grasp its limit, so too the Buddha is immeasurable—this is the meaning.
Just as space is unobstructed space, infinite and devoid of end, so too the Tathāgata is unshakeable, impossible to shake.
The meaning is "one who is impossible to agitate. 571.
Next, showing the words of forgiveness from the Paccekabuddha, he says: "Always patient, O great heroes," and so forth.

In that context, "great heroes" (mahāvīrā) refers to the Buddhas, who possess supreme energy; and "ascetics" (tapassino) refers to those who have received the name "tapas" because of their scorching (tapanato) of evils.
The connection is as follows: those endowed with energy, patient, perfected in patience, and forgiving of the offenses of others—those who are forgiving and ever-enduring at all times.
"Of those who are patient and forgiving" refers to those Buddhas who are patient, joined with patience, forgiving of the offenses of others, and enduring.
The meaning is that there is no going along wrong paths by means of desire and so forth.
Having spoken these words, the Fully Enlightened One— or the Solitary Buddha— dispelling, repeatedly dispelling the fever,
the burning that has arisen in beings, stood before the great multitude of people assembled there, including the king.
"Face-to-face" means that at that time, in that moment, he rose up into the sky, the atmosphere; this is the meaning.

(Verse 573) "O wise one, by that deed"—O wise one (*dhīra*), endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), by that deed, namely the act of disrespect committed toward a Paccekabuddha, I attained a state of inferiority and baseness in this final existence, the birth of a barber serving as a courtier for kings.
The meaning is "having approached" or "having arrived. "Having completely transcended that birth" means having thoroughly and utterly transcended that birth which is dependent on others.
"I entered the city free from fear" means I entered and had entered the great city of Nibbāna, the city of Nibbāna devoid of fear.
Even then, O Great Hero, O Supreme among Heroes— even at that time, when I had offended the Paccekabuddha—
the Self-Existent Paccekabuddha dispelled and removed the fever, the distress of body and mind, which had arisen because of my offense.
He [dispelled] me, who was burning, burning with remorse and anxiety right after that, and being tormented.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: having seen the fault well-established as a fault, and having seen it clearly established, he asked for forgiveness and endured that transgression.
(575) "Even today, O Great Hero"—O Supreme Hero—even today, at the time of our meeting, by the three fires:
either those known as the fire of passion, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; or those known as the fire of hell, the fire of the hungry ghosts, and the fire of saṃsāra.
The Blessed One caused me— who was burning and experiencing suffering— to reach, that is, to attain, the state of coolness known as the tranquility of body and mind,
or indeed Nibbāna itself, by destroying my mental distress. The connection [of the meaning] is that he extinguished, that is, pacified, those three fires described in the aforementioned manner.

576. Having thus shown his own humble past conduct to the Blessed One, he now spoke the words beginning with "Those who have the ear ready" in order to exhort others as well and urge them toward listening.
In this context, "those of you who have the ear ready"—that is, who possess the application of the ear, the fixing of the ear—listen to my words as I speak and instruct you.
"Pay attention. I shall declare the goal to you"—the connection is as follows:
"In whatever manner and by whatever means the state (*pada*), which is Nibbāna, was seen by me, in that very manner I shall declare to you the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) known as Nibbāna.
577. Showing that, he said: "Having disparaged the Self-Existent One (*sayambhu*)," and so forth. In that context, *sayambhuṃ* means "one who has become [enlightened] by himself."
Having insulted and shown disrespect toward a Paccekabuddha— one born of noble birth, with a peaceful mind and concentrated—
by that unwholesome karma performed, I have today, in this present time,
been born and reborn into a lowly womb, a life dependent on others, as one born of the class of barbers.
578. "Do not miss the opportunity" means: do not let the moment of a Buddha’s arising pass you by;
do not let it slip away. For indeed, beings who have missed the opportunity—having passed over and transcended the moment of a Buddha’s arising—grieve;
they grieve, thinking, "We are unfortunate and dull-witted. This is the meaning: they grieve in this way regarding their own welfare (*sadatthe*).
"You should strive for growth; exert energy! You have secured, established, and attained the opportunity—the moment of a Buddha's appearance.
(579) Thereafter, demonstrating the danger (*ādīnava*) inherent in those wandering in *saṃsāra* by means of similes and their subjects, he says: "And of some..."
He spoke beginning with "vomiting" (*vamananti*). The connection is as follows: for some individuals there is vomiting, that is, ejecting upwards;
for others there is purging, that is, discharging downwards; for some there is *halāhala* poison, the poison that causes fainting;
and for certain individuals there is medicine, a means of protection—the Blessed One has thus declared these in their respective order.

580. "For those who have entered upon the emetic" means that for those who have entered the path and possess the factors of the path (*maggasamaṅgī*), the Blessed One declared the emetic to be the casting off of *saṃsāra*, the liberation from *saṃsāra*.
"For those established in the fruits" means for those abiding in the fruits, he declared the purgative to be the draining away of *saṃsāra*.
"For those who have attained the fruits" means for those who have obtained the fruits and remain therein, [he declared] the medicine of *nibbāna*.
He proclaimed. The connection is as follows: he proclaimed to those seeking—the human and divine attainment of Nibbāna—to those searching for the Saṅgha, which is a field of merit. 581.
"Of those opposed to the Teaching" means those who are adversaries of the Teaching; their *halāhala* is curiosity, evil, and unwholesome.

The connection is with the word "declared" (*akkhāsī*). Just as a venomous snake (*āsīvisa*)—because it brings suffering to those faithless persons who have committed evil in *saṃsāra*—is like a venomous snake;

just as a snake whose venom is activated by sight (*diṭṭhavisa*) consumes the man bitten by it, burning him and causing him pain; so too does that faithless man who has committed evil [consume himself].
The connection is as follows: "It burns in the four states of misery" means that it consumes the *halāhala* poison; it dries it up. 582.
"Once drunk, the *halāhala*": the *halāhala* poison, once drunk—that is, drunk a single time—obstructs and destroys life.
A person who, having missed the teaching within the dispensation (*sāsana*) and committed an offense, [remains] for ten million eons (*koṭi-kappa*).
"Even for an eon it burns; it broods," is the meaning.
(583) Having thus shown the fruit and result for persons lacking faith, he now spoke the verse beginning with "With patience" in order to demonstrate the majesty of the Buddhas.
In that context, the Buddha who taught emetics and so forth—that Buddha, through patience...
By means of patience, by non-violence toward beings— that is, by not harming them— and by possessing a mind of loving-kindness, that is,
by being endowed with a heart of loving-kindness, he carries across, causes to transcend, and cools the world including its devas as it exists;
for that reason, you should not offend the Buddhas, meaning you should not be able to oppose them, but should instead practice according to the Buddha’s teaching.
In gain and in loss, they do not cling, they do not associate, and they do not become attached.
In honor and respect, and in dishonor and disrespect, the Buddhas remain unshaken like the earth;
for that reason, those Buddhas are not to be opposed by you, nor should they be opposed, meaning it is impossible to oppose them.

585. Showing the Buddhas’ state of equanimity, he said, “Devadatta,” and so forth. In that context, the meaning is: the Sage who is equal toward all beings, whether they are murderers or those who do not murder, whose mind is impartial—that is the Buddha-Sage.
586. “In these there is no aversion”: in these Buddhas, there is no aversion (*paṭigha*), nor ferocity, nor a mind of hatred;
it does not exist. “In these no lust is found”: in these Buddhas, even lust—passion, attachment, clinging—is not found.
It does not exist, it is not found; for that reason, the connection is that the Buddha is equal toward all—toward both the executioner and his own biological son—and possesses an even mind.
(587) Furthermore, demonstrating the very majesty of the Buddhas, he said, "Having seen on the road those wearing saffron robes," and so forth. Therein:
Having seen upon the road or path a saffron robe— stained with filth, mixed with excrement, dyed with astringent dyes, born of the power of the *ṛṣis*,
the banner of the Noble Ones, their requisite— cast aside, one should join the ten fingers in reverential salutation, place the hollowed palms to the head,
and pay homage with the head to that banner of the *ṛṣis*, the banner of Arhatship, which illuminates the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples.
The meaning is that the robe is to be revered, honored, and worshipped.
588. *Abbhatītā* means those who have passed away, gone beyond, and attained Nibbāna.

And those Buddhas who are present, those Buddhas who have arisen now, and those Buddhas who are yet to come—those not yet born, not yet become, not yet produced, not yet manifested. By this banner they are purified.
By means of this robe produced by the power of *iddhi*, these Buddhas are purified, become pure, and shine forth.
Therefore, for that reason, these Buddhas are "to be honored" (*namassiyā*); the meaning is that they are to be venerated and saluted.
There is also a reading, “*etaṃ namassiyaṃ*,” which means “this [robe] produced by *iddhi* is to be honored.”
589. Thereafter, demonstrating his own virtue, he spoke the verse beginning with "satthukappaṃ. In this context, the meaning is:

"I bear in my heart—that is, in my mind—through hearing, memorizing, and so forth, that which is like the Teacher (satthukappa), similar to the Buddha, well-disciplined (suvinaya), having beautiful discipline (sundaravinaya), and which subdues the three doors in a beautiful manner;
I reflect upon it. Thus, while paying homage to the Vinaya, the Vinaya Piṭaka...
"Paying homage and showing respect for the Vinaya, I shall dwell"—the meaning is that I shall make my residence at all times, at every moment.

(590) "The Vinaya is my abode" means that the Vinaya Piṭaka is my dwelling place; it is my home in the sense that it serves as a space for hearing, memorizing, attending to, grasping, and engaging in inquiry.
"The Vinaya is my standing and walking" means that the Vinaya is [my domain] through the performance of duties such as hearing and so forth.

"The place for standing and the place for walking. "I make my dwelling in the Vinaya" means that I make, I perform, a dwelling—a staying—by way of hearing, memorizing, and practicing the Vinaya-tantra within the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"The Vinaya is my resort" means that the Vinaya Piṭaka is my resort, my nourishment, my food, by way of constant memorization and mental attention; such is the meaning.
591. "One who has reached perfection in the Vinaya" means one who has attained the ultimate limit or consummation in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
"And skilled in calming" means one who is expert and proficient in the calming, the pacification, and the resolution of the seven classes of offenses beginning with the Pārājikas;
or alternatively, one who is skilled in the settling of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).
“Dispute, accusation, likewise the legal issue arising from an offense,
and the legal issue concerning business— these are considered the four legal issues.
And among the legal issues thus stated:
“Face-to-face settlement, verdict of past insanity,
admission of the offense, majority decision, and likewise the ‘covering over as with grass’”—
the meaning is that he is highly skilled and expert in these seven methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*) thus spoken. O Great Hero, Upāli!
"Venerable Mahāvīra, for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons,
you, the Teacher endowed with vigor who has attained omniscience and instructs gods and humans— your disciple Upāli pays homage at your pair of feet; this is the meaning."

592. Thus, having gone forth, paying homage and prostrating before the Fully Enlightened One, and having understood the excellence and the sublime nature of the Dhamma—the ninefold supramundane Dhamma taught by that Blessed One—I shall wander from village to village and from city to city ahead of me, paying homage to the Dhamma as well; such is the connection [of the verses].

593. "The defilements have been burnt away by me": by means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship realized by me, all the defilements numbering one thousand five hundred within the continuum of my own mind have been burnt, withered, utterly dried up, and destroyed.
"All states of existence have been eradicated": all nine states of existence, beginning with sensual existence (kāmabhava), have been thoroughly uprooted and exhausted by me.

"Shattered. "All taints are utterly destroyed" means that all four taints—the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*)—have been utterly destroyed and brought to total exhaustion. Now, at this time of attaining arahantship, there is no further becoming;
the meaning is that there is no more birth, which is characterized by renewed arising and existence.
594. Uttering an inspired utterance (*udāna*) by way of further joy, he said, "Welcome," and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:
"In the presence (*santike*), that is, in the vicinity (*samīpe*) of the Best of Buddhas, the Supreme Buddha—whether in the same city or elsewhere—my arrival was indeed welcome;

it was truly a good arrival, a beautiful arrival; it was, in fact, entirely auspicious. The "threefold knowledge" (*tisso vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

"Attained and reached" means made manifest. "The Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished" means that the instruction taught by the Blessed Buddha—the teaching—has been accomplished and brought to fruition;
it means it has been achieved through fulfilling the practice of duties, attending to the meditation subject, and attaining the knowledge of the path to arahantship.

"595. 'The four analytical knowledges' (paṭisambhidā) means that the four types of wisdom, beginning with the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), have been realized and made directly manifest.

'And the eight liberations' (vimokkhā): the connection is that these eight liberations—the four knowledges of the path and the four knowledges of the fruit—means of release from saṃsāra, have been realized. 'The six direct knowledges' (chaḷabhiññā) have been realized."
“Supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others,
knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints”—
these six direct knowledges have been realized and made manifest. The meaning is that by the realization of these knowledges, the Buddha’s dispensation has been fulfilled.
"Ittham" means by the manner described below. "Sudam" is a particle used merely to fill out the meter.

"The Venerable Elder Upāli"—meaning a disciple endowed with qualities such as steadfast virtue—spoke these verses which illuminate his past deeds; this is the meaning of "abhāsittha," which signifies that he spoke them.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upāli is completed.
3–7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña.
"Padumuttara-sambuddha," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. It is said that this...
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the attainment of liberation throughout various existences,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great householders in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity,
one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhu as foremost in his own dispensation.
Seeing that he was being placed in the foremost position among those who know the Dharma realized first, he himself aspired to that same rank.
Having offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Blessed One, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, he made a formal vow.
The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, prophesied his future success. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life.
While the stupa was being erected after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna,
he had a jeweled chamber constructed within the stupa and had thousands of objects worth a thousand pieces of gold fashioned to surround the stupa.
Having performed such meritorious deeds, he passed away from there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, [reappeared] at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
At that time, having become a householder named Mahākāla, he plowed a field measuring eight karīsas to expose the rice shoots.

Having taken the rice grains, he prepared milk-rice (pāyāsa) with unmixed milk; into this he added honey, clarified butter, sugar, and other ingredients, and offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Each spot from which the rice shoots had been plucked was filled again. At the time of threshing—

He gave the first-fruits of the threshing floor. He gave the first-fruits of the winnowing, the first-fruits of the sheaves, the first-fruits of the bundles, the first-fruits of the granary, the first-fruits of the storehouse, the first-fruits of the measuring, and the first-fruits of the barn.
In this way, he gave the gift of the first-fruits nine times for a single crop;
yet that crop became even more abundant and successful.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born even before the arising of our Blessed One, in a prominent brahmin family in the brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu. By his clan name, he was Koṇḍañña.
Thus his name became "Āgata. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and attained perfection in the science of marks and mantras.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, descending from the Tusita heaven, was born in the city of Kapilavatthu in the household of King Suddhodana.
On the day of his naming ceremony, when one hundred and eight brahmins were brought forward, those eight—
The brahmins were brought to the great terrace for the purpose of examining his physical marks.

Being the youngest among them all, he perceived the perfection of the Great Man’s marks; having reached the conclusion that "this one will certainly become a Buddha," he wandered about, awaiting the Great Being’s Great Renunciation.
The Bodhisatta, too, growing up with a great retinue, gradually reached maturity and attained the ripening of his wisdom.
In his twenty-ninth year, setting out on the Great Renunciation, he went forth as a wanderer on the banks of the Anomā River.
Proceeding by stages, he went to Uruvelā and applied himself to striving. At that time, the young brahmin Koṇḍañña learned of the Great Being’s state of having gone forth.
Having heard this, he went forth into homelessness with his four sons, including the young brahmin Vappa, making himself the fifth.
In due course, he approached the Bodhisatta and attended upon him for six years.
Becoming weary of the Bodhisatta’s consumption of substantial food, he departed and went to Isipatana. Then the Bodhisatta...
Having gained physical strength through the consumption of solid food, he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the full moon day of Vesākha upon the invincible throne;
having crushed the heads of the three Māras and attained full enlightenment, he spent seven weeks right there at the seat of awakening.
Then, knowing that the wisdom of the group of five monks had reached maturity, he went to Isipatana on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī.
He preached to them the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, on the fifth day of the fortnight, through the preaching of the Discourse on the Characteristic of Non-Self, he realized Arhatship.
596. Having thus attained Arahatship, he reflected, "By what deed have I attained this supramundane happiness?

Examining his own past karma, he came to know it through direct experience. Out of joy, and as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he recounted the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One," and so forth.
The meaning of this has already been explained above.
"Lokajeṭṭhaṃ vināyakaṃ" means the eldest and foremost of the entire world of sentient beings; that is the meaning.

He is called a "Vināyaka" (Guide) because he specifically leads (*neti*) and brings (*sampāpeti*) those beings who are to be trained to the further shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*, namely, the great *nibbāna* of the deathless;
[he is] that Vināyaka. "Buddhabhūmimanuppattaṃ" refers to the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), which is the ground or the place of establishment for a Buddha.

"Omniscient knowledge" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) means that he has reached and penetrated it; thus, "having reached the stage of a Buddha" (*buddhabhūmi*) means having attained omniscience and become a Buddha—this is the meaning.
"First I saw him as 'I'" means that on the first full moon night of Vesākha, at the time of dawn, I beheld the Sambuddha Padumuttara who had become a Buddha—this is the meaning.
597. "As many as were gathered together in a mass at the foot of the Bodhi tree, as many as were near the Bodhi tree— those *yakkhas* who,

with palms joined (having placed the ten fingers together in a hollowed gesture) and having set that hollowed palm upon their heads, pay homage and revere the Fully Enlightened One, the Buddha who has become awakened"— this is the syntactical connection.
598. “All the gods, their minds delighted, have come to the place where the Buddha has become; all those gods, with joyful hearts, move through the sky”—this is the connection [of the verse].
“The dispeller of the darkness of deep gloom”: the meaning is that this Buddha, who dispels—that is, drives away—the exceedingly profound darkness of delusion, has arrived.
599. "Of those overcome with laughter" means of those deities endowed with laughter—that is, joy and gladness—a great roar, a great sound, arose and proceeded;
the connection is: "In the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One, we shall burn away the defilements, the corruptions, and the [unwholesome] states. 600.
"Having understood the speech of the deities" means having recognized the sound of the deities uttered together with words of praise.
The connection is as follows: "With a joyful heart, with a mind accompanied by gladness, I gave the first alms-food to him who had become a Buddha.
(602) "Having gone forth for seven days" means: having gone forth in the Great Renunciation and having practiced striving for seven days.
The meaning is: "I attained, I reached, Bodhi—which is known as the knowledge of the path to Arahatship and has omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) as its proximate cause.

"This was my first meal" means: this meal, which sustains the body, was given by this son of the gods to me, who am a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī), the highest way of conduct; it was the first [meal] given to me.

603. "For having come here from the Tusita realm"—meaning, having come here to the human world from the Tusita abode—"that son of the gods who brought and gave me alms, that son of the gods I shall praise, I shall speak of, I shall make manifest.
The connection is: "Listen to my words as I speak them. Hereafter, we shall explain only those words that are not self-evident.

607. *Tidasā* refers to the realm of the Thirty-three (*tāvatiṃsa-bhavana*). *Agārā* means that he will dwell together with the Bodhisatta, who has gone forth after leaving his own arisen brahmin household and performed austerities for six years.
608. *Tato sattamake vasse*: from the time of his going forth, in the seventh year.
"The Buddha will speak the truth" means that after performing austerities for six years, having become a Buddha in the seventh year—

The meaning is that, at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī, he will preach the Discourse on Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma, wherein he will explain the Four Noble Truths known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
"By name Koṇḍañña" means that by way of his personal name and clan name, he is named Koṇḍañña.
"Will realize first" means that among the group of five, he will be the very first to realize the knowledge of the path of stream-entry right from the beginning.
"Sacchikāhiti" means he will realize it, that is, he will make it manifest before his own eyes.
"Nikkhantenānupabbajin" means having gone forth together with the Bodhisatta who had gone forth, he followed him in his renunciation.
Having thus followed him in his renunciation, I performed the exertion of striving well; that is, I practiced it thoroughly and with firm resolve.
"Katam" means "what. "For the sake of burning up the defilements" means for the sake of drying up the defilements, for the sake of destroying them;

"I went forth into homelessness"—that is, I entered upon the practice of the Teaching which is detrimental to the household life and devoid of such activities as farming and trade—this is the meaning.
(610) "Having approached the All-Knowing One": all that is reckoned as the past, future, and present, or as formations, change, characteristics, Nibbāna, and designations.
The meaning is that, knowing the knowable while conversing with the devas, the Buddha went to and approached the Migāra’s Deer Park monastery in the seven worlds;
having approached, he beat— that is, sounded— the drum of the Deathless, the great drum of the Deathless Nibbāna,
by means of this knowledge of the path to stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) realized by me.

611. "So now"—meaning that I, having first become a stream-enterer, have now, by means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship, attained and reached the deathless, peaceful state whose very nature is tranquility;
the meaning is that I have arrived at and realized the unsurpassed Nibbāna, which is devoid of anything higher.
"Having fully understood all taints" means having fully understood all taints, such as the taint of sensual desire and the rest.
"Having abandoned [them] through full understanding as abandonment, I dwell free from taints and free from defilements; I pass my time in the dwelling of the postures.
The verses beginning with "The four analytical knowledges" have their meaning already explained.
Then, at a later time, the Teacher, in the great monastery of Jetavana, in the midst of the community of monks, seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne prepared for him—
Sitting there, demonstrating that he was the first to penetrate the nature of the Dhamma, the Buddha placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are long-standing in the faith: namely, Aññā Koṇḍañña.
Desiring to avoid the supreme prostrations being performed toward himself by the two chief disciples, as well as the crowded living conditions found in village dwellings, [he departed].
Desiring to dwell in delight in seclusion, yet considering even the performance of hospitality toward laypeople and renunciants who approached him to be a hindrance (*papañca*),
he requested leave from the Teacher, entered the Himālayas, and dwelt for twelve years on the banks of the Chaddantada Lake, being attended by the Chaddanta elephants.
While the Elder was dwelling there in this manner, one day Sakka—
The King of the Devas approached, paid homage, and stood to one side, saying: "It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble one would teach me the Dhamma.

The Elder taught him the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha—the Dhamma containing the Four Noble Truths, struck by the three characteristics, associated with emptiness, variegated by various methods, and plunging into the Deathless. Having heard it, Sakka, making known his own faith, said:
“I have even greater confidence now that I have heard the Dhamma of great flavor;
the Dhamma taught is dispassion, leading to total non-clinging. Thus he offered praise.

Having lived for twelve years on the banks of the Chaddanta Lake, when the time for his final passing was near, the Elder approached the Teacher, requested permission for his final passing, and having gone back to that very place, he attained Parinibbāna.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña is completed. 3–8.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja begins with the verse starting "The Conqueror named Padumuttara. This [Venerable] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn in the womb of a lion during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. He lived in a cave at the foot of a mountain.
When the Blessed One had gone out for almsfood to favor him, he entered the lion’s cave and attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
He sat down. Having taken his food and returned, Sīha stood at the entrance of the cave; seeing the Blessed One, he was filled with joy and satisfaction.

Having made an offering of water-born and land-born flowers while purifying his mind, he remained there with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, letting out a lion’s roar at the three times of day to ward off other wild beasts for the sake of protecting the Blessed One. Just as...
On the first day he made offerings in this manner for seven days. The Blessed One, thinking, "After the lapse of seven days, having emerged from cessation, he will turn the wheel of the Dhamma;
such is his supporting condition," departed through the air and returned to the monastery even as Sīha was looking on.
Unable to endure the suffering of separation from the Buddha, Sīha passed away and was reborn in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he went to the monastery together with the city-dwellers. Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he was filled with faith;

for seven days he offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered through successive births among gods and humans until the time of our Blessed One at Kosambī.
He was reborn as the son of the royal chaplain of King Udena. His name was Bhāradvāja.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and was teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins;
however, because his conduct was inconsistent with his high status, he was abandoned by them. He went to Rājagaha and [observed] the gains and honor of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having seen this, he went forth in the Teaching, but lived without moderation in food.
The Teacher, establishing him in moderation through a skillful means, had him apply insight meditation, and before long he became one possessed of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijña*).

Having attained the six supernormal powers, he declared in the presence of the Blessed One before the community of monks: "Whatever is to be attained by disciples has been attained by me. In the midst of the bhikkhu-saṅgha...
And he uttered this lion’s roar: “Let whoever has doubt regarding the path or the fruit question me.
For that reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who utter the lion’s roar, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja is the foremost.”

613. Having thus reached this supreme state and recollecting the store of merit accumulated in the past, he spoke the words beginning with “Padumuttara,” manifesting his own account of meritorious deeds through a sense of joy. The meaning of that has already been explained above.
“In front of Himavanta” means in the eastern direction from the Himalaya mountain. “He dwelt on Cittakūṭa at that time.”

When I was Sīha, the king of beasts, dwelling near the Himavat mountains, at that time the Teacher named Padumuttara dwelt upon the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa—the summit of Mount Citta—due to its variegated beauty with many medicinal herbs and many jewels; such is the connection.
(614) "Abhītarūpo tatthāsiṃ" means that I, the king of beasts, being of a fearless nature and of a state free from fear, was there.
*Attha*: the meaning. *Catukkamo*: capable of going in a sequence from the four directions. *Yassa saddaṃ suṇitvāna*:
having heard the sound of which—the lion’s roar of that king of beasts—many people, many beings, are struck with awe; they are especially paralyzed with fear. 615. *Suphullaṃ padumaṃ gayha*:
having taken a fully blossomed lotus flower and adorned [the Blessed One] out of faith in the Blessed One.
"I approached the Bull among Men, the leader of men, the supreme, the most excellent, the Fully Awakened One"—

the meaning is that I went into his presence. "Of him who had emerged from meditative absorption" means that I offered and honored that flower to the Buddha who had emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

616. *Catuddisaṃ namassitvā* means: having paid homage in the four directions, having gladdened one’s own mind and established it with reverence, they uttered a lion’s roar—a roar of fearlessness—this is the meaning.
617. Then, revealing the prophecy given by the Buddha, he spoke the verse beginning with *Padumuttaro*. Its meaning is already explained. 618. *Vadataṃ seṭṭho*:
the best among those who say, “We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas,” namely, the followers of other sects.
"The connection is: 'The supreme Buddha has arrived. The meaning is: 'We shall hear—that is, we will listen—to that Dhamma of the Blessed One who has arrived.
(619) 'Of those overcome by laughter' means of those gods and humans who were possessed by, or overwhelmed with, laughter—that is, with joy.
'The Leader of the World' means the leader of the world, the one who brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation; [hearing] my voice..."

He proclaimed, revealed, and explained my lion’s roar; he is one who sees afar, seeing into the future, a great sage among sages, a mighty muni. The remaining verses are easily understood. [Verse 622:
Having been a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī) by name Paduma, he will exercise sovereignty, lordship, and rule for sixty-four births—this is the meaning.
623. “In a hundred thousand aeons” (*kappasatasahassamhi*): this is a locative used in the sense of equality; the meaning is “at the conclusion of a hundred thousand aeons.
624. “When the teaching was proclaimed” (*pāvacane pakāsite*): the meaning is that it was proclaimed and taught by that Blessed One Gotama in the three baskets (*piṭakatraya*).
“He will become a kinsman of Brahmā” (*brahmabandhu bhavissati*): at that time, during the era of the Blessed One Gotama, this Sīha, the king of deer, was born into a brahmin family.

The meaning is "he will be reborn. "Having gone forth from the brahminhood" (brahmaññā abhinikkhamma) is connected with "having departed from the brahmin family, he will go forth in the teaching of that Blessed One.
"One whose mind is directed toward striving" (padhānapahitatta) means one whose consciousness is sent forth for the purpose of exerting energy. Of the defilements known as acquisitions (upadhi)...
"By way of non-existence, he is without acquisitions (*nirupadhi*). By way of the non-existence of the distresses of the defilements (*kilesa-daratha*), he is peaceful.

Having fully understood and abandoned all taints (*āsava*)—that is, every single taint—he will be taintless and free from defilement; he will be extinguished through the final extinction of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*); this is the meaning.

(626) "In a secluded, remote lodging" means in a dwelling in the distant forest, free from the crowding of people. "Swarming with wild beasts" means crowded or filled with packs of fierce animals such as black lions and the like. The rest has already been explained.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja is completed.
3–9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Khadiravaniya:
"The Ganges named Bhāgīrathī," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Khadiravaniya. He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of ferrymen.
While performing work on a ferryboat at the Payāga ford on the Mahāgaṅgā river, one day he saw the Blessed One, accompanied by his Saṅgha of disciples, arrive at the riverbank.
Having seen this, with a mind full of faith, he prepared a boat-raft and, after transporting [the Buddha] to the opposite shore with great honor and hospitality,
saw a certain bhikkhu being established by the Teacher in the foremost position among forest-dwelling bhikkhus.
Aspiring to that very status, he offered a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and made a formal aspiration.
He made [this aspiration]. The Blessed One declared that his aspiration would not be in vain.
From then on, accumulating merit and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence;
and now, during this appearance of a Buddha, he was conceived in the womb of a brahmin woman named Rūpasārī in the village of Nālaka in the kingdom of Magadha.
He was born. When he reached maturity, his parents, desiring to bind him with the fetters of the household life, made this known to him.

Having heard that the Elder Sāriputta had gone forth, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: "My elder brother, the noble Upatissa, has abandoned this wealth and gone forth;
how could I possibly enjoy what he has vomited out like a globule of spittle? Thus he became stirred.
Like a deer that does not approach a snare, he deceived his kinsmen; then, urged on by the excellence of his own causal conditions, he went into the presence of the monks.
Having announced that he was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, he declared his desire for the going-forth.
The monks ordained him, and having conferred full ordination upon him when he had reached twenty years of age, they assigned him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, having taken up his meditation subject and entered the acacia grove, he rested, exerted himself, and strove;
and because his knowledge had reached maturity, before long he became an arahant possessed of the six super-knowledges.
Having become an arahant, he put away his lodging, took his bowl and robe, and set out to pay homage to the Teacher and the Dhammasenāpati, eventually arriving at Sāvatthī.
Having reached Jetavana and entered it, he paid homage to the Teacher and the Dhamma-Senāpati, and dwelt for several days at Jetavana.
Then, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among the forest-dwelling bhikkhus, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are forest-dwellers, namely Revata."

628. Having thus attained this foremost position and recollecting his own past karma, he spoke the words beginning with “The Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī,” proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct) out of joy and gladness.
Therein, it is called the Gaṅgā because she goes while singing (*gāyamānā*) and making a sound (*ghosaṃ kurumānā*).
Alternatively, "go" refers to the earth (*pathavī*); she is called the Gaṅgā because she has gone to and flows upon that [earth]. [He visited] Lake Anotatta three times...
In the place where it went after making a circumambulation, it was called the Āvaṭṭagaṅgā; in the place where it went over the mountain peak, it was called the Bahalagaṅgā;
in the place where it went piercing through the Tiracchānapabbata, it was called the Umaṅgagaṅgā;

and in the place where it struck the thick mountain and traveled five yojanas through the air, it was called the Ākāsagaṅgā; and the place where it fell broke open the earth, giving rise to [the river].
Having burst through the bank of the lotus pond over five *yojanas* in width, she there became five streams like the five fingers [of a hand].

Having five names—Ganges, Yamunā, Sarabhū, Mahī, and Aciravatī—and having divided Jambudīpa into five parts and five portions, she has gone to, reached, and flows through those five parts and five portions; thus she is called Bhāgīrathī. And she is the Ganges.

Because she belongs to Bhāgīratha, she is the Gaṅgā-Bhāgīrathī. It should be understood that although one should say "the Gaṅgā is Bhāgīrathī," it is stated as "Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā" for the sake of metrical ease and in accordance with ancient usage.
Regarding "originated from the Himavanta": *hima* is so called because it harms (*hiṃsati*), strikes, agitates, and churns beings with its cold;
that which possesses this *hima* is *himavā*; from that *himavanta* (the Snowy Mountain), starting from there...

"Pabhāvitā pavattā sandamānā" means "originating from the Himālaya. "Kutitthe nāviko āsiṃ" means that at a treacherous crossing where the current of that Gaṅgā became violent, I was born into a family of fishermen and was a boatman; this is the meaning.
"Orime ca tariṃ ahaṃ" means that whenever people arrived, I crossed them over from the further bank to this bank; this is the meaning.

629. “Padumuttara, the Leader, the supreme among bipeds, the Guide who brings beings to Nibbāna—the Buddha Padumuttara, while bringing forth my perfection of merit—reached the ford to cross the Ganges stream together with one hundred thousand masters and one hundred thousand whose taints were destroyed;
such is the connection.”

630. "Having brought together many boats" means that upon seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One who had arrived, they brought together many boats that had been well-constructed and finished by carpenters;
having joined two boats together as one and having made a canopy-covering for the boat, they honored the Bull among Men, the Sambuddha Padumuttara—this is the meaning.
631. "Having come," meaning having arrived there by means of a boat thus assembled; "and having boarded that most excellent boat"—this is the syntactical connection.

"Standing in the midst of the water, the Teacher"—meaning the Teacher, having boarded the boat and being situated in the middle of the waters of the Ganges, spoke these verses associated with joy; this is the syntactical connection.
632. “He who ferried across the Fully Awakened One” means that the boatman ferried the Fully Awakened One across the current of the Ganges.
“And also the stainless Saṅgha” means that he did not merely ferry the Fully Awakened One across, but also the stainless, undefiled Saṅgha;
this is the meaning. “By that clarity of mind” means by that clarity of mind accompanied by joy which arose at the time of pushing off the boat.
"He will delight in the world of the gods within the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure; he will experience divine prosperity"—this is the meaning.

633. "A celestial mansion shall arise for you": for you who have been reborn in the world of the gods, a celestial mansion (*byamha*, *vimāna*) that is well-constructed, perfectly formed, and not unstable—meaning it does not wobble like a ship—shall arise and become manifest; this is the meaning.

"A canopy of flowers in the sky" means that as a result of the construction of the upper pavilion on the ship, a canopy of flowers will always be maintained in the sky wherever he goes; this is the connection.
"In fifty-eight eons" means after fifty-eight eons have passed from the time he began performing these meritorious deeds.
The connection is as follows: "By name Tāraka, a kṣatriya wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī), a lord over the four continents, a conqueror who has achieved victory, shall come to be.
The remaining verses are of plain meaning. 637.

"By name Revata"—because he was born under the Revatī constellation, he will receive the name "Revata"; "a kinsman of Brahmā" means he will be born as the son of a brahmin, arising within a brahmin family; this is the meaning.
639. "Nibbāyissatināsavo" means that, being free from defilements (*nikkilesa*), one will attain *nibbāna* through the final extinction of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*). 640.
"'Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ'"—thus was I prophesied by the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having gradually reached the pinnacle of the perfections (*pāramitākoṭi*), my energy (*vīriya*) is unflagging energy; it is the yoke-bearer, the bearer of the burden, and the sustainer of the burden.
The meaning is that it was the bringing about and the attainment of Nibbāna, which is secure and fearless through yogic practices.
"I bear my final body" connects to the sense that, "Now I bear the final physical frame within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Later on, having gone to his own birthplace, he [addressed] his three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā.
Having brought his three nephews—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—and having ordained them, he assigned them to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
They dwelt devotedly engaged in that meditation subject.
At that time, a certain illness arose in the Elder; hearing of this, the Elder Sāriputta [said]: “Revata’s...
Thinking, “I shall inquire after his health and ask about his spiritual attainments,” he approached him.
When the Elder Revata saw the General of the Dhamma approaching from afar, he spoke the verse beginning with “Cāle” as an exhortation intended to arouse mindfulness in those novices.
In that context, “Cāle, Upacāle, Sīsūpacāle” is an address to them; [the names] are Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā.
Indeed, even though those three boys—who had received their names according to their feminine gender—had gone forth into the religious life, they were still addressed in that same way.
And some say: “Cālī, Upacālī, and Sīsūpacālī were their names.
To show for what purpose he used the vocatives “Cāle,” etc., he said, “Dwell mindful, indeed,” and stated the reason for this: “He has come...”
"Like a hair-splitter. "Patissatā" means mindfulness. "Kho" is used for emphasis. "Āgato" means he has come. "Vo" means to you.
"Vālaṃ viya vedhī" means like a hair-splitter. This is the summary of the meaning here:

the venerable Mātula, who is like the Teacher himself and resembles a hair-splitter due to his sharp, swift, and penetrating wisdom, has come to you; therefore, establish the perception of him as a recluse.
"Abide indeed endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension; be diligent in the dwelling you have attained.

Having heard this, those novices performed the duties such as going out to meet the Dhammasenāpati, and at the time of the two maternal uncles, the elders, receiving their greetings, they sat down not far away, having entered into meditative concentration. [Then] the Dhammasenāpati, together with the elder Revata...
Having exchanged greetings with them, he rose from his seat and approached those novices.
Because they had already established a time limit, they rose, paid homage, and stood aside as the Elder approached.
The Elder asked, "In which various dwellings do you reside? When they replied, "In such-and-such a place," the Elder, thus training even the children, said: "As for me..."
"Truly, this brother is a speaker of truth and one who lives in accordance with the Dhamma," he said, praising the Elder as he departed. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Khadiravaniya is completed.
3-10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ānanda.
"Emerging from the gate of the monastery," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Ānanda.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī as the half-brother of the Teacher; his name was Sumanas.

[He] was born. His father, however, was named King Nanda. When his son, Prince Sumanakumāra, had reached maturity, the king gave him the city of Bhoganagara, located two hundred yojanas from the city of Haṃsavatī.
From time to time, he would come and see both the Teacher and his father. At that time, the king [was staying with] the Teacher and the Saṅgha of monks numbering one hundred thousand.
He himself served him with great care and did not allow others to do so.
At that time, the border regions were in revolt. Without informing the king of the state of the rebellion, the prince himself pacified it.
Hearing this, the king was delighted in heart and said, "I grant you a boon; choose what you will."
The prince said, “I wish to make my life fruitful by attending upon the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for three months.
[The king replied,] “That is not possible; ask for something else. “Your Majesty, there are no two kinds of speech among kṣatriyas.
Grant this to me; I have no need for anything else. If the Teacher permits it, it is as good as given. He [the prince] [considered] the Teacher’s mind...
“I shall find out,” he thought, and went to the monastery. At that time, the Blessed One had entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi).
He approached the monks and said, “Venerable sirs, I have come to see the Blessed One; please let me see him.
The monks said, “There is an elder named Sumana who is the Teacher’s attendant; go to him. So he—
Having approached the Elder, he said, "Venerable sir, please show me the Teacher.
Then the Elder, even as the prince was looking on, sank into the earth and approached the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see you.
[The Buddha replied,] "In that case, monk, prepare a seat outside. The Elder then prepared the Buddha’s seat once more.
Having taken it, he vanished within the Fragrant Chamber and appeared outside the monastery courtyard while the prince was looking on;
he then prepared a seat in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber. Seeing this, the prince thought, "How great indeed is this monk!
The Blessed One also emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and sat down on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Teacher.
Having offered hospitality, he asked, "Venerable sir, this elder seems to be dear to you in the Dispensation.
"Yes, prince, he is dear. "By doing what, venerable sir, has he become dear? "By performing meritorious deeds such as giving and the like.
"Lord, I too wish to become dear in the future Buddha-Dispensation just as this elder is. Then, [he made offerings] headed by the Buddha...
Having provided food for the Saṅgha in the military camp for seven days, on the seventh day he said, "Venerable Sir, I have received from my father a boon to provide for your needs for three months;
please accept my invitation to spend the three-month rains retreat with me.
Having perceived the Teacher's consent, he took the Blessed One and his retinue, and at every *yojana* along the way, for the Teacher and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha...
Having had suitable dwellings constructed here and there and causing them to reside therein,
he had him enter a monastery built for a hundred thousand coins in a beautiful garden named Sobhana, which he himself had purchased for a hundred thousand coins near his own residence,
saying: "It was bought by me for a hundred thousand, and it was built for a hundred thousand."
“The garden named Sobhana— accept it, O Great Sage.
Having thus offered water, he performed a great almsgiving for the Teacher on the day of entering the rains retreat,
and having instructed his wife, children, and ministers, saying, “You should give alms in this manner,” and enjoining them to perform the duties of charity, he himself [approached] the Elder Sumana.
Dwelling right near his own residence, he thus attended upon the Teacher for three months in that very place where he lived.

When the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) was approaching, he entered a village and, having offered a great almsgiving for seven days, on the seventh day he placed his three robes at the feet of the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and after paying homage, said: "Venerable Sir, as for this..."
"Starting from the time I established my military camp, I have performed meritorious deeds; I did not do so for the sake of attaining the status of Sakka or other such states.
Rather, I made this aspiration: 'May I too, like the Elder Sumana, become a beloved attendant to a future Buddha.
Seeing that there would be no obstacles to his fulfillment, the Teacher gave him a prediction and departed.
Thus, having performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand years during that appearance of a Buddha,
and thereafter accumulating further sublime meritorious kamma throughout various existences, he wandered among gods and humans until, at the time of the Blessed One Kassapa,
he was reborn in a noble family; and having reached maturity, he took hold of the alms-bowl of a certain elder who was wandering for alms.
Having made it his upper robe, he performed an act of worship. Reborn again in heaven, and passing away from there, he became the king of Bārāṇasī.
Having seen eight paccekabuddhas, he fed them and, in his own Maṅgala Garden, had eight leaf-huts constructed.
For their use as seats, he prepared eight thrones made entirely of precious gems along with jeweled water-vessels.
He performed service for ten thousand years; these [deeds] are well known.
However, for a hundred thousand eons, accumulating merit in various states of existence, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta.
Passing away from there, he was reborn in the household of King Amitodana, and all...
Because he was born bringing joy to his kinsmen, he received the name Ānanda.
Having gradually reached maturity, gone forth, and attained supreme enlightenment, the Blessed One set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma.
When he first went to Kapilavatthu and subsequently departed from there, Bhaddiya and others, who were going forth to join his retinue, followed him.
Having gone forth together with him and received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One,
he heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, during the first twenty years after the Blessed One’s enlightenment, there were no fixed attendants.
At one time Nāgasamāla was wandering about with his bowl and robes; at another time it was Nāgita; at another time Upavāna; at another time Sunakkhatta;
at another time the novice Cunda; at another time Sāgata; and at another time Meghiya.
For the most part, they did not satisfy the Teacher’s mind. Then, on a certain day, the Blessed One was seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne prepared in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber.
Seated surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old;
when some monks say, 'I will go by this path,' they go by another path;
some set down my bowl and robe on the ground; and as for one monk who was my constant attendant—"
“Understand this! Upon hearing this, a sense of spiritual urgency arose among the bhikkhus.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, “Venerable sir, I shall attend upon you. The Blessed One declined his offer.
By this same means, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna, all the great disciples [offered to do so], saying, “I shall attend upon you; I shall…”
“I shall attend upon him,” they rose, with the exception of the Venerable Ānanda. The Blessed One, however, refused them as well.
But Ānanda remained silent. Then the monks said to him, “Friend, you too should request the position of the Teacher’s attendant.
“What kind of thing is it called ‘attending upon the Teacher’ that one receives by requesting it? If it pleases him, let the Teacher himself [choose].”
“He will speak,” [the Elder thought]. Then the Blessed One said, “Monks, Ānanda need not be urged by others; having known it himself, he will attend upon me.
Thereupon the monks said, “Rise, friend Ānanda, and request the Teacher for the position of attendant.
The Elder rose and said, “If, venerable sir, the Blessed One would grant me the choice food that he has received himself...”
“I will serve the Blessed One in this way: I will not give him a robe; I will not give him choice almsfood;
I will not allow him to dwell in the same fragrant chamber; and having accepted an invitation, I will not go [to it with him].
These four refusals were intended to clear him from reproach, showing: “What burden is it for one who receives such virtues to attend upon the Teacher?”
“Venerable sir, if the Blessed One will accept the invitation I have received, and if I am permitted to see him as soon as anyone arrives from other regions,
and if I am permitted to approach the Blessed One and ask questions whenever a doubt arises in me,
and if the Blessed One will explain to me again the Dhamma taught in his absence, [I shall come].”

“In this way, I shall attend upon the Blessed One. These four requests were made for the purpose of clearing away the reproach that he had not received even such a favor from the Teacher’s presence, and for the purpose of fulfilling his status as the Dharma-treasurer (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika).
Having taken these eight boons, he became a constant attendant. For the sake of that very position, [he practiced] for a hundred thousand eons.
He attained the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled.
From the day he obtained the position of attendant, he served the One of Ten Powers with two kinds of water, three kinds of tooth-sticks,
the massaging of hands and feet, the rubbing of the back, and the sweeping of the fragrant chamber and its courtyard.
Attending to him with such duties as these— thinking, "At this particular time, it is fitting for the Teacher to receive such-and-such,
and it is fitting to perform such-and-such"— he remained in the Teacher's presence throughout the day. Then, during the night, taking a large staff-lantern,
he would circumambulate the Gandhakuṭi courtyard nine times so that he might give a prompt reply when the Teacher called out to him.
For the purpose of dispelling sloth and torpor, the Teacher, while seated in the Jeta Grove in the midst of the noble assembly,
praised him in many ways and established him in the foremost position among the monks who are learned, mindful, wise, resolute, and devoted attendants. Thus,
having been placed by the Teacher in these five foremost positions, he was endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities.

This great elder, who was the guardian of the Teacher’s treasury of Dhamma, while still a trainee (*sekha*), was—after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna—exhorted by the monks in the manner described above and moved by a deity, [to think]: "Now indeed the recitation of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgīti*) must be performed;
yet it is not fitting that I, being a trainee with duties still to be done, [should sit] together with the elders who are beyond training (*asekha*)."
Thinking, "I shall go to the assembly to sing the Dhamma," he was filled with enthusiasm. Having established insight (vipassanā), he practiced the work of insight for much of the night;
yet, failing to attain a balance of energy while walking on the meditation path (caṅkama), he entered the monastery and sat upon his bed.
Desiring to lie down, he bent his body, but before his head had reached the pillow, his feet left the ground.
As soon as he was released, within that very interval, his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging, and he became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Thus, adorned with qualities such as the six supernormal knowledges, having attained the foremost position among attendants and others due to his own virtues,
and remembering his former deeds, he spoke the words beginning with "Having gone out from the gate of the monastery," showing his own past conduct out of a sense of joy.

Therein, "at the monastery gate" means that the Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Padumuttara, having emerged from the door of the monastery for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to all beings, sat upon a well-prepared, excellent Buddha-seat in the center of a pavilion constructed near the outer gate.
"Raining down the rain of the Deathless" means raining down the Dhamma-rain by means of the great, deathless streams of Dhamma-teaching. He brought [them] to nibbāna.
“*Mahājanam*”: he extinguished and pacified the fire of the defilements within the mental continuum of the great multitude;
the meaning is that he brought the great multitude to peace and coolness through the nectar-drink of *nibbāna*.

(645) “*Satasahassaṃ te dhīrā*” is said while demonstrating the excellence of his retinue. [He was surrounded] by the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), which consist of the categories of knowledge such as the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhā*).
Endowed with great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) because they possess supernormal powers capable of traveling in an instant across many hundreds of thousands of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*),
those wise ones— whose taints (*āsava*) were exhausted by the hundreds of thousands—

surrounded that Blessed One, the Sambuddha Padumuttara, like a shadow that never departs; the meaning is that they surrounded him and listened to the Dhamma, remaining inseparable from him like a shadow.
646. "I was mounted upon the back of an elephant" means that at the time of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, I was seated on the back of an elephant;
this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "holding the white umbrella, the most excellent," the connection is:

while holding over my head the white umbrella, which is the most excellent and worthy of being aspired to, I was seated upon the back of an elephant. "Having seen his exceedingly beautiful form... [is the continuation].
"Having seen the Fully Enlightened One teaching the Dhamma—beautiful, lovely, and possessing a heart-stealing form—joy, contentment, and gladness arose within me; the meaning is that they arose.
(647) "Descending from the elephant's shoulder": having seen the Blessed One seated there, he descended from the back of the elephant.
"Having descended, I approached the bull among men, the preeminent man"—the meaning is that I went into his presence.
"A jewel-adorned parasol for me"—the connection is: "I held a parasol adorned with jewels over the head of the Supreme Buddha.
648. "Knowing my intention"—that is, having understood the intention arisen through my faith, in the midst of the seers...
"The Blessed One Padumuttara was one who had become great. "Setting that aside" means:
setting aside the discourse on the Dhamma being taught by himself, he spoke these verses for the purpose of giving me a prediction;
this is the meaning. If one asks, "How? he says: "He who... and so forth. That prince of mine, adorned with golden ornaments, [held] a parasol...
"He bore it upon his head"—this is the connection. "I shall praise him"—that is, I shall praise that prince;
I shall make him known. "Listen to my speech"—the meaning is: listen to the words of me as I speak, with attentive ears and with focused attention.
650. “Having gone from here, this person”—meaning this prince—having passed away from this human world and gone to the Tusita heaven, will dwell there;
he will abide there. The connection [of the meaning] is that, honored and surrounded by celestial nymphs (accharā), he will experience the splendor of the Tusita realm.

651. "Thirty-four times" means that after passing away from the Tusita heaven, he will be reborn thirty-four times in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the Lord of Devas (Devinda) and exercise sovereignty over the gods; this is the connection.

"A commander of forces eighty times" means that after passing away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he was reborn in the human world as a commander of forces—the leader and chief of a fourfold army—during eight hundred births.
"Having become a regional king (padesarājā), he will dwell upon the earth, the land abounding in many excellent jewels; 'he will dwell upon the earth' is the meaning.

(652) "Forty-eight times" means that in forty-eight births he will be a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī rājā). "He will exercise extensive and incalculable regional sovereignty over the great earth," that is, over the entire territory of Jambudīpa.
(654) "Of the banner of the Sakyan clan" means that he will be a kinsman of the Buddha, who serves as the banner for the lineage of the Sakyan kings.
655. "Ardent" means possessing energy. "Circumspect" means endowed with wisdom characterized as discernment (*nepakkasaṅkhātāya paññāya*).

"Skilled in the many sciences" means expert and proficient in the state of great learning and in the mastery of the Three Piṭakas. "Of humble conduct" means not being contemptuous and free from arrogance—that is, devoid of the haughty state of physical posturing and so forth.
The connection [of the passage] is: "He will become a reciter of all, a bearer of the entire Three Piṭakas."
656. "One who is resolute in exertion" refers to the Elder Ānanda, whose mind was directed toward the application of energy.

"Peaceful and free from acquisitions" means he is devoid of the acquisitions of passion, hatred, and delusion; because the defilements to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry have been abandoned, he is peaceful, with body and mind calmed.
657. “There are forest-dwellers” means those who dwell in the wilderness, born in the great forest. “Sixty years old” means those whose strength has declined at the age of sixty.
“With three-fold rutting-fluid flowing” means those from whom the rutting-fluid flows from three places, namely the eyes, the ears, and the temples.

“Mātaṅgas” means those born in the Mātaṅga elephant lineage. “With tusks like chariot-poles” means those with tusks resembling the poles of a chariot. “Exalted” means fit to be vehicles for kings. They are designated as “kuñjara” (elephants).

Just as there exist and are found elephant-kings among the *nāgas*, so too there exist wise, highly powerful *arahant-nāgas* numbering in the hundreds of thousands, who are reckoned as those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). All those *arahant-nāgas* belong to the Buddha, the King of *Nāgas*.
"They are not such in their aspiration" means that they are not like that in their aspiration; why? Because all of them are terrified by fear of their own [defiled] nature.
The meaning is that they were unable to remain stable. The remainder is of plain meaning because it follows the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Ānanda-thera-apadāna* is completed.
With this, the commentary on the first section, the *Buddhavagga*, is finished.
The first part is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In the Khuddaka Nikāya...
Apadāna-Ṭīkā (Second Part): The Apadāna of the Elders (Therāpadāna)
2. The Chapter on the Lion Throne (Sīhāsaniyavagga) 1.
The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka "Nibbute lokanāthamhi...
and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka. This [Elder], too, [attained his status] under previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha into a family endowed with wealth and faith.
While the Blessed One was still living, he dwelt in the world of the devas; after the Blessed One had passed away, he was born here and attained the state of discernment.
Upon seeing a shrine containing the bodily relics of the Blessed One, he thought: "Alas, what a loss for me!

Thinking, "It has not yet arrived during the time the Blessed One is living," he cleared his mind toward the cetiya and, filled with joy, had a lion throne made for the Dhamma-seat out of every kind of jewel, resembling one fashioned by a deity; he honored it as if the Buddha were still alive.
Above that, he also constructed a dwelling like a celestial vimāna, and he even provided a footstool for setting the feet upon.
Thus, having performed manifold kinds of worship throughout his life with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, and so forth, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the devas.
Having experienced successive divine splendors in the six realms of sensual bliss, and having experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch among humans many times,
and having experienced the prosperity of regional sovereignty beyond counting, [he appeared] during the time of Kassapa...
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and practiced the duties of a recluse, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans during that interval.
In this present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth;
upon reaching maturity, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, received full ordination, and took up a meditation subject.
Exerting himself and striving, he attained *arahantship* before long.
