Having thus attained the fruit of *arahantship*, he recalled his own past karma, gave rise to joy, and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the verse beginning with "When the Protector of the World had passed away.
In this context, the "Protector of the World" (*lokanātha*) is so called because he is the preeminent lord (*nātha*) of the world (*loka*).
The meaning is "the Lord of the three worlds. The grammatical connection is: "when the World-Protector Siddhattha has attained Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "when the teaching has been expanded":
the meaning is that when the teaching—the three Piṭakas—has been expanded, spread, and made manifest. Regarding the phrase "when the Dispensation is well-known":

the meaning is that when the Buddha’s Dispensation, which comprises the Three Trainings, has been known and realized by many people numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions who have destroyed their taints (āsava).

2–3. "With a serene mind, joyful" means that at that time, while the Buddha was still living, I—having not yet reached [final liberation]—passed away from the deva world and was reborn in the human world.

Upon seeing the relic-shrine (dhātucetiya) of that Blessed One, with a serene mind, a mind associated with faith, a beautiful mind, and having conceived great devotion and confidence, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful my arrival! How well-timed my arrival! I felt such joy.

Thinking, "It is fitting for me to perform a single meritorious deed for the attainment of Nibbāna," he fashioned a lion throne near the Blessed One’s stupa, having adorned it with gold, silver, jewels, and other precious materials in honor of the Blessed One.
He also had a footstool made for the Blessed One to place his feet upon while seated there.
Furthermore, for the purpose of preventing the lion throne from becoming damp, he placed [a covering] over it.
And he built a house. Therefore it was said: “I had a lion-throne made… and there I had a house built.
By that mental clarity means: because I had made a lion-throne for the Blessed One while he was still living, by that mental clarity.
“He was reborn in Tusita” means he was reborn in the Tusita realm.

4. "In length twenty-four": for me, having been reborn there as a god, that which was well-made, produced by merit, and manifested—meaning it came into being at the very moment of my birth—was twenty-four *yojanas* in height (length) and fourteen *yojanas* in width (breadth). The rest is easy to understand.

9. "In ninety-four aeons from now" means in ninety-four aeons from this present aeon; whatever deed I performed or did back then, from that time forward, by the power of my merit, I have not known any miserable rebirth (*duggati*).
The meaning is that no miserable rebirth was ever experienced by me. 10. "In seventy-three aeons from now" means in seventy-three aeons from this present aeon.
"Three persons named Indra" means three universal monarchs (*cakkavatti-rājāno*) named Indra; in a single aeon, across three births, there was a universal monarch named Indra.
Meaning: "In the seventy-second aeon" means in the seventy-second aeon from this present one. Three persons named Sumanā were Cakkavatti kings three times.
"In the seventy-first aeon" means in the seventy-first aeon from this present one, neither more nor less; [therein] those named Varuṇa... Varuṇa.
"Cakkavattīs" means that three kings named Cakkavatti, endowed with the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana), were lords over the four continents;
this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekatthambhikatthera.
The passage beginning with "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha" is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Ekatthambhadāyaka.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [attained his present state].
In the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth after having been a forest worker.
At that time, all the faithful and devoted lay followers, being of one mind, thought, "Let us build an assembly hall for the Blessed One.
Having entered the forest for the sake of timber materials, they saw that lay follower and said to him, "Give us a pillar."

They made their request. Having heard of that situation, he said, "Do not worry," and after dismissing them all, he took a pillar made of heartwood, showed it to the Teacher, and gave it to those very people.

Born with joy because of that very act, and making that his foundation, he performed other meritorious deeds such as giving; then, passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and from there to another.
Having experienced divine prosperities in the six sensual realms, having repeatedly experienced the prosperity of a supreme universal monarch among humans,
and having experienced the prosperity of regional sovereignty for incalculable ages,
he was reborn in this current arising of a Buddha into a family endowed with faith; there, together with his parents, he [listened to] the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having heard this, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and upon receiving full ordination, took up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
As he applied his mind to it, before long he became an *arahant*.
Having thus attained *arahantship*, he recollected his own past deeds and, filled with joy, [recited] the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
Explaining this, he said, "Of Siddhattha," and so forth. Therein, "of Siddhattha" means of the Blessed One, the Fortunate One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

"A great multitude" (*mahāpūgagaṇo*) means a great assembly of lay followers (*upāsaka*); "there was" (*ahu*) is the meaning of "it was" (*ahosi*). "And they went for refuge to the Buddha" means those lay followers went for refuge to the Buddha, they honored him, or they understood him as "the Buddha-refuge. [Likewise] the Tathāgata.
"They have faith" means they place the qualities of the Buddha within the continuum of their own minds.
"All having come together and consulted" means all having assembled and gathered, having consulted and persuaded one another,
and having become of one mind, they built— that is, they constructed— the upper story (*māḷa*), the hall of attendance, for the sake of the Teacher.
The connection is as follows: "While searching for a single pillar among the timber materials in the great Brahma-forest. 15.

"Having seen them in the forest": having seen those lay followers (*upāsaka*) in the forest, having approached the group—that is, having gone near—and having raised my joined palms—that is, having placed the joined palms, with the ten fingers pressed together, upon my head—I [spoke].
The connection is as follows: at that time, he questioned the *gaṇa*, the assembly of lay followers (*upāsaka*), asking, "For what purpose have you come to this forest? (16).
Those virtuous lay followers, being questioned by me, answered—that is, they explained in detail—"Desiring to build a pavilion (*māḷa*), we could not obtain a single pillar. This is the connection.

17. "Give me a single pillar; I shall give it to the Teacher. I will bring the pillar; let these venerable ones be free from concern and devoid of effort regarding the bringing of the pillar"—this is the connection [of the text].
24. "Whatever womb I enter" means whatever birth—whether as a deity or as a human—I approach.
Or, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative: "in whichever world," meaning either in the world of the gods or in the world of humans. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekatthambhika is completed. 3.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Nanda begins with the words "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," etc. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences,
he was reborn in a certain family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity and hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One,
he saw that the Teacher had designated a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties.

Seeing him being appointed [to that position], and himself aspiring for that very office, he offered a great almsgiving accompanied by abundant honor and worship to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
and made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, may I in the future become such a disciple of a Buddha like you."
From that time forth, wandering among gods and humans, during the era of the Blessed One Atthadassi, he was reborn by way of natural law as a large tortoise in a river named Dhammā.

One day, seeing the Teacher standing on the bank about to cross the river, and desiring to ferry the Blessed One across himself, he lay down at the Teacher’s feet. The Teacher [perceived] his intention...
Having understood this, he climbed onto his back. Joyful and elated, cutting through the current with speed, he brought him safely to the opposite shore even more quickly.
The Blessed One, pronouncing a blessing of thanksgiving for him and describing his future prosperity, departed.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering only among the happy realms, he was born here in this era of a Buddha’s appearance in Kapilavatthu.
He was conceived in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the chief queen of King Suddhodana.
On the day his name was given, because he was born bringing joy to the assembly of kinsmen, they gave him the name "Nanda.
When he reached maturity, the Blessed One—having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma and bestowing favor upon the world—gradually arrived at Kapilavatthu.
Having gone to the gathering of his kinsmen, he provided the occasion for the discourse by recounting the Vessantara Jātaka.
On the following day, having entered the city for alms, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) with the verse beginning, “Arise, do not be negligent.
Then, returning to the palace, he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry with the verse beginning, “One should practice the Dhamma well-conducted.”

Having ordained him, and knowing that he was oppressed by dissatisfaction precisely because of that ordination, the Elder dispelled that dissatisfaction through a skillful means.
By reflecting thoroughly and establishing insight, he attained Arahantship before long.
On the following day, the Elder approached the Blessed One and said: "Venerable Sir, as for that which the Blessed One stood as surety for me..."
“For the sake of obtaining five hundred celestial nymphs with the feet of peacocks, Venerable Sir, I release the Blessed One from this promise.
The Blessed One said, “Nanda, when your mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging, at that very moment I was released from this promise.
Then the Blessed One [instructed him] on the guarding of the sense doors with particular detail.

Recognizing that quality and cultivating it, [the Buddha] placed him in the foremost position for guarding the doors of the sense faculties, saying: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples in guarding the doors of the sense faculties, namely Nanda.
For the Elder thought: "Nanda has fallen into this misfortune because of a lack of restraint over his sense faculties; I shall thoroughly restrain him."

Having become energetic and possessed of strong moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of wrongdoing (*ottappa*), and because he had performed service there, he reached the highest perfection in the restraint of the sense faculties.
Having thus attained this foremost position, he recollected his own past deed and, filled with joy, proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), beginning with the words:
"To the Blessed One Padumuttara... [He said: "A linen cloth (*khoma*) was given by me," referring to the Khoma kingdom.
The meaning is: "A cloth born [of merit]," that is, "I have given this most exquisite linen cloth out of serene confidence in the Blessed One and with great reverence and esteem.
"To the Self-Become" (*sayambhu*) means to one who has become or been born by himself through noble birth, having arisen [without a teacher].
"To the Great Seer" (*mahesi*) means to one who seeks or searches for the great aggregates of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The connection is: "O Great Seer, a linen cloth was given by me for the sake of a robe for that Great Seer, the Self-Existent One.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha explained that to me": here, *taṃ* (that) is in the accusative case used in the sense of similarity; the meaning is:
"The Buddha specifically explained—that is, spoke of—the fruit of the gift of that donor of cloth to me. "Named Jalajuttama" means named Padumuttara.
There is also a reading, “Jalaruttamanāyako,” which means: the supreme leader (nāyaka) and foremost (padhāna) among the shining gods and brahmās.
By this gift of cloth—by the result of this gift of cloth—you will, in the future, be of a golden hue, a beautiful golden color.
29. "Having experienced two prosperities" means having experienced the two prosperities consisting of the divine and the human.
"Urged by the roots of merit" means urged or impelled by the factors of merit, by the portions of merit;
the meaning is that he was as if sent with the words, "By this merit, propagate the Teacher’s lineage. [He was told: "You shall be the younger brother of the Blessed One Gotama."
The connection is with the word "explained" (byākāsī).

30. "One who is intoxicated by passion, whose virtue is pleasure": one who is intoxicated by and attached to the defilements of sensual desire, whose nature is the experience of bodily and mental pleasure.
"Entangled in greed for sense-pleasures" means bound and joined by craving, which is termed "greed," toward the objects of sense-desire. By the Buddha...

"Since you were then urged on by greed for sensual pleasures, therefore, having been urged and incited to go forth by your own brother, the Buddha Gotama, you shall go forth in his presence"—this is the connection. 31.
"Having gone forth there"—meaning, having gone forth in that teaching of the Blessed One Gotama.

"Urged by the root of the wholesome, which serves as the foundation for the accumulation of merit, and enjoined to spiritual cultivation, you shall—having fully understood and abandoned all taints (āsava) in their entirety—become free from disease, free from suffering, and attain Nibbāna;
you shall reach the state of non-appearance; you shall go to the state of being indefinable (apaṇṇattika)—this is the meaning. "In a thousand kalpas plus a hundred," means:
in a period of one thousand kalpas plus a hundred kalpas prior to this present kalpa, [there was] one named Ceḷa.
The meaning is that they were four wheel-turning monarchs (*cakkavatti-rājāno*). Regarding "sixty thousand eons" (*kappasahassāni*):
having passed sixty thousand eons, within one eon below that, four persons named Upaceḷa were wheel-turning monarchs in four births;
this is the meaning.
33. "In five thousand aeons" means that in a period of one thousand aeons plus five additional aeons, four men named Ceḷā became Cakkavatti kings, endowed and possessed of the seven treasures;
they were sovereigns and preeminent rulers over the four continents—namely Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha—each separately. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nanda is complete.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka begins with the verse: "The Victor named Padumuttara... This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, whatever is to be said here by way of the origin of the story has already been told in the Mahāpanthaka-vatthu of the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta.
This, however, is the distinction: after the Elder Mahāpanthaka had attained Arahatship, through the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*),...
While passing his time [in meditation], he thought: "How indeed might it be possible to establish Cūḷapanthaka in this same happiness?
He approached his own grandfather, Dhanaseṭṭhi, and said:
"If you grant permission, Great Merchant, I would ordain Cūḷapanthaka. "Ordain him, venerable sir," he replied. The Elder ordained him. He—
Established in the ten precepts, he stood before his brother and said:
“Just as a fragrant red lotus may be in full bloom at dawn, its fragrance unabated;
behold Aṅgīrasa shining brightly, like the sun scorching in the sky.”
While learning a verse, Cūḷapanthaka was unable to master it in four months; even when learned, it did not remain in his heart.
Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, “Cūḷapanthaka, you are incapable in this dispensation;
since you cannot grasp even a single verse in four months, how will you bring the purpose of your going forth to its fulfillment?”
"Go out from here! Thus addressed by the Elder, he stood weeping near the gateway, bowing down.

At that time, the Teacher was dwelling in Jīvakambavana. Then Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go and invite the Teacher together with five hundred bhikkhus. At that same time, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka...
He was the distributor of alms-food. When told, "Accept alms for five hundred bhikkhus," he replied, "I accept for all except Cūḷapanthaka.
Upon hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became even more deeply distressed.
The Teacher, perceiving his mental anguish, thought, "Cūḷapanthaka will attain awakening through a method devised by me."
Appearing before him at a nearby spot, he asked, "Why are you weeping, Panthaka?
He replied, "Venerable Sir, my brother has sent me away. "Do not worry, Panthaka; you shall go forth in my teaching.
Come, take this and attend to it, thinking, 'The dust-remover, the dust-remover. With his psychic power, [the Buddha] provided a clean piece of cloth.

Having prepared it, he gave it to him. The Teacher took the piece of cloth given to him and sat down, rubbing it with his hand while saying, "Dust-remover! Dust-remover! As he rubbed it, it became soiled;
as he rubbed it further, it became like the residue from a mortar. Because of the ripening of his knowledge, he thought thus:
“This piece of cotton is naturally pure, yet by depending on this appropriated body it has become defiled and changed;

therefore, just as this is impermanent, so too is the mind. Having thus established the contemplation of decay and fall, he developed the jhānas upon that very sign, used them as a basis for the jhānas, and then established insight.
He attained Arhatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). As soon as he had attained Arhatship, the Three Piṭakas and the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) came to him.
The Teacher went with four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus and sat upon a seat prepared in the residence of Jīvaka.
However, Cūḷapanthaka did not go because his own alms-food had not been accepted. Jīvaka [prepared] rice-gruel...
He began to give it. The Teacher covered the bowl with his hand. When asked, "Why, venerable sir, do you not take it?
he replied, "Jīvaka, there is a certain bhikkhu staying in the monastery. He sent a man, saying, "Go, my good man, and bring the noble one who is sitting in the monastery.
Now, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka was such that neither in physical appearance nor in conduct could anyone distinguish him from another.
Having created a thousand monks who were his very likeness, he sat down.
When that man saw the great number of monks in the monastery, he went and told Jīvaka: "The community of monks in this monastery is more numerous than the one here;
I do not know which venerable one should be summoned. Jīvaka asked the Teacher: "Who is it, Bhante, in the monastery?"
“Is there a monk sitting here named Cūḷapanthaka? “There is one named Cūḷapanthaka, Jīvaka.
“Go, my man, ask ‘Which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? and bring him here. He went to the monastery and asked, “Venerable sir, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka?
At that moment, even a thousand monks cried out all at once, “I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!”

He related it. When he returned and reported that occurrence to Jīvaka, Jīvaka—having understood the situation through inference because he had himself penetrated the Truths, thinking, "The noble sir is surely possessed of psychic power"—said, "Go, my man;
when the noble sir is first speaking, tell him, 'The Teacher summons you,' and take hold of the corner of his robe. He went to the monastery and did exactly as instructed. At that very moment,
The created monks vanished. Taking the Elder with him, he departed.
At that moment, the Teacher accepted the rice gruel and the various kinds of solid food.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he commanded the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, "Give the blessing. He, whose analytical knowledges were fully developed, [proceeded] like Mount Sineru...
As if churning the great ocean, agitating the Buddha-word contained in the Three Piṭakas, and grasping the Teacher’s intention, he offered his expression of gratitude.
When the One of Ten Powers had finished his meal and returned to the monastery, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall:
“Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas! For it is said that in four months he was able to grasp even a single verse.”
"Even though they were unable [to do so themselves], they made him of such great psychic power in a mere moment.

For indeed, while seated in Jīvaka’s residence, the Blessed One, knowing that "Cūḷapanthaka’s mind is thus concentrated and his insight has entered the path," showed himself while remaining exactly as he was and said:
"Panthaka, this rag is not at all stained or covered in dust."
Furthermore, showing that there is yet another defilement and stain within the discipline of the Noble One, he says:
“Lust is the stain, and not dust is so called; ‘stain’ is a designation for lust.
Having utterly abandoned this stain, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of Him who is free from stain.”
“Hatred is dust… [as before] …in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
Delusion is dust… [as before] …in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
Having spoken these three verses, at the conclusion of the verses, Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
"He has attained it. Having heard the conversation between those bhikkhus, the Teacher approached, sat upon the Buddha’s seat, and asked, "What are you discussing, bhikkhus?

When they replied, "This, venerable sir," he said, "Bhikkhus, by now Cūḷapanthaka has obtained the supramundane inheritance by abiding in my instruction; but in the past, he obtained a mundane inheritance."
Having spoken thus, when requested by them, he related the Cūḷaseṭṭhijātaka.

Later on, while seated upon the Dhamma-seat surrounded by a host of noble ones, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those monks who manifest mind-made bodies and those skilled in the turning away of the mind.
Thus, having attained this foremost position and recollecting his own past deed, through a state of joy and gladness, he [recited] this account of his former conduct.
Proclaiming this, he said, "The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth. Therein, the meaning of the first two phrases is already explained.
"He who was secluded from the group" means that the Teacher named Padumuttara was secluded from the group—that is, from the great assembly of monks—and having become separate, he attained solitude.
At that time, during my period as an ascetic, near the Himalayan mountains in the Himavanta...
He made his dwelling there; the meaning is that he lived by means of the four postures.

36. "And I... 'then' (tadā): when that Blessed One, having approached the Himavat, dwelt there, then I too—near the Himavat, in a hermitage (assama) so named because 'all' (ā) perils (parissaya), consisting of afflictions of body and mind, are stilled (samanti) therein—[dwelt]."

"I dwell in forest retreats" is the connection. "The Great Hero who has recently arrived" means they approached that Blessed One, the Leader of the World, who possesses great heroism and had just come after his exertion; the meaning is that they went to him at the very moment of his arrival.
"Having taken a flower parasol" refers to approaching in this manner while holding a parasol covered with lotus, water-lily, and other flowers.
"Taking a flower-made parasol and approaching the Blessed One—the bull among men, the best of men—while shading him, I drew near";
this is the meaning. "While he was entering into meditative absorption" refers to the connection:
"I created an obstacle for him as he sat having entered into and attained the fine-material-sphere absorption (rūpāvacara-jhāna)."
38. "Taking it with both hands" means that I raised up that well-adorned flower-parasol with both hands and gave it to the Blessed One;
this is the connection [of the words]. "He accepted" means that the Blessed One Padumuttara received that flower-parasol given by me;
the sense is that he graciously consented to it.

41. “Having taken up a hundred-petaled parasol” means that he took up with great care and respect a flower-parasol covered with lotus flowers, each of which had a hundred petals by way of having one hundred petals on every single lotus blossom;
this is the meaning. “I shall praise him” means that I, [the Buddha], shall praise that ascetic, that is, I shall make him known.
"Listen to my words as I speak them and attend to them.

(42) "For twenty-five eons" means that by virtue of this gift of a flower-parasol, he will act as the king of the gods, having been Sakka twenty-five times in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; such is the connection. And "thirty-four times" means thirty-four occasions.
In the world of humans, he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
43. Whichever womb—whether among human wombs or others—he transmigrates through, goes to, or is reborn in;
in each such womb, he stands, sits, or remains like a lotus placed in an open space or a vacant spot.
"Will uphold" means "will cover over from above. 45.

"When the teaching has been proclaimed": when the entire three baskets (piṭakat-taya) have been proclaimed and illuminated by that Blessed One, one will obtain human status—that is, one will be reborn into the human race.
"In the mind-made body": by means of the mind, namely, the consciousness of meditative absorption (jhāna-citta).
"Reborn" means mind-made (*manomaya*); the meaning is that he moves his body according to how his mind functions, making it follow the course of the mind.
In that mind-made body, that ascetic will become one named Cūḷapanthaka, supreme and foremost—this is the meaning.
The remainder is easily understood, as it has already been explained below and is self-evident.
52. "I plunged into the *kokanada* lotus": the meaning is that while I was wiping the cloth offered by the Blessed One, I plunged into the *kokanada* lotus.
Regarding the phrase "my mind was liberated therein," the connection is as follows: my mind became intent upon and attached to that *kokanada* lotus, and from that, I attained *arahantship*.

53. "I have reached the perfection, the culmination, in all respects and in all [instances] regarding bodies made of mind, which are of the nature of thought"—this is the connection. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka is complete.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Pilindavaccha Thera begins with the words, "When the Protector of the World had attained Nibbāna...

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī; there, in accordance with the manner described below, he came into the presence of the Teacher.
While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among the deities for his being dear and pleasing to them.

Having aspired to that very rank and performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed away from there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he paid homage to his stupa.
Having offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha, he passed away from there and experienced the two kinds of excellence among gods and humans.
When no Buddha had yet appeared, he became a wheel-turning monarch; having established the great masses in the five precepts, he made them destined for heaven.
Even before our Blessed One had appeared, he was reborn in Sāvatthī in a brahmin family as Pilindotissa.
They gave him the name [Pilinda] and his clan was Vaccha; later, he became known as Pilindavaccha.
However, due to a great sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding *saṃsāra*, he went forth as a wandering ascetic (*paribbājaka*).

Having mastered the spell called Cūḷagandhāra, through that spell he became a traveler through the air and a knower of others' minds, dwelling in Rājagaha having attained the pinnacle of gain and the height of fame.
Then, after our Blessed One had attained full enlightenment, he gradually arrived at Rājagaha.
From that time on, through the power of the Buddha, his knowledge did not succeed and he could no longer accomplish his own purpose. He thought:
"I have indeed heard the teachers of old saying: 'Wherever the Mahāgandhārī spell prevails, [it does not work]...'"
"In this regard, my Cūḷagandhāra spell is not succeeding. From the time the ascetic Gotama arrived, [he thought:
"This spell of mine is no longer effective; undoubtedly the ascetic Gotama knows the Mahāgandhāra spell.
What if I were to attend upon him and learn that spell from his presence? He [approached] the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this: “Great Ascetic, I wish to master a certain branch of knowledge in your presence;
please grant me the opportunity. He replied, “In that case, go forth in my presence.

Thinking, “Going forth is the preliminary practice for the acquisition of knowledge,” he went forth. After the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma, he gave him a meditation subject suitable to his temperament.
He gave [it]. Because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he soon established insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*.

As for those deities who, in a previous birth, had been reborn in heaven by following his advice, they—out of gratitude and having conceived great reverence for him—would attend upon the Elder morning and evening before departing. Therefore, the Blessed One [addressed him as follows].
Because of his exceedingly dear and pleasing nature to the deities, he placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"This is the foremost among my disciples, monks, those bhikkhus who are dear and pleasing to the deities, namely Pilindavaccha.

Thus, having attained the foremost place regarding alms-bowls and recollecting his own past karma, he proclaimed this account of his former conduct out of joy and gladness when [the Buddha] had passed away.
He spoke the words beginning with "Lokanāthamhi.

Therein, he is the "Lord of the World" (lokanātha) because he is the protector and the preeminent one over the worlds of desire, form, and formlessness. Wisdom (medhā) refers to the knowledge of omniscience, the unobstructed knowledge, and so forth;
he whose wisdom is beautiful or excellent is "Sumedha. He is the "Supreme Person" (aggapuggala) because he is both supreme and a person.
The connection is: "When that Sumedha, the Leader of the World, the Supreme Person, had attained final Nibbāna through the parinibbāna of the aggregates.

With a clear mind and joyful heart—meaning with a mind clarified by faith and a beautiful mind through gladness—I performed the stupa worship, the worship of the shrine, for that Blessed One Sumedha; such is the meaning.
56. "And those who have destroyed the taints there"— that is, in that assembly, those who have destroyed the taints, who have abandoned the defilements, who possess the six direct knowledges,
who are endowed with the six higher knowledges, and who are of great psychic power, being possessed of great supernormal powers—
all those who have destroyed the taints, having gathered them together there with great care and respect, [I shall provide] a meal for the Saṅgha for the entire Saṅgha.
"I provided the meal that was to be given; the meaning is that I fed them.

(57) "At that time he was my attendant" means that at that time, when I was giving a meal to the Saṅgha, there was a disciple attendant named Sumedha—after the Blessed One—meaning he was called Sumedha. That disciple offered me his appreciation for the honor and hospitality.
The meaning is that he spoke of the benefits after having expressed his appreciation.
"By that clarity of mind" means that by means of the clarity of mind arisen through performing the worship of the stupa, I was reborn—meaning I arrived—in a divine mansion in the world of the devas;
the sense is that "I have been born there. "Eighty-six thousand" [refers to the number].
The connection [of the verse] is: "In that celestial mansion (*vimāna*), sixty thousand celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*) delighted my mind and caused it to rejoice.

(59) "Following after me alone" means those nymphs, while attending upon me with all divine sensual pleasures—the objects of desire such as forms and so forth—followed me alone and always, at all times, acted according to my word; this is the meaning. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pilindavaccha is completed.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Rāhula:
"Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Rāhula. This Venerable One...

Having performed services under previous supreme Victors and accumulating merits conducive to the realization of *vivaṭṭa* (the turning away from existence) in various births, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those desirous of training (*sikkhākāma*). Seeing this, he himself...
Aspiring to that state, he performed sublime meritorious deeds such as cleaning and illuminating the dwelling place, and made a formal resolution (*paṇidhāna*).
Passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing both types of excellence.
Then, during this arising of a Buddha, having been conceived in the womb of Queen Yasodharā on account of our Bodhisatta, he was born.
Named Rāhula, he grew up surrounded by a great retinue of kṣatriyas. The account of his ordination is found in the Khandhaka itself.
Having gone forth, he received excellent instruction from many discourses in the presence of the Teacher;
with matured knowledge, he applied himself to insight and attained arahantship. Having become an arahant and reflecting upon his own practice, he declared his realization:
“Endowed with both qualities, the wise call me Rāhula the Fortunate:
that I am the son of the Buddha, and that I am one who possesses vision regarding the Dhammas.
That my taints are exhausted, and that there is no further becoming.”
“I am an arahant worthy of offerings, one possessed of the three knowledges, a seer of the Deathless.
Blinded by sensual desire, shrouded in a net, covered by the veil of craving,
they are bound by their negligent kinsman like fish in the mouth of a trap.”
“Having abandoned that sensual desire, having severed Māra’s bond, and having uprooted craving, I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
Thus he spoke these four verses. Therein, “endowed with both” refers to the excellence of birth and the excellence of practice.
He was endowed and possessed of both kinds of excellence. Regarding the phrase "the wise know me as Rāhulabhadda":

my fellow practitioners of the holy life recognize me as "Rāhulabhadda. For when the Great King Suddhodana heard the announcement of his birth, he took up the words spoken by the Bodhisatta—"Rāhu is born; a bond is born"—and gave him the name "Rāhula."
In this regard, at the beginning, he spoke using the very same expression uttered by his father: “The wise call me Rāhula-bhadra.
*Bhadra* is simply a word of praise. Later, because of his desire for training (*sikkhākāmatā*), the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying:
“This is the foremost among my disciples, monks, those who are desirous of training, namely Rāhula.”

68. Thus, having attained this foremost position and remembering his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the words beginning with "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara...
Regarding the phrase "in the seven-storied palace" (*sattabhūmimhi pāsāde*): it is called a *pāsāda* because it produces serene confidence (*pasāda*) and joy;
that palace which has seven stories situated one above the other is the "seven-storied," and in that [palace].

"In the seven-storied palace: 'I spread out a mirror' means that having prepared a mirror-surface, I gave a carpet for the World-Chief, the Blessed One, the Neutral One; the meaning is that after spreading it, I honored him. 69.

'Surrounded by thousands of those whose taints were destroyed' means surrounded and encompassed by thousands of Arahants. 'The Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men, the Great Sage'—the meaning is that he, the Lord of bipeds, approached and entered the fragrant chamber together with them."

70. Shining forth, beautifying that very fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), the god of gods among gods, the bull among men among men, the eldest, the Teacher—having sat down in the midst of the community of monks—he spoke these verses of explanation;
such is the connection [of the text].
71. "By whom this bed was illumined": by which lay follower (*upāsaka*) this bed, known as the palace, was illumined, made radiant, and set ablaze.
It was spread out so that it was perfectly level, like the surface of a mirror made of bell-metal (*kaṃsaloha*).
"I shall praise that lay follower" means I shall make him manifest. The rest is easy to understand.

81. "It is impossible that such a one"—meaning for whatever reason such a one is "such" (tādī) due to having a nature unshakable by the desirable and the undesirable—that he should attain or reach a state of attachment (*allīnabhāva*) to the household, to the life of a householder; this reason is "impossible," meaning it is not a valid cause.

82. "Having gone forth from the home"—having departed from the household life and having abandoned it like a blade of grass—he, being well-vowed and well-trained, will go forth. By the name of Rāhula—thus sent by the Great King Suddhodana.
Having heard the news of the prince’s birth, his father Siddhattha said, "Rāhu is born; a bond is born," and because he was given that name, the meaning is that he is named Rāhula.

Just as the asura lord Rāhu approaches and goes toward the moon and sun by defiling their celestial mansions with his radiance, even so, this one [was named] as if to create an obstacle to my going forth and renunciation.
It should be understood that this was said with the intention that "Rāhu has been born";
the meaning is that he will become an Arahant—one endowed with such a decisive support (*upanissaya*), who is devoted to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), and whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted.
"As a hen would protect her egg": just as a hen, protecting her egg—that is, the seed—remains vigilant, [so too should one guard] virtue (*sīla*).

One should protect it just as a yak protects its tail; like a yak that, while protecting its tail, refuses to pull away even when its hair gets caught in thorns for fear of breaking it, and thus dies rather than break its tail, one should protect one’s virtue even at the cost of life, without breaking it.
"The prudent one, endowed with virtue": *nepakka* is said to be wisdom (*paññā*); possessed of that *nepakka*, the prudent one [guards against] the state of being broken, torn, or otherwise impaired.
"Because he will protect [the precepts] after having attained them, he will be one perfected in virtue (sīlasampanna)"—thus did the Blessed One give this prediction.

Having thus attained the fruit of Arahatship, one day while sitting in a secluded place, out of a sense of gladness, he spoke these words beginning with "Thus the Great Sage protected... This is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Rāhula is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta begins with the verse:
"To the Blessed One Padumuttara... and so forth. This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta.
This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds in previous lives under former Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*),
was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, he went into the presence of the Teacher and, while listening to the Dhamma, [saw] the Teacher [appoint] one bhikkhu as the most serene on all sides (*samantapāsādikānaṃ*).
Seeing him being placed in the foremost position, he performed acts of service for the Teacher, aspired to that same status, and practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in the village of Nālaka, in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī;
his name was Upasena. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas.
Having mastered [the teachings] and heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth,

and upon reaching the first year of full ordination (*upasampadā*), thinking, "I shall increase the noble lineage," he ordained a certain son of good family in his own presence and went with him into the presence of the Teacher.
And the Teacher [assigned] that unordained monk to be the resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of that [junior] bhikkhu.
Having heard this, he was rebuked: "O foolish man, you have indeed turned back too quickly toward abundance!

Thinking, "Now, if I have been rebuked by the Teacher on account of the assembly, I shall win the Teacher's favor by means of that very assembly," he applied himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arhatship. Having become an Arhat, he himself...
He practiced by undertaking all the ascetic virtues (dhutaṅgas), and he encouraged others as well for that purpose;
therefore, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position among those who are "all-round beautiful" (samantapāsādikas).
Later, when a dispute had arisen at Kosambī and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was split into two factions, he—desiring to avoid that quarrel with one bhikkhu—[said]: "At present..."
When asked, "A quarrel has arisen and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has split; how indeed should I proceed?", [the Elder] explained his own practice, beginning from his dwelling in seclusion.
Thus, by means of giving this exhortation to that bhikkhu, the Elder declared his own state of realization, demonstrating that he had practiced in such a manner.

86. Thus, having attained this foremost position and recollecting his own past karma, he spoke the words beginning with "The Blessed One Padumuttara," proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct) out of a sense of joy.
Regarding the phrase "sitting on a slope" (*pabbhāramhi nisīdantaṃ*): a "slope" (*pabbhāra*) is that which has its burden bent or inclined forward;
it refers to one desiring seclusion, sitting in a self-arisen mountain slope in the midst of a forest.
"I approached the Blessed One, the supreme among men" means that I went into his presence.
"Seeing a *kaṇikāra* flower" means that while approaching in that manner, I saw a *kaṇikāra* tree in full bloom in that place.
"Having cut it from its stalk at that time" means that at the moment I saw the Tathāgata, I [cut] that flower from its stalk.
"Having cut it at the stalk," means having severed it. "Having adorned it upon the parasol" means having covered the parasol with that flower.
"They offered it to the Buddha" means they placed it upon the head of the Buddha seated on the mountain slope.
(88) "And alms-food for his feet" means I gave alms-food in a special manner to the Blessed One while he was seated right there.
The meaning is "he fed. *Paramannaṃ subhojanaṃ* means the supreme food known as *paramanna*, which is excellent food, the highest nourishment.

*Buddhena navame tattha* means that in that secluded place, together with the Buddha as the ninth, he fed eight monks who were recluses who had stilled their evil and whose taints were exhausted; this is the meaning.

"He whom they call Sumedha" refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One Gotama, who possesses vast wisdom (*bhūripañña*)—wisdom equal to the earth—and is "Sumedha," meaning one endowed with beautiful, all-knowing wisdom and so forth.

The connection is that the wise say, "He who is called Sumedha, the one of beautiful wisdom, will become this Perfectly Enlightened One Gotama one hundred thousand aeons from now. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta is completed.
8. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla:
"Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Raṭṭhapāla. This Venerable One...
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to the attainment of liberation throughout various existences,
he was reborn even before the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great householders in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Upon reaching maturity, after his father’s passing, he established himself in the life of a householder as the superintendent of the treasury of jewels.

Having seen the immeasurable wealth displayed that had been inherited through his lineage, he thought, "My father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth, were unable to take this vast heap of wealth with them when they departed; yet it is fitting that I should take it with me.
Having reflected thus, he gave a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, and others. He then approached an ascetic who had attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and, by him—

Appointed as the ruler of the world of the gods, he performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his life. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods and experienced divine splendor.
Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan, he passed away and was reborn in the human world as the only son of a family capable of restoring a divided kingdom. At that time—

The Blessed One Padumuttara, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, led those beings who were ready to be trained to the land of safety known as the Great City of Nibbāna.
Then, that son of noble family, having gradually attained maturity, went one day to the monastery together with lay devotees;
seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, he sat down at the edge of the assembly with a mind full of serene faith.
Now at that time, the Teacher placed a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith.

Seeing this, the man, with a mind full of serene confidence, gave a great almsgiving for seven days to the Blessed One, who was surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, and aspired to that same position.
The Teacher, seeing that it would be accomplished without obstacle, said: "In the future..."
“He shall become the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama,” he prophesied.
Having paid homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, he rose from his seat and departed.

Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as his lifespan lasted, and passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans; ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Phussa—
In that time, while the Teacher’s three half-brothers were attending upon him, he performed the duty of assisting them in their meritorious deeds.
Having thus accumulated much wholesome karma through various existences and wandering only among happy destinies,
during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born in the merchant Raṭṭhapāla’s family in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the kingdom of Kuru.
He was reborn in a household capable of restoring a broken kingdom; therefore, his name was inherited from his lineage as Raṭṭhapāla.
Growing up with a great retinue, he gradually reached the prime of youth and was united by his parents with a suitable wife.
Established in great glory, he enjoyed a prosperity resembling that of divine bliss.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the countryside through the kingdom of Kuru, arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika.
Having heard this, the noble son Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher; having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and, desiring to go forth, fasted for seven days.
After much difficulty and hardship, he obtained his parents' permission.
Having approached the Teacher and requested the going-forth, he was ordained in the presence of a certain elder by the Teacher’s command.
Performing his duties with wise attention and increasing his insight, he attained arahantship.
Having attained arahantship, and having obtained the Teacher’s permission, he went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his mother and father; and there—
While wandering for alms from house to house, he received some last night’s sour gruel at his father’s residence;
partaking of it as if it were nectar, he accepted his father’s invitation for the following day.
On the second day, having finished his meal at his father’s house, he approached the women of the harem who were dressed in their finest attire and asked, “What kind of people are they?”
Having said such things as, "Noble son, these are the nymphs for whose sake you lead the holy life," they began to employ seductive tactics.
Having turned their intention aside, he preached the Dhamma connected with impermanence and other such themes, saying:
"Behold this painted image, a body of sores piled together; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“Behold this form fashioned by the mind, which is afflicted and full of many thoughts, and for which there is no lasting stability— adorned with gems and earrings,
yet it is a skeleton wrapped in skin that shines along with its garments.”
“Feet adorned with anklets, face smeared with powder—
this is enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
Hair arranged in eight-part patterns, eyes anointed with collyrium— ”
Enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for one seeking the further shore:
Like a freshly painted collyrium box, this putrid body is adorned;
Enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for one seeking the further shore.
“The hunter set the snare, yet the deer did not fall into the trap;
having eaten the bait, we depart while the deer-trappers wail.
The hunter’s snare is severed; the deer did not fall into the trap.”
"Having partaken of our fodder, we depart; the deer-trappers grieve.
Having spoken these verses, he rose up into the air and sat down upon the auspicious stone slab in King Koravya’s Migājina forest park.
It is said that the Elder’s father had caused bolts to be fixed at seven gate-towers.
The King gave orders: "Do not let him go out; having removed his saffron robes, have him dressed in white garments.

Therefore, the Elder departed through the air. Then King Koravya, having heard that the Elder was seated there, approached him, exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, and said: "Sir Raṭṭhapāla, one who goes forth here—"
“Some go forth having encountered the loss of health, or the loss of wealth, or the loss of relatives; but why do you go forth when you have not experienced any such loss?
He asked. Then the Elder replied to him: “The world is swept away, it is unstable;
the world is without shelter, without a lord; the world is without refuge, and everything must eventually be abandoned and departed from; the world is deficient and unsatisfied.”
Having declared that he himself had realized these four summaries of the Dhamma—“a slave to craving”—he spoke this verse as a sequel to that teaching:
“I see people in the world with wealth who, having acquired riches, do not give them away out of delusion.
Greedy, they hoard their wealth and desire even more sensual pleasures.”
“A king, having conquered the earth by force and dwelling upon the great land as far as the ocean’s edge,
might still be unsatisfied with what lies on this side of the sea and long for even the further shore beyond.
Both the king and many other men, not being free from craving, come to death.”
Having offered less than they had intended, they abandon the body; yet there is no satiety with sensual pleasures in this world.
Their relatives, scattering their hair, wail for them, saying, "Alas! Oh, that we were not dead!
Having wrapped him in cloth and carried him out, they pile up the funeral pyre and then burn him.
“Thus he is burned while being impaled on stakes, having abandoned his wealth for a single garment.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor companions can be a refuge for one who is dying.
His heirs take away his riches, but the being goes wherever his karma leads.”
No wealth whatsoever follows one who is dying—not sons, nor wives, nor riches, nor the kingdom.
One does not obtain long life through wealth, nor can one ward off old age with riches.
For the wise say this life is short here, impermanent, and subject to change.
“The wealthy and the poor alike experience contact; the fool and the wise person are touched by it in the same way.
For the fool lies prostrate, as if slain by his own folly, while the wise person does not tremble when touched by contact.
Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth, for by means of it one attains security in this world.”
For because of not having reached the end of existence, one performs evil deeds out of delusion.
One enters a womb and the other world, undergoing the succession of saṃsāra;
the person of little wisdom, placing full confidence in that, enters a womb and the other world.
"Just as a crow caught at the opening of a trap is slain by its own deed, so too, when people pass away to the next world, they are slain by their own evil deeds.
For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; in their various forms, they agitate the mind."
“Having seen the peril in the strands of sensual pleasure, O King, I have therefore gone forth.
Young men and the aged alike fall like fruits from a tree upon the dissolution of the body;
seeing this too, O King, I have gone forth. The life of a recluse is certainly better, for it is unerring.”
“Out of faith I went forth, having entered the teaching of the Victor;
my going forth has not been in vain, and free from debt I enjoy my food.
Having seen sensual pleasures as a blazing fire and gold as a blade, [I have renounced them].”
“From the descent into the womb comes suffering, a great terror in the hells.
Having understood this danger, I then attained a sense of spiritual urgency;
being thus pierced [by that realization], I have now reached the destruction of the taints.”
“I have served the Teacher; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
For the sake of which I went forth from the home to the homeless life—”
“Thus my goal has been attained: the destruction of all fetters”—these verses he spoke.

Having thus taught the Dhamma to King Koravya, the Elder went back into the presence of the Teacher. Later on, while seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith.
97–8. Thus that Elder, having attained this preeminent status and remembering his former deeds, became filled with joy as he recounted the account of his past conduct.
Explaining this, he said, "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," and so forth.

"A choice elephant was given by me" means that, having gained confidence in the physical body (*rūpakāya*) of that Blessed One, [he gave] a choice, supreme, and excellent elephant—one with tusks like the poles of a chariot, well-trained, capable of bearing burdens, and worthy of a king.
"Adorned with a white parasol" means attended by a white parasol raised over its back.
Shining. Furthermore, what distinguished this noble elephant? It was well-trained and adorned with ornaments on its trunk.
For the sake of providing a dwelling for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, I caused a monastery and a vihāra to be built.
99. Regarding "fourty-five thousand": within that vihāra which was thus constructed, there were forty-five thousand palaces.

"And I caused [them] to be made"—this is the meaning. "Having performed a great flood-like gift" means having prepared a great gift resembling a vast flood, complete with all requisites, and dedicated it to the Sage, the Great Seer—this is the meaning.
"The Great Hero rejoiced" refers to his resolve that remained uninterrupted throughout four hundred thousand times ten million aeons (*asaṅkhyeya*).
By means of his energy, the Great Hero—the self-become one who had become [enlightened] by himself, having attained the knowledge of omniscience, the foremost and most excellent person—rejoiced;

he performed an expression of appreciation for the dwelling. "Making all people laugh" means making all gods and humans throughout the entire infinite and immeasurable world laugh, bringing them to satisfaction by delivering a teaching on the Dhamma of the Four Truths connected with the deathless Nibbāna.
"Taught, proclaimed, revealed, analyzed, and made clear"—this is the meaning.
"He explained that to me" means he made manifest to me specifically the power of the merit I had performed. "Named the Supreme among Water-born Ones":
*jalaja* means "water-born," referring to the lotus (*paduma*); thus the meaning is "named Padumuttara. There is also a reading: "The Leader named Supreme among Water-born Ones."

In this context, those who shine by their own radiance are the "shining ones" (*jalanā*), namely the moon, the sun, the gods, and the brahmās; the supreme among those shining ones is the "supreme shining one" (*jalanuttama*).
He is the "leader" (*nāyaka*) because he is the foremost leader of all beings, or because he leads (*neti*) and causes beings endowed with the necessary requisites to attain *nibbāna*.
Thus, he is the "supreme shining leader" (*jalanuttamanāyaka*). [He dwells] in the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅghe*).
"Having sat down" means that, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he spoke these verses; the meaning is that he recited them clearly.
The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla is completed.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sopāka.
"Of him who was clearing the mountain cave," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sopāka.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various births the merits conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), [served] Siddhattha...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn as the son of a certain householder.
One day, having seen the Teacher, he offered *bījapūra* fruits to the Master; out of compassion for him, the Blessed One partook of them.
That bhikkhu, having gained deep faith in the Teacher and the Saṅgha, established a system of providing meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) on behalf of the Saṅgha.

He gave milk-rice to three monks for as long as he lived. By virtue of those merits, experiencing successive successes among gods and humans, he was once reborn in the human womb and gave milk-rice to a Paccekabuddha.
Thus, having performed meritorious deeds here and there and wandering only through happy destinies, by the natural result of his former karma during this current appearance of a Buddha—
In Sāvatthī, he took rebirth in the womb of a certain destitute woman.
After she had carried him in her womb for ten months, when the fetus was fully developed and it was time for delivery, she was unable to give birth;
she fell into a swoon and lay for a long time as if dead. Thinking he was dead, her relatives carried him to the cemetery, placed him upon the funeral pyre, and...
When a wind and rainstorm arose, by the power of the deity, they departed without lighting the fire.
Because the boy was in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*), by the very power of the deity he emerged from his mother’s womb healthy; however, the mother passed away.
Then the deity, assuming a human form, took him and placed him in the house of a cemetery-keeper, where for some days she remained in a suitable guise.
He nourished him with food. Thereafter, the cemetery keeper raised him as his own son.
As he grew up in this way, he played about together with a boy named Suppiya, who was the keeper's biological son.
Because he had been born and raised in the cemetery, he became known by the name Sopāka.

Then one day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One spread out the net of his knowledge and, surveying those susceptible to his teaching as if they were kinsmen, saw that the boy was caught within the net of his knowledge; he then went to the charnel ground.
Urged on by his past causes, the boy approached the Teacher with a serene mind, paid homage to him, and stood before him. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to him.
Having heard this Dhamma and requested ordination, he was told by his father, "You have my permission. He then led his father into the presence of the Teacher.
His father, having paid homage to the Teacher, gave his consent, saying, "Venerable sir, please ordain this boy.
After ordaining him, the Blessed One directed him toward the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*). Having taken up the meditation subject of loving-kindness, he went to the charnel ground.
While dwelling there, before long, having made the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*) his foundation and having developed insight (*vipassanā*), he realized *arahantship*.
Having become an *arahant*, in order to show other forest-dwelling monks (*sosānika-bhikkhu*) the method for the cultivation of loving-kindness, he spoke this verse: "Just as toward an only son...
This is what is meant: just as a mother and father act for the welfare of an only son who is dear and beloved...

One should be intent on the absolute welfare [of others]; thus, one should be skilled in being intent on the absolute welfare of all beings— whether distinguished by the directions such as the east and so forth,
or by the states of existence such as the realm of sense-desire and so forth, or by all stages of life such as childhood and so forth—
without establishing boundaries such as "friend," "neutral person," or "enemy," but rather by breaking down those boundaries.
Having spoken this verse, "One should cultivate loving-kindness that has a single flavor everywhere," he gave this instruction: "Venerable sirs,
if you cultivate loving-kindness in this way, you will certainly partake in those eleven benefits of loving-kindness which were described by the Blessed One, beginning with 'one sleeps in comfort.'"
112. Thus, having attained the fruit [of his goal] and reflecting upon the merit he had performed, he became joyful;

and in order to show the account of his former conduct, he spoke the words beginning with "While cleaning the mountain cave. Therein, "mountain cave" (*pabbhāra*) refers to a secluded place on a rocky mountain;
because it was suitable for one who has gone forth, he constructed a wall of bricks and a door-panel for it.
Having prepared it, he gave it for the monks to dwell in; because it was to be sought after with great effort (*pakārena bharo*), it is called a *pabbhāra*.
While I was clearing it away, the Blessed One named Siddhattha came and arrived in my presence. 113.
"Seeing the Buddha who had approached" means: seeing him who had thus come into my presence, [the one] who is the same toward the desirable and the undesirable (*tādino iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu*).

Having prepared and finished arranging a spread of grass, leaves, and so forth, as well as a wooden seat, for the Buddha—the world’s elder endowed with the quality of equanimity (*tādi*) and immovability—I gave him a flower-seat, a seat made of flowers. 114.
Having sat down on that flower-seat thus prepared, the Leader of the World, Siddhattha, [sat].
The Blessed One, "knowing my destiny"—that is, having known and understood my future destination and place of rebirth—proclaimed and spoke of impermanence, the state of being impermanent:
"Impermanent, alas, are all conditioned things. Indeed, conditioned things (*saṅkhārā*), produced by coming together and meeting with conditions, are entirely impermanent.
All conditioned phenomena (*sappaccaya-dhammā*), being subject to conditions, are impermanent in the sense of non-existence.

"Subject to arising and passing away" (*uppādavayadhammino*) means they have the nature of perishing after having arisen; the meaning is that these formations (*saṅkhārā*), having arisen and become manifest, cease and perish.
"Their subsiding is bliss" (*tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho*) means that the specific pacification of those formations is bliss; it is that which brings about their subsiding.
The meaning is that Nibbāna alone is absolute happiness.
Having spoken this— the All-Knowing One, the Blessed One who knows all phenomena, the Eldest of the worlds, the Mature One, the Bull among men,
the Preeminent One, the Hero— having thus spoken and delivered this Dhamma teaching connected with impermanence, [he stood] in the sky.
The connection is: "Like a king of swans in the sky, he rose up into the open firmament.
(117) Having abandoned—having relinquished—one's own view (*diṭṭhi*), that is, one's own tenet (*laddhi*), inclination (*khanti*), preference (*ruci*), and disposition (*ajjhāsaya*).
"I cultivated the perception of impermanence" means: I cultivated, increased, and attended to the perception that occurs regarding the impermanent as "impermanent. Therein, at the time...
"Where was I born?"—in that [life], from that birth, I passed away, died.
(118) "Having experienced two prosperities"—having experienced the two prosperities known as human prosperity and divine prosperity.
"Urged on by white roots"—urged on by former roots of merit, or by wholesome roots that serve as a foundation.
"Urged on": when my final existence had arrived, when my last birth had been reached.
"I approached the womb of cooked food" (*sapākayonim upāgamiṃ*): I approached a womb where there was one's own cooked food (*sapāka*).
The meaning is: I was reborn in a *caṇḍāla* family, a family whose own cooked food was not to be eaten by others. Alternatively, "cooked food" (*sapāka*) refers to a dog.
The meaning is that he was born into a family of outcasts (caṇḍāla) who eat food left over by dogs. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the legend of the Elder Sopāka is complete.
10. Commentary on the Legend of the Elder Sumaṅgala.
"Desiring to offer an oblation," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Sumaṅgala Thera. This Venerable One had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;
accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn as a tree deity during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassi.
One day, having bathed the Teacher, [he offered] a single robe.

Seeing him standing there, he was filled with joy and clapped his hands. By virtue of that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this present age of a Buddha in a poor family in a certain village not far from Sāvatthī, due to the ripening of that same karma;
his name was Sumaṅgala. When he reached maturity, he possessed the tools of a hunchbacked laborer: a sickle, a plow, and a hoe.

Having offered [the land], he made his living by farming. One day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was providing a great almsgiving for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he arrived carrying a jar of curd along with men who were bringing the requisites for the gift.
Seeing the honor and respect shown to the bhikkhus, he thought: "These recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, are dressed in fine garments..."
Having eaten fine foods and dwelling in dwellings sheltered from the wind, he thought, "What if I were to go forth as well?
Having approached a certain great elder, he informed him of his intention to go forth.
Out of compassion for him, the elder ordained him and explained a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to him. While dwelling in the forest, he lived in solitude.

Having become disillusioned and weary, desiring to depart, he was traveling toward his native village when, on the way, he saw men plowing a field—men who had tied up their hair, were dressed in soiled garments, whose bodies were covered in dust on all sides, and who were withering under the wind and sun.
Seeing them, he thought: "Alas, great indeed is the suffering these beings endure for the sake of a livelihood!"

"...experiencing them," he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Because his knowledge had reached maturity, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as it had been grasped appeared before him.

Approaching the foot of a certain tree, having attained seclusion, and reflecting with wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), he increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and, following the sequence of the paths, attained Arahatship.

124. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahatship and remembering his own past kamma, he spoke the words beginning with “Desiring to offer an oblation,” while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds) out of joy.
Therein, “oblation” (*āhuti*) refers to various kinds of offerings and honors, such as food and drink.
“Desiring to offer” (*yiṭṭhukāmo*) means desiring to sacrifice, that is, desiring to give a gift. “Having prepared the meal” (*paṭiyādetvāna bhojanaṃ*) means having prepared the food.
"Having prepared [it]. "Seeking out brahmins" means seeking out recipients who have gone forth in pure renunciation.
"Standing in a spacious courtyard" means standing in a vast courtyard, beautiful with a ground of pure, white sand. 125–7.

Regarding the passage beginning "Then I saw the Sambuddha," [the Buddha is described as] of great fame and having a great retinue, [who appeared] to the whole world, that is, to the entire world of sentient beings.
The trainer, the preeminent leader, the one who brings about the attainment of Nibbāna, the Self-Become One (*sayambhu*), who has arisen by himself without a teacher,
the Supreme Person, the Best of Persons, the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) endowed with qualities such as good fortune,
the radiant one possessed of blue, yellow, and other splendors, honored and surrounded by disciples, shining and resplendent like the sun, [was walking] along the street.
The connection is: "They saw the Fully Enlightened One named Piya-dassī, who was traveling along the road.
Having raised his hands in añjali—meaning, having placed his joined palms upon his head—he gladdened his own mind;
the meaning is that he inspired confidence in the virtues of the Blessed One who had become thus, and made his heart clear. He invited him with his mind alone.
"I invited him with my mind: 'May the Great Sage come!'—may the Sage, the Blessed One, who is honored and worthy of worship, come to my dwelling.

(128) Having understood my intention—that is, having known the resolve of my heart—the Teacher, who is unsurpassed in the world, the world of beings, and is devoid of any superior, approached and arrived at my gate, my house-gate, surrounded by a thousand who have destroyed the taints, a thousand Arhats."
129. When the Teacher had arrived, I paid him homage in this way:

"O Noble Steed among men (*puruṣājanya*), O Supreme One among men, let my homage be unto you! O Supreme Being among men (*puruṣottama*), distinguished by superior qualities, let my homage be unto you!
Having ascended my dwelling, which produces serenity (*prasāda*),"
"They sit upon the lion-throne, the supreme seat"—this is the meaning of "they requested. 130.

"The Tamed One, surrounded by the tamed": he himself is tamed by means of the three doors [of body, speech, and mind], and is likewise surrounded by a retinue consisting of the four assemblies known as monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
"The Crossed One, the best of those who cross": he himself has crossed over, having transcended saṃsāra.

The Blessed One—the foremost, most excellent, and supreme among distinguished persons who have set out to ferry others across—having ascended the palace through my service, sat down upon the noble, preeminent seat; having taken his seat, he remained there.
(131) "Whatever material goods I possess in my own home"—whatever food was presented, prepared, and gathered in heaps within my own house—[I offered it all].
"Atthi" means: "I gave that material gift (āmisa) to the Buddha, to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha;

the meaning is that I gave it with thorough (pa-) respect (ādarena). "Pasanno sehi pāṇibhī" means: having taken it with my own two hands while my mind was full of faith, I gave it; this is the meaning.
132. With a clear mind, with a mind whose intentions are serene, joyful and of beautiful disposition;
filled with rapture, with rapture arisen—that is, with joy having been produced—one with palms joined, placing the hollowed palms upon the head, pays homage to the Best of Buddhas.

The meaning is: "I perform an act of salutation to the Best of Buddhas. "Oh, how sublime is the Buddha!"—this refers to the sublimity, the greatness, of the Teacher who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths.
"Aho acchariyaṃ" means "Oh, how wonderful!

(133). Regarding "among the eight who attend upon": among those eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) who are attending upon [the Buddha] while eating, it means that the *khīṇāsava* Arhats alone are the most numerous.
"This power belongs to you alone" means this power—such as walking through the sky, emerging from and submerging into the earth, and so forth—belongs to you alone.
"It is indeed your own majesty, not that of others.
We go to you for refuge" means: we go to you who are thus, to you as a refuge, a protection, a shelter, and a final resort; the sense is that we approach, we go to, or we know [you]. 134.

The World-Champion, the Bull among Men, the Lovely-to-Behold Blessed One, having sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses of explanation; the meaning is that he uttered them. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Sumaṅgala-thera-apadāna* is completed.
The commentary on the second chapter, the *Sīhāsana-vagga*, is completed.
3. The *Subhūti-vagga*.
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Subhūti.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Subhūti begins with the words "Not far from the Himalayas.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [lived] one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
Even before the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Lord of the World, had appeared, he was reborn as the only son of a certain wealthy brahmin in the city of Haṃsavatī;
they gave him the name Nanda-māṇava. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in them, [he departed] together with his retinue of forty-four thousand young brahmins.

Having gone forth together with him into the ascetic life of a seer at the foot of a mountain, he attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha samāpattiyo*) and the five supernormal powers (*pañca abhiññāyo*).
He also explained a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to his pupils, and they too, before long, became attainers of *jhāna*.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having appeared in the world, was residing near the city of Haṃsavatī.
While dwelling there, one day at the time of dawn, as he surveyed the world,

the Blessed One perceived that the matted-hair ascetics who were disciples of the ascetic Nanda possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship, and he saw that the ascetic Nanda himself, being endowed with two factors, had made a resolve for the status of a disciple.
Having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, he took up his bowl and robe at the time of the forenoon.
Without addressing anyone else, like a lion wandering alone, while the disciples of the ascetic Nanda had gone out for fruits,
he descended from the sky and stood upon the earth even as the ascetic Nanda looked on, thinking, "May he know my state as a Buddha.
Seeing both the majesty of a Buddha and the perfection of his marks, the ascetic Nanda [recited] the *lakkhaṇa-mantra*.
Having reflected thus, and knowing, "One endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home, becomes a wheel-turning monarch; if he goes forth,
he becomes an omniscient Buddha, a breaker of the veil in the world—
this noble steed among men is undoubtedly a Buddha," he went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and prepared a seat.
He gave it. The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him. The ascetic Nanda also took a seat suitable for himself and sat down to one side.

At that time, forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics arrived in the presence of their teacher, carrying various most excellent and nutritious fruits; they observed the manner in which both the Buddhas and their teacher were seated.

Having looked, they said, "Teacher, we used to wander about thinking, 'There is no one in this world greater than you,' but this man, we think, is even greater than you. The ascetic Nanda replied, "Sons, what are you saying?
Do you wish to compare Mount Sineru, which rises six million eight hundred thousand yojanas high, with a mustard seed?"

"Do not compare me with the All-Knowing Buddha," he said. Then those ascetics, thinking, "If this man were insignificant, our teacher would not have brought such a comparison. How great indeed is this noble being!
fell at his feet and paid homage with their heads. Then their teacher said, "Sirs, among our Buddhas..."
“There is no suitable gift to be found, yet the Blessed One has arrived here at the time for the alms-round;
therefore, we shall give whatever gifts we can according to our means. Bring forth each and every fine fruit that you have brought.
