Having had them brought, she washed them with her own hands and personally placed them into the Tathāgata’s bowl.
As soon as the Teacher had accepted the various fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence. The ascetic himself strained the water and gave it to him.

Then, when the Teacher had finished his meal and was seated, he summoned all his resident disciples and sat down beside the Teacher, engaging in a conversation of recollection. The Teacher said, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus..."
"Let him come," he thought. Knowing the Teacher's mind, about one hundred thousand *khīṇāsavas* arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood there.
Then the ascetic Nanda addressed his pupils: "Sons, even the seat for the Buddhas to sit upon is low, and there is no seating for a hundred thousand recluses.
It is fitting for you today to perform a magnificent honor for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"Bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain," he said.

Because the scope of supernormal power (iddhi) is inconceivable, they brought flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and taste in an instant and prepared a flower-seat one *yojana* in extent for the Buddhas;
for the chief disciples, three-quarters of a *yojana*; and for the remaining bhikkhus, various sizes such as half a *yojana*.
They prepared a seat for the youngest member of the Saṅgha that was the size of a bull.

When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Nanda stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined in reverence and said, “Venerable Sir, for our long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend and sit upon this flower-seat.
The Blessed One sat down on the flower-seat. When the Teacher was thus seated, [the Teacher’s...]
Having understood the signal, the bhikkhus sat down each on his own seat. The ascetic Nanda stood holding a large flower parasol over the head of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher, thinking, "May this honor paid to these ascetics bear great fruit," entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Knowing that the Teacher had entered that state, the bhikkhus also entered the attainment.

They entered [the attainment]. While the Tathāgata remained seated for seven days in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*), the resident monks, when the time for alms-round arrived, partook of forest roots and fruits;
at other times, they stood with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddhas.
However, the ascetic Nanda did not even go on alms-round; carrying a flower parasol, he spent those seven days solely in the bliss of rapture (*pītisukha*).

The Teacher, having emerged from cessation, commanded a disciple endowed with two qualities— namely, the quality of dwelling in non-conflict (*araṇavihāra*) and the quality of being worthy of offerings—
to offer words of appreciation for the "flower-seat" given by the group of seers.
Like a great warrior who has received a vast reward from a wheel-turning monarch, he, with a joyful heart, stood within his own domain and [recited] the Three Piṭakas...
Having reflected upon the Buddha’s word, he offered an expression of appreciation. At the conclusion of his teaching, the Teacher himself preached the Dhamma.
At the end of the Teacher’s discourse, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained arahantship.
The Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks," and at that very moment their hair and beards vanished.
Eight requisites were fastened upon his body; they surrounded the Teacher like elders of sixty years’ standing.
But the ascetic Nanda, because his mind was distracted, did not attain any distinction.
It is said that from the moment he began to listen to the Dhamma of the elder Araṇavibhaṅgika, he thought: “Oh, may I too in the future—”
The thought arose in him: "May this disciple obtain the same qualities obtained by me under the teaching of a single Buddha.
However, because of that thought, he was unable to penetrate the path and its fruition. Then, having paid homage to the Tathāgata and standing before him with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"Venerable Sir, regarding the monk who offered words of appreciation for the flower-seats to the company of seers..."

“Who is this among you in the Dispensation? “Venerable sir, this bhikkhu has attained the foremost position by virtue of his practice of dwelling in non-conflict (*araṇavihāra*) and his status as one worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
“Venerable sir, I do not aspire to any other success through the merit of having performed this service for seven days by holding the flower-parasol;
however, in the future, [may I be born] under a single Buddha...”
He made this aspiration: "May I become a disciple endowed with these two factors, just like this elder in the Teaching.
The Teacher, wondering, "Will this ascetic's aspiration be fulfilled? sent forth his knowledge of the future and looked;
seeing that it would be fulfilled after the passing of one hundred thousand aeons, he said, "Ascetic, this [aspiration] of yours..."
"Your aspiration will be in vain; after a hundred thousand future eons have passed, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and it will be fulfilled in his presence.
Having spoken these words of Dhamma, he leapt into the air, surrounded by the community of monks.
As long as the ascetic Nanda did not pass beyond the range of the Teacher’s vision, [the Teacher remained] with the community of monks...

And having raised his hands in *añjali*, he stood there. Later on, from time to time, he approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and—without falling away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*)—passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having passed away from there, for another five hundred births he went forth into homelessness and remained a forest-dweller; even during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he did so.
Having gone forth, he became a forest-dweller and fulfilled the practice of going and returning.
It is said that there are none who attain the status of a Great Disciple without fulfilling this practice;

as for the practice of going and returning, it should be understood according to the method described in the Aṭṭhakathās. Having fulfilled the practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, he passed away.
Having done so, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world.
Thus, by way of being reborn again and again in the Tāvatiṃsa abode, he experienced divine prosperity;
then, passing away from there, he became a wheel-turning monarch and a regional king many hundreds of times in the human world, enjoying sublime human prosperity.

Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn during the time of our Blessed One in Sāvatthī, in the house of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi, as the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika. His name was Subhūti.
At that time, our Blessed One, having appeared in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dharma, proceeded by stages...
Having gone to Rājagaha, he dwelt in the Sītavana forest near Rājagaha, performing a benefit for the world by means of accepting the Veḷuvana grove and other such acts.
At that time, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having taken merchandise for export from Sāvatthī, went to the house of his friend, the merchant of Rājagaha;
there he heard of the appearance of the Buddha and [learned that] the Teacher was at the Sītavana.
Having approached the Teacher while he was dwelling there, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry at the very first sight; then, having requested the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī,
he erected monasteries along the forty-five-yojana road at intervals of one yojana each, making donations of a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for each,
and [finally acquired] the parkland of Prince Jeta in Sāvatthī, measuring eight karīsas.
Having purchased it by covering the ground with ten million pieces of gold, he had a monastery built there for the Blessed One and gave it to him.
On the day of the monastery’s consecration, this householder Subhūti went together with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika; while listening to the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth.
Having been ordained, he mastered the two Matikas, requested a meditation subject, and practiced the duty of a recluse in the forest.
Having cultivated the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*) and made it a foundation, he developed insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*.

Because he taught the Dhamma according to the method established by the Teacher, teaching it in a non-specific manner, he became known as the foremost of those who dwell in the state free from conflict (*araṇa-vihārī*).
Furthermore, because while wandering for alms he would enter the attainment of the meditation on loving-kindness in every house, [he was so named].
Having risen, he accepts alms-food thinking, "In this way, it will be of great fruit for the donors.

Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). For that reason, the Blessed One placed him in the position of preeminence endowed with two qualities, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who dwell in non-conflict (*araṇa-vihārin*) and who are worthy of offerings, Subhūti is the foremost."
Thus this great elder, having reached Arahantship—the pinnacle of the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled himself—became renowned and distinguished throughout the world.
Traveling through the countryside for the welfare of many people, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
King Bimbisāra, hearing of the elder’s arrival, approached him, paid homage, and said: “Venerable sir, please dwell right here.”
Having said, "I will provide you with a place to dwell," he departed and forgot about them. The Elder, unable to find a lodging, spent his time in the open air.
Through the power of the Elder, the rain did not fall. Distressed by the lack of rain, the people raised a clamor at the gate of the king’s palace.
The king, investigating the matter, wondered, "For what reason does the rain not fall?"

Thinking, "I suppose it is not raining because the Elder dwells in the open air," she had a leaf-hut built for him and said, "Venerable sir, please dwell in this leaf-hut. Having paid homage, she departed.
The Elder entered the hut and sat cross-legged upon a grass mat. At that time, the rain fell only lightly and intermittently, not in a steady downpour.
He pours it out. Then the Elder, desiring to dispel the world’s fear of drought and demonstrating the absence of any internal or external danger for himself, spoke the verse:
“My little hut is roofed. The meaning of this has already been explained in the *Theragāthā*.
But why did these great elders proclaim their own virtues? Because [these qualities] had never before been attained by them throughout this long period of time.

Having reflected upon the supremely profound, exceedingly peaceful, and sublime supramundane Dhamma realized by themselves, the Noble Ones—possessing supreme fewness of desires—reveal their own virtues for the purpose of illuminating the exalted joy inspired by the surge of rapture, and for the purpose of demonstrating the world-transcending nature of the Dispensation.
Just as the Lord of the World, according to the inclinations of those to be enlightened, [declared]: "Endowed with the ten powers..."
“Monks, the Tathāgata is confident, possessing the four grounds of self-confidence,” and so forth; in this way he proclaims his own virtues.
Thus, this verse of the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*) also came to pass.
Having thus attained the fruit of Arhatship and attained the status of being foremost among those who have reached that state, he remembered his own past karma and was filled with joy.
While elucidating the *apadāna* of his former conduct, he said, "Not far from the Himavanta," and so forth. Therein, "of the Himavanta" means of the Himalaya mountain;
"not far" means nearby, close, at the foot of the mountain, in a place frequented by people for coming and going.
"A mountain named Nisabha" refers to a rocky mountain named Nisabha because it is the eldest among mountains.
The connection is with the word *ahosi* ("was"). "A well-made hermitage for me": on that mountain, a hermitage—a forest dwelling—was well-constructed for my residence.
The meaning is that it was built in a beautiful form, complete with huts, places for standing and sitting, day-quarters, night-quarters, enclosures, and so forth.
"A leaf-hut well-erected": a hut covered with leaves was well-constructed for my dwelling.
"Measured out and completed"—this is the meaning.
"By name Kosika"—by the name given by his parents, he was named Kosika. "Of lofty asceticism"—one whose austerity is manifest, one of fierce austerity.
"Solitary"—because of the absence of others, I alone am one. "Without a second"—devoid of a second ascetic; a *jaṭila* (wearer of matted hair).
The connection is as follows: "At that time, on that mountain Nisabha, I lived and dwelt as an ascetic wearing matted hair.

(3) "Fruit, root, and leaf—I did not eat those at that time": at that time, while dwelling on that Nisabha mountain, I did not eat fruit such as *tiṇḍuka*, roots such as *muḷāla*, or leaves such as *kārapaṇṇa*, having plucked them from the trees.
The meaning is as follows. To show how one lives when this is the case, he said: "I live by means of what has fallen of its own accord. Therein, the connection is:

"By making food out of leaves and so forth that have fallen—having arisen spontaneously (*pavattaṃ*) and fallen by their own nature (*supātaṃ*)—I, for my part, live and maintain my life at that time. [This refers to] "fallen, withered leaves" (*pavattapaṇḍupaṇṇāni*).
Or [there is] the reading "vā"; the meaning is: "I live depending upon the withered leaves and tree foliage that have fallen of their own accord.

4. "I do not corrupt my right livelihood": even while giving up life and making sacrifices, I do not corrupt—that is, I do not destroy—my right livelihood through the pursuit of food such as fruits and roots under the influence of craving; this is the connection. I fulfill it.
"My own mind" means my own mind, my own thought; I satisfy and gladden it with fewness of wishes and contentment.
"I avoid wrong search" means I avoid and keep far from wrong search—that is, improper seeking—such as through the practice of medicine or acting as a messenger. 5.
"A mind associated with lust" means whenever, at whatever time, a mind conjoined with lust arises in me.
Then, I myself examine it by means of my own knowledge and, having scrutinized it, I dispel it.
"Single-mindedly, I shall tame that": being single-mindedly concentrated upon one object of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*), I tame—that is, I subdue—that mind of lust.
"If you are attached to what is attractive": if you are attached—that is, clinging—to an object of form or other such bases that are attractive and worthy of attachment.
"You are corrupting": in that which is to be corrupted—the object that causes corruption—you are a corrupter.
"You are deluded, in that which is to be deluded": in that object which causes delusion, you are deluded; you are bewildered.
Therefore, "you must depart from the forest"—that is, go away from dwelling in the wilderness—in this way I shall tame myself. This is the connection of the passage.
24. “Timbarūsakavaṇṇābho” means having the luster of the color of a golden *timbarūsaka* fruit; that is to say, having the color of Jambū-river gold. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Subhūti is complete.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upavāna.
"Padumuttaro nāma jino," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Upavāna Thera. This Venerable One had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;
having accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was born into a poor family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having reached the age of discretion, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna...
Having taken the relic, when stūpas seven *yojanas* in height and made of the seven precious gems had been constructed by humans,
devas, *nāgas*, *garuḷas*, *kumbhaṇḍas*, *yakkhas*, and *gandhabbas*, he hung his own well-washed upper robe upon the top of a bamboo pole,
fastened it there as a banner, and performed an offering. Taking that [banner], the *yakkha* general named Abhisammataka was appointed by the devas for the purpose of guarding the stūpa worship.
Having placed it there with his body invisible, he circumambulated the shrine three times while supporting it in the air.

Seeing this, his mind became even more filled with serene faith; through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in the family of a brahmin in Sāvatthī during the appearance of this Buddha, and upon reaching maturity, he received the name Upavāna.

Having witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural power at the acceptance of the Jeta Grove, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight meditation, attained Arahantship and became possessed of the six super-knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Whenever the Blessed One was unwell, the Elder would offer him warm water and suitable medicinal drinks. Thus, for his Teacher...
The illness was pacified. The Blessed One offered him words of thanksgiving.

52. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahatship and reached the foremost position among those who have realized this excellence, he recalled his own past karma and, out of joy, proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), beginning with the words: "The Conqueror named Padumuttara... and so forth. Therein:
The Conqueror named Padumuttara, who had reached the further shore and the culmination of all mundane and supramundane phenomena,
the Blessed One who had conquered the five Māras, like a mass of fire,
having blazed with the six-colored rays of a Buddha and illuminated the entire world with the light of the Dhamma, was a Perfectly Awakened One, truly awakened from the sleep of ignorance.

The connection is as follows: having awakened from the slumber of the defilements along with their latent tendencies within the world of beings, he whose lotus-eyes have blossomed has attained final Nibbāna;
being extinguished by the Nibbāna of the aggregates, he has gone beyond sight.
57. "Jaṅghā" refers to the series of steps being constructed for the purpose of placing the bricks that are to be piled up at the time of building the cetiya.
88. "Well-washed" means it was thoroughly washed and made perfectly clean by a man who is a washerman, a cloth-cleanser.
"My upper garment" (*uttareyya-paṭa*) means my upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). Having fastened it to the tip of a bamboo pole and made it into a banner, I raised it up;
the meaning is that I hoisted it into the sky, into the atmosphere. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upavāna is complete.
3. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Tisaraṇagamaniya begins with the verse "In the city of Bandhumatī. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī in a noble family in the city of Bandhumatī. There, he attended upon his blind parents.
One day he thought: "While I am attending upon my parents, I am not permitted to go forth; what if I..."
"I shall take the three refuges; thus I will liberate myself from an evil rebirth.
Having approached Nisabha, the foremost disciple of the Blessed One Vipassī, he took the three refuges.

Having observed them for those hundred thousand years, through that very kamma he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Thereafter, wandering among gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a great *sāla*-tree family in the city of Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, while still only seven years old and surrounded by other children, he went to a certain monastery.

There, a certain elder whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsavatthera*) taught him the Dhamma and granted him the refuges (*saraṇāni*). Having received them, he recalled the refuges that had been protected by himself in the past.
Having recollected [his past] and increased his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship. Once he had attained Arahatship, the Blessed One ordained him.

Having attained Arahatship and been ordained, he recollected his own former karma and, out of joy, proclaimed the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words, "In the city of Bandhumatī... Therein, he was the attendant to his mother.
The connection is as follows: "I was the attendant and supporter of my parents in the city of Bandhumatī.

(108) "Covered by that darkness" means covered and shrouded by the darkness of delusion (*moha*). "They burn with the three fires" means all beings burn with the three fires known as the fire of lust (*rāga*), the fire of hatred (*dosa*), and the fire of delusion (*moha*).
(114) "We obtain eight causes" means "I obtain eight reasons," that is, eight causes that serve as conditions for happiness. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tisaraṇagamaniya is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pañcasīlasamādāniya begins with the verse "In the city of Candavatī... This too...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi. Due to unwholesome karma committed in a previous life, he became poor, lacking food, drink, and sustenance;
living by working as a servant for others, he came to understand the peril of *saṃsāra*.
Although he desired to go forth, not obtaining ordination, he undertook the five training rules in the presence of the Elder Nisabha, a disciple of the Blessed One Anomadassi.
Because he had arisen during a long-lived age, he maintained his virtue for one hundred thousand years.
By that kamma, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in Vesālī during this current appearance of a Buddha.

He was reborn into a family of great wealth. Seeing his parents undertaking the precepts, he recollected his own past virtue, increased his insight (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship*, and went forth into homelessness.
Recalling his own former deeds, filled with joy, he proclaimed this account of his past conduct as a spontaneous utterance (*udāna*).
He spoke the verse beginning with "In the city of Candavatī. "At that time I was a hired laborer" means that at the time I was performing meritorious deeds, I was a hired laborer, a worker for wages.
"Engaged in the service of others" means I was appointed (*āyutta*) or assigned (*yojita*) to perform work for others for wages;
because there was no opportunity, I did not obtain the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) for the sake of liberation from *saṃsāra*.
135. *Mahandhakārapihitā* means covered, enclosed, and obstructed by the great darkness of the defilements (*kilesa*).
*Tividhaggīhi ḍayhare* means they are being consumed by three fires, namely those known as the fire of hell, the fire of the hungry ghosts (*peta*), and the fire of saṃsāra.
"But by what means and for what reason might I become dissociated from them? is the meaning.
136. "I have no object suitable to be given, such as food, drink, and so forth;
in the absence of that, I am a wretched person, suffering, a hired laborer living on wages. What if I were to observe the five precepts?
Having undertaken the five precepts and fulfilling them, what if I were to guard them well—excellently and beautifully?"
"Having performed them, one should preserve them"—this is the meaning.
"I myself experienced that fame": the meaning is that by the power and influence of those virtues, I experienced great fame among gods and humans.
Even while praising the fruit of those virtues for ten million eons (*kappakoṭi*), it would be only a single portion.
The meaning is: "One should make it known and proclaim it. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pañcasīlasamādāniya is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Annasaṃsāvaka.
"Golden-hued, the Perfectly Enlightened One"—this is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Anusāsaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
While he was wandering for alms, [he beheld the Buddha] adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the halo of a fathom-wide radiance.

Having seen the Blessed One, with a mind full of serene confidence, he invited the Blessed One, led him to his home, satisfied him with excellent food and drink, and after offering hospitality, fed him.
By virtue of that very clarity of mind, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas;
having experienced celestial glory, and then passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world and experienced human prosperity.
Having experienced various successive fortunes among gods and humans, he was reborn into a certain family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having gained faith in the Teaching, he went forth, developed insight, and attained Arahatship.
On account of the name of the merit he had performed in the past, he became well known by the name Annasamsāvaka Thera.
155–6. Later on, having remembered his own former karma and being filled with joy, he thought, "Thus, by the power of this accumulation of merit, I have attained Arahatship.
Proclaiming his own account of past conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*) by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ... and so forth.
In that context, "suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ" means that the Blessed One whose complexion (*vaṇṇa*) is like the color of gold is "suvaṇṇavaṇṇa"; [he refers to] him who is "suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ."
"Sambuddhaṃ siddhatthaṃ" means the Perfectly Enlightened One, Siddhattha. "Gacchantaṃ antarāpaṇe" means while he was walking through the middle street of the merchants' market rows.

"Kañcanagghiyasaṅkāsaṃ" means resembling a golden archway; endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks, the light of the world who has become a lamp for the entire world, immeasurable—devoid of measure—and incomparable—devoid of likeness.

The connection is as follows: "Having seen Jutindhara, the bearer of light, the possessor of the six-colored Buddha-rays such as blue and yellow—the one who holds the meaning of 'Siddhattha'—I obtained supreme, most excellent joy. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Annasamsāvaka is completed.
6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhūpadāyaka.
"Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dhūpadāyaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), [attained this state] under Siddhattha.
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha,
he inspired confidence in the heart of that Blessed One and performed an offering of incense in his Gandhakuti with many types of incense, such as sandalwood, agallochum,
and black aloe-wood. By that merit, experiencing both celestial and human success in each successive birth, he was reborn in various states of existence.
Having become worthy of worship, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Through the power of his accumulation of merit, he went forth into the Dispensation, developed insight, and attained Arahatship.
Because of the merit of having offered incense, he became renowned everywhere as the Elder Dhūpadāyaka (the Incense-giver). Having attained the fruit of Arahatship, he recollected his own past kamma.
Born with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "of the Blessed One Siddhattha" while showing the *apadāna* of his former conduct.
He is "Siddhattha" because the purpose (*attha*)—consisting of qualities such as omniscience—is accomplished (*siddha*) and perfected in that Blessed One;
he is the Blessed One Siddhattha, who possesses the qualities of fortune and the like, the eldest in the world, and the supreme being of the entire world.
"Of such a one" (*tādino*) means of one who is unshakable in nature regarding the desirable and the undesirable. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dhūpadāyaka is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pulinapūjaka.
The legend (*Apadāna*) of the Venerable Thera Pulinapūjaka begins with the words, "Of the Blessed One Vipassī," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. With a mind full of faith toward the Teaching, he [attended] upon the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa*).
Having removed the ancient sand and strewn a new, white sandy shore resembling a bed of pearls, he adorned the platform.

By that deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods; there, having enjoyed divine splendor in a golden celestial mansion shining with divine jewels for many yojanas, he passed away from there and was born in the human world endowed with the seven treasures.

Having been a universal monarch (cakkavattī rājā) and experienced human prosperity, he wandered through successive births until, during the present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth.
Having gained faith in the Teaching (sāsana), he went forth into homelessness, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship.
He became well known by the name Pulinapūjakatthera, which corresponded to the name of the merit he had performed.

165. Thus, having recollected his own former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “Of the Blessed One Vipassī,” demonstrating the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct).
Therein, he is called Vipassī because he sees in various ways (*vividhaṃ passati*); or, he is called Vipassī because he sees having become detached (*vivicca passati*);

or, he is called Vipassī because he sees manifold meanings (*atthe*) such as those pertaining to one’s own welfare and the welfare of others; or, he is called Vipassī because he sees manifold [levels of truth] such as conventional reality (*vohāra*) and ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

Or, he is called Vipassī because he sees clearly. At the supreme and most excellent foot of that Vipassī Bodhisatta’s tree of awakening, within the circular pavilion of the Bodhi-tree, I discarded the old sand and strewn down a pure, white, fresh layer of sand. The rest is easy to understand.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pulinapūjaka.
8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uttiya.
The passage beginning with "On the banks of the Candabhāgā River" is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Uttiya.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Siddhattha...
In the time of the Blessed One, having been reborn as a crocodile in the river Candabhāgā, he saw the Blessed One approaching the riverbank.
With a mind full of confidence and desiring to carry him to the other side, he lay down right near the bank. Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One placed his foot upon his back.
Delighted and elated, through the force of his joy, the crocodile became possessed of great strength and began cutting through the current.
With swift speed, he brought the Blessed One to the opposite shore. The Blessed One, perceiving his clarity of mind, declared:

"Having passed away from here, this man will be reborn in the world of the gods; from that point on, wandering only through happy destinies, he will attain the Deathless after ninety-four aeons. Having thus prophesied, he departed.
Thus, wandering through happy realms alone, he was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha as the son of a certain brahmin in Sāvatthī;
they gave him the name Uttiya. When he reached maturity, thinking, "I shall seek the Deathless," he became a wanderer.
One day, having seen the Blessed One, he approached him, paid homage, and listened to the Dhamma.
Having gained faith and gone forth into the teaching, he was unable to produce any distinction because his virtue and view were not purified.
Seeing another bhikkhu who had produced a distinction and proclaimed his realization, he approached the Teacher and requested a brief exhortation.
The Teacher then addressed him with the words, "Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the beginning," and so forth.
He gave him brief instruction. Standing upon the Teacher’s instruction, he began the practice of insight (vipassanā).

While he was engaged in insight practice, an illness arose. When the illness arose, he became stirred with a sense of urgency; recognizing the basis for the arousal of energy, he further developed his insight and attained Arahatship.
Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahatship in accordance with the provisions he had prepared, he remembered his own past karma and was filled with joy.
While elucidating the *apadāna* of his former conduct, he spoke the words beginning with "on the bank of the river Candabhāgā.
Therein, it is called the river Candabhāgā because it flows making a sound— resounding with the splendor of the moon’s radiance—
due to its banks of pure, white sand and because it is filled with sweet, clear water endowed with luster.
The connection is that there was a *susumāra* (crocodile) on the bank of that river Candabhāgā.
In this context, it is called a *susumāra* because it kills small shoals of fish, tearing them into pieces; the meaning is "fierce fish" or "kumbhīla.
"I was intent upon my food" means I was occupied and engaged with my own feeding ground. "I went to the river-ford" refers to the time when the Blessed One was approaching.
I went to the river crossing; I have arrived.

At that time, when I was going to the crossing, the Blessed One Siddhattha—the foremost person, the eldest and best among all beings, the self-become, who arose by himself and became a Buddha—was at the river.
Desiring to cross over, he approached the riverbank.

(172) “My paternal domain” means that which has been handed down through my father, grandfather, and so forth; the meaning is: the crossing performed by those of great power who have attained prosperity.
(173) “Having heard my roar” means having heard my shouting—that is, my propitiation—the Great Sage, the Blessed One, ascended; such is the connection. The rest is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the *Uttiya-thera-apadāna* is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Ekañjalika-thera-apadāna*: "Suvaṇṇavaṇṇa...
and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Ekañjalika. This one, too, [was born] during the time of previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Triple Gem.
Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī wandering for alms, he stood with a devout mind, raising his hands in reverential salutation (añjali). He...
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he became worthy of honor everywhere and experienced both kinds of prosperity.

Then, being born into a family endowed with great wealth during the arising of this present Buddha, he gained faith in the Teaching, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight, established himself in Arahatship.
On account of the merit performed in the past, he became renowned as the Elder Ekañjalika (the One-Handsal).
180. Thus, remembering his own past karma and seeing it as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of his hand, he spoke the words beginning with "Suvaṇṇavaṇṇa...
while proclaiming the *Apadāna* of his former conduct by way of a spontaneous utterance (*udāna*). Regarding the phrase "Vipassi, the leader of the caravan":

one who carries (*vahati*) and brings across (*tāreti*) merchants through a wilderness is a "caravan-leader" (*satthavāha*). [This refers to] wild-beast wildernesses, thorn-brake wildernesses, famine wildernesses, and waterless wildernesses.
The meaning is that he carries across, brings out, leads forth, and delivers from the wilderness of *yakkhas* and the wilderness of food-scarcity, leading them to the land of safety.
Who is he? He is the chief merchant. Because of his similarity to a caravan leader (*satthavāha*), this Blessed One is also a caravan leader.
For he [leads] beings who have performed the equipment of merit and aspire to the threefold enlightenment across the wilderness of birth, the wilderness of old age, and...

The meaning is that he carries across, brings out, delivers, and leads forth from the wilderness of disease, the wilderness of death, the wildernesses of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and from the entire wilderness of *saṃsāra*, and establishes them on the ground of *nibbāna*.
He is the leader of the caravan, the foremost, the best, and the preeminent; thus he is the "Foremost Leader of the Caravan. [I pay homage] to that Vipassī, the Foremost Leader of the Caravan.
The connection is with the word “Sambuddha. “Naravaraṃ vināyakaṃ” means: he is a “nara-vīra” (hero among men) because his prowess is unyielding among men;
him. He is a “vināyaka” (guide) because he leads beings who have specially accumulated the requisites of merit to the city of Nibbāna;
him. 181. “Adantadamanaṃ tādiṃ” means: because of being associated with the defilements such as lust, hatred, and delusion, [he is the tamer] through the doors of body, speech, and mind...

He who tames beings that are untamed is the "Tamer of the Untamed" (adantadamana); he is the "Such-like One" (tādin), because he possesses qualities such as imperturbability toward the desirable and the undesirable.
He is the "Great Debater" (mahāvādin) and the "Greatly Wise One" (mahāmati): he is a Great Debater because among the proponents of his own and other systems there is no person equal to him;
he is Greatly Wise because his wisdom is vast, like the earth and like Mount Meru. [The text refers to] that Great Debater.
"Mahāmatiṃ Sambuddhaṃ"—this is a construction in grammatical apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekāñjalika is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Khomadāyaka.
The legend of the Venerable Khomadāyaka Thera begins with the words, "In the city of Bandhumatī...

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, he became deeply devoted to the Dispensation and held the Triple Gem in high esteem.
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of khoma cloth.
Taking that very act as his foundation, he performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life and was reborn in the world of the devas.

After experiencing divine bliss by passing from one celestial realm to another among the six classes of devas, he passed away from there and attained various human prosperities in the human world, such as that of a universal monarch (cakkavatti).
Having experienced the ripening of his accumulated store of merit, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher; having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness. By developing insight, he attained Arahatship before long.
He became well known by the name Khomadāyaka Thera, "The Elder Who Gave a Linen Cloth," on account of the merit he had performed.
184. Thus, recollecting his own past karma and filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "In the city of Bandhumatī" in order to show the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
Therein, "bandhu" means a kinsman; that city in which those kinsmen dwell together in close association is called "Bandhumatī.
"I plant the excellence of seeds" refers to the perfection of the seeds of merit, such as generosity, virtue, and so forth.
"I plant" means "I establish.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Khomadāyaka is completed.
The commentary on the third Subhūti-vagga is completed.
The commentary on the Four Recitation Sections is finished.
4. The Chapter on Kuṇḍadhāna. 1.
Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna.
"Secluded for seven days," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kuṇḍadhāna.

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; and having approached the Blessed One in the manner previously described, he—
While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those receiving the first voting-ticket (*salāka*).
Aspiring to that very station, he wandered about performing meritorious deeds appropriate to that goal.
One day, when the Blessed One Padumuttara had emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and was seated, [he offered] a mass of ruby powder (*manosilācuṇṇa*).
He presented a large plantain leaf-stalk; the Blessed One accepted it and ate it.
By that meritorious deed, he exercised sovereignty among the gods eleven times. And twenty-four times he was a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
Having thus performed successive acts of merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he became a terrestrial deity during the time of Buddha Kassapa.
Having offered it, he was reborn. For those Buddhas who possess long lifespans, there is no half-monthly Uposatha.
Thus, for the Blessed One Vipassi, the Uposatha occurred every six years;
however, the Great Sage Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha every sixth month. At the time of his recitation of the Pātimokkha, those residing in various directions...
Two companion monks were going along, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha. A certain earth-deity thought to herself:
"The friendship between these two monks is exceedingly firm; would it break even in the presence of a schismatic, or would it not?
Keeping watch for an opportunity, she followed them at no great distance.
Then one elder, having placed his bowl and robes in the hand of another, went to a place near water for the purpose of washing his body;
having washed his hands and feet, he emerged from the vicinity of the thicket.
A terrestrial deity followed behind that elder, appearing as a woman of exquisite form, and as if shaking out her hair and arranging it, she bound it together.
As if wiping dust from her back and as if arranging her garment to put it on, she emerged from the thicket following the Elder step by step.
Seeing this situation, her companion Elder, who was standing to one side, became sorrowful and thought:
"I have now lost my long-standing affection for this monk; if I..."
Thinking, "If I were to recognize such a state of being, I would not have placed my trust in him for all this time," he spoke as the other was still approaching:
"Take back your bowl and robe, friend; I will not travel along the same path with such a wicked man.
Upon hearing those words, the heart of that modest bhikkhu was pierced by a sharp spear.
It was as if he had been pierced. Then he said to him: "Friend, what is this you say?
For all this time I have not known even a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Yet today you call me 'evil. What have you seen?
What is the use of seeing anything else? Why do you speak thus to me while I am together with a woman so beautifully adorned and prepared?"
"Did you set out having been in one place? "This is not so, friend; I do not see such a woman.
Even though he spoke thus up to three times, the other elder, disbelieving him, took his own experience as the very truth and, instead of going with him by the same path, went by another.
He went to the presence of the Teacher by one path; the other monk also went to the very same place where the Teacher was, but by a different path.

Then, at the time when the Saṅgha of monks was entering the Uposatha hall, that monk saw the other monk in the Uposatha hall, recognized him, and thought: "In this Uposatha hall there is such a wicked monk; I will not [sit] with him."
Thinking, "I shall perform the Uposatha together with him," he went out and stood outside.

Then a terrestrial deity, thinking, "A grievous deed has been committed by me," approached him in the guise of an elderly lay follower and asked, "Venerable sir, why does the noble one stand in this place? [The monk replied,] "Lay follower, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall."
“I am standing outside because I will not observe the Uposatha together with him. “Venerable sir, do not think so;
this bhikkhu is pure in virtue. It was I whom you saw as a woman.
I did this for the purpose of testing you, observing whether the friendship of these elders was firm or not, and whether it would break or not.”
“That deed has been done. “But who are you, good sir? “I am a terrestrial deity, venerable sir.
Even as he was speaking, the young god stood by means of his divine power, fell at the elder’s feet, and having entreated the elder, saying, “Venerable sir, forgive me;
this is not the fault of the elder, let us perform the Uposatha,” he entered the Uposatha hall.

He was ordained. That elder first observed the Uposatha together with him in one place; however, due to their friendship, he did not live with him again in the same place thereafter. He did not speak of the elder’s fault.
Later on, the elder who had been censured performed the work of insight meditation and attained Arahatship.
Due to the outflow of that karma, that earth deity was not released from the states of misery for the duration of an entire interval between Buddhas.
However, whenever he returned to the human state at intervals, whatever harm was done by anyone else would fall upon him alone.
He was reborn in the city of Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One into a brahmin family; his name was Dhāna Māṇava.
They gave him a name. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas;
later in life, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and having gained faith, he went forth in the Dispensation.

From the day of his full ordination, whenever he entered that village, a certain woman, fully adorned and prepared, would enter with him, and when he departed, she would depart as well, [and likewise] at the monastery...
"When he enters, she enters with him; when he stands, she stands"—thus she was perceived as a constant companion.
Yet the Elder did not see her. However, due to the ripening of his own past karma, she appeared to others.
While women in the village were giving alms of rice-gruel, they said, "Venerable sir, this one bowl of gruel is for you; this other one is for her."
“Of our companion,” they said, making sport of him. This caused the Elder great distress.
Even when he went to the monastery, the novices and young bhikkhus surrounded him and made sport of him, saying, “A *koṇḍa* (a deformed person) has been born!
Thus, for that very reason, the name Kuṇḍadhāna Thera arose for him. Rising up again and again from those [troubles], he...
Unable to endure the sport being performed, he fell into a state of madness and said, "You are Koṇḍas! Your preceptor is a Koṇḍa!
Your teacher is a Koṇḍa! Then they reported this to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, Kuṇḍadhāna speaks such harsh words together with the young novices.
The Teacher had him summoned and asked, "Is it true, Dhāna, that you [said this]?"
He asked, "Why do you speak harsh words to the young novices? When he replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha said, "Why do you speak thus?
He answered, "Venerable Sir, being unable to endure constant harassment, I speak in this way.
[The Buddha said,] "You have not been able to exhaust the karma you committed in the past until this very day; yet again, you speak such harsh words."
Having said, "Do not speak, O monk," he spoke further:
"Do not speak harshly to anyone; when spoken to, they may retort.
For contentious speech is painful, and counter-blows may strike you."
“If you do not harm yourself, like a bronze gong that has been struck, you have reached Nibbāna; no further agitation exists for you.
And they also reported this matter of the elder wandering with a woman to the King of Kosala.
The king, having sent [messengers] saying, "Go, my men,
and investigate him," went himself with a small retinue to the presence of the Elder and stood to one side, watching. At that moment,
the Elder was sitting engaged in needlework, and that woman appeared as if standing not far away.
Seeing her, the king thought, "There must be a reason for this," and went to the place where she was standing.
As he approached, she acted as if she had entered the Elder’s leaf hut. The king also entered the leaf hut with her;
looking everywhere but not seeing her, he thought, "This is no ordinary woman; it is a single karmic result of the Elder's."
Having formed this perception, even though he was walking near the Elder first, he did not pay homage to him.

Realizing that the reason for this was untrue, he emerged from the leaf-hut, paid homage to the Elder, and sitting to one side, asked, "Venerable sir, I hope you are not distressed by lack of almsfood?
The Elder replied, "It is sufficient, Great King. [The king said,] "I know this..."
"Venerable sir, how can anyone have confidence in you who live with such a defilement?
From now on, you must not go anywhere else. I shall provide for you with the four requisites;
do not neglect wise attention," he said, and established a regular supply of almsfood for them.
Having obtained the Elder as a supporter, the King’s mind became one-pointed through suitable food;
thus, by increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship*. From that time on, that woman vanished.
At that moment, Mahāsubhaddā, while living in a family of wrong views in the city of Ugganagara, thought: "May the Teacher have compassion for me."
Having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha and becoming free from the stench of raw flesh, she stood on the upper terrace of the palace and performed an act of truth, saying:
"May these flowers remain suspended in mid-air and form a canopy over the head of the One of Ten Powers;
by this sign, may the One of Ten Powers, together with five hundred bhikkhus, accept my alms tomorrow. Having thus made her declaration, she... eight.
He scattered handfuls of *sumana* flowers. When the flowers arrived at the time of the Teacher’s preaching, they remained suspended above the Teacher’s head like a canopy.
Seeing that *sumana* flower canopy, the Teacher mentally accepted Subhaddā’s alms-offering;
then, on the following day when dawn had risen, he said to the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, we...”
“Today we shall go on a long alms-round; do not give voting tickets to the worldlings (puthujjana), but give them only to the noble ones (ariya).
The Elder informed the monks: “Friends, the Teacher will go on a long alms-round today.
Let the worldlings not take [tickets]; let only the noble ones take the voting tickets. Then the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna said, “Bring the voting ticket, friend!”
He extended his hand first. Ānanda, having formed the thought, "The Teacher does not have voting tickets given to such monks;
he gives them only to the Noble Ones," went and informed the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Give a voting ticket to him who asks for one.
The Elder thought: "If it is not proper to give a voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna, then..."
“The Teacher will reject it; there must be a reason for this,” he thought, and thus he set out with the intention, “I shall give the voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna.

Even before Ānanda arrived, Kuṇḍadhāna attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge, stood in the air by means of psychic power, and said, “Bring it, friend Ānanda; the Teacher knows me; do not [give it to] a monk such as I.”
"The Teacher does not forbid one who takes the first voting ticket," he said, and reaching out his hand, he took a ticket.
Taking that as the occasion for instruction, the Teacher established the Elder in the foremost position among those who take the first voting ticket in this Dispensation.
Because this Elder, having obtained the support of the king and through the acquisition of suitable food, had attained a concentrated mind...
While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he became possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*) due to his excellence of natural support (*upanissaya*).
Even though this elder was such as this, ordinary monks (*puthujjana-bhikkhu*), unaware of his virtues, gave rise to doubt, thinking, "He takes the first voting ticket;
what indeed could this mean? In order to dispel that doubt of theirs, the elder [ascended] into the sky.
Having ascended and displayed a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*) under a pretext, reciting the verse beginning with "One should cut the five.

Thus, having become an *arahant* in accordance with the store of merit he had fulfilled, and having attained the foremost position (*etadaggaṭṭhāna*), he recalled his own past deeds and, out of joy, proclaimed his account of former conduct, saying: "For seven days I remained in seclusion," and so forth.
In that place, the Teacher remained for seven days in seclusion through the dwelling in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
the meaning is that he was one who had become secluded. The rest is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna is completed.
2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sāgata.
The account beginning with “He who was known by the name Sobhita” is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sāgata.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Padumuttara...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn into a certain brahmin family and attained mastery in all arts.
Known by the name Sobhita, he became one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha, the analysis of phonemes, and the Itihāsa as the fifth;
he was a master of exegesis and grammar, and was fully proficient in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man. One day...

Seeing the Blessed One Padumuttara, resplendent with the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, passing through the gate of the pleasure grove, he, with a heart of extreme faith, offered praise by means of many methods and many eulogies of his virtues.
Hearing that praise, the Blessed One said: "In the future, under the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama, there will be one named Sāgata..."

“He shall become a disciple,” he gave this prediction. From that time forth, performing meritorious deeds, he lived out his lifespan and, passing away from there, was reborn in the world of the devas.

After experiencing the dual excellences among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in a certain family home during the arising of this Buddha. His parents were filled with joy.
Because he increased [their merit] and was well-born, they gave him the name Sāgata. Having gained faith in the Teaching, he went forth, developed insight, and attained Arahantship.
Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship in accordance with his accumulation of merit, he remembered his own past karma and was filled with joy.
He spoke the words beginning with “he who was named Sobhita,” while proclaiming the *apadāna* of his former conduct. Therein, the connection is as follows:
at that time, when the equipment of merit was being fulfilled, there was a brahmin named Sobhita by name.
(21) “Having raised [them] from the wrong path” means having lifted up and removed them from hostile paths, evil ways, or byways.

"Point out the path, O Blessed One," means: "You, the Omniscient One, point out—explain, teach, analyze, and clarify—the path, the way of the true person, the means for attaining Nibbāna. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sāgata is complete.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāna.
"Of the Lord Padumuttara," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kaccāna.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating, in various existences, the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the turning away from saṃsāra, [attained his state] under Padumuttara.
Having been born during the time of the Blessed One into the household of a wealthy merchant of a great clan, he grew up and one day,

while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief. Desiring that same position for himself as well, he—
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he wandered among gods and humans; during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha,
having become a master of spells (vidyādhara) and traveling through the air, he saw the Teacher seated in a certain forest grove and,
with a devout mind, made an offering of kaṇikāra flowers.
Thus, by that meritorious deed, he transmigrated from one happy destination to another, and during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī.

After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he made an offering at the site where the Golden Stupa was built, using a golden brick worth ten thousand pieces, and thought: "In whatever place the Blessed One is reborn, may he be born for me..."

"May my body become golden-colored," he made this aspiration. Then, having performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, he was reborn during the present arising of a Buddha in the house of the family priest of King Caṇḍapajjota in Ujjain.
On the day of his naming, his parents said, "Our son is golden-colored..."
“Since he has come taking his own name with him,” they gave him the name Kañcanamāṇava.
As he grew up, having mastered the three Vedas, he obtained the position of family priest upon his father’s passing. He became known by the name Kaccāna according to his clan.
King Caṇḍapajjota, having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, said, “Teacher, go there and bring the Teacher here.”
He sent him. He, being the eighth including himself, approached the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher taught the Dhamma to him.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he, together with those seven people, became established in Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks. At that very moment, they had hair and beards only two finger-breadths long and were wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhimaya*).

They were like elder monks of sixty years' standing. Thus, having accomplished his own purpose, the Elder informed the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, King Pajjota wishes to pay homage at your feet and hear the Dhamma.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, you yourself go there; even when you have gone, the king will gain confidence. Then the Elder, accompanied by himself as the eighth...
Having gone there, he won over the king, established the teaching in the Avanti region, and returned once more to the presence of the Teacher.
Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship, he was designated as foremost among the disciples in this way:
"Bhikkhus, my disciples who analyze in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief, Mahākaccāna is the foremost."
Having realized his own past karma and recollecting the account of his former deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Lord Padumuttara.
In this context, the term "Paduma Cetiya" refers to the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) residence of the Blessed One itself,
which is worthy of worship as a shrine (*cetiya*) because it was covered with lotuses or constructed in the shape of a lotus— just as one speaks of the "Gotamaka Cetiya" or the "Āḷavaka Cetiya."

When it was said that the dwelling place of those *yakkhas* is called a *cetiya* because it is a place worthy of worship, so too this dwelling place of the Blessed One is called a *cetiya*; it should not be understood as a *dhātucetiya* (a relic shrine).
For since the Blessed One had not yet attained final Nibbāna, there were no bodily relics (*sarīradhātu*) present, and thus he did not construct a relic shrine. [This refers to] the stone seat.
"Having had it made" means: having had a stone seat made of crystal for the lower part of that Perfume Chamber named Padumā, in order to serve as a flower-stand.
"They coated it with gold" means: they specially coated—that stone seat—with Jambūnada gold;
the sense is that they covered it.

32. Having taken up a parasol made of jewels, fashioned from the seven precious gems, and holding it over his head, and having taken up a yak-tail fan and a white, excellent chowrie, I offered them to the Buddha.

"To the Friend of the World, the Neutral One" (lokabandhussa tādinoti) means: to the Buddha who is like the Friend of the entire world and who possesses the quality of neutrality (tādi). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākaccāna is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kāḷudāyi begins with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara... This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse,
he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who inspire confidence in families, and he made a corresponding aspiration.
Having done so, he aspired for that position.
Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, on the very day the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of our mother,
he himself took rebirth in Kapilavatthu in the house of a minister, by means of the Bodhisatta’s [merit].
Because he was born on the very same day as [the Bodhisatta], they placed him on a cushion of fine linen that very day and led him away to attend upon the Bodhisatta.

For on this same single day, seven things were born together with the Bodhisatta: the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four treasures, the elephant Āṭānāṭiya, the horse Kaṇṭhaka, Ānanda, Channa, and Kāḷudāyin.

Because he was born together [with the Bodhisatta], they were called "born-together" (*sahajāta*). Then, on the day of his naming—on a day when the entire city was filled with exultant hearts—they gave him the name Udāyin because he had been born on such an occasion.
However, because his complexion was somewhat dark, he became known as Kāḷudāyin.
He grew up playing childhood games together with the Bodhisatta.
Later on, when the Lord of the World had gone forth on the Great Renunciation, had gradually attained omniscience,
and was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
King Suddhodana heard this news and dispatched a minister accompanied by a thousand men, saying: "Bring my son here."

Thus, having gone into the presence of the Teacher at the time of the Dhamma teaching and standing at the edge of the assembly, they heard the Dhamma and, together with their retinue, attained arahantship.
Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became as if sixty-year-old elders, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*). From the attainment of arahantship...
But from that point on, the Noble Ones remained impartial. Therefore, he did not convey the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers.
When the king thought, "He neither goes nor does his message reach me," he dispatched another minister with a thousand men.
When that one also acted in the same manner, he sent yet another; thus, [he sent] nine times with nine thousand men.
He sent for his ministers. Having all attained *arahantship*, they remained silent.
Then the king thought: "Because these people lack affection for me, they said nothing to the One of Ten Powers regarding his coming here.
This Udāyin, however, was of the same age as the One of Ten Powers; he played in the dust with him, and he is devoted to me."

Thinking, "I have affection for him; I shall send him," he summoned him and said, "Dear son, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha) here. Having said this, he sent him off.
As he was departing, however, [the son] said, "If I may receive the going-forth, O King, then I will bring the Blessed One here," and having said this, "Whatever must be done..."
When he was told, "Show me my son," he went to Rājagaha;

standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s time for preaching the Dhamma, he heard the Dhamma, and together with his retinue, attained Arahantship and was established in the state of an "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come, monk). Having attained Arahantship, however, he thought:
"This is not yet the time for the One Possessed of Ten Powers to go to his native city; but when the spring has arrived..."
“The time for departure will come when the forest groves are in bloom and the ground is covered with green grass.
Thus, while awaiting the right time, when spring had arrived, he praised the path to the Teacher’s native city, saying:
“O Blessed One, now the trees are leafless, having shed their foliage though they are destined to bear fruit.”
They shine forth like those possessed of radiance; O Great Hero, the time for the chariots has come.
"These trees are in full bloom, delightful, and their fragrance wafts in all directions.
Having cast off their leaves, they hope for fruit; O Hero, it is time to depart from here."
“Neither too cold nor yet too hot, O Blessed One, is this pleasant climate for the journey;
let the Sākiyas and the Koḷiyas see you crossing the Rohiṇī river facing westward.
With hope one plows the field; with hope the seed is sown.”
"Traders go out to sea with hope as their carriers of wealth;
may that hope for which I stand be fulfilled for me.
May it not be too cold, nor too hot, nor too plagued by famine and drought."
"The ground is green and lush; this is the time, O Great Sage.
Again and again they sow the seed; again and again the king of the gods sends rain;
again and again the farmers plow the field; again and again grain comes to the kingdom."
“Again and again do beggars wander; again and again do givers of gifts give.
Having given again and again, the givers of gifts go again and again to the heavenly state.
Indeed, a hero purifies seven generations in whichever family that one of vast wisdom is born.”
"I believe the God of Gods is capable [of this], for from you was born the Sage whose name is Truth.
Suddhodana is the name of the Great Seer’s father, while the Buddha’s mother is named Māyā;
having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, she rejoices in the Heaven of the Thirty-three upon the dissolution of her body."
“Gautamī has passed away and departed from here, having become endowed with celestial pleasures.
She rejoices with the five strands of sensual pleasure, surrounded by those hosts of deities.
These verses he spoke. Therein, “aṅgārinā” means “like charcoal,” thus “charcoal. Charcoal is the color of red coral.
"Of trees" means *rukkhānaṃ*. "Possessing flowers and fruits" means those which have them; thus they are called *aṅgārino* (possessing coals).

The meaning is that, with their intensely red blossoms and sprouts, they appear as if strewn all over with a shower of coals. "Now" (*dāni*) means at this time. "Trees" (*dumā*) means *rukkhā* (trees). "Venerable Sir" (*bhadante*):
because "bhadanta" has "bhaddaṃ" at its end, it is spoken of by eliding one *da*-sound, as in "bhadante. [He is] endowed with distinguished virtues.
And the Teacher is the foremost among those endowed with distinguished qualities. Therefore, "Bhadante" is simply an address to the Teacher;
it is a singular form ending in -e, as in such examples as *sugate*, *paṭikamme*, *sukhe*, *dukkhe*, *jīve*, and so forth.
Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of an invocation. Hence it was said: "‘Bhadante’ is an address. [It is] "a different word having the same meaning as the word *bhadda*."
"Phalesino" means those seeking fruits (*phala*). For even in the case of insentient things, he speaks of the activity of a sentient being.

Thus requested by the Elder, the Blessed One—seeing that many would attain distinguished spiritual achievements upon going there—set out from Rājagaha toward the road leading to Kapilavatthu by way of a journey without haste, accompanied by twenty thousand whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). By means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), the Elder [reached] Kapilavatthu.
Having gone before the king, he stood in the air; seeing him in a form never seen before, the king asked, "Who are you?
To show him, "You do not know me, whom you sent as a minister’s son into the presence of the Blessed One; rather, you should know me thus," he said:
"I am the son of the Buddha, the conqueror of the unconquerable, of Aṅgīrasa, the peerless Tathāgata."
“You are my father’s father, O Sakka; by Dhamma, Gotama, you are my grandfather,” he said in this verse.
Therein, “I am the son of the Buddha” means I am the son of the offspring of the Omniscient Buddha. “Asayhasāhino” means from the time of his full enlightenment...
Because, prior to the Great Bodhisatta, it was impossible for others to bear or carry the entire burden of the requisites for enlightenment and the office of great compassion—
which were thus "unbearable" (*asayha*)— he bore and carried them; and because thereafter,
it was likewise impossible for others to bear or overcome them, he bore and overcame the five "unbearable" Māras.

Because he bears the Buddha-work—which is called "instruction" (anusāsani) and is beyond the capacity of others—by understanding the distinctions of the dispositions (*āsaya*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), temperaments (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*) of those to be trained, and thereby providing instruction to them as is appropriate through the mundane and supramundane ultimate goals pertaining to this life and the life hereafter;
or because he acts with excellence therein, he is "one who accomplishes the impossible" (*asayhasāhī*).
"Aṅgīrasassa" means one who has taken upon himself the perfection of virtue and other qualities. "Of him whose radiant luster streams forth from every limb."
Others [say this]. Some, however, say: "The two names, Aṅgīrasa and Siddhattha, were indeed given by his father. "Appaṭima" means peerless.
"Tādino" refers to one who has attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādi*) toward both the desirable and the undesirable.
"You are my father's father" means that, according to the noble lineage (*ariyajāti*), you are the father of my father, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in accordance with worldly convention.

“Sakka,” he addresses the king by way of his clan. “By the Dhamma” means by way of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the two types of birth—the noble birth and the worldly birth—through the convergence of their respective natures.
“Gotama,” he addresses the king by way of his lineage (*gotta*). “You are my grandfather” means you are my paternal great-grandfather.
And here, by saying “I am the son of the Buddha,” and so forth, the Elder answered with something other [than the question].
Having thus made himself known, the king, delighted and joyful, had him seated upon a magnificent couch;
then, filling a bowl with various choice foods prepared for himself, he offered it to him.
When the king asked, "Venerable sir, why do you wish to depart? Please eat," he replied, "I shall go to the presence of the Teacher and eat there."
“But where is the Teacher? “He has set out on the road with a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus for the purpose of seeing you.
“You eat this almsfood yourselves; take some other to the Blessed One.
Until my son reaches this city, bring almsfood for him from here,” he said, and the Elder—
Having performed his meal duties and preached the Dhamma to the king and his assembly, and even before the Teacher’s arrival,
he inspired the entire royal palace with deep faith in the Triple Gem; then, while everyone was looking on,
he released into the air the bowl filled with the food intended for the Teacher, and rising himself into the sky, he offered the alms-food.
Having offered it, she placed it in the Teacher’s hand. The Teacher consumed that alms-food.
Thus, as the Blessed One traveled one *yojana* each day along the sixty-*yojana* road, she brought and gave him alms-food from the royal palace itself every day.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This woman is purifying my father's entire residence," declared: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost..."

“Among my disciples, those monks who inspire confidence in families, Kāḷudāyin is indeed the foremost,” he said, thus placing him in the position of being the chief among those who inspire confidence in families.

(48–9) Having thus attained Arahantship in accordance with the store of merit he had previously accumulated and having obtained this foremost position, he recalled his own past karma and, out of joy, proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words: “Of the Buddha Padumuttara... and so forth.
"Of one who has set out on the journey" means of one setting out upon a long road for the purpose of going to the western country (*apararaṭṭha*).

"While wandering on his tour at that time" refers to the Blessed One, the Buddha Padumuttara, as he was wandering on his tour through the three circles—the inner circle, the middle circle, and the outer circle—at that time;
[he saw] a lotus that was well-blossomed, thoroughly bloomed, and fully awakened.
"Having taken"—meaning having grasped—not only the *paduma* lotus, but also the blooming *uppala* and *mallika* jasmine;
"having taken with both hands," the connection is that they filled [the vessels]. "Having taken the supreme rice" means:
having taken the most excellent, best, sweet, and perfectly cooked *sāli* rice, I gave it to the Teacher and fed him; such is the meaning.

97. "One who generates joy for the Śākyans" means one who generates and produces joy and satisfaction for the Śākya royal family—the Blessed One’s kinsmen—through his excellence of stature, girth, beauty, youth, speech, and conversation.
"He will be a known relative" means he will be a well-known and manifest kinsman.
The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kāḷudāyin is completed.
5. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mogharāja begins with the verse "Atthadassī tu bhagavā" and so forth. This [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those who wear coarse robes. Having seen this, he...
Desiring a particular state of existence, he made a resolution and performed meritorious deeds in various births; then,
during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, having been reborn again in a brahmin family and having attained mastery in the sciences and arts of the brahmins,
one day he saw the Blessed One Atthadassi walking along the royal road surrounded by the community of monks.

Seeing him, with a mind full of faith, he prostrated himself with the fivefold greeting, placed his hands in añjali at his head, and after praising him with the six verses beginning with "As far as there are embodied teachers," he filled a vessel and offered honey to the Teacher.
The Teacher accepted it and gave a blessing of thanksgiving. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he...
During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn as a minister to the king named Kaṭṭhavāhana.
Sent by the king to bring the Teacher, he went into the presence of the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
Having practiced the ascetic life for twenty thousand years, when he passed away from there, he remained only in the happy destinies throughout one entire interval between Buddhas.
In this dispensation of the Buddha, having been reborn in a brahmin family, he received the name Mogharāja.
Having mastered the arts in the presence of the brahmin Bāvari, he became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and went forth as an ascetic.
Surrounded by a thousand ascetics, he was sent along with Ajita and the others into the presence of the Teacher; he was the fifteenth among them.
Having offered an oblation and asked a question, he attained arahantship at the conclusion of the answer.

Having attained arahantship, however, he wore rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) that were especially endowed with a threefold coarseness: coarseness of the needlework, coarseness of the threads, and coarseness of the dye.
Because of this, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes.

64. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arhatship in accordance with his aspiration, and seeing his own prior accumulations of merit, Atthadassī, the Blessed One, spoke the words beginning with "Atthadassī tu bhagavā," while proclaiming the account of his former deeds (*pubbakammāpadāna*).
All of that is of plain meaning. 73. *Puṭakaṃ pūrayitvāna*: "Puṭaka" refers to a vessel (*vāraka*) or a jar (*ghaṭa*).
Having filled a jar with pure, faultless, small-bee honey—free from flies or larvae—and having grasped it with both hands, he took hold of it with great care and respect.
