The connection is: "They presented [it] to the Blessed One, the Great Sage. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mogharāja is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Adhimutta.
"Nibbute lokanāthamhi... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Adhimutta Thera.

Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated virtues conducive to the attainment of liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family when the World-Lord Atthadassi had attained final *parinibbāna*. With faith in the Triple Gem, he [honored] the Saṅgha of monks...
Having invited [the monks], he had a pavilion constructed of sugarcane, offered a great almsgiving, and at its conclusion made a resolve for the state of peace (*santipada*).
Passing away from there, he experienced the dual excellences among both gods and humans;

then, being reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha, he gained confidence in the Teaching and, because he was firmly established in faith, became renowned as the Elder Adhimutta.

84. Having thus attained Arahatship by means of the equipment he had prepared, and having remembered his own former karma, he became filled with joy. Recounting the account of his past conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning, "When the Lord of the World had passed away... All of this is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Adhimutta is completed. 7.
Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka (The Garlic-Giver)
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Lasuṇadāyaka Thera begins with the words "Not far from the Himālaya," and so forth.

This Venerable One, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the attainment of liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, he perceived the dangers of the household life.
Having abandoned his home and gone forth into the ascetic life, he dwelt in a forest depending on the Himalayas.
There he planted many garlic bulbs and lived subsisting only on forest roots and fruits. Taking many garlic bulbs in a carrying-pole, he brought them to a human settlement;
having offered them with faith as a gift, he gave them for the sake of medicine to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
He departed. Thus, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he wandered among gods and humans by the power of that very merit, experiencing both types of excellence.
Eventually, during the arising of this present Buddha, he was reborn;
having gained faith and gone forth, he developed insight and before long attained Arahantship. By virtue of his past karma, he became renowned as the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka (the Garlic-Giver).
89. Having remembered his own former karma and feeling joy, he spoke the account of his past conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words "Not far from the Himālayas," and so forth.

Therein, the connection is as follows: when the Blessed One Vipassī arose at a place frequented by humans at the edge of the Himalaya mountains, at that time I was an ascetic (*tāpasa*). "I lived by means of garlic" means that I planted red garlic and [lived upon it].
The meaning is: "Making that very thing my field of activity, I maintain my livelihood. Therefore it was said: "Garlic is my food. 90.

"Having filled the khāris" means: having filled the ascetics' vessels with garlic, taking them on a carrying-pole, [he went] to the monastery—the dwelling place of the Saṅgha—during the three seasons beginning with winter, to the vihāra where the Saṅgha dwells in the four postures.
"I went" means "I went there. "Joyful with a joyful mind" means "being satisfied, with a mind associated with gladness, I gave garlic to the Saṅgha"—this is the meaning. 91.
Of Vipassī... [and so on]... "to the one who delights in him," that is, to this Blessed One Vipassī, the foremost and best among men.
The connection is: "I am devoted to the Dispensation, entirely delighted by it. Regarding "of the Saṅgha... they rejoice":

the meaning is that after I gave the gift of garlic to the Saṅgha, I rejoiced—being well-pleased and satisfied—while experiencing divine prosperity for the duration of a lifespan in the highest heaven of the celestial worlds. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka is completed.

8. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Āyāgadāyaka begins with the verse: "When the Lord of the World had passed away... This [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn in a certain family home at the time of the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One Sikhi.
With faith in the Teaching, he gave wages to carpenters and had a long, most enchanting dining hall constructed;
then, having invited the Saṅgha of monks, [he served them] with excellent food.

Having fed him and given a great gift, he gladdened his heart. Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as his life lasted, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of prosperity.
Now, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a noble family;
having acquired faith and gone forth into homelessness, he applied himself with diligence and effort, developed insight, and before long attained Arahantship.
He was well known as Āyāgathera because he had come [to this state] by virtue of merit performed in the past.
(94) Thus, having attained arahantship through the equipment of merit performed, and being filled with joy upon recollecting the wholesome kamma he himself had done in the past,
he spoke the words beginning with "When the Lord of the World had passed away," while proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
In that context, "nibbute" means that the Blessed One, the Lord of the Flame (Sikhī), who was the most excellent and supreme among those claiming to be Buddhas, has attained final Nibbāna.
"Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cetasā" means: being joyful because of his faith, he was exceedingly glad;
with a heart uplifted by a state of mind associated with joy, he paid homage—that is, he bowed down—to the most excellent stupa, the best of shrines.
95. "Having had it measured by carpenters" means having had the measurement determined by asking, "What is the size of the dining hall?
"Having given them wages at that time" means that at that moment, for the purpose of the construction work, I gave wages to those carpenters;
being satisfied and with a mind full of joy, I had the *āyāga*—that is, the long and extensive dining hall—built.
"I caused [it] to be made"—this is the meaning. The remainder is easy to understand. 97.
"This is the fruit of the āyāga" means this is the result (*vipāka*) of the gift of a dining hall.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Āyāgadāyaka is completed.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhammacakkika.
This is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Dhammacakkika, beginning with the words "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
This [Elder] also, having performed his duties under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births—

During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn in a certain noble family; having reached maturity and increased with sons and daughters, he became endowed with wealth and great prosperity.

Having conceived faith and devotion toward the Three Jewels, he had a jeweled Wheel of Dhamma fashioned and placed behind the Dhamma-seat in the Dhamma assembly hall, and he made offerings to it. By that meritorious deed, among gods and humans...
Having experienced the prosperity of Sakka and the glory of a wheel-turning monarch in various rebirths, he was eventually born into a wealthy family during this current dispensation of a Buddha.
Having developed faith, he went forth into homelessness, and by increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he soon attained *arahantship*.
He became renowned as the Elder Dhammacakkika, named after the wholesome deeds he had performed in the past.

102. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship in accordance with his accumulation of merit, and having remembered his own past karma, he—filled with joy and proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct)—spoke the words beginning with "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha...

The phrase "in the presence of the lion-throne" (*sīhāsanassa sammukhā*) means in front of the Blessed One while he was seated on the lion-throne; that is, in the place facing the Buddha’s seat. [The Blessed One turned] the Wheel of Dhamma...

"Established by me" means that I had a Dhammacakka made—displaying lion figures on both sides with a mirror-like surface in the middle—and it was established and worshipped. What kind of thing was it?
It is connected thus: it was well-made, praised, and extolled as "exceedingly beautiful" by the wise and intelligent.
103. "Cāruvaṇṇova sobhāmī" means "I shine and radiate like one of beautiful complexion.

There is also a reading, "catuvaṇṇehi sobhāmī," which means "I shine and radiate by means of the four castes," namely those comprised within the four castes known as Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, and Sudda.
"Sayoggabalavāhano" means [endowed] with vehicles such as golden palanquins and so forth, as well as with generals, great ministers, and the like.
The meaning is: "together with servants and forces, and with vehicles consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots.
The connection is: "many people—meaning numerous men—who follow me and act in accordance with me, constantly, at all times, surround [me].
The rest is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhammacakkika is completed.
10. The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kapparukkhiya begins with the words "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," etc.; this too is [the account] of the Venerable Elder Kapparukkhiya.
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that serve as the means for attaining Nibbāna in various states of existence,
he was reborn at the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha into a family endowed with great wealth and vast possessions.
With faith in the Teacher, he had a golden wishing-tree (kapparukkha) fashioned, adorned with the seven kinds of gems, and offered it to Siddhattha.
Having placed it before the shrine of the Blessed One, he made offerings to it. Having performed such merit, he lived out his lifespan;
when he passed away from there, he wandered only through happy destinies and, in due course, was reborn in a certain family home during the arising of this Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he established a household life, gained faith in the Triple Gem, and having heard the Dhamma—

Having gained faith and pleased the Teacher, he went forth into homelessness; not long thereafter, having attained *arahantship*, he became renowned as the Elder Kapparukkhiya by virtue of the wholesome deeds he had performed in the past.
Having thus attained the fruit of *arahantship* and recollecting his own former karma, he [proclaimed] his *pubbacaritāpadāna* out of a sense of joy.
Explaining this, he said, "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," and so forth.
"In the presence of the most excellent stupa" means in the place before the most excellent, supreme stupa—a shrine where the relics are enshrined.

Having fastened and hung them upon variegated cloths—cloths such as *cinapaṭṭa* and *somārapaṭṭa*, which are charming due to their diverse, manifold, and dissimilar patterns—I established the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*).
The meaning is: "I established [it]. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kapparukkhiya is completed.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is completed.
5. Upāli-vagga 1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upāli, the Nephew of the Elder Upāli:
"With a thousand [monks] whose taints were destroyed," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Upāli, the nephew of the Elder Upāli.

For this elder had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas; accumulating merit in various successive existences, he was reborn into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, seeing the peril in the household life, he abandoned his home and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic (*isi*).
Having attained the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he dwelt in the Himalayas.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring seclusion, entered the Himālaya mountains.

Seeing from afar the Blessed One shining like the full moon, the ascetic, with a mind full of faith, placed his deerskin mantle upon his shoulder, raised his joined palms in salutation, and while still standing, pressed his ten-fingered palms together above his head; then, with many...
He praised the Blessed One with many similes and words of eulogy. Upon hearing this, the Blessed One gave him a prophecy, saying:
"In the future, this ascetic will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One named Gotama and will become the foremost among those of sharp wisdom regarding the Vinaya.
Having lived out his full lifespan without falling away from jhāna, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. From there...

Having passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing various fortunes, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in the city of Kapilavatthu as the nephew of the Elder Upāli.
Gradually reaching maturity, he went forth into homelessness under his maternal uncle, the Elder Upāli.
Having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and developed insight (*vipassanā*), he became an *arahant* before long.
Because he had lived in the presence of his own teacher, Upāli became sharp-witted regarding questions on the Vinaya.

Then the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are sharp-witted in answering questions on the Vinaya, the foremost is the bhikkhu Upāli, my nephew."

1. Thus, having attained this foremost position and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the verse beginning with "khīṇāsavasahassehi" and so forth.
In that context, they are called *āsavā* because they flow (*savanti*) and proceed everywhere (*ā*), up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).

There are four taints (*āsava*), such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*); those by whom these have been exhausted (*khīṇa*), dried up (*sositā*), completely dried up (*visositā*), and destroyed (*viddhaṃsitā*) are [the ones referred to].
"Khīṇāsavā" means those very thousands who have destroyed the taints; "by those thousands of khīṇāsavas. The connection is as follows:
the Leader of the World, surrounded and encompassed by them—He who leads the world to Nibbāna, devoted to seclusion, goes to dwell in solitude, to be alone.
2. "Clad in an antelope skin": I am covered with the skin of the ajina deer; the meaning is that I am dressed in an antelope skin.
"Carrying a triple staff" means carrying a triple staff that has been taken up for the purpose of setting down the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*).
The connection is: "He saw the Leader of the World surrounded and encompassed by the community of monks. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upāli, the Nephew, is completed.
2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Soṇakoḷivisa.
The passage beginning with "Of the Sage Anomadassi" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Koḷivisa.
This one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various births the merits conducive to the turning away from saṃsāra, [encountered] Anomadassi...
Having been reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he grew up with a wife and children and became endowed with great wealth.

For the purpose of providing a walking path for the Blessed One, he had a beautiful *caṅkama* constructed; having had it plastered with lime, he made it level and radiant like the surface of a mirror.
Having adorned it with lamps, incense, flowers, and other offerings, he dedicated it to the Blessed One and [invited] the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
He honored the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with exquisite food. Having performed meritorious deeds in this manner for as long as he lived, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the devas.
There, having experienced divine splendor in the manner described in the Pāḷi, he was subsequently born into the Okkāka clan—all of which should be understood according to what is stated in the Pāḷi.
In his final existence, however, he was born into the royal lineage of the Koliyans.
Because he wore an earring worth ten million when he reached adulthood, he became known as Koṭikaṇṇa (Ten-Million-Ear) and Kuṭikaṇṇa (Crooked-Ear).
Having gained faith in the Blessed One after hearing the Dhamma, he went forth into homelessness;
and by developing insight, he soon attained arahantship.

25. Having thus become an Arahant and recollecting his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the verse beginning with "Of Anomadassi, the Sage.

Therein, "Anomadassi" means one whose vision (*dassana*) is not inferior (*anoma*), not base, but beautiful, because of being adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and because of being resplendent with the halo of fathom-wide radiance; [this refers to his] height and circumference.
Because he was endowed with such qualities, the body of that Blessed One was beautiful to behold; thus, "of that Anomadassī, the Sage" is the meaning.
"Tādi" means one whose nature is unshakable regarding the desirable and the undesirable.

"Having made a plastering with lime" means having had the walkway (caṅkama) smeared with lime and decorated with lamps, incense, flowers, banners, flags, and so forth; it is there that I had the walkway constructed.
The meaning is "he wished. The meaning of the remaining verses is easily understood by following the text (*pāḷi*). 35.

He who bears glory (*yasa*), which consists of the perfection of retinue and the perfection of wealth, is *Yasodhara*; the connection is that all these seventy-seven wheel-turning monarchs were of one name, namely *Yasodhara*.
52. *Aṅgīrasa*: he from whose body (*aṅga*) rays (*rasmi*) have issued forth is *Aṅgīrasa*; [he is so called] because he is free from desire, hatred, delusion, fear, and wrong courses of action.
Or, because he does not go to the four states of misery due to his conduct being free from evil, he is a *nāga*;
and since he is a great *nāga* who is honored, he is a "Great *Nāga*" (*Mahānāga*). The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Koḷivisa is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhaddiya, Son of Kāḷigodhā.
The passage beginning with "Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷigodhā.
This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas in various existences, [accumulated] merits conducive to the turning away from saṃsāra.
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching adulthood and being blessed with children and a wife, he saw the city-dwellers performing meritorious deeds;
desiring to perform merit himself as well, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and prepared many costly couches, such as those with thick cotton mattresses.
Having prepared the place, while the Blessed One sat there together with the Saṅgha, he fed them with exquisite food and gave a great almsgiving.

Having thus performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his life and experienced the two kinds of excellence among gods and humans, in a later time, during this current arising of a Buddha, he was reborn as the son of the queen named Kāḷigodhā. When he reached the age of discretion—

He became well known as Bhaddiya Kāḷigodhāputta because of his auspiciousness due to the perfection of his physical form— his height, girth, hands, and feet— and because he was the son of Queen Kāḷigodhā.
Having gained faith in the Teacher and won over his parents, he went forth into homelessness and,
before long, became an arahant.

54. Having thus become an Arahant and recollecting his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of past conduct), spoke the verse beginning with "Padumuttara Sambuddha.
The meaning of that has already been explained above. Regarding the term *mettacitta*: it is called *mettā* because it "moistens" (*mijjati*), "endears" (*sinehati*), and "rejoices in" all beings;
a mind accompanied by such loving-kindness is a "mind of loving-kindness" (*mettacitta*). This [Blessed One] possessed that [mind].
"Atthi" means "possessing a mind of loving-kindness (mettā)," referring to that very mind of loving-kindness. "Mahāmuni" refers to the Great Sage because of his greatness among all monks;
the connection is that he is the Sambuddha Padumuttara. "Sabbā janatā" means the entire body of people, that is, all the inhabitants of the city.
"Sabalokagganāyaka" means the foremost and best of the entire world, because he leads and brings [beings] to Nibbāna.
The connection is that the people approach and go near the Leader, the Sambuddha Padumuttara.
"Both bound and unbound meat" refers to the bait known as *baddhasattu* (meat tied up) and *abaddhasattu* (meat not tied up).

Alternatively, the connection is that they take food and drink—such as boiled rice, cakes, snacks, hard foods, and gruel—which are called "bait" (*āmisa*) because they are to be consumed within the day—and give them to the Teacher in the unsurpassed field of merit.

58. "A seat fit for a Buddha" means a seat suitable for a Buddha, worthy of a Buddha, appropriate for a Buddha, made of the seven precious gems; this is the meaning. The rest is easily understood by following the same method.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷigodhā, is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka.
"Having built a small hut in the forest," and so forth, is the legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, he remained bound by the ties of the household and lived in domestic life.

Seeing the peril [of sensual pleasures], he abandoned both the objects of desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of desire (*kilesakāma*), and established a forest dwelling in a mountain range not far from the Himalayas.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara arrived at that place out of a desire for seclusion.
Then, upon seeing the Blessed One, that ascetic, with a mind full of serene faith, paid homage and prepared a layer of grass for him to sit upon.
He gave [it]. While the Blessed One was seated there, he satisfied him with many sweet fruits, such as *tiṇḍuka* and others.
By that meritorious deed, when he passed away from there, wandering on from gods to humans, he experienced two states of prosperity.
Then, in this current arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain family home; endowed with faith, he went forth into homelessness.
Having increased his insight (*vipassanā*), he became an *arahant* before long.

Because he remained perfectly established in *nibbāna*—the state of peace—with effortless ease, as if reaching the fruit of *arahantship* on the very tip of a razor, he became renowned as the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka.
Having become an *arahant*, however, he recollected his own past deeds and, filled with joy, [recited] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*.
He spoke the words beginning with “having built a hut in the forest,” demonstrating this. Therein, “in the forest” (*araññe*):

it is called a forest (*arañña*) because people do not take pleasure in it, do not delight in it, and do not settle there due to the fear of lions, tigers, and other such beasts; [he dwelt] in that forest. “A hut” (*kuṭikaṃ*):
having built a grass-thatched hut, he dwelt among the mountains; the meaning is that he made his abode there. And by gain...
The connection is: "He dwelt contented with non-gain, with ill-repute, and with disrepute.
72. Regarding the phrase *jalajuttamanāmakaṃ*: that which is born in water is *jalaja*, meaning a lotus; the most excellent among those born in water is *jalajuttama*;

one whose name is equal to the most excellent among those born in water is *jalajuttamanāmaka*; [the Buddha] is thus called *jalajuttamanāmaka*. Thus, [he refers to] the Buddha named *jalajuttamanāmaka*.
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is easily understood by following the method of the Pāḷi text.
Thus ends the commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka.
5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcahatthiya.
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Pañcahatthiya Thera, beginning with "The Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha; and upon reaching maturity, he lived with faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, they brought five handfuls of blue lotuses. With those five handfuls of blue lotuses, he honored the Blessed One, Sumedha, as he was walking along the street.
Those flowers, having gone up into the air, formed a canopy, providing shade as they moved along with the Tathāgata himself.
Seeing this, he was filled with joy; his body suffused with rapture, for the rest of his life he [remained] devoted to that very [practice].
Having recollected his merit, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the gods.
Wandering on from one existence to another, he was reborn in an eminent family during this current dispensation of a Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him;
he went forth into homelessness, developed insight, and before long became an arahant. He became well known by the name Katakusala as the Elder Pañcahatthiya.

77. Thus, recollecting his own former karma and manifesting the account of his past conduct as seen through direct wisdom (*paññā*), the one named Sumedha spoke these words beginning with "the Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha.

In this context, *sumedha* means that the Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One (*sambuddha*) whose intelligence (*medhā*)—consisting of the penetration of the Four Truths, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and other forms of wisdom—is beautiful;
he is the Blessed One Sumedha, the Fully Enlightened One, who was walking in the market square, in the middle of the street. This is the grammatical connection.
"With downcast eyes" means with eyes cast downwards. "Speaking in moderation" means having the habit of speaking after knowing the proper measure;
the meaning is that he taught the Dhamma after knowing the measure. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Pañcahatthiyatthera-apadāna* is completed.
6. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumacchadaniya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Padumacchadaniya begins with the words, "When the Lord of the World had passed away...

This [Elder] also, having accumulated the equipment of merit by performing meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras, was amassing merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various births.
During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a certain noble family; having reached maturity, he gained faith in the Triple Gem.
After the Blessed One Vipassī had attained final Nibbāna, he honored the funeral pyre with lotus flowers.
By virtue of that very confidence of heart, he lived out his full lifespan and, wandering through the happy destinies thereafter, experienced both celestial and human prosperity.
Having experienced two types of prosperity on many occasions, he was reborn in a noble family during this present time of our Perfectly Enlightened One.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into the Dispensation.
By striving and exerting himself, he became an Arahant before long. As he was dwelling here and there—in places such as his night-quarters and day-quarters— [The remainder of the passage follows.]
His monastery was covered with lotus flowers; therefore, he became well known as the Elder Padumacchadanīya.

Recalling his own past karma and proclaiming his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct) out of a sense of joy, he spoke the verse beginning with "When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna.
In that context, "Nibbūte" means when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*).

The meaning is: while the funeral pyre for the body of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī was being prepared and had been set upon the pyre, I took a cluster of full-blown lotuses and placed them upon the pyre as an offering.
Since the method for the remaining verses has already been explained below, their meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumacchadanīya is completed.
7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sayanadāyaka.
"Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sayanadāyaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), [attained this state] under Siddhattha...

In the time of the Blessed One, a certain person was reborn in a particular family. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and had a couch made for the Blessed One’s use out of ivory, gold, and other precious materials;
having spread it with priceless and variegated coverlets, he honored the Blessed One.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted it and used it. Through that meritorious deed, he experienced celestial and human prosperities.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher’s dispensation, went forth into homelessness, and having commenced insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he became an *arahant* before long.
He became well known by the name Sayanadāyaka Thera, due to the merit he had performed in the past.

88. Thus, one day, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "To Siddhattha, the Blessed One," while proclaiming the *Apadāna* of his former conduct. Since all of that is easily understood by following the method of the Pāḷi, [no further explanation is needed].
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sayanadāyaka is complete.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Caṅkamanadāyaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Caṅkamanadāyaka Thera begins with the words "Of the Sage Atthadassi.

This Venerable One had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various births, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi. Having attained maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher.

Having had a walkway constructed on a high foundation, plastered with lime, shining like a heap of silver, and having spread out a white sand surface resembling pearls, he offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One accepted it;
and having accepted the walkway, he entered into a state of pleasant concentration of body and mind, [thinking]: "In the future, in the teaching of the Blessed Gotama..."

“He will become a disciple,” he prophesied. By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering from one state to another among gods and humans and experiencing two types of prosperity, he was reborn in a certain family home at the time of this Buddha’s appearance.

Upon reaching maturity, endowed with faith, he went forth into the teaching; not long after, having attained Arahantship, he became renowned as the Elder Caṅkamanadāyaka (the Giver of the Walking Path) because of the merit he had performed.

93. Thus, on one occasion, having recollected the meritorious deeds he had previously performed and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Sage Atthadassi," proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).

Therein, *Atthadassissa* means: he who sees (*dakkhati*) or beholds (*passati*) the purpose (*attha*), the motive (*payojana*), growth (*vuddhi*), increase (*virūḷhi*), and Nibbāna, is called *Atthadassi*; or alternatively, [he is so called because] he sees the purpose, which is Nibbāna.
"One whose nature is seeing and one whose nature is knowing" means *atthadassī*. The connection is as follows:

"They had a delightful, heart-captivating, cultivable, and mind-to-be-attended walking-passage (*caṅkama*) made for that Blessed One, the sage (*muni*), who is endowed with the sage’s wisdom (*mona*).
The remainder is easily understood by following the method already explained.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Caṅkamanadāyaka is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Subhadda begins with the verse: “Padumuttaro lokavidū... This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties in various existences while accumulating merit for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a wealthy and faithful family of noble birth.
Having reached maturity, though bound by the shackles of the household life, he placed his faith in the Triple Gem; and while lying upon the bed of final Nibbāna, he beheld Padumuttara.

Having seen the Blessed One and having seen the devas from the ten thousand world-systems who had assembled there, he, with a devout mind, made offerings with many fragrant flowers such as *nigguṇḍika*, *eṭaka*, blue *kāsoka*, and *asita*. By that meritorious deed, he remained for the duration of his lifespan;
then, passing away from there, he experienced divine splendors among the Tusita heaven and other realms, and thereafter among humans.
Having experienced human success, he was honored with fragrant flowers in each place where he was reborn.
However, having been born into a family endowed with great wealth during this current appearance of a Buddha,
and having reached maturity, although he saw the danger in sensual pleasures, he did not obtain a vision of the Blessed Buddha until the time of the Buddha’s final passing away (parinibbāna).
Having gone forth at the very moment he was lying on the bed of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, he attained Arahatship.
He became well known by the name Subhadda, due to the merit he had performed in the past.
Recalling his own former deeds, and out of joy, he proclaimed the account of his previous conduct, beginning with Padumuttara.
He spoke the verse beginning with "knower of the world" (*lokavidū*). That has already been explained in its literal sense. "Listen to me as I speak...
[omission] ...he shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints"—this was prophesied by the Blessed One Padumuttara while he was lying upon his deathbed.
The commentary on the fifth recitation section is completed.
115. Thus, demonstrating his own practice, he said: “Bound by former karma,” and so forth. “One-pointed” means one whose mind is concentrated.

“Well-composed” means thoroughly composed; the meaning is that his body and mind are tranquil. “The Buddha’s legitimate son” means that having heard the instruction and admonition issued from the Buddha’s breast—that is, from his heart—he attained the fruit of arahantship. “I am a pillar of the Dhamma.”
"Sunimmito" means that I am well-fashioned according to the Dhamma—that is, born from the Dhamma of the meditation subject—and well-formed through noble birth;

the sense is that I am one for whom all duties have been perfectly accomplished. "Upagamma dhammarājaṃ" means having approached the Blessed One, who is the King of Dhamma, the sovereign lord over all beings by virtue of the Dhamma.

"Having approached" means having gone near. "I asked the supreme question" means I asked a supreme question concerning the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), dependent origination (*samuppāda*), and so forth.
"And as he spoke my question" means this Blessed One of ours, speaking—that is, answering—my question.
"He led me to the stream of Dhamma" refers to that which is reckoned as the *nibbāna*-element without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
"Entered the stream of Dhamma, the flow of Dhamma"—this is the meaning.
118. *Jalajuttamanāyaka* (the Supreme Leader of the Lotus-Born): this is a conventional designation formed by changing the letter *m* to *y* in the name Padumuttara.
"He attained Nibbāna without clinging": having not grasped the five aggregates as clinging, he attained Nibbāna; he was no longer manifest, he passed beyond sight.
"He went" means that he did not remain established anywhere, such as in the human world or elsewhere. "Like a lamp when the oil is exhausted" connects thus:
like a lamp, it was extinguished due to the exhaustion—that is, the absence—of the oil of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭatela*).
119. "It was seven yojanas [in height]" refers to the jewel-encrusted [stupa] of that Blessed One Padumuttara after he had attained *parinibbāna*.

"The stupa was seven yojanas high" means it had become so. "There they honored the banner" means that there, at that cetiya, they honored the banner which was auspicious in every way, excellent on all sides, and delightful in every respect.
"And of the Buddha Kassapa" refers to [the lineage] that has come down from the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
The connection is as follows: "As I was wandering among gods and humans, my own legitimate son named Tissa was the foremost disciple of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One;
he was an heir to the Victor’s teaching, the Buddha’s teaching.
Regarding the phrase "with his inferior mind": with that inferior, lowly mind of my son Tissa, the foremost disciple.
"With my mind and heart, [thinking it was] unwholesome, unsightly, and improper, I spoke and uttered these words:
'He is the ender, the last one'—this is the meaning. "By the ripening of that kamma" means by the ripening of that unwholesome kamma consisting in the devouring of an arahant.
"In the end I saw the Victor" means in the end, at the conclusion, at the time of his final nibbāna, in the Upavattana of the Mallas.
The meaning is: "I saw our Gotama, the Sammasambuddha, the Victor who has conquered all Māras, reclining on his bed of final Nibbāna in the Sāla grove.

There is also a reading: *pacchā me āsi bhaddakan*. The meaning of that is: "Afterwards—at the end of that Blessed One's life, at the time close to his Nibbāna—there was for me a 'bhaddaka', a beautiful penetration of the Four Noble Truths."

122. “The Great Hero ordained me”: the connection is that the Great Hero—the one of great prowess, devoted to the welfare of all beings, endowed with compassion, the Sage who has conquered Māra—while still lying upon his final bed in the Sāla grove at Upavattana among the Mallans, on the couch of his Parinibbāna, ordained me.
123. “My ordination was this very day”: my ordination was this very day, on the very day of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna;
likewise, my full admission (*upasampadā*) was this very day; and this very day, in the presence of the Supreme among Bipeds, the Parinibbāna took place.
The connection [to the present] is as follows. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Subhadda is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Cunda.
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Cunda Thera, beginning with "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha.

Having accumulated the equipment of merit through deeds of virtue performed under previous Buddhas, and having gathered merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, he was reborn at the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and [offered] a vessel made of the seven precious gems.
Having had a golden casket made and covering it with *sumana* flowers, he honored the Blessed One.
Those flowers rose up into the air and remained there in the form of a canopy. Then the Blessed One prophesied concerning him:
"In the future, in the dispensation of the Blessed One named Gotama, there will be a disciple named Cunda. By that meritorious deed, from that point on...
Having passed away from the deva-world and been reborn there, he experienced happiness in due course among the six classes of sense-sphere devas;

then, having experienced the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such attainments among humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in a brahmin family as the younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta, being the son of Rūpasārī. When he reached the age of discretion, his physical stature, proportions, beauty, and age—
Because of his beauty, they changed the letter *ka* to *ca* and gave him the name Cunda. When he reached maturity,
seeing the disadvantage of the household life and the benefit of the going forth, he went forth in the presence of his elder brother and,
having developed insight, attained Arahantship before long.

125. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahatship, one day he remembered his own past karma and, filled with joy, spoke the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), beginning with the words "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
The meaning of that has already been explained above. The terms *agghiya* and so forth are also of plain meaning. 128.

"The Sambuddha who has transcended doubt" (*vitiṇṇakaṅkho*) means that because doubt (*vicikicchā*) has been exhausted through the specific attainment of the Path, he is one who has transcended doubt.

"He is the Buddha without doubt. "Surrounded by those who have crossed the floods" means that because he has crossed over and transcended the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), he is surrounded and attended by those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) and who have likewise crossed the floods. The verses of explanation are of plain meaning. 139.
"I served the Great Hero" means for the sake of attaining and reaching the supreme goal, Nibbāna, during [the period of] more than one hundred thousand aeons...

The meaning is that because he had performed the exertion of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*) over four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*), he waited upon and served the Great Hero, the Buddha.

Furthermore, "and many other virtuous ones" means that he did not only serve the Buddha, but also many other disciples who were virtuous, of lovely character, endowed with moral discipline, and who had attained the highest excellence; and also my own brother, the Elder Sāriputta.
The connection is "they attend upon. 140.

"Having attended upon my brother" means: having attended upon my brother and performed his duties and services, at the time of his final passing away (parinibbāna), because the Blessed One was the first to pass away after him, they took his relics and placed them in the bowl.
"Having scattered [it], I offered it to the Buddha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men"—this is the meaning. 141.
"Taking it with both hands": the Blessed One, having taken that great relic given by me with both his own hands, clearly displayed that relic while praising the Elder Sāriputta, the chief disciple.
The meaning is "he proclaimed. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Cunda is completed.
The commentary on the fifth chapter is completed.
6. Bījanīvagga 1.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vidhūpanadāyaka "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Vidhūpanadāyaka. This [Elder] also, under previous Victors...

Having fulfilled the equipment of merit and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence in various successive births, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, endowed with great wealth and having conceived faith, he became devoted to the Blessed One.
During the summer season, he had a fan made of gold, silver, pearls, and gems, and [presented it] to the Blessed One.

He gave [it]. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans and having experienced two types of success, he was reborn in a noble family at the time when our Fully Enlightened One appeared.
Having been bound by the fetters of the household life, seeing the danger in domestic existence and seeing the benefit in going forth, being endowed with faith, in the Teaching...
Having gone forth and developed insight, he became an Arahant before long.
Reflecting on his own past karma, wondering, "By what meritorious deed was this supramundane success obtained by me?",
and knowing it through direct realization, he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," while proclaiming the account of his former conduct.
That has the same meaning as explained below. Regarding "a fan was given by me":
it is called a *bījanī* because it extinguishes the heat of beings who are especially tormented and generates a cool breeze; thus, *bījanī* itself is *bījanikā*.
The meaning is: "I had this fan made of the seven precious gems, shining brightly, and gave it."
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vidhūpanadāyaka is completed.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sataraṃsi begins with the verse: “Having climbed the lofty rock...”. This [Elder] also, among the previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, he became proficient in the Sakkaṭa grammar and the three Vedas;
then, abandoning the household life, he entered the forest and went forth as an ascetic, dwelling in the Himalayas.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring solitude, ascended a high mountain and sat down like a blazing flame.
Seeing the Blessed One seated in that manner, the ascetic was filled with joy;

raising his hands in reverent salutation, he praised him with many verses. By virtue of that meritorious deed, when he passed away from there, he was reborn among the devas of the six sense-sphere heavens.
Having experienced divine prosperity, he was subsequently reborn in the human world as a wheel-turning monarch named Sataraṃsi.
Having enjoyed that prosperity many times over, he was now reborn in this present age of a Buddha in a certain noble family.
Due to the ripening of his knowledge through the power of his prior accumulation of merit, he went forth at the age of only seven and attained arahantship.
8–9. Thus, remembering, "By what kamma have I attained the state of peace while still only seven years old?

and seeing his past kamma directly through his knowledge, he became joyful. Reciting his former life's legend (*pubbacaritāpadāna*) by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he spoke the words beginning with "Having climbed the lofty rocky mountain," and so forth.
Therein, "Padumuttara" refers to the Buddha who sat after having ascended the high mountain made of rock.
The connection [of the passage] is as follows: "Not far from the mountain" means in a place near the mountain where the Blessed One was seated.
"A brahmin who has mastered the mantras" means a certain brahmin who has reached the further shore, the end, the limit, of the three Vedas known as mantras;
he identifies himself as it were with another, saying, "I am this one who has mastered the mantras. He had entered.

To the Great Hero, the Victorious One endowed with heroism, seated upon that mountain—how distinguished is he? To the God of Gods, the supreme deity surpassing all the gods of the sense-sphere and the Brahma-world;

to the Bull among Men, the best among men; to the Leader of the World, who guides the entire world of sentient beings and leads them to Nibbāna—I, having raised my hands in the añjali gesture, the hollow of which is formed by the joining of ten fingers, to my head and crown, [pay homage].
"Having established [him], they praised and thoroughly extolled him"—this is the connection. 12. "He spoke":
he prophesied, "By whom this salutation with joined palms was given... [omitted] ...he shall become an Arahant. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sataraṃsi is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sayanadāyaka.
“Of the Buddha Padumuttara,” etc., is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Sayanadāyaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various births the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the cessation of rebirth, [served] Padumuttara...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn in a certain noble family. Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household, he lived in comfort.
Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith in the Teacher and had a costly couch made of ivory, gold, silver, pearls, and gems.
Having spread upon it Chinese silk, woolen blankets, and other fine coverings, he gave it to the Blessed One for his use as a bed. The Blessed One—

Showing him favor, he lay down there. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced corresponding pleasures such as traveling through the air and sleeping in comfort.

Now, during this current appearance of a Buddha, having been reborn into a family endowed with great wealth and having reached the age of discretion, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and became filled with serene faith.
Having gone forth and practicing insight, he became an Arahant before long.

Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth; the meaning of that has already been explained above.

Regarding the phrase "the excellence of seed in a good field": just as seeds sown in a fertile field that is free from weeds and debris and possesses such qualities as being well-watered, [will flourish].

Just as [crops] produce sweet fruits, even so, gifts given in a field of merit consisting of a pure mental continuum—one free from the weeds and refuse of the one thousand five hundred defilements such as lust and hatred—yield great fruit despite being small; this is the meaning.
The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sayanadāyaka is complete.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gandhodakiya begins with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara... This [Elder] was also among the former excellent sages.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences,
he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, seeing the city-dwellers performing worship to the Bodhi tree,
he filled a variegated jar with fragrant water mixed with sandalwood, camphor, aloe-wood, and other scents, and [approached] the Bodhi tree.
He was consecrated. At that moment, the rain-god poured down in great torrents. Then, he passed away by the force of a thunderbolt.
By that very meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods; remaining right there, he uttered the verses beginning with, "Oh, the Buddha!
Oh, the Dhamma! Having thus experienced prosperity among gods and humans, he became entirely free from all feverish distress in every place where he was reborn.
Having attained a state of coolness and being happy, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.

Upon reaching maturity, he placed his faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and by applying himself to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and practicing insight (*vipassanā*), he soon attained *arahantship*.
Because of the merit he had performed in the past, he became renowned as the Elder Gandhodakiya.

25. Thus, one day, having remembered his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "Padumuttarassa," proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
That has already been explained. "The great festival of the Bodhi tree took place" (*mahābodhimaho ahū*) means that there was a worship (*pūjā*) of the Great Bodhi Tree.
"Taking a variegated jar" (*vicittaṃ ghaṭamādāya*) means [a jar] adorned with various works of painting and gold-work.
The meaning is: "having taken a shining jar filled with scented water.
"I gave scented water" (*gandhodakamadāsaṃ*) means "I sprinkled [it] with scented water. 26.
"And at the time of the Bodhi-tree's bathing" means "at the time of performing worship for the Bodhi-tree. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gandhodakīya is complete.
5. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Opavayha begins with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," etc.; this [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth at a time when the Conqueror Padumuttara had appeared in the world.

As he grew up, possessing vast riches and great enjoyments, while living the life of a householder, he became devoted to the Teaching and filled with faith and great reverence for the Teacher; he then made an offering with a noble Sindhu horse.
Having performed the offering, he thought, "Elephants, horses, and the like are not permitted for ascetics such as the Buddhas;

I shall give them allowable articles. Having had that [elephant] appraised, he gave robes made of cotton, wool, and silk, as well as medicinal requisites such as camphor and *takkola*, in exchange for the same value in *kahāpaṇa* coins. By that meritorious deed, for as long as his life lasted...
Having remained there, when he passed away from that state, he was reborn among gods and humans, where he enjoyed happiness endowed with many vehicles such as elephants and horses.
In this present era of a Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn in a certain family home;

upon reaching maturity, being endowed with faith, he went forth into the Dispensation, took up a meditation subject, developed insight, and established himself in Arahatship through the successive stages of the Path.
By virtue of the accumulation of merit performed in the past, he became well known as the Elder Opavayha.
Reflecting, "For what reason have I attained this state of peace?", he directly perceived his former karma through his knowledge.
Filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past deeds by way of an inspired utterance, beginning with the words, "Of the Buddha Padumuttara... and so forth.
That has the meaning already explained. “I gave a noble thoroughbred horse” means that I gave a noble, high-bred Sindhu horse;
the sense is that I honored [him] with it. 35. “One who bears his own equipment” (sapattabhāra): he whose own eight requisites (patta) are his burdens is one who bears his own equipment;

the sense is that he is endowed with the eight requisites. 36. “I gave what is suitable for endurance” (khamanīyam adāsim): the sense is that I gave robes and other allowable requisites appropriate for endurance.
40. "Carima" means the end, the ultimate limit; such is the meaning. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Opavayha is completed.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saparivārāsana.
"Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Āsanatthera together with his retinue.

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a family endowed with great wealth. Upon reaching maturity, he conceived faith and became devoted to the Teaching.
Having faith in the fruit of giving, he offered alms-food to the Blessed One consisting of various kinds of choice delicacies;

and having given it, he adorned the seats in the dining hall where they sat for the meal with jasmine, *jātisumana*, and other flowers. The Blessed One then gave a discourse of thanksgiving (*bhattānumodanā*).
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced manifold [rewards].
Having experienced prosperity, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, being faithful and confident, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an Arahant.
Having thus attained the state of peace, he reflected with knowledge: "By what merit have I reached this state of peace?"

Reflecting upon his past karma and seeing [the results], he was filled with joy; thus, while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth.

That has already been explained in meaning. Regarding the phrase "I gave alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*)," alms-food is so called because it is food to be eaten and consumed by making morsel after morsel of the alms obtained here and there; that alms-food I gave to the Blessed One.
The meaning is: "They fed the Blessed One.
44. "He proclaimed the alms-food" means he explained the virtues and benefits of the alms-food given by me.
48. "Restrained in the Pātimokkha" means restrained, guarded, and shielded by the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.

The meaning is as follows: "And among the five faculties" refers to the five faculties beginning with the eye-faculty; the meaning is that he was protected by the restraint of the faculties regarding forms and so forth, and thus he was protected by the virtue of restraint of the faculties.
The rest is easy to understand. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sāparivārāsana is completed.
7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcadīpaka.
"Of the Buddha Padumuttara," etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pañcadīpaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout his successive births, [served] Padumuttara...

Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he lived as a householder until he reached maturity. Having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, he was established in right view;

being faithful and confident, he saw the great multitude performing worship to the Bodhi tree and, surrounding the Bodhi himself, lit a lamp and made offerings. By that meritorious deed, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.

Wandering through saṃsāra, having experienced the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such blessings, he dwelt in radiant celestial palaces and similar abodes, shining brightly in every birth he took.
Now, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a wealthy and noble family;
upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him, and having gone forth into homelessness, he soon became an arahant as a result of his offering of lamps.
The Elder Dīpaka was well known.
One day, having remembered his own past karma and filled with joy, he spoke the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth.
The meaning of that is exactly as stated. He said, "I was one of upright view," meaning he was free from crooked wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
The meaning is that, having abandoned crookedness for straightness, he attained right view directed toward Nibbāna.

51. Regarding "I gave the gift of lamps": here, a *padīpa* is so called because it shines (*dibbati*) or glows (*jotati*) in various ways (*pakārena*); the giving of that is *padīpadāna*. "I gave that" means I performed the offering of lamps. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pañcadīpaka is completed.
8. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dhajadāyaka.
The passage beginning with “Of the Buddha Padumuttara” refers to the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Dhajadāyaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a prerequisite for the cessation of rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [encountered] Padumuttara...

Having been reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he gained maturity and, having developed faith in the Teacher, had a banner made with many beautiful cloths and performed an offering of that banner.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in high-born families in each successive existence and became worthy of honor. Later, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain noble family.
Having been reborn, he grew up and increased in wealth through his sons and wife; possessing great fortune and renown, he conceived faith and became devoted to the Teacher.
Abandoning the household life, he went forth into homelessness and, before long, became an Arhat.
Having attained the fruit of Arhatship, he recollected his past karma and, filled with joy, [related] his own account of former deeds.
Explaining this, he said: "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth. Its meaning has already been stated previously. "Joyful with a joyful mind" means:
because it is associated with a mind accompanied by gladness (*somanassa*), he is joyful;
his physical form is complete, and because his mind is endowed with faith, it is "joyful"—that is to say, a satisfied mind. "I raised a banner" means: it shakes or trembles.
"It moves," thus it is called a banner (*dhaja*); the meaning is that they honored it by raising that banner and fastening it to the top of a bamboo pole.
58–9. "Having taken the fallen leaves" means having taken the Bodhi-tree leaves that had fallen, [thinking] "I shall discard them outside"—this is the meaning.
"Pure within, pure without" refers to the internal continuum of mind known as the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the external physical body consisting of the eyes, ears, and so forth.

And having especially attained purity, being liberated from the defilements and free from taints (*anāsava*), he bowed down—that is, he performed a prostration—as if in the very presence of the Fully Enlightened One (*Sambuddha*)—to that supreme Awakening;
such is the meaning. The rest is everywhere of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dhajadāyaka is completed.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paduma.
The account of the venerable Elder Paduma begins with the words, "Proclaiming the Four Truths," and so forth.

Having accumulated the requisites for merit through wholesome deeds performed under previous Buddhas, he was reborn in a certain family home while the Sage Padumuttara was illuminating the world with the lamp of the Dhamma.
Having established a household, he became well-known as one endowed with great wealth.

Having gained faith in the Teacher, while listening to the Dhamma together with the great multitude, he stood holding a cluster of lotuses along with his banner. He tossed that cluster of lotuses together with the banner into the air;
seeing that marvel, he was filled with exceeding joy. For as long as he lived, he performed wholesome deeds.

Having done so, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven; prominent like a banner throughout the six sense-sphere realms, honored, and having experienced celestial splendors, and later having experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch among humans, he was now reborn in this present age of a Buddha in a wealthy and faithful family home.
Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him, and at only five years of age he went forth into homelessness, and before long—
Having become an Arahant, he became well known by the name Paduma Thera, a title bestowed because of his merit.
Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (the account of former deeds), he spoke the words beginning with "proclaiming the Four Truths.
In this context, "Truth" (*sacca*) means that which is real, not unreal, and not perverted; it refers to the truths by way of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The four truths combined are the "Four Truths" (*catusacca*); the meaning is that he makes those Four Truths manifest, making them known in the world.
"Proclaimer of the Excellent Dhamma" (*varadhammappavattako*) means the proclaimer who sets forth the supreme Dhamma.

"Raining down the nectar-shower" (*amataṃ vuṭṭhiṃ*) means raining down, pouring forth, the stream of the great nectar of Nibbāna, cooling the world together with its devas and extinguishing the fever of all defilements (*kilesa*).
The meaning is that he rains down the rain of the Dhamma while extinguishing [the fires].
68. “He took the lotus together with its banner” means he took the lotus—the cluster of lotuses—having joined it together with the banner.
“I stood in the middle of the treasury” means I stood having lifted up both [the banner and the lotus]. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Paduma Thera Apadāna* is completed.
10. The commentary on the *Asanabodhiya Thera Apadāna*:
"At seven years of age," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Asanabodhiya Thera. This [Thera] also, among the Buddhas of the past...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Tissa into a certain noble family.
Upon reaching maturity and attaining happiness, he became devoted to the Teaching.
Having taken a fruit from the Asana Bodhi tree and then having taken the young shoots that had emerged from it, he planted the Bodhi tree so that it would not perish.
Likewise, having protected it by performing acts such as sprinkling water, he honored it.
Through that merit, after experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.

Because his requisites were fully matured, even while still only seven years old, he went forth and attained Arahatship at the very moment of shaving his head; he became renowned by the name Asanabodhiya Thera, derived from the merit performed in the past.
78. Thus, having recollected his former provisions and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “When I was seven years of age” while proclaiming the account of his past conduct.
Therein, “jātiyā” means from the time of emerging from the mother’s womb;
“sattavasso” means seven years old, having reached full maturity. The connection is: “I saw the Leader of the World, the Blessed One Tissa.”

"Pasannacitto sumano" means one whose mind is clearly serene, undisturbed, and unshaken; "sumano" means a beautiful mind, a mind accompanied by joy (*somanassa*). 79. Regarding "Tissassāhaṃ bhagavato":
he is called Tissa because he was born three times—from the mother's womb, from the human species, and [from the lineage].
The meaning is: having become liberated from the five aggregates, he was born, produced; "the Buddha was born. The connection is:
"We shall plant the supreme Asana Bodhi for that Blessed One Tissa, the Tādin, the Eldest of the World.
(Verse 80) "By the name 'Asana'" means: by way of designation, by way of the conventional term "name," it is the Asana tree named "Asana" that is the Bodhi.
The meaning is "there was. Regarding the term *dharaṇīruhapādapa*: it is called *dharaṇī* because it supports (*dhāreti*) creepers, trees, mountains, the Ganges, the ocean, and so forth.
What is it? It is the earth (*pathavī*). That which grows and is established upon that [earth] is *dharaṇīruha*. A *pādapa* is so called because it drinks with its feet;
the meaning is that it drinks the water sprinkled by means of what is termed its "feet"—its roots—and thus sustains the moisture of the essence of water. Thus it is *dharaṇīruha*.
"And that tree" means the tree growing from the earth; the meaning is that for five years I served and nourished that supreme *asana* tree, the Bodhi tree.

81. "Having seen the flowering tree": having seen that *asana* Bodhi tree, which I had nourished, flowering—extraordinary because its blossoms were worthy of the *accharās* (divine nymphs) and causing one's hair to stand on end—I was proclaiming my own deed, speaking in detail about my own work.
The meaning is that they went into the presence of the Best of Buddhas. The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Asanabodhiya is completed.
The commentary on the Sixth Chapter is completed.
7. The Chapter on Those Who Contemplate Themselves (Sakacintaniyavagga) 1.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sakacintaniya "Having seen a forest, a grove... and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sakacintaniya. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, at the conclusion of that Blessed One’s lifespan, he failed to reach the Blessed One while he was still living;
however, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he went forth as an ascetic (*isi*).
Dwelling in the Himālayas, he entered a certain delightful forest for seclusion;

there, having fashioned a sand-stūpa (*pulina-cetiya*) at a cave, he made a mental image of the Blessed One and a mental image of his relics, worshipped with forest flowers, and paid homage while serving him.
By that meritorious deed, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he attained the supreme excellence among the two highest [classes].
Having experienced the supreme fortune of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), he was reborn in a certain noble family during this current arising of a Buddha.
Endowed with great wealth and endowed with faith, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and became an *arahant* possessing the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former deeds while in the forest.
He said, "Having seen a forest," and so forth. Therein, *pavana* means a forest that is spread out, extensive, and dense in its growth.

*Kānana* means a place where the face (*ānana*)—that is, the opening—is undesirable (*avakuccha*), or where there is constant carrying away (*avahana*) by lions, tigers, yakṣas, rākṣasas, elephants, horses, birds, and serpents;
or it is called *kānana* because it is thick with the sounds of flocks of birds, cocks, and cuckoos. That forest, designated as *kānana*, is what is meant by *pavana*.
"Free from noise" means being devoid of the sounds of humans; the sense is that it is quiet and silent. "Untroubled" means not turbid, that is, free from calamities.
"Practiced by the seers" means practiced and cultivated by the seers (isī), namely those comprised of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Arahants, and those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsavas).
"Receptacle for offerings" means it is the recipient of what is called an "offering" (āhuna), which is to say, worship and honor.
"Like a house" is the meaning. 2.
"Having made a stupa with bamboo" means having constructed a cetiya with bamboo slips.
"Scattering various flowers" means I scattered and worshipped with many flowers such as the *campaka* and others. "As if in the presence of the Sambuddha."

The meaning is: "I paid special homage—that is, I performed a prostration—to the monument (cetiya) that was manifested and produced as if in the very presence of the Fully Enlightened One while he was still living. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sakacintaniya is completed.
2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Avopupphiya.
"Having gone forth from the monastery," etc., is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Avopupphiya.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation, [encountered] the Blessed One Sikhī.
Reborn at the proper time in a noble family, having reached maturity and being endowed with faith, he heard the Dhamma and was filled with joy.
Taking various flowers in both hands, he scattered them over the Buddha.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced the excellence of the celestial worlds as well as the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, everywhere.
Having been honored during this appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain noble family.

Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teaching (*sāsana*), went forth, and before long became an *arahant*. He is known as the Elder Avopupphiya because he was strewn with flowers (*avakiritattā*) in that space (*ākāsa*); for "space" (*ākāsa*) is so called because it shines and radiates (*kāsati*) on all sides (*samantato*).

7. Thus, having attained a state of peace and remembering his own former karma, he became filled with joy. Recalling the account of his past conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the words beginning with "Having gone forth from the monastery" (*vihārā abhinikkhamma*).

In this context, a "monastery" (*vihāra*) is so called because it specifically carries (*harati*) and brings about (*āharati*) the continuity of one's personal existence (*attabhāva*)—which does not fall away—by means of the four postures; it is where this occurs. Therefore, "from the monastery" (*vihārā*) means specifically from that place.
"Having gone out, having gone out. He rose up and walked the walking-path;
he especially rose up for the purpose of walking, meaning he ascended it. "Proclaiming the Four Truths":
while walking on that walking-path, proclaiming—that is, making manifest—the Four Truths known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, [he proclaimed] the Deathless.
The connection is that he walks back and forth while teaching, analyzing, and clarifying the state of *nibbāna*. 8.
"Having understood the speech of Sikhin, the Best of Buddhas, the Tathāgata":

having understood—that is, having known—the voice, the sound, and the utterance of Sikhin, the Buddha who is the Best and who possesses the qualities of a Tathāgata. "Having taken various flowers": [having taken] many [flowers], such as the *nāga*, *punnāga*, and others.
Having taken flowers and brought them, "I scattered them in the air" means that as the Blessed One was walking back and forth, I scattered them in the sky above his head and paid him homage. 9.
By that kamma, "O Lord of bipeds"—the chief among bipeds, namely gods, brahmās, and humans—"O Bull among men."
"Become a leader among men": Having gone forth in your presence, I have attained the immovable state;
I have reached Nibbāna, the unshakable state. "Having abandoned victory and defeat":
having cast aside both victory, consisting of celestial and human prosperity, and defeat, consisting of the suffering of the four lower realms, I have attained Nibbāna.
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Avopupphiya is completed. 3.
Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Paccāgamaniya.
This is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Paccāgamaniya Thera, beginning with the words "On the bank of the river Sindhū.
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated, throughout various existences, the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*),
he was reborn at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī in the womb of a ruddy goose (*cakkavāka*) near the river Gaṅgā, due to his prior accumulation of requisites.
The peacock was wandering about, not eating any living creatures but subsisting solely on algae. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassi, seeking to bring benefit to sentient beings, went there.
At that moment, the cakravāka bird, seeing the radiant Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, plucked a *sāla* flower from a *sāla* tree with his beak and approached to offer it. By that very act...

Through his clarity of mind, he passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the gods; after experiencing successive attainments among the six classes of sense-sphere deities, he passed away from there and was reborn in the human world.
Having experienced the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such blessings, he was born into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher by virtue of his past conduct and went forth into homelessness.

Before long, he became an *arahant*. Having been a cakravāka bird, he saw the Blessed One, went somewhere to fetch flowers, and because he had offered them in worship, he became renowned as the "Thera of the Return through Former Merit" (*paccāgamaniya-thera*).
Recalling his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds) at Sindhuyā.
He said, "On the bank of the river," and so forth. It is called *sindhu* because it makes the sound *sī* while shaking and trembling; it is called *nadī* because it goes making the sound *nada*.

As for the *cakkavāka*, he said, "I was that [bird] at that time": it is called *cakkavāka* because it moves swiftly like a wheel (*cakkam*) whether in water, on land, or in the air, flying with great speed. At that time, [he saw] the Blessed One Vipassī.
The meaning is: "At the time of seeing [the Buddha], I was a cakravāka crane.

"I dwell eating pure moss" means that because it is unmixed with other types of food, I live consuming only pure moss. "And well-restrained among the wicked" means that, by virtue of former habitual tendencies (*pūrvavāsanā*), one is thoroughly restrained in committing evil;
being restrained through the three doors, one is well-trained.
