14. "I saw the stainless Buddha"—because he was free from lust, hatred, and delusion, I saw and beheld the stainless, undefiled Buddha.
"Going through the wind-swept path"—I saw the Buddha traveling through the wind-swept path, the path of the sky.
"With my beak"—having grasped and taken up a *tāla* flower and a *sāla* blossom with my own mouth-beak, I offered them to Vipassi.
The meaning is: "They made an offering to the Blessed One Vipassī. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Paccāgamaniya is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Parappasādaka.
The legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Parappasādaka Thera begins with the words: "Usabhaṃ pavaraṃ vīraṃ...

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha into a brahmin family as one who had mastered the three Vedas along with Itihāsa as the fifth, and was a scholar of the *pada*.
A master of exegesis, well-versed in the *Nighaṇṭu* and *Keṭubha* lexicons along with the analysis of phonemes, and unerring in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man—
known by the name of the Brahmin Sela— he beheld the Blessed One Siddhattha, who was himself resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics;
seeing him thus, with a mind full of faith, he [spoke] for many reasons and in many ways.

He proclaimed praise through similes. By that meritorious deed, having experienced the six celestial attainments of the sense-sphere—beginning with Sakka and Māra—in the world of the gods, and having experienced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch among humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth.

Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth; not long thereafter, Please note: The provided text ends abruptly, so the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.
Having attained the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he became one whose taints were utterly destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Because he inspired faith in the minds of all beings by praising the Buddha, he became renowned as the Elder Parappasādaka.
One day, recollecting his own past deeds, he was filled with joy and proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct).
He spoke these words beginning with "the bull, the preeminent hero. In that context, "bull" (*usabha*) refers to four types of preeminent leaders: *vasabha*, *nisabha*, *visabha*, and *āsabha*.
Among them, the leader of a hundred cows is a *vasabha*; the leader of a thousand cows is a *nisabha*; the leader of a hundred thousand cows is a *visabha*;
and the leader of ten million cows is an *āsabha*. This applies to anyone whatsoever.
When learned brahmins who are well-versed in the scriptures offer praise, they do so according to their own individual wisdom;
yet there is not even one person capable of praising the Buddhas in every respect. For the Buddha is immeasurable. Indeed, it has been said:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha for an entire eon, without speaking of anything else...”
“An eon might pass away in the course of its vast duration, but the praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted”—this is the beginning [of the verse].
This brahmin, because it had ascended to his lips and because of his singular confidence, said “usabha” and so forth when he ought to have said “āsabha.
It is called a *vara* because it is to be chosen or desired. He is a *vīra* (hero) because of the exertion he performed over many hundreds of thousands of eons. Great...
One who seeks and searches for the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and the rest is a great seer (*mahesi*); [I salute] that Buddha, the great seer.
One who has specifically conquered Māra—the aggregates, the defilements, and so forth—is a victor (*vijitāvī*); [I salute] that perfectly enlightened one (*sambuddha*), the victor.

That perfectly enlightened one whose complexion is like the color of gold is "golden-hued" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇa*); having seen that golden-hued perfectly enlightened one, what being indeed would not be filled with confidence?
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Parappasādaka is completed. 5.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhisadāyaka begins with the words "Vessabhū by name... This [Elder] also, among the previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in the Himālayas during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū and lived there as an elephant.
At that time, the Blessed One Vessabhū, desiring solitude, went to the Himālayas. Upon seeing him, that noble elephant felt a mind of serene faith.
Having taken lotus roots and stalks, he fed the Blessed One. By that meritorious deed, when he passed away from his birth as an elephant, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

having experienced the six kinds of excellence in the sense-sphere heavens there, he returned to the human state and, among humans, experienced the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such blessings.
Now, during this current appearance of a Buddha, [he was born] into a family of great wealth...
Born into a noble family, he gained faith in the Teacher through the power of his past impressions (*pubbavāsanā*) and, having gone forth, became an *arahant* before long.
He became well known as the Elder Bhisadāyaka, named after the wholesome deed he had performed in the past.
Recalling his own former karma and wishing to display the account of his previous conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Vessabhū by name."
In this regard, he is called Vessabhū because he "consumes" (bhunāti) or transcends the merchant class (vessa).

Alternatively, he is called Vessabhū because he consumes—that is, overcomes—the merchant's craft, sensual lust and the like, wholesome deeds and the like, or the objects of desire and the defilements of desire.
Thus, the Blessed One was by name Vessabhū. He was the third among the seers (isī), for he sought after wholesome states.
“He seeks,” thus he is a seer (*isi*); because [the previous Buddhas] were called “Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū,” this third seer was the third Blessed One—this is the meaning.
“Having plunged into the forest grove” means having entered, having gone down into the grove known as a forest;

this is the meaning. “Having taken the lotus root and stalk”: it is called a *bhisa* because it devours, injures, or destroys the hunger of bipeds and quadrupeds; what is it? It is the lotus bulb (*padumakanda*). The *bhisa* and the stalk (*muḷāla*) together are the “lotus root and stalk”; the meaning is, “having taken that lotus root and stalk.”
31. "And because it was touched by the hand, Vessabhū, the supreme Buddha, the one of highest intelligence, said:
'That gift given by me was touched and made contact with by the palm of the hand of Vessabhū, the supreme Buddha.
I do not know of any happiness equal to that; from what could there be anything superior? By that happiness, I do not know of any happiness equal to it, nor anything superior to it."
The meaning is: "Where else could there be a happiness greater than that? The remainder is easily understood by following the same method.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhisadāyaka is complete.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sucintita.
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Thera Sucintita, beginning with the words "He dwelt in mountain fastnesses. This [Thera] also,
having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences,
was born during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi in a hunter's family in the Himalayan region, where he lived by killing and eating deer, pigs, and other such animals.
He was dwelling there. Then the Lord of the World, out of compassion for beings and for the welfare of the world, went to the Himalayas.
There, upon seeing the Blessed One, the hunter’s heart was filled with faith, and he gave him the choice, sweet meat he had brought for his own consumption.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted it; having eaten it and delivered a blessing, he departed.
Thus, through that very merit and that very joy, when he passed away from there and wandered through happy destinies, he experienced the six types of prosperity in the sense-sphere realms;
having experienced the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such states among humans, he was reborn in a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and, before long, became an arahant.

36. Having attained the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*), the five superknowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*), and other such qualities, and having recollected his own past karma, he became filled with joy.

Recounting the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke these words beginning with "I was one who dwelt in mountain fastnesses" (*giriduggacaro āsiṃ*). That which makes sound is called *giri*. What is it? It is a mountain consisting of rock and dust.
That which is difficult to traverse because of hardship is *dugga*. Thus, [the compound] is *giridugga* (a mountain fastness).
*Giriduggaṃ* means a difficult mountain pass; in that mountain pass, among the mountain ranges, I was one who roamed, having the habit of wandering. *Abhijātova kesarī*:
like a lion born with a mane—meaning, being especially (*abhi*) born or produced (*jāta*), like a maned lion (*kesarī*), I roam in the mountain pass.

40. *Giriduggaṃ pavisiṃ ahan ti*: "I entered the mountain pass"—at that time, having become filled with joy and gladness due to that gift of meat, I entered the mountain range. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sucintita is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vatthadāyaka begins with the verse:
"Then I was born as a bird... This [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various states of existence, he was reborn in the womb of a supaṇṇa during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
Seeing the Blessed One Atthadassi traveling toward Mount Gandhamādana, his mind became filled with serene faith; abandoning his supaṇṇa form, he manifested the appearance of a young brahmin.
Taking a costly divine garment, he honored the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having accepted it and delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, departed.
He spent his time in that very joy; having lived out his lifespan, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas.
Wandering from one state to another there, and having experienced the fruits of his merit, he subsequently attained the excellence of human birth among men.
In all his births, he obtained costly garments and ornaments; wherever he went, he dwelt in the shadow of those garments.
In this present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn into a certain noble family, and upon reaching maturity, having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth into homelessness.
Not long thereafter, he attained the six supernormal powers and became one whose taints were exhausted. Previously—
He who was known by the name Katapuñña became famous as the Elder Vatthadāyaka.

Recalling his own past deeds, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), spoke the verse beginning, "At that time I was born as a bird," and so forth.
In this context, "born as a bird" (*pakkhijāto*) refers to a winged creature; it is called a "wing" (*pakkha*) because by means of it one leaps (*pakkhandati*) or flies (*upalavati*).
One who has wings (*pakkha*) is a *pakkhī*; the meaning is that he was born and produced within the womb of winged beings.
A *supaṇṇa* is one whose wing (*paṇṇa*) or feather is beautiful; the meaning is that he possesses the great burden of wings that are golden-hued, catching the wind, and blazing with light.
They are called *garuḷas* because they swallow heavy burdens, such as rocks, for the purpose of seizing *nāgas*. Of these *garuḷas*...
"Adhipo rājā" means the Lord of Garuḍas; "he saw the stainless Buddha" is the connection [of the sentence].
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vatthadāyaka is complete.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ambadāyaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Ambadāyaka Thera begins with "Anomadassī, the Blessed One," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī in the womb of a monkey; he lived as a king of monkeys in the Himālaya mountains. In that...
At that time, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One Anomadassi went to the Himalayas.
Then that king of monkeys, seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, offered him a very sweet mango fruit and some small honey.
Then the Blessed One, while he was looking on, consumed it all and, having uttered words of thanksgiving, departed. Thereupon, his heart filled with joy, he—
By means of that very joy and gladness, he remained for the duration of his lifespan; passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Having experienced celestial bliss there again and again, and having experienced human prosperity among men, he was now reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a family endowed with great wealth.
Having gained faith in the Teacher and gone forth into homelessness, before long—
He attained the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). He became well known as the Elder Ambadāyaka by virtue of his past merit.
Later on, seeing the seeds of wholesome karma he himself had sown, he was filled with joy;

and proclaiming the account of his own former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "The Blessed One Anomadassī... [and continued]: "He pervaded the world with loving-kindness, immeasurable and free from attachment."

The Blessed One, by means of the words beginning with "May all beings in the entire world be happy," suffused, extended, and increased his mind of loving-kindness—making them free from acquisitions (*an-upadhi*) and devoid of acquisitions (*upadhivirahita*)—toward immeasurable beings; this is the meaning. 54.
"I was a monkey then" means that at the time of her arrival, he was a king of monkeys; this is the meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ambadāyaka is completed. 9.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sumanas begins with the words, "He who was named Sumanas," and so forth. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi in a family of garland-makers.

Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him; with a mind full of serene confidence toward the Blessed One, he took handfuls of *sumana* flower garlands and offered them with both hands. By that merit, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Having experienced two perfections, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a certain family home.
Having grown up and increased with a wife and children, he became well-known by the name Sumanā. Having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an Arahant.
Having become an Arahant, he recollected his own past karma and, filled with joy, [related] his own account of former deeds.
Explaining this, he said, "Named Sumana," and so forth. He whose mind (*mano*) or consciousness (*citta*) is beautiful (*sundara*) is "Sumana.
Endowed with faith, serenity, and great respect, I was at that time a garland-maker named Sumana by name.

63. Regarding "Sikhin, the Kinsman of the World": he who shines (*kāseti*) from the crest (*sikhā*) or the head (*muddhā*) is "Sikhin. Alternatively, [it refers to] the association of associated states (*sampayutta-sampayoga*).
He consumes and destroys, thus he is "Sikhī" (the Flame-possessor). What is that? It is the flame of fire. He is called Sikhī because he is illuminated by a crest (sikhā) like a flame of fire.

Just as a flame of fire shines and becomes manifest, and just as the flame burns grass, wood, foliage, and so forth, even so this Blessed One shines with rays of blue, yellow, and other colors, becoming manifest throughout the entire world-system. [He burns] all the defilements existing within his own continuum...
"Soseti" (cools), "viddhaṃseti" (destroys), and "jhāpeti" (burns away) are the conventional names, the designation, and the appellation of that Sikhin.
"Lokabandhu" means a kinsman and relative to the entire world; thus, it refers to the Blessed One Sikhin, the Friend of the World. The meaning is: "I offered and worshipped a *sumana* flower to him.
The commentary on the *Sumanatthera-apadāna* is completed.
10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pupphacaṅkoṭiya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pupphacaṅkoṭiya begins with the verse: "Like a fearless lion...
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Sikhī...
At one time, having been reborn in a noble family and attained maturity, he was endowed with great wealth.
Having gained confidence in the Teacher and wishing to demonstrate his faith, he plucked an *anoja* flower of golden hue, filled a casket with them, and offered them to the Blessed One.
He made this aspiration: "Blessed One, by the result of this deed, may I be of golden complexion and worthy of veneration in every place where I am reborn."
Having made an offering, he formed the aspiration: "May I attain Nibbāna. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among gods and humans;
everywhere he was honored, possessing a golden complexion and being handsome. Later, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn in a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained confidence in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness. Having developed insight, [he attained the goal].
Before long, he became an Arahant.

Having attained the fruit of Arahantship and recollecting his own past karma, he was filled with joy; proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he spoke the verse beginning with "Like a fearless lion," and so forth.
In this context, "lion" refers to beings such as those with two feet or four feet.
"He overcomes and overwhelms," thus he is a lion (*sīha*); one who is fearless in form and fearless in nature. The connection is:
"They pay homage to him who sits like that fearless lion. Like the foremost of birds, the king of *garuḷas*;
like the preeminent and supreme king of tigers; and like the maned lion, the distinction among all lions, who has arisen with excellence for the three worlds.

I take refuge in Sikhi, the Perfectly Enlightened One. What is he like? The connection is as follows: he is the "Immovable One" (*aneja*), free from defilements (*nikkilesa*), unconquered by the Māras of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*) and the rest, and seated as the "Crested One" (*Sikhi*). Regarding the phrase "the supreme slayer of Māra":

he is the foremost and best among all things for the slaying, withering, and destruction of all defilements; even though there exist Paccekabuddhas and disciples of the Buddha who also slay the defilements, he is superior to them.
"Supreme" (*agga*) is the meaning. The connection is: "surrounded by and seated before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. 70.
"Having placed it in a casket" (*caṅkoṭake ṭhapetvāna*): having filled a basket with the finest *anoja* flowers, I honored the most excellent Sambuddha Sikhī; this is the meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pupphacaṅkoṭiya is completed.
The commentary on the Seventh Chapter is completed.
8. The Chapter of Nāgasamāla. 1.
Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nāgasamāla.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Nāgasamāla Thera, beginning with "I [offered] a flowering *āpāṭali* tree," is as follows:

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household life, through association with such virtuous persons...
Having failed to perform acts of seeing, hearing, or making offerings to the Teacher while he was still living,
one may— after the Blessed One has attained final nibbāna— deposit his bodily relics, inspire confidence of mind toward the stupa built over them,
offer a *pāṭala* flower, and give rise to joy; then, having lived out their full lifespan, by virtue of that very joy, they pass away from there and are reborn among the Tusita devas and others.
Having experienced happiness in the six celestial realms and subsequently having enjoyed human prosperity among men, he was reborn into a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, because his body was as delicate as the young shoots of a *nāga* tree, his parents gave him the name Nāgasamāla.
Having gained faith in the Blessed One and gone forth into homelessness, he became an Arhat before long.
1. Thus, having later recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "I took a *āpāṭali* flower" while proclaiming the account of his former conduct.
Therein, "*Āpāṭali*" means that I took a *pāṭali* flower from all sides (*ā*) or with care (*ādarena*), and offered it as worship upon the stupa (*thūpa*).
"*Ujjhitaṃ sumahāpathe*" means [the flower] discarded on the great highway by all the city-dwellers.
It was erected on the main road in the middle of the city, in a street, for the purpose of paying homage and making offerings;
the meaning is that it was constructed with brickwork, plasterwork, and so forth. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method explained below and its meaning is plain.
The commentary on the *Nāgasamāla* Thera’s Apadāna is completed.
2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Padasaññaka.
"Having seen the footprint that had been stepped upon," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Padasaññaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in each successive birth, [served] the Blessed One Tissa...
Born at one time into the home of a lay follower endowed with faith, he reached maturity and became devoted to the Triple Gem.

Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One showed him a footprint shrine (*padacetiya*); seeing it, he was filled with serene joy, his hair stood on end, and he offered great reverence through acts such as prostration and worship.
By that very merit well-performed in that fertile field, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the heavenly realms, where he experienced celestial bliss.
In a later time, having been born among humans and experienced all the perfections of human life, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, he conceived faith, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arahant.
He became renowned by the name Padasaññaka Thera, owing to the merit performed in his previous lives.
5. Thus, one day, remembering his own former karma and proclaiming the account of his past conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with "And having seen the footprint that was stepped upon.

Therein, "stepped upon" means trodden or shown. While the gait of all Buddhas is always at a height of four finger-breadths above the ground, this [being], knowing his perfection of faith, thought, "Let him see this," and [thus acted].
He showed him the footprint-cetiya; therefore, having gained confidence in it, he performed acts of honor such as salutation and worship—this is the meaning.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the legend of the Elder known as Padasaññaka is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Buddhasaññaka.
The passage beginning with "A wearer of rag-robes at the crossroads" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Buddhasaññaka.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [encountered] the Blessed One Tissa...
Born at one time into a noble family, having reached maturity and developed faith, he saw the Blessed One’s rag-robe (paṃsukūlacīvara) hanging on a tree.
With a devout mind, thinking, “This is the banner of the Arahants,” he paid homage and performed acts of worship such as offerings.
Through that meritorious deed, after experiencing the prosperity of gods and humans, during this present appearance of a Buddha, he was born into a family endowed with great wealth.
Having been reborn in a certain noble family, he was born with faith; having gone forth, before long he became an Arahant.

Having attained the realization of Arahantship, he remembered his own past karma and, filled with joy, proclaimed the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "A wearer of rag-robes on a difficult path.
In this context, that which shakes or trembles is called a *duma* (tree). It also means to suck or to fill.
Or, "dumagga" means the top of a tree; "dumagge" means on that tree-top. It is called *paṃsukūla* because it goes toward (*ulati*) a state of repulsiveness and unpleasantness like dust (*paṃsu*).
That which is made of *paṃsukūla* is *paṃsukūlika*.
Having seen the Teacher’s rag-robe caught on the tree-top, I raised my hands in reverential salutation and paid homage to that *paṃsukūla*.
The meaning is "he made a prostration. *Taṃ* is merely a particle. The remainder is entirely obvious in meaning everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Buddhasaññaka is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhisāluvadāyaka.
"Having seized the forest grove... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Thera Bhisāluvadāyaka.

This [Thera] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was dwelling in a forest retreat near the Himalayas during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, subsisting on forest roots and fruits, and having attained [insight] through seclusion (*viveka*).
Having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a mind full of serene confidence, he gave him five *sāluka* roots.

The Blessed One, in order to gladden his heart, consumed them while the man was still looking on. Through that mental serenity, after passing away, he experienced prosperity among the Tusita devas and other realms;
subsequently, having experienced human prosperity, during this current appearance of a Buddha, in one [place]...
Having been reborn in a noble family and attained great wealth, he renounced it all, went forth in the Dispensation, and before long reached Arahantship.
Recalling his own past deeds from that point on, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the verse beginning, “I entered the forest and the woods.
The meaning of this has already been explained above. “I dwell in the wilderness” refers to his life of seclusion.
The connection is "I dwell [there]. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhisāluvadāyaka is completed.
The commentary on the sixth section (*bhāṇavāra*) is finished.
5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekasaññaka.
"Khaṇḍa was his name... and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ekasaññaka.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Vipassi...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, he developed a mind of faith toward the Triple Gem.
Seeing that Teacher’s chief disciple named Khaṇḍa wandering for alms, he gave him an offering of food out of faith.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, after experiencing the prosperity of gods and humans, he was born in Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Reborn in a certain noble family, he reached the age of discretion and, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith.

Having gone forth, before long he became an Arahant. One day, because he applied his mind to the perception of alms-food and attained a distinguished distinction therein, he became renowned as the Elder Ekasaññaka (the One-Perception).
18. Later on, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "He was known by the name Khaṇḍa.
In this context, that chief disciple Thera was named Khaṇḍa because his defilements (kilesas) had been cut away (khaṇḍita).
The rest is self-evident throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekasaññaka is completed.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Tiṇasantharadāyaka begins with the verse "Not far from the Himalayas... This too...

Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Because this had arisen even before the appearance of that Buddha, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest ascetic; dwelling near a lake not far from the Himalayas, he...
He was dwelling there. At that time, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One traveled through the air.

Then that ascetic, seeing the Blessed One standing after having descended from the sky, with a mind full of faith, gathered grass, prepared a grass mat, and having seated [the Blessed One], he paid homage with great reverence and respect by prostrating himself on his five limbs, then sat down to one side.

Having made the offering, he departed. He remained for the duration of his lifespan, and after passing away from there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing manifold prosperity, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth;
not long thereafter, he became an arahant.

22. Later on, having remembered his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of past conduct), spoke the verse beginning with "Not far from the Himālayas," and so forth. The meaning of that has already been explained above. Regarding the phrase *mahājātassaro*:
here, "lake" (*saraṃ*) means that bipeds, quadrupeds, and other beings who desire water resort (*saranti*) to it; or alternatively, they resort to it...
“Rivers, caves, and so forth” refers to a lake (*sara*); and because it is great and has arisen by itself, it is a “great self-arisen lake” (*mahājātassara*).
It should be understood that it is called a “great self-arisen lake” because its name is not well-known, unlike the Anotatta or Chaddanta lakes.

“Covered with hundred-petalled [lotuses]” means that each individual flower possesses a hundred petals, thus it is a “hundred-petalled” one; [it is covered] with white hundred-petalled lotuses (*satapatta-setapaduma*).

"Covered and become dense" is the meaning. "A haunt for various birds" means it is a haunt—that is, the dwelling place—of birds known as *sakuṇa* because many kinds of birds, such as swans, wild fowl, *kukkuha*, and *deṇḍibha*, together utter sounds.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tiṇasaṇṭharadāyaka is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sūcidāyaka begins with the verse: "In thirty thousand aeons... This [Elder] also, under previous Victorious Ones...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
Upon reaching maturity, he offered five needles to perform the Blessed One’s robe-work (*cīvarakamma*).
Having experienced the fruits of that merit among gods and humans, and wandering through successive births as they arose...
Having become one of sharp wisdom, he was reborn in a certain family home during this appearance of a Buddha.
As he grew up, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness; due to his sharp wisdom, he attained *arahantship* at the very edge of the razor-sharp blade [of the shaving stage].

Later, reflecting upon his merit and seeing it, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the verse beginning with "In thirty thousand kappas... The intermediate portions here are indeed easy to understand.

31. Regarding the phrase "Five needles were given by me": here, *sūci* means that which pierces, makes a hole, or pricks; thus, "five needles" (*pañcasūcī*) means five in number of needles. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sūcidāyaka is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pāṭalipupphiya.
"Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Pāṭalipupphiya.

This [eulogy] concerns one who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and, accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Tissa as the son of a merchant in a certain noble family; and having reached maturity...
Knowing what is wholesome and unwholesome, he gained confidence in the Teacher, took a *pāṭali* flower, and offered it to the Teacher.
Through that merit, experiencing manifold success and happiness as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an *arahant*.

36. Thus, at a later time, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words, "The Golden-Colored Sambuddha.

In this context, "in the marketplace" (*antarāpaṇe*): it is called a *āpaṇa* because they trade, sell, and display goods such as gold and silver on all sides (*ā*) there; the space within that marketplace is the street, hence it is called *antarāpaṇa*.
In that marketplace, having seen the Fully Enlightened One—who was golden-hued, resembling refined gold, and possessed of the thirty-two marks of excellence—he offered a *pāṭali* flower;
this is the meaning. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pāṭalipupphiya is finished.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ṭhitañjaliya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ṭhitañjaliya begins with the words, "In former times he was a deer-hunter...
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various successive births, [reached the presence] of Tissa...
In the time of the Blessed One, due to a certain faulty deed committed in the past, he was reborn in the womb of a hunter;
having reached maturity, he lived in the forest, making his living by killing deer, pigs, and other animals through his work as a hunter.

At that time, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One went to the Himālaya mountains. He [the Blessed One] was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and a fathom-wide aura of radiance.
Seeing the Blessed One measuring out the water, he was filled with joy; having paid homage, he went and sat down on a bed of leaves.
At that moment, the sky thundered and lightning struck. Then, recollecting the Buddha at the time of death, he again joined his palms in reverence.
By that merit—having performed wholesome deeds in a fertile field—he warded off the ripening of unwholesome karma and was reborn in heaven.

Having experienced the prosperities of the sense-sphere realms and, subsequently, having experienced the human prosperities among men, he was later reborn in a certain family home during this arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, through his former latent tendencies, he gained confidence in the Teacher and went forth;
not long thereafter, he became an Arahant.

42. Thereafter, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "In former times I was a deer-hunter," while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of past conduct).
In this context, "deer-hunter" (*migaluddo*) means one who approaches (*upagacchati*) for the purpose of killing deer (*miga*).
They are called "deer" (*miga*) because they go swiftly, running with the force of the wind; he is a hunter (*luddo*), meaning cruel (*dāruṇo*), toward those deer.
"Lobhī" means a deer-hunter. "In former times, at the time of seeing the Blessed One, I was a deer-hunter"—this is the meaning.
Regarding "araññe kānane": it is called *arañña* because a multitude of deer (*arati*) goes there;

or alternatively, it is called *arañña* because noble persons (*sappurisa*) who have attained great essence—such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others—who delight in seclusion, are "attached" (*rajjanti*) to it on all sides (*ā*).
*Kānanaṃ* means that which cries out (*nadanti*) with a wretched sound or a terrifying sound, or that which finds (*vindanti*) joy (*āna*);
thus it is a forest. The connection is: "In that forest, in that *kānana*, I was formerly a deer-hunter.

Regarding the phrase "there I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*addasaṃ sambuddhaṃ*): the meaning is that there, in that forest, I saw (*addakkhim*), I beheld, the Perfectly Enlightened One who had arrived.

The vision occurred previously and not far away; therefore, by following the door of the mind, the eye-consciousness precedes and brings about the attainment of the body-consciousness—this is the meaning.

44. "Then there was a thunderbolt-fall for me": it thunders and roars all around (*ā*), thus it is a *asanī*; the falling of the thunderbolt is a *asanīpāta*, meaning a divine punishment. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ṭhitañjaliyati is completed. 10.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tipadumiya begins with the words, "The Victor named Padumuttara," etc. This [Elder] also, among the previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of garland-makers. Upon reaching maturity,
while living and performing the work of a garland-maker, one day he took many kinds of flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial, and went into the presence of the king.

Desiring to go, he thought thus: “If the king, upon seeing these flowers, were to become pleased and give me a thousand pieces of wealth or a village and such, yet by worshipping the Lord of the World I obtain the deathless treasure of Nibbāna—what is the use of these to me?
Therefore, [he resolved]: “It is fitting to worship the Blessed One in order to bring about the attainments of heaven and liberation.”
Having reflected thus, he took exceedingly beautiful red flowers and offered them in worship. Those flowers went and stood covering and overspreading the sky.
The city-dwellers, filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, raised thousands of hand-claps.
Seeing this, the Blessed One gave a blessing of thanksgiving. Through that merit, having experienced prosperity among gods and humans, he...
Born into a householder’s family during this appearance of a Buddha, he grew up and, having gained confidence in the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, acquired faith.
He went forth into homelessness and, before long, became an Arahant.
Recalling his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), spoke of Padumuttara.
He spoke the words beginning with "The Victor" (*jina*). Its meaning has already been explained above.

"One who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānaṃ pāragū*) means one who has reached and realized through direct experience the further shore of all nine supramundane phenomena, which is Nibbāna.

"Tamed, surrounded by the tamed" means that he himself is tamed in body, speech, and so forth, and is surrounded by disciples established in the foremost ranks. The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere by virtue of the context.
The commentary on the *Tipadumiya Thera Apadāna* is completed.
The commentary on the eighth chapter is completed.
9. The Chapter on Timira.
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Timirapupphiya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Timirapupphiya begins with the words "On the bank of the river Candabhāgā. What is its origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various births the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the turning away from saṃsāra (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn in a certain noble family. Upon reaching maturity, he established a household and lived there;
however, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the life of a householder and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic.
He lived near the Candabhāgā River, but out of a desire for solitude, he went to the Himālaya mountains and sat down beside Siddhattha.
Having seen the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and gained confidence in his virtues, he took a *timira* flower and offered it as worship.
By that merit, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, he wandered through the cycle of existence until this arising of a Buddha, when he was reborn in a certain family home.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an *arahant*.
1. Later on, having remembered his former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "On the bank of the river Candabhāgā," while proclaiming the account of his past conduct.

The meaning of this has already been explained above. Regarding the phrase "Let us go to Vajā": because of dwelling near the Ganges and because of its delightful nature everywhere, I go—that is, I travel—along the course of the stream below the Ganges, dwelling here and there.
The meaning is as follows: "Having seen the ascetic seated" means having seen the Fully Enlightened One, who is designated an "ascetic" (samaṇa) because he has stilled evil and dried up evil.

2. "Thus I thought at that time": this Blessed One has himself crossed over and will cause all beings to cross; he delivers them from saṃsāra. This Blessed One, himself tamed through the doors of body and so forth, tames others. 3.
"Himself comforted, having attained comfort"—freed from the fever of the defilements, he comforts all beings, [establishing them] in a state of peace.

He causes others to attain it. Being himself peaceful, with a body and mind that are peaceful, he causes the bodies and minds of others to attain peace. Being himself liberated, having been released from saṃsāra, he will liberate others from saṃsāra.
"This Blessed One, being himself extinguished—extinguished by the fires of the defilements—will cause others also to be extinguished by the fires of the defilements";
this is the meaning of what I thought at that time.

4. Having taken that which, by its dark blue rays, makes the entire forest expanse appear as if it were darkness—like the *timira* flower—and having grasped its pericarp and stalk, I scattered it in the sky above my head;
the meaning is that I offered it in worship. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Timirapupphiya is completed.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Gatasaññaka begins with the verse: "When I was seven years of age... This [Elder] also, during previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Through the influence of past latent tendencies, faith arose within him;
he went forth even at the age of seven and became well-known simply by paying homage to the Blessed One. One day, [he saw] exceedingly deep-blue gem-like radiance...
Having taken seven flowers that had grown in a place where a plough had been used, he offered them in the air.

Having practiced the duties of a recluse for as long as his life lasted, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that merit. In this present dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain family home;
upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth, and before long he became an Arahant.
10. Later on, having remembered his own former karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct, saying:
"When I was seven years of age," and so forth. In this context, "seven years of age" means that he had completed seven full years from the time of his emergence from his mother’s womb.
"I went forth into homelessness": *āgāriya* is that which is beneficial to the household (*agāra*).
"Household work such as farming and trade does not exist for one who is homeless"; thus, "I went forth into homelessness" means that I entered the religious life in the Buddha’s teaching.

12. "The path followed by the Sugata" means the path traversed by the Buddha. Alternatively, it connects with "having worshipped with a joyful mind and a contented heart" by way of fulfilling the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti) as taught by the Sugata. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gatasaññaka is completed.
3. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nippannañjalika:
"While sitting at the foot of a tree... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Nippannañjalika. This [Elder] also, among the Buddhas of the past...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation over many existences, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into homelessness and dwelt in the forest, fulfilling the ascetic practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree.
At that time, a severe illness arose; oppressed by it, he reached a state of supreme compassion.

Then the Blessed One, out of compassion for him, went there. Thereupon, while still lying down and unable to rise, he placed his palms together in reverence at his head and paid homage to the Blessed One. Passing away from that state, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
having enjoyed the excellence there, and having thus experienced the six types of prosperity in the sense-sphere realms, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
Reborn in a certain noble family, he reached maturity and, having gained faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness.
Before long, he became an Arahant and became renowned as Nippannajalika Thera on account of his past merit.
Later, reflecting upon the excellence of his own meritorious deeds, he was filled with joy and [recited] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*.

"Manifesting [this], he sat at the foot of a tree," and so forth. In this context, it is called a *rukkha* (tree) because it grows (*ruhati*), grows back (*paṭiruhati*), and ascends higher and higher (*uddham-uddham ārohati*).

"At the foot of that tree" means in its vicinity. "Afflicted by a supreme illness" means afflicted by a disease or sickness that is most intense, excessive, harsh, and cruel; the meaning is, "I am possessed by a disease. "I have reached a state of supreme compassion"—this refers to having attained the highest degree of pity.
The connection is as follows: "I have reached a state of extreme, excessive compassion, a state of wretchedness, and a state of suffering in the forest, in the wilderness.
(20) "There were five indeed who had great crests (*sikhā*). Here, *sikhā* refers to a topknot (*cūḷā*) in the sense of being worn upon the head.
One who possesses a crest-jewel—that is, a shining diadem—is called *sikha*. There were five Cakkavattins who possessed that very same name; they existed, they came into being.
The meaning [of the rest] is clear.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nipannañjalika is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Adhopupphiya.
"Abhibhū by name was that bhikkhu"—this is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Thera Adhopupphiya.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) over many existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household life, he later perceived the danger in sensual pleasures.

Having seen this, he abandoned it and went forth into the ascetic life; having attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, and having gained mastery over the psychic powers, he dwelt in the Himalayas.
Now, the Blessed One Sikhī had a chief disciple named Abhibhū, who, delighting in solitude, had gone to the Himalayas. Then that ascetic [saw] that chief disciple, the Elder...
Having seen this, as the ascetic climbed the mountain where the Elder was staying, he took seven fragrant and beautiful flowers from the base of the mountain and offered them in worship.
Then the Elder expressed his appreciation for the offering. That ascetic also returned to his own hermitage.
There, being afflicted by a snake, at a later time, he did not fall away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) due to that very calamity.

Having died while thus afflicted, he was destined for the Brahma-world; after experiencing the excellence of the Brahma realm and the excellence of the six sense-sphere heavens (*kāmāvacara*), and having exhausted his human excellences among men, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, and with a mind full of serene confidence, he went forth into homelessness, and before long—
He became an Arahant. Later on, he became well known as the Elder Adhopupphiya, after the name of the merit he had performed.
One day, having recollected his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words:
"That monk named Abhibhū... In this context, he is called *Abhibhū* because he overcomes others through virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
He is called *abhibhū* because he overcomes or overwhelms the Māras, beginning with the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*);

or alternatively, he is called *abhibhū* because he overcomes, afflicts, and destroys the defilements (*kilesa*) residing within his own continuum and those of others. He is a *bhikkhu* because his nature is to beg or his nature is to solicit;
or alternatively, he is a *bhikkhu* because he wears robes made of rags and tatters. The meaning is that the chief disciple named *Abhibhū* was a *bhikkhu*. [This refers to the time of] Sikhī.
The connection is: "He was the foremost disciple of the Blessed One.

Regarding the phrase "A python oppressed me": a great python snake oppressed such an ascetic—one endowed with virtue and endowed with meditative absorption—due to an enmity arising from evil deeds committed in the past.
Oppressed by that very affliction, he [remained] without falling away from his meditative absorption.
Having passed away, he was destined for the Brahma-world. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Adhopupphiya is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Raṃsisaññaka.
"On a mountain in the Himālayas," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Raṃsisaññaka.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having reached maturity and established a household life, he perceived the danger in sensual pleasures.
Having abandoned the household life and gone forth into the ascetic renunciation, he lived in the Himalayas wearing a deerskin.

At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī went to the Himalayas. Then, seeing the Blessed One who had approached him, that ascetic was filled with faith upon beholding the six-colored rays of light emanating from the Blessed One’s body, and he joined his palms in reverence.

Having taken [the offering], he performed an act of homage with the five limbs. By that very merit, when he passed away from this life, he experienced celestial prosperities among the Tusita gods and others;
subsequently, having experienced human prosperities as well, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he established a household life, but seeing the defects therein, he abandoned his home and went forth into homelessness.
Before long, he became an arahant.
Later on, remembering his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his past conduct, spoke the verse beginning with "On a mountain in the Himālayas.
In that context, it is called a *pabbata* because it expands (*brūhati*) or increases (*vaḍḍheti*) in a distinct manner (*pakārena*).
“Himavanta” means one who possesses snow (*himas*); since it is both snow-possessing and a mountain, it is called the Himavantapabbata (the Snowy Mountain).
Although one should say “on the Himavantapabbata,” the phrase “on the mountain Himavanta” was stated for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.
The connection is: “In that Himavanta mountain, I formerly made my dwelling. The rest is clear everywhere according to the method [of interpretation].
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṃsisaññaka is completed.
6. The commentary on the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dutiyaraṃsisaññaka begins with the verse: "On a mountain in the Himālayas... This too...

Having performed wholesome deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in each successive birth, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Upon reaching maturity, he established a household;
however, seeing the defects therein, he abandoned it and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic. Dwell­ing on the Himālaya mountains, he wore garments of bark-fiber.

He dwelt in the bliss of seclusion. At that time, seeing the Blessed One Phussa arrive at that place, he beheld the six-colored rays of a Buddha issuing from his body, streaming hither and thither like the flickering light from a raised torch.
Full of faith, he extended his hands in reverential salutation, paid homage, and gladdened his heart; through that very joy and gladness, he—

Having passed away, he was reborn among the Tusita devas and others; there, after experiencing the six kinds of prosperity of the sense-sphere realms, and later, having experienced human prosperities as well, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into homelessness due to the influence of his former mental impressions and, before long, became an Arhat.

35. Thus, at a later time, having recollected his former deed and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the *Apadāna* of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "On a mountain in the Himālayas... All of that is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Raṃsisaññaka is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phaladāyaka.
"On a mountain in the Himālaya," and so forth, is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Phaladāyaka Thera.

Having accumulated a store of merit through wholesome deeds performed under previous Buddhas, and having gathered merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa.
Having attained happiness and subsequently renounced all that for the ascetic life of a forest-dweller, he—
Having gone forth, he lived wearing coarse antelope skins. At that time, seeing the Blessed One Phussa arrive there, he took sweet fruits with a devout mind and fed him.

By virtue of that wholesome deed, after experiencing the excellence of merit in the world of the gods and other realms, he was born into a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having been reborn, and having gained maturity, he placed his faith in the Teacher, went forth, and before long became an Arahant.

Later on, recollecting his own past karma and proclaiming the *Apadāna* of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with "On a mountain in the Himālayas... Since all of that follows the method already explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phaladāyaka is completed.
8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Saddasaññaka.
The verse beginning with "On a mountain in the Himalayas" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Saddasaññaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [was born during the time of] the Blessed One Phussa...
Born at one time into a noble family, he reached adulthood and developed faith;
having gone forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic in the Himalayas, he heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One who had approached out of compassion for him.
Having gained serene confidence in the teachings, he lived out his full lifespan and, passing away later on, was reborn among the six classes of devas beginning with Tusita.
Having experienced the prosperities of the sense-sphere realms and the human prosperities among men, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him; having gone forth into homelessness and developed insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship*.

Later on, remembering his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former deeds, spoke the verse beginning with "On a mountain in the Himālayas. All of that is clear in meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saddasaññaka is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bodhisiñcaka begins with the words "Of the Blessed One Vipassī," etc.; this [Elder] also [lived] among the Buddhas of the past.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to the turning away from existence over many births, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having gone forth into the Dispensation and beautifying the Teaching through the practice of the observances, he saw the great multitude performing an offering to the Bodhi tree;
he then had them take many flowers and fragrant water and made an offering. He...

By that merit, he was reborn in the world of the gods; after experiencing the six kinds of celestial success in the sense-sphere realms, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him, and having gone forth into homelessness, he became an Arahant before long.
Having become an Arahant, he spent his time in the bliss of the fruits of meditative absorption (jhāna); then, recollecting his former karma, he was filled with joy.

Explaining the *apadāna* of his former conduct, he spoke the words beginning with "of the Blessed One Vipassī. In that context: he is called Vipassī because he sees (*passati*) the distinguished ultimate reality (*paramattha*), which is Nibbāna;
or, he is called Vipassī because he specifically perceives (*passati*) those people who are capable and incapable [of attaining liberation];
or, he is called Vipassī because his nature is to see while contemplating (*vipassanto*) and to perceive the Four Noble Truths. This is the Great Bodhi Festival of that Blessed One Vipassī.
This is the connection. In that context, "Great Enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*) refers to the knowledge (*ñāṇa*) in the four paths;
because the Blessed One, seated there, penetrates it, even the *kaṇikāra* tree is called "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
Furthermore, it is honored by gods, brahmās, humans, and asuras, and it is enlightenment, thus it is "Great Enlightenment. It is the enlightenment of the Great Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Or [for] Great Enlightenment"—the meaning is that there was a great offering for it. The rest is entirely obvious in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bodhisiñcaka is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumapupphiya.
"Entered the lotus grove," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Padumapupphiya.

This [Venerable] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa; and as he grew up, he became possessed of lotuses.
Having entered a lotus pond and eating the roots and stalks of the lotuses, he saw the Blessed One, Phussa, walking not far from the pond;
with a mind full of faith, he gathered lotuses from there, tossed them into the air, and offered them to the Blessed One.
Those flowers remained suspended in the air, forming a canopy. With even greater devotion, his mind was filled with faith.

Having gone forth and fulfilled the ascetic life (samaṇadhamma), the essence of which is the practice of the observances (vattapaṭipatti), he passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven as if making it his own abode.

Thereafter, having experienced in succession the six types of prosperity in the sense-sphere realms and the prosperity of human birth, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, faith arose within him, and he went forth into homelessness.
Before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, having recollected his own former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "He entered the lotus forest," and so forth.
In this context, they are called *pokkharā* because they pierce (*khanti*) in various ways (*pakārena*) with their stalks, leaves, and other parts.
A "lotus forest" (*pokkharavana*) is so called in the sense that it arises from lotuses;
the meaning is that I entered the center adorned with clusters of lotus thickets. The rest is entirely clear.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumapupphiya is completed.
The commentary on the Ninth Chapter is completed.
10. The Chapter on Sudhā. 1.
Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sudhāpiṇḍiya.
"This is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Sudhāpiṇḍiya Thera, beginning with the words 'He worships those worthy of worship.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, was unable to perform merit while the Blessed One Siddhattha was still living; however, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna..."
When a cetiya was being constructed after the relics had been enshrined, he gave a lump of plaster.

By that merit, from ninety-four aeons ago until this present time, he did not see the four states of misery; instead, having experienced the prosperity of gods and humans, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness, and before long he became an arahant.

1–2. Later on, having remembered his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “one worthy of worship” while proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).

In that context, those “worthy of worship” (*pūjāraha*) are the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), teachers (*ācariya*), preceptors (*upajjhāya*), parents, venerable ones, and so forth.

For a person who worships those worthy of worship with garlands and the like, lotuses, garments, ornaments, the four requisites (*catupaccaya*), and so on—while they are in the act of worshipping— [The text continues: ...for that person who is worshipping, [there arises] merit... [and so forth].
The meaning is that even by someone of great power, it would not be possible to calculate the portion of merit by means of numbers such as hundreds,

thousands, or hundreds of thousands. This same principle applies not only to one who worships the Buddha and others while they are still living, but also to the stūpas, images, Bodhi trees, and so forth, of the Blessed One after he has attained final nibbāna.

3. To illustrate this, he said, "of all four continents," and so forth. Therein, "of all four continents" means that having taken together the four continents known as Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha, along with the two thousand minor islands associated with them, one would exercise sovereign wheel-turning kingship throughout the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
"For the sake of a single act of worship" refers to [worship] at a cetiya within a relic chamber.
All this wealth in the entire Jambudīpa, beginning with the seven precious gems, does not equal even a sixteenth part of a single offering made at a cetiya;
that is to say, it is not worth even one-sixteenth part when divided sixteen times. 4. "Of Siddhattha... between the fruits":
of the Blessed One Siddhattha, the foremost and best among men, [between] the fruits... [etc.]... within the interval.

While the stucco work was being performed in the relic chamber of the cetiya, in the middle between the two boundaries—or alternatively, in the space between the places where flowers were offered—I gave a lump of stucco and smeared it; such is the connection [of the verse].
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sudhāpiṇḍiya is completed.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sucintita:
"Of Tissa, the Lord of the World," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sucintita. This one also [arose] during the previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit over many births for the attainment of Nibbāna, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.

Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and offered a pure, well-crafted, wooden, priceless seat for the Teacher to sit upon. By virtue of that meritorious deed, he experienced the happiness of the fortunate realms.
Wandering here and there through the cycle of rebirths, he was born into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness; not long thereafter, he became an Arahant.

Having attained the fruit of Arahantship, he recollected his past deeds and, filled with joy, spoke the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Conduct), beginning with the words, "Of Tissa, the Protector of the World," and so forth. All of that is clear in meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sucintika is completed.
3. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Aḍḍhaceḷaka:
"Of the Blessed One Tissa... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Aḍḍhaceḷaka. This elder, too...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various births, he was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Tissa into a family of the poor due to a single unwholesome kamma.
Upon reaching maturity, having learned of the teaching of the True Dharma, he became devout in mind and gave half a measure of cloth for the sake of a robe. He...
Having passed away through that very joy and gladness, he was reborn in heaven;
after experiencing the excellence of the six sense-sphere realms, when he fell from there, he experienced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch—the pinnacle of human excellence—among men.
Then, being reborn in a certain middle-class family during this arising of a Buddha, he reached maturity and [heard] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Having heard this, with a mind full of faith, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an *arahant*.

Later on, remembering his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the words beginning with "I [served] the Blessed One Tissa. All of that is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Aḍḍhaceḷaka is completed.
4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sūcidāyaka.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sūcidāyaka begins with the words, "In former times I was a smith...
This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; filling the seeds of wholesome karma from time to time, during the era of the Blessed One Vipassī...
Due to a single flaw in his karma, he was reborn in a family of smiths;

having reached maturity and attained proficiency in his own craft, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and, with a mind full of faith, gave a gift of needles for the purpose of sewing robes.
By that merit, after experiencing celestial prosperity, he later arose among humans as a Wheel-turning Monarch and so forth.
Experiencing prosperity in each successive birth he arose, he possessed sharp wisdom and the diamond-like knowledge (*vajirañāṇa*).
Gradually, having been reborn during this appearance of a Buddha, he reached maturity, became wealthy, and was endowed with faith and sharp wisdom.
One day, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he directed his knowledge according to the Dhamma and became an *arahant* even while sitting on his seat.
19. Being an Arahant, having remembered his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "In the past I was a smith...
and so forth. In this context, *kammāro* means one who lives by, thrives, grows, and prospers through work such as iron-work or metal-work;
thus, it means "I was a smith" (*kammāro*) at the time when he was formerly performing meritorious deeds.
The meaning [is as explained]. The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sūcidāyaka is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gandhamāliya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Gandhamāliya Thera begins with the words, "Of Siddhattha, the Blessed One," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha; he possessed great wealth and vast enjoyments.
Having gained faith in the Teacher, he cultivated many fragrant substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and kassuta.
He had a fragrant stupa built for the Teacher and covered it above with *sumana* flowers, and he offered the eightfold service to the Buddha.
Through that meritorious deed, after experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha in a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness.
Before long, he became an Arahant.

Later on, having recollected his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha... All of that is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gandhamāliya is complete.
6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tipupphiya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Tipupphiya begins with the words, "In former times I was a deer-hunter.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassi in a hunter's family due to some intervening lapse in unwholesome conduct.

Having become a deer-hunter, he lived in the forest. At that time, seeing the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Vipassi—its leaves and sprouts fully developed, green in color, with a blue luster, and enchanting—he worshipped it with three flowers, discarded a withered leaf, and paid homage to the great Bodhi tree of Pāṭali as if in the very presence of the Blessed One.
By that merit, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.

Having been reborn there, he experienced divine prosperity again and again; passing away from there, he was born among humans, where he enjoyed the fortune of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and other such blessings.
Now, in this present era of a Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in a certain noble family.
Upon reaching maturity, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, his heart was filled with joy; he renounced the household life and went forth into homelessness.
Before long, he became an *arahant*.
Having thus attained perfection, he recollected his own past karma and, filled with joy, spoke the account of his former deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words:
"In the past, I was a deer-hunter... In this context, one who goes toward and reaches death is called a *miga* (deer).
Alternatively, he is called a *miga* because he moves about here hunting; a hunter who is greedy and covetous in the killing of deer is a *migaluddaka*. The connection is:
"In former times, during my period of performing meritorious deeds, a deer-hunter lived in the great forest known as the Kānana.
Regarding the phrase "having seen the green *pāṭali*": it is called *pāṭali* because it exists there with a surface that is red in color; [it is so called] because of its flowers...
It is called "pāṭali" because of its red color; the meaning is that he saw the Bodhi tree of the Pāṭali, which was green and blue-colored due to the greenness of its leaves.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tipupphiya is finished.
7. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Madhupiṇḍika.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Madhupiṇḍika begins with the words, "Having seen [him] in the forest grove...
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Siddhattha...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn among the *nesāda* hunters and lived in a great forest.
Then, seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha—who had attained delight in solitude—he offered him very sweet honey as he arose from his meditative absorption.
With a mind full of faith, he paid homage and departed. By that very merit, experiencing successive states of prosperity...
Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family during this current arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth into homelessness; before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, remembering his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former deeds, said:
"In the forest, in the grove," and so forth, he said. Therein, "in the forest" (*vivane*): a forest (*vana*) that is especially extensive is a "great forest" (*vivana*);
the meaning is that it is devoid of and free from the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as from the objects of sensual desire and the defilements of sensual desire.

The connection is with "in the great wilderness known as a grove" (*kānana*). "Shining like a medicinal herb" (*osadhiṃva virocan-taṃ*): [it is] whatever is desired and sought after by those people who increase existence (*bhava*).

It is called *osadha* because it produces [a healing effect]. It is called *osadhi* because they rise up and take hold of that star by means of which they extract [the essence], depending on the cause for the production of nutritive essence (*ojā*).

While it would be more accurate to say "shining like the *osadhi*-star," the phrase "shining like the *osadhi*" was stated for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition. The rest is entirely obvious throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Madhupiṇḍika is completed.
8. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Senāsanadāyaka:
"Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Senāsanadāyaka. This too...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher;
then, when the Blessed One arrived at a forest grove where he himself was staying, he paid homage to the Blessed One, spread out a mat of leaves, and [prepared a seat].
He gave [it]. Having constructed a boundary wall all around the place where the Blessed One was seated, he performed an offering of flowers.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, he was reborn into a noble family at the time of this Buddha’s appearance.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth; before long, he became an Arahant.

45. Thus, at a later time, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "To the Blessed One Siddhattha," while demonstrating the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*). Since all of that follows the method already explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Senāsanadāyaka is complete.
9. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Veyyāvaccakara.
"Of the Blessed One Vipassī," and so forth, is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Veyyāvaccakara Thera. Its origins and other details are to be understood according to the system already explained below.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Veyyāvaccakara Thera is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Buddhupaṭṭhāka Thera.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka begins with the words "Of the Blessed One Vipassī," and so forth.
