This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a family of conch-blowers. Upon reaching maturity, he became proficient in his own craft, the blowing of the conch.
He became skillful and, at all times, honored the Blessed One by blowing his conch shell; indeed, he worshipped with the sound of the conch alone.
By that merit, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he was everywhere renowned, possessing a great voice, a great resonance, and a sweet tone.
In this present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn into a prominent family, and upon reaching maturity, he was known for his sweet voice.
Having gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an Arahant. Later on, he became well known as the Elder Madhurassara.
One day, recollecting his own past kamma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with "Of the Blessed One Vipassī.
That has already been explained above. "I was a conch-blower" (*ahosiṃ saṅkhadhamako*): *saṃ* means "well" (*suṭṭhu*).
"He goes digging" means "conch"; the meaning is that he moves and wanders as far as the edge of the ocean water.
One who blows that conch, making a sound, is a "conch-blower"; the meaning is that I was indeed such a conch-blower.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka is completed.
The commentary on the tenth chapter is completed.
11. The Chapter on the Giver of Alms-food.
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhikkhādāyaka.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Bhikkhādāyaka begins with the words, "The Fully Enlightened One, golden-hued...
This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors; thus, throughout various existences, he accumulated merits that served as the necessary conditions for his liberation.
During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn in a certain noble family;
having grown up endowed with wealth and having conceived faith, he went out from his residence and, seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha wandering for alms, offered him food with a devout mind.
The Blessed One accepted it, delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, and departed. By that very wholesome deed...
Having remained for the full span of his life, at the conclusion of that life he was reborn in the world of the devas.

There, having experienced the six kinds of prosperity of the sense-sphere devas, and having experienced human prosperity among humans, he was reborn into a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, faith arose in him; he went forth into homelessness and, before long, became an arahant.
1. Later on, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former conduct, beginning with the words, “The Golden-Hued Sambuddha.
All of that is exactly according to the method explained below. Regarding the phrase *pavarā abhinikkhantā*:
it is called *pavara* because it is to be chosen (*varitabba*) or aspired to (*patthetabba*) in an excellent (*paka*) manner; it is that which has become delightful and secluded.
The meaning is that it has emerged with particular distinction from its own dwelling (*vihāra*).

Or, "from craving (*vāna*) it has come to *nibbāna*": here *vāna* is said to mean craving (*taṇhā*); because it has emerged from that, it is *nibbāna*. The meaning is that, having made the craving called *vāna* its primary object, it has abandoned all defilements and attained *nibbāna*.
2. "Having given alms-food with a ladle" (*kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ datvāna*): A ladle (*kaṭacchu*) is a spoon to be held in the palm of the hand.
"Alms-food" (*bhikkhā*) means that which is begged for or requested; or, it is that which is to be specially eaten or consumed.
Alms-food taken with a ladle is "alms-food with a ladle" (*kaṭacchubhikkhā*); the meaning is "having given rice with a spoon. The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhikkhādāyaka is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika:
"The Perfectly Enlightened One, golden-hued... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Ñāṇasaññika. What is its origin?

This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.

Upon reaching maturity, he developed faith and became devoted and yearning for the hearing of the True Dhamma. Following the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he directed his knowledge [toward it], and because its fame was immeasurable...
Having placed his trust in the knowledge of the Blessed One and paid homage by performing the five-limbed and eight-limbed prostrations, he departed.

Passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas; experiencing the divine splendors of the six sense-sphere heavens there, he passed away from that state and was born in the human world.
Having experienced the excellence of being a wheel-turning monarch and other such attainments while in the womb there, in this [life]...
Having been reborn in a noble family endowed with great wealth at the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he grew up, gained faith in the Teacher, and went forth;
before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, remembering his own past deeds, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, said:
He said, “The Perfectly Enlightened One, golden-hued,” and so forth. That has the same meaning as already explained. “Like a bull of noble breed” (*nisabhājāniya*):
*nisabha* is the leader of a hundred thousand cows; he is both a *nisabha* and a *ājāniya*—noble, excellent, and supreme—thus he is a *nisabhājāniya*.

The meaning is: “just as the *nisabhājāniya*, so too is the Blessed One. This was spoken by way of designation (*paññatti*) according to the conventional understanding of the world. He is incomparable.
Indeed, Blessed One. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Uppalahatthiya.
The legend of the Venerable Uppalahatthaka Thera, beginning with "A resident of Tivarā," is as follows:
Having performed wholesome deeds under previous Victors, he accumulated merit conducive to the realization of *vivaṭṭa* (the turning away from saṃsāra) in various births.
During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn into a family of garland-makers; and upon reaching maturity, through his work as a garland-maker, [he produced] many flowers.

He lived by selling them. Then one day, while wandering about with flowers he had gathered, he saw the Blessed One walking like a jewel of priceless value and honored him with a cluster of red lotuses.
When he passed away from there, he experienced the fruits of that merit in the happy realms;
and now, having been reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha, he attained faith as he grew up, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arhat.

13. Thus, at a later time, having remembered his own former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "I was a resident of Tivarā," while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds).
Therein, "Tivarā" refers to a well-fortified, concealed city built in three tiers;
"a resident of Tivarā" means one who was habitually dwelling there, or one living in a house situated within that place of residence.

The meaning is as follows: "At that time I was a garland-maker" means that at the time of performing the accumulation of merit for the sake of *nibbāna*, I was a garland-maker, a florist who lived by buying and selling flowers; this is the meaning.

(14) "I gave a handful of flowers" means that upon seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha, I gave him a bunch of blue lotuses as an offering; this is the meaning. The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Uppalahatthaka is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padapūjaka begins with the words "Of the Blessed One Siddhattha," etc.; this [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn into a noble family.

Upon reaching maturity, he developed faith in the Teacher and honored him at the soles of his feet with a *sumana* flower. By virtue of that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced the prosperity of Sakka;
and now, in this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn into a noble family and reached adulthood.
Having gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth into homelessness; by developing insight, he was established in the fruit of arahantship.

Later on, remembering his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), spoke these words beginning with "To the Blessed One Siddhattha...
[He said: "I gave *jātipuppha* flowers," meaning I gave *jātisumana* jasmine flowers.
Where "aham" should have been said, it is stated with the elision of the word *sumana* for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse.
In that context, it is called *sumana* because, being born from its species, it brings joy (*somanassa*) to people even as it blossoms;
it is called *puppha* in the sense of blooming or opening. Thus, it is a *sumana-puppha* because it is both *sumana* and a *puppha*; [the plural] refers to those *sumana-puppha* flowers.
The meaning is: "I shall worship the Blessed One Siddhattha. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padapūjaka is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Muṭṭhipupphiya.
"Sudassano by name"—this is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Muṭṭhipupphiya.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a family of garland-makers.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in his own craft; one day—
Having seen the Blessed One, with a mind full of serene faith, he scattered *jātisumana* flowers from both hands at the base of the Blessed One’s feet as an offering.
Through that accumulation of merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of prosperity, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha;
and having reached maturity, by virtue of his former mental impressions (*pubbavāsanā*), he—
Having gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an Arahant.
Later on, recollecting his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words, "He who was named Sudassana...
In this context, "Sudassana" refers to him by virtue of the beauty of his stature, proportions, form, symmetry, youthfulness, and splendor.

"Sudassano" means "beautiful to behold. The meaning is that, having become a florist named Sudassano, he worshipped the Blessed One Padumuttara with *jāti-sumanā* flowers. The rest is entirely clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Muṭṭhipupphiya*-Thera Apadāna is completed.
6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Udakapūjaka.
"Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ... and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Udakapūjaka.

This [Elder] also, having accumulated a store of wholesome deeds under previous supreme Victors, was fulfilling the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) in various states of being.
In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a certain noble family.

Having grown up and come to understand wholesome and unwholesome deeds, he became inspired with faith upon seeing the six-colored rays of light emitted by the Blessed One Padumuttara as he traveled through the sky.
Taking water in both hands, he made an offering. The water thus offered rose into the sky like silver bubbles.
He stood there. With deep faith and that very joy, he was reborn among the Tusita devas and others;
after experiencing celestial splendors and later experiencing human prosperity, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth, and before long became an arahant.

29. Later on, having remembered his own former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "The Golden-Colored Sambuddha," proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds).
That has already been explained above. Regarding the phrase "blazing like a ghee-lamp": *ghata* means clarified butter (*sappi*);
the "seat" (*āsana*) of the ghee—that is, its receptacle—is the "ghee-seat" (*ghatāsana*), which refers to fire. Alternatively, it is so called because it consumes that [ghee] when it exists.

"Ghaṭāsana" means like fire. Just as when a vessel is sprinkled [with oil] and placed over a fire, the flame of the fire blazes intensely, so too the meaning is that the Blessed One was blazing like a mass of fire.
"Like the sacrificial fire that has been kindled" (*ādittam va hutāsanam*): "huta" refers to offerings and honors;
the "seat" (*āsana*) of such offered honors is the "hutāsana. He was like the blazing sun, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The connection [of the verse] is that they saw the Golden-Colored Sambuddha, shining with circles of fathom-wide radiance, traveling through the sky as clear as the atmosphere.
The rest is self-evident throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Udakapūjaka is completed.
7. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Naḷamāliya.
The passage beginning with "Of the Buddha Padumuttara" is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Naḷamāliya.

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) over many births, [encountered] Padumuttara...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, and having reached maturity and established a household life, he perceived the danger in sensual pleasures;
abandoning his home, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic. While dwelling in the Himalayas, he saw the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, there;
filled with faith, he paid homage and spread out a layer of grass. Then, for the Blessed One who was seated upon it, [he offered] bundles of reeds...
Having made it a fan and fanned him, she gave it to him. Out of compassion for her, the Blessed One accepted it and offered words of thanksgiving.
By that merit, as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, he was free from the fever and torment of arising states;
having attained physical, mental, and spiritual happiness and experienced manifold joys, he was born into a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having been reborn, through the power of his former mental impressions (*pubbavāsanā*), he gained faith in the Teacher; having gone forth, before long he became an *arahant*.

Later on, remembering his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth. That has already been explained above.
"Taking a reed garland" (*naḷamālaṃ gahetvāna*): it is called a "reed" (*naḷa*) because it is without essence, without substance, thinner and lighter even than a bamboo stalk.
"Born as Naḷa"—the flower of Naḷa is "naḷamāla"; the grammatical connection is that they had a fan made from that naḷamāla.
A "bījanī" is so called because the wind is fanned (*bījissati*) or generated by it; the meaning is that I offered that fan to the Buddha and he accepted it.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Naḷamāliya is finished.
The commentary on the seventh recitation section is finished.
8. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Āsanupaṭṭhāhaka.
"Having seized the forest grove," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Āsana-paṭṭhāka.

This [Venerable One] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
While living the life of a householder, he perceived the faults therein and [renounced] the household life.
Having abandoned the ascetic life and gone forth, while living in the Himālayas, he saw the Blessed One who had arrived there;
filled with faith, he offered him a lion-throne. When the Blessed One was seated upon it, he took a bouquet of garlands, honored him, circumambulated him, and departed.
By that merit, as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, in each birth he was reborn...

He was of noble birth and possessed of great wealth. In the course of time, having been reborn into a family home during this arising of a Buddha, he grew up and, gaining faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness. Not long after, he became an Arahant.

Being an Arahant, he recollected his own past karma and, filled with joy, spoke the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), beginning with the words, “Having seized the forest and the woods,” and so forth. All of that has already had its meaning explained below.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Āsanupaṭṭhāhaka is complete.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Biḷālidāyaka begins with the verse "Not far from the Himalayas," etc. This [Elder] also, under former Victorious Ones...

Having fulfilled his duties in various states of existence while accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity and living the life of a householder, he perceived the defects therein;
abandoning the household life, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic (*tāpasa-pabbajjā*) and lived in the Himalayas, being exceedingly modest and contented.
He lived subsisting on *ālu* roots and other such foods. Then, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One Padumuttara went to the Himālaya mountains.

Seeing him, the man was filled with faith; he prostrated, took some *biḷāli* plants, and scattered them into the Buddha’s bowl. Out of compassion for him, the Tathāgata consumed them, inspiring joy in his heart.
By virtue of that deed, when he passed away from there, he experienced the dual excellences among both gods and humans.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth into the Dispensation and, before long, became an Arahant.
Later on, recollecting his own wholesome karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, said:
He spoke the words beginning with “Not far from the Himālayas. Since all of that follows the method already explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
*Āluva*, *karambha*, and so forth, are merely the names of various species of tubers.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Biḷālidāyaka is completed.
10. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Reṇupūjaka.
"Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ... and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Reṇupūjaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Supreme Victors and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, [saw] Vipassi...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he grew up and, having gained faith in the Teacher, reached the age of discretion.
Seeing the Blessed One shining like a mass of fire, his mind was filled with serene confidence; he took a *nāgapuṣpa* filament and offered it as worship.
Then the Blessed One gave him a discourse of thanksgiving.
62-3. By that merit, having passed away from there and wandering among gods and humans, he experienced both kinds of excellence;
being honored everywhere in each successive birth, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Having attained maturity, through the power of his former mental impressions, he placed his faith in the Teacher and went forth in the Dispensation. Not long thereafter, he became an Arahant.

Having seen his own past deeds with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), he became joyful and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), spoke the verse beginning with "the golden-colored Sambuddha.
The meaning of that has already been explained above. "Like the sun with a hundred rays" (*sataraṃsiṃva bhānumaṃ*):

that sun whose rays—that is, its radiance—are a hundred in number, or measure a hundred, is "one with a hundred rays"; [this is stated] for the sake of the ease of the metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
"Four-rayed" (*sataraṃsi*) is what was said; the meaning is "having many hundreds of rays" or "many hundreds of thousands of rays. *Bhāṇu* means radiance;

he who has radiance is *bhāṇumā*. Having seen the Blessed One Vipassī—who is like the sun known as *bhāṇumā*—I took a *nāgapuppha* flower with its filaments and offered it in worship; this is the meaning. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Reṇupūjaka is completed.
The commentary on the eleventh chapter is completed.
12. The Chapter on the Great Retinue (*Mahāparivāravagga*).
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahāparivāraka.
The passage beginning with "The Blessed One named Vipassī" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Mahāparivāraka.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation, [saw] Vipassī...

At the time when [this] arose for the Blessed One, [the deity] was reborn in the yakkha realm with a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of yakkhas, dwelling on a certain small island experiencing divine happiness. On that island there was a monastery adorned with a cetiya;
the Blessed One went there. Then that commander of the yakkha army [learned] of the Blessed One’s arrival there.
Having seen [this], he took celestial garments, went and paid homage to the Blessed One, and honored him with those celestial garments; together with his retinue, he went for refuge.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.

Having experienced the sixfold sensual pleasure there, and having passed away from there, he experienced the happiness of a supreme universal monarch and other such states among humans. Later, during this current appearance of a Buddha...
Having been reborn in a noble family and reached the age of discretion, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth; before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, remembering his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), spoke the words beginning with "The Blessed One named Vipassī.
In this context, he is called Vipassī because he sees (*passati*) the distinction (*visesa*), the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), which is Nibbāna.
Alternatively, he is "Vipassī" because he sees the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), in their various forms;
or he is "Vipassī" because he perceives individually each of the various beings who are to be awakened.
That Blessed One Vipassī went to the Dīpa Cetiya, a monastery that was a place of worship on the island (*dīpa*). The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahāparivāraka is completed.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sumaṅgala begins with the verse: "Atthadassī, the supreme Victor... This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, he was reborn as a tree deity near a certain pond.
At that time, the Blessed One, having emerged from his monastery and desiring to bathe, went to the bank of that pond; having bathed there, he stood clad in a single robe.
He stood there like Brahmā, like the sun, or like a golden disk.
Then that son of the gods, filled with joy, offered praise with palms joined and presented an offering with his own divine songs and musical instruments.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, after experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, he was later reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having reached the age of discretion, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arahant.
Later, remembering his past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the verse beginning with "Atthadassī, the supreme Victor.
In this context, he is called Atthadassī because he sees (*dakkhati*) or beholds (*passati*) the ultimate goal, Nibbāna. Then...
Or, he is an "Atthadassī" (Seer of Meaning) because his nature is to see the purpose and benefit for all beings, which consists of the Four Noble Truths.

He is a "Jina" (Conqueror) because he has conquered, is conquering, and will conquer the defilements (*kilesa*). He is a "Vara" (Excellent One) because he is to be chosen and aspired to by all beings.
Thus, he is the Atthadassī Jina who is also the Vara; hence, "Atthadassī Jinavara. He is the "Lokajeṭṭha" (Eldest in the World) because [the world] is broken and dissolves.

The world (*loka*) is so called because it is seen by the Buddhas and others, or because it has reached the beyond (*pāra*). Alternatively, "world" refers to the world, the worldly person (*lokī*), and that which is perceived;

thus, through the compound of single-remainder (*ekasesa-samāsa*), where one should have said "worlds," it is expressed as "the world. The eldest of the world is the "eldest of the world" (*lokajeṭṭha*);
the meaning is that he is the bull among men (*narāsabha*) who is the eldest of the world. The rest is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sumaṅgala is completed.
3. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saraṇagamaniya:
"Of both the kings of the gods... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Saraṇagamaniya. This one, too, [arose] during the time of previous Buddhas.
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in successive births,
he was reborn in the Himālayas as a king of the gods during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Later, when another king of the *yakkha*-gods approached for the purpose of battle,
these two— each surrounded by many thousands of *yakkhas* and with shields, weapons, and other gear in hand— [encountered one another].

They drew up their battle lines for the sake of combat. Then the Blessed One Padumuttara, having conceived compassion for those beings, went there through the air and taught the Dhamma to the two divine kings and their retinues.
At that time, they all cast aside their shields and weapons, and with profound reverence and esteem, they paid homage to the Blessed One and went for refuge.

This was the first refuge he went to among them. By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having grown up and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an Arhat.
20. Later on, having recollected his former wholesome deeds and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "Of the two divine kings.

Therein, by way of a designation, he spoke of the two unnamed kings of the *yakkhas*—who were not well-known by name or clan like Suciloma, Kharaloma, Āḷavaka, Kumbhīra, Kuvera, and others—saying, "Of the two divine kings," and so forth.
"Battle has been set up": *saṅgāma* means "approaching for the sake of strife";
it is well (*saṃ*) set up (*uppaṭṭhita*), meaning it has come together and stands in one place. "It was arrayed":
it was well (*saṃ*) gathered into a mass in close proximity (*samīpe*).

21. "He stirred the great multitude": seated in the air, the Blessed One thoroughly stirred (*saṃvejesi*) those yakkhas gathered in a heap by means of a teaching on the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths;
the meaning is that he caused them to take up [the practice], made it known to them, and awakened them by showing the dangers [of worldly existence]. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saraṇagamaniya is completed.
4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekāsaniya.
The account beginning with "Varuṇo nāma nāmena" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ekāsaniya.
This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [attained birth] under Atthadassi...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn as a king of the gods named Varuṇa.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, he and his retinue honored him with perfumes, garlands, and the like, as well as songs and instrumental music.

Subsequently, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he and his retinue [honored] the Great Bodhi tree with all kinds of musical instruments and cymbals, as if it were the sight of the Buddha himself.
He made this offering. By that merit, after passing away from there, he was reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven.
Having thus experienced celestial prosperity, and having been born among humans as a human being, he experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti).
Now, in this present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family; upon reaching maturity, he went forth in the Teacher’s dispensation and, before long, became an Arahant.

31. Thus, later on, having recollected his own deed and understood it as it truly was, Varuṇa—filled with joy and proclaiming the account of his former conduct—spoke the words beginning with "By name Varuṇa.
Therein, the connection is as follows: "When I made offerings to the Buddha and to enlightenment for the sake of awakening, at that time I was a king of the gods named Varuṇa."
34. *Dharaṇīruhapādapanti*: Here, it is called *dharaṇī* because it supports trees, creepers, mountain ranges, jewels, and so forth.
That which grows and establishes itself upon that [earth] is *dharaṇīruha*. It is called *pādapa* because it drinks with its feet;
the meaning is that it drinks the water repeatedly poured upon it through its feet—that is, its roots—and thus spreads the essence of water through the trunk, branches, and twigs of the tree. That...
The connection is that the tree growing from the earth is the Bodhi-tree.
"Delighted by one's own karma" means delighted and confident by one's own wholesome karma; the connection is that he was confident in the supreme enlightenment. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Ekāsaniya*-Thera Apadāna is completed.
5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Suvaṇṇapupphiya.
The account beginning with "The Blessed One named Vipassī" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Suvaṇṇapupphiya.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the turning away from saṃsāra (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), [reached the presence of] Vipassī...
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn as a terrestrial deva in a certain place;
having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of four golden flowers.
Those flowers became a golden canopy in the sky and covered [the Buddha], and the radiance of the golden flowers and the radiance of the Buddha’s body merged into one, becoming a great effulgence.
Thus, with even greater faith, he remembered [the Buddha] even after returning to his own home.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through happy realms such as the Tusita heaven and experiencing celestial prosperity, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, gave his heart to the Dispensation, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arahant.

40. Thus, at a later time, having remembered his past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "The Blessed One named Vipassī," proclaiming the account of his own former conduct. The meaning of this has already been explained above.
44. "Having generated gladness" means having produced powerful rapture (*pīti*).

As in such passages as, "Gladness is rejoicing, delighting, laughter, loud laughter, cheerfulness, elation, and mental satisfaction," it means having generated a state of mental satisfaction within one's own nature.
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is entirely obvious throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Suvaṇṇapupphiya is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Citakapūjaka.
"I dwell at Rājāyatana," and so forth, is the legend (Apadāna) of the Venerable Citakapūjaka Thera. This [Thera] also,
having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and thereafter accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout each successive existence,
was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi as a deity of the Rājāyatana tree, dwelling there from time to time together with other deities.

Having heard the Dhamma, he became confident in the Blessed One. After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he took perfumes, lamps, incense, flowers, drums, and other offerings, and together with his retinue, went to the place of the Blessed One’s funeral pyre.
There, having honored him with lamps and other offerings, he worshipped him with many musical instruments and various kinds of instrumental music.
From that time forth, even when he had entered his own palace, he kept only the Blessed One in mind.
He pays homage as if in the Blessed One’s very presence. By that very merit and that clarity of mind, after passing away from Rājāyatana, he was reborn among the Tusita devas and others;
having experienced divine prosperity there, and subsequently experiencing human prosperity among men, he was now reborn into a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Having attained maturity, he conceived a clear confidence in the Blessed One.
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, he became an Arhat not long thereafter.
Later on, remembering his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words:
"I dwell at Rājāyatana. Regarding "Rājāyatana": it is the abode (*āyatana*) of the king of gods; thus, it is Rājāyatana. Of that...

Or it is the name of the tree. "The Blessed One has attained final nibbāna" (parinibbute bhagavati) is connected with "of Sikhi, the Kinsman of the World," at the time of final nibbāna—that is, at the moment of attaining final nibbāna when the aggregates have completely and without remainder ceased. 50.
"They went to the funeral pyre" (citakaṃ agamāsuṃ): it refers to that which was piled up with fragrant woods such as sandalwood, agarwood, devadāru, camphor, and *takkola*.
*Rāsigataṃ* means heaped up; *citakaṃ* is simply that which is heaped up. The meaning is: "Out of reverence for the Buddha, I went near the funeral pyre for the purpose of worshipping it.
In that context, showing what was done after going there, he said, "Having had musical instruments played there," and so forth.
All of this is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Citakapūjaka is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Buddhasaññaka begins with the verse:
"When Vipassī was the Supreme One in the World... This [Elder] also [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas.

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn as a son of the gods in a certain terrestrial celestial mansion (*bhūmaṭṭhaka-vimāna*) during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī relinquished the volitional formations of life (*āyusaṅkhāra*).
Then, the entire ten-thousandfold world system, including its oceans and mountains, trembled.
At that moment, even the abode of that son of the gods trembled. At that instant, the son of the gods, seized by doubt, thought, "What indeed is the cause of this earthquake?

Having realized that the Buddha was relinquishing the volitional formations of his lifespan, he was overcome with great sorrow and dejection. Then the Great King Vessavaṇa arrived and said, "Do not grieve."
He comforted him. That son of the gods, passing away from there, transmigrating among gods and humans by virtue of that merit, was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Having reached maturity and renounced the life of a householder, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an Arahant.
Later on, remembering his own former karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his past conduct, said:

When he said, "Vipassī, the supreme one in the world," and so forth: *āyusaṅkhāramossajji* means that "āyu" (life) is so called because it "yunoti" (binds together) or protects beings on all sides (*ā*).
The "saṅkhāra" (determination) of life is the state of its accumulation; thus, *āyusaṅkhāra*. He "ossajji" (relinquished), that is, he abandoned or gave up that *āyusaṅkhāra*;
this is the meaning. At that relinquishing of the determination of life, the entire earth of the ten-thousandfold world-system, together with the oceans girdled by water, [shook].
"Kampittha" (it shook) is the connection [with the previous]. 58. "Otataṃ vitthataṃ mayhaṃ": my abode was overspread and expanded;
my mind was variegated—my mind, pure and perfectly purified, was shining and variegated with many kinds of jewels, and it shook in a manifold way.
"Kampitthā" means "shaking. The remainder is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Buddhasaññaka is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggasaññaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Maggasaññaka Thera begins with the words "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," and so forth. This venerable one had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;

subsequently, accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn as a son of the gods in the Himālayas during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having gone into the forest, he showed the way to those who were lost.
Having fed those disciples who were searching for him, he pointed out the path to them.
By that merit, having experienced the excellence of gods and humans, he remained undeluded and mindful in every birth throughout his successive existences.
Then, being reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha, he attained maturity; unattached to the life of a householder, he went forth and before long became an Arhat.

66. Thus, at a later time, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Buddha Padumuttara," while proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
Regarding the term *sāvakā*: they are called disciples (*sāvaka*) because they listen properly and with reverence to the words spoken by the Blessed One;
or alternatively, they are so called because they direct their wisdom according to the Blessed One’s teaching and listen to the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*).

"Disciples": the connection is that the disciples who wander in the forest, roaming through the woods, having become lost and bewildered regarding the path, wander about like the blind, being deprived of sight, in the great wilderness. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggasaññaka is completed.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka begins with the verse: “Atthadassimhi sugate...
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [attained this state].
At the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, he was reborn in the womb of a yakkha;
because he had not obtained a vision of the Blessed One while the Blessed One was still living, he remained thereafter overcome with great sorrow once the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.

For at that time, the Blessed One’s chief disciple named Sāgata was instructing him, saying: "The veneration of the relics of the Blessed One is the same as the veneration performed while the Blessed One was still living."
Having said, "Just as [the merit] becomes of great fruit through the power of serenity of mind," he was exhorted, "Build a stupa," and so he had a stupa constructed.
After worshipping it, when he passed away from there, he experienced the attainments of gods, humans, Sakka, and universal monarchs;
then, in this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain family home in Sāvatthī, and upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher.
Not long after going forth, he became an Arahant.
Later on, remembering his own meritorious deed, filled with joy and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning, "In the Sugata Atthadassi," and so forth.
That has already been explained above. Regarding the phrase, "They were reborn in the yakkha womb": here...
Furthermore, they are called *yakkhas* because they go (*yanti*) about, eating whatever comes into their presence.
The "yakkha-yoni" is the womb or birth-state of *yakkhas*; the meaning is that one has been reborn in the *yakkha*-womb.
(73) "Alas, it was a poor gain for me"—the status I have gained through me is a poor gain; [this refers to] the Teacher who has become a Buddha.
The meaning is: "having failed to perform hospitality" or "having offended. *Duppabhātaṃ* means a poorly broken dawn; the sense is:
"the breaking of the night was not well done for me. *Duruṭṭhitaṃ* means badly established; the sense is:
"the rising of the sun was a bad rising for me. Everywhere else, the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka is completed.
10. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Jātipūjaka:
"At the birth of that Vipassi... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Jātipūjaka. This one, too, [was born] during the time of previous Buddhas...

Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, he heard from the astrologers the signs and characteristics described regarding the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"It is said that this prince, having become a Buddha, will be the supreme and most excellent one for the entire world."
“Having heard [this], he will deliver all beings from saṃsāra. Having heard this, even while still a youth, he performed a great offering to that Blessed One as if to a Buddha.
Later, in due course, having passed through those three stages of time—youth, the period as a prince, and the period as king—and even after the Buddha had appeared, he performed a great offering;
then, passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven and other realms, where he experienced divine bliss.
Afterwards, having experienced human happiness such as that of a wheel-turning monarch among men, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
At the age of only seven or eight years, he gained faith in the Blessed One, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight,
he became an arahant before long.

82. Thus, at a later time, having remembered his own past karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “Jāyaṃ tassa Vipassissa,” proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds). That has already been explained in meaning above. 84.
Regarding the phrase “Having heard the words of the *nemittas*”: here, those who know the *nimitta*—that is, the cause or the reason for the attainment of pleasure and pain—are called *nemittas*.
The meaning is: “having heard the speech of those *nemittas*, the astrologers. The rest is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Jātipūjaka is completed.
The commentary on the twelfth chapter is completed.
13. The Chapter on Sereyya.
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sereyyaka The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sereyyaka begins with the words, "A reciter, a bearer of mantras...

This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors, and thereafter, throughout a thousand successive existences, he accumulated merits that served as the necessary conditions for his liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a brahmin family; having reached maturity and mastered the three Vedas, he attained the pinnacle of all brahminical sciences such as the Itihāsas.
One day, while standing in the open air with his retinue, he saw the Blessed One and, with a devout mind, took a Sereyya flower and offered it by tossing it into the air.
Those flowers formed a canopy in the sky and remained there for seven days before vanishing.
Having seen that marvel, his mind became exceedingly serene; through that very joy and gladness, he passed away and was reborn among the Tusita devas and others.
There, after experiencing celestial happiness, and subsequently human happiness, he was born into this present age of a Buddha.
Having been reborn in a noble family and reached the age of discretion, he gained faith in the Teacher through the power of his former mental impressions (*pubbavāsanā*).
Having gone forth, before long he became an *arahant*.

Later on, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed in the past, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former lives (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), spoke the words beginning with "A student of the Vedas, a bearer of the mantras," and so forth. The meaning of this has already been explained above.
3. "Having taken *sereyyaka*": *Sirisa* is the *jāti* flower; *sereyya* is that very same thing, and *sereyyaka* is simply *sereyya*.

The connection is: "having taken that *sereyyaka*. Since there was no time for one who has faith in the Blessed One to arrive there and offer flowers such as *jāti*, *sumana*, *makuḷa*, or *campaka* after having set them down, he took that *sereyyaka* flower which had arrived there.
"Having taken [it], they honored it"—this is the meaning. The rest is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sereyyaka is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pupphathūpiya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Pupphathūpiya Thera begins with the words "Not far from the Himavat...

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī Buddha. Having attained maturity and reached proficiency in his own craft, he there—
Seeing no essence in the household life, he abandoned his home and entered the Himalayas.

Together with five thousand disciples who accompanied him, he developed the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments. Having built a leaf-hut near a mountain named Kukkura, he resided there.
At that time, having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, he went into the presence of the Buddha along with his disciples.
Desiring to depart but oppressed by a certain illness, he entered a leaf-hut and, having heard from his disciple concerning the power and the marks of the Buddha, became serene in mind.

Having had many flowers—campaka, asoka, tilaka, keṭaka, and others—brought from the Himālaya, he constructed a stupa and worshipped it as if it were the Buddha. Having passed away, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. Then...
Those disciples, having prepared his funeral pyre, went into the presence of the Buddha and reported what had occurred.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the situation with his Buddha-eye, made it manifest through his knowledge of the future.
Later, in this present dispensation of the Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī; having reached maturity, by the power of his former mental impressions, [he recognized] the Teacher.
Having gained faith and gone forth, before long he became an *arhat*.
Then, recollecting his own former wholesome deeds, filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "Not far from the Himālayas," and so forth.
The meaning of that has already been explained above. "The mountain named Kukkura" refers to a mountain...
Because its peak was shaped like a dog—standing in the form of a dog—it became known as "Kukkurapabbata" (the Dog Mountain).
The meaning is that he lived near it, having constructed a leaf-hut and dwelling there together with five thousand ascetics.
Following this method, all the remaining points are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pupphathūpiya is complete.
3. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pāyasadāyaka:
"The Fully Enlightened One, golden-hued... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Pāyasadāyaka. This one, too, [was born] during the time of previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various states of existence, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a wealthy family.

Upon reaching maturity and living as a householder, he was endowed with great wealth consisting of elephants, horses, property, grain, and the seven precious gems; moreover, he was possessed of faith in the fruit of kamma.
Having gained faith, he had about a thousand golden bowls made, filled each with a thousand portions of milk-rice porridge, and taking them all, he went to the Simbali grove.
At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī, emitting six-colored rays, was walking back and forth, having established a walkway in the sky. When the merchant saw that marvel, he...
Being exceedingly pleased, he set out the bowls, paid homage, and announced them for acceptance. Then the Blessed One, out of compassion, accepted them;
having accepted them, and in order to inspire joy in him, he partook of them together with a Saṅgha of one thousand bhikkhus, while the remaining portion was consumed by many thousands of bhikkhus.
Thus, wandering through happy destinies by virtue of that merit, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having reached maturity, he developed faith, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arahant.

Later on, reflecting upon his own wholesome deeds and recollecting them, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with "The Golden-Colored Sambuddha. This has already been explained above.
28. *Caṅkamaṃ susamārūḷho*: "He walks (*kamati*) by taking steps (*padavikkhepaṃ*) while moving about (*caḍinanto*)," thus it is called a *caṅkama*.
The meaning is that the portion of ground which serves as the support for the walking—that is, for the taking of steps—is what is named a *caṅkama*.
The connection is: "He has especially ascended (*susamārūḷho*) to this *caṅkama*. Regarding *ambare anilāyane*: "It is covered (*varīyati*) or shielded (*chādiyati*) by this," thus it is a *vara*.
They do not obstruct the *ambara*; the meaning is that it is like the sky, resembling a white cloth. It is called *anila* because there is no hiding or concealment therein.
It is called *āyana* because those possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*) go and move by means of it on all sides (*ā*).

Thus, *anilāyana* means that which is both *anila* and *āyana*. The meaning is: "they construct a walking path (*caṅkama*) in that *ambara*, in that *anilāyana*. Everywhere else, the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pāyasadāyaka is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gandhodakiya begins with the verse "Sitting in the excellent palace," etc. This [Elder] also, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to Nibbāna in various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a family of wealthy merchants.

Having attained maturity, possessing great wealth and vast enjoyments, and experiencing human happiness as if it were celestial bliss, he sat one day in an excellent palace. At that time, the Blessed One...

He wandered through the streets like the great golden Mount Meru. Seeing the Blessed One wandering there, he approached with a devout mind, paid homage, and honored him by sprinkling fragrant water over the Blessed One.
Through that merit, as he transmigrated among gods and humans, he was reborn in a certain family home during this appearance of a Buddha; having reached maturity, he lived the life of a householder.

Without clinging [to worldly things], he went forth in the presence of the Teacher, received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and by developing insight (*vipassanā*), he became an *arahant* before long.

Later, remembering his own past wholesome deeds and filled with joy, he sat down and spoke the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words "In a magnificent palace...
and so forth. In that context, "palace" (*pāsāda*) means that which produces or generates serene confidence (*pasāda*) and gladness (*somanassa*).
The meaning is that, having seen the palace—variegated with many kinds of work such as garlands, paintings, and goldwork—it produces delight in the people who enter it.
Furthermore, it is a "supreme palace" (*pāsādavara*) because it is supreme in the sense of being desirable;
the connection is that, having sat down in that supreme palace, they saw Vipassī, the supreme Victor. The rest is entirely obvious throughout.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gandhodakiya is completed.
5. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sammukhāthavika:
"When Vipassi was being born... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sammukhāthavika. This one, too, [made offerings] during the time of previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. At the age of seven, he attained perfection in his own craft;
and while living after having established a household, when the Bodhisatta Vipassī appeared, [he beheld] the marks of all Buddhas.
Appearing in the three Vedas, they prophesied both the marks of the Bodhisatta Vipassī and his future Buddhahood to the multitude of people headed by the king;
he thus pacified the minds of the people and offered many words of praise.
By that wholesome karma, after experiencing the six types of success in the sense-sphere realms, he [experienced] the successes of a wheel-turning monarch among humans.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in a noble family during this arising of a Buddha;
having reached maturity and developed faith, he went forth and before long became an Arahant. He became well known by the name Katakusala as the Elder Sammukhāthavika. 41.
Recalling his own former karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct while being born:

He said, "In Vipassi," and so forth. When Vipassi, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was being born—arising and emerging from his mother’s womb—I proclaimed, explained, and made manifest the sign, the cause, the reason for his Buddhahood;
that is, I displayed many wonders. The rest is easily understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sammukhāthavika is complete.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kusumāsaniya begins with the verse "In the city of Dhaññavati... This [Elder] also, under previous Victors...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he became one of great wealth and vast possessions;
having mastered the three Vedas and reached the pinnacle of brahminical arts, he was skilled in both his own and others' doctrines and desired to honor his parents.
Having placed five bunches of blue lotuses near himself and sitting there,
he saw the Blessed One Vipassī approaching, surrounded by the community of monks; and seeing the dense Buddha-rays of blue, yellow, and other colors, with a mind full of serene faith,
he prepared a seat, spread those flowers upon it, and had the Blessed One sit down there.
Taking all the hard and soft foods prepared for his mother’s sake in his own house, he personally served and fed the Blessed One together with his retinue.
At the conclusion of the meal, he presented him with a handful of blue lotuses.
Filled with joy, he made a formal aspiration. The Blessed One, having offered words of thanksgiving, departed. By that merit, he—
Having experienced two types of prosperity among gods and humans, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a family endowed with great wealth in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, he flourished in riches and renown; then, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth, becoming an Arahant before long.

65. Thus, at a later time, having recollected his former wholesome deeds through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *apadāna* of his former conduct, spoke the verse beginning with "In the city of Dhaññavatī.
It is called Dhaññavatī because it is a source (*ākara*) for many families of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and great landowners who are "grain-like" (*dhañña*), meaning meritorious;
or alternatively, because it is a source for the seven kinds of grain and the seven treasures, such as pearls and gems.
It is "rich in grain" (*dhaññavatī*) because it is a source (*ākara*) of things for enjoyment and use;

or alternatively, it is "rich in grain" because it is a source of monasteries, hermitages, and so forth, which are dwelling places for the "grain" of those who have exhausted their taints—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and *khīṇāsavas*. Of that "rich-in-grain" [city].

"City" (*nagara*): it is called a city because people seeking enjoyment and use resort (*patthenti*) there; or else, it is "naga" because [people] do not go away from it (*na gacchati*), [referring to] kings, crown princes, great ministers, and so forth.
A dwelling place. It is called a *nagara* because it takes (*ādadāti*) or seizes (*gaṇhāti*) the mountain;
the meaning is that a *nagara* is a delimited area surrounded by walls, moats, and so forth, which constitutes a collection of dwelling places for kings and others.
When I received the prophecy in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, at that time, in that city of Dhaññavatī—
"He was a brahmin"—this is the connection. The rest is entirely clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kusumāsaniya is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phaladāyaka.
The legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Phaladāyaka Thera begins with the words, "A reciter of the scriptures, a bearer of the mantras," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to the turning away from the round of rebirths (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) over many existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having attained maturity, he reached the pinnacle of his own craft, including the three Vedas and other branches of knowledge.

At that time, the Teacher, the leader of many thousands of brahmins, having failed to see the ultimate limit of his own crafts and perceiving no essence therein, abandoned the life of a householder and went forth as an ascetic.
Having established a hermitage not far from the Himalayas, he made his dwelling there together with his disciples. At that same time, the Blessed One Padumuttara [was wandering] for alms.
While wandering, out of compassion for him, he arrived at that place. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic’s mind was filled with serene faith;
he set aside for himself some sweet lotus fruits that had been hung from the top of a tree in a leaf-woven basket, and gave them to the Blessed One along with honey.
To cause joy to arise in the ascetic, the Blessed One consumed them while the ascetic was still looking on, and [vanished] into the sky.
Having stood there and spoken of the benefits of giving the fruit [of his gift], he departed.

75. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that merit, and having experienced both types of excellence, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth; and at only seven years of age, he attained Arahantship.

Having attained [the state of a Buddha] and having remembered the wholesome kamma performed in the past, he became filled with joy; thus, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), he spoke the verse beginning with "ajjhāyako mantadhara.
In this context, one who "thinks" (*ajjheti*) or "reflects" (*cinteti*) is an *ajjhāyi*; an *ajjhāyi* is precisely an *ajjhāyaka*.

Here, the letter *a-* [in *ajjhāyaka*] is used among the ten meanings stated as follows: "The letter *a-* [is used] in the sense of negation, in the sense of increase... [and so on] ... the letter *a-* [is used] in the sense of absence or slightness."
It functions in its presence. One who studies (*ajjheti*), reflects upon, and recites for the benefit of his pupils by means of hearing, memorizing, and so forth, is an *ajjhāyaka*;
the meaning is "a thinker. One who holds and exercises in mind all the mantras learned in the presence of a teacher is a *mantadhara*.
Regarding the phrase "one who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas": here, "Veda" refers to knowledge (*ñāṇa*); by means of that knowledge...
They are called *vedas* because they are to be known (*veditabba*) and realized (*bujjhitabba*). They are the three collections of texts known as the *Iruveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*.
One who has gone to the further shore (*pāra*), the end, the limit of those *vedas*, is a *pāragū*. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phaladāyaka.
8. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika.
The verse beginning with "On a mountain in the Himalayas" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ñāṇasaññika.

This [Elder], too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout each successive birth, [attained this state].
During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a noble family; having reached maturity, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest ascetic.
Having constructed a leaf-hut in a mountain range not far from the Himalayas, he dwelt there after attaining the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
One day, seeing a pure and white sandy bank, [he thought]: "Such purity..."
Thinking, "The Buddhas possess such perfectly pure Buddha-knowledge," he recollected both the Buddha and that knowledge and praised them.
By means of that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, having experienced both kinds of excellence, he was reborn in a certain family home during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into homelessness in the Dispensation and, before long—
Having attained *arahatta*, and recollecting the merit he had performed in the past, he became filled with joy;
proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning, "On a mountain in the Himālayas. Regarding the phrase "seeing the beautiful sand" (*pulinaṃ sobhanaṃ disvā*):

it is called "sand" (*pulina*) because it exists and remains in a state purified by a fine, even surface as if perfectly fashioned; "beautiful" refers to seeing excellent sand, [and thus] the supreme Buddha.
"Recall"—this is the meaning. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gaṇṭhipupphiya.
"Golden-hued is the Sambuddha"—this and more is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Gaṇṭhipupphiya Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit over many births, was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Not lacking in means of enjoyment and luxury, one day he [beheld] the Blessed One Vipassī.
Seeing him together with his retinue, he offered worship with flowers and parched grain as the fifth item, his mind full of serene faith.
By virtue of that very clarity of mind, he lived out his lifespan and was reborn in the world of the devas, where he enjoyed celestial splendor.
Later, having experienced human prosperity among men, he was reborn in a certain family home during this current appearance of a Buddha, endowed with faith.
Not long after going forth, he attained arahantship.

One day, recollecting the merit he had performed in the past, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming his own account of former deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*) by saying, "By means of this wholesome deed, I have reached Nibbāna," he spoke the verses beginning with "The Golden-Hued Sambuddha. All of that—
Because it follows the method explained below, the meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gaṇṭhipupphiya is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumapūjaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Padumapūjaka Thera begins with the words, "Not far from the Himālaya," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having attained maturity and reached proficiency in his own craft, there—
Seeing no essence [in worldly life], because he had appeared before the arising of a Buddha and thus had not received instruction or admonition,
he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. Having established a hermitage at a mountain called Gotamaka, not far from the Himalayas,
he developed the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, and dwelt there solely in the bliss of jhāna.
Then the Blessed One Padumuttara, having become a Buddha, went to the Himalayas out of compassion for him, in order to deliver sentient beings from saṃsāra.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic, with a mind full of faith, gathered his own disciples and had them bring lotus flowers, with which he made an offering.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence.
In this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī; having become faithful and confident, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an Arahant.
(97) Recalling his own meritorious deed, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke these verses beginning with "Not far from the Himālaya.
He said, "Gotama Mountain," because it was established as the dwelling place for many *yakkhas* and deities named Gotama.
He became well-known as "Gotama" because of his lineage (*gotra*). That which moves and stands is a mountain (*pabbata*).
That which is covered with *nāga* trees is a tree (*rukkha*), for it grows and stands. Alternatively, that which grows upward while digging into the earth is a tree;
various and manifold kinds of trees, such as the *campaka*, *kappūra*, *nāga*, *agaru*, and *candana*, are "various trees" (*nānārukkhā*); by those various trees...

The connection is: "Gotama is covered and strewn over by the mountain. Regarding the term *mahābhūtagaṇālayo*: they are called *bhūtā* because they come into being (*bhavanti*), are born (*jāyanti*), arise (*uppajjanti*), and grow (*vaḍḍhanti*).
Those that are both great (*mahantā*) and *bhūtā* are the *mahābhūtā*.
A group (*gaṇo*) or collection (*samūho*) of these *mahābhūtā* is the *mahābhūtagaṇo*. That which is the abode (*ālayo*) or foundation (*patiṭṭhā*) of the *mahābhūtagaṇo* is the *mahābhūtagaṇālayo*.
98. "In the midst of that" means that a hermitage was manifested, produced, and constructed within the interior of that mountain of Gotama. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumapūjaka is completed.
The commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter is completed.
14. The Chapter on Sobhita.
1. Explanation of the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sobhita.
"The Victor named Padumuttara," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sobhita. This [Elder] also, among the previous Buddhas...
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household life, one day, while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma, he praised Him with various kinds of hymns, his mind filled with joy and serene confidence. By that very [act]...
Having died with a mind full of joy, he was reborn among the devas;
there, having experienced divine happiness, and subsequently experiencing human happiness among humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in a noble family at Sāvatthī.
Having gone forth at the age of only seven, before long he became an arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers.

1. Later on, having recollected his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words, "The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth. Since all of that follows the method already explained below, it is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sobhita is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sudassana.
The legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Elder Sudassana begins with "On the bank of the river Vitthata," and so forth.
This [Elder] also, having performed service under previous Victors and accumulated a store of merit through various births, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household life, he lived near the river named Vitthata.
While searching for the fruit of the *pilakkhu* tree, he saw the Sammasambuddha, who was sitting on its bank like a crest of blazing fire.
With a mind full of serene faith, he cut a *ketakī* flower by its stalk as if it were a branch and, making an offering, spoke thus:
“Venerable Sir, I pay homage with this very knowledge by which you have become a Sammasambuddha, a Buddha of such great majesty.”
Then the Blessed One gave his expression of appreciation. By that merit, he was born among gods and humans, experiencing both types of excellence.
In this current arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain family home; having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an Arahant.
10. Thus, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed and filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “on the broad riverbank” while proclaiming the *apadāna* of his former conduct.
Therein, "broad" (*vitthatā*) means that which spreads out, extends, and becomes wide;
"river" (*nadī*) means that which roars, makes sound, has gone, and flows; those crossing the river, having reached this [place], are said to have "crossed."
“*Hontīti tīran*” means the bank; because of its width, it means “on the bank” or “near the bank” of that river. “*Ketakiṃ pupphitaṃ disvā*” means:
that which cuts (*chindati*) and pierces (*vijjhati*) the hand of those who grasp it with a vile manner is *ketaṃ*;
this flower belongs to that, thus it is the *ketakī* flower. The connection is: “having seen that, having cut its stalk.”
11. Regarding the phrase "Sikhino lokabandhuno": *Sikhī* means fire; he whose dense rays of six colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—are blazing like fire is *Sikhī*.
He who is the kinsman and relative of the world—that is, of the entire threefold world—is the *Lokabandhu*.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "Having cut the stalk of the *ketakī* flower, they shall worship that *Sikhī*, the *Lokabandhu*."
The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sudassana is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Candanapūjanaka.
The legend of the Venerable Cūḷa-Candanapūjaka Thera begins with the words, "On the bank of the Candabhāgā River," and so forth. This venerable one,
having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi in the Himālaya region near the river Candabhāgā, in the womb of a Kinnara, subsisting on flowers.

Clad in flowers and adorned with the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, and other scents, he dwelt like a terrestrial deity in the Himalayas, enjoying manifold pleasures such as garden sports and water sports.

At that time, the Blessed One Atthadassī, out of compassion for him, went to the Himalayas, descended from the sky, spread out his outer robe, and sat down. That kinnara beheld the Blessed One shining brilliantly...
Seeing him seated there, he honored him with fragrant sandalwood with a devout mind. The Blessed One gave him a discourse of thanksgiving.
By that merit and that joy, he lived out his full lifespan; when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
After experiencing successive successes in the six realms of sense-sphere existence, he attained the prosperity of a universal monarch among humans, as well as regional and local sovereignty.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in a noble family during this arising of a Buddha; having reached maturity and gone forth, he attained *arahantship* before long.
Recalling his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his past conduct, spoke the words beginning with "On the bank of the Candabhāgā River.
In that context, it means he was born as if having known [her] moon-like mind, taste, and disposition.

"Canda" means the moon. Because it possesses a moon-disk and water that is clear and stainless on both sides, as well as a white sandy bottom resembling a spread of pearl scales, its parts (*bhāga*) are similar to the moon;
thus it is "Candabhāgā. The meaning is: "on the bank, near that river Candabhāgā.
All the rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Candanapūjanaka is completed.
The commentary on the eighth recitation section is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pupphacchadaniya.
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Pupphacchadanīya, beginning with the words "He who was named Sunanda by name.

This [Venerable One] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation through many existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; and having reached maturity, he attained proficiency in his own crafts.

Possessing great wealth and great fame, he was devoted to giving. One day, thinking, "Let no one in all of Jambudīpa be able to say, 'I have not received a gift,' regarding these beggars," he prepared a great distribution of alms.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara was traveling through the air with his retinue. Seeing him, the brahmin’s heart was filled with faith, and he summoned his own disciples.
Having had flowers brought, he scattered them in the air as an offering. They remained, covering the entire city, for seven days.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, after experiencing happiness among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in a certain family home in Sāvatthī.
Having developed faith, he went forth into homelessness and attained Arahantship at the very moment of shaving his head. Regarding himself...
Having recollected his past karma, Sunanda, filled with joy, spoke the words beginning with "By name Sunanda," while proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
Since that follows the method already explained below, it is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pupphacchadaniya is completed.
5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rahosaññaka.
The account beginning with "Not far from the Himalayas" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rahosaññaka.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, during a period when a Buddha was absent from the world...
Born into a brahmin family in the Middle Country, he attained maturity and achieved proficiency in his own crafts; yet,
seeing no essence therein and perceiving nothing but the filling of his belly and unwholesome states such as anger,
intoxication, and pride, he abandoned the household life, entered the Himalayas, and went forth as a seer (isipabbajjā), dwelling near Mount Vasabha surrounded by many hundreds of ascetics.
Having established a hermitage and dwelling for three thousand years right there in the Himalayas, he became overcome with dejection, thinking:
"I am recognized as the teacher of so many disciples, held in high esteem, worthy of honor, and venerable; yet I have no teacher myself.
Having gathered all those disciples together, he declared that in the absence of Buddhas there can be no attainment of Nibbāna, and then he himself—
Sitting alone in a secluded place, as if sitting in the very presence of the Buddha,
he brought the perception of the Buddha to mind; having generated joy with the Buddha as its object, he sat cross-legged in the hall and,
passing away, was reborn in the Brahma-world.
