34. Having dwelt there for a long time in the bliss of *jhāna*, he was reborn in a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.

Without clinging to sensual pleasures, he went forth at the age of seven and attained *arahantship* on the very day his hair was shaved. Having become possessed of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*), he recalled his own past karma through the knowledge of previous existences (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).
With joy having arisen within him, he proclaimed the *Apadāna* of his former conduct, beginning with the words: "Not far from the Himālaya... and so forth.

"Vasabha by name is a mountain": the meaning is that it is a mountain designated as "Vasabha" because, apart from the Himavanta mountains, it is the highest and most excellent among all other mountains.
The rest is entirely clear in meaning everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Rahosaññaka is completed.
6. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Campakapupphiya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Campakapupphiya begins with the verse: "Shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower...

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the attainment of liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, [served] Vessabhu...
During the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity and attaining proficiency in his own crafts, seeing no essence therein, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic.
Dwelling in the forest, he made offerings of *campaka* flowers brought by his disciples to the Blessed One Vessabhū. The Blessed One gave him a discourse of thanksgiving.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that very wholesome karma, he experienced both types of excellence.
Having been reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha, and having reached maturity, he did not cling to the household life due to the power of his former mental impressions;
instead, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an Arhat.

41. Thus, at a later time, having remembered his own former meritorious deed and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with "Shining like a *kaṇikāra* tree," while proclaiming the account of his past conduct. In that context, "like a *kaṇikāra*" refers to the *pāṭali* tree;
for when all its leaves and foliage have fallen away and it is ready to take up flowers, it forms a cluster (*kaṇṇikā*) and takes up flower buds in the shape of a cluster.

"Pakatā" means *kaṇikāra*; it should be understood that although it ought to be called "kaṇṇikāra," it is stated as "kaṇikāra" by eliding one of the two *ṇa*-sounds according to the rules of phonology (*nirutti*).
The meaning is: they saw the Buddha shining like that flowering *kaṇikāra* tree. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Campakapupphiya is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Atthasandassaka begins with the verse: "Seated in a spacious hall... This [Elder] also, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit over many lifetimes, he was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in his own crafts; however, seeing no essence therein, he abandoned his home and went to the Himalayas.
There, having built a leaf-hut in a delightful place, he dwelt there out of compassion for sentient beings.
Having seen the Blessed One Padumuttara who had arrived at the Himālaya, with a mind full of faith, he paid homage with the five-fold prostration and praised him with words of eulogy.
By that merit, having lived out his lifespan and passed away, he was reborn in the Brahma world.
Later, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family; having reached maturity, he [approached] the Teacher.
Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he acquired faith, went forth into homelessness, and attained *arahantship*.
47. Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning, "Seated in a spacious hall," and so forth.
In that context, "in a spacious hall" (*visālamāḷe*) means a spacious, extensive, wide, and large hall; thus it is called a "spacious hall."
The connection [of the verse] is: "Seated and sitting in that spacious hall, I saw the Leader of the World. This is indeed easy for them to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Atthasandassaka is complete.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekapasādaniya:
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Ekapasādaniya Thera, beginning with "Nārada" as my name.

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having cultivated skillfulness through many births, was reborn into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
Known by the name Kesava, he reached maturity, abandoned the household life, and went forth; while living there, one day—
Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, with a mind full of serene confidence, he raised his joined palms and departed, filled with exceeding joy and gladness.
Having lived out his lifespan, he passed away with that very same gladness and was reborn among the devas;
there, having experienced celestial splendors, he was reborn among humans, where he experienced worldly success, and then in this [life]...
Having been reborn in a certain noble family during the arising of a Buddha, he attained maturity, gained faith in the Teacher, and went forth into homelessness;
before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed, he was filled with joy and [began] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (the Legends of Former Deeds).
Proclaiming this, Nārada said, "Thus is my name," and so forth. Therein, "Nārada" means that because his body is pure by birth, there is no *raja*—dust or impurity—for him; thus he is "Nārada.
By changing the letter *ja* to *da*, "Nārada" is his family-given name (*kuladattika-nāma*).
"Kesava" means that because he was born in the Kisavaccha clan, he is "Kesava. Thus people know me as "Nārada-Kesava."
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekapasādaniya.
9. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sālapupphadāyaka.
“‘The King of Beasts was there at that time,’ etc., is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Sālapupphadāyaka.

This [being], having performed meritorious deeds in various previous lives and accumulated a store of wholesome karma, was reborn in a lion’s womb in the Himalayas due to a certain lapse in his karma;
he lived there surrounded by many lions. At that time, the Blessed One Sikhī, out of compassion for him,”
He went to the Himavat mountains. Seeing that he had approached, the lion, with a serene mind, took a *sāla* flower together with its stalk and buds by breaking off a branch and offered it to him.
The Blessed One gave him a blessing of thanksgiving.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, in this [life]...
"Born into a noble family at the time of a Buddha’s appearance, having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and attained *arahantship*.
Remembering his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words:

'At that time I was the king of deer... In this context, they are called "deer" (*migā*) because they go toward death (*maraṇaṃ gacchanti*), or alternatively, because they seek out grass (*ghāsaṃ magganti*).

They are called *migā* because they seek (*gavesanti*). A king of deer is a *migarāja*. Although he was the king of all four-footed creatures, he is called "king of deer" by beginning with the term "deer" for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition.
The meaning is: "At the time when I saw the Blessed One and, having broken off a branch of a *sāla* tree laden with flowers, offered it as worship, I was the king of deer."
62. "Sakosaṃ pupphamāharin" means that I brought a *sāla* flower together with its stalk to offer it; this is the meaning. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sālapupphadāyaka is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Piyālaphaladāyaka.
"Parodhako was then... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Piyālaphaladāyaka.

This [Venerable] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was born into a hunter's family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi;
in a certain mountain cave in the Himalayas, he slaughtered deer.
He lived there, making his livelihood by hunting. At that time, seeing the Blessed One Sikhi who had come there, he paid homage morning and evening with a devout mind.
Seeing no other gift to offer, he gathered some sweet piyāla fruits and gave them to Him.
The Blessed One partook of them. That hunter’s body was continuously suffused with rapture directed toward the Buddha.
With his mind detached from evil deeds and subsisting on roots and fruits, he passed away before long and was reborn in the world of the devas.

Having experienced divine splendors there, and having experienced various kinds of prosperity among humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance into a householders’ family. Upon reaching maturity and establishing a domestic life, while living there—
"Being dissatisfied, I abandoned my home and went forth in the presence of the Teacher; having developed insight, I attained Arahantship before long.
Recalling the deed of giving fruit that I had performed, I was filled with joy and spoke this account of my former conduct, beginning with the words:
'At that time I was a hunter... In this context, when I gave a *piyāla* fruit and [set] my mind...
"I was then a harasser"—this is the connection [of the verse]. "Harasser" (*parodhaka*) means one who obstructs other beings, one who causes them affliction.
Where it should have been "pararodhaka," the letter *r* of the preceding word has been elided, and thus it is stated as "parodhaka.
"I served the Leader"—the meaning is that I invited and pleased that Teacher, the bringer of Nibbāna, saying, "Venerable Sir, please partake of this fruit. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Piyālaphaladāyaka is completed.
The commentary on the Fourteenth Chapter is completed.
15. The Chapter on the Umbrella.
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Aticchiya The passage beginning with “When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna” is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Aticchiya.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, [was born during the time of] Atthadassi...

Having been reborn in a certain noble family during the time of the Blessed One, because he had not seen the Blessed One while he was still living, he thought at the time of the Blessed One’s parinibbāna,
"Alas, what a loss for me! Having resolved, "I shall make my birth fruitful," he had a parasol-with-a-parasol-canopy (chattādhichatta) constructed and worshipped it,
enshrining within it a relic-chamber containing a bodily relic of that Blessed One.
In a later period, having had a flower-parasol made, he honored that very same relic chamber.
By virtue of that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, he was reborn in this current arising of a Buddha into a householders’ family.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and taking up a meditation subject, he strove and before long attained Arahatship.

1. Having recollected his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he spoke the words beginning with "When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
In this context, *chattātichatta* means: that which protects or shields from the heat is a *chatta* (parasol);
an *atichatta* for a *chatta* is a parasol placed above a parasol, a parasol upon a parasol. Above and above the parasol...
"Chatta" means a parasol. "Abhiropayim thūpamhi" means: it is called a *thūpa* because it is piled up (*thūpiyati*) or heaped together;
or else, it is called a *thūpa* because, by way of its stability, it attains growth, increase, and abundance, and thus stands firm.
In that *thūpa*, I have caused a parasol to be placed; the meaning is that I have specially raised it and honored it by way of placing it one above the other.

2. "Having made a floral canopy" means having made a canopy—an awning above the umbrella—using many fragrant, blossoming flowers, and thus having honored [the Buddha]; this is the meaning. The rest is everywhere of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Aticchattiya is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Thambhāropaka.
"Nibbute lokanāthamhi... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Thambhāropaka Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Dhammadassi.
Being faithful and confident, when that Blessed One had attained final *parinibbāna*, [he...]
Having driven a pillar into the courtyard of the relic chamber, he raised a banner. Having tied together many *jātisumana* flowers, he climbed up by means of a ladder and made offerings.
After living out his full lifespan and passing away, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing both types of excellence.
Honored everywhere during this appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a certain noble family;
from his childhood onwards, he was worthy of veneration, possessed firm faith in the Teaching, and having gone forth, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Recalling his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), beginning with the words: "When the Lord of the World had passed away... and so forth.

In this context, "when the Protector of the World had attained Nibbāna" means that when the Teacher—the Lord of the entire world, the preeminent one, and the refuge—had attained Parinibbāna through the dissolution of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*), he had become invisible, like the flame of an extinguished lamp.

"Dhammadassī Narāsabha" means one who sees the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; or alternatively, one who sees the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

"Dhammadassī" means one whose nature is to see and whose nature is to perceive the Dhamma; "narāsabha" means the preeminent, supreme bull among men; "Dhammadassīnarāsabha" refers to that Dhammadassī who is a bull among men—in him, Dhammadassīnarāsabha.
"I raised a banner on a pillar" means that having driven a pillar into the ground within the courtyard of the cetiya, I raised a banner there.
"Having bound [it], they placed it"—this is the meaning.
6. "Having caused a ladder to be built": that by which one leans, goes, or ascends to the top is a *nisseṇi* (ladder);
having caused that *nisseṇi* to be measured out, constructed, and bound, they ascended the best of stūpas—this is the connection. [The word] *jātipupphaṃ*.
"Having taken" means: it is called *jātisumana* because it produces a beautiful mind (*sumana*) in people even as it is being born;
thus, while it should be called *jātisumanapuppha*, the word *sumana* has been elided for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse, and it is therefore called *jātipuppha*.
Having taken that *jātisumanapuppha* and having strung them together, I offered them upon the stupa.
"Having raised it up, they honored it"—this is the meaning. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Thambhāropaka is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vedikāraka.
"Nibbute lokanāthamhi... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Vedikāraka Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating merits conducive to the attainment of *vivaṭṭa* (the turning away from rebirth) in various existences, was reborn at the time of the Blessed One Piyadassi into a family endowed with great wealth. Having reached maturity and established a household life, he...

Having placed his faith in the Teacher who had attained Nibbāna, he caused a railing to be made for the Teacher’s stupa; having filled it with the seven kinds of jewels, he performed a great offering.

By that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans over many hundreds of thousands of births, he was worthy of worship, possessing great wealth and great enjoyments, and after experiencing both types of happiness, he was born into a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Reborn endowed with great wealth, he went forth and, through diligent effort, became an Arahant before long.
One day, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed in the past, he was filled with joy;

proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning, "When the Lord of the World had passed away," etc. The meaning of that has already been explained above. [In the phrase] "Piyadassī, the best of men..."

"Piyadassī" means one whose appearance is dear and brings joy; the meaning is that his appearance is excellent, generating great confidence in the multitude through his height, proportions, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide halo. "Naruttama" means the supreme among men;
thus, he is both Piyadassī and the supreme among men, i.e., Piyadassīnaruttama. When that Piyadassīnaruttama had attained Nibbāna, [the relics were placed] in the relic-chamber.
The connection is: "I had a railing made. The meaning is: "At the end [of the structure], for the purpose of supporting the flowers, I had a circular railing made.

11. "Surrounded by jewels": that which shines, glows, and radiates light is a *maṇi*; or alternatively, that which has gone from here, proceeding while filling the minds of people and producing joy, is a *maṇi*.
[It was surrounded] by many kinds [of gems], such as natural-colored gems (*jātiraṅgamaṇi*) and beryl gems (*veḷuriyamaṇi*).
The meaning is that they surrounded [the stupa] with a circular railing made of jewels and performed the supreme great worship. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vedikāraka is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saparivāriya.
“Padumuttaro nāma jino” and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Saparivāriya Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) over many births, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara;
upon reaching maturity, he became one of great wealth and great possessions. Then, during the time of Padumuttara...
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the great multitude enshrined his relics, erected a great stupa, and paid him honor.
At that time, this lay devotee constructed a shrine for the stupa out of sandalwood and performed a great offering ceremony.
By virtue of that merit, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence, and now, during the arising of this Buddha—
Having been reborn in a certain noble family, he performed wholesome deeds and, upon reaching maturity, went forth into the teaching out of faith.
Before long, he became an Arhat.
Later on, remembering his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former life, spoke this narrative of his previous conduct:
He spoke the words beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara. In this context, "omatta" means a state of inferiority, lowliness, or suffering;
the meaning is: "I do not see, nor do I know, nor have I ever before seen a state of lowliness. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saparivāriya is completed.
5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Umāpupphiya.
The verse beginning with "When he who was honored by the world had attained Nibbāna... is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Umāpupphiya.
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Siddhattha...
Reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached maturity, established a household, and lived there.
While a festival for the shrine of the Parinibbūta Blessed One was being held, he took an *umā* flower with the color of a sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*) and offered it as worship.
By that merit, wandering only through happy destinies and experiencing celestial and human prosperity in each successive birth, he...
He was generally blue-complexioned, well-born, and possessed of great wealth. In this present age of a Buddha, he was reborn into a wealthy family;
having reached maturity, he conceived faith and went forth into homelessness, and before long he attained Arhatship.
21. Recalling his past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct beginning with "When the World-Honored One had passed away," and so forth.
It has been said. Therein, "honored by the world" (*lokamahita*) means one who is honored and worshipped by the worlds; thus, the connection is:

"when that Siddhattha, the Blessed One, who was honored by the world, had attained final Nibbāna. Regarding "the recipient of offerings" (*āhutipatiṭṭhā*): "offerings" (*āhutino*) refers to acts of worship and honor;
he is worthy of receiving those offerings, thus he is "the recipient of offerings. This is a compound formed with the elision of the *ta*-suffix (*aluttaka-tanta-samāsa*).
"In him, the Blessed One, the receiver of offerings, having attained final nibbāna"—this is the meaning.

22. *Umāpuppha*: It is called *umāpuppha* because it flowers and blooms, emitting a blue luster higher and higher; the meaning is that, taking that *umāpuppha*, they performed an offering at the cetiya. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the legend (*apadāna*) of the Elder Umāpupphiya is completed.
6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Anulepadāyaka.
The passage beginning with "Anomadassīmunino" is the Apadāna of the venerable elder Anulepadāyaka.
This [elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Anomadassī...
Born at that time into a noble family of great wealth and vast possessions, he had a railing constructed around the base of that Blessed One’s Bodhi tree,
had it plastered with lime, and arranged for a bed of sand so finely spread that it was like a silver celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
By virtue of that merit, having attained happiness, in birth after birth he appeared in silver celestial mansions, silver houses, and silver palaces.
Having experienced happiness, he was reborn in a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he placed his faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and applied himself to insight meditation; before long, he became an Arahant.
Later on, he wondered, "What wholesome deed did I perform to attain this distinction? and by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), [he investigated].

Having recollected in succession and having known the wholesome deeds performed in the past, he became filled with joy; thus, while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), he spoke the verse beginning with "Anomadassīmunino.

Therein, "Anomadassī" refers to one whose vision (*dassana*) is not inferior (*anoma*)—that is, whose body is beautiful and worthy of being seen—because his body is resplendent and radiant with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura.
"Sundaradassano" means "of beautiful appearance. "Having given a lump of lime" means having had a railing made for the Bodhi-house and applied a coating of lime throughout the entire Bodhi-house.
"They performed hand-work" means having fashioned hand-boards from heartwood, they performed the polishing work with those hands. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Anulepadāyaka is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggadāyaka begins with the verse “Having crossed the river...”; this [Elder] also [lived] under the previous Victors.

Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merit over many existences for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, he was reborn into a family esteemed by the world during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.

As he grew up and lived the life of a householder, one day, seeing the Blessed One crossing a certain river and proceeding through the forest, his heart was filled with serene faith, and he thought: "Now..."
Thinking, "It is fitting that I should level the path for the Blessed One," he took a pickaxe and a basket,
leveled the Blessed One’s route, scattered sand over it, and having bowed at the Blessed One’s feet, he said: "Venerable Sir, by this act of adorning the path,
may I be worthy of honor in every place where I am reborn, and may I attain Nibbāna."
He made an aspiration. The Blessed One, saying words of appreciation, "May your intention be fulfilled," departed.
By that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was honored everywhere.
Now, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a prominent family; having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth, and by increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), [attained realization].
Having attained *arahatta* before long and having directly realized his own past karma, he became filled with joy.

While proclaiming the account of his former deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Having crossed over the river" (*uttaritvāna nadikaṃ*). Therein, it is called a *nadī* because it makes a sound (*nadati*) as it flows;

a *nadikā* is simply a small river (*nadī*). The meaning is: "having crossed over," that is, having passed beyond, that *nadikā*. "Taking up a spade and a basket" (*kudālapiṭakamādāya*)... [text continues].
What is called "earth" (pathavī) is that which is capable of being split, crushed, or cut; thus it is a "pickaxe" (kudāla).
A "basket" (piṭaka) is what carries soil, sand, and so forth, a vessel made from palm leaves, rattan, bamboo, and the like.
"Pickaxe and basket" (kudālapiṭaka) means taking and holding both the pickaxe and the basket. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggadāyaka is completed.
8. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phalakadāyaka begins with the verse: "In a former time, I was a cartwright... This [Elder] also, among the Buddhas of the past...
Having performed his duties and accumulated a store of merit through many successive existences, he was reborn into a family of carpenters during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
With faith in the Triple Gem, he fashioned a support-board out of sandalwood and offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One pronounced a blessing of thanksgiving for him.
37. Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that merit, he experienced both types of excellence at all times, his mind nourished with happiness.
Having been reborn in a noble family during this arising of a Buddha and having attained maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma;
inspired with faith, he went forth and, through diligent effort, before long attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having reached [this state] and recalled his own past karma, he became filled with joy; then, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he said:

"In the past, I was a maker of vehicles," and so forth. Therein, "maker of vehicles" (*yānakāra*) means: that by which one goes to whatever desired place is a "vehicle" (*yāna*); one who makes that is a "maker of vehicles.
"In the past" (*pure*) means at the time of seeing the Buddha, I was a maker of vehicles—this is the meaning. *Candanaṃ*.
"Having made a board": it is called *candana* because it gladdens (*candati*) or allays feverish distress (*pariḷāha*).

Alternatively, it is *candana* because they anoint the body with it for the sake of fragrance (*sugandhavāsanattha*). Having made that [board] into a support-board (*ālambanaphalaka*), he gave it to the Teacher, the Friend of the World (*lokabandhu*).
"Friend of the World" means one who has become a kinsman and relative to the entire world; the meaning is that he gave it to that Teacher, the Friend of the World. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Phalakadāyaka is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vaṭaṃsakiya begins with the verse:
"He who was named Sumedha... This [Elder] also, among the former Lords of Sages...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Upon reaching maturity, he established a household;
however, seeing the defects therein, he abandoned his home and went forth as a forest ascetic, dwelling in the great forest. At that time, Sumedha...

The Blessed One arrived at that forest out of a desire for seclusion. Then, upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic, with a mind full of faith, took a blooming *saḷala* flower, tied it into the shape of a crest-ornament, placed it at the feet of the Blessed One, and made an offering.
The Blessed One offered words of appreciation for the sake of his mental clarity. By that merit, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Having experienced both kinds of prosperity while wandering in saṃsāra, he was born in this present age of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, having become faithful and confident, he went forth into homelessness and before long became an Arhat.
Later on, remembering his past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former deeds, said:

"Named Sumedha," and so forth, has been stated. "Cultivating seclusion" means that, having abandoned the state of being crowded by people, he entered—that is, went deep into—the great forest while cultivating, increasing, and making much of both seclusion from people and seclusion of mind.
The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vaṭaṃsakiya is completed.
10. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka:
"Of the Blessed One Sumedha," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka. This one, too, [arose] among the Buddhas of the past...

Having performed his duties and accumulated a store of merit over many existences for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha into a household of laypeople.
Upon reaching maturity, endowed with great wealth, he gained faith in the Teacher;
having heard the Dhamma, he had a couch made of the seven precious gems fashioned for that Teacher and performed a great act of worship. He...
By that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was honored everywhere.

In due course, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth. Having reached maturity and established a household, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma;
filled with faith, he went forth into homelessness and, before long, attained Arahantship. By the name of the merit he had performed in the past...
The Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka became well known. Just as below, so too above, the names of the elders should be understood in this same way according to the merit performed in their previous lives.
On one occasion, he recalled his own past karma and, filled with joy, proclaimed his account of former deeds.
He spoke the words beginning with "To Sumedha, the Blessed One," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "a couch was given by me":

a *pallaṅka* is that upon which one sits or rests after having assumed the cross-legged posture (*ūrubaddhāsana*); such a couch, made of the seven precious gems, was given and honored by me—this is the meaning.
"With a canopy and a coverlet" means together with a canopy (*uttaracchada*) and together with a coverlet (*pacchada*).
"With an over-canopy" means having tied a canopy above and covered the seat with the finest cloths. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka is finished.
The commentary on the fifteenth chapter is finished.
16. The Chapter on Bandhujīvaka.
1. The Explanation of the Elder Bandhujīvaka’s Apadāna.
“Like the moon, stainless and pure,” etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Bandhujīvaka. This Venerable One...
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi. Upon reaching maturity and establishing a household life while living there,
he beheld the excellence of the Blessed One Sikhi’s physical form and, with a mind full of serene faith, took some bandhujīvaka flowers.
He made an offering at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One offered a blessing of thanksgiving (*anumodana*) for the sake of increasing his clarity of mind.
Having lived out his full lifespan, he was reborn in the world of the devas by that very merit.

After experiencing the six types of excellence in the sense-sphere heavens and the excellences among humans, such as those of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), he [encountered] this our Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

Having been reborn in a household at the time of his birth, having attained the pinnacle of physical beauty and the summit of heaven, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, conceived faith, abandoned his home, went forth, and attained *arahantship*. 1.

Recalling the wholesome kamma performed in previous lives by means of the knowledge of past existences (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), he became filled with joy and [related] this account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
Explaining this, he said, “Like the moon, stainless and pure,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:
“Like the moon, stainless and pure” means like the moon freed from the stains of the five defilements—namely, clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu;

and because the fifteen hundred stains have been abandoned, it is “stainless” (*vimala*), and because it is free from afflictions (*nikkilesa*), it is “pure” (*suddha*) and serene. [He addresses] the Sambuddha, the Crested One (*Sikhi*). Of the mud of the afflictions...
"Untroubled by way of non-existence": because of the total exhaustion of that powerful attachment known as delight-in-becoming (*nandībhava*), it is "one for whom delight-in-becoming is exhausted.
"Crossed over in the three worlds": crossed over, having transcended, from the threefold world. "Clinging" (*visattikā*): clinging is said to be craving;
the meaning is "free from craving."

2. "Nibbāpayantaṃ janatan" means causing the people—the multitude of beings—to attain *nibbāna* (extinction) and to be pacified by the absence of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*), while raining down the rain of the Dhamma.

"Saying himself crossed over from *saṃsāra*, causing all beings to cross over and transcend *saṃsāra*, a sage (*muni*) because of his knowing and realizing the four Truths—this is the connection [to] the Sambuddha Sīkhī."

"Contemplating in the forest" (*vanasmiṃ jhāyamānaṃ*) means contemplating, reflecting, and developing with the mind by means of contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*);

the meaning is "in the midst of the forest. "Having seen the Sage, the Crested One (*sikhī munim*)" is the connection; it refers to one whose mind is one-pointed (*ekaggaṃ*), whose mind is concentrated (*ekaggacittaṃ*), and whose mind is well-established and fixed upon the object (*susamāhitaṃ*).
3. "Bandhujīvaka flowers" means: the *bandhu* (kinsmen) are one's relatives; their *jīvaka* (life-sustainer) is the flesh and blood of the heart.
A *bandhujīvaka* flower is a flower whose color is identical to that flesh and blood of the heart.
Having taken such a *bandhujīvaka* flower, they honored the World-Kinsman Sikhin—this is the meaning. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bandhujīvaka is finished.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Tambapupphiya begins with the verse: "Appointed to foreign service... This Venerable One...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a poor family due to an unwholesome deed committed in the past during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassi.
Upon reaching maturity, he sustained his livelihood by performing work for others on wages. Living thus in hardship, he...
Having committed an offense against others, he fled out of fear of death and entered a forest. Upon reaching that place, he saw a *pāṭalibodhi* tree;
having paid homage to it and swept around it, he saw a copper-colored flower on one of its trees.

He plucked all those blossoms from their stalks and performed an offering to the Bodhi tree. Having inspired confidence in his heart there, he paid homage and sat down, folding his legs in the cross-legged posture.
At that moment, those men followed him step by step and arrived at that place.
When he saw them, while still reflecting upon the Bodhi tree, he fled and fell into a terrifying mountain precipice, where he died.
Because he had recollected the worship of the Bodhi tree, through that very joy and gladness, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and others.

Having experienced the prosperity of the sense-sphere realms and having enjoyed the excellence of universal monarchs and other high positions among humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma;
with a mind full of serene confidence, he went forth into homelessness. Not long thereafter, having become an Arahant and recollecting his own past karma, he was filled with joy.

While elucidating his own past conduct (*pubbacarita-apadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "engaged in the transport of others' goods. In this context, "others' works" (*parakamma*) refers to the tasks of others;
the meaning is that he was "engaged," "joined," or "appointed" in their "transport" (*āyana*), which is to say, in their performance, carrying, and maintenance. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tambapupphiya is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vīthisammajjaka.
The Apadāna of the venerable Elder Vīthisammajjaka begins with the verse: "The rising sun shines forth...
This [Elder] also had performed his duties under previous Buddhas; having accumulated a store of merit over many hundreds of births, he [was born during the time of] the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having been reborn in a noble family at the proper time and living the life of a householder, he saw the Blessed One being led along the street while it was being decorated by the city-dwellers.
With a mind full of serene faith, he leveled the street and raised a banner there.
By that very merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, having experienced both kinds of excellence, in this [life]...
Having been reborn in a certain family at the time of a Buddha’s appearance, and having attained maturity, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma;
having gained faith and a heart full of great reverence, he went forth into homelessness. Having received full ordination, he became an Arahant not long thereafter.
Recalling his own past karma and knowing it through direct experience, he proclaimed the account of his former conduct, beginning with the verse: "The rising sun... and so forth.
In this context, "rising" means ascending; "possessing a hundred rays" (sataraṃsi) refers to having a hundredfold radiance.
The phrase "like the sun possessing a hundred rays" is merely a conventional designation for the teaching; the meaning is that he was like the sun with its many hundreds of thousands of beams.

"Like the radiant moon with yellow rays" means that having seen the Fully Enlightened One—who possesses yellow rays because his radiance has contracted—just as the moon-disk is radiant and powerful, the meaning is established. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vīthisammajjaka is completed.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kakkārupupphapūjaka begins with the verse:
"I was a son of the gods... This also [is the account] of the venerable Elder Kakkārupupphapūjaka.
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulated a store of merit through various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi as a deity dwelling on earth.
Upon seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhi, he took a *dibbakakkāru* flower and offered it in worship.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of thirty-one eons, he experienced both types of happiness.
Having experienced [the results of his deeds], he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and before long became an Arahant.

Having directly realized his own past karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the narrative of his former conduct, saying, "I am a son of the gods," and so forth. In that context, they "divine" (dibbanti) means they sport.
"With the five divine strands of sensual pleasure" means: *devā* (gods); *devaputta* (son of a god) means one who is the son of gods, or a god himself as a son;

being such a *devaputta*, existing [as one], I took a divine *kakkāru* flower and, having grasped it in a special manner, offered it to the Blessed One Sikhī—this is the meaning. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kakkārupupphapūjaka is completed.
5. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mandāravapupphapūjaka begins with the verse:
"I was a son of the gods... This too [is the account] of the Venerable Elder Mandāravapupphapūjaka.
The Elder, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi as a deity dwelling on the earth. Upon seeing the Blessed One Sikhi,
his mind became filled with serene faith, and he made an offering of celestial mandārava flowers.
25. Thus, everything beginning with "By that merit... is to be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the immediately preceding Elder.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mandāravapupphapūjaka is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kadambapupphiya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Thera Kadambapupphiya begins with the words, "Not far from the Himālaya," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various births, was reborn into a certain family when the world was empty of a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having reached maturity and lived the life of a householder, he perceived the peril therein.
Having abandoned the household life and gone forth into the ascetic order, he dwelt having established a hermitage on the mountain named Kukkuṭa near the Himālayas.
There, seeing seven paccekabuddhas, he gathered blossoming kadamba flowers with a devout mind and offered them to those paccekabuddhas.
They, in turn, offered words of thanksgiving beginning with, "May what was wished for and prayed for... and so forth.

30. Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by means of that merit and having experienced both types of excellence, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha.

Upon reaching maturity, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and not long thereafter became an Arahant. Recalling his former deed, he was filled with joy.
While elucidating the *apadāna* of his former conduct, he said, "Not far from the Himālaya," and so forth. That has already been explained.
As for the mountain named Kukkuṭa: because it possesses mountain peaks on both sides shaped like the crests of a cock (*kukkuṭacūḷa*), it received the designation "Kukkuṭa.
It stands firm, appearing distinctively, thus it is called a "mountain" (*pabbata*). "At the foot of that mountain" means at the base of that mountain.
Near that mountain. "Seven Buddhas dwell" means that seven Paccekabuddhas dwell in a leaf-hut at the foot of that Kukkuṭapabbata mountain. 31.
"Like the risen king of lamps": the king of lamps is the lamp-king; [it refers to] all the lamps, which are like shining stars.

The meaning is "the king Canda" (the Moon). Alternatively, because he shines throughout all four continents—namely Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, and Uttarakuru—as well as the two thousand minor islands, he is called the "Moon" and the "King of Lamps" due to his pervading radiance.
Having seen that flowering *kadamba* tree, which was like the moon risen in the sky, [he took] a flower from it...
Having picked them up with both hands and grasped them firmly, I scattered them over the seven Paccekabuddhas;
"I scattered" means I thoroughly covered them, honoring them with reverence. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Kadambapupphiya* Thera-apadāna is complete.
7. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tiṇasūlaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Tiṇasūlaka begins with the words, "Not far from the Himalayas...
This elder, having accumulated the equipment of merit under previous Victors and amassing wholesome deeds in each successive birth, lived during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī.
Having been reborn in a noble family and established a household life, he perceived its faults therein and, abandoning it, went forth as an ascetic.
While dwelling near the Himalayas, he saw the Fully Enlightened One, Sikhi, who was living on the mountain named Bhūtagaṇa and cultivating solitude;
with a mind full of faith, he took a flower from a blade of grass and offered it at the Buddha’s feet. The Buddha, too—
He offered his appreciation for that.

35. By virtue of that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a family of great wealth in Sāvatthī; and upon reaching maturity, [he entered] the Teaching.
Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), he attained *arahantship* before long.
Recalling his former karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words: "Not far from the Himalayas...
The mountain named Bhūtagaṇa is so called because it is like a dwelling place, being the abode for hosts of spirits (*bhūtagaṇa*), that is, groups of gods and *yakkhas*.

And because it exists as an unchanging mass, the mountain is called Bhūtagaṇa; the meaning is that in it dwells the Conqueror, the Buddha who has conquered Māra, alone and without a second, abiding in divine, brahmic, and noble postures and modes of conduct. 36.
For ninety-nine thousand kappas he was not reborn in the states of deprivation, by virtue of the fruit of having performed that offering of grass, thorns, and flowers.
The meaning is that, for ninety-nine thousand eons without interruption, he was not subject to rebirth in the lower realms;
being liberated from the four states of misery, he was reborn only in the attainment of heavenly bliss. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Tiṇasūlaka* Thera Apadāna is completed.
8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nāgapupphiya.
The account beginning with "He who was known by the name Suvaccha" is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Nāgapupphiya.

This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and Bulls (Buddhas), accumulated in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in the three Vedas and other branches of his own craft;
however, seeing no essence therein, he entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life, and spent his time in the bliss of meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*).
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, out of compassion for him—

He went there. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic—being skilled in the treatises on marks and being inspired by the Blessed One’s perfection of physical marks and form—paid homage and stood with palms joined in reverence.

Because he had not descended from the sky and no offerings of honor had been made, he departed through the air just as he was. Then that ascetic, together with his disciples, gathered *nāgapuṣpa* flowers.
With that flower, he honored the path leading toward the direction where the Blessed One had gone.

By that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing both types of excellence and being honored everywhere, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during this appearance of a Buddha; and as he grew up, he became endowed with faith.
Having gone forth and beautifying the Dispensation through his observance of the proper conduct, he soon became an Arahant.
Reflecting, "By what wholesome deed was this supramundane attainment obtained by me? and perceiving his past karma directly, he experienced great joy.
Recalling his former life, he spoke these words beginning with "By the name of Suvaccho," while proclaiming the account of his previous conduct.
In this context, he is called "Vaccha" because he was born in the Vaccha clan, and since he was a beautiful Vaccha, he is "Suvaccha.
By name, he was a brahmin named Suvaccha who had mastered the mantras; the meaning is that he had reached the pinnacle of the entire body of mantra literature, such as the three Vedas.
The remainder is of plain meaning, as it follows the method explained below.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nāgapupphiya is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Punnāgapupphiya begins with the verse "Having entered the forest grove... This [Elder] also, under previous Victors...

Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Phussa into a hunter’s family.
Having entered the great forest, he saw a *punnāga* flower in full bloom there;
because he was endowed with the necessary causes, through the joy inspired by the Buddha as his object, he recollected the Blessed One and [offered] that flower together with its calyx.
Having gathered sand and fashioned a stupa, he made offerings to it.
By that merit, for ninety-two eons, he experienced exclusively the prosperity of gods and humans without interruption.
Now, in this current arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in a family of great wealth in Sāvatthī; and as he grew up, by the power of his former mental impressions (*pubbavāsanā*), he...
Having gained faith in the Dispensation and gone forth, he strove and before long became an Arahant.

Recalling the wholesome deeds performed in the past, he was filled with joy; and as he proclaimed his own account of former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning, "Entering the forest and the woods," and so forth.
Since all of that has already been explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Punnāgapupphiya is completed.
10. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kumudadāyaka begins with the verse "Not far from the Himalayas," etc. This elder, too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout many births,
he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara as a bird named Kukuttha in a great lake near the Himalayas;
although he was a bird due to some unwholesome karma, he possessed great intelligence by virtue of his previously accumulated merit.
He was skilled in both merit and demerit, virtuous, and abstained from taking life as his food.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara came through the air and walked back and forth near him.
Then, seeing the Blessed One, the bird, with a mind full of faith, took a white water-lily and offered it at the Blessed One’s feet. The Blessed One, for the purpose of producing joy in him—
Having accepted it, he offered a blessing of thanksgiving.
By that merit, having experienced the happiness of the dual excellence among both gods and humans, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a certain family in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, possessing great wealth and vast enjoyments, [he placed his faith] in the Three Jewels.
Having gained faith upon hearing the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he went forth into homelessness.

Not long after, having become an Arahant and directly perceiving his own past karma, he was filled with joy. Recounting the account of his former deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Not far from the Himālaya...
Regarding the phrase *padumuppalasañchanne*: here, it refers to a white lotus (*setapaduma*) that is fully covered by a hundred petals.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "And there was a great natural lake that was completely filled, dense, and covered with three blue, red, and white lotuses, as well as *paduma* and *uppala* flowers.
"Covered with white lotuses" (*puṇḍarīkasamotthaṭo*) means it was covered and filled with white lotuses, which are red lotuses (*rattapaduma*).
The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kumudadāyaka is completed.
The commentary on the sixteenth chapter is completed.
17. The Chapter on Excellent Service (*Supāricariyavagga*).
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Supāricariya.
The account beginning with "Paduma by name" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Supāricariya.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under the pre-eminent sages of former times and accumulating merit conducive to liberation in various states of existence, [served] Padumuttara...
At that time, having been reborn in the yakkha realm, he went to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himalayas.
Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma to the devas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and nāgas, his mind became serene; joining both hands together, he clapped them and paid homage.
By that merit, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the higher celestial worlds. Having experienced divine bliss there, he [was later reborn] among humans.
Having experienced the prosperity of a universal monarch and other such attainments, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a householder’s family at Sāvatthī.
Wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, he placed his faith in the Three Jewels;
having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he conceived faith, went forth into homelessness, and before long attained arahantship.
1. On one occasion, having recollected his own former karma and being filled with joy, he spoke the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "He who by name was Paduma...

Therein, "Paduma" refers to the Blessed One who, at the time of setting down his foot, caused a lotus to spring up from the earth and receive the sole of his foot; by that sign, the Blessed One was designated as "Paduma."
"Gone" here refers to the Blessed One Padumuttara. The connection is that the Blessed One, having departed from his dwelling-place in the forest and entered the midst of the woods, taught the Dhamma.

"The assembly of yakkhas" means there was a gathering of deities; such is the meaning. "They looked on for a while" means that at the time of that teaching they looked on intently; the meaning is that they became characterized by especially keen observation. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Supāricariya is complete.
2. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kaṇaverapupphiya begins with the verse: "The Blessed One named Siddhattha... This too...
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he was reborn into a pure family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a guardian of the royal inner apartments. At that time, the Blessed One Siddhattha, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, entered the royal street.
Then, as he was walking along, that guardian of the inner apartments saw the Blessed One and, with a mind full of serene faith—
Having offered a *kaṇavera* flower to the Blessed One and paid homage, he stood there.
By that merit, after experiencing only the attainments of happy destinies, he was reborn in a certain family during this arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and before long became an *arahant*.

7. Thus, having remembered the wholesome deeds performed in the past and having become joyful, Siddhattha—the Blessed One—spoke the words beginning with “Siddhattha by name,” proclaiming the *Apadāna* of his former conduct. Since all of that has already been explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kaṇaverapupphiya is complete.
3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Khajjakadāyaka.
This is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Khajjakadāyaka, beginning with the words "Of Tissa, the Blessed One.

This [Venerable] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, was reborn into a family of pure status during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Having seen the Blessed One, with a mind full of serene confidence, he offered various fruits such as mango and rose-apple.
He gave sweet fruits, coconuts, and fried cakes. The Blessed One, for the sake of increasing his faith, consumed them while he was looking on.

By that merit, having experienced only the attainments of happy realms, he was reborn in a noble family at Sāvatthī during this appearance of a Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Having conceived faith and great reverence, he went forth into homelessness; adorning the Dispensation by his observance of the proper conduct (*vatta-paṭipatti*), and graced with the ornament of virtue, he attained Arahantship before long.
Recalling his past karma, he was filled with joy, thinking, "In the past, I performed wholesome deeds in a fertile field; it was well done!"
Explaining the *apadāna* of his former conduct, he spoke the words beginning with "Of the Blessed One Tissa.
In that context, he was called Tissa because he was given that name by his parents on account of the excellence of his existence (*bhavasampatti*) at birth;

or alternatively, he was called Tissa because he was born as a Buddha who provides consolation and instruction through the three refuges, establishing individuals endowed with the necessary causes in both heaven and liberation.

He is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he is endowed with the "blessings" (*bhaga*) such as the qualities of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). The connection [of the sentence] is: "I gave fruit to that Blessed One Tissa in the past.
Regarding the phrase "a coconut and foot-ointment": a coconut is a fruit that grows in the shape of a tube (*nāḷika*);
the meaning is that I gave that fruit. Regarding "the snack was highly esteemed": a snack (*khajjaka*) is something to be eaten; it was highly esteemed (*abhisammata*).

The meaning is: "He gave a food offering that was especially prepared by mixing honey, sugar, and other ingredients, which was considered, known, and highly esteemed as beautiful and sweet. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Khajjakadāyaka is completed.
4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Desapūjaka.
The account beginning with "Atthadassī tu bhagavā" is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Desapūjaka.
This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences...

At the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn in a noble family; as he grew up, he became faithful and confident, one who held the Buddha as his guide, the Dhamma as his guide, and the Saṅgha as his guide.

At that time, the Blessed One Atthadassī, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, traveled through the air like the moon or the sun. That lay follower [honored] the direction in which the Blessed One had gone with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Having paid homage with palms joined in reverence, he stood there worshipping.
By that merit, he was reborn in the world of the gods and experienced the splendors of heaven;

subsequently, having experienced human excellence among men, he was reborn in a certain family during this arising of a Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he was endowed with all manner of enjoyments and luxuries.
Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, with a mind full of serene confidence, he did not cling to the household life but went forth.

Being perfect in his conduct, before long he became an Arahant. Recalling his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), he spoke the verse beginning, "Atthadassī, the Blessed One...
The meaning of that has already been explained above. [The word] *anilañjase*...
Because it is stated as a synonym that "the path, the road, the way, the track, the direct course, and the journey," *anilañjasaṃ* means the direct course for the wind—that is, the air;
thus, it refers to the sky. The remainder is of plain meaning. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Desapūjaka is completed.
5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya.
"Vessabhū, the Fully Enlightened One," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Kaṇikārachattiya.

This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various births the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), [attained this state].
During the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, he was reborn into a noble family and, upon reaching maturity, became endowed with faith.
At that time, the Blessed One Vessabhu, desiring seclusion, entered the great forest and sat down.
Then that lay follower, having gone there on some business, saw the Blessed One sitting like a blazing mass of fire.
Seeing this, with a mind full of serene faith, he plucked a *kaṇikāra* flower, fashioned it into a parasol, and offered it as a canopy over the place where the Blessed One was seated.
Through the power of the Blessed One, it remained there for seven days without wilting, standing exactly as it had been placed.
The Blessed One, for his part, dwelt having entered into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and he marveled at that wonder.
Seeing him, he was filled with joy; having paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One, emerging from his meditative attainment, went back to the monastery.
By virtue of that merit, after experiencing success among gods and humans, he was born in Sāvatthī during this current dispensation of a Buddha.
Born into a noble family, having attained maturity and being endowed with faith, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Detached from the household life, he went forth into homelessness and, beautifying the Conqueror’s dispensation through his observance of the proper conduct (*vatta-paṭipatti*), soon became an Arahant.
Recollecting his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his former deeds; he was named Vessabhū.

He spoke the words beginning with "the Fully Enlightened One" (*sambuddha*). Regarding that: *Vessabhū* means he who "dwells in" or "overcomes" the commoners (*vessa*) among the people of the *vessa* class;
thus he is Vessabhū. Alternatively, he is Vessabhū because he "overcomes" or "surpasses" the fivefold Māra among the *vessa*.

He is a "Fully Enlightened One" (*sambuddha*) because he has awakened to the Truths by himself alone; the meaning is that the Fully Enlightened One named Vessabhū. [The sage] for the sake of his midday rest... (*munī divāvihārāya*).
It is called *divā* because it shines (*dibbati*), that is, it makes each respective object manifest.
The period delimited from sunrise until sunset is "day. "Dwelling" (*vihāra*) is the proceeding by means of the four postures;

"dwelling during the day" (*divāvihāra*) is the dwelling for the sake of the daytime. For the purpose of that daytime dwelling, the Elder of the World, the Bull among Men, the Sage Buddha, [entered] the great forest.
"Having gone down and entered" is the meaning. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya is finished.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sappidāyaka.
“Then there was the Blessed One named Phussa... and so forth is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Sappidāyaka Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) over many existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa.
At that time, the Blessed One, walking along a street surrounded by the community of monks, [saw him].
He arrived at the door of that lay follower’s house. Then, upon seeing the Blessed One, the lay follower, with a mind full of faith, paid homage and gave him a bowlful of ghee and oil.
Having offered his blessing, the Blessed One departed. By virtue of that very joy, he lived out his full lifespan;
when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas through that merit, where he experienced divine happiness.

Having experienced [the fruits of his deeds] among humans, he was reborn; in each successive birth, having enjoyed happiness while possessing sweet foods such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses, he was now reborn in a certain family at Sāvatthī during this appearance of a Buddha.

Upon reaching maturity, endowed with faith and wisdom, and having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he became serene in mind, went forth into homelessness, and became perfect in his conduct.
Before long, he became an *arahant*.
Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with "Then there was a Blessed One named Phussa.
In this context, he is called "Phussa" because he was so named by his parents due to being born under the conjunction of the constellation Phussa.
He is Phussa by name. Alternatively, he is Phussa because he touched (phusi), saw, and realized Nibbāna.

Or again, he is Phussa because he touched, saw, and fully understood all the thirty pāramīs, the seventy-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā), and the entire Dhamma of the scriptural tradition (pariyatti) consisting of the Three Piṭakas.
He is Bhaggava because he possesses portions of merit such as "fortunate" (bhagyavā) and "suitable" (yutta).
"Bhagavā" [is explained as follows]: "Receiver of offerings" (*āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho*) means that "offerings" (*āhutī*) refers to acts of worship and honor;

he is worthy of receiving those offerings, thus he is the "receiver of offerings. The connection is: "Then at that time, the Hero named Phussa, the Blessed One, who brings relief to the great multitude, was walking along the street. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sappidāyaka is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Yūthikāpupphiya begins with the verse "On the bank of the Candabhāgā River... This venerable one...
Having performed services under previous Lords of Sages and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from existence over many hundreds of births,
he was reborn into a pure family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Upon reaching maturity,
while traveling downstream for some business on the bank of the river Candabhāgā, he saw the Blessed One Phussa, who desired to bathe, [like] a mass of fire.
Seeing it shining like fire, he was filled with joy; having plucked a *yūthikā* flower grown there, he offered it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One gave him a blessing of thanksgiving (*anumodana*).
By means of that portion of merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence.
Having been reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha, and having reached maturity, he heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.
With a mind full of faith, he went forth into homelessness and, beautifying the Dispensation through his observance of the proper conduct, he soon became an Arahant.
Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former deeds, he spoke these verses beginning with "On the banks of the river Candabhāgā."
All of that has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Yūthikāpuṣpiya is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dussadāyaka.
The legend of the Venerable Dussadāyaka Thera begins with the words, "In the delightful city of Tivarā... This Venerable One had performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors;

having accumulated merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn into a royal family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Upon reaching maturity, he attained the status of crown prince.
Having obtained a certain province, Pākaṭa became its ruler and gathered all the inhabitants of that province through the four means of attraction (*saṅgahavatthu*):
generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. At that time, the Blessed One Siddhattha arrived in that province.
Then, having received a gift, that crown prince [presented] the Blessed One there with fine cloth.
He made offerings. The Blessed One, having touched that cloth with his hand, leapt into the air.
That cloth followed the Blessed One alone. Then, seeing that marvel, the crown prince was exceedingly pleased and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Wherever the Blessed One arrived, all the people, seeing that marvel, [did the same].
Filled with wonder and amazement, they stood with their hands joined in reverential salutation. The Blessed One then returned to his dwelling.
By that very wholesome deed, the crown prince passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the gods;

having enjoyed divine splendors there, and subsequently experienced the prosperity of a universal monarch and other such attainments among humans, he was now born into this era of a Buddha’s appearance in a family of great wealth.
Born into a certain family and having reached maturity, he established a household life.
Having gained faith in the Triple Gem after hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he went forth into homelessness. Exerting himself, before long he became an Arahant.
One day, remembering his own past karma, he was filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former deeds, said:
He spoke the verse beginning with "In the delightful city of Tivarā. Therein, the meaning is:
"In the beautiful city named Tivarā, having been a prince, I honored the Blessed One Siddhattha with a cloth. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dussadāyaka is complete.
9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Samādapaka.
The passage beginning with "In the city of Bandhumatī" is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Samādapaka.

This elder, too, having accumulated the equipment of wholesome deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas and amassing merits conducive to the turning away from existence throughout many births, [attained this state].
During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a noble family; having grown up and established a household life, he lived performing meritorious deeds.
Being faithful and confident, he gathered many lay followers and, becoming the leader of the group, said, "Let us build a pavilion.
Having encouraged them all, he had a single pavilion constructed with level ground and white sand.
Having scattered [the flowers], he offered them to the Blessed One. By that merit, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

after experiencing the six kinds of prosperity of the sense-sphere heavens and the prosperity of universal monarchs and others among humans, he was reborn in a noble family during this appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Blessed One, and having heard the Dhamma, his mind became serene and he was filled with conviction.
Having gone forth, endowed with virtue and perfected in the observance of duties, he attained *arahantship* before long.
Later on, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed and filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past conduct, beginning with the words, "In the city of Bandhumatī...
In this context, they are called "bound" (*bandha*) because they are connected as one through kinship, clan, and so forth.
"Bandhu" means those who dwell in the entire city; "Bandhumatī" means that in which such kinsmen (bandhus) exist.
The meaning is that in that city named Bandhumatī, there was a great multitude, a community of lay followers (upāsakas). Regarding the phrase "We shall build a *māḷa* for the Saṅgha":
here, "mā" takes the sense of the minds of the people who have gathered; thus, it is a *māḷa*. Alternatively, [it refers to] the groups of the three types of people who have gathered.

“*Māḷaṃ*” means that which is sufficient for the seclusion of the mind; *māḷakaṃ* is simply the same as *māḷaṃ*. The meaning is: “We shall build a pavilion (*māḷakaṃ*) for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the legend (*apadāna*) of the Elder Samādapaka is completed.
10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcaṅguliya.
The account of the Elder Pañcaṅguliya begins with the words, "There was a Blessed One named Tissa.

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the attainment of liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). Under the Blessed One Tissa...
At one time, having been reborn in a certain family and having reached maturity, he established a household life and became endowed with great wealth.
Being faithful and confident, he saw the Blessed One entering the street from his monastery;
taking many fragrant flowers such as *jātisumana* and various ointments such as sandalwood, he went to the monastery, honored the Blessed One with flowers, and [anointed him] with ointments.
Having made a five-fingered mark on the Blessed One’s body and paid homage, he departed.
By that merit, having experienced the two kinds of excellence among gods and humans, he was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth;
and as he grew up, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he attained realization.
Having gone forth with a serene mind and having developed insight, he soon became an Arahant.
Recalling his past karma and knowing it through direct realization, he spoke the words beginning with “The Blessed One named Tissa,” proclaiming the account of his former life, thinking:
“By performing such wholesome karma, I have attained this kind of supramundane success. All of that is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pañcaṅguliyatthera is completed.
The commentary on the seventeenth chapter (*vagga*) is completed. 18.
The Chapter on the White Lotus (*Kumudavagga*).
1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kumudamāliya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kumudamāliya begins with the words, "On a mountain in the Himalayas...

This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as the necessary condition for liberation throughout various existences, [attained this state].
In the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn as a rakkhasa near a spring in the vicinity of the Himavat mountains.
Seeing the Blessed One Atthadassī who had arrived there, he became joyful in heart, gathered water-lilies (kumuda), and offered them to the Blessed One.
Having given his blessing, the Blessed One departed.
1. By virtue of that merit, having passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas;

after experiencing the six kinds of excellence in the sense-sphere heavens and experiencing the excellences among humans, such as those of a wheel-turning monarch, he was born into a noble family during this arising of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith in the Triple Gem, he went forth and, through striving, attained the end of the holy life: Arahantship.

Having reached that place, remembered his own past karma, and being filled with joy, he spoke the words beginning with “On a mountain in the Himālaya,” while proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds).
Therein, “a *rakkhasa* born there” means a *rakkhasa*— one who eats the blood and flesh of others, merciless, of terrible appearance,
fearsome by nature, and possessed of great strength— who was born and produced in the vicinity of that lake.
The meaning is: "I was a powerful and harsh yakkha.

Regarding the phrase "the kumuda flower blooms there": when the rays of the sun are absent from that great lake, in the evening, the flower—which has received the name "kumuda" because it becomes bud-like, shriveled in form, lusterless, and unsightly—blooms, that is, it opens up.
