The meaning is as follows: "They are born wheel-sized" means those flowers are born having the measure of a chariot wheel.
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kumudamāliya is completed.
2. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nisseṇidāyaka.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Nisseṇidāyaka begins with the words, "Of the Blessed One Koṇḍañña...
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating merits conducive to the turning away from saṃsāra over many births, [met] the Blessed One Koṇḍañña.
At that time, a man was reborn in a family of carpenters; being faithful and confident, upon hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he became joyful in mind.
For the purpose of ascending to the Blessed One’s residence on the upper story, he fashioned a ladder made of strong wood, raised it up, and set it in place.
To increase his faith, the Blessed One ascended to the upper story of the residence while the man was looking on. He [the carpenter] was exceedingly...
Having passed away with that very joy and gladness of mind, he was reborn in the world of the devas;
there, having experienced divine splendor, when he was born among humans, he was reborn into a noble family by the result of his gift of the ladder, and after experiencing human happiness,
he was reborn into a certain family during the appearance of this Buddha and heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Having conceived faith, he went forth and before long became an *arahant*.
Recalling his own past karma, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his former conduct, he spoke the words beginning with "Koṇḍañña of the Blessed One.
In that context, "of Koṇḍañña": one who moves about (*ḍeti*) while being base (*kucchito*) is a *koṇḍa*, a lowly being.
*Koṇḍañño* means "one who is other than Koṇḍa"; the sense is that he was a superior man (*uttamapurisa*) beyond ordinary measure.
Alternatively, because he was born into the *Koṇḍañña* clan among the Brahmin clans, his name is "Koṇḍañña" by way of his lineage; [the text says] "of that Koṇḍañña. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nisseṇidāyaka is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rattipupphiya.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rattipupphiya begins with the words, "In former times I was a deer-hunter...

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various births the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), [encountered] Vipassi...
At that time, one born into a hunter’s family who was wandering in the forest to kill deer saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking in the wilderness out of compassion.

With a mind full of faith, he plucked a blooming flower called *rattika* and a *kuṭaja* flower along with its stalk, and offered them with a heart of joy. The Blessed One, having given a blessing of thanksgiving, departed.

13. Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that very merit and having experienced both types of excellence, he was reborn into a noble family during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Triple Gem;

having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth into homelessness and, before long, attained Arahantship. He [then reflected] upon his own past kamma.

Having remembered, "The wholesome deed performed by me when I was a hunter was excellent," he became filled with joy and spoke the verses beginning with "In former times I was a deer-hunter," while proclaiming the account of his past conduct.
In this context, *migaluddo* means one who is a hunter of deer, a violent slayer; thus, the meaning is: "In former times I was a hunter (*nesāda*).
Alternatively, *migaluddo* means one who is greedy for deer; thus, the meaning is: "In former times I was a hunter."
14. “Having seen it blooming at night”: many flowers, such as the lotus and others, bloom by day through contact with the rays of the sun and become buds at night.
However, many other flowers, such as the *jātisumana* and the jasmine (*mallikā*), bloom at night and not by day.
Therefore, because they bloom at night, there are many [species] designated as "night-blooming."
The meaning is that they took fragrant flowers and *kuṭaja* flowers and offered them. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Rattipupphiya is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Udapānadāyaka.
"Vipassī, the Blessed One," and so forth, is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Udapānadāyaka Thera.

This Thera, too, having performed his duty under previous Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit through many existences, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, he thought: "I must give a gift of drinking water, and that continuously."
Thinking, "It is fitting to have one constructed and established," he had a well dug.
When it was filled with water, he had it lined with bricks and made sturdy. He then dedicated that well, full of the water rising therein, to the Blessed One Vipassī.
The Blessed One offered a blessing of thanks (anumodana) illustrating the benefits of the gift of drinking water. By that merit, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in various places where he enjoyed happiness provided with lotus ponds, wells, drinking water, and other amenities.
In this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn into a certain family; having grown up, he became faithful and confident, went forth into homelessness, and before long attained Arhatship.
18. Later on, having recollected his own former karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct, beginning with the words, "Of the Blessed One Vipassī.
In that context, regarding the phrase "a well was made by me": it is called an *udapāna* because water is drunk (*pibanti*) there;
this is a designation for a pit, a lotus pond, or a lake. That well, the pit, was made for the sake of the Blessed One Vipassī.
"Kato" means "dug. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Udapānadāyaka is complete.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka.
"Nibbute lokanāthamhi... and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Sīhāsanadāyaka Thera.

This [Thera], having performed meritorious deeds in various previous births for the sake of attaining *nibbāna* and having accumulated a store of merit, was reborn into a family of householders during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity and hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he placed his faith in the Triple Gem.
Full of faith in that Blessed One who had attained final Nibbāna, he had a lion throne inlaid with the seven precious gems constructed and honored the Bodhi tree;
he also honored it with many garlands, perfumes, and incense.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence everywhere, he...
Having been honored during this appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity and living the life of a householder, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching; with a mind full of faith, he renounced his circle of kinsmen and went forth into homelessness.
Not long after, having become an Arahant, he recalled the store of wholesome merit accumulated in the past and, filled with joy, [related] the account of his former deeds.
Explaining this, he said, "When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna," and so forth. Regarding that, "I gave a lion-throne" (*sīhāsanam adāsim*):
a throne inlaid with gold, silver, and precious gems in the form of lions is a "lion-throne"; or, it is a throne worthy for the fearless Blessed One to sit upon;
or, it is the best and most excellent seat, thus it is a "lion-throne. I gave that; the meaning is, "I honored the Bodhi tree."
The rest is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka is complete.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggadattika.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Maggadattika Thera begins with “Anomadassī, the Blessed One,” and so forth. This Venerable One had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;

having accumulated there, in various existences, the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī. Having reached maturity and established a household life, while living there, [he saw] Anomadassī...

Seeing the Blessed One walking back and forth in the sky and observing the scattering of flowers at each step as he walked upon those footprints—a marvel—he, with a mind full of faith, threw flowers into the air; they remained there, forming a canopy.
By that merit, wandering only through happy destinies and being honored everywhere, he experienced happiness until, in this [present life]...

Having been reborn in a certain family during the appearance of a Buddha, he gradually reached youth, conceived faith, went forth into homelessness, became perfected in his conduct, and before long attained Arhatship.
Because of his devotion to walking meditation, he became renowned as the Elder Maggadattika.
Remembering his past deeds and filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of former lives, beginning with the time of Anomadassī.

The Blessed One spoke these words beginning with "bhagavā. "For the sake of happiness in this present life" means: for the sake of the happiness of bodily lightness and so forth, obtained through walking meditation (*caṅkama*) within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"He walked in the open air" means: he walked in the open space, in the courtyard;
the meaning is that he made strides and moved about on foot.

"When the foot is lifted, flowers": the meaning is that as he was walking, when his foot was lifted, lotuses, blue lilies, and other flowers rose up from the earth and scattered upon the walkway (*caṅkama*). "They remain beautifying the head":
the meaning is that they remained upon the Buddha’s head, adorning it. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maggadattika is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Ekadīpiya begins with the verse "Of the Sage Padumuttara... This Venerable One [also] [lived] under the most excellent of previous Victors.

Accumulating the equipment for skillful deeds and merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation in various states of existence, he was reborn into a householders’ family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, being faithful and confident, he offered a single-lamp offering at the Blessed One’s Salala Great Bodhi tree;
having made it permanent, he established a supply of oil for the purpose of constantly offering that single lamp.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that merit, shining brightly everywhere with clear vision, he experienced both types of happiness.
Now, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a family of great wealth in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, he placed his faith in the Triple Gem, went forth into homelessness, and before long attained Arahantship, having gained special attainments through his offering of a lamp.
The Elder Ekadīpiya is well known.

Later on, having recollected his own past karma and being filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words, "Of the Sage Padumuttara... All of that is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekadīpiya is completed.
8. The Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maṇipūjaka.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Maṇipūjaka begins with the words, "Within the Himalayas...
This elder, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] Padumuttara...
Having been born into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One and having established a household life, he perceived the peril therein;
abandoning the household life, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic. Building a leaf-hut near a river on the slopes of the Himalayas, he lived there.
Out of a desire for seclusion and out of compassion for him, the Blessed One Padumuttara approached that place.
Seeing this, with a mind full of faith, he honored the Blessed One with a jeweled couch.
To increase his faith, the Blessed One sat there. Becoming even more deeply inspired, he made an aspiration for the attainment of Nibbāna.
After the Blessed One had expressed his appreciation, he departed. By virtue of that merit, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was honored everywhere.
Having experienced happiness, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a family endowed with great wealth in Sāvatthī.
While living the life of a householder, one day, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth,
and before long became an arahant.

34. Thus, one day, recollecting the wholesome deeds he had performed and feeling joy arise within him, he spoke the words beginning with "Within the Himālaya" while proclaiming the account of his former life.
Therein, "orena" means having left the further side of the Himālaya;
it is an instrumental form used in the sense of the locative, meaning "in that direction. "The river flows" (*nadikā sampavattati*).
The meaning is that there was a certain river with an unmanifest name, flowing well, streaming, and rushing along.

"In its vicinity" means in the neighborhood of the bank of that river. "The Self-Existent One dwelt then" means that when I was worshipping the jeweled couch, at that time, having become a Buddha by myself without a teacher, he dwelt there.
The Blessed One dwells; this is the meaning. 35.
Regarding "having taken up the jewel, [he sits] cross-legged": it is called a *maṇi* because it pleases the mind and produces joy;
or else, it is called a *maṇi* because it measures (*māti*) and serves as an ornament (*ābharaṇa*); or else, even kings, crown princes, and others [value it] until death.
They do not abandon it, but engage in battle for its sake; thus it is called a "gem" (maṇi).
Having taken up—that is, having grasped—that gem and a delightful, well-fashioned, and beautifully variegated couch made of gems, he offered it to the Best of Buddhas;
this is the meaning. All the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Maṇipūjaka is completed. 9.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tikicchaka begins with the verse "In the city of Bandhumatī... This venerable one [lived] under previous Victors.

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī in the city of Bandhumatī into a family of physicians.
Being highly learned, well-trained, and skilled in the art of medicine, he treated many who were afflicted by disease.
[He served] the elder named Asoka, who was an attendant to the Blessed One Vipassī.

He treated the disease. By that merit, experiencing happiness successively among gods and humans, he became free from illness, long-lived, and possessed a body of golden hue in every birth he was reborn in. 39.
In this present dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a household of lay devotees in Sāvatthī; and having grown up, he [became proficient] in all the arts.
Having attained success, being healthy, happy, and endowed with wealth, he was devoted to the Triple Gem. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he gained faith;
abandoning the household life and going forth, he became an Arahant before long.
Recalling his former karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his account of past deeds, beginning with the words: "In the city of Bandhumatī... and so forth.
Since all of that has been explained according to the method stated below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Tikicchaka is complete.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka.
"Under Vessabhu, the Blessed One," and so forth, is the *apadāna* of the venerable Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka.

This elder, too, having accumulated the equipment of wholesome deeds under previous Buddhas and amassing merits conducive to disengagement from existence throughout many births, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu as the son of a monastery attendant; and having reached maturity, he became endowed with faith.
Full of faith, he performed the work of an *ārāmika* (monastery attendant) in the monasteries and served the Saṅgha with diligence.

By virtue of that very wholesome kamma, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence. Now, during this appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a householder family in Sāvatthī;
having reached maturity, endowed with great wealth and established in happiness, he became well-known for attending the Teacher’s Dhamma teachings.
Having heard [the Dhamma], he placed his faith in the Teaching, went forth, and became perfected in the observance of the duties.
Adorning the Dispensation and increasing his insight, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long.
Possessing the six supernormal powers, he became renowned as the Elder Saṅghupatthāka on account of the wholesome kamma performed in a previous life.
45. Thus, one day, thinking, "What kind of karma did I perform in the past to obtain this supramundane success?

he recalled his own former deeds. Having known them through direct experience, he became filled with joy and, making manifest the account of his former conduct, spoke the words beginning with "Under the Blessed One Vessabhu...
Therein, "I was a monastery attendant" means that I was [the attendant] of Vessabhu.
The meaning is that he was an attendant in the monastery of the Blessed One. The remainder is easily understood, as it follows the method already explained below and its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka is completed.
The commentary on the Eighteenth Chapter on the Equal Ones is completed.
19. The Chapter on the Kuṭaja Flower: 1–10.
Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kuṭajapupphiya and others.
Furthermore, regarding these ten elders—beginning with the elder Kuṭajapupphiya—who appear in this nineteenth chapter, there is nothing new [to be told].

For the well-known names and native cities of these elders, who had accumulated a store of merit in the presence of previous Buddhas, are to be understood in the same manner as stated below. Therefore...
The entire *Apadāna* is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the nineteenth chapter is completed.
20. The Chapter on the Tamāla Flower.
1–10. Commentary on the Legends of the Elder Tamālapupphiya and Others.
In the twentieth chapter, the legend of the first elder is self-evident. 6.
Regarding the legend of the second elder: "The seer who dwelt in the forest" refers to his state of living in the woods after having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.

Known as the sage Dāyavāsika, he gathered and cut whatever grass was there for the purpose of roofing the dwelling-maṇḍapa of the Teacher Siddhattha, who had come to that forest out of compassion for himself;
having constructed a roof of *dabba* grass and built a maṇḍapa with many small sticks, he covered it with that grass for Siddhattha.
"I gave to the Blessed One" means "I honored him. 8.

"They maintained it there for seven days": the meaning is that the gods and humans staying there in that pavilion maintained—that is, sustained—the Teacher while he remained seated having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for seven days. The rest is of obvious meaning.
Regarding the *Apadāna* of the third Elder, in the case of the Elder Khaṇḍaphulliya, here "khaṇḍa" refers to the state of being worn out due to the decay of the timber.
"Chinna-bhinna-ṭṭhānaṃ" means the places that are broken or split. "Phullaṃ" refers to the flowering of things such as *kaṇṇikita* and *mahicchattaka* fungi at spots where wood has decayed.
"Khaṇḍaṃ ca phullaṃ ca" means broken and flowering; the repairing (*paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ*) of what is broken and flowering—that is, making it firm again and again—is "khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ.
Now, at the time when this elder was fulfilling the requisites for the Blessed One Phussa—
Applying a lump of plaster to a place on a *cetiya* that has been broken or split in order to make it firm is called "the repair of what is broken and dilapidated" (*khaṇḍaphulla-paṭisaṅkharaṇa*).
Therefore, he became well known as the Elder Khaṇḍaphulliya. This is the third [chapter].
17. Regarding the legend of the fourth elder: "He was a bound servant to the king" means he was an attendant or a laborer for the king.

19. *Jalajuttamanāmi*: "Born in water" (*jalaja*) means born in the water (*udaka*). What is that? It is the lotus (*paduma*). The meaning is: "The Blessed One whose name is equal to the lotus," namely Padumuttara. Alternatively, the meaning is: "The Blessed One whose name is the supreme lotus. This is the fourth [verse]. The fifth has its meaning already explained. 28.
Regarding the sixth [verse], "in the city of Dvāravatī": it was [surrounded] by gates, windows, door-panels, fences, walls, watchtowers, gatehouses, moats, water-trenches, and ditches.

And "the city Sampanna" refers to the city of Dvāravatī; because the city was characterized by its gates (*dvāra*) and its enclosure (*vati*), people conventionally called it "Dvāravatī City," which is why it is said, "in the city of Dvāravatī.
The meaning is: "The flower garden Mālāvaccha was mine."
31. "Those are sprouts, those are *aśoka* shoots. This is the sixth [verse].
The seventh, eighth, and ninth have their meanings already explained. In the tenth as well, there is nothing new.
The commentary on the twentieth [chapter] is completed.
21–23. The Chapter on Kaṇikārapupphiya and Others.
1–30. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārapupphiya and Others.
From this point forward, we shall provide a commentary on all the words that have not been previously explained. [This applies to] the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-third [vaggas].
In all the chapters, the names of all the elders obtained through their own performed merit, the diversity of the merit they performed,
the names of the Buddhas who gave them their prophetic declarations (*byākaraṇa*), and the cities where they dwelt— all these are indeed clear,
as they follow the method already explained below. Furthermore, the meaning of the verses of the *Apadāna* is easily understood by following the same method.
24. Udakāsanavagga 1–10.
Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elders who Gave Water and Seats, etc.
In the twenty-fourth chapter, the first and second Apadānas are indeed straightforward.
9. Regarding the third *apadāna*: "In the city of Aruṇavatī. It is called *aruṇa* because it rises, making light (*āloka*) all around;
that [city] possesses this [light], thus it is *Aruṇavatī*. The meaning is that in that city, the sun rises, making light.
Although the rising of the sun occurs in other cities as well, this is a specific designation for the earth of all four-footed creatures.

It should be understood that this is stated by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), just as one says "a buffalo" (*mahiṃsa*) because it sleeps on the ground even though it is capable of sleeping elsewhere.

Alternatively, it is called Aruṇavatī because it possesses light, shining like the rising sun through the radiance of the seven treasures—gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth—from its walls, palaces, and watchtowers;
in that city of Aruṇavatī, there was a baker who made his living by selling cakes.
The meaning is "making it so. 14. Regarding the fourth *apadāna*:
"In the delightful city of Tivarā"—it is called Tivarā because it was surrounded and enclosed by three walls;
it is called delightful (*ramma*) because it was pleasing through various kinds of food and drink, clothing and ornaments, dancing, singing, and so forth. In that [city]...
The connection [of the verse] is: "In the delightful city of Tivarā, I was a reed-worker.
The meaning of the fifth *apadāna* is already clear.
In the sixth *apadāna*, the phrase "I was a dyer then" means that one produces garments by way of colors such as blue, yellow, red, and so forth.
"One who colors" (*vaṇṇakāra*) means one who dyes. The meaning is that, having become a cloth-dyer, he dyed cloths of various colors when it was time to cover the stupa with cloths.
27. "Having seen a flowering *piyāla* tree" means having seen a *piyāla* tree in full bloom. On the path traveled...
"I scattered" means that, having been a deer-hunter and a hunter, I gathered *piyāla* flowers and scattered them on the path by which the Buddha had gone, in order to offer worship.
30. In the eighth *apadāna*, "not arrogant in one's own craft" means not being conceited in one's own skills such as logic (*takkabyākaraṇa*) and so forth.
"Established and clever, I went to the forest"—having seen the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassi, traveling through the midst of the woods.
"I gave a mango offering"—the meaning is that I gave a gift of mangoes. 33. In the *Navama-apadāna*:

"A terrace was caused to be made by me"—the meaning is that at the shrine where the bodily relics of the Blessed One Atthadassi were enshrined, a terrace known as the *chinnabhinna-ālinda-pupphādhāna* was caused to be constructed and built by me.
The tenth *apadāna* has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter is completed.
25. The Chapter on the Giver of Haste (*Tuvaradāyaka-vagga*).
1–10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tuvaradāyaka, etc. 1.

In the first apadāna of the twenty-fifth chapter, the phrase *bharitvā tuvaramādāya* means that having filled [the vessel] with *tuvara* seeds—which are like mung beans or peas—and having roasted and flowered those *tuvara* seeds, he took them in a container and gave them to the Saṅgha as it entered the forest; "gave" (*adāsi*) is the meaning.

4–5. Regarding the second account: “Having made the bow straight” means that while wandering about with a bow strung for the purpose of killing deer and other animals, he saw the filaments [of flowers] fallen;
that is, having seen a small, well-flowered *sara* tree, he offered it to the Buddha.
The meaning is: “I, having calmed my mind, offered and honored it to the Blessed One Tissa when he had arrived in the forest.”
9–10. In the third *apadāna*, "the water-fowl" refers to a cock wandering in a lake.
"Seizing the lion with his beak" means that while the Blessed One Tissa was traveling through the air, [the fowl] bit a lotus flower with his beak and offered it as an act of worship;
this is the meaning. 14. In the fourth *apadāna*, "taking the *virava* flower": it is called *virava* because it makes various sounds (*viravati*); thus, it is a sound-maker.

Having taken—that is, having gathered—the mass of flowers known as "virava" because they blossom at the very moment a sound is made, I offered them to the Buddha Siddhattha; the meaning is that I honored him.
17. In the fifth *Apadāna*, "Kuṭigopaka" refers to a guardian of lodgings. "I would fumigate from time to time" means at every appropriate occasion as they arose.
"I perfumed" means that I made it fragrant with incense. "I perfumed" means that I scented it with the incense following the fragrance of the Blessed One Siddhattha’s Perfume Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*).
The sixth and seventh *apadānas* have their meaning already explained.

27. In the eighth *Apadāna*, "seven *sattalipuppha* flowers" means seven flowers counted as seventy; the meaning is that, taking seven flowers with his head, he offered them in worship to the Blessed One Vessabhu.
31. In the ninth *Apadāna*, "bimbijālaka flowers" means red *aṅkuravaka* flowers; the meaning is that he offered them in worship to the Blessed One Siddhattha. 35.

In the tenth *Apadāna*, "having taken an *uddālaka*" means having plucked an *uddālaka* flower grown in a lake (*jātassara*) or a bird-pool (*vihaga-sobbha*), he offered it in worship to the Blessed One Kakusandha. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Twenty-fifth Chapter is complete.
26. The Chapter on Praise (Thomakavagga): 1–10. Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Thomaka and others.
In the twenty-sixth chapter, the first account (*apadāna*) is self-evident. 5–6.
In the second account, “having abandoned the celestial form” means having abandoned—that is, cast off—the body of a deity and fashioned a human body.
“Desiring to perform a service” means desiring to perform a superior deed, that is, an accumulation of merit (*puñña-sambhāra*).

"Devara" means "I am the king of the gods. The meaning is that, together with my wife, out of reverence for the teaching of the Supreme Buddha, I have come here to this human world. Regarding the phrase "alms were given by me to him":
when the Blessed One Padumuttara had a disciple named Devala, it was to that disciple that alms were given by me with a mind full of serene confidence.
"Alms were given" means that alms-food was bestowed.
9–10. Regarding the third offering: "The Sambuddha named Ānanda"—the meaning is that he was a Paccekabuddha named Ānanda because he produced joy (*ānanda*).

"In a forest inhabited by non-humans" means that he attained final Nibbāna in a great wilderness (*mahārañña*), a forest under the protection of non-human beings, through the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

"Disappeared" means he went out of sight. "I cremated his body there" means that having come here from the world of the gods, I cremated—that is, performed the burning of—the Blessed One’s body there in the forest; such is the meaning.
The fourth and fifth apadānas are indeed self-evident.
20. Regarding the sixth gift: "I was known by the name Candana" means that I was designated as "Candana" by way of my name.

"The son of the Fully Enlightened One" means that before he became a Paccekabuddha, I was his biological son. "A single pair of sandals was given by me" means that one pair of sandals was given by me.
"May you attain enlightenment through me" means [may you attain it] through me, by means of that pair of sandals.
The meaning is: "Having attained the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*), you shall bring it to fulfillment.
23–24. In the seventh *apadāna*, regarding the phrase "having made a *mañjarika*": having taken *mañjeṭṭhi* flowers and green *caṅkoṭaka* leaves, I set out upon the highway and the street;
while proceeding in that manner, I [encountered] the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) preceded by the community of monks.
The connection is that they saw the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the foremost of ascetics, the supreme and best among the ascetic monks,
surrounded [by his retinue]. "They offered it to the Buddha" means that having seen him, they took up that flower with both hands,
lifted it up, and offered it— paid homage— to the Blessed One, the Buddha Phussa.

28–29. Regarding the eighth *apadāna*: "I am one who eats saltless leaves" means that having gathered milk-leaves and other greens through the practice of gleaning (*uñchācariyā*), I cook and eat leaves devoid of salt; thus, "I am one who eats saltless leaves" is the meaning.
Furthermore, "restrained in the observances" means restrained in the perpetual five precepts known as observances, such as abstaining from taking life and so forth.
"Covered" (*pihita*) is the meaning. "When the morning meal had arrived" means when the time before the midday meal had come.
"Siddhattha approached me" means that the Blessed One Siddhattha approached and reached my presence.
"I gave those to the Buddha" means that I gave that saltless leaf-food to that Buddha; such is the meaning.
The ninth *apadāna* is self-evident. 37–38.

Regarding the tenth *apadāna*: "Sikhin, Sikhin, just as... refers to the Blessed One Sikhin, who was blazing and illuminating with the six-colored rays issuing from his body; "Sikhin, just as a flaming mass of fire" refers to him.
"Taking the *aggaja* flower" means having taken the flower named *aggaja*, he offered it— that is, honored it— to the Blessed One Sikhi Buddha.
The commentary on the twenty-sixth chapter is completed.
27. The Chapter on Throwing the Lotus (Padumukkhipavagga).
1–10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ākāsukkhipiya, etc.

1–2. In the twenty-seventh chapter, regarding the first apadāna: "Two [lotuses] are to be taken from the foremost of water-born things" means from the foremost among those born in the water, that is, in the liquid.
Having taken two flowers, such as blue lotuses and so forth, she approached the Buddha;
the meaning is that she placed one flower at his feet as an offering and threw the other flower into the air.
The second *apadāna* is self-evident.
10. Regarding the third offering: "At the supreme Bodhi tree, the best of trees," means that at the foot of that Bodhi tree, many flowers were offered by me in the shape of a half-moon;
this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "the tree growing from the earth" (*dharaṇīruhapādapa*): it is called *dharaṇī* because it supports (*dhāreti*) trees, mountains, jewels, and so forth;
thus it is the earth. That which grows (*ruhati*) and is established upon the earth is [a tree].

A "dharaṇīruha" is a tree; it is called a "pādapa" because it drinks water through its root, which is designated as the "foot" (pāda), and because it spreads [its growth] through its trunk, branches, and so forth.
Thus, "dharaṇīruhapādapa" means a tree that grows from the earth. The meaning is: "I have worshipped with flowers upon that tree growing from the earth."
The meaning of the fourth *apadāna* is already clear. 18–19.
In the fifth *apadāna*, "not far from the Himavat" means in the vicinity of the Himavat.

"A mountain named Romasa" means that because it was devoid of trees, creepers, and thickets, and was covered solely with coarse grass (*dabbatiṇa*) and the like, it was called the Romasa Mountain. In that [place]...
"At the foot of the mountain" means on that edge of the mountain. "The ascetic with developed faculties" (*samaṇo bhāvitindriyo*):
an ascetic is one whose evil has been stilled and whose defilements have been pacified; "with developed faculties" means one whose faculties, such as the eye-faculty, are guarded.

Alternatively, "with developed faculties" means one whose faculties, such as the faith-faculty, have increased. The meaning is: "I gave him to that ascetic, having taken him by the tail and the neck."
The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth chapters are self-evident in their meaning.
The commentary on the twenty-seventh chapter is completed.
28. The Chapter on the Golden Pillow (Suvaṇṇabibbohana-vagga).
1–10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Suvaṇṇabibbohanīyatta and others.
In the twenty-eighth chapter, the first apadāna is self-evident.
In the second apadāna, the phrase “with a mind-made body” (manomayena kāyena) means with a body that proceeds by the power of the mind.
10. Regarding the third *apadāna*, "near the great ocean" (*mahāsamuddaṃ nissāya*) means in a mountain cave located between mountains situated close to the great sea.
The Blessed One, Siddhattha, dwelt and resided there out of a desire for seclusion.
"Having gone forth to meet him" (*paccuggantvā*) means that I, having gone out to meet that Blessed One and approached his presence, performed meritorious acts such as paying homage.
"Desiring" means I wished for it. "I gave a flower-filled basket" means that I offered and honored a *kadamba* basket filled with flowers to the Blessed One Siddhattha.
In the fourth *Apadāna*, "of one whose mind was not harsh" means of one whose mind was gentle; the word *atha* is used here as a verse-filler (*padapūraṇa*).
19. Regarding "while dwelling at the udumbara tree": while the Blessed One Tissa was dwelling in the shade of the root of an udumbara tree.
"On a prepared leaf-mat" means: while he was seated on a seat made of broken branches, upon a leaf-mat that had been arranged and secured.
"A secluded place has been given by me" means: a secluded place, a space enclosed by a pavilion, a gate, and so forth, has been granted by me.
"Given" means "accomplished. 24.

Regarding the gift of books in the sixth *Apadāna*: "A book has been given by me"—having beaten a roll of cloth or a leather cover, having taken the thread produced from unevenly rubbed cow-hide, having spun it, and with that thread...
The meaning is: having had a cloth woven for the purpose of a sitting mat or for the purpose of a ground-covering, [he thought], "I have given this cloth to the Triple Gem.
27. In the seventh *apadāna*, "on the bank of the Candabhāgā River" means from the bank of the river named Candabhāgā;
this is a locative expression used in the sense of the ablative. "Downstream" means following the current, below it; the meaning is: "I go, I travel down the Gaṅgā."
"Seven *māluva* flowers": the meaning is that I took seven *māluva* flower petals and, having made a stupa out of sand upon a funeral pyre—a heap of sand—I honored it.
(31–32) In the eighth *Apadāna*, "Mahāsindhu Sudassanā": [she is so called] because she was adorned by beautiful sights and by white sandy banks with lovely waters.
There was a river of water named Mahāsindhu that was exceedingly captivating.

There, in that river Sindhuvāri, I saw one who was radiant with splendor, beautiful to behold, of lovely form, endowed with supreme tranquility, possessed of the highest peace, and free from passion—this is the meaning.
Having seen him, I was struck with wonder in my heart, thinking: "Such a terrifying [being]..."
"How did he reach the Himālaya?"—the meaning is that his intention was filled with wonder, his mind struck by a sense of marvelousness and amazement.
"I gave him an *ālu* root"—the meaning is that with a mind full of faith, I respectfully gave an *ālu* tuber to that Arahant.
The ninth and tenth gifts are self-evident.
The commentary on the twenty-eighth chapter is completed.
29. The Chapter on the Giver of Leaves (Paṇṇadāyaka-vagga). 1–10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paṇṇadāyaka and others.
1–2. In the first rule of the twenty-ninth chapter, "eating leaf-food" (*paṇṇabhojana*) means that I was sitting in a leaf-hut for the purpose of eating leaf-food such as milk-leaves and so forth.
"While I was seated" (*upaviṭṭhaṃ ca maṃ santaṃ*) means while I was present, having sat down in the leaf-hut.
"The great seer approached" (*upāgacchi mahāisī*) [refers to one who has attained] the great aggregates of virtue and so forth.
"The Great Seer, seeking [alms], the Lamp of the World, the Light of the World, Siddhattha, the Blessed One, approached;
the meaning is that he came into my presence. 'To him seated upon a bed of leaves'—the connection is: 'Having approached, I gave him the cooked leaves for his meal as he sat upon the bed of leaves.'"
5–7. In the second *apadāna*, the connection is as follows: "Siddhattha, the Blessed One, who is equal to Sineru and comparable to the earth.
Having emerged from meditative absorption (*samādhi*) means having emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that is, having come out of it.
"He stood before me for alms" means that at the time for wandering for alms, [the Blessed One thought]: "Today, whoever gives me anything as a gift, for them it will be of great fruit."
The meaning is that he approached and came into my presence while I was sitting there after having reflected.
"Harītaka... and phārusaka fruits"—the meaning is that all those fruits were given by me with a mind full of serene confidence to that Great Seer Siddhattha, who has compassion for the entire world.
11–12. In the third *apadāna*, the connection is as follows: "Just as a lion roams in the forest, so [he] roamed like the lion-king Siddhattha, the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "just as a bull of the *nisabha* breed": there are four types of pre-eminent bulls—*vasabha*, *nisabha*, *visabha*, and *āsabha*.
Among these, the *vasabha* is the leader of a hundred cows; the *nisabha* is the leader of a thousand cows.
*Nisabha* means the eldest, the leader of a hundred thousand cattle; *visabha* means the eldest, the leader of ten million cattle;
*āsabha* means the eldest, the leader of a billion cattle. Here, however, *āsabha* is called *nisabha*, meaning like a noble, fearless, and immovable king of bulls.
"Like a shining *kakudha*" means like a *kakudha* tree resplendent with flowers and sprouts.
The meaning is that, upon seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha approaching— the bull among men, the peerless leader of men, the supreme one—
they went out to meet him with a mind serene because it was associated with faith.
The fourth birth story and the others, up to the tenth, are indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the twenty-ninth chapter is completed.
30. The Chapter on Those Who Worship the Pile (Citakapūjakavagga). 1–10. Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Citakapūjaka and others.
1–2. In the first rule of the thirtieth chapter: “Desiring to offer an oblation” (*āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmo*) means desiring to perform an act of worship and honor.
“Bringing various flowers” (*nānāpupphaṃ samānayiṃ*) means I brought well (*saṃ*) many kinds (*nānā*) of flowers, such as *campaka* and *salala*;
the meaning is that I made a heap of them. “Of the crested one, the kinsman of the world” (*sikhino lokabandhuno*) refers to the kinsman related to the entire threefold world.

The meaning is: having seen the funeral pyre—the cremation mound—of the Blessed One Sikhi burning and blazing with a heap of wood, I scattered those flowers gathered into a heap over it as an act of worship.
6–7. In the second *apadāna*, "wearing a deerskin upper garment" means wearing a deerskin (*ajina*) as one's upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).

"Acchādana" means clothing. "The five higher knowledges were produced" means that the five kinds of direct knowledge (abhiññā), beginning with the various supernormal powers (iddhividha), were produced, generated, and brought to completion. "The polisher of the moon" means one who polishes around the lunar disk;
the sense is that he touched it. "Vipassī, the lamp of the world" means [one who is] like a lamp throughout the entire threefold world.
The Blessed One Vipassī had come into my presence, having arrived with distinguished attainment. Having seen him, [the meaning is:
"I brought Pāricchattaka flowers from the world of the gods and held them over the head of the Teacher Vipassī in the form of a parasol."
11–13. Regarding the third *apadāna*: "My son has gone forth" means that my son went forth out of faith (*saddhā*).
"Clad in saffron robes" (*kāsāyavasano*) refers to the time he went forth; the meaning is that he did not go forth by way of an external renunciation.
"And he attained Buddhahood" means that my son, among the four Buddhas, [attained] the state of a disciple-Buddha (*sāvakabuddha*).
"Suṭṭhuppatto" means he has attained [the goal] well; the meaning is that he has attained *arahatta*.
"Nibbuto lokapūjito" means honored by the entire world and extinguished (*parinibbuto*) through the final extinction of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*).

"Vicinanto sakaṃ puttaṃ" means that after asking him for the direction of his departure, I went back, searching for my own son; the meaning is that I followed after him. Regarding the one who has been extinguished...

"Of the Great One" means: "I went to the funeral pyre, the place of the pyre, at the site of the enshrinement of that Great One—my son, the Arahant—who was endowed with the great aggregates of virtue and so forth. "Having raised my joined palms there" means:
having raised my joined palms—the bringing together of the ten fingers—at that site of enshrinement, and placing them upon my head, I [went] to the pyre.
"Having paid homage and made obeisance to the mass of burning wood, and having taken up the white parasol"— the meaning is that not only did I pay homage,
but having taken up and raised the white parasol, I placed it [there], that is, I established it.
(17–18) "When the sun had not yet risen" in the fourth *apadāna* means when the sun had not risen or appeared, i.e., at the time of dawn.
The meaning is as follows: "Great was my confidence" means that for me, who was oppressed by illness, a vast and exceeding confidence of mind arose through the recollection of the Buddha.
The connection is: "The manifestation and appearance of the Great Sage, the Best of Buddhas, occurred in the world.
"I heard the report there" means that when that manifestation took place, I heard the report: "A Buddha has arisen; I am ill."
"I heard, yet I do not see that Conqueror"—the meaning is that I do not see the Perfectly Enlightened One who has conquered the five Māras;
because of my severe illness, I am unable to go and see him. "And death has arrived"—the meaning is that I have reached the time near to death;
being one whose death is imminent. "I recollected the perception of the Buddha"—I recollected the name "Buddha."
The meaning is: "He directed his mind toward the Buddha as its object.
21–23. Regarding the fifth *apadāna*: "Having gone out from the gate of the monastery" means having departed from the monastery gate by way of the paths leading out from the gate of the Saṅgha.
"A cow-head rug was spread for me" means that on that path leading out from the gate, [a rug] for the Blessed One and the community of monks...
The meaning is: "I spread out the ox-head bone for the sake of their treading upon it, so that their feet might not step in the mud.

"I experience my own karma" means: by the power of my own deed of spreading the ox-head bone, I experience the results of maturation such as noble thoroughbreds, swift horses with the speed of the wind, and fast vehicles. "Aho! This act is a supreme act"—in this fertile field...
"Regarding the Saṅgha, even a small service well-performed by me yields great fruit; therefore, it is a supreme deed, the highest duty—how wonderful!

is the meaning. Just as rice seed sown in fields free from defects such as weeds yields a great harvest, even so, in the field of the Saṅgha—which is free from the defects of passion, hatred, and so forth, and whose bodily and verbal conduct is utterly pure—the act of spreading out a cow-hide rug is likewise [of great fruit].
The meaning is: "What has been done by me gives great fruit. Regarding the phrase "nothing else is worth a sixteenth part," the connection is:
"Any deed performed in other, external teachings is not worth even a sixteenth part, a part, or a fraction of the service and honor rendered to the Saṅgha."
The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth recitations are self-evident.
The commentary on the thirtieth chapter is completed.
31. The Chapter on Lotus Filaments.
1–10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Padumakesariya, etc. 1–2.

In the first *apadāna* of the thirty-first chapter: "In the past, among the assembly of seers (*isisanghe*)" means that in the past, at the time of fulfilling the requisites for enlightenment, while in the presence of the assembly of seers—that is, the multitude of seers who were *paccekabuddhas*—on the Himavanta mountain, in the lineage of the Mātaṅga elephants...
The connection is that he was a *vāraṇa*, a fierce elephant. He is called a *vāraṇa* because he wards off (*vāreti*) humans and others;
or else, he is a *vāraṇa* because he roars with his voice, uttering the cry of a *koñca* crane. "By the grace of the chief queens" means by the grace of the chief queens of the *paccekabuddhas*.
"Among those supreme among the *paccekajinas*, who have shaken off passion and are such as they are" refers to the *paccekabuddhas* who are unshaken by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
The connection [of the verse] is: "They scattered lotus filaments and lotus pollen and sprinkled [the ground].
The second and third verses are straightforward. 13–16.
In the fourth verse, it is said, "There was a great festival for the Bodhi tree," because the Blessed One Vipassī possessed the state of being the basis for the knowledge of the four paths.
The meaning is that there was an offering to the tree which had received the name "Bodhi.

At the time of the Bodhi-pūjā, to the great multitude assembled there, the Fully Enlightened One—the World-Chief, the Bull among Men—appeared as if standing upon the tree, like the very essence of the tree;
such is the meaning. "The Blessed One at that time" means at that occasion when the Bodhi-pūjā was being performed.
The Blessed One, preceded by the community of monks and surrounded by the community of monks, uttered the roar of his voice;
that is to say, speaking and articulating with a soft, smooth, sweet, and supreme sound, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths—the meaning is that he taught them.
And "teaching both in brief" means teaching in accordance with the inclinations of the individuals to be trained, both in summary and in detail.
The meaning is "he taught. Regarding the term *vivaṭṭacchado*: lust (*rāga*) is a covering, hatred (*dosa*) is a covering, delusion (*moha*) is a covering; all defilements (*kilesa*) are coverings.
He by whom these coverings have been uncovered, opened, removed, and destroyed is *vivaṭṭacchada*, the Fully Awakened One (*sambuddha*).
He extinguished that great multitude by means of his teaching; the meaning is that he stilled their feverish distress. Of him, I—
"Having heard the Dhamma" means having heard the Dhamma being taught by that Blessed One.

In the fifth Apadāna, "bearing fruit in hand, full of longing" means that upon seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, he took sweet fruits and, being full of longing, went slowly and unhurriedly to his hermitage; this is the meaning.
The sixth and seventh Apadānas are self-evident.

40. When the eighth *apadāna* is completed, "and in the new work" (*navakamme*) means when the new work on the boundary (*sīmā*) has been finished. "They gave an anointing" (*anulepamadāsuṃ*) means that afterwards they gave a plaster of lime; they had it plastered with lime—this is the meaning.
The ninth and tenth *apadānas* are indeed self-evident.
The commentary on the thirty-first chapter is complete.
32. Ārakkhadāyakavagga: 1–10.
Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Ārakkhadāyaka and others.
The first, second, and third apadānas in the thirty-second chapter are indeed easy to understand.

16. Regarding the fourth *apadāna*, "I sprinkled with water-born [flowers]": the meaning is that I sprinkled and worshipped with the most excellent water-born flowers, such as the blue lotus (*utpala*), the red lotus (*paduma*), and so forth.
The fifth *apadāna* is self-evident. 26–27.
Regarding the sixth *apadāna*, "the supreme shrine named Sikhin, the Kinsman of the World": this refers to [the Buddha] who is the kinsman of the entire triple world.
The connection is as follows: "The supreme shrine of my kinsman, the Blessed One Sikhi, was in a wilderness—a forest devoid of human traffic, a great jungle free from the clamor of people.

Regarding the phrase "At that time I wandered about blind": at that moment in the forest, because I was lost on the path, I was blind—not blind in the sense of lacking eyes—but I wandered about the way like one who is blind.

The meaning is "I am searching. "By me departing from the forest" means by me departing from the great forest, the lion-throne—the supreme seat, or the seat of the Blessed One who is like a lion—was seen; this is the meaning.
"Having placed my joined palms to one side" means having arranged the upper robe to one side and placing the joined palms upon the head; this is the meaning. "I praised the Leader of the World."
The meaning is that he offered praise to that which leads to Nibbāna, the principle of the threefold world, which has been extolled. 34.
In the seventh apadāna, "Sudassano Mahāvīro" means: he of beautiful appearance, because his body is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
he of captivating appearance, the Blessed One Siddhattha, who possesses great heroism—this is the connection. "In the most excellent dwelling-house" means in the supreme [abode].
The meaning is that he dwells in a monastery.
The eighth, ninth, and tenth acquisitions are self-evident.
The commentary on the thirty-second chapter is completed.
33. The Chapter on Umāpupphiya (Umāpupphiyavagga).
1–10. Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Umāpupphiya and Others.
In the thirty-third chapter, the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth apadānas are indeed straightforward.
55. In the *Sattamāpadāna*, "I went to the assembly" means "I went to the gathering place, to the assembly. 62.
Regarding "Abbuda and Nirabbuda": because it is stated that "one hundred thousand times ten million *koṭis* is an *abbuda*;
one hundred thousand times ten million *abbudas* is a *nirabbuda*," the lords of men who have gone there possess a great lifespan measured by *abbuda* and *nirabbuda*.
The eight kṣatriya wheel-turning monarchs existed in groups of eight during twenty-five thousand eons;
this is the meaning of "they were. The eighth, ninth, and tenth chapters of the *Apadāna* are indeed well-known.
The commentary on the thirty-third chapter is completed.
34–38. The Chapter on Perfumed Water and Other Offerings (Gandhodakādivagga). 1–50. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gandhadhūpiya and Others.
The thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth, thirty-sixth, thirty-seventh, and thirty-eighth chapters are indeed self-evident in their meaning.
In the thirty-ninth chapter, from the first *apadāna* up to the eighth *apadāna*, the meaning is already clear.
39. The Chapter on the *Avaṭaphala* (The Untorn Fruit). 9. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Soṇakoṭivīsa.
The *Apadāna* beginning with "In the dispensation of Vipassi" and so forth is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Soṇa Koṭivīsa Thera.

This Thera, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassi into a family of great wealth belonging to a guild-leader; and upon reaching maturity...
Having become a merchant, he went to the monastery together with lay devotees;

having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, with a mind full of serene confidence, he had the Blessed One’s walking path plastered with lime, constructed a cave-dwelling, spread the floor of the cave with cloths of various colors, and fashioned a canopy above it.
Then, having dedicated it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, for seven days...
Having given a great gift, he made a formal aspiration (paṇidhāna). The Teacher offered words of appreciation (anumodana).

Through that wholesome deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing both types of excellence, when the Blessed One Kassapa—the Great Sage—had attained final Nibbāna and our own Blessed One had not yet appeared, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī. Upon reaching maturity, [he stood] on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having built a leaf-hut, he respectfully served a certain paccekabuddha who was dwelling there for three months with the four requisites.
When the paccekabuddha had completed the rainy season retreat and his requisites were fulfilled, he returned to Gandhamādana.
That noble son also performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived; passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
In the time of our Blessed One, he took rebirth in the house of Aggaseṭṭhi in the city of Campā.
From the moment of his conception, the merchant’s great mass of wealth increased.

On the day he emerged from his mother’s womb, there was great gain, honor, and respect throughout the entire city, due to his previous gift of a red woolen blanket worth one hundred thousand pieces to a Paccekabuddha.
His physical form was golden-hued and exceedingly delicate; therefore, they gave him the name Soṇa. He grew up with a great retinue.

The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were the color of the bandhujīvaka flower, and their touch was as soft as cotton that has been carded a hundred times. On the soles of his feet, there were hairs the color of jeweled earrings.
He was born. When he reached maturity, they had three palaces built for him, suitable for the three seasons, and provided him with female dancers.
He dwelt there enjoying great prosperity like a young god.
Then, when our Blessed One had attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he resided near Rājagaha.

While staying there, he was summoned by King Bimbisāra; together with those eighty thousand village headmen, he came to Rājagaha, went into the presence of the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, acquired faith.

Having obtained permission from his mother and father, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Having received full ordination, he took a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher.
In order to avoid the company of people, he dwelt in the Sītavana forest. While living there, he reflected:
"My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness merely through ease; it is right to practice the duty of a recluse even by wearying the body.
Having thus resolved upon standing and walking meditation alone, he applied himself to striving, even though blisters arose on the soles of his feet.
While maintaining equanimity toward feeling, he exerted firm energy; however, being unable to produce any distinction due to over-exertion of energy, he thought:
"Even though I am striving in this way, I am unable to produce the paths and fruits. What is the use of my renunciation?
It would be better for me to return to the low life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds. Then the Teacher [addressed] him...
Having understood Soṇa’s mental disposition, the Teacher went to him and, after exhorting him with the parable of the lute, showed him the method for applying evenness of energy.
Having thus purified his meditation subject, he returned to Vulture Peak.
Soṇa, for his part, having received this exhortation from the Teacher, applied evenness of energy, intensified his insight, and established himself in Arahantship.

49. Having thus become an Arahant and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke the verse beginning with "In the dispensation of Vipassī.
Therein, "Vipassī" means one who sees specifically or one who sees in various ways; thus he is Vipassī.
"Pāvacane" means that which is spoken forth clearly (*pakārena vuccati*), namely the Three Pitakas. "In the dispensation of that Vipassī"—that is, in those Three Pitakas.

The meaning [of the terms]: "Leṇa" means a shelter (*leṇa*); it is called *leṇa* because people hide or dwell within it; thus, it refers to a monastery (*vihāra*). "In the royal capital of Bandhumatī":
those who bind themselves to one another through the succession of their lineage are called *bandhū*, which means kinsmen.

Because they reside there, it is called *Bandhumā*; or, because it possesses kinsmen (*bandhu*), it is *Bandhumā*. A place where kings dwell is a royal capital (*rājadhānī*); [thus, it is] Bandhumatī.
And because it was both that [place] and a royal capital, it is the royal capital of Bandhumatī; the connection is “by me a shelter was made in that royal capital of Bandhumatī.
The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Soṇakoṭivīsa is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Buddha Pubbakammapilotika. 64.

Regarding the tenth *apadāna*, the phrase "near the lake Anotatta" (*anotattasarāsanne*) means that because it is shielded by mountain peaks, there is no water here that has become heated or warm from the scorching heat of the sun and moon;
thus, it is called *Anotatta*. They remember (*saranti*), go to (*gacchanti*), and originate from it (*pabhavanti*).

A lake (*sara*) is so called because great rivers flow forth from it. The meaning is that the great rivers issuing from the Lion’s Mouth and other openings flow out, circling three times to the right each time, and then proceed in the direction from which they issued.
That lake is Anotatta; thus, it is the "Anotatta Lake. A place situated near or close to that lake is "near the Anotatta Lake" (*anotattasarāsanna*).

"In its vicinity" means near that Anotatta Lake. "Delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) means it is a place to be enjoyed and frequented by gods, asuras, gandhabbas, kinnaras, uragas, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others;
[it is] in that delightful place. "Upon a stone slab" means upon a solid rock slab of a single mountain.
"Shining with various jewels" means shining clearly with many various gems, such as ruby and beryl.

While [the Buddha] was shining forth. "In the midst of a forest thick with various fragrances" means that he was seated upon a stone slab in the interior of a forest made dense by many kinds of fragrant flowers, such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *tāmāla*, *tilaka*, *asoka*, *nāga*, *punnāga*, *ketaka*, and so forth.
(65) "By a great community of monks" refers to one that was great both in terms of its noble qualities (*guṇa*) and its numerical size; "surrounded" means encompassed or encircled by it.
The Leader of the World, the Fully Enlightened One who has conquered the three worlds, sat there upon the stone seat and explained his own past deeds, specifically making them manifest;
this is the meaning. The rest here is easily understood, as it has already been stated below in the *Buddhāpadāna* and its meaning is straightforward.
Although [the deeds] are included within the *Buddhāpadāna*, they are mentioned here in this *Apadāna* because they indicate both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The Elder Councilors compiled [the texts] by way of grouping them into chapters.
The commentary on the *Buddhāpadāna* as a fragment of past karma is completed.
The commentary on the thirty-ninth chapter is completed.
40. Pilindavaccha Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
In the fortieth chapter of the Apadāna, beginning with "In the city of Haṃsavatī," [is contained] the account of the Venerable Elder Pilindavaccha.

The Apadāna. This [person], too, having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various states of existence, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of gatekeepers;
he possessed great wealth and vast enjoyments. Looking upon his hoard of a billion coins of wealth, while sitting in private, he thought: "This..."

Thinking, "It is right for me to depart after properly taking all my wealth," and having resolved, "It is right to give a gift of all requisites to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha," he had all his articles of use and requisites manufactured by the hundreds of thousands,
beginning with one hundred thousand parasols, and [presented them] to the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having invited [the Sangha], he gave a great almsgiving to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

Having thus given alms for seven days, on the final day he made an aspiration for the attainment of Nibbāna; and having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, at the end of his life he was reborn in the world of the gods, where he experienced the divine splendors of the six sense-sphere heavens, and among humans, the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and other such attainments.
Having experienced [the results of his past deeds], he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance into a brahmin family;
having attained mastery in all arts and sciences, he became well-known by the name Pilindavaccha according to his clan.
One day, having heard a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and before long—
Having become an arahant and recollecting his own past kamma, he became filled with joy;
proclaiming it by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "In the city of Haṃsavatī. Its meaning has already been explained above.
"I was a doorkeeper" means that in the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a gatekeeper at the king's palace. "Unshakable and immeasurable wealth" refers to the king’s...
The meaning is: "In my house there has been accumulated and heaped up immeasurable, boundless wealth—vast riches that cannot be shaken or moved by others. 3.
"Many riches have been attained": the meaning is that many riches were acquired, reached, and obtained by me.
The names of the requisites, such as the *satthavāsi* (carpenter’s tool), are easily understood through the application of the method [of analysis].
The benefits of giving these requisites are likewise easily understood. Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
The second, third, fourth, and fifth *apadānas* are indeed straightforward.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bākula:
In the sixth *apadāna*, the *apadāna* of the Elder Bākula begins with the words "Not far from the Himavat... This Elder, it is said, was...

In the past, at the very beginning of an incalculable eon exceeding one hundred thousand kalpas prior to the appearance of the Blessed One Anomadassi, he was reborn into a brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas;
however, seeing no essence therein, he thought, "I shall seek that which pertains to the future life," and having gone forth as an ascetic, he dwelt at the foot of a mountain.
Dwelling as one who had attained the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he heard of the appearance of a Buddha.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he was established in the refuges.

When the Teacher fell ill with a wind-disorder (*vātābādha*), he brought medicinal herbs from the forest and cured him. Having dedicated that merit for the sake of [the Teacher’s] health, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having been reborn and wandering among gods and humans for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), he was born into a certain family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma;
seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those with little illness, he himself, desiring that same status, made a formal aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).
Having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived and having accumulated merit, he wandered only through the happy realms.
Even before the arising of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī.

Having attained mastery in all the arts and sciences, seeing no essence therein, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*). Having become a possessor of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he dwelt at the foot of a mountain.
Vasanta, having heard of the arising of a Buddha, went into the presence of the Teacher and established himself in the refuges.

When the disease known as *tiṇapupphaka* arose among the bhikkhus, he pacified it. Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that state and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
From there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa—
Having been reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī and living the life of a householder, he saw a great monastery that was old and decaying;
having had all the dwellings there, such as the Uposatha hall, constructed, and having prepared all medicinal requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
he performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and spent an entire interval between Buddhas among gods and humans.
While wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn even before our Blessed One’s appearance in the family of a merchant in Kosambī.
After emerging from his mother’s womb, while he was being bathed in the Yamunā by nurses for his health, he slipped from their hands and was swallowed by a fish.
Fishermen caught that fish with a net, and [it was brought] to the merchant’s wife in Bārāṇasī.
They sold her. Having taken her and while she was splitting [the wood], she saw that the boy was healthy due to the fruit of merit performed in the past;
thinking, "I have gained a son," she took him and raised him. When his biological parents heard of this occurrence, they came and made a claim, saying, "This is our son;
give us back our son. To which the king replied, "He belongs to both parties equally."
Having been established as the adjudicator for the inheritance dispute between two families with the words, "Let it be so," he received the name Bākula.
Upon reaching maturity, while enjoying great prosperity, he resided for six months at a time in each of two merchant families.
When their turn arrived, those families would construct a double-hull ship and erect a jeweled pavilion upon it.
Having had the fivefold musical instruments prepared and having seated the boy there, they proceeded to the central meeting place between the two cities along the Ganges;
other merchant men likewise made preparations, went to that spot, and having placed the boy there, departed.
As he grew up in this manner, he reached eighty years of age and became well known as "The Son of Both Merchants."
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth.
Striving for seven days, on the eighth day he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having become an Arahant, he recollected his own former karma; filled with joy, he proclaimed the account of his past conduct.
"He lived not far from the Himavanta," and so forth, he said. Its meaning has already been explained above. The meaning of the *Apadāna* text is also easy to understand.
Having attained Arahatship, dwelling in the bliss of liberation, and having a lifespan of six hundred years, he passed away into Parinibbāna.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bākula is complete.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Girimānanda.
In this seventh *apadāna*, the account of the venerable Elder Girimānanda begins with the words, “My wife has passed away,” and so forth.

This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; in various existences, he accumulated the roots of merit that serve as the necessary conditions for the cessation of rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he was reborn into a noble family. Upon reaching maturity, he established a household and lived there;
however, when his wife and children passed away, he was pierced by the arrow of grief.
Entering the forest, subsisting on wild fruits that appeared of their own accord, he dwelt at the foot of a tree. At that time, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One Sumedha went there.

Having gone there and taught the Dhamma, he extracted the dart of sorrow. Having heard the Dhamma, with a mind full of faith, he honored the Blessed One with fragrant flowers, prostrated himself on his five limbs, and having placed his joined palms to his head, he praised him.
By that merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans and experiencing happiness in both places, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
He was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of the royal chaplain to King Bimbisāra; his name was Girimānanda.
Upon reaching maturity, he witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during the Teacher’s arrival at Rājagaha.
Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness and, while practicing the duties of a recluse, stayed for several days in a village residence before going to pay homage to the Teacher.
He went to Rājagaha. When King Bimbisāra heard of his arrival, he approached him and invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, please stay right here;
I shall serve you with the four requisites. Although the king had departed after making this invitation, because of his many duties, he did not remember [to visit].
[Thinking], "The Elder dwells only in the open air," the deities, fearing that the Elder would become wet, [sent] a rain-shower.
They detained him. The king, having investigated and understood the reason for his distress, had a small hut built for the elder.

While dwelling in that hut, the elder—having attained mental concentration through the acquisition of a suitable dwelling, having balanced his energy, and having intensified his insight—reached the state of Arahatship.

419. Thus, having attained Arahantship and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct, spoke the words beginning with "My wife has passed away.

Both that report to the Blessed One and the instruction given by the Blessed One, as well as the account of the attainment of the Path and its Fruit, are easily understood according to the sequence of the text.
The commentary on the *Girimānanda Thera-apadāna* is completed.
The eighth, ninth, and tenth *apadānas* are of clear meaning.
The commentary on the fortieth chapter is completed.
41. Metteyya-vagga. 1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tissa-Metteyya. 1.
In the first apadāna of the forty-first chapter, beginning with the words "relying on Pabbhārakūṭa," [is the account] of the Elder Tissa-Metteyya.

The Apadāna. In this regard, there is no need for further explanation concerning the fact that he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic and gave a deerskin to the Blessed One Padumuttara for the purpose of a sitting mat;
the remainder is easily understood from the text of the Apadāna itself.
2. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Puṇṇaka.
29. The second Apadāna, beginning with "Dependent upon the peak of the mountain slope," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇaka.

In this account, the only distinctive feature is the construction of a funeral pyre for the Paccekabuddha who had attained final Nibbāna while serving as a general of the Yakkhas in the Himavat mountains.
The remainder is easily understood by following the text.
45. The third *Apadāna*, beginning with "Not far from the Himālayas," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Mettagu Thera.
Therein, having lived as an ascetic on Mount Asoka near the Himālayas while residing in a leaf-hut, he saw the Sambuddha Sumedha;
the distinction was that he took a bowl and filled it with ghee. The remaining fruits of merit are easily understood. [This concludes] the verses of the *Apadāna*.
The meaning is indeed clear.
72. In the fourth *Apadāna*, beginning with "The Ganges named Bhāgīrathī," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Thera Dhotaka.
Therein, having been a brahmin, seeing monks crossing the Ganges river named Bhāgīrathī, with a mind full of faith he [built] a bridge...
The distinction lies solely in the fact that [the offering] was dedicated to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
The meaning of the verses illustrating the fruit of merit is easily understood by following the method of exposition.
100. In the fifth Apadāna, beginning with "Not far from the Himālaya," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Upasīva.

This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic (isipabbajjā). Having seen the Blessed One Padumuttara in the Himālaya mountains, he [prepared] a grass mat...
The distinction here is that after spreading [the cloth], he made an offering of *sāla* flowers to the Blessed One as he sat there; the rest is self-evident.
161. The legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Nandaka Thera begins with the words, "In former times, I was a deer-hunter.
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a *karavika* bird and, while uttering its sweet song, [he offered it].
He circumambulated the Teacher. Later on, having become a peacock, he joyfully cried out with a sweet voice three times a day at the entrance of the cave where a certain Paccekabuddha dwelt.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds in various successive existences, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One.
Having received the name Nandakoṭi, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight, attained Arahantship.
At a later time, recollecting his own past karma and filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words:
"In the past, I was a deer-hunter... and so forth. In this account, the specific detail is that he constructed a pavilion for the Paccekabuddha and covered it with lotus flowers.
183. The legend of the Venerable Hemaka Thera begins with the words, "Dependent upon the peak of a mountain slope," and so forth.
Therein, having gone forth as an ascetic and dwelling in the Himālayas, he saw the Blessed One Piyadassī approaching;
having spread out a throne made of jewels, he stood there. For the Blessed One seated upon it, he offered a *jambu* fruit the size of a water-jar.
Having brought it, he gave it [to the Buddha]. The Blessed One consumed that fruit for the sake of gladdening his mind. This much is the distinction.
224. The legend (Apadāna) of the Venerable Elder Todeyya begins with the words, "O King, you were named Vijaya.
Therein, "O King, you were named Vijaya" refers to his victory in all battles from the time of his youth, and by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
The meaning is that there was a king named Vijaya because he delighted (*rañjana*) and won over (*allīyana*) the people.

Regarding the phrase "in the supreme city of Ketumatī": *ketu* refers to banners and flags; or alternatively, it refers to jeweled archways erected in the center of the city for the sake of its beauty.
Since those *ketus* were constantly raised and graced the city, it was called Ketumatī. It filled all the people with wealth and grain.
They call it a city. And since that city, Ketumatī, is supreme in the sense of being the most excellent, it is called "Ketumatīpuruttama" (the supreme city of Ketumatī);
[he] dwelt in that supreme city of Ketumatī. The connection is: "A king named Vijaya, fearless and endowed with valor, resided there. Having abandoned such a city and all its property and vehicles—
Having entered the Himālaya mountains and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, while dwelling there, he saw the Blessed One Sumedha;
having conceived great joy, his specific deed was the offering of sandalwood. 276.
This is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Jatukaṇṇī, beginning with the words "In the city of Haṃsavatī."
