In this regard, the distinction lies in his state of dwelling in a golden palace as the son of a merchant, his state of living endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, and the fact that people from all regions and those skilled in all crafts came to serve him. 330.
In the tenth Apadāna, beginning with "Not far from the Himalayas," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Udena Thera. Therein:

The distinction lies in the fact that while living near the Himavat mountains, having gone forth into the ascetic life in reliance upon Mount Paduma, he took a lotus flower and offered it in worship to the Blessed One Padumuttara. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Forty-first Chapter is completed.
42. Bhaddāli-vagga: 1–10. Commentary on the Apadānas of Bhaddāli Thera and others.
In the forty-second chapter, the first, second, and third apadānas are easily understood by following the established method.
106. The fourth *Apadāna*, beginning with "In the city of Bandhumatī," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Madhumaṃsadāyaka Thera.
Therein, "pig-butcher" refers to one who makes his living by selling pork.
"Having cooked the *ukkoṭaka*" means having cooked the flesh of the *pihakapapphāsa* (the lungs) and sprinkling it over the sweet meat (*madhumaṃsa*). With that meat, [he filled] the bowl.
The meaning is that, having filled [the bowls] and given them to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they attained Arahatship in this present dispensation of a Buddha by means of that meritorious deed.
There is also the fifth *Apadāna* of the Elder Nāgapallava, the sixth *Apadāna* of the Elder Ekadīpiya, the seventh *Apadāna* of the Elder Ucchaṅgapupphiya,
the eighth *Apadāna* of the Elder Yāgudāyaka, and the ninth *Apadāna* of the Elder Patthodanadāyaka.
Even the tenth *apadāna* of the Elder Mañcadāyaka is entirely easy to understand.
The commentary on the Forty-Fourth Chapter is completed. 43–48.
The Chapter on the Once-Sweeper, etc. (*Sakiṃsammajjakādivagga*).
1–60. Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Sakiṃsammajjaka and others:
In the forty-third chapter, all the elders’ Apadānas are indeed clear. The distinction lies solely in the diversity of the elders' names and the diversity of their merits.
In the forty-fourth chapter as well, all the Apadānas are likewise manifest. The distinction lies solely in the diversity of their merits and the diversity of their fruits.
1. In the forty-fifth chapter, the first *apadāna*, beginning with "Kakusandha, the Great Hero," is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Vibhīṭakamiñjiya Thera. 2.

Regarding that, the meaning of "he gave the seeds and kernels" is that he split open the Vibhīṭaka fruits, took the seeds and kernels, mixed them with honey and sugar, and gave them to the Blessed One Kakusandha. All the subsequent *apadānas*, beginning with the second, are indeed easy to understand.
The various names of the elders and so forth should also be understood according to the recitation. 1.

In the first account of the forty-sixth chapter, "I had a *jagati* made" means "I had a veranda (*āḷinda*) built all around the tree of supreme enlightenment. All the remaining accounts, beginning with the second, are likewise self-evident.
In the forty-seventh chapter, the first account and those following are easily understood by following the Pāḷi text.
In the forty-eighth chapter, the first and second accounts are indeed self-evident. 30. Regarding the third account:
"The Blessed One named Kosiya" means that he was a Paccekabuddha named Kosiya because he was born into the Kosiya clan (*gotra*).
"At Cittakūṭa" refers to among the mountain peaks—such as Cittakūṭa, Kelāsakūṭa, Sānu, and Kūṭa—that stand concealing Lake Anotatta.
The meaning is that on the Citrakūṭa mountain, which was variegated with various jewels, medicinal herbs, and so forth, that Paccekabuddha resided.
The fourth and fifth accounts (*apadāna*) are indeed plain. 56. Regarding the sixth account:

"I gave eight-fold offerings" means that among the various types of alms-food such as *pakkhika-bhatta* (fortnightly food), *uposathika-bhatta* (food for the observance day), *dhura-bhatta* (regular food), and *salāka-bhatta* (ticketed food), I gave the eight-fold ticketed food (*aṭṭha-salāka-bhatta*) by way of *kusa* leaves. This is the meaning.

61. In the seventh *apadāna*, "Sobhita": because his body was radiant with height, circumference, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the fathom-wide halo, and so forth, the meaning is that the Perfectly Enlightened One was named Sobhita (the Radiant).

66. In the eighth *apadāna*, "He dwelt then in Takkarā": the meaning is that he dwelt then in that royal capital called Takkarā, which is so named because people who perform those ten bases of meritorious action (*dasapuññakiriyavatthu*) reside there. "In that Takkarā, he dwelt then."
72. In the *Navama-apadāna*, "taking a well-made *pānadhi*" means taking a pair of sandals that have been fashioned in a beautiful form. The tenth *apadāna* is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the forty-eighth chapter is finished. 49.
The Chapter on Rags from Refuse (*Paṃsukūla-vagga*).
1–10. Commentary on the Legends (Apadāna) beginning with the Elder Saññaka of the Rag-Robes.
The first legend in the forty-ninth chapter is indeed easy to understand. 14. Regarding the second legend:

"Buddhas who arise without a cause" (*adhiccuppattikā buddhā*) means those who arise spontaneously (*adhiccena*), that is, without a specific cause; they are self-become (*sayambhūtā*). The meaning is that they have arisen, been born, and become manifest through self-originated knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), being devoid of any instructors such as other gods, Brahmās, or Māras.
16. "Like the Udumbara flower" means that a flower on the Udumbara tree is as difficult to find as something whose appearance is rare.
"As the hare-mark in the moon" means that the form of the hare-line within the lunar disc is as difficult to find.
"Like milk for crows" means that milk is as difficult for crows to obtain as it is, because they are constantly oppressed by hunger day and night.

Thus, the meaning is that the Leader of the World is difficult to encounter; for after fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*) for four incalculable eons, eight incalculable eons, or sixteen incalculable eons, and hundreds of thousands of aeons, he becomes a Buddha—therefore, the Leader of the World is rare.
30. Regarding the third *apadāna*: "Honey flows with lotus stalks" means it flows and drips from the filaments of the lotuses in the honey-lotus pond.
"Khīraṃ sappiṃ muḷālibhī" means that milk and the essence of ghee flow and drip from the lotus roots;
therefore, the meaning is: "May the Buddha accept both of these as my own.
The fourth, fifth, and sixth verses are self-evident.
119. Regarding the eleventh *apadāna*: "Forty birds" (*dijā*) means those born twice; thus they are called *dijā*.
Because their teeth, which had emerged in childhood, fell out and then grew back again, they are *dijā*, and these are their teeth. The explanation has already been given below in the *Nidānakathā*.
The eighth *apadāna* is self-evident.
171. Regarding the *Navama-apadāna*, it says: "At that time, I was a young brahmin (*māṇava*).
When the wise Sumedha received his prophecy from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, I was a brahmin youth named Megha.

Having gone forth as an ascetic along with the ascetic Sumedha, I trained in the precepts; however, through association with a certain evil companion, I fell under the influence of the fault of such association.
Having fallen under the sway of evil thoughts and the like, he experienced the suffering of fiery flames and other torments in hell due to the kamma of matricide.
Passing away from there, he was reborn as a great *timiṅgala* fish in the ocean. Desiring to swallow a large ship passing through the middle of the sea, he went toward it.
Upon seeing him, the merchants were terrified and cried out, "Oh, the Blessed One Gotama! Then—
The great fish, having generated reverence for the Buddha through the influence of past impressions (*pubbavāsanā*), passed away from there and was reborn in Sāvatthī into a wealthy brahmin family.
Endowed with faith and confidence, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, went forth, and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Going to pay his respects three times a day, he remembered [his former life] and paid homage. At that time—
The Blessed One said to me, "Ciraṃ Dhammaruci.
Then that elder praised him with verses beginning, "O you who possess the hundred marks of merit for a very long time. "Bhante, O Gotama who bears the hundred marks of merit!
By 'patipubbena visuddhapaccaya' is meant that previously, at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, the equipment for the perfections was fully completed."
The meaning is: "I have not seen [him] for a very long time. Regarding the phrase *ahamajjasupekkhanam*:

today, on this very day, I shall indeed behold (*passāmi*)—that is, see (*dakkhāmi*) with certainty—the one named Gotama, whose beautiful sight (*suppekkhanam*) is a lovely vision (*sundaradassanam*), or rather, a lovely form (*sundaradiṭṭham*), a peerless body (*nirupamaṃ viggahaṃ*), a physique beyond comparison (*upamārahita-sarīram*). This is the meaning.
185–186. "By me, darkness has been long dispelled"—the meaning is that you, whose darkness is especially destroyed and whose delusion is shattered, have been well praised by me for a very long time.

"The river of craving has been dried up by beautiful guarding"—the meaning is that this river of craving has been specifically dried up by beautiful guarding and protection; it has been rendered incapable of arising by you. "For a very long time, the stainless has been purified."
The meaning is: "The stainless *nibbāna* has been especially purified by you for a very long time, over a vast duration; it has been well accomplished and attained.

"O Great Sage, the eye consisting of knowledge"—the meaning is: "O Great Sage, O Great Ascetic, the eye consisting of knowledge, namely the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), has been acquired and reached by you for a long time. "Unperished" (*avinaṭṭho*).
"Again I was lost within," means that once more, in the midst of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), I had perished and fallen away.
"Today I have come together with you again," means that today, at this time, I have once more come together with you, become one with you, and dwell together.
"For deeds done do not perish, O Gotama," [means] O Gotama, the Omniscient Buddha, [deeds done] do not vanish along with you.
The meaning is that the meetings and so forth performed will not be lost; they will not be separated [from one another] until the final nirvana of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*).
The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dhammaruci is completed.
The tenth *apadāna* is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the forty-ninth chapter (*ekūnapaññāsamavagga*) is completed.
50–53. The Chapter on Kiṅkaṇipuppha and Others.
1–40. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kiṅkaṇipupphiya and others:
All the *Apadānas* in the fiftieth chapter, the fifty-first chapter, the fifty-second chapter, and the fifty-third chapter are indeed clear.
54. The Kaccāyana Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāyana.
In the fifty-fourth chapter, the first apadāna begins with "The Conqueror named Padumuttara," etc., which is the apadāna of the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana.

This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; in various existences, he cultivated the necessary conditions for the turning away from the cycle of rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
While accumulating merit, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara into a great household of wealthy merchants.

Having reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw a certain bhikkhu whom the Teacher had designated as foremost among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief. Seeing this, he himself...
Having made an aspiration while longing for that particular state, and having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he wandered among gods and humans.
During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he became a master of the sciences (vidyādhara) and, traveling through the air, saw the Blessed One seated in a certain forest grove;
with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of *kaṇikāra* flowers.
Thus, by that merit, wandering from one happy destination to another, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he made an offering of a golden brick worth a hundred thousand [pieces] at the site of the Golden Shrine (Suvaṇṇacetiya),
and through the result of this, in every place where he was reborn, his body—

"May he be golden-colored," she made this aspiration. Then, having performed wholesome deeds throughout her life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in Ujjain, in the house of the royal priest of King Caṇḍapajjota.
On the day of his naming, his mother said, "My son is golden-colored; let him take a name for himself..."

Thinking, "He has arrived," they gave him the name Kañcana-māṇava. As he grew up, having mastered the three Vedas, he obtained the position of domestic priest upon his father’s death. He became known by the family name Kaccāyana.
Then King Caṇḍapajjota, having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, said, "Teacher, go there yourself and bring the Teacher here."

He sent him forth. He, being the eighth including himself, approached the presence of the Teacher; the Teacher taught the Dhamma to him, and at the conclusion of the teaching, together with the other seven persons, he was established in Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having thus attained the fruit of Arahatship and remembering his own past karma, he became filled with joy and [recited] the account of his former conduct.

Proclaiming this, he spoke the words beginning with, "The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth; the meaning of that has already been explained above. Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.

At that very moment, they came to possess hair and beards only two finger-breadths long, and they wore robes and bowls made of supernormal power (*iddhi*), appearing like elder monks of sixty years' standing. Having thus accomplished his own purpose, the Elder said, "Venerable Sir, the King..."
"Pajjota wishes to pay homage at your feet and hear the Dhamma," he announced.
The Teacher said, "Kaccāna, you yourself go there; when you have gone, the king will place his trust in you. By the Teacher's command, the Elder went there as the eighth member of the group.
Having won the king’s confidence and established the Teaching in the Avanti country, he returned once more to the presence of the Teacher.

Having arrived, he expounded the three treatises—the *Kaccāyana-pakaraṇa*, the *Mahānirutti-pakaraṇa*, and the *Netti-pakaraṇa*—in the midst of the Saṅgha, by virtue of his own former aspiration. Then, being well-pleased, the Blessed One declared:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples in analyzing in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief: that is to say, Mahākaccāna."
Having been established in this foremost position, he dwelt in the bliss of the supreme fruit.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākaccāyana.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vakkali.
The second *Apadāna*, beginning with "A hundred thousand [aeons] from now," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Vakkali Thera.
This Elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various births,
was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, and attained maturity.
Having gone to the monastery with the lay followers who were proceeding to the presence of the Teacher,
he stood at the edge of the assembly and listened to the Dhamma. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those resolved through faith,
he himself aspired to that very station and, for seven days, [attended] upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having given a great gift, he made an aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacle for him, gave his prediction.
Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during the time of our Blessed One in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī;
they gave him the name Vakkali. In this context, *kali* refers to faults such as blemishes, moles, or black spots.
This is a synonym. Because he was like a mass of refined gold, he was called *Vakkali*—the syllable *va* being added because his blemish (*kali*) had departed (*apagata*) or vanished (*byapagata*).
Having reached maturity and mastered the three Vedas, he attained perfection in the Brahminical arts.
Upon seeing the Teacher, unsatisfied with merely beholding the excellence of his physical form, he traveled about together with the Teacher.
Thinking, "If I live in the midst of a household, I will not obtain a constant vision of the Teacher," he went forth in the presence of the Teacher.

Except for the time of eating and the time of attending to bodily needs, at all other times he would abandon whatever other duties he had and dwell looking toward the Blessed One, standing wherever it was possible to see the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher—
As he was waiting for his knowledge to reach maturity, while Vakkali had been wandering about for a long time merely looking at his physical form, the Buddha said nothing to him.
Then one day he said: "Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body of mine?
Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, he sees me; whoever sees me, he sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, it is the Dhamma..."
“While passing by, he saw me,” he said. Even though the Teacher spoke thus, the Elder was unable to leave the sight of the Teacher and go elsewhere.

Then the Teacher, thinking, “This monk will not attain awakening without experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega),” on the day of the retreat at the onset of the rains, dismissed the Elder, saying, “Go away, Vakkali! Having been dismissed by the Teacher, he... [the Elder] toward the Teacher.
Unable to stand before him, [the monk] thought, "What is the use of my life, since I do not obtain the opportunity to see the Teacher?

and climbed to a precipice on Mount Vulture Peak. The Teacher, knowing his situation, thought, "If this bhikkhu does not receive consolation from me, he will destroy the underlying tendency for the paths and fruits," and so [appeared] himself.
Having shown this, he emitted a radiance and said:
"A bhikkhu full of gladness, with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the stilling of all formations."

Having spoken this verse, he extended his hand, saying, "Come, Vakkali. The Elder, thinking, "I have seen the One of Ten Powers, and I have even received the invitation 'Come,'" gave rise to powerful joy and gladness.
Without even realizing where he was going or his own state of departure, he leaped into the air before the Teacher;
while his first foot was still on the mountain, [the second was already in the sky].

It is recorded in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Dhammapada-vaṇṇanā* that while reflecting upon the verses spoken by the Teacher, he suppressed his rapture even in mid-air and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
However, it should be understood here as follows: having been exhorted by the Teacher with the words, "What [do you have], Vakkali? and so forth, on Vulture Peak...
While dwelling there, he established insight meditation (*vipassanā*), yet because of the excessive strength of his faith, the insight did not enter its proper course.
The Blessed One, knowing this, purified a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and gave it to him. However, he was still unable to bring that insight to its ultimate perfection.
Then, due to a deficiency in food, a wind-disorder arose in him; while he was being oppressed by that wind-disorder, [the Blessed One said:]
Knowing this, the Blessed One went there and asked:
"Afflicted by a wind-disease, dwelling in the forest grove,
with coarse food scattered for alms, how will you fare, O bhikkhu?"
He said: Having heard that, the Elder replied:
"Filling my entire body with abundant rapture and bliss, though enduring even what is coarse, I shall dwell in the forest."
“Cultivating the foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, and the powers;
and cultivating the factors of enlightenment, I shall dwell in the forest.
With energy aroused, resolute, and always firm in my exertion...”
“Having seen them united and in harmony, I shall dwell in the forest.
Recalling the Fully Awakened One— the supreme, the tamed, the concentrated—
I shall dwell in the forest, untiring by day and night.”
He recited four verses. Their meaning has already been explained in the commentary on the *Theragāthā*. Thus, having intensified his insight (*vipassanā*), the elder attained Arahantship.

(28) Having reached Arahantship, he recollected his own past karma; filled with joy, he proclaimed his *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), beginning with the words, "A hundred thousand [aeons] from now...
Therein, "from here" refers to the auspicious eon (*bhaddakappa*) during which Kakusandha and the other Buddhas appeared.
"At the summit of a hundred thousand kalpas below" is the meaning.

29. "Face like the form of a lotus": a face as beautiful as a fully blossomed lotus. "Eyes like lotus petals": eyes resembling the petals of a white lotus flower; this is the meaning. 30. "Fragrance like that of the Padumuttara [Buddha]":
the meaning is one whose mouth has the fragrance of a lotus.

31. "Like eyes for the blind" means he is like an eye for beings deprived of vision; the meaning is that through his teaching of the Dhamma, he is the giver of the eye of wisdom and other such eyes to all beings.
"Peaceful in nature" means his very essence is peaceful and his modes of conduct (īryāpatha) are tranquil.
"A treasure-store of virtues" means a repository of virtues; the meaning is that he is the locus where the entire multitude of virtues is stored. "A mine of compassion and wisdom."

He is the mine, that is, the source or foundation, of compassion—which consists of the stirring of the hearts of the virtuous—and of the wisdom that discerns what is beneficial and what is harmful. 32.
"Honored by Brahmās, Asuras, and Suras" means he is honored and worshipped by the Brahmās, the Asuras, and the gods.
33. "And with his sweet voice" means he delights all people with a sound as sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird.
"Intimacy" (*santhava*): he was intimate with his own disciple, meaning he praised him through sweet Dhamma teachings. "Devoted to faith" (*saddhādhimutta*):
the meaning is that he was devoted to and established in the Teaching through the faith of conviction. "Eager for a sight of me" (*mama dassanalālasa*): he was intent upon and dedicated to seeing me.

35. *Taṃ ṭhānam abhirocayin* means: I delighted in that state of being intent upon faith; the meaning is that I desired and longed for it. 40. *Pītamaṭṭhanivāsanaṃ* means: clad in garments of smooth, golden color;

the meaning is that she was dressed in such clothes. *Hemayaññopacitaṅgaṃ* means: her limbs were adorned with golden ornaments; the meaning is that her body was decorated with golden chains. 47–48. *Nonītasukhumālaṃ maṃ* means:
me, whose hands and feet are as soft and delicate as fresh butter. *Jātapallavakomalaṃ* means: [me, who am] tender like a newly sprouted leaf.
"Soft as the tender sprouts and leaves of the *aśoka* tree" is the meaning.
"Terrified by the fear of a *piśācī*" means that at that time, another *piśācī*, a certain *rākṣasī*, terrified and frightened me while I was in such a state.
Then, they laid me down at the feet of the Great Seer, the Perfectly Enlightened One. My parents were dejected in mind and their hearts were filled with fear.
"We give this boy to you; may he be your refuge, O Lord, O Leader"—this is the connection.

49. Then he accepted him as counsel: at that time, when he was given by my mother, the Blessed One [accepted him] with his soft and tender hand, which was marked with the wheel-sign and other characteristics, and possessed a webbed network of fingers.
The meaning is: "He took hold of me. (52) *Sabbapāramisambhūtam*:
arisen and born from all the perfections, such as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and the rest. *Nīlakkhinayanaṃ varam puññasambhārajam*:
possessing excellent, dark-blue eyes, produced by the accumulation of merit. *Sabbasubhākiṇṇam*: adorned with every kind of beauty and complexion.
The meaning is: "having seen the form of the Blessed One’s hands, feet, head, and so forth, which is crowded with [various parts] by way of shape and has become dense";
"I dwell without having reached satiety" is the connection. 61.
At that time, when I had attained Arahantship—"at the end of my course"—refers to the fifteen qualities beginning with virtue (sīla) at the moment I reached that state.
The meaning is that he reached the end of the duties to be practiced, having attained the conclusion and fulfilled them.

There is also a reading, "maraṇantago. The meaning of that is: he reached the end of death, which is Nibbāna. The connection is: "He designated [him] as the foremost among those resolved through faith.
Then the Teacher, seated in the midst of the community of monks, said: "Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples..."
It is said: "He placed me in the foremost position among those resolved through faith, namely Vakkali. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vakkali is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākappina.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Kappina Thera begins with the words, "The Conqueror named Padumuttara," and so forth.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma.
Hearing this and seeing that the Teacher had established one bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who give exhortation,
he performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that very station.
Having practiced wholesome deeds there for as long as he lived, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, not far from Bārāṇasī, in a certain place...
At that time, he was reborn in the house of the senior weaver in the village of Pesakāra.
About a thousand Paccekabuddhas, having spent eight months in the Himālaya mountains, were dwelling in the countryside during the four months of the rainy season.
On one occasion, they descended not far from Bārāṇasī and sent eight [messengers] to the presence of the king, saying, "Request manual labor for the purpose of preparing our lodgings."
They sent [the invitation] to the Paccekabuddhas. At that time, however, it was the king’s sowing festival (*vappamaṅgala*).
Having heard, “It is said that the Paccekabuddhas have arrived,” he went out, asked the reason for their coming, and said, “Venerable sirs, there is no opportunity today;
tomorrow is our sowing festival, and we shall attend on the third day. Having spoken thus, he did not even invite the Paccekabuddhas.
He entered. The Paccekabuddhas set out, thinking, "We shall enter another village.
At that time, the wife of the chief basket-maker was going to Bārāṇasī on some business;
seeing those Paccekabuddhas, she paid homage to them and asked, "Venerable sirs, why have you noble ones arrived at an improper hour? They [replied] from the beginning...
They began to speak. Hearing this, a woman endowed with faith and wisdom invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept our alms tomorrow.
"We are many, sister," they replied. "How many, venerable sirs? she asked. "About a thousand, sister," they said.
"Venerable sirs, we lived in this village as a group of about a thousand; each one of us gave alms to each monk."
“Give alms, monks; accept [my invitation], and I myself shall have a dwelling place built for you,” she said.
The Paccekabuddhas accepted. She entered the village and proclaimed: “Mothers and fathers, having seen a thousand Paccekabuddhas, I have invited them;
prepare a seating area for the noble ones and provide rice porridge, food, and so forth. In the center of the village, she erected a pavilion.
Having had seats prepared and having seated the Paccekabuddhas on the following day, she served them with excellent hard and soft foods.
At the conclusion of the meal, taking all the women of that village with her, she paid homage to the Paccekabuddhas along with them.
Having obtained their promise to stay for the three-month rains retreat, she then made a proclamation throughout the village.
—“Mother and father, let one man from each family take axes, hatchets, and other tools, enter the forest, bring back building materials, and construct a dwelling place for the noble ladies.
Hearing her words alone, the village dwellers each took their turn;
including the night and day watch-posts, they completed ten thousand leaf-huts, each person contributing their own.
When a Paccekabuddha arrived at a leaf-hut, they would say, "I shall attend upon him with diligence;

I shall attend upon him with diligence," and so they attended upon him. At the conclusion of the rains retreat, she exhorted them, saying, "Prepare robes for the Paccekabuddhas who have completed the rains retreat in their respective leaf-huts," and for each one, [she provided] a thousand...
He had a robe worth a thousand pieces given to them. Having delivered the blessing after their rains-retreat, the Paccekabuddhas departed.
The village dwellers, having performed this meritorious deed, passed away from there and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as deities known as the Gaṇadevatās.
After enjoying divine splendor there, they were reborn in the households of householders during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa.
Formerly, the eldest weaver was the son of the eldest householder, and his wife was the daughter of another eldest householder.
The wives of the others were the daughters of the other householders;
when they all reached marriageable age and went to their husbands' families, they returned to those very same homes. Then, one day, at the monastery during the preaching of the Dhamma—
When it was announced that "the Teacher will teach the Dhamma," all those householders, hearing this, went to the monastery together with their wives, thinking, "We shall hear the Dhamma.
At the very moment they entered the midst of the monastery, it began to rain.
Those who had personal attendants or novice monks related to them as kinsmen entered their respective cells and other quarters. They...
But because there were no such people, they were unable to enter anywhere and remained right in the middle of the monastery.
Then the head householder said to them: "Look, sirs, at our misfortune! Is it not fitting for those called sons of noble family to feel shame even to this extent?
They replied: "Noble sir, what shall we do? He said: "Because we lack a place of trust..."
“Having reached this state of distress, let us all pool our wealth and build a monastery. “Very well, noble sirs,” said the eldest brother, and he gave a thousand pieces of gold.
The others each gave five hundred. The women each gave two hundred and fifty.
Having brought that wealth, they built a great monastery with a thousand-pinnacled gabled hall for the Teacher’s residence.
They had it named. Because the new construction work was so vast and their wealth was insufficient, they gave half again, and then half again more, than the wealth previously given.

When the courtyard was finished, while holding a great festival for the monastery, they offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days, and prepared robes for twenty thousand monks.
But the wife of the elder householder, being established in her own wisdom, thought: "I shall not treat him as my equal, but rather with greater honor;

I will worship the Teacher. Taking an anojā-flower basket along with a thousand-piece cloak the color of an anojā flower, she worshipped the Teacher with the anojā flowers, placed that cloak at the Teacher’s feet, and said, "Venerable Sir,..."
He made this aspiration: "In every place where I am reborn, may my body be the color of the *anoja* flower, and may my name be 'Anoja' itself.
The Teacher gave his approval, saying, "So be it.

They all lived out their full lifespans and, passing away from there, were reborn in the world of the gods. When this Buddha appeared in the world, they passed away from the world of the gods; the eldest...
Having been reborn in the royal family of the city of Kukkuṭavatī, he reached maturity and became known as King Mahākappina.
The others were reborn in the families of the ministers. The wife of the eldest was reborn in the royal family of Sākala in the kingdom of Madda;
her body had the color of an anojā flower, so they gave her the name Anojā.
When she reached maturity, she went to the house of King Mahākappina and became known as Queen Anojā.
The other women also, having been born into the families of the ministers, reached maturity and went to the houses of those very sons of the ministers.
They all enjoyed prosperity equal to that of the king himself. For whenever the king was adorned with ornaments, [they likewise appeared].
When he wandered about mounted on an elephant, they too wandered about in that very same way. When he wandered about by means of a horse or a chariot, they too wandered about in that very same way.
Thus, being together, they experienced prosperity all at once through the power of the merits they had performed together.
As for the king, there were Vāla, Vālavāhana, Puppha, and Pupphavāhana.
"Supatta" refers to five horses. Of these, the king himself mounted the horse Supatta;
he gave the other four horses to the horsemen for the purpose of delivering his message. Having fed them early in the morning, the king said: "Go, my men!
Roam for two or three *yojanas* and find out whether the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha has appeared."
"Having heard it, announce my pleasant message," he sent them. They departed through the four gates and wandered for two or three *yojanas*, but returned without having obtained any message at all.
Then one day, the king, having mounted his horse Supatta and being surrounded by a thousand ministers, was going to the pleasure garden when [he saw] those who appeared weary...
Seeing about five hundred merchants entering the city, [the king] thought, "These people must be weary from their journey;
I shall surely hear a wonderful message from them. He had them summoned and asked, "From where have you come?
They replied, "Your Majesty, there is a city named Sāvatthī at a distance of two thousand yojanas from here; we have come from there."
“But has any news arisen for you in this region? “Your Majesty, there is nothing else; a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared.
At that very moment, the king’s body was so overwhelmed by powerful joy that he was unable to perceive anything else.
After waiting for a short while, he asked, “Sirs, what do you say? “A Buddha, Your Majesty, has appeared.”
The king spent the second and third times in the same manner. On the fourth occasion, having asked, "What do you say, dear ones?
and being told, "A Buddha has appeared," he said, "Dear ones, I give you a hundred thousand pieces for the sake of hearing such pleasant news.
Then he asked, "Is there any further message, dear ones? They replied, "There is, Your Majesty; the Dhamma has appeared. The king—
Having heard that as well, he passed three rounds in the same manner as before;
when it was said on the fourth round, "The Dhamma has appeared," he said, "I shall give you another hundred thousand here as well," and asked, "Is there any further message, dear ones?
"There is, Your Majesty: the Saṅgha has appeared. Having heard that too, the king likewise passed three rounds in the same manner.

On the fourth occasion, when it was said, “The Saṅgha has arisen,” he said, “I shall give you another hundred thousand here as well,” and after looking at his thousand ministers, he asked, “Sirs, what shall we do? They replied, “Your Majesty, what will you do?
He said, “Sirs, having heard that ‘the Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Saṅgha has arisen,’ I shall not turn back again.”
“Having gone for the sake of the Blessed One, I shall go forth in his presence. “We too, Your Majesty, will go forth together with you,” they replied.
The king had letters inscribed on a golden plate, gave it to the merchants, and said:
“Give this to the queen named Anojā; she will give you three hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and furthermore—”
"You should say to him: 'The King has indeed granted you authority; enjoy prosperity as you please.
But if he asks, 'Where is your king?', report that he has gone away, saying, 'He has gone forth into homelessness for the sake of the Teacher.
Thus he spoke. The ministers likewise sent such a message to their respective wives.
Having dispatched the merchants, the king mounted his horse and set out at that very moment, surrounded by a thousand ministers.
On that same day, as the Teacher surveyed the world at dawn, he saw King Mahākappina together with his retinue and thought:
"This Mahākappina, having heard from the merchants that the Three Jewels have appeared, [will go to them]..."
"Having honored these words with three hundred thousand [offerings], he will renounce his kingdom and, surrounded by a thousand ministers, desire to go forth under me;
tomorrow he will depart, and together with his retinue, he will attain *arahantship* along with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
I shall go out to meet him. On the following day, like a universal monarch, [he went] to the king who was the lord of the small village.

Going out to meet him, the Teacher himself took his bowl and robe and, having traveled two hundred yojanas along the road to welcome him, sat down at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the river Candabhāgā, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha.
As the King was approaching, he reached a certain river and asked, "What is the name of this river? "It is called Aparacchā, O King. "What of it?"
“What is its size, dear? “It is one *gāvuta* in depth, O gods, and two *gāvutas* in width.
“But is there a boat or a raft here? “There is none, O gods. “While we look for boats and such, birth leads us toward old age, and old age toward death.
Having become free from doubt, I have gone forth for the sake of the Three Jewels; for them—”

Through my power, having focused on the virtues of the Triple Gem with the thought, "May this water not be like water," and recollecting the Buddha's qualities by reflecting, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One:
the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," he and his retinue leaped upon the surface of the water with a thousand horses.
The thoroughbreds leaped as if onto the backs of solid rocks; only the tips of their hooves were wetted.
Having crossed that river and proceeding forward, he saw another river and asked, "What is the name of this one?
"It is named Nīlavāhā, O Lord," they replied. "What is its size? "In both depth and breadth, it is half a yojana, O Lord.
The rest is exactly as before. Upon seeing that river, he practiced the recollection of the Dhamma, thinking: "Well-proclaimed is the Dhamma by the Blessed One."
Recalling [the Buddha], he leaped across it. Having crossed that as well, as he was going on, he saw another river and asked, "What is the name of this?
"It is called the Candabhāgā, O King. "What is its size? "In both depth and breadth, it is one *yojana*, O King.
The rest is exactly as before. But upon seeing that river, [he thought]: "The Blessed One has entered the right path..."
He leaped forward while recollecting the recollection of the Saṅgha, thinking, "This is the Saṅgha of the disciples.
Having crossed that river as well, as he went along, he saw the six-colored rays of the Buddha’s body issuing forth and illuminating the branches, twigs, and foliage of the banyan tree;
seeing this, he thought: "This radiance belongs neither to the moon, nor to the sun, nor to the devas, Māras, Brahmas, Supaṇṇas, or Nāgas."
“Surely, as I was coming along with the Teacher in mind, I must have been seen by the Perfectly Enlightened One,” he thought.
Immediately, dismounting from the back of his horse, he approached the Teacher with his body bowed low, following the direction of the reins;
he entered within the Buddha’s rays like one sinking into liquid emerald. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he stood to one side.
He sat down together with his thousand ministers. The Teacher delivered a gradual discourse to them.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the king, along with his retinue, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then they all rose and requested the going-forth. The Teacher considered, "Will these sons of noble family come [to understand]?"
Reflecting on the phrase "alms-bowls and robes made by supernormal power," he realized: "These sons of noble family gave a thousand robes to a thousand Paccekabuddhas;
during the time of Buddha Kassapa, they also gave twenty thousand robes to twenty thousand bhikkhus.
It is no wonder that these sons of noble family have obtained alms-bowls and robes made by supernormal power. Having understood this, he [raised] his right hand...
Stretching out his hand, he said, "Come, monks; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
At that very moment, wearing the eight requisites and appearing like elder monks of sixty years' standing, they rose into the air, descended, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

Those merchants went to the royal palace and, having announced the message sent by the king, entered when the queen said, “Let them come,” and stood to one side. Then the queen asked them, “Sirs, for what reason have you come?
“We have been sent to you by the king; please give us three hundred thousand [pieces of gold], it is said. “That is much.”
“Tell me, tell me! What have you done in the presence of the king? For what reason is the king so pleased with you that he has had this much wealth given to you?
“Your Majesty, we have done nothing else; we merely delivered a single message.
“But can you, dear ones, deliver it to me as well? “It is possible, Your Majesty,” they replied. Then, having rinsed their mouths with a golden pitcher, they spoke.
“Queen, a Buddha has appeared in the world. Upon hearing this, her body thrilled with joy;
she failed to notice anything for three times, but on the fourth occasion, having heard that “a Buddha has appeared,” she asked, “Dear ones, what was given by the king for this word?
“A hundred thousand pieces of gold, Queen. “Dear ones, the king has acted unworthily in giving such a reward for a mere report.”
"Having heard that you are giving a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], I shall give you three hundred thousand for my poor-quality merchandise.
Is there anything else you have to report? They reported these and those other two messages as well.
The queen, as before, did not perceive them for three times each; then, on the fourth time, she [perceived] the three...
He gave three hundred thousand [pieces]. Thus, they all received twelve hundred thousand.
Then the queen asked them, "Where is the king, dear ones? "Queen, the king has gone, having said, 'I shall go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Teacher.
"What message did he give me? "It seems he entrusted all his sovereignty to you."
“[The King] has given you leave, saying, ‘You may enjoy your prosperity as you please.
But where are the ministers, dear? “They too have gone with the King, thinking, ‘We shall go forth,’ O Queen.
She then had their wives summoned and asked, “Ladies, your husbands have gone with the King, thinking, ‘We shall go forth. What will you do?”
“But what message did they send us, O Queen? “They have reportedly entrusted their own prosperity to you, saying:
‘You may enjoy this prosperity as you please. “But what will you do, O Queen?
“As for us, that king of ours is stationed on the road with three hundred thousand [attendants] to provide for the Three Jewels.”
Having worshipped and abandoned his prosperity like a lump of spittle, he has gone forth, thinking, “I shall go into homelessness.
Having heard the teaching of the Three Jewels, I too have worshipped them with nine hundred thousand [offerings].
Indeed, this so-called prosperity is not painful for the king alone; it is painful for me as well. Who would [accept] a lump of spittle discarded by the king on their knees?
“Having set foot upon the ground, I shall take it up with my mouth; I have no need for prosperity.
I shall go forth into homelessness under the Teacher. “Queen, we too shall go forth together with you.
“If you are able, that is well. “We are able, Queen. Thereupon, saying “Come,” she had a thousand chariots harnessed, and having mounted a chariot—
Having departed with them, when they first saw a river along the way, he questioned her exactly as the king had previously asked.
Having heard the entire account, he said, "Look for the path taken by the king.
When it was replied, "We do not see any hoofprints of thoroughbred horses," the king performed an Act of Truth, saying: "I have set out for the sake of the Three Jewels."
"Having performed [this act] and recollected the virtues of the Three Jewels, he has gone; I too have gone forth for the sake of the Three Jewels.
By their power, thinking, 'May this water not remain as water,' I sent a thousand chariots while recollecting the virtues of the Three Jewels. The water became like solid rock, and the wheels—"
They crossed at the very topmost spot. By this same means, they also crossed the other two rivers.
The Teacher, knowing that they had arrived, made a resolution such that they would not see the monks who were their husbands sitting near him.
As the queen was approaching, she saw rays of light issuing from the Teacher’s body.
Having reflected thus, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and standing to one side, asked:
"Venerable sir, King Mahākappina has gone forth for your sake; where is he? Let him show himself to us. "Sit down for now;
you shall see him right here," he replied. All of them, joyful and delighted, thought: "It seems he is indeed right here!"
Thinking, “Let us sit so that we may see our husband,” they sat down. The Teacher delivered a gradual discourse.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Queen Anojā attained the fruit of stream-entry together with them.
Having heard the Dhamma being taught to them, the Elder Mahākappina, along with his retinue, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). At that moment—

The Teacher showed those bhikkhus to them. For if, at the very moment they arrived, they were to see their own husbands wearing saffron robes with shaven heads, their minds would not become one-pointed, and they would not be able to realize the path and its fruit.
Therefore, from the time they were established in unwavering faith, the Teacher showed those bhikkhus to them only after they had attained arahantship.
Seeing them as well, they prostrated with the fivefold salutation and said, "Venerable Sir, your duty as renunciants has reached its consummation.
Having spoken thus, they paid homage to the Teacher, stood to one side, and requested ordination.
When this was said, the Teacher considered the arrival of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā; at the very moment the Teacher thought of her, she appeared.
Having come through the air and taken all those women, he led them through the air to the bhikkhunīs’ residence and ordained them.
Before long, they all attained arahantship. The Teacher, taking a thousand bhikkhus, went through the air to Jeta’s Grove.
There, indeed, the Venerable Mahākappina, while at his night-quarters and other places, exclaimed: "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"
He wandered about uttering this inspired utterance: "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! The monks reported this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, Mahākappina wanders about uttering the inspired utterance, 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! It seems he is uttering it with reference to the happiness of his own kingship.
The Teacher summoned him and asked: "Is it true, Kappina, that you [uttered this] with reference to sensual pleasure?"

“Did he utter an inspired utterance? [The king replied: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows whether that inspired utterance was made concerning my son, or whether it was made concerning someone else.
Then the Teacher said: “Monks, my son does not utter an inspired utterance concerning sensual pleasure or the pleasure of kingship;
rather, as my son practices the Dhamma, there arises in him what is called ‘Dhamma-rapture.’”
Having established the connection by saying, “Thus, with reference to the Deathless, the Great Nibbāna, he uttered this inspired utterance,” he taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
“The one who drinks the Dhamma sleeps happily with a serene mind;
the wise person always delights in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.”
Then one day the Teacher addressed the monks: “Monks, does the monk Kappina teach the Dhamma to the monks?
“Venerable sir, he dwells free from concern, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life; he does not give even a mere exhortation.
The Teacher summoned the Elder and said: “Is it true, Kappina, that you [neglect] your pupils?”
“...did you not give even a single word of instruction? “It is true, Blessed One. “Brahmin, do not act thus;

from this day forward, teach the Dhamma to the monks who approach you. “Very well, Bhante,” the Elder accepted the Blessed One’s words with his head and, by means of a single instruction, established the thousand ascetics in Arahatship. Because of that, him—
The Teacher, assigning his disciples to their respective ranks in order, placed him among the foremost, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples who give exhortation to the bhikkhus, namely Mahākappina.
Thus the Elder, having attained the fruit of Arahatship and remembering his own past karma, was filled with joy and [recited] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*.
He spoke the words beginning with "Proclaiming the Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth. "Risen in the cloudless sky" means risen, emerged, and become manifest throughout the entire sky.
"In the autumnal firmament" means like the sun, the *sūriya*, in the sky during the autumn season; such is the meaning.
(70) "At that time there was one Akkhadassa" means that during the era of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the teacher Sāradassī—meaning "one who sees benefit"—was well-known; such is the meaning.
71. Regarding the phrase *sāvakassa katāvino*: "of that Blessed One" (*tassa bhagavato*) refers to my own mind (*me manaṃ mama cittaṃ*).

The connection is as follows: having heard the words of the disciple (*sāvakassa*), who was fulfilling his duty with perseverance (*katāvino*), who was tireless in his task (*sātaccakiccayuttassa*), and who—while satisfying (*tappayantassa*) and pleasing (*tosayantassa*) me, while proclaiming the virtues (*guṇaṃ*) of his instructor (*ovādakassa*), and while establishing himself in the foremost position (*aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentassa*)—spoke thus.

73. *Haṃsasamabhāgo* means one who walks like a swan. *Haṃsadundubhinissano* means one whose voice is like the cry of a swan and the sound of a drum or kettledrum; the connection [of the sentence] is: "Behold this great minister, O monks," he said. 74.
*Samuggatatanūruhaṃ* means having body hair that has grown well upward—that is, with hair standing erect—or it means having a joyful mind.
*Jīmūtavaṇṇaṃ* means having a color equal to a pearl; the meaning is that his beautiful body possesses a radiant luster. *Pīṇaṃsaṃ* means a full shoulder.
"Pasannanayanānanan" means "of those with clear eyes and clear faces.
(75) "Katāvino" refers to a bhikkhu who has performed his duties and stands at the very pinnacle; the connection is that he aspires for this through a mind uplifted by sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
(81) "Sataso anusāsiya" means having instructed by means of the Dhamma, by what is just, by speech, and by way of reasoning.

"In the vicinity of Bārāṇasī" means in the weaver’s village near Bārāṇasī. "Born of the Keniya caste" means he was born into a family of weavers, belonging to the class of those who work with thread; the rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākappina is completed.
4. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dabbamallaputta:
In the fourth Apadāna, beginning with "The Conqueror named Padumuttara," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dabbamallaputta.
This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; in various existences, he accumulated merits conducive to the attainment of liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in the city of Haṃsavatī as the son of a wealthy merchant and possessed great fortune.
Having gained faith in the Teacher, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who assign lodgings.
With a mind full of serene confidence, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha.
Having given a great gift for seven days, at the end of those seven days he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and aspired for that place.

The Blessed One, knowing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, gave him a prediction. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, when he passed away from there, he experienced celestial splendor among the Tusita and other devas; then, passing away from there, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī—
Born into a certain family, although he knew that a monk was an arahant disciple of that [Teacher], he slandered him with a falsehood due to association with wicked people.
He gave milk, sugar-cane, and alms-food to that very person’s disciples.

Having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing both types of excellence, [he encountered] Kassapa, the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
Born into a noble family at the proper time, he went forth into homelessness in the Dispensation at its final stage.

After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna and a great clamor had arisen throughout the entire world, seven monks who had gone forth climbed a mountain in the midst of a forest in a frontier region and cast down a ladder, saying:
"Let those with hope for life descend; let those without attachment sit here. He was the one who gave them this exhortation.

Within seven days, the Elder Jeṭṭhaka became an Arahant. The Elder immediately following him became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), and the other five, possessing pure virtue, passed away from there and were reborn in the world of the gods.

Having experienced divine bliss there for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, they appeared in this present dispensation of the Buddha as these four: Pukkusāti, Sabhiya, Bāhiya, and Kumārakassapa.
They were born here and there. But this one was born in the city of Anupiya in the kingdom of the Mallas.

While he had not yet emerged from his mother’s womb, his mother passed away; then, someone placed her body upon a funeral pyre for cremation, took the boy who had fallen among the brushwood, and raised him.
Because he had fallen among the brushwood (*dabba*), he was called Dabba Mallaputta.

He became well-known. Later, he went forth by virtue of his prior accumulations; devoted to his meditation subject, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long.
Then the Teacher, on account of his impartiality and his possession of supernormal power, [appointed him] as the lodging-keeper for the monks.
He appointed him to the task of announcing the meal and assigning the portions. The entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus approved of this, as recorded in the Vinaya-khandhaka.
Later on, the Elder assigned a ticket-meal from a donor of choice tickets to the Mettiya and Bhūmajaka bhikkhus.
They were overjoyed and said, "Tomorrow we shall eat rice mixed with bean curry and honey."
They became filled with zeal. But when that lay follower heard that it was their turn, he commanded his slave-woman:
"Woman, whatever bhikkhus come here tomorrow, serve them with broken rice and sour gruel.
She did exactly so; when the bhikkhus arrived, she had them sit at the mouth of the granary and fed them. Those bhikkhus were displeased.

Making a *taṭataṭa* sound with their fists, they harbored resentment toward the elders and sat down, suffering and dejected, thinking, "It is he who has appointed this very person to give us unpalatable food instead of the sweet food we used to receive.
Then a nun named Mettiyā asked them, "Venerable sirs, why are you dejected? They replied, "Sister, while we were being harassed by Dabba Mallaputta..."
“Do you look on with indifference? they asked. “Venerable sir, what could I possibly do? “Lay the blame upon him,” [the monks said].
She then proceeded to make false accusations against the Elder here and there. Hearing this, the monks reported it to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One summoned Dabba Mallaputta and said: “Is it true, Dabba, that you [acted as Mettiyā says]?”
“Did you cause the nun to be corrupted? he asked. “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One know me as he knows me.
“Dabba, those who are truly worthy do not evade questions in this way; speak whether you are the perpetrator or not the perpetrator.
“I am not the perpetrator, venerable sir. The Blessed One said, “Having expelled the nun Mettiyā, investigate those monks.”

He said: The monks, headed by the Elder Upāli, having caused that nun to be expelled and having interrogated the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks, reported the matter to the Blessed One when those monks replied, "That nun was instigated by us.
The Blessed One then laid down a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks on the basis of groundless charges.
And at that time, while the Elder Dabba was assigning lodgings to the monks, he sent monks from the eighteen great monasteries surrounding the Veḷuvana monastery to those of similar status;
during the darkness of night, he lit a lamp with his finger and sent out monks who lacked supernormal powers using only that light.
Thus it was in the Elder’s duties of assigning lodgings and designating meals.
When this became known, the Teacher, while in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, established the Elder Dabba in his position, declaring:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are assigners of lodgings; that is to say, Dabba Mallaputta.
Then the Elder, recollecting his own past karma, filled with joy, began to proclaim the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (the account of his former conduct).
He spoke the words beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara. All of that has already had its meaning explained below. The connection is:
“In the ninety-first aeon from now, the Leader named Vipassī arose in the world.
(125) “With a wicked mind” means with a defiled mind; the sense is that his mind was not serene due to association with the unwholesome. He reviled a disciple.
"Tassā" means: I reviled that Blessed One’s disciple whose taints were exhausted; I ascribed false words to him;
the meaning is that I made a groundless accusation. 132.
"Dundubhiyo" means drums, so called because they produce the sound "dunduṃ. "Nādayiṃsu" means they made a sound.
They did so. Regarding the phrase "thunderbolts from all sides": *asaniyo* means those things engaged in striking (*asana*) or destroying from every direction;
the connection is that the terrifying divine rods (*devadaṇḍa*) burst forth.

(133) "Torches fell from the sky" means that masses of fire fell from the atmosphere. "And the comet was seen" means that a mass of fire accompanied by streaks of smoke was seen and perceived. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Dabbamalla-putta is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kumāra-Kassapa:
In this fifth *Apadāna*, beginning with the words "A hundred thousand [aeons] ago from here," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kumāra-Kassapa.
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family.

Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among those who discourse on the mind.
Desiring that same position for himself, he made a formal aspiration and performed meritorious deeds corresponding to that goal.
Having lived out his full lifespan while performing [these deeds], he passed away from there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, experienced both types of excellence.
During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn into a noble family;

having gone forth in the teaching of that Blessed One and practiced the duties of a recluse, he wandered only among the happy destinies, experiencing celestial and human bliss until this present arising of a Buddha.
He was reborn in Rājagaha in the womb of a certain merchant’s daughter. It is said that even while she was still a young girl, she desired to go forth;
however, having requested her parents and failing to obtain permission for the going-forth, she went to her husband’s family. There she conceived a child, but being unaware of it, she thought:
"By pleasing my husband, I shall cause him to grant me permission to go forth. While she was thus striving to please her husband, [she addressed him as] "Noble Son"—
“If this body were outside, rather than within,
one would surely take up a staff to drive away the crows and jackals”—
thus she won him over by pointing out the defects of the physical body.
Having been permitted by her husband and unaware that she was pregnant, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs who were followers of Devadatta.
When the bhikkhunīs saw that she was pregnant, they questioned Devadatta about it. He declared, "She is not a samaṇī.
She then said, "I did not go forth under Devadatta; I went forth under the Blessed One," and [she approached] the Blessed One.
Having gone into his presence, he questioned the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher assigned the Elder Upāli to the case.
The Elder summoned the families residing in the city of Sāvatthī and the female lay devotee Visākhā; then, adjudicating the matter before the assembly including the King, he declared:
"The pregnancy was conceived previously; her going forth is blameless. Hearing this, the Teacher said: "Well adjudicated by Upāli!"
She gave her approval to the Elder, saying, "It is well.

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking that "the care of a child is an impediment for bhikkhunīs," had him entrusted to nurses and raised him; they gave him the name Kassapa.
Later, having adorned him and brought him into the presence of the Teacher, he ordained him.
Because he had gone forth while still a youth, when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa; give this fruit or this hard food to Kassapa," they asked, "Which Kassapa?
and replied, "The Youth-Kassapa. Thus he received that name, and because he was the king's son who was to be cherished, [he was known as] Posāvanīya-putta.
Even in his old age, he was known only as Kumārakassapa.
From the time of his going forth, he applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and mastered the word of the Buddha.
Then, having practiced the duty of a recluse with him on a mountain peak, he became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) and was reborn as a Great Brahmā in the Suddhāvāsa realm.

Having formulated fifteen questions with the thought, "I shall provide the means for the arising of the Path and its Fruits by showing the gateway to insight (vipassanā)," he instructed [the novice] while dwelling in the Andhavana forest, saying, "You should ask the Teacher these questions.
Thereupon, he asked the Blessed One those questions, and the Blessed One answered them for him as well. The Elder, by the Blessed One—
Having mastered the instructions exactly as they were told, he brought insight (vipassanā) to maturity and attained Arahatship.
Having reached Arahatship, he remembered his own past karma and, filled with joy, began to proclaim the account of his former conduct, starting with the words:
"A hundred thousand [aeons] ago... Regarding this, the method already explained below and the meaning which is self-evident—
We shall not comment on all of that; we shall comment only on the obscure passages. 169.
"My mother has conceived a being" means my mother is heavily pregnant, gravid, and close to giving birth.
173. "The body like an anthill": the so-called body is like an anthill, just as an anthill [is covered] here and there...
"The house-lizard and the ant have their dwellings in holes and crevices;

even so, this body has nine openings and is constantly oozing"—this was taught and proclaimed by the Buddha, the Blessed One. Having heard this, my mind, not grasping at the taints (*āsava*) and leaving none remaining, was liberated from the defilements (*kilesa*);
the meaning is that I was established in Arhatship. Later, in various places, for the monks...

Having heard of his state as a speaker on the wonderful Dhamma, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are speakers on the wonderful Dhamma, this Kumārakassapa is the foremost.
Thus ends the commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kumārakassapa.
6. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bāhiya.
In the sixth Apadāna, beginning with "A hundred thousand aeons ago from here," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Bāhiya Dārucīriya.

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences the roots of merit that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having attained proficiency in the brahminical arts and becoming thoroughly versed in the Vedangas, one day he went into the presence of the Teacher.

While listening to the Dhamma with a serene mind, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge; desiring to attain that same position, he—
Having given a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of those seven days,

he prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet and said: "Bhante, on the seventh day from now, just as the Blessed One has placed that monk in the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge,
may I too, in the future, in the dispensation of a certain Buddha, [be established] among those of quick higher knowledge."

He made a resolution, saying, "May I become the foremost. The Blessed One, having surveyed the future with his knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) and knowing that it would be fulfilled, prophesied:
"In the future, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed Gotama, he will become the foremost among those of swift direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*).

Having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his life, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods, where he enjoyed the six kinds of celestial prosperity belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Having experienced the prosperity of universal monarchs and other such attainments among humans for many hundreds of millions of eons, he was reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he went forth into homelessness;
and at a time when the Dispensation was declining, he became filled with spiritual urgency upon seeing seven monks transgressing the conduct of the four assemblies.
Having entered the forest, thinking, "Until the disappearance of the Dispensation, we shall establish our own foundation," they paid homage to the Golden Cetiya.
There, seeing a mountain in that forest, he said, "Those who have attachment to life may turn back;
those without attachment, let them ascend this mountain. Having constructed a ladder, they all ascended that mountain.
Having set up a ladder, they practiced the duties of a recluse. Among them, the senior of the Saṅgha attained Arahatship after the lapse of a single night.
Having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* at Lake Anotatta and rinsed his mouth, he brought back almsfood from Uttarakuru and said to those bhikkhus, "Friends, eat this almsfood. They replied:
“Venerable sir, did we make such an agreement as this: ‘Whoever first attains arahantship, let the rest eat the almsfood brought by him’?
“No, friends. “In that case, if we too should achieve a distinction like yours, we shall bring it ourselves and eat; thus they did not wish to accept it.
On the second day, the second elder, having become a non-returner, brought almsfood in the same manner and invited the others.
They said, "But friend, was an agreement made that we would not eat the almsfood brought by the senior elder, but would instead eat what was brought by the next elder?
"No, friends. "If that is so, then we too, like you..."
“Having produced a distinction, we shall eat when we are able to do so through our own individual manly effort,” they did not wish [to eat].
Among them, the elder who had attained *arahantship* passed away into *parinibbāna*; the second, an *anāgāmī*, was reborn in the Brahma-world;
and the other five, being unable to produce a distinction, withered away and died on the seventh day, [reborn] in the world of the gods.
They were reborn there. Having experienced divine bliss there, they passed away from that state and were reborn among humans during this appearance of a Buddha.
Among them, one became King Pukkusāti; one was Kumāra Kassapa in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra;
one was Bāhiya Dārucīriya; one was Dabba Mallaputta; and one was Sabhiya the Wanderer. Of these, this one—
Bāhiya Dārucīriya was reborn in a merchant family in the port city of Suppāraka;
he attained proficiency in the merchant’s craft and became very wealthy and possessed of great riches.

While traveling abroad by ship with merchants bound for Suvaṇṇabhūmi, he had traveled for a few days when his ship was wrecked, and he found himself among those who were about to become food for fish and turtles.
Only one person remained; taking hold of a single plank, he strove on until on the seventh day he reached the shore of the port of Suppāraka.

Having no lower garment or upper robe, and seeing nothing else, he wrapped some dry sticks with grass fibers to wear as a lower garment and an upper robe, and taking an alms-bowl from a shrine, he entered the port of Suppāraka.
He arrived. When people saw him, they offered him rice porridge, alms-food, and other provisions, and they honored him, thinking, "This one is an Arahant.
When garments were presented to him, he thought, "If I wear them or put them on, my gains and honor will diminish," and so he rejected them and continued to wear only rags from the woodpile.
Then, while he was being esteemed by many as "an arahant, an arahant," this reflection arose in his mind:
"Whoever in the world are arahants or have entered the path to arahantship, I am one of them.
In that manner, he maintained his livelihood through that practice of hypocrisy.

During the dispensation of the Sevenfold-Powered One (Kassapa), while seven persons were practicing the ascetic life after climbing a mountain, one became a non-returner (anāgāmī) and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma-world.

Looking upon his own excellence as a Brahmā and reflecting on the place where he had come from, he saw the mountain where he had climbed to practice the ascetic life; however, he did not see the place where the others had been reborn.
Reflecting, he knew that one had attained final Nibbāna (parinibbāna) and that the other five had been reborn in the world of the sense-sphere devas;
from time to time he reflected upon them, wondering, "At this moment, where indeed are they?
Reflecting thus, he saw Dārucīriya living by means of deceit near the port of Suppāraka, and thought, "Alas, this fool is lost!"
"In the past, while practicing the duties of a recluse, he would not even consume almsfood brought by an Arahant due to his extreme asceticism;
yet now, though not an Arahant, he falsely claims to be one for the sake of his belly, wandering about deceiving the world. He does not know that the One Possessed of the Ten Powers has appeared.
I shall go, stir him with a sense of urgency, and make him aware of the Buddha’s arising. With this thought, in an instant—
Descending from the Brahma world, he appeared before Dārucīriya at the port of Suppāraka just as night was falling.
Seeing a radiance in his own dwelling place, he went outside;
seeing the Great Brahmā, he raised his hands in reverential salutation and asked, "Who are you? [The Brahmā replied: "I am your old friend, the one who has attained the fruit of non-returning."
“Having reached the Brahma-world, I was reborn there; having become an Arahant, I have attained final Nibbāna as the eldest of us all, while you five persons were reborn in the world of the gods.
Now, seeing you living here by means of fraudulent practices, I have come to subdue you. Having said this, he spoke this reason: “Indeed, Bāhiya, you—”
“You are neither an Arahant nor have you entered the path to Arahantship; that practice by which you might become an Arahant or enter the path to Arahantship does not exist for you.

Then, having informed him that the Teacher had appeared and was residing in Sāvatthī, and having sent him away with the words, “Go into the presence of the Teacher,” he returned to the Brahma-world itself.
But Bāhiya, standing in the air and looking at the Great Brahmā as he spoke, thought:
"Alas, a grievous deed has been done by me! I thought, 'I am an Arahant,' though I am not worthy;
yet this one says to me, 'You are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship. Is there perhaps another Arahant in the world? Then he [addressed him].
He asked: “Then who, indeed, in this world with its devas are arahants or have entered the path to arahantship?
Then a deity informed him: “Bāhiya, there is a city named Sāvatthī in the northern regions;
there the Blessed One currently resides—he is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha. For that Blessed One, Bāhiya...”

“He is an Arahant and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of Arahantship. Having heard the deity’s words during the night, Bāhiya, with a heart stirred by spiritual urgency, departed from Suppāraka at that very moment. Traveling for only one night, he arrived at Sāvatthī;
and as he went, through the power of the deity and the power of the Buddha, he traversed a road of two hundred leagues.
He arrived at Sāvatthī; at that moment, the Teacher had entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having entered Jetavana, he asked a number of bhikkhus who were walking back and forth in the open air, "Where is the Teacher now?
The bhikkhus replied, "He has entered Sāvatthī for alms," and then they asked him, "But from where have you come?"
“We have come from Suppāraka. “When did you set out? “I set out yesterday at evening time.
“You have come from far away; sit down now, wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest for a while.
When you have rested, you will see the Teacher upon your arrival,” they said. “Venerable sirs, there is a threat to the life of either the Teacher or myself.”
“I do not know how he did it; without stopping anywhere and without sitting down, he has come this path of two hundred yojanas in a single night.

Only after seeing the Teacher shall I rest,” he said. Having spoken thus, he entered Sāvatthī in great haste and, seeing the Blessed One moving about with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha, exclaimed, “At long last, Gotama the Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared to me!”

"Seen! Having gone from the place where he had seen him with his body bent low, he prostrated himself with the fivefold contact in the middle of the street, grasped the Teacher’s ankles firmly, and said:
"May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma, which will be for my welfare and happiness for a long time. Then the Teacher said to him, "It is not the right time..."
“Bāhiya, we have already entered among the houses for alms,” he replied, declining.
Hearing this, Bāhiya said, “Venerable sir, while wandering through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), no morsel of food has ever been unobtained by me;
nor do I know whether there will be an end to the life of either you or myself. Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma; let him teach it.”
"O Sugata, the Dhamma," he requested again. The Teacher refused a second time in the same manner. For it occurred to him thus:
"From the moment he saw me, his entire body has been continuously overwhelmed by rapture;
with such a powerful surge of joy, even after hearing the Dhamma, he will not be able to penetrate it. Let him first attain equanimity."
"Let it be; let even the intense exhaustion of one who has come from a road of two hundred leagues in a single night be stilled for now.
Having thus refused twice, when he was asked for the third time, [the Blessed One], while standing right there in the middle of the street, said:
"Therefore, Bāhiya, you must train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there shall be only the seen,'" and so forth.

He taught the Dhamma by means of various methods and in many ways. While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he exhausted all taints and attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
At the very moment he attained Arahatship, he recollected his past karma and, filled with joy, [recounted] the account of his former deeds.

Explaining this, he said, "From a hundred thousand [aeons] ago," and so forth. Since that follows the method already stated below, its meaning is self-evident; we shall provide an explanation only for those words whose meaning is not yet clear.
181. *Hasanapaccavekkhaṇaṃ* means a reflection born of perfect joy; the sense is that the youthful complexion is exceedingly delicate. 182.
*Hemayaññopacitaṅgaṃ* means a body (*deha*) whose limbs (*aṅga*) are adorned with golden threads (*hemasutta-yañña*), that is, a body whose parts are embellished with golden cords.
"Palambabimbatamboṭṭhaṃ" means endowed with a pair of lips that are red in color, resembling hanging *bimba* fruits.
