"Setatiṇhasamaṃ dijaṃ" means having even teeth; the meaning is that they are like teeth made level by being rubbed with a sharp, keen iron file.
183. *Pītisamphullitānanan* means that the face—the mouth—is well-expanded and blossomed by joy; the sense is that he possesses a face resembling the surface of a mirror. 184.
*Khippābhiññassa bhikkhuno* means of a bhikkhu who is capable of knowing with specific distinction right at the very moment the teaching is delivered. 186.
*Saggaṃ agaṃ sabhavanaṃ yathā* means they went to the heavenly world as if to their own home.
196. “Na tvaṃ upāyamaggaññū” means that you were not one who knew the path that serves as the means for attaining Nibbāna. 200. “Sadā jinanta satthuno” means:

always, at all times, conquering the Conqueror (Jina), with my anger defeated, I shall see the stainless face of the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)—a face like the surface of a mirror;
“I am going out to see it,” is the construction [of the sentence]. I asked the brahmin (Dija).
"Where is the Delighter of the World?"—in what place is the Teacher who brings joy to the world? "I ask the twice-born brahmins and the bhikkhus"—this is the meaning.

(201) "Like a hare, quickly [he reaches him], eager for the sight of the Sage"—the meaning is that, like a hare, he who is eager (*ussuka*), that is, filled with zeal (*ussāha*) for the sight of the Sage, the Tathāgata, quickly reaches him.

(202) "Having gone swiftly"—having gone rapidly. "For the sake of alms, free from longing here"—with respect to alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), he is free from longing (*apiha*), devoid of craving (*apagatapīha*), and without attachment (*agidha*), free from thirst (*nittaṇha*).
203. The connection is as follows: they saw him wandering for alms in the supreme city of Sāvatthī, looking neither hither nor thither with undisturbed patience (*alolakkhanti*).
"Resembling an abode of glory" means resembling a shining portal, an abode of the splendor of the primary and secondary marks of beauty (*lakkhaṇānubyañjana-sobhā*).
"With a face bearing the radiance of the sun" means like the brilliantly shining orb of the sun.
[His] face-disk shining brightly. 204.

"For me who have strayed onto a wrong path"—that is, for me who am lost on a contemptible path, a road beset by calamity, who have entered upon a false practice—be a refuge, be a support. "Gotama," he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.
218. "There the bright ones do not shine"—the shining herbs, stars, and so forth, endowed with white radiance, do not shine there.

They did not shine. The rest is of plain meaning. Having thus proclaimed his own past deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), he immediately requested the Blessed One for ordination (*pabbajjā*). When asked, "Is your bowl and robe complete?
he replied, "They are not. Then the Teacher said to him, "In that case, go and seek a bowl and robe," and departed. It is said that he [had been seeking them] for twenty thousand years.
While performing the duties of a recluse, he said, "It is proper for a bhikkhu, having obtained requisites himself,
to use them alone without looking to another," yet he did not show favor to even a single bhikkhu by means of an alms-bowl or a robe.
Knowing that because of this, no supernaturally produced bowl or robe would arise for him, the Blessed One [ordained him] by the "Come, bhikkhu" formula.

He did not grant him the going-forth. While he was still searching for that very bowl and robe, gathering scraps of cloth from a rubbish heap, a non-human being who harbored an old grudge against him became obsessed with the body of a young cow with a calf and struck him on the left thigh, bringing him to his death.
The Teacher, having wandered for alms and finished his meal, [returned].
As he was departing together with many bhikkhus, he saw Bāhiya’s body fallen in a rubbish heap.
Standing at the door of a house, he commanded the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, take this Bāhiya Dārucīriya!
Bring a bier, carry this body out through the city gate, cremate it, collect the relics, and erect a stupa. Thus he gave his orders to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus, having erected a stupa over the relics on the great highway, approached the Teacher and reported the deed they had performed.
Thereupon, a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha:

"The Tathāgata caused the funeral rites for his body to be performed by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, and having had the relics taken, he caused a cetiya to be built; which path, indeed, has been attained by him?"

“Was he a novice monk, or was he a bhikkhu? Taking that as the occasion for a teaching, the Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, Bāhiya Dārucīriya has been established in Arahatship,” and he expanded upon this further with a discourse on the Dhamma. Having declared his state of final Nibbāna, he said:
“Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are bhikkhus, this is the foremost of those possessing swift higher knowledge—namely, [Bāhiya].”
"Bāhiya of the Tattered Robe," he placed him in this foremost position.
Then the monks asked him, "Venerable sir, you say, 'Bāhiya of the Tattered Robe has attained arahantship.
When did he attain arahantship? "At the time he heard my Dhamma, monks. "When was that?"
“Venerable sir, has the Dhamma been taught by you? “While walking for alms, standing in the middle of the street.
“Venerable sir, the Dhamma taught by you while standing in the middle of the street is but a small amount;
how could it produce such distinction with only that much? Then the Teacher said to them, “Monks, my Dhamma is neither ‘little’ nor ‘much’...”
"Do not think thus. For even many thousands of verses connected with useless matters are not as good as a single verse-line grounded in the meaning.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"Even if there were a thousand verses Connected with useless matters..."
“A single verse-line is better, hearing which one attains peace.
At the conclusion of this teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the legend of the Elder Bāhiya is complete.
7. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika.
The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Mahākoṭṭhika begins with the verse: "In the dispensation of the Conqueror named Padumuttara...

What is its origin? This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, [accumulated] the necessary conditions for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various births.
Accumulating merits during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great wealth.
Having reached maturity and established his household after the passing of his parents, while living the life of a householder,
one day at the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara’s preaching of the Dhamma, the inhabitants of the city of Haṃsavatī went forth with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
Seeing them walking with their minds inclined toward, leaning toward, and tending toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, they approached the Blessed One together with them.

Seeing the Teacher place a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), [they thought]: "This one is the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges in this Dispensation; what if I too..."

Thinking, "May I become the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) in the teaching of a single Buddha," he approached the Blessed One after the assembly had risen at the conclusion of the Teacher’s discourse and invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept almsfood at my home tomorrow. The Teacher consented. He then paid homage to the Blessed One.
Having performed a circumambulation and returned to his own residence, he adorned the places where the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus would sit throughout the entire night with perfumes,
garlands, and other offerings; he had various kinds of solid and soft food prepared,
and at the end of that night, [he served] the Teacher, surrounded by a hundred thousand bhikkhus, with a variety of rice gruels and refreshments in his own residence.
Having fed [the monks] with fragrant rice and food accompanied by soups and condiments, at the conclusion of the meal, he thought: "I am aspiring for a great position;
however, it is not proper for me to aspire for that position by giving alms for only a single day.
I shall give alms in succession for seven days and then make my aspiration. He, by that very [means]...
Having given a great almsgiving for seven days according to the established rule,
at the conclusion of his meal duties, he had the storehouse of cloth opened; he placed exquisite, fine garments sufficient for the three robes at the feet of the Buddha,
and having given the three robes to the hundred thousand bhikkhus, he approached the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable Sir, that bhikkhu whom you [spoke of] seven days ago from now..."

At the conclusion of the day, he was established in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). [The monk] prostrated at the feet of the Teacher and made this aspiration:
"May I too, like that bhikkhu, go forth in the dispensation of a Buddha who will arise in the future and become the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges.
The Teacher, knowing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, said: "In the future..."
"Exactly one hundred thousand eons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world;

under his dispensation, your aspiration shall be fulfilled," he prophesied. Having performed meritorious deeds there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that state, experienced the excellence of the deva realms, and wandered successively through the worlds of gods and humans.

Thus, wandering among gods and humans and accumulating the requisites of merit and knowledge in various states of existence, he was reborn during this arising of a Buddha in Sāvatthī into a prominent brahmin family; they gave him the name Koṭṭhika.
Why did they not take the name of his mother, or that of his grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth, but instead give him such a name?
Why? It should be understood that they gave him this name because it was appropriate to his character:

due to his own possession of wisdom, he moved about striking, hammering, and piercing people with the weapons of his mouth whenever he saw them—being skilled in the *vedaṅgas*, the *Satakkara* and *Takkas*, the *Nighaṇḍus* and *Keṭubhas*, the *Sakkharappabhedas*, and all the *Vyākaraṇas*.
When he reached maturity, [he mastered] the three Vedas...
Having mastered the brahminical arts and attained proficiency, he went one day into the presence of the Teacher;
having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and from the time of his full ordination began practicing insight meditation.
Attaining Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and having gained mastery over those analytical knowledges, he fearlessly addressed the Great Elders.
Even when approaching to ask a question, he approached the One of Ten Powers and asked questions regarding the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) alone.
Thus, because of the service he had performed there and his mastery attained therein, this elder became the foremost among those who have reached the analytical knowledges.
Then the Teacher, making the *Mahāvedalla-sutta* the occasion for its delivery, [addressed] those who have reached the analytical knowledges...
He placed him in the foremost position, saying: "This is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), namely Mahākoṭṭhika.
Later on, experiencing the bliss of liberation and filled with joy, he [began to] recount the narrative of his own former conduct.

He spoke the words beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara, making [the Dhamma] clear,” and so forth. All of that has already been explained according to the method stated below, and thus its meaning is plain.

Regarding the phrase “Thus indeed, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika”: here, *sudam* is a particle used as an indicator (*nidassane*). *Āyasmā* is a term of respect, just as in the expression “the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is completed.
8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uruvelakassapa.
In the eighth Apadāna, beginning with "The Conqueror named Padumuttara," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Uruvelakassapa.
This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; in various states of existence, he accumulated the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation.
While accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a noble family. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those with a great retinue, he himself aspired to that same status.
Having given a great alms-offering, he made a formal vow (paṇidhāna). And the Blessed One [spoke] to him...
Seeing that there would be no obstacles, he prophesied: "In the future, within the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, he will become the foremost among those with a great retinue.

Having performed meritorious deeds there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that state and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn ninety-two aeons ago as the half-brother and younger sibling of the Blessed One Phussa.

He also had two other younger brothers. Those three, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and honored them with the highest worship, performed wholesome deeds for as long as they lived.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, they were reborn even before the arising of our Blessed One as three brothers in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī.
By virtue of their clan name, all three were named Kassapa. When they had reached maturity, the three of them mastered the three Vedas.
The eldest brother had a retinue of five hundred young brahmins, the middle one three hundred, and the youngest two hundred.
As they examined the essence of their own texts, they saw that the benefit therein pertained only to the present life, and thus they [sought] the going-forth.
They set out. Among them, the eldest brother went to Uruvelā with his own retinue and, having gone forth as an ascetic, became known as Uruvelakassapa;
the middle one went forth at the bend of the river Gaṅgā and became known as Nadīkassapa;
the youngest went forth at Gayāsīsa and became known as Gayākassapa. Thus, among them, the ascetic life was undertaken.
After we had gone forth and lived here and there for many days, our Bodhisatta, having made the Great Renunciation,
attained the knowledge of omniscience, and having gradually set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
established the five bhikkhus of the group in Arahatship, [and then addressed] the fifty-five people headed by the noble son Yasa...
Having trained sixty arahants among his companions and dismissed them with the words, "Go forth, monks, on your wanderings," and having trained the thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group,
he went to the dwelling place of Uruvelakassapa; entering the fire-hall there for the purpose of staying,
he converted Uruvelakassapa along with his retinue by means of three thousand five hundred miracles performed by Nāgadama and others who had gone there.
He ordained him. Both the procedure for his ordination and the performance of the miracle of psychic power will be made clear in the Apadāna commentary of Nadī-Kassapa.

Upon hearing of his state of having gone forth, the other two brothers also came with their retinues and were ordained in the presence of the Teacher. All of them wore robes and bowls produced by means of psychic power.
They became those who were summoned by the words "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*). The Teacher, taking that thousand of recluses with him, went to Gayāsīsa;
sitting upon the Back Stone (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*), he established them all in Arahatship by means of the discourse on the series of burning fires (*ādittapariyāyadesanā*).

Having thus attained Arahatship, filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past conduct, beginning with the words, "The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth. We shall explain only the difficult passages (*anuttānapada*).
268. "Having destroyed all darkness" means that the Blessed One Phussa, having shattered the darkness of defilements such as lust, hatred, and delusion;

"having disentangled the great tangle" means having disentangled, broken, and split apart the great, chaotic tangle of defilements consisting of one thousand five hundred groups of defilements, such as craving and conceit.
"Together with the world of devas" means including the celestial realms.
The construction is as follows: "satisfying the entire world-dwelling, satisfying it, nourishing it, he rains down the deathless rain, causing the stream of the great Nibbāna-rain to flow.
For at that time, in the phrase "in Bārāṇasī," the word *bārasa* (twelve) functions as a numeral (*dvādasarāsī*), as in the expression "twelve men" and so forth.
In ancient times, seers from the Himālaya and seers reckoned as *paccekabuddhas* from Gandhamādana used to come through the air and go there, descend, and enter; thus it is called Bārāṇasī.

Alternatively, it is the city where hundreds of thousands of those reckoned as perfectly enlightened Buddhas descended for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; [the feminine form] is due to a change of gender.
Having [established it] by way of the feminine gender, it is called "Bārāṇasī"; in that Bārāṇasī.

273. Having made the bordering region one where the sword is laid down—meaning having abandoned the sword, having cast down weapons, and having rendered the frontier province free from violence—they "approached again," meaning they arrived having once more come near to and reached that city.
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Uruvelakassapa is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Rādha.

296. The legend of the Venerable Elder Rādha begins with the words, "In the ninth dispensation, the Conqueror named Padumuttara," and so forth. All of this is easily understood by the wise through following the text and reflecting upon the method; it consists solely of the diversity of merit.
The commentary on the legend of the Elder Rādha is complete.
The tenth legend, that of the Elder Mogharāja, is likewise easily understood.
The commentary on the Catupaññāsamavagga is completed.
55. Bhaddiyavagga 1.
Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
In the first *apadāna* of the fifty-fifth chapter, beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara," is the *apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having reached the age of discretion, while sitting listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of sweet voice.

Aspiring to that very station for himself, he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, consisting of honey mixed with ghee, sugar, and other sweet flavors, and said: "Venerable Sir, may I too in the future..."
“May I, like this bhikkhu, become the foremost among those with sweet voices within the dispensation of a single Buddha,” he thus made his aspiration.
The Blessed One, seeing that there would be no obstacle for him, gave a prediction and departed.
Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as his life lasted, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he experienced both types of excellence.
In the time of the Blessed One Phussa, he was reborn as a peacock.
While carrying a sweet mango fruit from the king’s garden in his beak, he saw the Teacher and, with a mind full of faith, resolved, "I shall give this to the Buddha.
The Teacher, knowing the movement of his heart, took his bowl and sat down. The peacock then placed the ripe mango into the bowl of the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher, for the purpose of generating joy in him, consumed it while the cuckoo was looking on.
Then that cuckoo, with a mind full of serene confidence, spent seven days in that very rapture and happiness.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, in each successive birth he possessed a sweet voice. During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, having been born into a family of carpenters—

Having become the chief architect, he became well-known. When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna and they began to construct a stupa seven *yojanas* in extent to enshrine his bodily relics, he said, "Let us make it one *yojana* in width and one *yojana* in height.
They all adhered to his word. Thus, he caused a monument of limited measure to be built for the Buddha who is immeasurable.
In the place where he was reborn by virtue of that kamma, he was inferior to others in stature.

During the time of our Blessed One, having been reborn in a noble family, he became known as Lakunḍaka Bhaddiya because of his extreme shortness and his beautiful body, which resembled a golden statue.
Later on, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he gained faith and went forth into homelessness.
Having become one who was learned and a preacher of the Dhamma, he preached the Dhamma to others with a sweet voice.
Then, on a festival day, a certain courtesan traveling in a chariot with a brahmin saw the Elder and smiled, showing her teeth.
The Elder took the sign of her teeth as his object, and having developed meditative absorption (*jhāna*), [attained liberation].
Making that his foundation and increasing his insight, he became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
Dwelling frequently in mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagatāsati*), one day, while being exhorted and instructed by the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, he established himself in *arahantship*.
Some monks and novices, not knowing that he had attained *arahantship*, [addressed him] in their ears...
They seized him and dragged him; taking him by the head, the arms, or the hands and feet, they shook him and tormented him while playing.
Then the Blessed One, having heard this, said: "Monks, do not torment my son.
From that time forth, recognizing him as an Arahant, they did not torment him.
12. Having thus become an Arahant and feeling joy, he spoke the words beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara," proclaiming the account of his own former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*).
"With a sweet cooing" (*mañjunābhinikūjaham*) means that I uttered a sound with a sweet, lovely voice;
"I cooed" (*abhinikūjin*) is the meaning. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kaṅkhā-Revata: 34.
In the second *Apadāna*, beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara," is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kaṅkhā-Revata.

This [being] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, was reborn into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; all of that is easily understood by following the text.
The commentary on the *Kaṅkhārevata*-Thera Apadāna is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīvali The third apadāna begins with the words, "In the third apadāna, the Victor named Padumuttara... This is the apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sīvali.
He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the realization of Nibbāna.
In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family, he went to the monastery in the manner described above.
Standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who receive gains.
Thinking, "It is fitting that I too should become such a person in the future," he invited the One Possessed of Ten Powers [for a meal].

Having given a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by means of this meritorious deed, I do not seek any other success;

rather, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I also become the foremost among those who receive gains, just like that monk whom you have established in this foremost position. The Teacher—
Seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, he prophesied, "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future in the presence of the Buddha Gotama," and then departed.
That noble son performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, and after experiencing both types of excellence among gods and humans,
he was reborn in a village not far from the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
At that time, the inhabitants of the city of Bandhumatī, having conversed with the king, gave alms to the One of Ten Powers.
One day, while all were giving alms together, they looked among their offerings and thought, "What indeed is lacking in our gift?
and they saw neither honey nor sugar-curd. They resolved, "We shall bring it from somewhere," and [set out] along the roads leading into the city from the countryside.
They stationed men there. At that time, this son of good family, taking a vessel of sugar and curd from his own village, set out for the city thinking, "I shall fetch something.

While looking for a convenient place to enter after washing his face and rinsing his hands and feet, he saw a honeycomb as large as the head of a plough, free of flies and stalks. He thought, "This has arisen for me through my merit."
Having taken it, he entered the city. A man stationed by the citizens saw him and asked, "Sir, for whom are you carrying this?
"For no one at all, master; this is for sale," he replied. "In that case, take this coin and give me this honey and sugar-curd."
He thought: "This is not worth much to me, yet he gives much all at once;
I shall test him. Then he said to him: "I do not give for a single kārṣāpaṇa. "If that is so, take two kārṣāpaṇas and give them to me.
"Even for two I will not give. By this means, increasing the amount until it reached a thousand, he thought: "It is too much to press him further."
"It is not proper; let it be for now, I shall ask what task must be performed with this. Then he said to him:
"This is not of great value, yet you give much; for what purpose do you take this? [The man replied:

"Sir, here the city-dwellers, having come into conflict with the king, were giving alms to the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin at the head of the offering assembly, and they gave these two items there."
“They are searching for me without seeing me. If they do not find these two, the citizens will suffer defeat.
Therefore, I shall take them by paying a thousand pieces of gold. [The other asked: “Is this permissible only for the citizens, or is it also permissible to give them to others?
[He replied: “It is not forbidden to give them to anyone at all. [The other asked: “But is there...?”
“Is there anyone among the citizens who gives a thousand [pieces of money] in a single day for alms? “There is none, Sir.
“Do you know that these two are worth a thousand each? “Yes, I know it. “In that case, go and inform the citizens:
‘A certain man does not give these two for their price; he wishes to give them with his own hand along with you yourselves.’”
“Be free from discursive thought because of these two reasons. Having said, “You shall be the bodily witness for the portion of the eldest in this gift,” he departed.
Then that clansman took five pungent spices with a kahāpaṇa he had received as travel expenses from the village;
having ground them into powder, he stirred some curd into it, pressed a honeycomb into it, and [mixed it] with the powder of the five pungent spices.
Having prepared it, placed it in a lotus leaf, and secured it, he took it and sat down not far from the One of Ten Powers.
While observing his turn for the honor being offered by the great multitude, he waited for an opportunity;
then, approaching the Teacher, he said, "Venerable Sir, this is my offering of alms for the poor; out of compassion for me, [accept it]."

“Please accept it. Out of compassion for her, the Teacher accepted it with a stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings, and he made a resolution such that it would not be exhausted even as it was served to the six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.
When the noble son had finished his meal duties, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, sitting to one side, said: “I have seen...”
“Venerable Blessed One, today the residents of the city of Bandhumatī have presented an offering to you;
by the power of this merit, may I too, in each successive birth, attain the highest gain and the supreme state.
The Teacher said, “So be it, noble son,” and having offered words of thanksgiving for the meal to him and the city-dwellers, he departed.

Thus, that clansman, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived and wandering among gods and humans, took rebirth in the womb of Suppavāsā, the daughter of a king, during this current appearance of a Buddha.
From the time of his conception, five hundred offerings were brought to Suppavāsā every morning and evening. Then, she, in order to test his merit—
She stood there, causing a seed-basket to be touched by her hand. From each single seed, a hundred or even a thousand slips would emerge;
from each single *karīsa* field, fifty or sixty loads, measured by wagons, would arise.
Even at the time of filling the storehouse, as the princess touched the door with her hand, through her merit, whatever was being taken by those who received it would appear again.

It filled up. Even when the rice-pot was full to the brim, they would say, "This is for the merit of the princess," and as long as they did not draw it out while giving to anyone, the rice would not be exhausted. Seven years passed while the child was still in the womb;
however, when the fetus had matured, she experienced great suffering for seven days. She addressed her husband, saying: "Before..."
Thinking, "While I am still alive, I shall give a gift before I die," she sent a messenger to the Teacher, saying: "Go, sir, report this news to the Teacher and invite him;
whatever the Teacher says, take careful note of it and, having returned, tell it to me.
He went and reported her message to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, [the Teacher]..."
“The daughter of the Koḷiyas is worshipping at your feet. Out of compassion for her, the Teacher said: “May the daughter of the Koḷiyas, Suppavāsā, be happy and free from illness;
may she give birth to a healthy son. Having heard this, he paid homage to the Blessed One and set out toward his own village.
Even before he had arrived, from Suppavāsā’s womb, a caul...
The fetus emerged like water; the people sitting around her began to weep with tearful faces, while one person, joyful and delighted, went to report the news of her husband's joy.
Seeing their gestures, he thought, "I suppose the discourse spoken by the One of Ten Powers must have reached its conclusion. He returned and [related] the Teacher’s words to the princess.
He spoke. The princess said, "The meal you have been invited to provide will itself be a meal of auspiciousness for your life;
go and invite the One of Ten Powers for seven days. He did accordingly. For seven days, they offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
That boy, cooling the fevered hearts of his kinsmen, brought them to a state of calm.
Thinking, "He was born while performing [this act]," they gave him the name Sīvali. Because he had dwelt in the womb for seven years, from the time of his birth he was capable of all tasks.
On the seventh day, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, engaged in conversation with him.
The Teacher also spoke this verse:
“He who has transcended this mire, this difficult path, this cycle of existence and delusion;
who has crossed over, reached the further shore, meditative, unshaken, free from doubt;
who, through non-clinging, is extinguished—him I call a brahmin.”
Then the Elder said to her: "But is it not fitting for you to go forth after having experienced such suffering?

"I would go forth, venerable sir, if I were permitted," she replied. Seeing her conversing with the Elder, Suppavāsā thought, "What is my son talking about with the General of the Dhamma? and approaching the Elder, she asked him.

—“Venerable sir, what is my son saying to you? Having related the suffering of dwelling in the womb that he himself had experienced, he said, “With your permission, I shall go forth. “Very well, venerable sir, let him go forth,” they replied.
The Elder led him to the monastery, gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*), and while ordaining him, said, “Sīvali,…”
“There is no need for you to give me any other instruction; simply reflect upon the suffering you have experienced for seven years.
“Venerable sir, the burden of ordination rests with you alone; as for what I am able to do, I shall know that myself.
At the very moment he shaved off his first circle of hair, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry; at the second...
At the moment his hair was shorn, he established himself in the fruit of Once-returning; at the third [shaving], he was established in the fruit of Non-returning.
For all of them, the shaving of the hair and the realization of the fruit of Arhatship occurred neither before nor after one another.
Then a discussion arose among the community of monks: "Oh, even though this Elder was so meritorious, for seven months and more..."
“Having dwelt for years in his mother’s womb, he has now dwelt for seven days in a difficult birth.
The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, this was not a deed performed by this son of good family in this present birth,” and he related the past.
"Monks, having brought this back from the past: even before the appearance of the Buddha, this son of good family was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī.
Upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingdom and became renowned and possessed of great wealth.
At that time, a certain frontier king, thinking 'I shall seize the kingdom,' came and besieged the city; having established a military camp, he remained there. Then—"
The king, being of one mind with his mother, had the gates closed in the four directions for seven days within the city of the royal camp;
thus, those entering and leaving were bewildered at the gates. Then the Paccekabuddhas in the Migadāya monastery raised a cry.
Hearing this, the king had the gates opened, and the bordering king also fled.

Thus, having experienced suffering in the hells and other realms as the ripening of that karma, even though he was reborn into a royal family during this current appearance of a Buddha, he experienced such suffering together with his mother.
However, from the time of his going forth, the four requisites for the Saṅgha of monks arose for him according to his wish. In this way, the story originated here.
Later on, the Teacher went to Sāvatthī. The Elder paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I wish to test my own power of merit;
please give me five hundred bhikkhus. “Take them, Sīvalī,” he replied.
Taking those five hundred bhikkhus, he set out toward the Himalayas and traveled along a forest path. First, for him—
The deity dwelling in the banyan tree gave alms for seven days. Thus it was said:
"First he saw the Banyan Tree, secondly Mount Paṇḍava;
thirdly the Aciravatī River, and fourthly the excellent ocean."
“He went to Himavanta as the fifth, to Chaddanta as the sixth, to Gandhamādana as the seventh, and then to Revata as the eighth.
In all these places, they gave gifts for exactly seven days each. However, on Mount Gandhamādana, the divine king Nāgadatta—
During those seven days, on one day he gave an alms-offering of milk, and on another day he gave an alms-offering of ghee.
Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus said to him: "Friend, neither milch cows being milked nor the churning of curds are seen belonging to this royal deva;
from where, O royal deva, does this arise for you? [He replied: "Venerable sirs, it is from the Dasabala Kassapa."
“This is the fruit of giving milk-rice at the proper time,” said the King of Devas.
Later, the Teacher went out to meet the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana forest. How so?
Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, it is said that my younger brother, Revata, has gone forth.”
"Whether he finds pleasure there or not, I shall go and see him. The Blessed One, knowing that Revata was practicing insight (vipassanā), twice refused the request;
but on the third occasion, knowing that he had attained arahantship, he said:
"Sāriputta, I too will go; announce this to the bhikkhus. The Elder, having assembled the bhikkhus, said: "Friends, the Teacher..."
"I wish to go on a journey; let those who wish to go come," he announced to everyone.
When the One Possessed of Ten Powers was about to depart for his journey, those monks who remained behind were few;
for the majority, being desirous of going, were even more numerous, thinking, "We shall see the Teacher’s golden-hued body, or we shall hear his sweet discourse on the Dhamma. Thus spoke the Teacher.
Accompanied by a great community of bhikkhus, he set out, thinking, "We shall see Revata.
Then, at a certain place, having reached a fork in the road, the Elder Ānanda asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, there is a fork in the road here;
by which path should the community of bhikkhus go? "Which path, Ānanda? [the Blessed One replied.]
“Is it the straight road? “Venerable sir, the straight road is thirty leagues long and is a path frequented by non-humans. But the detour road is sixty leagues long, safe and well-supplied with food.
“Ānanda, has Sīvali come along with us? “Yes, venerable sir, he has come.
“In that case, let the Saṅgha go by the straight road; we shall test Sīvali’s merit. The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, [set out].
In order to test the merit of the Elder Sīvalī, he ascended a road thirty *yojanas* long.

From the point where he began his ascent, at every *yojana*, the host of devas constructed cities and prepared monasteries for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha to dwell in. The sons of the devas [prepared these] for the king...
Acting like hired laborers, they went about carrying rice gruel, solid food, and other provisions, asking, "Where is the noble Sīvalī?
The Elder, having caused them to receive honors and respect, proceeded into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher partook of the meal together with the community of monks. In this very manner, the Teacher experienced such hospitality every day for a distance of up to a league.
Having traveled and crossed a wilderness of thirty yojanas, he arrived at the dwelling place of the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana forest.
Knowing of the Teacher’s arrival, the Elder used his supernormal power to create, at his own residence, a monastery sufficient for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha,
as well as a fragrant chamber for the One Possessing the Ten Powers, along with places for night-quarters and day-quarters.
He went out to meet the Tathāgata. The Teacher entered the monastery by way of a path adorned and prepared for him.
Then, when the Tathāgata had entered the Fragrant Chamber, the monks entered their respective lodgings according to seniority.
The deities, thinking, "It is not yet time for food," brought eight kinds of beverages. The Teacher [partook of] the beverage together with the Saṅgha.
Thus, while experiencing such honor and respect from the Tathāgata, half a month passed by according to this very routine.
Then, some discontented monks sat down in one place and started a conversation:
"The One of Ten Powers, saying 'He is the younger brother of my chief disciple,' [has appointed] such a construction-worker monk..."
“Now that he has arrived, what will the Jetavana Monastery or the Veḷuvana Monastery and others do in comparison to this monastery?
This monk is a builder of such new construction work; what indeed will he do for the duties of a recluse?
Then the Teacher thought: “If I dwell here for a long time, this place will become crowded; those who live in the forest...”
“Since these monks are seekers of solitude, Revata will not have a comfortable stay.
Then the Elder went to his day-quarters. The Elder, too, was alone; leaning against a support-board at the end of his walking-path, he sat upon a stone slab.
Seeing the Teacher approaching from afar, he went out to meet him and paid homage.
Then the Teacher asked him: "Revata, this is a place for wild beasts;
when you hear the sounds of fierce elephants, horses, and so forth, what do you do? "Venerable Sir, as I listen to their sounds, a certain 'forest-rapture' arises within me.
At this point, the Teacher spoke to the Elder Revata on the benefits of the forest using five hundred stanzas.

On the following day, after walking for alms in a nearby place, he addressed the Elder Revata and caused those monks who had spoken in dispraise of the Elder to forget their walking sticks, sandals, oil-flasks, and sunshades.
When they returned to retrieve their requisites, even as they went back by the same path they had come, they were unable to recognize that spot.

They were unable [to proceed]. For previously they had gone by way of a path prepared and adorned, but on that day, traveling by an uneven path, they went on their knees, sitting down in a squatting posture at various places.
Crushing bushes, shrubs, and thorns, they reached the place resembling their own dwelling, and there, at various acacia stumps...
They recognized their own parasols, sandals, walking sticks, and oil flasks.
At that moment, realizing, “This monk possesses supernormal power,” they took their belongings and departed,
saying, “Such is the kind of hospitality prepared for the One Endowed with the Ten Powers.”
When the bhikkhus arrived first, while she was sitting in her own house, the laywoman Visākhā asked, "Venerable sirs, is Revata’s dwelling place pleasant? "It is pleasant, laywoman;
that lodging resembles the Nandana Grove and the Citra-latāvana Grove. Then, when the bhikkhus arrived later, she asked them, "Noble sirs, is Revata’s..."
“Is this his dwelling place? “Do not ask, laywoman; it is an improper matter to discuss. This is merely a wilderness of barren ground, gravel, stones, and uneven khadira forests;
that bhikkhu dwells there.
Having heard the accounts of both the earlier and later bhikkhus, Visākhā wondered, “Whose words are true?”
After her meal, having taken perfumes and garlands, she went to attend upon the One of Ten Powers;
having paid homage and sat down to one side, she asked the Teacher: “Venerable sir, some noble ladies praise the dwelling place of the Elder Revata, while others blame it.
What is this, venerable sir? “Visākhā, whether that place be delightful or not, in whatever location—”
"The mind of the noble ones delights [there]; therefore, that very place is called delightful," he said, and then recited this verse:
"In the village or in the forest, in the lowlands or on the high ground—wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful."

In a later period, while the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, he placed the Elder among the foremost, saying: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who receive offerings, namely Sīvalī.
Then, the Venerable Elder Sīvalī, having attained Arahatship and reached that state of being foremost, recalled his own past karma.
Filled with joy, he proclaimed his *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), beginning with the words: "The Victor named Padumuttara... and so forth.
We shall provide an explanation of the meaning of the words without leaving anything obscure. 55.
"His virtue is incalculable" means that the virtue of that Blessed One Padumuttara was incalculable.
"Nine thousand crores, and eight hundred crores..."
“Fifty-one hundred thousand, and another thirty-six:
these rules of restraint and discipline were proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
they are pointed out by way of summary in the training of the restraint of discipline.”
The training rules (sikkhāpada) thus spoken were taught by way of the instruction given to disciples. However, the Blessed One’s virtue (sīla) is truly incalculable;
the meaning is that it is impossible to calculate or enumerate it. His concentration (samādhi) is like a diamond (vajira):
just as a diamond pierces through jewels such as sapphires, emeralds, lapis lazuli, crystal, and cat's-eye, making them perforated here and there.
In the same way, the supramundane path-concentration of the Blessed One Padumuttara pierces, breaks, and utterly eradicates the opposing and contrary states—
this is the meaning. The immeasurable, supreme knowledge of that Buddha is for the purpose of knowing and penetrating the four truths,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
“Capable” means the multitude of knowledges, such as self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which is incalculable;
the meaning is that it is devoid of calculation due to its divisions into past, future, present, and so forth.

“And liberation is incomparable” means that because they are liberated from defilements, the four liberations beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) are beyond comparison, devoid of likeness; the meaning is that they cannot be compared by saying, “They are like this.”
The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sīvali is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vaṅgīsa.
The fourth Apadāna, beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa Thera.

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī; and having reached maturity...
Having gone to the monastery with the city-dwellers who were going to hear the Dhamma, while listening to the Dhamma,
he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being the foremost among those possessed of ready wit. Having performed an act of service for the Teacher,
he made a resolution, saying, "May I too in the future become the foremost among those possessed of ready wit," and was thus prophesied by the Teacher.

Having performed wholesome deeds for as long as life lasted, and having experienced the twofold prosperity among gods and humans, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
Later, because his mother was a female wanderer (paribbājikā), he became well-known as a wanderer;
having received the name Vaṅgīsa, he mastered the three Vedas. Thereafter, having pleased his teacher, [he learned] the spell for knowing the heads of corpses.
Having learned this art, he would strike a corpse’s head with his fingernail and know: “This being has been reborn in such-and-such a womb.
Thinking, “This is our means of livelihood,” the brahmins took Vaṅgīsa and traveled through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
When three years had passed, Vaṅgīsa had the heads of even those who had died brought to him; striking them with his fingernail, he would say: “This being...”
Having said, "I was reborn in such-and-such a womb," he would bring various people forward to cut through the doubts of the great multitude and have them each declare their own destiny.
Because of this, the great multitude placed great trust in him.
Relying on that, he received from the hands of the multitude even hundreds and thousands [of coins]. The brahmins took Vaṅgīsa and, according to their pleasure...
They wandered about. Having heard of the Teacher’s virtues, Vaṅgīsa desired to approach the Teacher.
The brahmins, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama will ensnare him with his magic,” dissuaded him.
Disregarding their words, Vaṅgīsa went into the presence of the Teacher; having exchanged greetings, he stood to one side.
He sat down. The Teacher asked him, "Vaṅgīsa, do you know any craft? "Yes, Master Gotama, I know one called the 'Head-End of a Corpse';
by means of it, even if someone has died three years ago, I can determine the place where they have been reborn by tapping their head with my fingernail.
Then the Teacher [showed him] one head that had been reborn in hell, one among humans, and one...
Among the gods, he had the head of one who had attained final Nibbāna brought and showed it to him.
Having struck the first head, he said, “Venerable Gotama, this being has been reborn in hell. “Excellent, Vaṅgīsa! You have seen well.
He asked, “Where has this being been reborn? “In the human world. “And where is this one? “In the world of the gods. [He asked] of all three as well.
He described the place where [the Buddha] was reborn. But when he struck the head of the one who had attained final Nibbāna with his fingernail, he could see neither the end nor the limit.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Are you unable, Vaṅgīsa? He replied, "Behold, Master Gotama;
let me first examine it. And though he turned it over again and again, even with the external mantras, he could not [find the end of] the head of the one whose taints were exhausted.
He was unable to know it. Then sweat broke out from the crown of his head. Feeling ashamed, he remained silent.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa? "Yes, Master Gotama; I am unable to know the place where this person was reborn.
If you know it, please tell me. "Vaṅgīsa, I know this, and I know even more than this," he said, and then—
“He who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth,
who is unattached, well-gone, and awakened— him I call a brahmin.
Whose destination neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor humans know...”
“He who has destroyed the taints, the Arahant—him I call a brahmin.
He spoke these two verses. Then, showing his reverence, he said, “In that case, Master Gotama, give me that knowledge,” and sat down in the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher said, “We give it to one who shares our same outward marks. Vaṅgīsa said, “Whatever...”
Having said, "It is fitting that I receive this mantra," he approached the brahmins and said, "Do not worry about me when I go forth;
once I have mastered the mantra, I shall become the foremost in all Jambudīpa, and by that, it will only be well for you as well.
For the sake of the mantra, he went into the presence of the Teacher and received the going-forth.
He made his request. At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was standing near the Blessed One, and the Blessed One commanded him:

“Nigrodhakappa, ordain this man. Following the Teacher’s command, the Elder ordained him and said, “First, learn the protective charms,” and then he explained to him the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects as well as the meditation subject of insight. He [the newly ordained monk] [applied himself to] the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects...
While reciting his lessons, he established himself in the meditation subject for insight (*vipassanā*).
The brahmins approached him and asked, "Master Vaṅgīsa, have you learned any craft in the presence of the ascetic Gotama? "Yes, I have been trained.
"In that case, come, let us go. "What is the use of learning a craft? You may go; I have no need for you."
"What remains to be done? The brahmins replied, "Now even you have fallen under the sway of the ascetic Gotama and been ensnared by his magic;
what more can we do for you? With these words, they departed by the very path they had come.
Vaṅgīsa, having further developed insight, realized arhatship.

96. Thus, having attained Arahatship and recollecting his own past karma, the Elder, filled with joy, spoke the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Past Deeds), beginning with the words, "The Conqueror named Padumuttara... We shall explain only those parts whose meaning is not immediately evident. 99.
"Anurañjanto pabhāhi" means that the Blessed One Padumuttara, by means of rays of six colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—was coloring, blazing, beautifying, and shining;
such is the sense. "Veneyyapadumāni so" refers to the Sun Padumuttara [illuminating] the lotuses of those capable of being trained (*veneyya*).

The meaning is that, by means of his own speech—which is like the rays of the sun—he especially awakens and fully rouses the lotuses that are the people to be trained, causing them to blossom through the attainment of the path of arahantship. 100.
"Endowed with intrepidities" means—
“Regarding obstacles, regarding the way out, regarding Buddhahood, and regarding the destruction of the taints—
the Buddha is thoroughly confident in these four points.
Thus, the meaning is that he is endowed with, possessed of, and equipped with the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence as they have been described.

105. *Vāgīso vādisūdana*: He is the lord (*īso*) or chief among disputants—that is, among wise people who engage in debate. Although he should be called "lord of disputants" (*vādīso*), it should be understood that this term is used by changing the letter *d* to *g*.
He is a "destroyer of disputants" (*vādisūdano*) because he causes the doctrine of his own welfare and the welfare of others to flow forth, or because he makes it manifest.

110. *Māramasano*: It is called *māramasano* because it devours (*masati*), clutches (*parāmasati*), and destroys the five Māras, beginning with the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*). *Diṭṭhisūdano*:

It is called *diṭṭhisūdano* because it clarifies, causes to flow forth, and illuminates the vision of views known as conventional and ultimate truth (*vohāra-paramattha*). 111. *Vissāmabhūmi santānaṃ*:

For those weary in the entire ocean of saṃsāra, it is a "resting ground" (*vissāmabhūmi*) by means of attaining the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) and so forth; the meaning is that it is a place of rest and a place of pacification.

132. "Tatohaṃ vihatārambho": from that point on, by the sight of the body of the Paccekabuddha, I was one whose aggressive intent (*ārambha*) was destroyed, whose prideful exertion (*sārambha*) was ruined;
having had my conceit (*māna*) destroyed and becoming free from vanity (*nimmada*), I properly entreated him for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*);
"I entreated" means I made a formal request. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Vaṅgīsa-thera-apadāna* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Nandaka-thera-apadāna*:

The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Nandaka begins with the verse, "In the fifth *apadāna*, the Conqueror named Padumuttara," and so forth. That he too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and all such matters, are easily understood by following the text.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nandaka is completed.
6. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kāḷudāyi:
"In the sixth *Apadāna*, the Victor named Padumuttara... and so forth, is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kāḷudāyi.
This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of being,
was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he [saw] the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who inspire confidence in families.
Seeing him being appointed, he performed an act of resolution (*abhinīhārakamma*) appropriate for that occasion and aspired to that position. The Teacher also made a prediction regarding him.

Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, on the day of the conception of our Bodhisatta in the womb of his mother, he passed away from the world of the gods and was reborn right there in Kapilavatthu into a family of ministers.

He took rebirth. Born on the very same day as the Bodhisattva, they placed him on a soft *dukūla* cotton mattress that very day and brought him to attend upon the Bodhisattva. For together with the Bodhisattva, these seven were born:
the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four treasures, the state elephant Ārohaṇiya, Kaṇṭhaka, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī.

Because he was born on the same day, they were called "Born Together" (*sahajāta*). Then, on the day of his naming—on a day when the entire city was filled with uplifted joy—they gave him the name Udāyin.
However, because his complexion was somewhat dark, he became known as Kāḷudāyin.
He grew up playing childhood games together with the Bodhisatta.
Later on, when the Lord of the World had gone forth on the Great Renunciation, had gradually attained omniscience,
and was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha after setting in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
King Suddhodana, having heard this news, dispatched a minister accompanied by a thousand men with the command: "Bring my son here."
Thus, at the time of the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, they went into the presence of the Teacher;
standing at the edge of the assembly, they heard the Dhamma and, together with their retinue, attained Arahantship. Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, “Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became as if sixty-year-old elders, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*). From the attainment of Arahantship...
From that point on, those called noble ones (ariya) remain indeed neutral; therefore, he did not report the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers.
[Thinking], "The king neither comes nor is his message heard," he dispatched yet another minister accompanied by a thousand men.
When that one also acted in the same manner, he dispatched yet another—in this sequence, nine thousand men were sent with their retinues.
He dispatched nine ministers. Having all gone and attained *arahantship*, they remained silent.
Then the king thought: "Because these many people lacked affection for me, they said nothing regarding the arrival of the One of Ten Powers here;
but this Udāyī is of the same age as the One of Ten Powers and was his playmate since childhood. In me..."
“...and full of affection; I shall send him. Then, having summoned him and said, “Dear son, go with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One of Ten Powers here,” he sent him off.
As he was departing, however, he said, “If I may be permitted to go forth, O King, then I shall bring the Blessed One here. The king replied, “Even if you go forth, my son—”
Having been told, "Go see [the Teacher]," he went to Rājagaha.

Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s time for preaching the Dhamma, he heard the Dhamma and, together with his retinue, attained Arahatship and was established in the state of an "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come, monk). Having attained Arahatship, he thought:
"This is not yet the time for the One of Ten Powers to go to his own native city; rather, when the rainy season has arrived, on the mountains..."
“The time for traveling will come when the forest thickets have ground covered with green grass.
Thus, anticipating the time for departure, he praised the journey as the rainy season arrived, so that he might go to the Teacher’s native city. And this was said in the Theragāthā:
“O Blessed One, the trees are now like glowing coals, having shed their foliage and bearing fruit.”
They shine forth like those possessed of radiance; O Great Hero, this is the season for the juices.
"These trees are in full bloom, delightful, and their fragrance wafts in every direction.
Having shed their leaves, they hope for fruit; O Hero, it is time for you to depart from here."
“Neither too cold nor yet too hot, O Blessed One, is the pleasant climate on this journey;
let the Sākiyas and the Koḷiyas see you crossing the Rohiṇī river facing westward.
With hope one plows the field; with hope the seed is sown.”
"Traders set out upon the ocean, seeking to bring back wealth, driven by hope;
may that hope by which I stand be fulfilled for me.
May it not be too cold, nor too hot, nor too plagued by famine and drought."
“The ground is green and lush; this is the time, O Great Sage.
“Again and again they sow the seed; again and again the king of gods sends rain;
again and again the farmers plow the field; again and again grain comes to the kingdom.”
“Again and again beggars wander about; again and again the masters of giving give.
Having given again and again, the masters of giving go to the heavenly realm again and again.
Indeed, a hero purifies seven generations in whichever family that one of vast wisdom is born.”
I believe the God of Gods is capable, for from you was born the Sage whose name is Truth.
Suddhodana is the name of the Great Seer’s father, while the Buddha’s mother is named Māyā;
having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, she rejoices in the Heaven of the Thirty-three after the breaking up of the body.
“That Gotamī has passed away and departed from here, having become endowed with celestial pleasures.
She rejoices with the five strands of sensual pleasure, surrounded by those hosts of devas.
“I am the son of the Buddha, the conqueror of the unconquerable, of Aṅgīrasa, the peerless Tathāgata.”
“You are my father’s father, Sakka; by Dhamma, O Gotama, you are my grandfather.
“Mangoes, breadfruit, and wood-apples, adorned with flowers and young shoots;
their firm fruits drip like small honeycombs.”
“While both sides are being served, it is time for you to go, O Greatly Famed One.
“The rose-apples are very sweet, as are the *nīpa*, *madhuka*, *gaṇḍī*, and *diva* fruits;
they shine on both sides—O Greatly Famed One, it is time for you to go.”
“Tiṇḍuka fruits and piyāla fruits, golden-hued and delightful;
small-apple trees always bearing fruit—O one of great fame, it is time to go.
Kadalī trees and pañcamocī trees, adorned with well-ripened fruit.”
“They hang on both sides; it is time to go, O Greatly Famed One.
‘The delightful peacock-trees always bear honey-fruit;
the small-apple trees always bear fruit; it is time to go, O Greatly Famed One.’”
“The rows of *hintāla* and *tāla* trees shine like a heap of silver;
covered with well-ripened fruit, they are small yet dripping with honey.
They eat those fruits, O one of great glory, for it is time to depart.”
“With the color of the *udumbara* flower and always bearing sweet fruit, trees hang down on both sides; it is time for you to go, O Greatly Renowned One.
Such are these many trees of yours, bearing various fruits.”
"They hang on both sides; it is time to go, O Greatly Famed One.
Campakas, salaḷas, and nāgas, fragrant and stirred by the breeze, shine with their blossoming tips and honor you with their sweet scent."
“Reverent and bowed low, O one of great fame, it is time to go.
The punnāga trees and mountain-punnāgas, those plants rooted in the earth, are in full bloom;
with their well-flowered tops they shine, honoring you with their sweet fragrance.”
“Reverent, with necks bowed low, it is time to go, O Greatly Famed One!
The *asoka* and *koviḷāra* trees are excellent, bringing forth joy;
the fragrant *kaṇṇikā* flowers are bound together, adorned with crimson hues.”
“Reverent, with heads bowed low, it is the time for you, O one of great fame.
The *kaṇṇikāra* trees are in full bloom, constantly emitting rays of golden light;
they waft divine fragrances, beautifying all directions.”
“With reverence and bowed heads, it is time for you, O one of great fame. The *supatta*,
the *gandhasampanna*, the *ketakī*, and the *dhanuketakī*—
fragrant and wafting their scent, they pervade all directions with their aroma.”
Reverently making offerings, they said: "It is time for you, O one of great fame!
Mallikā, Jātisumanā, Sugandhā, and Khuddamallikā—these flowers waft their fragrance in all directions, beautifying both paths."
They hang down with reverence; this is the time for you, O one of great fame.
The *sindhuvāra* trees, cool-scented and fragrant, stirred by the breeze, honor all directions and beautify both paths.
“Reverent, with necks bowed and uplifted, this is the time for you, O one of great fame.
‘The lions and maned lions, frequented by the four-footed beasts,
are fearless when drinking liquor— these majestic kings of beasts.’”
“With lion’s roars they worship you, those deer-conquerors full of reverence;
drawn up on both sides along the path, it is time for you, O one of great fame.
Tigers, Sindhava horses, and mongooses—well-formed and terrifying—are there.”
As they were flying through the air, fearless and seeking refuge with anyone at all, they bowed with great reverence to them, saying:
"The time has come for you, O Greatly Famed One!
The Six-Tusked Elephant—well-formed, with a beautiful voice and lovely appearance—is now split in three ways."
"Those seven factors established upon you, both of you, are resonant throughout the paths;
full of reverence, as if laughing, this is your assembly, O Greatly Famed One.
'Deer, wild boars, and spotted antelopes, variegated and beautiful birds;'"
"In height and girth, well-formed and with graceful limbs, you two are like singers on the path; this is the time for you, O you of great fame.
Like the Gokaṇṇa, Sarabha, and Ruru deer, you possess perfect proportions."
"Beautiful, with limbs perfectly formed, serving even as an Apsara;
serving them at that time, it was the right season for you, O one of great fame.
'Leopards, bears, hyenas, and always tudaras and varunas;'"
Now all of them have been trained in loving-kindness by you, O Neutral One;
they will surely serve you in return. This is the time for you, O Greatly Famed One.
There are jackals, mongooses, squirrels, and many black deer.
Those who are like saffron, heroes, and fragrant, singing alone— this is your time,
O one of great fame!
Those peacocks with blue necks, with beautiful crests and auspicious wings— this is your time, O one of great fame!
"Your peacocks and swans, resembling beryl and jewels, are crying out and paying homage; it is time for you to see your father.
And your golden-spotted swans and swift-swimming wild geese—"
All those birds have abandoned their nests and are intent on seeing the Conqueror;
they warble with sweet voices, for it is time for them to see their father.
"The swans, the cranes, the sunadas, the ruddy geese, and the river-dwellers..."
The cranes, the herons, the beautiful ruddy geese, the water-crows, and the wild fowl—all these are calling out with joyful voices;
this is the time for you to see your father.
The parrots, variegated, handsome, sweet-voiced, well-feathered, and well-plumed—
As they alight upon the treetops, both of them warble along the paths;
they warble here and there, for it is time for you to see your father.
“The cuckoos are all variegated, always possessing excellent and sweet voices.”
“You have amazed the people, including Surā, Saddhi, Mitta, and the others, as they worship you with arrows. It is time for you to see your father.
The bhiṅkās, kuraras, and sārās always fill the forest.”
Making the forest resound, gathered together with one another, they were singing as if with a melodic chant:
"The partridges are sweet-voiced and strong, the wild cocks are sweet-voiced; this is the time for you to see your father."
"Sweet-sounding and delightful, it is time for you to see your father.
Covered with white sand, well-founded and enchanting,
filled with sweet water, these lakes of yours shine forever."
“Having bathed and drunk there, it is time for you to see your kinsmen.
There are lakes of beautiful, cool water, teeming with crocodiles, sharks, and makaras, encircled by *valaya* and *muñja* reeds and *rohitaka* trees, and filled with darting fish and turtles.”
“Having bathed and drunk there, it is now time for you to see your kinsmen.
‘The lakes shine in many ways, strewn with blue lotuses and likewise with red lotuses,
and filled with white and blue water-lilies.’”
There the waters are cool; it is the right time for you to visit your kinsmen.
"Covered with white lotuses and strewn with red lotuses, the lotus ponds there shine on both sides of the paths here and there."
There they bathe in the waters; it is time for you to see your kinsmen.
Those beautiful rivers, strewn with white sandbanks, easy to ford, and delightful, are filled with great floods of cool water.
They flow along both paths; this is the time for you to see your kinsmen.
Along both sides of the road, crowded with villages and market towns, are people full of faith and confidence, devoted to the Triple Gem.
“For them, your purpose is fulfilled; it is time for you to see your kinsmen.
In various regions, both gods and humans alike honor them with perfumes and garlands;
it is time for you to see your kinsmen.”
Thus the Elder praised the journey of the Teacher with about sixty stanzas. Then the Blessed One, thinking, "Kāḷudāyī desires my departure;

I shall fulfill his aspiration," and seeing that many would attain distinguished spiritual progress upon traveling there, set out from Rājagaha at a brisk pace, accompanied by twenty thousand who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava).
Experiencing the various fruits of the kind already described, being honored with service and worship by multitudes of bipeds, quadrupeds, and others,
being perfumed with the scents of fragrant flowers of the aforementioned sort, and providing for the welfare of the inhabitants of villages and market towns,
he set out on the road toward the village of Kapilavatthu. Having traveled to Kapilavatthu by means of his psychic power, the Elder stood before the king.
Standing in the sky and seeing a form never seen before, when asked by the king, "Who are you?", he said,
"If you do not know the minister’s son who was sent by you into the presence of the Blessed One, then know him thus: "I am the son of the Buddha,
the conqueror of the unconquerable, of Aṅgīrasa, the peerless Tathāgata."
“You are my father’s father, O Sakka; by Dhamma, Gotama, you are my grandfather,” he said in this verse.

Therein, “I am the son of the Buddha” means that I am a legitimate son (*orasa-putta*) because I was born from the Dhamma-teachings produced through the exertion of the heart of the Omniscient Buddha.
“One who endures the unbearable” refers to those prior to his full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), excluding the Great Bodhisattvas.

Because it is impossible for others to endure or overcome the entire equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), which is "unbearable" (*asayha*); because he endures and overcomes that which is characterized by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
and because even beyond that, due to the impossibility of others enduring or overcoming him, he endures and overcomes the five "unbearable" Māras;

and because, through the awakening to the distinctions of their latent dispositions (*āsaya*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), temperaments (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*), he [guides] those to be trained (*veneyya*) according to what is appropriate.

"Of the Asayhasāhin": because he bears the burden of the Buddha’s work—which is called "instruction" (*anusāsani*) and is insuperable by others—by means of the ultimate truths pertaining to the present life and the future life;

or because he is one who performs well therein, he is "the bearer of the insuperable. "Of Aṅgīrasa": [this refers to] him who has taken upon himself (*aṅgīkata*) the perfection of virtue and so forth.
Others say: "Because of the radiance (*obhāsa*) streaming forth from every limb (*aṅga-maṅga*). However, some [say]: "'Aṅgīrasa' and 'Siddhattha'—these..."

"They say that two names were taken for the father alone. "Appaṭimassa" means of the peerless one; "tādino" means of the one who is such through the perfection of the characteristic of equanimity (*tādi*) toward the desirable and so forth.
"'Tuvaṃsi pitupitā mama'" means: by way of the noble lineage (*ariyajāti*), you are the father of my father, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*);

by way of worldly convention (*lokavohāra*), you are my father. "Sakka"—with this he addresses the king by his clan name. "Dhammena"—by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), [namely] by way of the noble lineage and the worldly lineage.
[This was] through the meeting of the natures of two castes. He addressed the king by his clan, saying "Gotama.
He was the grandfather, thus [the king said], "Noble sir, you are my grandfather. And here, by saying "I am the son of the Buddha," and so forth, the Elder answered another question.
Having thus made himself known, the king—joyful and delighted—had him sit upon a magnificent couch and [offered] to himself...
Having filled his bowl with the various kinds of exquisite food that had been prepared and having given it to him, [the man] made a gesture indicating he wished to depart.
When asked, "Why do you wish to go? Eat," he replied, "I shall eat after going into the presence of the Teacher.
"But where is the Teacher? "He has set out on the road with a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus for the purpose of seeing you."
"You eat this alms-food yourselves; take another portion for the Blessed One. Until my son reaches this city, bring him alms-food from right here.
Having finished his meal and having taught the Dhamma to both the king and his assembly, the Elder departed from the royal palace even before the Teacher’s arrival.
Inspiring in them all a deep faith in the virtues of the Triple Gem, he released into the air the Teacher’s bowl filled with alms-food while everyone was looking on;
then, ascending into the sky himself, he brought the alms-food and placed it in the Teacher’s hand.
The Teacher consumed that alms-food. Thus, in a single day, [he covered] a road of sixty yojanas.
Each day, as the Blessed One traveled a *yojana*, [Sujātā] would bring almsfood from Rājagaha and give it to him.
Eventually, the Blessed One reached the city of Kapilavatthu; on the following day, he walked for alms along the royal road.
Hearing of this, King Suddhodana went there and said, "Do not think such a thing should be done; this is not the tradition of our royal lineage."
“Great King, this is your lineage, but such is our Buddha-lineage,” he said, and added:
“One should rise up and not be negligent; one should practice the Dhamma of good conduct.
One who lives according to the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.”
“Practice the Dhamma in well-conducted conduct; do not practice ill-conducted conduct.
One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.
Thus he taught the Dhamma. The king was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then the king [provided for] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha...

Having invited him to his own residence, fed him, and offered him hospitality, and having heard the *Dhammapāla-jātaka* at the conclusion of the meal, he and his retinue were established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Later, while lying beneath the white parasol, he attained *arahantship* and passed into final *nibbāna*.
Thereafter, the Blessed One went to the palace of Queen Bimbā, the mother of Rāhula; having taught her the Dhamma, he [removed] her grief.
Having dispelled [his grief] by teaching the *Candakinnarījātaka* and having inspired faith [in him], he went to the Nigrodhārāma.
Then Queen Bimbā said to her son, Prince Rāhula: “Go, ask for the wealth belonging to your father.
The prince, saying, “Give me my inheritance, O ascetic,” followed after the Blessed One and said, “Is it well with you, ascetic?”
Saying, "It is a shadow," he departed. The Blessed One led him to the Nigrodha Monastery, and saying, "Receive the supramundane inheritance," he granted him the going-forth.
Then, while seated in the midst of the noble assembly, the Blessed One placed the Elder among the foremost, declaring:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who inspire confidence in families: namely, Kāḷudāyī."

165. The Elder, having remembered his own past karma and being filled with joy as he recalled his former deeds, spoke the verses beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara,” while proclaiming the *Pubbacaritāpadāna* (Account of Former Deeds). Among these, we shall explain only those words that are not self-evident (*anuttāna*).
166. *Guṇāguṇavidū*: "Guṇa" means virtue and "aguṇa" means vice; thus, "guṇāguṇa" refers to praise and blame, or the wholesome and the unwholesome.
One who knows this is a "knower of virtues and vices" (*guṇāguṇavidū*). *Kataññū*: one who recognizes the benefit performed by others is "grateful" (*kataññū*). Even for a single day...
He is grateful (*kataññū*) because he is capable of giving even his kingdom to one who has rendered assistance through such acts as providing food.
He is a "knower of what has been done" (*katavedī*); that is, he finds (*vindati*), experiences, and receives (*sampaṭicchati*) what has been done for him.

"He yokes beings to the ford" means that by means of the teaching of the Dhamma, he yokes, thoroughly yokes, and establishes all beings upon the path of skillful means—the way leading to entry into Nibbāna. The rest is self-evident.
The meaning of the verses on the praise of the departure has already been stated in the *Theragāthā*.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kāḷudāyi is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Abhaya.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Abhayatthera begins with the words, "In the seventh *apadāna*, the Conqueror named Padumuttara...

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Victors and accumulating merits that served as a supportive condition (*upaniṣad*) throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a brahmin family in the city of Haṃsavatī. As he grew up...
A master of the Vedangas and skilled in both his own and other systems, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma one day, he praised the Blessed One with verses with a mind full of faith.
Having lived there for the duration of his lifespan and performed meritorious deeds, he passed away from that state and was reborn in the world of the devas.
Wandering thus from one happy destination to another, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born in Rājagaha.
He was reborn as the son of King Bimbisāra, and they gave him the name Abhaya.
