When he reached maturity, while traveling about in friendly association with the Nigaṇṭhas, one day, having been sent by the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta to challenge the Teacher’s doctrine, he asked a subtle question;
and having heard the subtle answer, he gained confidence in the Teacher.
Having gone forth in the presence [of the Buddha] and directed his knowledge toward a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) appropriate for it, he attained Arahantship before long.

Having reached Arahantship and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the account of his former conduct (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), spoke the verses beginning with "The Victor named Padumuttara. All of that is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Abhaya is completed.
8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya.
In this eighth Apadāna, beginning with "In this auspicious aeon," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Lomasakaṅgiya.

This [Elder] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for the cessation of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
While amassing merit during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn into a brahmin family and became endowed with faith and serene confidence.
He had another friend named Candana; both of them, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, went forth with minds full of faith.
Having guarded their virtue for as long as they lived, possessing perfectly pure morality, they passed away from there and were reborn in the world of the devas.
They experienced divine bliss for one interval between Buddhas. Among them, this one was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha into the Sākyan clan;
having become another Candana-devaputta, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Then, at the Dhamma-teaching on Vessantara, which was delivered by the Blessed One—who had been entreated by Kāḷudāyin, who inspired faith in the Sākyan clan—in order to humble the pride of the Sākyan kings:
Having seen the miracle of the rain of lotuses, he went forth with a mind full of faith.
Having heard the teaching of the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta* as recounted in the *Majjhima Nikāya*, while dwelling in the forest, he recalled the instruction of that *Bhaddekaratta-sutta* teaching;
by directing his knowledge according to that and attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he attained Arahatship.

225. Having attained arahantship and recollecting his own former karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke these verses beginning with "In this auspicious *kappa*. Therein, first, a *kappa* is fourfold:
a *sārakappa*, a *varakappa*, a *maṇḍakappa*, and a *bhaddakappa*. Among these, that *kappa* in which a single Buddha arises is—
A *sārakappa* (essence aeon) is so named. That in which two or three Buddhas arise is called a *varakappa* (excellent aeon).
That in which four Buddhas arise is called a *maṇḍakappa* (ornamented aeon). That in which five Buddhas arise is called a *bhaddakappa* (fortunate aeon). But elsewhere—
“The Sārakappa, the Maṇḍakappa, and likewise the Sāramaṇḍakappa;
the Varakappa and the Bhaddakappa—these are the five kinds of aeons.
One, two, three, four, and five Buddhas appear in succession.”
“In these five aeons, the Leaders appear.

Thus, five aeons have been mentioned. Among them, this aeon is known as the “Auspicious Aeon” (Bhaddakappa) because it is adorned by five Buddhas—namely, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, Gotama, and Metteyya.
Therefore, the connection is: “In this auspicious aeon, the Leader named Kassapa appeared. The rest is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya is completed.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vanavaccha:
In this ninth *Apadāna*, beginning with "In this auspicious aeon... is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Vanavaccha.

This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated the merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma;
having conceived faith, he went forth into homelessness, lived the pure holy life, and after passing away from there, was reborn in the world of the gods.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the vicinity of certain monks in a forest region in the womb of a dove. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness toward them, he heard the Dhamma;
having passed away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Kapilavatthu.
Even while still in his mother’s womb, a pregnancy-longing (dohada) arose in his mother to dwell in the forest.
[She went] to give birth in the forest. Then, while she was dwelling in the forest according to her desire, the delivery of the fetus occurred.
When he emerged from the womb, they received him with a piece of kāṣāya cloth. That was the time when the Bodhisatta had been born;
the king had the prince brought and raised him together with [the others]. Then the Bodhisatta, having gone forth on the Great Renunciation—
Having gone forth and practiced austerities for six years, when the Buddha had appeared, he went into the presence of Mahākassapa.
Inspired by his instruction and having heard from him of the appearance of the Buddha, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having heard the Dhamma, he went forth and, before long, became an arahant possessed of the six super-knowledges.

251. Having attained Arahatship and recollecting his own past karma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former deeds), spoke these verses beginning with "In this auspicious aeon...
Therein, regarding the phrase "a kinsman of Brahmā, of great renown":
although it should be said "a kinsman of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇabandhu*)—meaning one who is a relative of the Brahmins—it is rendered as "brahmabandhu" for the sake of the metrical flow of the verse.
It should be understood that this has been said. He is of great renown because he pervades the three worlds. All else is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vanavaccha is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Cūḷasugandha.
The *Apadāna* of the Venerable Sugandha Thera, beginning with "In this auspicious kappa," is the tenth.

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa in a family of great wealth in Bārāṇasī; and having reached maturity, he—
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he paid homage at all times and gave great alms;
seven times a month, he anointed the Blessed One’s Gandhakuti with the four kinds of fragrant paste.
He made this aspiration: "In each place where I am reborn, may a sweet fragrance emanate from my body. The Blessed One gave him a prediction. He [lived] for the full span of his life.
Having performed meritorious deeds while remaining there, he passed away from that state and was reborn in the world of the gods.
Because he made the world of sense-desire fragrant with the scent of his body, he became renowned as the "Fragrant Deva-son" (Sugandha-devaputta).

After experiencing the splendors of the celestial realm, he passed away from there and was reborn into a family of great wealth during this current appearance of a Buddha. Even while still in his mother’s womb, his mother—
By the fragrance of his body, the entire house and the entire city became of one scent;
at the moment of his birth, the whole city of Sāvatthī was like a casket of perfumes, and so they gave him the name Sugandha.
He grew up. At that time, the Teacher, having arrived at Sāvatthī, accepted the great monastery of Jetavana.

Seeing him, with a mind full of faith, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One; and before long, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), he attained *arahantship*.
From the day of his attainment until his final *parinibbāna*, throughout this interval, a sweet fragrance alone wafted from the places where he lay and so forth.
Even the devas scattered celestial powders and divine fragrant flowers over him.

272. That elder, having attained arahantship and recollecting his own past karma, became filled with joy and, proclaiming the *pubbacaritāpadāna* (account of former conduct), spoke these verses beginning with "In this auspicious aeon...
Since all of that follows the method already explained below and its meaning is clear, it is easily understood;
the distinction lies solely in the variety of merit and the variety of names.
The commentary on the *Cūḷasugandha Thera-apadāna* is completed.
The commentary on the fifty-fifth chapter (*Pañcapaññāsa-vagga*) is completed.
56. The Chapter on Renown (*Yasa-vagga*).
1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Yasa:
In the fifty-sixth chapter, the first apadāna, beginning with “Having plunged into the great ocean,” is the apadāna of the Venerable Elder Yasa.
This one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, [accumulated] the necessary conditions for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of being.
Accumulating merit during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he became a Naga king of great power.
He led the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, to his own abode and offered a great almsgiving;
he clothed the Blessed One in a most costly set of three robes and presented each individual bhikkhu with a pair of costly separate garments and all manner of requisites.

With the requisites of a recluse. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he became the son of a merchant during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha and honored the Great Seat of Enlightenment with the seven kinds of jewels.
During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth into the teaching and practiced the duty of a recluse. Thus, wandering only through happy destinies, he [reached] our...

In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn in Benares as the son of a very wealthy merchant, in the womb of Sujātā, the merchant’s daughter who had given the Blessed One milk-rice porridge; his name was Yasa, and he was exceedingly delicate.
He had three palaces—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season—and it was in the rainy-season palace that he...
During the four months of the rainy season, he dwells being entertained by female musicians and does not descend to the lower palace.
During the four months of winter, he remains right there in the winter palace, where the windows and shutters are well-sealed against the wind.
During the four months of summer, he dwells right there in the summer palace, which is provided with many doors, windows, and lattices. Because of the delicacy of his hands and feet—
There was no need for him to sit upon the ground or perform other such tasks. Having spread out a bed made of *simbali* flowers and the like, he performed his duties there using them as pillows.
Thus, like a young god in the celestial realm, while he was provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure and was enjoying himself, sleep came upon him beforehand;
the attendants also fell asleep throughout the entire night.
And the oil lamp was burning. Then the young man Yasa woke up early and saw his own retinue sleeping:

one with a lute tucked under her arm, another with a hand-drum around her neck, another with a tambourine under her arm, some with disheveled hair, others drooling, and still others snoring like those in a charnel ground.
"I think that upon seeing it, the danger became apparent to him, and his mind settled into disenchantment.
Then the young man Yasa uttered this inspired exclamation: "Alas, how beset! Alas, how overwhelmed!
Then the young man Yasa, having put on his golden sandals, went toward the gate of his residence.

The non-human beings opened the gate, thinking: "May no one cause an obstacle for the clansman Yasa in his going forth from the home life into homelessness. Then the clansman Yasa approached the city gate;
the non-human beings opened the gate, thinking: "May no one cause an obstacle for the clansman Yasa in his going forth from the home life..."
“...to the going forth into homelessness. Then the young man Yasa approached Isipatana, the Deer Park.
Now at that time, the Blessed One, having risen at the end of the night during the early morning hours, was walking back and forth in the open air.
The Blessed One saw the young man Yasa coming from afar; seeing him, he descended from his walk.
He sat down on the prepared seat. Then the young man Yasa, not far from the Blessed One, uttered this inspired utterance:
"Alas, how beset! Alas, how oppressed! Then the Blessed One said to the young man Yasa:
"This, Yasa, is indeed unbeset; this is unoppressed. Come, Yasa, sit down; I shall teach you the Dhamma."
“I shall explain it. Then the young man Yasa, thinking, “This indeed is free from distress;
this is free from affliction,” being joyful and elated, took off his golden sandals and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the young man Yasa was sitting there to one side, [the Blessed One said:]
The Blessed One gave a gradual discourse, namely: a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven;
he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that the young man Yasa had a ready mind, a pliable mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, [he set forth the teaching of the Dhamma].
Then he proclaimed that Dhamma teaching which is uniquely excellent among the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would perfectly absorb dye, even so, while Yasas was on that very seat, there arose in him the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma.
—“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
Then the mother of the young man Yasa, having ascended the palace and not seeing the young man Yasa, approached the householder Seṭṭhi;
having approached him, she said this to the householder Seṭṭhi: “My son...”

“Householder, their fame is no longer seen. Then the merchant householder, having dispatched swift messengers to the four quarters, went himself toward Isipatana, the Deer Park. There the merchant householder saw the pair of golden sandals set down;
seeing them, he followed that very path. From afar, the Blessed One saw the merchant householder.
Seeing him approaching, the Blessed One thought: "Suppose I were to perform such a feat of psychic power that the householder Seṭṭhi, sitting here, would not see the young man Yasa sitting here.
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power. Then...
Then the householder merchant approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, might the Blessed One see the clansman Yasa? "In that case, householder, sit down; perhaps while sitting here you might see the clansman Yasa sitting here. Then the householder merchant...
“Sitting right here, I shall indeed see the clansman Yasa sitting here,” he thought;
thus joyful and elated, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the householder Seṭṭhi sat there, the Blessed One delivered to him a gradual discourse...
[as before] ...and being independent of others, he spoke thus to the Blessed One regarding the Teaching.

“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One through many lines of reasoning.”
“...has been explained. Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Thus he became the first lay follower in the world by means of the threefold formula.

Then, as the Dhamma was being taught to the clansman Yasa’s father, his mind was liberated from the acquisitions through non-clinging as he reflected upon the plane exactly as it had been seen and exactly as it had been understood. Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“As the Dhamma was being taught to the clansman Yasa’s father, [he reflected upon] the plane exactly as it had been seen and exactly as it had been understood...”

As he reflected, his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging. “The clansman Yasa is incapable of returning to the lower life to enjoy sensual pleasures as he did formerly when he was a householder;
what if I were now to withdraw that performance of psychic power? Then the Blessed One withdrew that performance of psychic power. [Yasa] saw...
When the householder merchant saw the young man Yasa sitting there, he said to him:
"My dear Yasa, your mother has fallen into lamentation and grief; give life back to your mother.
Then the young man Yasa looked up at the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One said to the householder merchant: "That..."
"What do you think, householder? Suppose a person has seen and known the Dhamma with the knowledge of a trainee and the vision of a trainee, just as you have;

and when that person reviews the ground exactly as it was seen and known, their mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging—would such a person, householder, be capable of falling back into the lower life to enjoy sensual pleasures?"
“Is it not just as it was before when he was still a householder? “Certainly not, Bhante.

“Householder, when the noble son Yasa saw and knew the Dhamma with the knowledge and vision of one in training (sekha) just as you have, his mind—upon reviewing the ground exactly as it was seen and known—was liberated from the taints through non-clinging. He is incapable [of falling back].”
“Householder, this clansman Yasa has indeed returned to the lower life to enjoy sensual pleasures, just as he did previously when he was a householder.
“It is a gain for the clansman Yasa, Bhante! It is a great fortune for the clansman Yasa, Bhante!
Since the mind of the clansman Yasa has been liberated from the taints through non-clinging, may you please consent [to my request].”
“Bhante, may the Blessed One accept today’s meal from me, with the young man Yasa as his attendant monk.

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Then the householder Seṭṭhi, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed. Not long after he had left, the young man Yasa...
The householder Seṭṭhi said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One;
may I receive the full ordination. “Come, monk,” the Blessed One said, “the Dhamma is well-expounded;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. That itself was that venerable one’s full ordination.
1. Having become an Arahant, filled with joy, and proclaiming the account of his own former conduct, he said, "Plunging into the great ocean," and so forth.
In this context, it is called *samudda* because it must be clearly (*su*) shown by means of the finger-seal (*aṅguli-muddā*);
or else, it is called *samudda* because it rises up (*udiyati*), is agitated, is stirred, and makes a roaring sound while being churned.
It is called the "great ocean" (*mahāsamudda*) because it is both great (*mahanta*) and an ocean (*samudda*); [the phrase] "that great ocean" refers to that *mahāsamudda*.
"Having plunged in" (*oggayha*) means having gone down into it, having entered within, having entered into the interior of that great ocean;

this accusative case should be understood here as expressing identity (*sāmyatthe*). Regarding the phrase "my dwelling well-constructed" (*bhavanaṃ me sumāpitaṃ*): herein, "dwelling" (*bhavanaṃ*) means that they exist, are produced, or reside there by means of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).

"Bhavana" means that which they make their dwelling in; "my bhavana" refers to that celestial mansion (*vimāna*), that palace (*pāsāda*), that city well-constructed with five walls and gabled chambers—the meaning is that it was perfectly fashioned by my own power.

"Sunimmitā pokkharaṇī" means a lotus pond that has become very great, having come into being, proceeded, occurred, been dug, or made; [it is so called] because of its fish, turtles, flowers, sandy banks, bathing places, sweet water, and so forth.

"Suṭṭhu nibbattā" means well-produced or fashioned. "Cakkavākūpakūjitā" refers to that lotus pond being resounded, made vocal, and filled with the cries of ruddy geese (*cakkavāka*), wild fowl, swans, and so forth;

this is how the phrase is to be connected. Following this, the description of the rivers, forests, islands, bipeds, quadrupeds, trees, and birds, as well as the invitation to the Blessed One Sumedha for his vision and the sequence of the Blessed One Sumedha’s acts of giving, are indeed easy to understand.
"Receiver of the world’s oblation": here, "world-oblation" (*lokāhuti*) means an oblation in the world;

it is called the "receiver of the world’s oblation" because he accepts the oblation—that is, the honor and worship—of the world comprised of the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness. This refers to the Blessed One, the Wise One (*sumedha*).
The remainder—the giving of the prophecy and the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship—is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Yasatthera-apadāna* is completed.
2. The commentary on the *Nadīkassapatthera-apadāna*:
"Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Nadīkassapa.
This person as well, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, one day,
seeing the Teacher wandering for alms, he conceived a heart full of faith and [offered] the first fruit that had appeared upon a mango tree he himself had planted.

He gave a single mango fruit the color of mana-silā stone. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha as the brother of Uruvelakassapa.
Upon reaching maturity, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he did not desire the life of a householder; instead, he went forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller.
Together with three hundred ascetics, he established a hermitage on the bank of the river Nerañjarā and dwelt there.

Because he lived by the river and belonged to the Kassapa clan, he received the name Nadī-Kassapa (River-Kassapa). The Blessed One granted him and his retinue ordination through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu*).
At Gayāsīsa, he [received] the Blessed One’s teaching known as the *Ādittapariyāya* (The Discourse on the Burning).
He established himself in arahantship.
Herein is the sequential account: after the Teacher had ordained the young man Yasa, he went to Uruvelā in order to subdue the three matted-hair ascetics who were brothers.
Now at that time, three matted-hair ascetics were residing in Uruvelā.
Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, and Gayākassapa—among them, Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic was the leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of five hundred matted-hair ascetics;
Nadīkassapa the matted-hair ascetic was the leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of three hundred matted-hair ascetics;
and Gayākassapa the matted-hair ascetic [was the leader] of two hundred matted-hair ascetics.
He was the leader, the guide, the foremost, the chief, the preeminent one.
Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa; having approached, he said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa, we would stay for one night in the fire-hall. "It is not troublesome for me, Great Ascetic," [he replied].
"Venerable sir, there is a nāga king here named Caṇḍa, possessed of psychic power, venomous, and of terrible poison; let him not harm you.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa... and a third time... "Let him not harm you.
At the very least, let him not harm me; come now, Kassapa, please permit me the fire-hall. "Dwell there, Great Ascetic."
"As you please. Then the Blessed One, having entered the fire-hall, prepared a grass mat and sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
That nāga saw that the Blessed One had entered; seeing him, he became dejected and emitted smoke. Then the Blessed One...
It occurred to him: "What if I were to overcome this nāga’s fire with my own fire, without damaging his skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or bone marrow?
Then the Blessed One, having performed such a feat of supernormal power, emitted smoke. Thereupon, unable to endure that insult, the nāga blazed up.
The Blessed One also entered the fire-element and blazed forth. As both were set ablaze, the fire-chamber became as if on fire, glowing, and radiant.
Then those matted-hair ascetics, having surrounded the fire-chamber, said this:
"How handsome indeed, sirs, is that great ascetic! He is being harassed by a serpent. Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One—

Then, without harming the skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow of that nāga, he consumed its fire with his own fire, placed it in his alms-bowl, and showed it to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, saying:
"Kassapa, this nāga has been consumed by me; its fire has been extinguished by my fire. Then, Uruvelakassapa...

It occurred to Jaṭila: “The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he will, by means of his own fiery energy, overcome the fiery energy of the fierce Nāga king, who possesses psychic power, is venomous, and is of terrible poison;
yet he is not an Arahant like I am.”
“On the Nerañjarā River, the Blessed One said to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
‘If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa, let us stay today in your fire-hall.
‘It is not troublesome for me, Great Ascetic; I merely wish to prevent you from doing so out of concern for your comfort.’”
“Caṇḍa the Nāga king is here, possessing psychic power, a venomous serpent with a terrible poison;
do not let him harm you.
“Even if he should not harm me, please, Kassapa, grant me permission for the fire-hall.”
Knowing that it had been given, he entered fearlessly, having transcended all dread.
Seeing that the seer had entered, the serpent-king was dejected and emitted smoke;
but the human-king, with a joyful mind and uplifted heart, also emitted smoke there.
Unable to endure the insult, the noble serpent blazed up like a fire;
skilled in the element of fire, the noble human likewise blazed there.
As both were set ablaze, they shone with light.
The fire-hall was ablaze, burning fiercely, and glowing with flames;
the matted-hair ascetics shouted from above, "Oh, what a handsome great ascetic!
He is being harassed by a nāga! they said.
Then, with the passing of that night, the flames of the nāga were extinguished,
but the flames of the one possessed of psychic power remained, appearing in many colors:
blue, red, madder-red, yellow, and the color of crystal.
Within the body of Aṅgīrasa, flames of many colors appeared.
Placing [the snake] in his alms-bowl, he showed the great serpent to the brahmin, saying:
"Kassapa, here is your snake; let fire be consumed by fire."

Then the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, having gained deep confidence in the Blessed One through this miracle of psychic power, said this to the Blessed One: "Stay right here, Great Ascetic; I shall provide you with regular meals.
This was the first miracle.
Then the Blessed One stayed in a certain grove not far from the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa.
...was dwelling there. Then, when the night had advanced, the four Great Kings, with their surpassing splendor illuminating the entire grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood in the four directions like great masses of fire. Then the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa—
When that night had passed, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

"It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready. Indeed, Great Ascetic, during the advanced part of the night, those of surpassing beauty approached you, illuminating the entire grove; having approached..."
Having paid homage to him, they stood in the four directions like great masses of fire.
"These, Kassapa, are the Four Great Kings; they approached me to hear the Dhamma. Then it occurred to the yogi Uruvelakassapa:
"Powerful indeed is this Great Ascetic, possessed of great majesty, in that even the four [Great Kings]..."
"The great kings will approach for the sake of hearing the Dhamma, but they will certainly not be as [worthy] as I am.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, dwelt in that very grove.
This was the second miracle.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire grove with his surpassing radiance,
approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One,
he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, more brilliant and more sublime than the splendor of his previous forms.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: “It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
Who was that, Great Ascetic, who at the end of the night, with surpassing beauty, [illuminated] the entire grove?”

Having illuminated [the area], he approached where you were; having approached and paid homage to you, he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, more brilliant and more sublime than his former radiance.
“This, Kassapa, was Sakka, lord of the devas, who approached me to listen to the Dhamma. Then...

Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa: "Powerful indeed is this Great Recluse, possessed of great majesty, since even Sakka, the lord of the devas, will approach him to listen to the Dhamma;
yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am. Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa...
He dwelt in that very grove.
This was the third miracle.
Then, when the night had advanced, Brahmā Sahampati, with a most radiant complexion, [approached] the entire extent of the grove.

Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, more brilliant and more sublime than the previous splendors.
Then, at the end of that night, Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
Who was that, Great Ascetic, who at the end of the night, with a most excellent complexion, having illuminated the entire grove, approached you;
and having approached and paid homage to you, stood to one side?"
“It is just as if there were a great mass of fire that is more brilliant and more sublime than the previous appearances of color.
“Kassapa, it was this Brahmā Sahampati who approached me for the sake of hearing the Dhamma.
Then, this thought occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa: “The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty.”
"For it is indeed remarkable that even Brahmā Sahampati will approach to hear the Dhamma,
let alone one such as I who am an arahant. Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the yogi Uruvelakassapa,
dwelt in that very grove.
This was the fourth miracle.
Now at that time, a great sacrifice had been prepared for the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa,
and the entire regions of Aṅga and Magadha were eager to come forth, bringing with them abundant solid and soft food.

Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa: "Now a great sacrifice has been prepared for me, and the entire region of Aṅga and Magadha will come forward bringing abundant food, both hard and soft.
If the Great Ascetic performs a miracle of psychic power before this great multitude, the gain and honor of the Great Ascetic will increase."
"My gains and honor will diminish; alas, what if the Great Ascetic were not to come for tomorrow's meal?

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, went to Uttarakuru, brought almsfood from there, ate it at Lake Anotatta, and spent the day’s rest right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: "It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
Why indeed, Great Ascetic, did you not come yesterday? Moreover, we were mindful of you, wondering, 'Why indeed does the Great Ascetic not come?'"
"And a portion of solid food and soft food has been set aside for you. Did it not occur to you, Kassapa:
"Now my great sacrifice is underway, and people from all of Aṅga and Magadha will come bringing abundant solid and soft food;
if the Great Ascetic performs a miracle of psychic power before this great multitude..."
"The gain and honor of the Great Ascetic will increase, while my own gain and honor will diminish;

oh, would that the Great Ascetic did not come tomorrow! Kassapa, having understood the reflection in your mind with my own mind, I went to Uttarakuru, brought almsfood from there, ate it at Lake Anotatta, and spent the day's rest right there.

He thought: "Then the ascetic Uruvelakassapa thought: 'The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he can even understand my mind with his own; yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal offered by the ascetic Uruvelakassapa, dwelt in that very grove."
The fifth miracle.
Now at that time, a rag-robe had arisen for the Blessed One. Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"Where indeed might I wash this rag-robe? Then Sakka, lord of the devas, [perceived the Blessed One's thought].
Having understood with his own mind the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, Sakka, lord of the devas, dug a lotus pond with his hand and said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One wash his rag-robe. Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“On what now shall I rub the rag-robe? Then Sakka, lord of the devas, [understood] with the Blessed One’s mind...
Knowing the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, she set down a large stone, saying, “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One rub his rag-robe here.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “What indeed shall I hold onto to climb up?
Then the deity dwelling in the *kakudha* tree, knowing with her own mind the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, [stretched out] a branch...
He inclined it, saying, “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One step up here, taking hold.
Then the Blessed One thought, “Upon what now should I set down this rag-robe?

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, set down a great rock, saying, “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One set it down here.”
“Let him cast away his rag-robe. Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: “It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
Why is it, Great Ascetic, that this lotus pond was not here before, yet now there is a lotus pond here?”
“Was this stone placed here before? By whom was this stone placed here? Was the branch of this *kakudha* tree bent down before?
This branch has been bent down now. “In this case, Kassapa, a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) came into my possession.
Then, Kassapa, this thought occurred to me: ‘Where indeed might I wash this rag-robe? And then...”
“Kassapa, Sakka, lord of the devas, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in my mind, dug a lotus pond with his hand and said this to me:
‘Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One wash his rag-robe.
Kassapa, that lotus pond was dug by a non-human being with a hand. Then, Kassapa, it occurred to me: ‘In what [shall I wash it]?’”

“...‘I shall rub this rag-robe’? Then, Kassapa, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in my mind, set down a great stone, saying: “Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One rub the rag-robe.
This stone, Kassapa, was set down by a non-human being. To me, Kassapa—
The thought occurred to me: “What indeed can I grasp to climb up?
Then, Kassapa, the deity dwelling in the *kakudha* tree, knowing with her own mind the reflection in my mind, bent down a branch, saying:
“Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One climb up by grasping this. That *kakudha* tree was one whose branches were within reach. Thus it was for me, Kassapa.
Then this thought occurred to me: "Upon what indeed should I cast away this rag-robe?
Then, Kassapa, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection in my mind, set down a great stone slab, saying:
"Here, Blessed One, may the rag-robe be cast away. That, Kassapa, was set down by a non-human being.

"Virtues. Then it occurred to Uruvelakassapa: "The Great Ascetic is of great psychic power and great majesty, since even Sakka, the lord of the devas, performs service for him; yet he is certainly not an Arahant in the way that I am.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, stayed in that very grove.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he announced the time to the Blessed One, saying, "It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
"Go, Kassapa, let us go," he said, and having dismissed the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, [he went] to the rose-apple tree...
Jambudīpa appeared [in his vision]; taking fruit from there, he arrived earlier and sat down in the fire-hall.
Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic saw the Blessed One sitting in the fire-hall, and having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"By which path have you come, Great Ascetic? I set out earlier than you, yet you..."

“Did you arrive first and sit down in the fire-hall? “Here, Kassapa, having dismissed you, I took a fruit from the rose-apple tree after which Jambudīpa is named; I arrived first and sat down in the fire-hall.
This rose-apple fruit, Kassapa, is endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of flavor. “If... [it is]...”
“Do you wish to enjoy it? “Enough, Great Ascetic; you alone are worthy of it; you alone should enjoy it.

Then this thought occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa: “The Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and great majesty, since, having sent me away first, he has [taken] fruit from that rose-apple tree after which the Rose-Apple Continent (Jambudīpa) is named.”
“Having taken [the food], he will return first and sit in the fire-hall, but he is certainly not an arahant like me.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the ascetic Uruvelakassapa, stayed in that very grove.
Then, at the end of that night, the ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he announced the time to the Blessed One: "It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready. "Go, Kassapa;
let us come," he said, and having dismissed the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, [he went] to the mango tree not far from the rose-apple tree by which Jambudīpa is named...
not far from that was the *āmalaka* tree... not far from that...
Having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, [the Blessed One] took a pāricchattaka flower and returned first, sitting down in the fire-hall.
The matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa saw the Blessed One sitting in the fire-hall;
having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One: "By which path did you come, Great Ascetic? I..."
“Did you depart earlier, and having arrived first, are you now sitting in the fire-hall?
“Here, Kassapa, after sending you away, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, took a pāricchattaka flower, and having arrived first, am sitting in the fire-hall.
This, Kassapa, is the pāricchattaka flower, endowed with beauty.”
"It is endowed with fragrance; if you desire it, take it. "Enough, Great Ascetic! You alone are worthy of it;
you alone should take it. Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and great majesty, since he sent me off first and then went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven..."
"Having taken a pāricchattaka flower, he will arrive first and sit in the fire-chamber;
however, he is certainly not an arahant like I am.
Now at that time, those matted-hair ascetics, wishing to tend the sacrificial fire, were unable to split the wood.

Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics: "Without a doubt, this is the power of the great ascetic’s supernormal might, such that we are unable to split the wood. Then the Blessed One said to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"Let the wood be split, Kassapa. "Let it be split, Great Ascetic. And at once—
Five hundred pieces of wood were split. Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that even pieces of wood are being split; yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am."
Now at that time, those matted-hair ascetics, wishing to tend the fire, were unable to kindle it.

Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics: "Without a doubt, this is through the supernatural power of the Great Ascetic, that we are unable to kindle the fire. Then the Blessed One [addressed] Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic...
He said this: “Let the fires be kindled, Kassapa. “Let them be kindled, Great Ascetic.
At once, five hundred fires were kindled. Then it occurred to Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic:
“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, since even the fires are being kindled; yet he is not [the Tathāgata].”
“Just as the Worthy One has said.
Now at that time, those matted-hair ascetics, having tended the fire, were unable to extinguish it.
Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics: “Without a doubt, this is the power of the psychic majesty of the Great Ascetic.”
“...so that we might not be able to extinguish the fire. Then the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“Let the fires be extinguished, Kassapa. “Let them be extinguished, Great Ascetic.
At once, five hundred fires were extinguished. Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa: “He is of great psychic power...”
"Indeed, this Great Ascetic possesses great power, in that even the fires have been extinguished; yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am.
Now at that time, during the cold winter nights in the intervals between the eighth days, while there was a falling of snow, those matted-hair ascetics...
They were emerging and submerging in the river Nerañjarā, performing acts of surfacing and diving.
Then the Blessed One manifested about five hundred fire-pits, where those matted-hair ascetics, having climbed out, could warm themselves.
Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics: "Without a doubt, this is the power of the psychic majesty of the Great Ascetic."
“Just as these ladle-mouths have been fashioned. Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“Powerful indeed is this Great Ascetic, possessed of great majesty, since he can even fashion so many ladle-mouths;
yet he is not an Arahant like me.”
Now at that time, a great unseasonal storm rained down, and a great flood arose;
yet the place where the Blessed One was staying was not submerged by the water. Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"What if I were to drive back the water on all sides and walk back and forth upon the ground in the middle, which is covered with dust?"
Then the Blessed One, having pushed back the water on all sides, walked back and forth upon the ground covered with dust in the middle [of the river].

Then Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic, thinking, "Let it not be that the Great Ascetic has been swept away by the water," went by boat together with many matted-hair ascetics to the place where the Blessed One was staying. He saw...

Seeing the Blessed One walking back and forth on the ground covered with dust in the middle [of the river], having caused the water to recede on all sides, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa said this to the Blessed One: "Is that you there, Great Ascetic?
"It is I, Kassapa," the Blessed One replied, and rising into the air, he stepped onto the boat. Then, to Uruvelakassapa...
The matted-hair ascetic thought: “The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he can even cause the water not to flow;
yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “For a long time this foolish man will continue to think thus.”
“The Great Ascetic is indeed possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, yet he is not an Arahant as I am.
What if I were to cause this matted-hair ascetic to feel a sense of spiritual urgency? Then the Blessed One said this to Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic:
“Kassapa, you are neither an Arahant nor have you entered the path to Arahantship; even that practice of yours—”
“There is no [quality] by which you might be an arahant or have entered the path to arahantship.
Then the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the full ordination. “Kassapa, you are one of the five [hundred ascetics].”
“The leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of the six hundred matted-hair ascetics—even they, you should first consult;
they will do as they deem fit. Then Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic approached those matted-hair ascetics;
having approached, he said this to them: “Sirs, I wish to lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic.”
“Go forth, and act as you think fit. “For a long time, sir, we have been devoted to the Great Ascetic;
if the Great Ascetic will practice the holy life, we all shall likewise practice the holy life under the Great Ascetic.
Then those matted-hair ascetics [discarded] their hair, their matted locks, and their bundles of carrying-poles.
Having cast the fire-oblation mixed with water into the water, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“May we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, Lord; may we receive the full ordination. “Come, monks,” the Blessed One said.
“The Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That itself was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
Then the matted-hair ascetic Nadīkassapa saw [them] with their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, and their fire-sacrifices.
While being carried away by the water, he saw [the elder] and thought, "May no harm have come to my brother.
He sent out the matted-hair ascetics, saying, "Go and find out about my brother," and he himself, together with three hundred matted-hair ascetics, approached the Venerable Uruvelakassapa.
Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Uruvelakassapa:
—“Now, Kassapa, which of these is better? —“Yes, friend, this is better.
Then those matted-hair ascetics, having cast their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, and their fire-offerings into the water, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One: “May we receive [the going forth]...”
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive full ordination?
“Come, monks,” the Blessed One said, “the Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
The matted-hair ascetic Gayākassapa saw the hair, the matted locks, the carrying-pole, and the fire-offerings floating in the water.

Upon seeing this, he thought, "May no harm have come to my brothers," and he sent out other matted-hair ascetics, saying, "Go and find out about my brothers. He himself, together with two hundred matted-hair ascetics, went toward the Venerable One.
Uruvelakassapa approached him; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Uruvelakassapa:
"Is this indeed better, Kassapa? "Yes, friend, this is better.
Then those matted-hair ascetics, having cast their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, and their fire-offerings into the water, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they said this to him:
"Venerable Sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive full ordination.
"Come, monks," the Blessed One said, "the Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering."
That was their full ordination.
"By the Blessed One’s resolve, five hundred pieces of wood did not split; they split. Fires did not ignite;
they ignited. They were not extinguished; they were extinguished. Five hundred cauldrons were conjured by supernormal power. Thus it was.
By this method, there are three thousand six hundred miracles.

Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as he pleased, set out on a journey toward Gayāsīsa together with a great saṅgha of bhikkhus—a thousand in number—all of whom were formerly jaṭilas. There...
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Gayā on Gayā’s Head together with a thousand bhikkhus.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, everything is burning. And what, bhikkhus, is that everything which is burning?
The eye, bhikkhus, is burning; forms are burning; eye-consciousness is burning; eye-contact is burning...”
It is burning. That feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is burning.
By what is it burning? It is burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
I say it is burning with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. [The same applies to] the ear...
It is on fire: sounds are on fire... the nose is on fire, odors are on fire... the tongue is on fire, tastes are on fire...
the body is on fire, tangibles are on fire... the mind is on fire, mental objects are on fire, mind-consciousness is on fire, mind-contact is on fire;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact, whether it be pleasant or...
Whether it be suffering or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, that too is burning. By what is it burning? It is burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion;
it is burning with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—thus I say.
Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, and he becomes disenchanted with forms.

One becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness, one becomes disenchanted with eye-contact, and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact.
One becomes disenchanted with the ear, one becomes disenchanted with sounds... [and so on] ...one becomes disenchanted with the nose, one becomes disenchanted with odors.
He becomes disenchanted... [as before] ...he becomes disenchanted with the tongue and with tastes...

he becomes disenchanted with the body and with tangibles... he becomes disenchanted with the mind and with mental phenomena, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact.
Whether it be pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one becomes disenchanted with that as well. Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate;

through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of those one thousand bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Having thus heard the teaching on the Discourse on the Burning, the Elder Nadī-Kassapa attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past conduct, beginning with the words: "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara... and so forth.
In this context, "the foremost fruit" means the supreme fruit, or the first fruit taken from a mango tree planted by oneself.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Nadīkassapa is completed.
3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gayākassapa In the third Apadāna, beginning with the words “Clad in a deerskin garment,” is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Gayākassapa.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) throughout various existences, [attained this state].
Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn in a noble family.

Upon reaching maturity, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest ascetic. Having established a hermitage in a woodland region, he lived there subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
At that time, the Blessed One, alone and without a companion, came near his hermitage; and he [saw] the Blessed One...
Having seen him, with a mind full of faith, he approached, paid homage, and stood to one side. Looking about for the right time, he offered some charming *kola* fruits to the Teacher.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this arising of a Buddha into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, due to his inclination toward renunciation, he [left] the household life.
Having abandoned the ascetic life of a forest-dweller and gone forth, he dwelt at Gayā together with two hundred ascetics.

Because he resided at Gayā and because of his lineage of the Kassapa clan, he received the name Gayā-Kassapa. After the Blessed One had granted him the ordination by the "Come, monk" formula along with his retinue, [the Blessed One] gave him the discourse on the burning analogy (*ādittapariyāya*), in the same manner as described for Nadī-Kassapa.
Being thus exhorted, he established himself in Arahatship.
Having attained Arahatship, filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past deeds, beginning with the words, "Clad in a garment of antelope skin.
In this context, "clad in a garment of antelope skin" means that, having gone forth as an ascetic, he wore an antelope skin as both an undergarment and an upper robe.

“*Khāribhāradharo*” means that during his time as an ascetic, he was one who carried a full khāri-measure of an ascetic’s requisites. “*Khārikatāpasaparikkhāre pūretvā*” means having filled [a khāri] with the requisites of an ascetic.
“*Kolaṃ ahāsi assaman*” means that having filled the hermitage with *kola*-fruit, he sat in the hermitage.
Regarding the reading “*agopayiṃ*,” the meaning is that after searching for *kola*-fruit, I protected—that is, guarded—the hermitage. All the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Gayākassapa is finished.
4. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kimila:
"When Kakusandha had attained Nibbāna," etc., is the *Apadāna* of the Venerable Elder Kimila. This too—

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence throughout various births, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha.

Upon reaching maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he erected a pavilion adorned with *salala* garlands in honor of the Teacher’s relics and performed an act of worship. By that meritorious deed, he...

Having been reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods and wandering from one state to another among gods and humans, he was born in this present age of a Buddha into the royal Sakya family in the city of Kapilavatthu;
they gave him the name Kimila. When he reached maturity, he lived heedlessly due to his abundance of wealth.
Knowing that his wisdom had reached maturity, [the Blessed One], while dwelling at Anupiya, [acted] for the purpose of generating a sense of spiritual urgency within him.

The Teacher, having conjured up a beautiful woman's form standing in the prime of youth and displayed her before him, then caused her to appear as if gradually overcome by old age, disease, and misfortune.
Upon seeing this, Prince Kimila was moved with extreme spiritual urgency; manifesting his agitation to the Blessed One, he declared his own sense of renunciation.
Having received instruction, he attained arahantship.
(42) Having reached arahantship, filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words, "When Kakusandha had passed away...
[The phrase] "In the brahmin who was possessed of wealth" refers to the Blessed One who had attained mastery through the five kinds of mastery (*vasitā*).
Because he was adorned with all the multitudes of qualities and had fully transcended [defilements], the Blessed One Kakusandha was a "Brāhmaṇa" (Brahmin);
the meaning is that [the Buddha] had attained final nibbāna. All the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Kimila is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vajjiputta.
The *Apadāna* of the venerable Elder Vajjiputta begins with the words, “The Blessed One, the thousand-rayed one,” and so forth.

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [lived] ninety-four aeons ago from this time.
Seeing a Paccekabuddha going for alms, he offered him plantains with a devout heart.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha as a Licchavi prince in Vesālī;
because he was the son of a Vajjī king, his name became Vajjiputta. While still young, even at the time of training in the art of elephant-riding and other skills—

Being endowed with the necessary causes, he wandered about with a disposition toward renunciation. Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
Performing the work of insight (vipassanā), before long he became possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña).
Later, having attained the six supernormal knowledges, when the Teacher had recently passed away, he made an appointment to recite the Dhamma.
While the great elders were dwelling here and there, on one occasion, seeing the Venerable Ānanda— though still a trainee (sekha)—
teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly, [the Buddha], inspiring him to strive for the attainment of the higher paths,
said: “Having gone into the thicket at the foot of a tree, having placed Nibbāna in his heart;”
"Meditate, Gotama; do not be negligent! What will that *biḷibiḷikā* tree do for you?"—thus he spoke this verse.

In this context, "the thicket at the foot of a tree" means a thicket consisting of the root of a tree. For there are thickets that are not the roots of trees, and there are roots of trees that are not thickets;
among these, by the mention of "the root of a tree," [it is indicated] because the place is endowed with shade.

By the mention of "shelter," he illuminates the absence of the perils of wind and sun; by the mention of "thicket," he shows the absence of the peril of wind due to being sheltered from the breeze, as well as the absence of crowding with people.
By both of these, he indicates fitness for spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "Having approached" (*pasakkiya*) means having drawn near.
"One should place Nibbāna in one’s heart" means [the thought]: "In this way, by practicing, Nibbāna is to be attained"—thus one should fix upon Nibbāna, the state of peace.
"Having placed [it] in the heart, having made it the object of the mind. "Meditate" means: meditate by means of the contemplation of the three characteristics;
cultivate the cultivation of the Path together with the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā*). "Gotama"—this he addresses to the Dharma-treasurer by his clan-name.

"And do not be negligent" means: do not fall into negligence regarding the higher wholesome states. Now, as to what kind of negligence this elder might have, [the following is said] by way of its prohibition:
Showing this, he said: "What will your *biḷibiḷikā* do? In this context, *biḷibiḷikā* refers to the act of *biḷibiḷi*;
just as the occurrence of the sound *biḷibiḷi* is useless, so too is the designation of a person (*janapaññatti*) similar to a *biḷibiḷikā*.
"What will it do for you? means: what kind of purpose will it accomplish for you? Therefore, having abandoned the designation of a person, one should be devoted to one's own true goal.
He gave this exhortation: "It shall be so.

Having heard it, stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) at the words spoken by others—words that smelled of the stench of worldly attachment—he spent much of the night walking back and forth (*caṅkama*).
Having intensified his insight (*vipassanā*), he entered his lodging; as soon as he sat down upon his couch, [he thought]: "Whatever..."
"I shall speak," he said; yet before his head had reached the pillow and while his foot was still raised from the ground, at the very moment his body entered the air, he attained *arahantship*.
Later, the Elder Vajjiputta, filled with joy, proclaimed his own account of past deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the words:
"The Blessed One, the thousand-rayed one... In this context, "the thousand-rayed one" refers to [the Buddha] who possesses many hundreds of thousands of rays.
It should be understood that the term "Sahassaraṃsī" was used for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Vajjiputta is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Uttara.
The sixth Apadāna, beginning with "The Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha," is the Apadāna of the venerable novice Uttara.

This one also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, became a master of secret sciences (vidyādhara) during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha and traveled through the air. At that time...
For the sake of favoring him, the Teacher sat at the foot of a certain tree within the forest, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha.
As he was traveling through the air, he saw the Blessed One;
with a mind full of serene faith, he descended from the sky and honored the Blessed One with vast, perfectly pure *kaṇikāra* flowers. By the supernatural power of the Buddha, the flowers...
They stood above the Teacher like a parasol; through that act, his heart became even more filled with serene confidence.

Later, having passed away and been reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he experienced divine splendor. Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan, when he passed from there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha.
He was reborn as a son, and his name was Uttara. Upon reaching maturity, he attained perfection in the brahminical sciences;
through his birth, appearance, learning, age, virtue, and conduct, he became highly esteemed by the world.
Seeing his success, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, desired to give him his own daughter.
He made known his own intention. Because of his inclination toward renunciation, he rejected that [offer] and, from time to time, attended upon the Dhamma-Senāpati;
having heard the Dhamma in his presence, he acquired faith, went forth, and, being perfect in his conduct, waited upon the Elder.
At that time, a certain illness had arisen for the Elder.

For the sake of medicine, the novice Uttara took his bowl and robes early in the morning and departed from the monastery. On the way, near a pond, he set down his bowl and went to the water’s edge to wash his face.
Then, a certain highway robber who had already committed a crime was being pursued by guards.

Pursued by the chief officer, the thief fled from the city; as he ran away, he placed the bundle of jewels he had taken into the novice’s alms-bowl and continued his flight. The novice also approached the vicinity of the bowl.
As the king’s men pursued the thief, they saw the bundle in the novice’s bowl and said, “This is the thief; this is the one who committed the theft,” and [seized] the novice.
Having bound his arms behind his back, they presented him to the brahmin Vassakāra.
At that time, Vassakāra was appointed to the king’s court of justice and was presiding over cases involving execution and mutilation.
Thinking, “Previously he did not heed my word and went forth among the pure heretics,” and desiring to kill him without even investigating the matter, he impaled him alive upon a stake.

Then the Blessed One, observing the ripening of his knowledge, went to that spot and placed his hand—whose fingers were webbed, soft, tender, and long, and whose white splendor was intensified by the rays of the jewels on his flashing fingernails, appearing like a flowing stream of molten gold from refined cinnabar—upon Uttara’s head, saying:
"Uttara, this fruit of your former karma has arisen; therein, by you—"
"By the power of reflection, you must practice acceptance," he said, and then taught the Dhamma according to Uttara’s disposition.
Through the contact of the Teacher’s hand, which was like a consecration with the Deathless, Uttara attained a state of serene joy born of faith;
having obtained sublime rapture and gladness, he ascended the path of insight as he had previously cultivated it, bringing his knowledge to full maturity.

Through his realization of the Truth and by the Teacher’s skillful teaching, he immediately exhausted all defilements according to the sequence of the Path and became one possessed of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Having attained the six supernormal powers, he rose from the stake and, standing in the air out of compassion for others, displayed a miracle.
The great multitude was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement. At that very moment, his wound healed; and by the monks—
When asked, "Friend, experiencing such suffering, how were you able to apply yourself to insight (vipassanā)?
he replied, "Friend, long ago in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the danger and the true nature of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) were well-seen by me;
thus, even while experiencing such suffering, I was able to increase my insight and attain distinction. [He spoke of] his previous birth:
"In my childhood, having caught a fly and taken a neem-wood skewer, I engaged in the game of impaling it on a spike;
thus, after experiencing the suffering of being impaled on spikes throughout many hundreds of births, I experienced such suffering as this in my final birth," he said. 55.

Then, at a later time, remembering his former karma and filled with joy, the Sambuddha named Sumedha spoke the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*, beginning with the words "The Sambuddha named Sumedha. Regarding that, we shall provide an explanation only of the words not already clear.

57. "I was then a *vijjādhara*": the meaning is that, having become capable of traveling through the air by means of the attainment of external spells (*mantādi-vijjā*) and so forth, and having preserved that spell by maintaining it without letting it perish, I existed in the womb of a *vijjādhara*.

Regarding the phrase "I was a traveler of the sky" (*antalikkhacaro aham*): the sky (*antalikkha*) is so called because it is written (*likhati*), that is, it marks the end, the limit, or the boundary.
Alternatively, *antalikkha* is so called because the end (*anta*) or limit (*pariyosāna*) is written upon (*likhyate*) or observed (*olokiyate*) by it;
thus, the meaning is "I am one whose nature is to move in that *antalikkha*, in the sky. "Taking up a well-fashioned trident" means a sharp spear, a pointed weapon.
A "well-fashioned trident" is a spear-weapon that has been excellently crafted for the purpose of piercing, grinding, crushing, and striking.

"Having taken it up" (*gayha*) means "having seized it from the sky"; such is the meaning. The remainder of all this is easily understood through the application of the method already explained below.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Uttara is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Aparauttara.
The legend (*apadāna*) of the Venerable Uttara Thera begins with the words: "When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna...

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha ninety-four aeons ago.
Having reached maturity and attained discernment, he conceived faith in the Teaching and declared himself a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
After the Teacher had passed into *parinibbāna*, he gathered his kinsmen together, collected many offerings and honors, and performed a worship of the relics.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this current dispensation into a brahmin family in Sāketa.
Having been reborn and received the name Uttara, he reached maturity and traveled to Sāvatthī on some business.
There, having seen the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree, he gained faith. Furthermore, his confidence increased through the teaching of the Kāḷakārāma Sutta;
he went forth, went with the Teacher to Rājagaha, received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and continued practicing in that very manner.
Having established insight meditation, he soon became one possessed of the six super-knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Having attained the six super-knowledges, while the Teacher was staying at Sāvatthī, he went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī for the purpose of attending upon the Buddha.
When asked by the monks, "Friend, have you brought your task of going forth to its ultimate conclusion?", he answered with a verse of realization (*añña*).

93. Having attained Arahantship, filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past conduct, beginning with the words, "When the Protector of the World had passed away... Since all of that follows the method already explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Aparauttara is completed.
8. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhaddaji.
The eighth Apadāna, beginning with "Having entered the lotus pond," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Bhaddaji Thera. This one,
too, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating virtues conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and attained maturity.
Having reached the further shore of the sciences and crafts of the brahmins, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic.

Dwelling in a hermitage he had established in a forest region, one day, seeing the Teacher traveling through the air, he stood with his hands joined in reverential salutation, his mind full of serene faith.
Perceiving his intention, the Teacher descended from the sky. Upon his descent—
Then he offered honey, lotus roots and stalks, ghee, and milk to the Blessed One.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted it and, having delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, departed. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Tusita devas;
having remained there for the full span of his life, when he passed away from there, he wandered successively through the happy realms alone until the time of Vipassi Buddha.
In the time of the Blessed One, having been a very wealthy merchant, he fed six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus and clothed them with the three robes.
Having performed such great merit, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Remaining there for the full span of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in the human world during a period when the world was empty of Buddhas, [where he served] five hundred paccekabuddhas with the four requisites.
Having served him, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in a royal family. While ruling the kingdom, he attended upon his own son who had attained the state of a Paccekabuddha.
After that [Paccekabuddha] had attained final Nibbāna, he took his relics, erected a cetiya, and made offerings.
Having thus performed various meritorious deeds in those various places, during this current appearance of a Buddha, in the city of Bhaddiya—
He was reborn as the only son of the merchant Bhaddiya, who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million; his name was Bhaddaji.
Indeed, his mastery over sovereignty, wealth, retinue, and excellence was like that of the Bodhisattva in his final existence.
At that time, the Teacher, having resided at Sāvatthī, [set out] with a great community of monks for the purpose of winning over the youth Bhaddaji.
Having gone together with him to the city of Bhaddiya, he dwelt in the Jātiyā Grove, awaiting the ripening of his wisdom.
He too, sitting on the upper terrace of the palace, opened the lion-window and looked out;
seeing the great multitude going into the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dhamma, he asked, "Where is this great multitude going? and [learned] that reason.

Having heard this, he too went into the presence of the Teacher with a great retinue; while listening to the Dhamma, even while adorned with all his ornaments, he destroyed all defilements and attained arahantship.
Now that he had attained arahantship, the Teacher addressed the merchant Bhaddiya:
"Your son, while listening to the Dhamma, has become established in arahantship, even though he was fully adorned."
“It is fitting for him to go forth this very day; if he does not go forth, he will attain final Nibbāna.
The merchant said, “There is no need for my young son to attain final Nibbāna while still a youth; let him go forth.
Having caused him to go forth and conferred full ordination upon him, the Teacher stayed there for seven days and then reached Koṭigāma, and that village—
It was on the bank of the Ganges. The inhabitants of Koṭigāma offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.

As soon as the Teacher had begun his expression of thanks, the Elder Bhaddaji went outside the village and, setting a time limit—thinking, "I shall emerge when the Teacher arrives at the vicinity of the path on the bank of the Ganges"—he entered into meditative attainment at the foot of a certain tree.
Having entered [the attainment], he remained seated. Even when the great elders arrived, he did not rise; it was only at the time of the Teacher’s arrival that he arose.
The bhikkhus who were worldlings grumbled: “This man has only recently gone forth;
when the great elders were coming, he became stiff with pride and did not rise.”
The inhabitants of Koṭigāma tied together many boats for the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The Teacher, thinking, “I shall manifest the power of Bhaddaji,” stood upon a boat and asked, “Where is Bhaddaji?
The Elder Bhaddaji approached the Teacher, and standing with palms joined in reverence, said, “It is I, venerable sir. The Teacher said, “Come, Bhaddaji; [come] with us.”
“Come, board the same boat. He leapt up and stood upon the boat where the Teacher was standing.
When they had reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher said, “Bhaddaji, where is the jeweled palace you inhabited during the time of Mahāpanāda?
“It is submerged at this spot, Bhante,” he replied. “In that case, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubt of your fellow celibates.”

At that moment, the Elder, having paid homage to the Teacher, went by means of his power of psychic potency (*iddhi*) and, having blocked the pinnacle of the palace with the space between his toes, he took the twenty-five-league palace and leaped into the air; as he was leaping, he lifted it fifty leagues high.
Now, those who had been his kinsmen in a previous existence, having become fish, turtles, and frogs due to the greed they felt for the palace, [remained there].
As the palace rose up, those who had been born there turned around and fell down.
Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, your kinsmen are suffering. At the Teacher’s word, the Elder released the palace;
the palace settled back in its original place. When the Teacher, who has gone beyond, was asked by the monks, "Venerable Sir, when did the Elder Bhaddaji [release the palace]?"
When asked, "Who inhabited this palace? he recounted the Mahāpanāda Jātaka and caused the multitude to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
But the Elder, having attained Arahatship and remembering his former accumulations of merit, was filled with joy;

wishing to proclaim the account of his past conduct, he began by saying, "Having plunged into the lotus pond... and so forth. In that context, "plunging into the lotus pond" refers to [entering] amidst various and manifold great floods.
Having entered—that is, having gone down into, having stepped into, and having plunged deep into—the reservoir of water named "lotus pond" because it was dug out;
the meaning is: having entered that lotus pond for the purpose of eating food, [I think] "I shall pull up the *bhisā*, the root of the white lotus (*padumapuṇḍarīka*).
The remainder is easily understood by following the method, as it has been explained in the manner stated below and its word-meanings are plain.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Bhaddajita is finished.
9. The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sivaka:
