In the ninth *Apadāna*, the account of the Venerable Elder Sivaka begins with the words, "While wandering in search... This too...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Blessed One wandering for alms, he filled the bowl with fermented rice gruel and gave it to him with a devout mind. By that [act]...
Migrating among gods and humans by means of meritorious karma, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Rājagaha and was named Sivako.
Upon reaching maturity, having attained proficiency in the sciences and arts, he abandoned sensual pleasures due to his inclination toward renunciation;
having gone forth as an ascetic and wandering about, he approached the Teacher and [heard] the Dhamma.
Having heard this, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long.

Having reached *arahantship*, filled with joy, he proclaimed his own account of past deeds (*pubbacaritāpadāna*), beginning with the verse: "While wandering in search... and so forth. All of that is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sivaka is completed.
10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upavāna.
The tenth Apadāna begins with the words "The Conqueror named Padumuttara," and so forth; it is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Upavāna.

It is said that this [Elder] had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and in various states of existence he accumulated merits conducive to the turning away from worldly existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Due to a certain lapse in his karma, he was reborn in a poor family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara;
having reached maturity after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he took a relic of the Buddha,

and when a stupa seven yojanas high made of the seven precious gems was constructed by humans, devas, nāgas, garuḷas, yakkhas, kumbhaṇḍas, and gandhabbas, he placed his own well-washed upper robe upon the tip of a bamboo pole there.
Having tied it up and made it into a banner, he performed an act of worship.

Taking that banner, the yakkha general named Abhisammata—who had been appointed by the devas to protect the stupa worship—held it aloft in the air with his invisible body and circumambulated the stupa three times.
Seeing this, his mind became even more filled with serene faith. By virtue of that meritorious deed, he...
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī.
Having received the name Upavāna, when he reached maturity, he witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during the acceptance of the Jeta Grove.

Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, he applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and became one possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Then, the Venerable Upavāna [approached] the Blessed One...
He became his attendant. At that time, a wind-related ailment arose in the Blessed One.
A brahmin named Devahita, who was the elder’s lay friend, was residing in Sāvatthī. He invited the elder to accept the four requisites.
Then the Venerable Upavāna, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of that brahmin.
The brahmin, thinking, "I suppose the Elder has come for some purpose," realized this and said, "Venerable sir, please tell us what you require.
The Elder, explaining his purpose to that brahmin, said:
"The Arhat, the Well-Gone One in the world, the Sage, is afflicted by wind."
“If there is warm water, O brahmin, give it to the Sage.
“Honored by those worthy of honor, honored by those worthy of respect,
revered by those worthy of reverence— I wish for him to depart.”
He spoke two verses.
Their meaning is as follows: He who is honored in this world by those worthy of worship—by the gods such as Sakka and others, and by the Great Brahmās and others;
who is venerated by those worthy of veneration—by King Bimbisāra of Kosala and others; and who is worshipped by those worthy of worship...
He is honored by great seers who are worthy of honor and whose taints are exhausted; he is an *arhat* because he is far removed from defilements;
he is a *Sugata* because of his beautiful gait and other qualities; he is the omniscient Sage, my Teacher, the God of gods, the Sakka beyond Sakka, and the Brahmā beyond Brahmā.
He has now become afflicted with an illness caused by the winds, due to the winds, on account of the agitation of the winds. If, O Brāhmaṇa, there were warm water...
"There is; I wish to give it to him to bring about the subsiding of his wind-affliction.

Upon hearing this, the brahmin presented the Blessed One with warm water and medicine suitable for dispelling wind. By that means, the Teacher's illness was cured. The Blessed One then offered him words of thanksgiving. 122.
Later, when the venerable Upavāna recalled his own past karma, he was filled with joy and [related] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*.
He spoke the words beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara,” proclaiming [the Buddha]. In that passage, the meanings of “Padumuttara” and so forth have already been explained previously.

(123) “A great multitude having gathered” means that the inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa had assembled in a mass. “Having made a funeral pyre” refers to the connection: having made a funeral pyre consisting of a heap of sandalwood one *yojana* in height, they placed the Blessed One’s body upon it.
(124) “Having performed the rites for the body” means having performed the task of cremation—that is, burning it with fire.

127–28. *Jaṅghā maṇimayā āsi*: regarding the stupa built by humans, the meaning is that the base (*jaṅghā*)—the part where people walk for the purpose of carrying flowers—is made of jewels, specifically of sapphire (*indanīla-maṇi*). *Mayampi*: the meaning is "we too [all the deities] shall build a stupa. 129. *Dhātu āveṇikā natthi*:
there is no separate, individual relic (*dhātu*) for the gods and humans to build a monument (*cetiya*) for each separately.
Demonstrating this, he said, "the body was gathered into a single mass" (*sarīram ekapiṇḍitam*). By the power of his resolve (*adhiṭṭhānabala*), the relics of his entire body [were unified].
The meaning is that it became one and the same, like a statue made of a single solid block of stone. "In this Buddha-thūpa" means:
in this golden thūpa built by all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, we shall all assemble and construct a casing-thūpa; such is the meaning. 133. *Indanīla* and *mahānīla*:
a gem with a luster like the color of an *indīvara* flower is an *indanīla* gem. Its color is superior to that [of the former].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having gathered together great maṇis, indanīla gems, mahānīla gems, and various kinds of *jotirasa* and *raṅga* gems, and having made them into a heap, they fashioned a covering-cloak (*kañcuka-thūpa*) for the golden stupa and covered it.
(144) "For the peerless Paccekabuddha" means that they built a separate stupa with its own individual upper covering for the supreme Buddha, the Lord.
147. "Kumbhaṇḍā and Guyhakā likewise": those gods whose eggs are the size of jars are called Kumbhaṇḍas;
because they conceal and hide themselves, they are known as Guyhakas (the Concealers). The meaning is that both those Kumbhaṇḍas and Guyhakas built a stupa.
151. "The others do not surpass its radiance": the radiance of the moon, the sun, and the stars does not surpass the radiance of that cetiya; it does not outshine it—this is the meaning.

158. "I too shall perform a service"—this means that for the monument (thūpa) of the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World, I too shall perform a service, a meritorious deed, a wholesome action, namely the *dhajapaṭāka* offering.
The commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Upavāna is complete.
11. Commentary on the *Apadāna* of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla.
The eleventh Apadāna, beginning with "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla Thera. This [Thera] also,
having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
lived in the city of Haṃsavatī even prior to the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having been reborn in a great wealthy household of householders, he reached maturity and, upon his father’s passing, established himself in the life of a householder.
Seeing the immeasurable wealth inherited through his family lineage that had been presented by the treasurer, he thought:
"My grandfather, great-grandfather, and others were unable to take away such a vast heap of wealth along with themselves, yet I am able to take it and go."
Thinking, "This is appropriate," he gave a great alms-offering to the poor, the destitute, and others.

While attending upon a certain ascetic who had attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he was urged by him toward the sovereignty of the deva-world. Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, when he passed away from there, he was reborn as a deva.
Remaining in that deva-world for the duration of his lifespan while exercising divine sovereignty, he passed away from there.
In the human world, he was born as the only son of a family capable of restoring a divided kingdom.
At that time, the Blessed One named Padumuttara appeared in the world;
having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he led those beings ready to be trained to the secure land known as the great city of Nibbāna. Then that noble youth—
Gradually reaching the age of discretion, one day he went to the monastery with some lay devotees.
Seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, he sat down at the edge of the assembly with a mind full of faith.
At that time, the Teacher designated a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those who had gone forth out of faith. [He saw] him...
Having seen this, with a mind full of faith, he fixed his intention upon that goal;
then, having offered a great almsgiving for seven days with immense honor to the Blessed One who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, he made a formal aspiration.

The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would succeed without obstacle, [said]: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, among those who have gone forth out of faith..."
“He will be the foremost,” he prophesied. Having paid homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he rose from his seat and departed.

There, having performed meritorious deeds for as long as his lifespan lasted, he passed away from that state and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, ninety-two aeons ago during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, while three royal princes who were the Teacher’s maternal cousins were attending upon him, [he was born].

He performed the duty of being a companion in their meritorious deeds. Thus, having accumulated much wholesome karma in various successive existences and wandering only among happy destinies, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in the merchant Raṭṭhapāla’s house in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the kingdom of Kuru;
for he was born into a family capable of sustaining a broken kingdom.
"Raṭṭhapāla" was his name, following his family lineage. Growing up with a large retinue, he gradually reached youth;
his parents then united him with a suitable wife and established him in great glory, where he enjoyed prosperity resembling celestial attainment.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of the Kuru realm—
While traveling, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. Having heard that news, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher;

having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith. After seven times interrupting his meals, and only with great difficulty and hardship having obtained his parents' permission, he approached the Teacher and requested the going forth. From the Teacher—
Having gone forth in the presence of a certain elder by means of a formal command, he performed his duties with wise attention,
increased his insight, and attained arahantship.
Then, at a later time, the Venerable One, recollecting his own past karma and filled with joy, [recited] the *Pubbacaritāpadāna*.
Explaining this, he said, "Of the Blessed One Padumuttara," and so forth.

"That beautiful elephant, Sunāga, was given by me" means that at the time when, having been a great wealthy merchant, he was distributing his entire fortune through acts of giving, the beautiful elephant king Sunāga, established on seven points, was given by him.
Demonstrating this, he said, "With tusks like plow-poles," and so forth. "With tusks like plow-poles" means with tusks the size of chariot-poles.
Thus, this noble elephant was given by me. "Urūḷhava" means capable of serving as a royal mount, or fit for a king.
"With a white parasol" means accompanied by a white parasol held over it for the sake of ornamentation.

"Resplendent" means endowed with the beauty of form through its proportions and dimensions. "With its trappings and its keeper" means equipped with elephant ornaments and accompanied by an elephant-keeper.
The meaning is as follows: "In this manner, this elephant-king was given by me to the Blessed One Padumuttara"—this is the meaning.

(181) "Having had food prepared by me" means: having established a permanent meal for the monks numbering in the tens of millions who were residing in the monastery caused to be built by me, [I] dedicated it to the Great Sage—this is the connection.

(183) "Named Jalajuttama": *jalaja* means "born from water"; what is that? The lotus (*paduma*). Because his name is identical to the lotus and because of his excellence, the Blessed One is named Padumuttara—this is the meaning. The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla is completed.
The commentary on the Great Chapter (Mahāvagga), the fifty-sixth, is completed.
Thus ends [the portion] of the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā* titled *Visuddhajanavilāsinī*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apadānas* of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Elder Disciples.
The Concluding Discourse:

To all beings, including the Elder Ānanda and others—who were endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires and who were lamps for the lineage of Elders on the Island of Ceylon—[this work is dedicated].
May the entire world, including the devas, know that this *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā* has been brought forth by a wise scholar who is a bearer of the Tipiṭaka,
adorned with the splendor of great universal virtues, and who— seeking the requisites for enlightenment through the attainment of exceptional skill over seven months by means of cutting,

subduing, and separating craving, pride, views, and the like, and through mindfulness, steadfastness, progress, energy, and valor— has done so for the sake of severing, restraining, and isolating them.

By this [merit], may the stains of greed and the like perish for all beings, as well as the various diseases of the eyes and other organs, and the sufferings born of fear such as quarrels; may thieves and other evildoers who cause harm in the world be destroyed.
May my five enemies and my evils perish, just as rain and wind vanish in the summer heat.
Having reached the city of Nibbāna by means of the noble eightfold path,
I cause others to enter it as well. Crushing all views and the evils of lust, hatred, and the like,
and having severed the cycle of saṃsāra, I attain heaven and liberation.
May all phenomena follow [the Dhamma] everywhere within the field of authority, from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence,
throughout the three worlds and even in the physical elements.
The Commentary on the Apadāna is complete.
